TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring wait times along the pathways of care in primary care
Keywords-MotsClés: COORDINATION OF CARE; ELECTRONIC MEDICAL RECORDS (EMR); HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; PRIMARY CARE; REFERRALS; WAIT TIMES
Abstract-Résumé: Family physicians who receive accurate information from other health care providers are able to provide better continuity of care to their patients, and with the likelihood of better health outcomes. The health care delivery system comprises many avenues, and family physicians (as well as their patients) experience periods of waiting as they navigate the twists and turns. So, the overarching goal of this research study is to provide information which can lead to timely communication and coordination across the health care sectors. Data, extracted in a secure research environment from electronic medical records of community-based family physicians, will show actual wait times in practice. And, using these wait times, we will provide estimates of wait times between primary care, on the one hand, and specialty care or out-of-office services, on the other. We also plan to calculate the wait times for the family physician's receipt of information after a patient is either seen by a specialist physician or discharged from a hospital and/or an emergency department. And, finally, we will examine, quantitatively, the coordination of care between primary care and community-based services. In showing which geographic areas are experiencing excessively long waits, we have two important hopes:  1. that health planners will consider providing additional health resources to these areas, and 2. that the newer primary care reform models will consider including health care personnel who could provide valuable assistance to patients with specific conditions, until they see the specialist physician.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sex-specific susceptibility windows for fetal origins of adult disease and transgenerational effects
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETIC; FETUS; FOLATE; GERM CELLS; SEX-SPECIFIC; TRANSGENERATIONAL
Abstract-Résumé: The prenatal period is a key time of fetal programming. In particular, one of the tissues of the fetus, the germ line, undergoes a genome-wide programming event that is critical for fertility of the resulting offspring and the health of future generations. Both animal and human studies have indicated that environmental exposures of male germ cells either during the period of fetal programming of male germ cells or prepubertally can lead to adult-onset diseases that are passed through a number of generations. Animal studies have linked these sex-specific, male-line transgenerational effects to epigenetic changes to the DNA of the developing germ cells. The epigenetic change identified was in the level of methylation of the DNA.  DNA methylation is a chemical modification or 'tagging' of genes that is essential for normal developmental programs; it regulates gene expression and provides a way for genes to be turned on or off at specific times. The fetal period is the key period when DNA methylation is reprogrammed in germ cells. However, while DNA methylation is erased in both male and female fetal germ cells, it is only re-established before birth in male germ cells whereas the DNA of female germ cells doesn't become methylated until after puberty. Due the presence of fetal germ line DNA methylation reprogramming in the male but not the female, we hypothesize that male fetal germ cells are uniquely vulnerable to epigenetic abnormalities resulting from environmental insults occurring during pregnancy.  Since epigenetic abnormalities are heritable, once induced, they have the potential to be passed on to future generations. Folate is a dietary exposure known to alter DNA methylation. In our research we are studying sex-specific susceptibility of male germ cells to perturbations of a key enzyme in the folate pathway, methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) and/or dietary folate deficiency and supplementation in the mouse and human.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional characterization of dynamic complexes involved in transcription, DNA repair and viral infection and their association to cancer formation.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DNA REPAIR; PHOSPHORYLATION; PML; SENESCENCE; SUMOLYATION; TFIIH; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; UBIQUITINATION; VIRAL INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: All living cells transfer the information from their genetic material (DNA) into a messenger (RNA) in a process known as transcription. To ensure that this is done in an accurate manner, any damaged DNA caused by environmental exposure to agents such as UV sunlight or toxic chemicals must be repaired. In this work, we will examine how transcription and repair of damaged DNA are intimately linked to ensure the proper transfer of genetic information. We have determined that several proteins involved in DNA damage repair after exposure to sunlight function like proteins that regulate transcription, and it now appears that the these factors regulate both processes. By using common factors, it appears that the two critical processes work together to make sure that everything is performed in the correct order and the integrity of our genetic information is protected. Failure to repair the damaged DNA prior to transfer of genetic information is known to lead to a number of different cancers. This is highlighted by the fact that there are many people who have defects in their DNA repair systems who suffer from a number of different anomalies including cancer. Interestingly, it appears that several different viruses function by mimicking these factors required for both transcription and DNA repair and as a result these viral infections are associated with different forms of cancer. Our goal is to understand how transcription and repair work together and the cancers associated with mutations in these systems and viral infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: NOD1 and NOD2 immunity regulate obesity-induced inflammation and insulin resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTES; CELL BIOLOGY; DIABETES; GLUCOSE; GUT BACTERIA; IMMUNITY; INFLAMMATION; INSULIN RESISTANCE; METABOLIC DISEASE; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: The rise in type 2 diabetes is alarming. Insulin resistance precedes diabetes, can last for decades and is reversible. This provides a chance to prevent the onset of diabetes. Over half of Canadians are overweight, which is the most significant factor contributing to insulin resistance. Obesity is associated with a chronic inflammation, which is critical in causing insulin resistance. The trigger for this inflammation is not clear.  We have discovered that a part of bacterial cell wall (i.e. peptidoglycan) links inflammation and insulin resistance during obesity. Different types of this bacterial cell wall are detected by two separate immune proteins. We discovered that one of these bacterial sensors (i.e. NOD1) causes inflammation and insulin resistance during obesity, but the other (i.e. NOD2) is actually protective. These bacterial sensors regulate the type of bacteria in our gut and how some of these bacteria can get into the surrounding fat tissue. This is a potential trigger for inflammation during obesity.  It is not yet understood why only certain obese individuals develop insulin resistance. This work can enhance the identification of people that are susceptible to diabetes by finding and linking bacterial and inflammatory markers of disease. Understanding the difference obesity-induced inflammation mediated by NOD1 and NOD2 provides a new way to probe bacterial and inflammatory causes of insulin resistance.  The objective of this research is to understand how NOD1 causes, but NOD2 protects against insulin resistance. This research will help direct novel nutritional interventions including specific prebiotics and probiotics and may identify new therapies that could prevent type 2 diabetes. This research is also relevant to patients with specific gut inflammatory pathologies. This work may direct changes in the monitoring or care of obese patients with gut diseases and/or diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stabilization of integrin-mediated monocyte adhesion to inflamed vascular endothelium: actin dynamics and signaling.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN CYTOSKELETON; ARREST STABILIZATION; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; ENDOTHELIAL ADHESION MOLECULES; FLOW CHAMBER STUDIES; INTRAVITAL MICROSCOPY; LEUKOCYTE INTEGRINS; MONOCYTES; SIGNALING PATHWAYS
Abstract-Résumé: The recruitment of white blood cells (leukocytes) from the blood into tissues is a key process in inflammation and contributes to atherosclerosis, autoimmune conditions and rejection of transplanted organs.  Monocytes are a subtype of leukocytes, and they play a critical role in atherosclerosis, a disease that results in heart attacks and strokes.  Therefore, inhibition of monocyte recruitment can constitute an important therapeutic approach for treatment of atherosclerosis, and understanding mechanisms of monocyte recruitment is critical to achieving this goal.  Adhesion molecules orchestrate monocyte recruitment.  They include monocyte alpha-4 integrins that bind to VCAM-1 on endothelial cells.  Endothelial cells line the inner wall of blood vessels.  During recruitment, adherent leukocytes experience the force of flowing blood.  Leukocytes must develop strong and stable adhesions in order to remain attached to endothelial cells and withstand the detachment forces imparted by flowing blood.  Our goal is to determine the mechanisms by which leukocytes stabilize their adhesion in flowing blood.  We will investigate signaling pathways, including those initiated by alpha-4 integrins, as well as a dynamic skeleton formed by actin molecules, that provides the leukocyte with tensile strength, a structural scaffold and regulates movement.

TitreApplicationTitle: Specification and morphogenesis of the urogenital system primordium
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL LINEAGE SPECIFICATION; COLLECTIVE CELL MIGRATION; DEVELOPMENTAL DISEASE; INDUCTIVE SIGNALS; LIVE IMAGING; MORPHOGENESIS; MOUSE GENETICS; PLANAR CELL POLARITY; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS PAX2 AND GATA3; UROGENITAL SYSTEM DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: At birth, a baby is composed of billions of cells organized in functional organs and tissues. To achieve this, the developing embryo has to multiply its cells but, more importantly, has to specify over 200 new cell types from "naive" cells and organize them in space such that they interact with the right environment and ultimately develop into a functional organs. A failure in this process can lead to developmental defects ranging from chronic diseases to embryonic death. We are studying the basic biological mechanisms of cell type specification and spatial organization. For this we use the mouse renal system that is relatively simple in its cellular composition and amenable to sophisticated developmental studies. We have previously identified the "master regulators" Pax2 and Pax8 that are both required and sufficient to induce the renal lineage. We built on this finding to identify the molecular network regulated by Pax2/8 and identified Gata3 as an important mediator of Pax2/8 function. Among other things Gata3 regulates the elongation of the renal primordium to form the embryonic kidney. In this proposal, we want to understand which signals from surrounding tissues activate Pax2/8 to specify provide the renal identity "naive" cells. We also propose to identify and characterize the biological forces driving the renal primordium to elongate in the embryo tail to connect to the bladder and form the kidney. A failure in renal promordium formation or elongation leads to a complete absence of kidneys and embryonic death. Importantly, partial failures in this process lead to a disease group called Congenital Anomalies of the Kidney and Urinary Tract (CAKUT). CAKUT affects as many as 1:100 newborn and is the most important cause of chronic kidney diseases and renal transplant in children. By elucidating the mechanisms of renal primordium specification and elongation we will help understand and better manage the treatment of children affected with CAKUT.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of human ovarian granulosa cell function by GDF9 and BMP15
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSISTED REPRODUCTIVE TECHNOLOGY; INFERTILITY; OVARY; SEX STEROIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Female reproductive disorders have significant medical, social and economic impacts on individuals and society. The overall goal of this research is to understand the hormonal control of human reproduction through a greater understanding of the regulation of ovarian function. Ovarian granulosa cells (GCs) are essential for normal oocyte development and steroid hormone production. The function of GCs depends not only on endocrine regulators but also on a variety of locally produced hormonal factors that exert their effects in an autocrine and/or paracrine fashion. In this next phase of research, our aim is to use our well-established human GC model to clarify the regulation of human GC function by GDF9 and BMP15, which is poorly understood in humans despite its important functional implications in a variety of animal studies. Not only will our results provide important insights into the normal and pathophysiological roles of these potent ovarian regulatory factors; but they might also lead to new ways of approaching fertility regulation, whether the objective is to develop alternative forms of contraception, treat human infertility, or develop better methods of inducing ovulation in assisted reproduction.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU SEIN; TUMEURS CEREBRALES (ET RETINIENNES)
TitreApplicationTitle: In Vivo Investigation of Mechanisms of Brain Metastasis and Metastatic Recurrence
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD BRAIN BARRIER; BREAST CANCER; CELL TRACKING; DORMANCY; METASTASIS; MRI; NANOPARTICLES; RADIATION THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: The spread of cancer from the breast to other organs, called metastasis, is responsible for most breast cancer deaths. When breast cancer is diagnosed early, before it has spread, survival rates are very high. In some cases, metastases can occur many years after treatment of the initial tumor, due to tumor dormancy. Dormancy refers to the ability for cancer cells to remain quiet in the body (not growing) for extended periods of time.  Dormant cells can be triggered to begin to grow, even many years after apparent successful treatment, and are believed to be responsible for cancer recurring.  Current therapies are increasing survival times for patients with metastases. However, one consequence of this improving the ability to treat metastatic disease is an increase in incidence of brain metastases. This is likely due to the difficulty of systemic treatments reaching metastases in the brain, because of the blood-brain barrier. Brain metastases thus are difficult to treat. They are often treated by whole brain radiation therapy, the use of strong beams of energy to kill cancer cells, but this can have severe side effects for patients. Thus, as the incidence of brain metastasis rises, there will be an increasing need to better understand the biology of brain metastases and how best to treat them.  Our group combines expertise in brain metastasis and dormancy of breast cancer, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and radiation therapy. We will study the role of two treatments (whole brain radiation and the drug called lapatinib) in mice, on actively growing metastases and dormant breast cancer cells. Together these studies will provide badly needed knowledge about the biology of brain metastases and how to treat them. This information will be increasingly important, as the rates of brain metastasis from breast cancer are rising, due to increasing success at treating metastases in other organs.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DE LA PROSTATE ET DE LA VESSIE; SYSTEME GENITO-URINAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Gata3 in prostate stem cells and cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL LINEAGE COMMITMENT; MOUSE GENETICS; MOUSE MODELS; PROSTATE CANCER; PROSTATE DEVELOPMENT; PTEN TUMOR SUPPRESSOR; REGENERATION; STEM CELLS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR GATA3; TRANSCRIPTIONAL PROFILING
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer-related death in men, mainly due to the development of aggressive tumors insensitive to hormone-deprivation therapies (castration-resistant tumors). It is therefore crucial to understand how these tumors arise and how they can be fought. We have recently shown that the loss of the transcription factor GATA3 is an important event for tumor progression as enforced GATA3 expression in a mouse model of prostate cancer effectively prevents cancer progression. Interestingly, it can do so when it is expressed in the cell nucleus (where it normally works), but the tumors sometimes exclude GATA3 from the nucleus, which allows tumors to progress. We find an equivalent situation in human as most advanced tumors (castrate-resistant) either lose GATA3 expression or exclude it from the nucleus.  We will follow up on these important findings by studying how GATA3 is retained outside the nucleus in advanced tumors. We will also use mouse models of cancer to determine the role of GATA3 in preventing tumor development, notably in the cell able to regenerate the prostate as evidence suggests they are the ones at the origin of the aggressive form of prostate cancer. The presence of GATA3 outside the nucleus in advanced tumors suggests a therapeutic strategy whereby GATA3 could be sent back in the nucleus to inactivate cancer-promoting signals and induce tumor cell differentiation or elimination. Our experiments will help design such therapeutic strategy by understanding how GATA3 is inactivated in tumors and what it normally does when functional.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards a better understanding of the language impairment and neural basis of primary progressive aphasia: A longitudinal study
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; DEMENTIA; LANGUAGE; LONGITUDINAL; NEUROIMAGING; PRIMARY PROGRESSIVE APHASIA; SPEECH PRODUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: A significant minority of (mainly) elderly people will develop dementia, which is progressive decline in intellectual functions (e.g., thinking,memory, reasoning). In some types of dementia, language is the earliest and most affected ability, and there is progressive deterioration in both production (speaking and writing) and comprehension. This disorder is called primary progressive aphasia (PPA)and is the focus of this study. Although difficulty with spoken language is a critical and disabling deficit, there has been remarkably little study of speech in people suffering from progressive aphasia. The goals of the this study are 1)to better characterize the language and motor speech impairments in the variants of PPA particularly with respect to sentence processing and connected speech; 2)to correlate patterns of performance (particularly language) and motor speech impairment with measures of brain atrophy (we will use two types of scans: magnetic resonance imaging, which provides clear detailed pictures of the brain tissue, and diffusion tensor imaging which reveals the networks of the fibers connecting different areas of the brain; 3) to improve early diagnosis and differentiation; 4) to identify measures which are sensitive to the deficits and may be suitable for clinical use. This work will improve our understanding of the neuroanatomical basis of language and speech processing in health and disease. It is also hoped that the findings will identify suitable goals for therapy supporting functional autonomy in these patient populations.

ClasseRechercheFR: DISTRIBUTION DES SOINS DE LA SANTE; RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Intensive Care Rehabilitation Study (ICARuS): Barriers to Early Physical Rehabilitation in the ICU - A Delphi Study.
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIERS; CRITICAL CARE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LONG-TERM OUTCOMES; MIXED METHODS; MORBIDITY; MORTALITY; MULTI-PROFESSIONAL CARE; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Patients who suffer from critical illness experience a range of new problems after their ICU stay - in particular weakness and limitations in physical function. This is related in part to immobility at the time of illness.  Research to date has shown that rehabilitation initiated after critical illness is not effective in improving physical function. However, rehabilitation initiated in the intensive care unit, while the patient is undergoing mechanical ventilation is safe and feasible. Furthermore, patients who are engaged in an active rehabilitation protocol while critically ill have better physical function at hospital discharge and less delirium during their ICU stay.  Despite this knowledge, implementation of early rehabilitation protocols has not been universal. Health care professionals of different disciplines play a key role in the day-to-day rehabilitation of ICU patients. Our study will use a mix of interview and survey techniques to understand the barriers to rehabilitation in patients on life support, as perceived by physical and occupational therapists, nurses, respiratory therapists and physicians. Our research findings will have direct implications for the design of an intervention intended to improve early rehabilitation in the ICU and by extension, the long-term outcomes of our patients.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; VIEILLISSEMENT
TitreApplicationTitle: A potential biomarker for vascular dementia
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; CEREBRAL AUTOREGULATION; CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW; CEREBRAL CORTEX; DEMENTIA; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; VACULAR DEMENTIA; VASCULAR RESERVE
Abstract-Résumé: As the population ages, more people are developing dementia. It is therefore increasingly important for the health care system to find solutions for slowing or even eliminating this condition. Individuals with declining brain function may be developing one of several different types of dementia that can be difficult to distinguish from each other early on. Knowledge of the dementia type is important for starting the right treatment as soon as possible. New research indicates that small blood vessels supporting the nerve cells are also under attack. One type of dementia is actually caused by injury only to the blood vessels themselves. Yet, in the other dementias, the relationship between blood vessel injury and direct injury to nerve cells is less well understood though it likely plays a role in Alzheimer's Disease. In the last 10 years our research team has developed a very accurate method for measuring how well the brain's blood vessels function to deliver blood to working nerve cells. This research proposal will use this method to better understand the role damaged blood vessels play in the development and progression of dementia. The method uses a unique breathing device where subjects breathe oxygen with different concentrations of carbon dioxide while MRI brain images are collected. Brain blood flow increases in healthy blood vessels when a small amount of carbon dioxide is inhaled but the flow does not increase as much in unhealthy vessels. We believe that the areas in the brain with unhealthy blood vessels will be seen at a very early stage of dementia allowing doctors to start the right kind of treatment sooner improving the future quality of life. Finally the method is accurate, affordable, safe as it has already been tested in over 600 patients, and is ready to be installed in almost any MRI scanner.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-Term Family Economic Consequences of a Childhood Cancer Diagnosis
Keywords-MotsClés: FAMILY FINANCIAL COSTS; PEDIATRIC ONCOLOGY; RECORD LINKAGE
Abstract-Résumé: Survival after childhood cancer has improved greatly over the last several decades. Increases in survival can largely be attributed to advances in therapy, particularly increases in the intensity of therapy. Due to the nature of the illness and the intensity of therapy, a childhood cancer diagnosis is not only emotionally and physically difficult, but has also been shown to pose a significant financial hardships on the families of children. Limited research exists that examines the economic impact of a childhood cancer diagnosis on the family. This study will examine the global economic impact on families that experience a diagnosis of childhood cancer and assess the family's economic trajectory over time. Should a family economic disadvantage that begins at diagnosis be identified, particularly a disadvantage that is a harbinger of long-term economic loss, policy changes that reflect more robust tax credits and/or incentives for paid parental leave of absence could be developed to mitigate.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF; MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: The high-resolution structure of the VacA toxin from H. pylori as determined by electron cryomicroscopy.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC INFECTIONS; CRYO-ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; GASTRIC CANCER; GASTRITIS; HELICOBACTER PYLORI; PORE FORMING TOXIN; ULCERS; VACA
Abstract-Résumé: The pathogenic bacterium Helicobacter pylori infects over half of the world's population. H. pylori infection is associated with gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, and gastric cancers.  The bacteria secrete a pore-forming toxin, VacA, which facilitate intracellular survival of the bacteria and bacterial colonization of the stomach.  Presence of the toxin is also associated with more severe disease including gastric cancer. The VacA toxin is activated upon secretion into the stomach where it interacts with gastric epithelia cells and host T-cells via cell-surface receptors, producing a myriad of downstream consequences.   While the VacA toxin has been characterized functionally, there exists little information about the structural and biochemical mechanisms that enable the toxin's activities.  We will use high-resolution electron cryomicroscopy to determine the structure of oligomeric VacA in its soluble, receptor-bound, and membrane-inserted and states.  These structures will allow us elucidate the conformational changes that occur upon receptor binding and membrane insertion.  The conformational changes will provide critical insight into the mechanisms that govern the toxic activity of VacA.  These findings will also provide the molecular information required to develop novel antibiotics for the treatment of H. pylori infection and new targets for treatment of gastric cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D on control of cell growth and differentiation
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE METASTASIS; BREAST; CANCER; KERATINOCYTES; KNOCK-OUT; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: A lack of vitamin D has been linked to several types of cancer including breast cancer. In earlier studies we have shown that vitamin D blocks the production of another hormone called parathyroid hormone related protein or PTHrP. PTHrP is produced by the great majority of breast tumors and when overproduced accelerates the development of bone metastases. Based on these observations we believe that we can target this vitamin D-PTHrP axis to counter the development of bone metastases. The majority of breast cancer patients who have a recurrence will develop cancer spread to the skeleton, which causes considerable suffering and morbidity. Bone metastases are currently treated with bisphosphonates that inhibit osteoclast bone lytic activity. Unfortunately, bisphosphonate treatment is not a cure and the number of patients experiencing skeletal complications is reduced by only 20%, which exemplifies the need for improving the efficacy of bisphosphonate therapy. Recent evidence points to the existence in tumors of a small population of multi-potent therapy-resistant cancer stem cells (CSC) that survive treatment to regenerate tumors locally and produce metastases. One aspect of this proposal is to examine the possibility of countering breast cancer metastatic spread to the skeleton by targeting of the CSC population through the vitamin D-PTHrP axis. We believe that the combination of vitamin D therapy, specific blockade of PTHrP activity, and bisphosphonate treatment in a co-targeting strategy will create an enhanced treatment addressing all levels of metastatic spread from breast to the skeleton. Another aspect of this proposal is to improve the efficacy of vitamin D by targeting specific signaling molecules that render the cancer cells resistant to the effect of vitamin D. Overall our goal is to develop pre-clinical models of vitamin D-based therapies. If successful, these strategies will constitute proofs of principle for therapeutic intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relapse prevention of ulcerative colitis by prebiotics: efficacy and protective mechanisms.
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA; CYTOKINES; PREBIOTICS; ULCERATIVE COLITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic relapsing inflammation of the colon ("colitis") affecting around 300 per 100.000 Canadians, the highest in the world.  It causes frequent episodes of bloody diarrhea ("flares") with loss of quality of life, employment and continuous use of expensive drugs. The current drug therapies are potentially toxic, as they are mostly directed towards the abnormal immune response.  The current theory is that a lack of protective ("probiotic") intestinal bacteria versus disease-inducing bacteria can lead to a flare of UC. Indeed, the ingestion of probiotics has been shown to treat and prevent UC. Non-digestible dietary carbohydrates are fibers that are easy to administer and very inexpensive versus drugs and even probiotics. These fibers stimulate protective bacteria that are already present in the gut whereas these bacteria produce natural products against inflammation.  We recently found that a mixture of non-digestible fibers not only reduced colitis in a rat model, but was also able to treat active mild to moderate UC in a small clinical trial. In this grant we will study if the same fiber mixture used in the rats and UC patients also prevent flares that occur despite standard drugs. If these fibers are effective, this inexpensive therapy will then prevent patients to add more potentially toxic drugs or even prevent loss of their colon.  There is still a lack of knowledge which bacteria induce (flares of) ulcerative colitis. By using molecular techniques analyzing the many gut bacteria that cannot be cultured plus what they are doing, we expect to identify which bacterial functions are stimulated before and during relapse, and especially what factors are associated with relapse prevention by our fiber mixture in each patient. This knowledge may unravel the cause of (relapses in) UC and could lead to novel (dietary), personalized therapies for this debilitating disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Obstetrical brachial plexus injury (OBPI): a clinical practice guideline
Keywords-MotsClés: BRACHIAL PLEXUS; CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH RESEARCH METHODOLOGY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; OUTCOMES RESEARCH; PEDIATRIC SURGERY; PERIPHERAL NERVE; PHYSIO AND OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY; PLASTIC SURGERY; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: The brachial plexus is a series of nerves that supplies motor function and sensation to the shoulders, arms and hands. These nerves exit the spinal canal in the neck and end in the arm. Obstetrical brachial plexus injury (OBPI) is a birth injury to the newborn child. During labour and delivery, forces applied to the child's head and neck to pull the child out of the birth canal can stretch and damage the brachial plexus. In the worst case, the nerves are pulled off of their origin at the spinal cord. OBPI occurs in 1 of every 1000 births. Hand and arm disability is seen immediately after birth. Some injuries will improve without surgery, but  40% of injuries will lead to permanent disability of the hand and arm.  OBPI cases should be referred to dedicated treatment centres, typically at university centres. Research has detected two "gaps" in care of these children. The first is timing of referral. The second are specific surgical indications in mild injuries. When discrepancies exist between the best evidence and care delivered to patients, "guidelines" can answer the challenge. "Guidelines" are a series of recommendations based on research. They must be agreed upon by OBPI surgeons and physiotherapists who are experts in care of OBPI.  We will review research and develop a set of recommendations for the physicians delivering children can follow. We will write a guideline for management of OBPI. It will guide referral and treatment reliably, based on best research evidence. If these children are referred to OBPI centres in a consistent manner, their outcomes will improve. Recommendations for surgical intervention will provide consistent care across Canada for all children, improving outcomes and parental uncertainty in a fragile population.

TitreApplicationTitle: NOD2 immunity and its protection against obesity-induced inflammation and insulin resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS OF METABOLIC DISORDERS; ENDOCRINOLOGY; INFLAMMATION; INSULIN RESISTANCE; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: More than half of the Canadian population is overweight or obese. Obesity causes insulin resistance and eventually type 2 diabetes. The rise in obesity negatively impacts the health of Canadians and causes a financial burden on the healthcare system and taxpayers.  This research aims to understand the relationship between obesity and insulin resistance/diabetes by investigating the immune system. Inflammation causes insulin resistance, and inflammation increases greatly during obesity. Inflammation is controlled by the immune system, which normally protects the body against disease. Good bacteria living inside the human gut are beneficial because they aid digestion, and these microbes constantly interact with the immune system to limit their growth. Studying how bacteria interact with the immune system is important because microbes activate pathways in inflammation, and therefore might be critical in preventing insulin resistance and diabetes during obesity.  This research will improve the health of Canadians by investigating therapeutic effects of small compounds found in certain types of gut bacteria that interact with parts of the immune system. These compounds activate specific immune responses and might be implemented as a "probiotic" health strategy to reduce the amount of inflammation during obesity, thereby reducing the rates of type 2 diabetes in overweight and obese Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the role of calcium-waves in human eosinophil migration and degranulation
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGIES; ASTHMA; CALCIUM SIGNALING; CALCIUM WAVES; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; DEGRANULATION; EOSINOPHIL; MIGRATION
Abstract-Résumé: One of the main signs of asthma is an increase in the lungs in the number of a special group of cells, known as eosinophils. Normally, they move around throughout the body via the bloodstream and wriggle into sites of infection to defend the body against invading organisms and particles that cause allergies. In asthma, they accumulate unnecessarily in the lungs and cause tremendous damage and other unwanted effects. A better understanding of how they move around and release their toxic weapons could lead to a better therapy for asthma.  We have found out that molecules that cause the eosinophil cells to move around also trigger a chemical signal inside the eosinophil consisting of a series of repetitive spike-like rises and falls in calcium concentration. These very same calcium spikes control other cell functions in other cell types - we believe they control movement of the eosinophil. We intend to learn more about how the eosinophil creates those calcium spikes, and how the calcium spikes control eosinophil movement. To do this, we can put a special dye into the eosinophil which allows us to see (using a microscope) the calcium spikes in individual living eosinophils without interfering with their normal function.  Very few people in the past have looked at these calcium spikes in eosinophils, and almost all of them used populations of millions of cells. This blurs the spikes being produced in each individual cell. The problem is similar to listening to a sound recording of a packed sports stadium from a distance, where all you hear is a continuous roar which dips and crescendos smoothly. On the other hand, close-up recordings from individual spectators sound quite different and contain much more information.  Our unique approach allows us to follow individual eosinophils and measure how fast or slow they move, how often they turn direction and how they behave all while measuring calcium spikes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the endonuclease domain of the mismatch repair factor MutLalpha in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA MISMATCH REPAIR
Abstract-Résumé: DNA Mismatch Repair (MMR) is a highly conserved process that corrects DNA replication errors. Two proteins are key to the initiation of the process: MutSalpha, which recognizes mismatches in DNA, and MutLalpha, which interacts with MutSalpha at the mismatch to nick the error-containing DNA and allow for correction of the error by downstream factors. Not surprisingly, mutations in these two proteins cause severe genomic instability and are the ultimate cause of hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) in humans. MutLalpha exhibits ATPase and endonuclease activities, which are located in separate domains connected by a flexible linker. While the ATPase activity of MutLalpha has been studied extensively, the regulatory mechanisms for its endonuclease activity and the role of the linker in its proper function are not clear. I will determine the stable boundaries of the endonuclease domain, which we hypothesize will extend into the linker, in order to solve a crystal structure of yeast MutLalpha using a combination of biochemical, biophysical and structural biology techniques. The outcome of this work will be a better understanding of the role of the linker in protein stability and the coordinated conformational changes that regulate the endonuclease activity of MutLalpha. This work will provide a framework with which to interpret the specific pathogenic effects of mutations within the endonuclease domain at a structural level. Knowledge of defects in tumour cells at the molecular level will allow for more precise diagnoses and more effective preventive treatments of HNPCC families that carry these mutations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding how fear of evaluation and reassurance seeking behaviour contribute to social anxiety disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL MANIFESTATIONS; CLINICAL INTERVIEWING; COGNITIVE VULNERABILITIES; PSYCHOPATHOLOGY MODELS; SOCIAL ANXIETY DISORDER; THERAPEUTIC APPLICATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: One in four Canadians will suffer from an anxiety disorder within their lifetime, which not only diminishes personal quality of life, but costs Canada $65 billion annually through direct (e.g., inpatient/outpatient care) and indirect (e.g., lost work productivity) expenses. Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) is an empirically-based treatment which addresses maladaptive thoughts and behaviours that contribute to anxiety problems. CBT demonstrates success rates as great as 90%, and is preferred over pharmacological treatment by the majority (60%) of people suffering from anxiety disorders. Research to improve our understanding of disorder presentation is needed to ensure accurate diagnoses, appropriate referrals to CBT practitioners, and to increase CBT efficiency. As the third most prevalent anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder (SAD) affects 13% of North Americans and is associated with intense fear of being watched or being the focus of attention. Fearing both negative and positive evaluation are maladaptive thought patterns associated with SAD that contribute to the fear of being observed. Excessively seeking reassurance about what one fears is a maladaptive behaviour pattern that also contributes to anxiety maintenance. Counter to this evidence, preliminary research suggests that individuals with SAD do not seek reassurance regarding evaluation of themselves or their performance. This discrepancy may be explained by the fact that reassurance is often in the form of positive appraisal, which individuals with SAD fear and avoid. The proposed study will extend previous research and clarify whether those with SAD avoid seeking reassurance about what they fear most (i.e., evaluation) and if this is because they fear positive appraisal. The results will improve understanding of SAD, facilitate diagnoses, and increase CBT efficacy, which will help eliminate costly inefficiencies in public health systems and alleviate the suffering of millions of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pharmacogenomic testing of atorvastatin efficacy and toxicity in secondary prevention of cardiovascular diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CORONARY HEART DISEASE; DIABETES; GENOTYPING; LDL-CHOLESTEROL; PHARMACOGENOMICS; STATIN
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, the number of individuals coping with heart disease is steadily increasing and now affects more than 1.3 million individuals. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) represents the most important health care spending in Canada and costs the Canadian economy $20.9 billion/year. Current standard of care requires patients with heart disease to be treated with lipid-lowering medications known as statins. Still, despite being treated with highly potent statins, the risk of cardiovascular events remained very elevated for these patients. We are at the forefront of CVD pharmacogenomic testing and are currently involved in several clinical trials and genetic consortia that aim at developing personalized medical tools to optimize management of CVD in Canada and around the world. Our objective is to take advantage of our increasing knowledge of the human genome along with the most recent technologies used for surveying it to identify genes that influence both the efficacy of these drugs and the risk of CVD in this population. On top of opening novel research opportunities on the newly discovered genes that influence CVD, this project will directly improve personal health by delivering molecular diagnostic tools able to identify patients that are likely to benefit the most from high-dose statin therapy. As a consequence, this approach will help determine whether or not a specific subgroup of patients do not drive any benefits from statin therapy and therefore expose themselves to avoidable potential side-effects in such a way that they are likely to derive more risk than benefits from statin therapy. The identification of better responsive patients could help avoid a considerable amount of useless prescriptions and provide substantial savings for healthcare systems across Canada and around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Omega current underlies SCN5A mutations associated with complex cardiac arrhythmias and dilated cardiomyopathy.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM; CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIAS; CARDIOMYOPATHY; HEART; ION CHANNELS; PATCH CLAMP; SODIUM CHANNELS
Abstract-Résumé: Dilation related cardiomyopathies are cardiac diseases that manifest as an enlargement of cardiac chambers and are the most common cause of heart failure in North America.  For over a decade, SCN5A gene has been associated exclusively to cardiac electrical abnormalities such as Brugada, the Long QT syndromes. Recently we identified a new SCN5A mutation where a hsitidien replaces the arginine on the S4 of the first domain (position 219) in a family with complex cardiac arrhythmias associated with DCM. We showed that that this resulted on leaky channels known as omega current. The association of the omega current with dilation characterized in this proposal is a novel hypothesis. We developed an in vivo model where the R219H human mutation was introduced in a mouse gene using gene targeting technique. The in vivo analysis of the homozygous and heterozygous mice showed that heart mice exhibit a dilation resembling what was described in human patient. The first objective is to characterize this mouse model and study the progression of the disease. The second objective of the proposal is to establish a cellular model of omega current using mouse embryonic stem cells differentiated into cardiac myocytes. This cellular model is of importance to ascertain that DCM is not the result of cardiac arrhythmias, know to generate dilated cardiac chamber as a compensatory mechanism. In conjunction with the mammalian expression model system, structural models containing DCM mutations will be undertaken as our third objective. The recent progress in crystallizing the homologous bacterial voltage-gated sodium channel, there is now sufficient understanding of the structure and function to anticipate useful data extrapolation for Nav1.5 function. As a forth objective we will express the isolated voltage sensors using a mammalian expression system this will provide a better signal-to-noise ratio.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of Amygdala Lesions on Human Emotional Processing
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYGDALA; EMOTION; TEMPORAL LOBE EPILEPSY
Abstract-Résumé: The amygdala is a critical structure for the perception and evaluation of emotional information. Studies in experimental animals have shown that lesions of this structure interfere with emotional processing. In humans, most lesion studies have been conducted in patients suffering from intractable temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) who underwent resection of medial temporal lobe regions, sometimes (but not always) including the amygdala. While in general these studies have confirmed the importance of the amygdala in emotion, results have been inconsistent in terms of the specificity of the deficits. These inconsistencies may be due in part to limitations in the assessment of the nature, location and extent of the assumed amygdala lesion, as well as in the experimental tasks employed. The goal of this proposal is to overcome these limitations by using advanced quantitative neuroimaging techniques and previously validated experimental paradigms in TLE patients before surgery. Results from these studies should further our knowledge of amygdala involvement in human emotional processing, as well as contribute to a better understanding of the emotional deficits in patients suffering from TLE.

TitreApplicationTitle: Étude pilote sur les pratiques médicales de fin de vie au Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: ENQUETE; FIN DE VIE; PRATIQUES MEDICALES; PROCESSUS DECISIONNEL; ETHIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: Les pratiques medicales en fin de vie au Canada sont actuellement sujets de debats aux plans ethique, social et politique. D'une part, des changements sont proposes pour une modification des lois et de la surveillance de ces pratiques. D'autre part, des recours judiciaires remettent en question les frontieres de la pratique medicale, soit en exigeant un elargissement des options en fin de vie (suicide assiste) ou en limitant le pouvoir medical actuel (decision d'abstention ou d'arret de traitement dans les cas d'incompetence du patient et de desaccord avec la famille). Toutefois, nous en savons bien peu sur la facon dont les medecins canadiens prennent des decisions en contexte de fin de vie. De telles informations sont necessaires pour alimenter les debats actuels, mais egalement pour identifier des pistes d'amelioration de la prise en charge des personnes en fin de vie. Sur le modele de grandes enquetes realisees dans divers pays, nous souhaitons mener une etude sur les pratiques medicales de fin de vie aupres des medecins canadiens. Or, il est avant tout souhaitable de mettre en place les conditions de reussite pour mener une telle enquete par le biais d'un projet pilote. Pour ce faire, nous creerons un comite d'experts charge d'etudier les questions prioritaires pour le Canada et de developper le questionnaire qui sera utilise pour l'enquete. L'outil fera l'objet d'un pre-test aupres de 25 medecins et d'une double traduction inversee comme processus de validation. Le protocole de recherche sera developpe et avalise par le comite d'experts. Ces etapes preparatoires permettront de preparer le terrain en vue d'une enquete nationale sur les pratiques medicales de fin de vie aupres des medecins canadiens.

TitreApplicationTitle: Disruption of immune functions by Virus infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN PRESENTATION; CYTOKINES; DENDRITIC CELLS; LYMPHOCYTIC CHORIOMENINGITIS VIRUS; MICE; TLR-SIGNALLING
Abstract-Résumé: Every day, millions of people worldwide get infected with new viral infections. Some of those infected, will be exposed to other microbial stimuli. Currently we have limited knowledge concerning how viral infections influence the immune response to other stimuli.  Our aim is to understand how viruses interfere with the initiation of cellular mechanisms that regulate an adequate immune response. We foresee that the knowledge gained from studying how viruses regulate host defences will provide important concepts to help in the development of new therapeutic approaches that alleviate viral-induced ill health.

TitreApplicationTitle: The consequences of cerebellar injury on brain development in premature infants
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN DEVELOPMENT; BRAIN IMAGING; BRAIN INJURY; CEREBELLUM; DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME; HIGH-RISK INFANT; INFANT DEVELOPMENT; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEUROBEHAVIORAL ASSESSMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The number of premature birth continues to increase every year with a growing survival rate among the smallest and sickest babies. These infants are at significant risk for brain injury. It is now recognized that injuries or the cerebellum are frequent in this population and will results in striking neurodevelopmental deficits.  This study seeks to understand the mechanism underlying brain development following CBI using novel imaging techniques to identify early markers of brain injury that are associated with postnatal and long-term neurodevelopment dysfunction. A better understanding of the mechanisms and consequences of premature-related injury will guide medical and rehabilitative therapies to optimize life quality and minimize functional disabilities. Results will improve both, the health population and health delivery system, as they will allow for improved medical management for these high-risk infants and the implementation of targeted early interventions that will improve life quality in survivors and their families.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Epithelial Cell Adhesion Machinery and Mechanisms in Tumour Metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN CYTOSKELETON; CADHERIN; CANCER; CATENIN; CELL ADHESION; METASTASIS; NMR; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; THERAPY DEVELOPMENT; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is a leading cause of death worldwide, and metastasized tumours cause a large fraction of the fatalities associated with cancer. In women, breast cancer is the most common cause of cancer death with approximately 90% of deaths due to distant metastases. Metastatic breast cancer cells are different from the primary breast tumour with increased drug resistance and the ability to spread to distant sites, making them especially challenging to cure. To develop appropriate therapeutics for metastatic cancers, we ought to understand how cells lose adhesiveness and how they metastasize in the body. Despite of tremendous efforts in modern cancer biology, these questions remain unsolved. For over two decades, our laboratory has been investigating the molecular and structural basis of cell adhesion with the ultimate goal of elucidating therapeutic opportunities in this amazingly complicated biological system. Our research team has been using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and X-ray crystallography to investigate fundamental biological processes relevant to metastatic cancer. Towards this goal, we have determined numerous high-impact three-dimensional structures of cell adhesion molecules. Since diminished cellular adhesion is one of the hallmarks of metastatic tumours, the elucidation of detailed structures of cell adhesion molecules will greatly contribute to gaining an understanding of what triggers tumour cells to metastasize. The scientific tools mentioned above enable us to visualize how cancer-specific mutations may cause structural damage to normal proteins as well as how modifications of these proteins play key roles in both morphogenesis and tumour progression.  We believe that atomic-resolution structural information on cell adhesion molecules and complementary analysis on their structure-function relationships will have a tremendous long-term impact on cancer treatment by providing new clues for therapeutic strategies to treat metastatic cancers.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: The directional selective retinal circuit: From ion channels to behavior
Keywords-MotsClés: GAP JUNCTIONS; NEURAL CIRCUITS; OPTOGENETICS; OPTOKINETIC REFLEX; PATCH-CLAMP; RETINA; SYNAPSE; TRANSGENIC MOUSE; TWO-PHOTON IMAGING; VISUAL PROCESSING
Abstract-Résumé: Slow neural processing is an inherent property that the brain must overcome in order to perceive the world in real time. For example, in the visual system, images are transduced by light detecting cells in the eye extremely slowly and the brain receives signals only ~50 ms after the image first falls on the screen (retina) of the eye. Why is this problematic? Consider what happens in tennis, when Nadal serves a tennis ball at 185 km/hour, which takes roughly 50 ms to cross the court. If Federer took 50 ms to see the ball, there is no way that he could face his opponent's serve. But we know Federer does very well to return serve, meaning that his brain can somehow compensate for delays. We believe, it is not the actual image of the ball that Federer sees, but an extrapolated image provided by his brain. How the brain can achieve this remarkable feat is not known, but is of obvious importance, not only in tennis, but in visualizing fast moving objects in our daily lives. In studying the responses of specialized cells in the retina (known as ganglion cells), we discovered that they have a remarkable ability to anticipate motion and compensate for processing delays. This is the first time in the visual system that a cell has been found to have properties to anticipate moving objects.  We demonstrate that these cells can anticipate because they are endowed with specialized connections called gap junctions, which allows them to communicate lateral signals with their neighbours and figure out that an object is approaching before it actually reaches them. These ganglion cells are also known to be important in directing our eyes, allowing us to track moving objects. In fact in certain diseases, these cells malfunction and their eyes undergo involuntary oscillatory movements (Congenital Idiopathic Nystagmus).  In order to find a cure for these diseases it is very important to first understand the mechanisms that govern responses of these particular ganglion cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating behavioural phenotype and function of networks of genes implicated in neurological and psychiatric disorders using an invertebrate animal model
Keywords-MotsClés: GENES AND BEHAVIOUR; HABITUATION; LEARNING AND MEMORY; NEURAL CIRCUIT
Abstract-Résumé: Although we have a number of new tools to identify genes that might play a role in Schizophrenia, however, this has not helped us to understand thsi disorder. There are several reasons for this: one is that we do not know the function of some of the genes, another is that so much data has been generated that it is not easy to understand what it all means.  An analogy would be having a large jigsaw puzzle with many small pieces, and no picture to help to understand how the pieces fit together. In this research we propose using a model organism, the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, with a small easily studied nervous system that can be studied much more rapidly than a mammal could be studied.  We will focus on a simple behavior that is altered in Schizophrenia.  This behavior is habituation, perhaps the simplest form of learning that is seen in all animals studied. Habituation is learning to ignore stimuli that do not predict anything good or bad- thus can safely be ignored. C. elegans shares a number of genes with humans (similar genes in different organisms are called homologues), and so our plan is use databases of genes implicated in human neurological disorders to study the role of their homologues in habituation in C. elegans.  We will use a new high-throughput behaviour analysis method to test habituation for all of the C. elegans genes homologous to genes implicated in Schizophrenia. Using data from these descriptions we will discover how the genes work together in gene pathways. Our hypothesis is that by understanding the role of gene networks in habituation in C. elegans we will shed light on how they contribute to a disorder and may lead to new ways to diagnose and treat this disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Spatial and temporal plasticity of transmitter release at a developing central synapse
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY BRAINSTEM; CALYX OF HELD SYNAPSE; CONFOCAL AND 2-PHOTON IMAGING; DEVELOPMENTAL NEUROBIOLOGY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MORPHOLOGICAL AND FUNCTIONAL REMODELING; NEUROTRANSMITTER RELEASE; PATCH-CLAMP ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; SENSORY DEVELOPMENT & COGNITIION; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION AND PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: The brain exhibits robust plasticity during its critical period of development in the early postnatal stage. Our research progam focuses on understanding the mechanisms underlying development and maturation of highly specialized connections (i.e. synapses) between nerve cells in the developing brain. Our goal is to gain insights into key molecular signaling pathways that govern developmental changes in the efficacy of neuronal communication and establish novel theories on experience-independent and -dependent plasticity in young brain. Our work will facilitate our understanding of how sensory experience shapes up brain functions, particularly auditory perception and related disorders such as deafness, hearing loss and audiogenic seizures.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; VIEILLISSEMENT
TitreApplicationTitle: Unraveling the Molecular Mechanisms of Non-homologous DNA End-joining
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; DNA DOUBLE-STRAND BREAK REPAIR; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NON-HOMOLOGOUS DNA END-JOINING; PROTEIN FILAMENT FORMATION; PROTEIN-DNA INTERACTIONS; V(D)J RECOMBINATION; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Maintaining DNA integrity is essential to all forms of life and prevention of cancer.  Despite its importance, it is continually damaged by exposure to many types of harmful agents.  Estimates put the frequency of DNA damage at up to one million events each day in every cell.  Although DNA is damaged in many ways, the most severe form occurs when DNA is broken into two or more pieces.  If not repaired, cells harboring this kind of damage will die.  If repaired improperly, genetic information will be altered, rendering such cells susceptible to misregulation events leading to the onset of cancer.  Fortunately, cells have a number of proteins that collectively act as guardians of the genome.  Although several of these guardian proteins have now been identified in humans the way in which they come together to form a functional DNA repair machine is not well understood.  Using methods (such as X-ray crystallography) that permit the detailed three-dimensional visualization of proteins, our lab is approaching the understanding of DNA repair machinery from the perspective of a molecular mechanic.  Our research is aimed at understanding specific parts of the 'machine' (ie. proteins) and their relationship to other parts of the machine.  By achieving a better understanding of how the DNA repair machinery functions normally, our proposed research will inform why a person's DNA repair machinery malfunctions during the development of cancer and ultimately allow measures to be taken to either 'fix' the repair machinery before cancer causing mutations occur, or exploit this knowledge to develop more effective chemotherapeutic drugs useful in the treatment of individual cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: The functional role of titin in muscle contraction
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC MUSCLE; CARDIAC MYOPATHY; CEREBRAL PALSY; MECHANISMS OF CONTRACTION; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; MYOFIBRILS; SARCOMERES; SKELETAL MUSCLE; TITIN
Abstract-Résumé: Titin is the third most abundant protein in muscles, and has been considered to have only passive structural roles until recently. However, in the past three years of CIHR support, we developed novel techniques that allowed us to study the properties of titin in completely new ways. By doing so, we discovered that titin increases its inherent stiffness and force when a muscle is activated, thereby contributing as much force to muscle contraction as the contractile proteins actin and myosin for some conditions. Since titin has also been shown to change its structure and function as a function of disease, injury, aging, disuse, and training, understanding its function, signaling, and force regulation in normal and diseased tissues has become a major thrust of scientific research in labs around the world.  In this proposal, we want to identify the molecular mechanisms of force regulation by titin and study this force regulation in normal and diseased heart and skeletal muscles, where force regulation through titin appears disrupted. Understanding these mechanisms, we hope to define muscle diseases more accurately, understand the mechanical implications of disease, and hopefully, contribute to the design of treatment options for cardiac and skeletal muscle diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Study of pre- and gamma/delta-T cell receptor signals regulating thymocyte differentiation
Keywords-MotsClés: DELTA-LIKE; EVA1; IMMUNE RECONSTITUTION; LYMPHOCYTE DEVELOPMENT; LYMPHOCYTE PROGENITORS; NOTCH SIGNALING; STROMAL CELLS; T CELL DEVELOPMENT; THYMUS; THYMUS EPITHELIAL CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The thymus is the essential organ that supports and allows for the development of T lymphocytes from bone marrow-derived stem cells. Thymic contributions result in the generation of mature T cells that are capable of recognizing foreign antigens/pathogens, while at the same time producing T cells that are tolerant to their own uninfected cells, preventing the initiation of autoimmune disease. This proposal provides a comprehensive study of key signaling pathways occurring at a critical checkpoint in T cell development. A deeper understanding of signaling cascades employed during normal T cell maturation is essential, as mutations in components of these signaling pathways may result in oncogenic events, leading to the onset of leukemia, such as aggressive thymomas or lymphomas. Cellular signals and molecular mechanisms underlying the differentiation of immature T cells remain unclear, hence our proposal aims to create in vitro and in vivo experimental systems in which to study the events governing a key stage during T cell differentiation.

TitreApplicationTitle: A community outreach and cardiovascular health (COACH)  program for individuals with stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SELF-MANAGEMENT; STROKE; TELEHEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is a common condition in older adults; 1 in 5 women, and 1 in 6 men will suffer a stroke after 55 years of age. The physical activity of individuals who have had a stroke declines dramatically after returning home from rehabilitation. This sedentary lifestyle increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, which in turn can lead to another stroke. In fact, up to 75% of stroke survivors have heart disease; 84% have hypertension; 75% are overweight; and 80% have impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes mellitus. Although these cardiovascular issues are responsive to regular physical activity, current stroke rehabilitation is primarily focused on functional recovery, with little or no long-term follow-up for the prevention of cardiovascular risk factors. Research shows that one-third of stroke survivors have another stroke within 5 years. Many of these recurrent strokes, however, are preventable by increased physical activity, and improved lifestyle and risk factor management.   The purpose of this study is to determine the effects of a comprehensive telehealth program targeted towards modifying health behaviours in community-dwelling stroke survivors that influence the risk of cardiovascular disease, such as physical activity, and lifestyle and cardiovascular risk factor management. This program, Stroke COACH (Community Outreach and Cardiovascular Health), will be delivered by telephone by community-based health-care workers.  We will use a randomized controlled trial to test the primary hypothesis that a 6-month Stroke COACH program will improve participation in physical activity as measured by weekly number of steps taken. Secondary hypotheses will test the effect of the program on dietary behaviour, and cardiovascular health outcomes, including resting blood pressure, lipid and glucose profiles, body mass index, and waist circumference.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analysis of DNA Methylation Data
Keywords-MotsClés: DATA INTEGRATION; FUNCTIONAL DATA ANALYSIS; HIDDEN MARKOV MODELS; MEQTL ANALYSIS; METHYLATION ARRAYS; METHYLC-SEQ; NORMALIZATION; WHOLE GENOME BISULFITE SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: DNA methylation describes a process where DNA nucleotides are altered by the binding of a small molecule. The presence of this molecule can alter how the DNA functions. It is now possible to measure, at specific locations along the genome, what proportion of cells in a sample of human tissue such as blood have this DNA methylation mark attached. There are several different technologies that can generate these data, but there are some challenges with obtaining accurate estimates of the proportion of cells that are methylated at any point, for all of the possible technologies. Methylation patterns vary along the genome, between different tissues, and between individuals. Since methylation can alter how DNA functions, there is great interest in understanding exactly how these patterns are related to gene activity and to disease. In order to understand these relationships, reliable statistical models are needed for characterizing the patterns and working with them. We propose to develop such tools, and to release user-friendly computationally efficient software packages to enable other researchers to perform these analyses on their data. One important feature of this proposal is a way to identify the most important places or sites in the genome for understanding methylation patterns and how they vary. If we had this set of sites, cheaper approaches to measuring methylation levels would be possible.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developmental relationships among social perceptual and social cognitive measures in infants at risk for autism spectrum disorders and in control infants
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SCREENING; BROADER AUTISM PHENOTYPE; EARLY AUTISM DETECTION; EARLY DEVELOPMENT OF AUTISM; PREDICTORS OF AUTISM; SOCIAL COGNITION; SOCIAL PERCEPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is associated with difficulty in social cognitive development, presenting severe challenges to developing children as well as parenting struggles in families dealing with the disorder. ASDs are increasingly prevalent, thus presenting an increasing social and economic challenge.  However, researchers know relatively little about the development of ASD in the first year, because ASDs are reliably diagnosed only when a child is about 2 years old, and children frequently are diagnosed at the age of 4, 5 or even later. The General Objective of this project is to use eye-tracking technology to measure early social perceptual measurement in the first year of life, and compare such early development to later social cognitive development. Siblings of individuals with autism serve as the "high-risk" group in this study. Because autism is heritable, we can identify children who may be at risk for autism by the existence of autism in the family. The control group comprises infants with no known autism in the family. This project measures early interest in social information to see if such measures predict later development of ASDs or of autistic characteristics.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Sleep and Obesity in Children and Adolescents: Identifying Pathogenic Pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; AMBULATORY MONITORING; CHILD HEALTH; CHILDREN; METABOLIC SYNDROME; OBESITY; PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGY; SCHOOL; SLEEP; STRESS RESPONSE SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: One in four Canadian children is overweight or obese. Over the past 25 years, the level of overweight and obesity has doubled. This is worrying because it has long term health consequences. Childhood obesity increases risk for many diseases such as high blood pressure, heart disease, and diabetes. While obesity levels have been rising, the amount of time children spend sleeping has been decreasing. There is convincing evidence showing that children who sleep less have a larger body size. However, the amount of timing spent sleeping might not tell the whole story. Having awakenings throughout the night or going to bed inconsistent with your internal clock may be more problematic. Researchers are still working to disentangle the pathways that link sleep and obesity. Some pathways include hormones dealing with appetite, the body's response to stress, and changes in metabolism and sensitivity to insulin. Most researchers look at these pathways singularly. Also, most studies use only self- (or parent-) reports of sleep times. This may not be the best way of capturing what happens during sleep. The goal of the current project is to consider different dimensions of sleep and how these pathways might link them to obesity. An in-depth measurement of sleep will be included to capture the subtle dimensions of sleep. The project will result in new information about why sleep may be linked to obesity. This information has potential to prevent and treat obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-term effects of creatine supplementation and exercise training on bone mineral density and bone strength in postmenopausal women
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MINERAL DENSITY; CREATINE MONOHYDRATE; DUAL ENERGY X-RAY ABSORPTIOMETRY; EXERCISE TRAINING; FALLS; FEMORAL NECK; FRACTURES; HIP STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS; OSTEOPOROSIS; POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis is an important health problem, costing the Canadian health care system over $2 billion per year. Loss of bone mineral and bone fragility is especially prevalent in postmenopausal women. Of all osteoporotic fractures, hip fractures are the most traumatic. Creatine monohydrate is a nutritional supplement that is often combined with strength training to increase strength and muscle mass. We recently completed a pilot study in a small number of postmenopausal women (n=33) that showed that creatine monohydrate significantly improved hip bone mineral density during a 1-year resistance training program. In our current proposal we want to determine whether creatine combined with strength training can have an even larger effect on bone mineral density at the hip if given over 2 years in a large group of postmenopausal women (n=240). We also want to determine whether this leads to reduced fractures in these women for up to a year after completing the creatine and strength training program.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reproductive and Work-Related Health in Female Welders and Electricians
Keywords-MotsClés: PREGNANCY; WORK-RELATED HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: This study seeks to identify risks to reproduction or health in women working in welding (welder, boilermaker, steam fitter, pipe fitter) and electrical trades. The proposal is based on a cohort that was set up at the request of the Canadian Standards Association's Committee on Safety in Welding out of concern that current guidelines and practices might not adequately protect the health of female welders or that of a fetus carried by a woman working as a welder.  The main study objective is to determine whether fertility and pregnancy outcomes are related to welding fume exposure, with the electricians acting as an unexposed comparison group. The cohort has recruited over 530 women welders and electricians across Canada, and has completed follow-up to 24 months for the earliest participants. We propose to expand the established cohort to 800 participants and to collect information on each woman and her pregnancies for up to 5 years, together with information on infertility and work-related ill-health. Our results will help to identify risks in these trades that can be modified to preserve the health of all welders and electricians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the role of caspase activity in cardiac hypertrophy
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; CARDIOVASCULAR; CASPASE; CELL DEATH
Abstract-Résumé: Heart/cardiac disease is a broad health concern for all post industrial societies.   A consistent feature to the many variants of cardiac illness is inappropriate growth of heart muscle, commonly referred to as cardiac hypertrophy.  The initial expansion in the size of the heart is often a beneficial response to an external stress (i.e. increased blood pressure) or damage to existing heart muscle, yet the muscle growth quickly leads to a loss of function, increasing the likelihood of adverse events such as heart failure.   Cardiac hypertrophy itself is derived from an excessive increase in the size of individual heart muscle cells and numerous individual genes and proteins have been implicated in driving this process forward.  Nevertheless, while these studies have greatly increased our understanding of how the heart muscle cell responds or accommodates growth, few studies have examined what factors inside the cell integrate various growth signals or control the restructuring process.   Here, we are examining whether cell death genes/proteins are required for this critical remodeling of heart muscle cells.  These proteins, referred to as caspases, are critical regulators of cell destruction or cell suicide (the scientific term is apoptosis) and act by targeting and destroying other cell proteins.  Our preliminary observations indicate that these 'cell death' proteins become active during cardiac hypertrophy and can induce growth of a heart muscle cell without causing the destruction of the cell.   Importantly, our observations suggest that caspases may represent viable and tractable targets for treating and limiting the pathology associated with cardiac hypertrophy.  The current research plan will build on this exciting area of investigation and provide the necessary information for designing and implementing appropriate pre-clinical models for the treatment of cardiac hypertrophy.
