TitreApplicationTitle: Alberta Physical Activity and Breast Cancer Prevention Trial: Ancillary Study Examining the Effect of Exercise on Oxidative Stress, Telomere Length and DNA Methylation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIOXIDANT ENZYMES; BREAST CANCER EPIDEMIOLOGY; CANCER BIOMARKERS; DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE; DNA METHYLATION; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; TELOMERASE; TELOMERE LENGTH
Abstract-Résumé: Physical activity reduces the risk of breast cancer by 25-30% when comparing the most to least active women. We conducted the Alberta Physical Activity and Breast Cancer Prevention Trial (ALPHA Trial) in Calgary and Edmonton between 2003-2007 to study how exercise reduces breast cancer risk. The ALPHA Trial was a year-long exercise intervention in 320 postmenopausal women aged 50-74 years who were healthy but inactive. It is the largest ever trial of its kind that has been conducted in the world, had excellent adherence to the exercise intervention and very few study drop outs. The study participants were randomly assigned to do either aerobic exercise or to maintain their regular lifestyle of no exercise. The exercise group did 5 days per week of aerobic activity of at least 45 minutes (3 days weekly were supervised and 2 were home-based sessions). Each woman had several measurements of her body taken at the beginning, six and 12 month time points including providing a fasting blood sample. We have previously reported that the exercisers had reduced levels of sex hormones, insulin resistance, inflammation, and all measures of body composition and body fat. We are now interested in understanding if other biological pathways may also be important. With bloods previously stored and frozen from our study participants, we will examine how exercise has influenced markers of oxidation as well as markers of DNA damage and repair (i.e telomere length and DNA methylation). This study is the first to examine several of these biomarkers within the context of a year-long controlled exercise trial in postmenopausal and will provide new insights on how exercise may decrease cancer risk.  Since all of the bloods have already been collected, this study leverages an existing resource and is consequently very cost efficient. This research will provide valuable new information to complement what has already been learned from the ALPHA Trial on how exercise reduces breast cancer risk.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the mechanisms of IRF1 in mediating innate resistance to mucosal HIV acquisition in HIV exposed seronegative (HESN) women.
Keywords-MotsClés: AFRICA; GENETICS; HESN; HIV; INNATE; IRF1; MICROBICIDE; MUCOSAL; PREVENTION; RESISTANCE
Abstract-Résumé: The ultimate solution to the HIV/AIDS pandemic, still, one of the greatest health issues facing humankind, is the development of an effective vaccine or microbicide. Almost all vaccines were derived out of an understanding, no matter how primitive, of what results in protective immunity.  We seek to understand the mechanisms of natural protection against HIV in women who are highly exposed to HIV yet escape infection.  Our earlier genetic studies showed that these HIV resistant women have reduced IRF1 expression in their blood cells. IRF-1 is an important regulator of human immunity and HIV replication.  To determine how IRF1 works in in protecting against HIV infection, this study will examine how artificially reducing IRF1 levels in cells and tissue from the female genital tract will limit HIV infection, and/or alter host immune responses at this site.  Findings from this study will generate new knowledge to determine if specifically reducing IRF1 will protect against HIV infection and if artificially reducing IRF1 could lead to  the eventual development of an effective HIV vaccine, microbicide or novel prevention strategy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Changes in regional brain activation predicted by the Transformation Hypothesis of memory consolidation
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CONSOLIDATION; FMRI; HIPPOCAMPUS; MEMORY; NEUROIMAGING; TRANSFORMATION HYPOTHESIS; VENTROMEDIAL PREFRONTAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: As memories age, their representation in the brain changes. Over time, highly detailed, perceptual elements of a memory are often lost. This loss is thought to be accompanied by a shift in brain regions involved in storage and recall of the memory. The goal of the present study is to assess how the passage of time affects the quality and neural representation of episodic memory (the 'what', 'where', and 'when' of a memory). Our study aims to determine the precise brain regions activated as a memory transforms over time from perceptually-detailed, to a more general, schematic version of the original memory. We will use functional neuroimaging to visualize patterns of regional brain activation as an individual retrieves memory for episodes we have presented to them after various delays, and we will compare this with the time-dependent loss of detailed memory of these episodes.  Understanding normal patterns of brain activation accompanying the loss of detail for episodic memory has profound implications for predicting and understanding the nature of memory deficits, and memory preservation, accompanying neurodegeneration associated with Alzheimer's disease and normal aging.

TitreApplicationTitle: NOD-Like Receptors and Inflammasomes in Kidney Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CELL SIGNALING; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; CLINICAL TRANSLATION; CYTOKINES; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNITY; RENAL FIBROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic kidney disease affects a large proportion of the population. Patients with chronic kidney disease experience a number of problems, including a risk of developing kidney failure that would require dialysis or a kidney transplant. Unfortunately, since the understanding is poor, there are almost no specific therapies for chronic kidney disease or to prevent the development of kidney failure. This proposal will examine how genes that control inflammation can affect kidney disease and the development of kidney failure. This research will increase the understanding of kidney disease that will lead to the development of new treatments or diagnostic tests.

TitreApplicationTitle: Standard Criteria Living Kidney Donor Safety Study
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; COHORT STUDY; HYPERTENSION; KIDNEY DONATION; KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION; ORGAN DONATION
Abstract-Résumé: Kidney failure is a serious health condition that affects more than 40,000 Canadians. The best treatment for kidney failure is a new kidney by transplantation. Unfortunately, patients with kidney failure often wait many years to receive a new kidney. Many patients die while they are waiting. Family and friends of patients who need a kidney often volunteer to donate one of their kidneys to their loved ones. Living kidney donation is now the major form of transplantation. Living kidney donation has few short-term risks; however, the long-term risks are uncertain. We are conducting a study to help understand these risks better. Since 2009, we have recruited 534 living kidney donors and 237 healthy non-donors from 12 transplant centres in Canada. We would like to follow this group of donors and non-donors for five more years to see if kidney donation increases a person's risk of getting high blood pressure. We will also collect blood and urine samples each year to test how well the kidney works. Finally, we will study the mental health and psychological outcomes of donors. This study will be the largest and most accurate study of its kind in the world. Information from this study will help potential kidney donors make informed decisions about becoming a living kidney donor. It will also help doctors care for living kidney donors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health and Social Impacts on the Family Following Fetal/Infant Death
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA BASE; BEREAVEMENT; CAUSAL INFERENCE WITH OBSERVATIONAL DATA; FETAL/INFANT DEATH; GRIEF; HEALTH CARE COSTS; HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTH SERVICES USE; MENTAL HEALTH; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The death of a baby pregnancy or the first year of life is frequently a life-transforming event for bereaved parents and families. Health and social care providers as well as society at large tend to underestimate the long-term impact that such a death can have on a family, often resulting in actions that are limited and possibly inappropriate. Evidence indicates that bereaved parents suffer from a range of physical, emotional, social, and financial concerns and is associated with heightened risk of mortality, particularly in the early weeks and months after the loss, and higher rates of hospitalization than among the non-bereaved, including psychiatric hospitalizations These serious negative sequelae can lead to decreased vibrancy and productivity, health and well-being for the bereaved as well as higher healthcare costs. There are no studies examining the impact of the death of a baby from a population health or health services use perspective in Canada. A better understanding of the risks and negative sequelae experienced by bereaved parents and families is needed to design effective interventions to mitigate them and to convince policy and decision makers of the need for action in this area. The purpose of this study is to determine, at a population health level, the mental health consequences, physical health consequences and social consequences for family members (parents and siblings) following fetal/infant death and their impact on health services utilization. Given the evidence for potential negative health impacts and the documented need for support, bereavement care must be integral to healthcare agendas and services. It requires a large system change through effective knowledge translation strategies, with key stakeholders across sectors and provinces.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Brain Fatty Acid-binding Protein in Malignant Glioma Progression
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN FATTY ACID-BINDING PROTEIN; CELL MIGRATION; MALIGNANT GLIOMA; PEROXISOME PROLIFERATOR-ACTIVATED RECEPTOR; POLYUNSATURATED FATTY ACIDS; RADIAL GLIA; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: The most common and deadly brain cancers in adults are called glioblastoma. Also referred to as malignant glioma or grade IV astrocytoma, these tumours originate in the brain and invade normal brain tissue, making treatment difficult. Patients diagnosed with these tumours usually die within two years in spite of being aggressively treated with a combination of surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy. Glioblastomas are difficult to treat because by the time the tumour is discovered, cells have already moved away from the main tumour mass. As a result, these cells can evade treatment centered on the main tumour mass. It is clear that new approaches are needed if we are to make a significant impact on disease outcome. A better understanding of the biology of glioblastoma and the cells from which these tumours are derived will provide important information on how to control the growth of brain tumours. In the brain, there are proteins that act as transporters of fatty acids. These fatty acid-binding proteins (B-FABP) are the focus of our study. We have previously discovered an association between B-FABP and the ability of tumour cells to spread within the brain. This observation has led us to propose that the growth and invasive properties of glioblastoma can be controlled through B-FABP. Our objectives are: (i) to investigate how B-FABP promotes cell spread in glioblastomas tumours, (ii) to identify ways of inhibiting cell spread in glioblastomas that express B-FABP, and (iii) to establish a live laboratory mouse model that will be used to examine how B-FABP, and the fatty acids that bind to B-FABP, can be manipulated to control tumour growth within the brain.

Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; GENETIC SCREENING; HUMAN GLOMERULAR DISEASE; PATIENT COHORT; PODOCYTE BIOLOGY; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS; TUMOR NECROSIS FACTOR ALPHA
Abstract-Résumé: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is in incurable progressive kidney disease that often necessitates kidney transplantation. This disease affects specialized kidney cells (podocytes) which normally work to prevent passage of proteins from blood into the urine. Unfortunately, in about one third of FSGS patients, FSGS recurs within hours of transplantation. This strongly suggests that the disease is caused by a toxic blood factor which damages podocytes. Patients with recurrent FSGS are destined for a life-long dialyses, and their lives are shortened dramatically.  We developed novel techniques to study the effects of patient's blood on podocytes. By applying these new methods, we discovered that the toxic blood factor activates TNF-alpha signaling pathway that drives pathogenesis of recurrent FSGS in some patients. In this project we will study the mechanism by which TNF-alpha affects podocytes. We will use a few approaches: 1) With the help of our colleagues from USA, Canada and France, we will amass a large collection of blood samples from the FSGS patients and will ascertain by using our novel functional and quantitative podocyte assays what proportion of FSGS cases may may be responsive to TNF-alpha blockade. 2) In the podocyte cultures, we will study the effects of TNF-alpha on cell adhesion and cell-cell contacts and other cellular and molecular mechanisms. 3) To test our hypothesis that inappropriate activation of TNF-alpha signalling in podocytes drives the disease, we will generate a transgenic mouse model to test whether a local podocyte expression of TNF-alpha will lead to the FSGS lesions. Our study is a strong example of a bench-to-bed scientific project and will have direct impact on the patients. Our results will facilitate development of novel treatment strategies for currently incurable form of FSGS and should allow us to use optimal strategy for individual patients in order to save their kidneys and improve their quality of life.

Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC BIOMARKERS; CARDIOLOGY; EMERGENCY MEDICINE; HEALTH SERVICES; RESOURCE UTILIZATION; TROPONIN
Abstract-Résumé: Identifying patients with heart attacks (MI) in the emergency department is challenging. One of the most important diagnostic tests for an MI is a blood test for cardiac troponin, a protein released into the bloodstream during an MI. Higher levels of troponin in the bloodstream are associated with a higher risk of death in patients with MI. A new troponin test, known as high-sensitivity troponin T (hs-TnT), has recently replaced older troponin tests in many Canadian hospitals. hs-TnT is much more sensitive than previous tests: It can detect much smaller levels of troponin in the blood. This means that MIs may be diagnosed earlier, doctors will miss fewer MIs, and patients with chest pain or breathing problems can have the diagnosis of a MI excluded faster than before.  The downside of this high sensitivity is that some patients with naturally high troponin levels may be misdiagnosed as having had an MI, and be subjected to risky additional tests without the prospect of benefit.  There is no agreementin the expert medical community as to how the hs-TnT tests ought to be used. There is insufficient scientific data to clearly identify what cutoff level provides the best diagnostic accuracy, minimizing both missed MIs and misdiagnosed MIs.  This research program has two objectives: First, we will identify what level of hs-TnT best identifies patients with chest pain who are at risk of short-term adverse outcomes (like death, MI or the need for emergency surgery or angioplasty) while minimizing misdiagnosis of patients with naturally high levels of troponin. This data will help doctors identify patients who need to be hospitalized for emergency cardiac testing. Second, we will identify what level of hs-TnT is associated with death among patients with chest pain. This information will help identify patients who require intensive monitoring during their hospital stay or additional testing to reduce their short- and long-term risk of death.

Abstract-Résumé: The prevalence of neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism spectrum disorders and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), has reached epidemic levels, affecting approximately 10% of school-age children. Children born to women with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) seem to have a substantially increased risk of these disorders compared to children born to healthy women. In a large population-based cohort using Quebec's administrative health data, we aim to determine if children born to women with SLE have an increased risk of autism spectrum disorders and ADHD compared to children born to women without SLE.

Abstract-Résumé: RNA interference is a controlling pathway in cells that uses small biological molecules called RNA to abrogate the production of proteins. The very recent discovery of this new process have rapidly contributed to better understand different aspects of biology as well as to bring realistic hopes for the development of new types of treatments to cure several human diseases as acknowledged by the Nobel committee in 2006. To use RNA interference has it full potential in laboratories and clinics, it is primordial to fully understand this new cellular pathway.  To achieve this, we propose in this project to study the proteins essential for this new process called Argonautes. The round worm as animal model will be put in contribution to decipher the functions of Argonaute proteins in cell.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating Factors Influencing Health Outcomes in Patients with Multimorbidity
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSTATISTICS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; MULTIPLE CHRONIC CONDITIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with multiple chronic conditions are common in the Canadian population (approximately 46% in those over the age of 65).  Furthermore, patients with multiple chronic conditions are more likely to die prematurely, be admitted to hospital, have poor quality of life, and experience a loss of physical functioning.  Research in this area is limited, so what represents best care for these patients is not known.  Therefore, we will quantify the impact of the presence of multiple chronic disease conditions in patients.    Using several large internationally well-recognized data sources with patient specific data (e.g., kidney function, cholesterol levels, blood pressure), we will address our research questions using typical health research methods. More specifically, our objective is to study the occurrence of multiple chronic conditions in the pneumonia population and the diabetes population as well as the impact of these multiple chronic conditions on unplanned healthcare encounters. My project has been created in collaboration with researchers, physicians, and policy makers.  Further collaboration will be undertaken to finalize the study design, as well as completion and distribution of results through various activities. I will be responsible for developing proposals and completing all aspects of this research.   Exploring this research questions will contribute to evidence leading to increased quality of life, improved quality of care, as well as decreasing the burden on the health care system in terms of cost and utilization for this complex population.

Keywords-MotsClés: CAMPUS FOOD BANK USE; CANADIAN COMMUNITY HEALTH SURVEY; EFFECTS OF HUNGER ON ACADEMICS; GENDER EFFECTS ON FOOD BANK USE; POST-SECONDARY STUDENT FOOD SECURITY; STRUCTURED SURVEYS
Abstract-Résumé: While food security has been well-studied among public school children and families of low socioeconomic status, its effects on post-secondary students have not been well-examined.  There have been some studies regarding the prevalence of food insecurity in post-secondary students, but little research has examined the food security, financial, psychological and physical health status of the students who use campus food banks.  In addition, there has been little investigation into gender differences with regards to food bank usage.  The study that is being proposed aims to examine the following factors among students who use the University of Alberta Campus Food Bank (CFB):  food security status; financial status; self-perceived mental and physical well-being; perceived effects of nutrition on academic success; and the relationship between gender and the aforementioned factors.  It is hypothesized that students using the CFB will have low food security, low financial status, and poor self-perceived well-being.  This study will elucidate how nutrition affects academics from the students' perspectives and if there is an association between food bank use and gender.  The data in the study will be collected from students who use the CFB, using structured surveys over a 12-month period.  After this period, the results will be analyzed with specific attention to patterns in the members' responses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Surgeon caseload and its association with breast conserving surgery and survival of early stage breast cancer patients in Alberta, Canada.
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST-CONSERVING SURGERY; CANCER HEALTH SERVICES; EARLY STAGE BREAST CANCER; MODIFIED RADICAL MASTECTOMY; POPULATION-BASED COHORT STUDY; SURGEON CASELOAD
Abstract-Résumé: Most women diagnosed with early stage breast cancer have the option of receiving either breast conserving surgery with radiation or modified radical mastectomy. Studies have shown that the rate of modified radical mastectomy is very high in Canada and Alberta, despite breast conserving surgery with radiation being a less invasive treatment with clinically proven survival rates comparable to that achieved by mastectomy. We will use a population-based cohort study design to investigate the relationships between the volume of breast cancer surgeries performed by individual surgeons, the type of surgery received, and survival rates of early stage breast cancer patients in Alberta from 2002-2010. Data sources include the Alberta Cancer Registry, physician billing, provincial hospital-based data (inpatient and outpatient), and the Canadian census. This study will generate information regarding the surgeon caseload-outcome relationship for early stage breast cancer patients and could be used to inform decision makers about how to best provide care for this population.

TitreApplicationTitle: ISTAR Clients' Experiences with, and Perceptions of, Psychological Counseling to Augment Stuttering Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIERS; CLIENT EXPERIENCES; COMMUNICATION DISORDERS; FACILITATORS; IMPACT OF STUTTERING; ISTAR; PSYCHOLOGICAL COUNSELING; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; STUTTERING; TREATMENT EFFECTIVENESS
Abstract-Résumé: Stuttering is a fluency disorder that can impact the overt speech, social interactions, perceptions, and life opportunities of individuals who are affected. Today, clinicians and researchers in the field of communication disorders are becoming increasingly aware that counseling is a critical component of stuttering therapy. However, no research in this field has been published to date on clients' experiences with psychological counseling as part of their stuttering treatment. In this project, I will carry out a qualitative research study, using a grounded theory framework, in order to learn about clients' experiences with, and perceptions of, psychological counseling services to accompany speech therapy for stuttering. Participants will be recruited from the Institute of Stuttering Treatment and Research (ISTAR)'s intensive stuttering treatment clinics in 2013. I will conduct semi-structured interviews with clients, and will invite them to share whether or not they chose to utilize the counseling service as part of their therapy. I will inquire as to some of the reasons why clients chose to access, or not to access, this service. Finally, I will ask clients if they perceive psychological counseling to be a helpful aspect of stuttering therapy, and if they can identify any ways in which this service could be improved. This study will reveal whether clients at ISTAR perceive counseling services to be beneficial, potential ways to improve counseling services, and perceived barriers and facilitators to accessing psychological services. Results of the current study will also lead to further research in order to explore counseling's contribution to speech therapy outcomes, ways to make counseling increasingly accessible for clients, and methods for improving and expanding counseling services in order to help clients cope with the social and psychological consequences of communication disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Qualitative Investigation of Facilitators and Barriers to Physical Activity Opportunities for Individuals with Disabilities in Rural Communities
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIERS; FACILITATORS; PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; RURAL COMMUNITIES
Abstract-Résumé: People with disabilities are at added risk of poor health because of barriers to physical activity. These barriers have been identified in past research. However, there is little information about the physical activity experiences of people with disabilities who live in rural communities. This project will specifically look at the experiences of people with disabilities in a rural community in Alberta, Canada. Through interviews with physical activity service providers and people with disabilities, information will be collected about this group's activity experiences and opportunities. The project will focus on identifying physical activity facilitators and barriers. Facilitators are understood to support taking part in physical activity. Barriers are thought to prevent participation in physical activity. By identifying what supports and prevents taking part in physical activity, this project may be able to provide direction to policy makers and service providers about how to improve access and programming for people with disabilities in rural communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Augmenting Functional Rewiring after Stroke with Chondroitinase ABC
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM IMAGING; CHONDROITINASE ABC TREATMENT; CORTICAL PLASTICITY AND RE-MAPPING; FUNCTIONAL RECOVERY AFTER STROKE; GROWTH INHIBITORY AND PERMISSIVE CUES; INTRINSIC OPTICAL SIGNAL IMAGING; ISCHEMIC STROKE; MULTI-PHOTON LASER SCANNING MICROSCOPY; PHOTOTHROMBOTIC STROKE; ROLE OF THE EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX IN STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: A stroke refers to brain damage that results from blocked blood flow in the brain. This damage often leads to deficits in speech, sensation, or movement for stroke survivors. Fortunately, adaptive changes take place where surviving brain tissue adopts the function of tissue damaged by stroke.  However, even with these changes stroke patients show only limited recovery from deficits even with rehabilitation therapy. Limited recovery may result from existing compounds in the brain that reduce the brain's ability to rewire. Treatments that can counteract these compounds may therefore increase the brain's ability to rewire and improve recovery after stroke. This project looks to see if injecting a compound called "Chondroitinase ABC" around the brain regions damaged by stroke can accelerate brain rewiring and recovery in a mouse model of stroke. If Chondroitinase ABC is able to do this, it may improve rehabilitation after stroke, perhaps even in patients for whom rehabilitation has not been effective.

TitreApplicationTitle: An examination of the relative contribution of GABA, 5-HT and NE towards neuropathic pain behaviours in male and female mice
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ANXIETY; COGNITIVE FUNCTION; GABA; INFLAMMATORY PAIN; MAO INHIBITOR; NEUROPATHIC PAIN; PAIN; SEROTONIN; SEX DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Although pain is a needed sensory experience to warn an individual of potential harm, pain can become a burden when not properly managed. This can happen with either acute pain (e.g. excessive pain after surgery), or with chronic pain conditions (e.g. chronic back pain). Chronic pain is also considered the most common health problem worldwide, with about one fourth of the population suffering from this condition. In addition to being a highly prevalent condition, chronic pain is a complex phenomenon with biological, psychological, and social components, meaning that how it works is still poorly understood. The proposed study will use different drugs to alter levels of neurotransmitters known to be involved in chronic neuropathic pain (persistent pain due to an injury to the nervous system) to try and better understand the mechanisms behind chronic pain. In addition, since it is known that chronic pain affects aspects of cognition like memory, attention, and anxiety in clinical patients, these factors will also be examined. It is the hope that studying the effects of both chronic and acute pain by manipulating different neurotransmitter level will help determine potential pathways for how pain and cognitive function interact. The proposed study will also focus on potential differences between male and female models of pain in all aspect of the research. Sex is an important factor to consider as significant sex differences in pain have been found with other animal models and in human laboratory research. For example, women have been found to experience a higher prevalence of most chronic pain conditions, suggesting that there may be underlying biological differences in pain between men and women. Overall, the proposed study hopes to gain a better understanding of pain and how it affects the daily function of individuals. It is also the hope that by using drugs to target potential pain pathways, future therapeutic targets will be discovered.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Physiology of P2X ATP Receptor Channels in Pain Pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALGESIA; ATP RECEPTOR CHANNELS; CHRONIC PAIN; MICROGLIA; RECEPTOR ANTAGONIST; SENSORY NEURONS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain affects as many as 1 in 5 people worldwide. Over the next two decades, as the population ages and modern medicine allows people to survive serious illness, the number of people affected by chronic pain is expected to rise to 1 in 3. Chronic pain can be debilitating, isolating, dehumanizing, and all too frequently, can turn deadly. Understanding the molecular basis of pain is key to the discovery of novel analgesics. Pain transducers are membrane proteins specifically sensitive to the danger signals heat, cold, chemical irritants or ATP. ATP receptors belonging to the P2X ion channel family have been shown to be involved in chronic pain in rodents and primates and they are candidate therapeutic targets for pain treatment without the negative side effects of morphine and pregabalin. P2X3 is expressed exclusively in the pain-sensing neurons located in spinal and trigeminal ganglia. P2X4 is upregulated in spinal microglia following nerve injury and P2X4 activation has been shown to contribute to neuropathy-associated pain hypersensitivity. We propose in this research program to investigate the function and integration of P2X3 and P2X4 receptors in sensory pathways, by understanding how other receptors talk to P2X receptors and by developing novel selective tools to probe P2X function. Our work will generate novel data to assess the potential of P2X receptors as valid targets for the pharmacological treatment of inflammatory and neuropathic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the function of ZBTB8A in adipogenesis and its requirement for normal metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOGENESIS; CHIP-SEQ; KNOCKOUT MICE; METABOLIC DYSFUNCTION; MOUSE MODELS OF DISEASE; OBESITY; RNA-SEQ; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is associated with an increased risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Although genetic predisposition contributes significantly to obesity, our knowledge of causative genes is far from complete.  We have discovered a novel protein with a structure suggesting that it controls the expression of many of genes. We found that down-regulation of ZBTB8A (named based on its structure) in mouse stem cells led to cell differentiation and an upregulation of genes that control fat cell differentiation and function. We therefore engineered mice to lack ZBTB8A. We found that mice lacking both copies of ZBTB8A became obese within 8 months and that mice lacking one copy of ZBTB8A had an intermediate level of weight and fat gain. We also found that these animals demonstrated many clinical features shared by individuals that are considered pre-diabetic. All of these experiments were performed in which that mice were fed standard (low fat) rodent food. We propose to thoroughly analyze the ZBTB8A mutant mice under specific dietary conditions including high fat and low fat diets. We also propose to analyze the molecular function of ZBTB8A in fat cells. Our findings that ZBTB8A mutant mice demonstrate dose-dependent abnormalities fat accumulation and metabolism that changes in ZBTB8A expression or function in the general population may genetically predispose individuals to obesity and type 2 diabetes. We expect that our work will be used in future studies to identify and test novel therapeutics designed to prevent or treat type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preventing falls on stairs: step geometry and the biomechanical risk factors in older adults with and without mobility impairment
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESSIBLE ENVIRONMENTS; AGING; BIOMECHANICS; BUILDING STANDARDS; ERGONOMICS; FALLS PREVENTION; MOBILITY; MOTION ANALYSIS; STAIR SAFETY; UNIVERSAL DESIGN
Abstract-Résumé: It must be acknowledged that research into falls has so far failed to reduce falls. Statistics show that fall-related injuries have remained persistently high over the past decades. In the case of stairs, particularly those found in homes, fall-related injuries are actually increasing. Older adults are at greatest risk as a fall frequently results in significant, disabling and fatal consequences. Many strategies have been proposed to address falls. However, changing environmental codes and practices may be the most effective and efficient way to have an impact on falls. It has been estimated that over half of falls on stairs each year are due to inconsistencies in stair geometry. However, there is little evidence on the relationship of stair design and precision of construction to user behaviour. This results in difficulty guiding safe stair design, improving stairway usability, and minimizing the risk of falls on stairs. This study will provide a comprehensive biomechanical analysis of stair ambulation with respect to aging and disability to understand how modifications in step geometry influence user behaviour and risk of falling when ambulating stairs. Importantly, the results of this research will be used to inform evidence to be presented to support changes in building codes. This empirical evidence is particularly crucial to the adoption of improvements to the Canada Building Code. Preventing falls through improved evidence-based design is of paramount importance to the health of Canadians and is an important component of the mandate to prevent disease and injury and promote overall health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intraspinal Neural Prosthesis for Restoring Function after Spinal Cord Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS OF WALKING; CONTROL ALGORITHMS; ELECTRICAL STIMULATION; HISTOLOGY; LOCOMOTION; MICROELECTRONICS; NEURAL PROSTHESIS; SPINAL CORD INJURY; SPINAL NETWORKS
Abstract-Résumé: We will develop and test a miniature implant that can electrically stimulate the spinal cord after paralysis so that standing and walking can be restored. The implant will be composed of very fine wires, smaller than the human hair that can be placed within the spinal cord in a region below the level of spinal cord injury. All wires will be implanted in a small area of the cord (only 3 cm long) known to contain neural circuits involved in controlling leg movements. In the past, we showed that when this technique was implanted in animals, minute levels of current were needed to produce powerful muscle contractions that could produce standing and walking. Now, we want to prepare this implant for human use. We want to understand how stable this implant can be when placed inside the spinal cord for long periods of time, and also whether the produced movements remain functional for long periods of time. Another thing we want to find out is where exactly, in the spinal cord of humans should the implant be placed so that the best standing and walking can be restored after paralysis. If this spinal micro-implant is found to be safe and capable of generating walking reliably, the results from this project could lead to the first trials of this technique in humans paralyzed because of a spinal cord injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Passive standing during the acute phase following a traumatic spinal cord injury: Does a high dose (> 5 hours/week) intervention attenuate declines in bone mineral density?
Keywords-MotsClés: DEXA; FORCE; IN-PATIENT REHABILITATION; OSTEOPOROSIS; PASSIVE STANDING; PREVENTION; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: A spinal cord injury is a traumatic life-altering event that causes paralysis and disability. Over 1,700 persons sustain an injury each year, and there are over 85,000 survivors of spinal cord injury living in Canada today.  There is currently no cure for a spinal cord injury, and treatment is likely decades away.  At the same time, spinal cord injury causes many health issues that arise soon after injury and continue throughout life. Every person paralyzed due to spinal cord injury will eventually develop osteoporosis, and with it, a much increased risk of bone fracture.  These osteoporotic fractures are referred to as fragility fractures because they happen without any known cause, while carrying out normal daily activities, or with very little force.  These fractures occur in up to 40% of those living with a spinal cord injury and cause loss of work, reduced quality of life and increased social and health care costs.  Able-bodied people can reduce their risk of osteoporosis by weight-bearing activities such as walking or running, but these options are not available to those living with spinal cord injury.  Therefore, we will test whether passive standing (in a supported standing frame), begun very early after injury, will reduce the rate of bone mineral loss, the clinical determinant of osteoporosis, occurring in the legs after injury.  A DEXA scanner will be used to measure the amount of bone mineral loss, and blood samples will be taken to measure markers of bone turnover.  Study participants will begin standing within 4 weeks of injury, and will stand for at least 5 hours per week for a 6-month period. DEXA scans will be administered at the beginning and end of the study, while blood samples with be collected at the beginning, middle, and end.  If this dose of standing reduces the rate of bone mineral density loss after spinal cord injury, we may be able to develop activity-based guidelines to reduce the risk of developing osteoporosis after spinal cord injury

TitreApplicationTitle: Establishing Accurate Phonetic Performance in Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; LANGUAGE LEARNING; PHONETIC PRONUNCIATION; REINFORCEMENT; SHAPING; VERBAL ATTEMPTS
Abstract-Résumé: The majority of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) have problems with language acquisition, particularly with accurate pronunciation. There is evidence to suggest that phonetics is one of the most challenging components of language learning.  Research has found that inaccurate phonetic performance is detrimental to the intelligibility of language. Therefore, ways to establish a more accurate phonetic performance would be greatly beneficial to this population. The effect of vocal shaping (i.e., rewarding vocal approximations to a target word) is well documented in the field of applied behaviour analysis. However, the few studies that focused on shaping with children with ASD relied on the therapist's ability to identify the similarity between vocal attempts and the target pronunciation. The present study will use purposely-developed software to increase the usability and effectiveness of vocal shaping procedures. Both normal adults (using second-language pronunciation as a proxy) and children with ASD will participate in the study. An initial treatment evaluation with normal adults will let us quickly test and fine-tune our procedure. In the evaluation with adults, English monolinguals will be presented with the native pronunciation of Icelandic words, and will be asked to reproduce it as accurately as they can. Participants will speak into a microphone and the software will compare the participants verbalization with the target native pronunciation. If the participant's response is more similar to the target pronunciation than the previous attempt, the response will be rewarded. In the case of repeated errors, the software will generate vocal prompts progressively similar to the target pronunciation. The procedure will continue until the target pronunciation is reached. The study will be replicated in children with ASD using English words. We expect that our shaping procedure will help children with ASD to acquire more accurate phonetic performance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Programming of bone development through early life exposure to soy isoflavones and folic acid
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICAL BONE STRENGTH; BODY COMPOSITION; BONE DEVELOPMENT; BONE MINERAL DENSITY; EARLY NUTRITION; FOLIC ACID; ISOFLAVONES; MICE; MUSCLE DEVELOPMENT; PROGRAMMING
Abstract-Résumé: Bone health of Canadians is worsening. With the aging population, it is estimated that one in two individuals in developed countries over the age of 50 will be at risk for fragility fractures from osteoporosis or low bone mass by 2020. There are no ideal treatments for osteoporosis. Prevention strategies that target the earliest stages of life provide an optimistic approach to reducing the risk of osteoporosis-related fragility fractures in adulthood. Using a well-established mouse model we have provided promising data that early life exposure to soy isoflavones, present in soy infant formula, and folic acid results in healthier and stronger bones at adulthood. This research follows from these previous findings, and will include analyses of muscle and fat tissues that can directly influence bone health through physical interaction (muscle) or secretion of chemicals that may influence bone health (muscle and fat tissue). Mice will be fed different levels of folic acid during pregnancy and lactation and their offspring will receive soy isoflavones, at levels that resemble the level of exposure to human infants fed soy formula, during the first days of life. Pups will be studied to young as well as later adulthood to understand if the intervention protects against deterioration of bone and muscle health during aging, and if these benefits are transferred to the next generation. We will measure a comprehensive set of indicators of bone health, as well as muscle and fat tissue as these tissues can influence bone development. These indicators include measures of whole bones and muscles, markers of metabolism in target tissues (bone, muscle and fat) and expression of genes that regulate these tissues. This research will identify long-lasting benefits of early life nutrition to bone and muscle health during aging and in the subsequent generation. Positive findings may help in developing nutritional guidelines that reduce the risk of osteoporosis-related fragility fracture.

TitreApplicationTitle: Estimating Health Service Utilization Associated with Multimorbidity: A Comparison of Self-Reported Health Service Utilization and Chronic Disease Status Data with Routinely Collected Administrative Health Care Utilization Data
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATABASE DATA; AGING; CHRONIC DISEASE; HEALTHCARE UTILIZATION; SELF-REPORTED QUESTIONNAIRE DATA
Abstract-Résumé: While much is known about the health care utilization associated with individual chronic conditions, less is known about health care utilization associated with multiple chronic conditions. At best, treating diseases in isolation is inefficient and can lead to duplication of care, however there is evidence that resulting fragmented and poorly coordinated treatment can be harmful for patients with multimorbidity. The problem is that Canadian health services research to date has used an overly simplistic approach to describing multimorbidity; little data is available on specific factors associated with, or modifying the relationship between, multimorbidity and health care utilization.  Attempts to study the impact of multimorbidity are complicated by the lack of consensus on how to define and measure the construct. As well, one must consolidate and interpret evidence from different data sources. Large health care utilization databases are also frequently used to study health service use and disease status. Prior methodologic studies have compared the agreement between health care utilization data from self-report and administrative sources but none have incorporated the concept of multimorbidity.  We propose to link individual-level data from Ontario residents 45 years and older participating in the Canadian Community Health Survey 2007/2008 with administrative databases to address the following objectives:  1) To compare the agreement between different sources of multimorbidity and health utilization data; 2) To examine the impact of using different definitions of multimorbidity, including specific constellations of chronic conditions,on estimates of health care utilization; and 3) To provide population-based evidence on how multimorbidity is associated with health care utilization and how this association is modified by other factors such as age, sex, and working status

TitreApplicationTitle: Cadherin switch: its regulation and downstream effects on cardiomyogenesis in mouse embryonic stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CA BINDING PROTEINS; DEVELOPMENT; ES CELLS; HEART DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The conversion of epithelia to mesenchyme (EMT) is essential for heart formation. The cadherin switch, ie, switch from expression of epithelial cell-cell adhesion protein, E-cadherin, to mesenchymal N-cadherin, is an integral part of EMT.  In ES cells, the cadherin switch occurs as cells exit from pluripotency and commit to a cell fate. Calreticulin (CRT) is a fetal cardiac gene: its expression is induced as cardiogenesis starts, peaks at the midpoint of it and is then repressed. CRT regulates activation of calcineurin (CaN), which controls translocation of a transcription factor, NFAT to the nucleus.  HYPOTHESIS: CRT and CaN control cardiogenesis by affecting the cadherin switch and ES cell community behaviour.  This occurs parallel to NFAT nuclear translocation and it is intra-nuclear NFAT that regulates cadherin-specific transcription factors.  The kinetics of E-to-N cadherin switch suggest a relationship between adhesion, expression of CRT, activation of CaN, nuclear translocation of NFAT and cardiomyogenesis. The cell surface properties affect cardiogenesis: hence we will first elucidate cell community behaviour of ES cells with manipulated CRT and CaN genes using microfluidics assays.  Inhibiting NFAT nuclear translocation induces a "super KO" phenotype in all ES cells, while expressing activated calcineurin induces a "super WT" phenotype. Using this system we will elucidate the mechanism of regulation of exit from pluripotency and subsequent progression of cardiomyogenesis from ES by CRT-CaN signalling. As we postulate that intranuclear NFAT regulates cadherins, we will next work out mechanisms of the inferred but so far undiscovered regulation of cadherin transcription factors by NFAT using EMSA and chromatin immunoprecipitation.   CRT is a modular protein, with a chaperoning and a Ca handling module, so by gain-of-function approach we will elucidate which of CRT's functional modules affects the cadherin switch and cardiac differentiation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Depression as a risk factor for type 2 diabetes: role of metabolic factors
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY STUDY; DEPRESSION; DIABETES; METABOLIC FACTORS; PROSPECTIVE STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: The relationship between depression and type 2 diabetes is of great interest since both conditions are major contributors to the global burden of disease. Metabolic factors, including obesity, high blood sugar, high blood pressure, high blood levels of triglycerides, and decreased high-density lipoprotein, are important risk factors for type 2 diabetes. It is likely that these metabolic factors are associated with depressive symptoms. Understanding the associations between depression, metabolic abnormalities and behavioral factors might lead to better intervention strategies in ways that would assist in preventing or delaying type 2 diabetes. Using a community sample of people aged 40 to 69 years, we plan to evaluate the interaction between depression and metabolic abnormalities on type 2 diabetes incidence. The main objectives are: a) to identify the association between depression with metabolic abnormalities and new diabetes diagnoses (5 years after baseline); b)to evaluate potential interactions between depression, metabolic abnormalities and behavioral diabetes risk factors (smoking, eating behavior, alcohol consumption, and physical activity) and their effect on new diabetes cases.   We will use recruit 2800 participants from the CARTaGENE study in Quebec, Canada. The CARTaGENE study is a general population-based public health survey of Quebec. Participants will be interviewed five years after baseline assessment.

TitreApplicationTitle: The cognitive structure of decisions under risk and uncertainty in Parkinson's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; NEURO-ECONOMICS; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; REWARD
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with Parkinson's disease are known to respond differently in situations that involve financial risk and reward (e.g. gambling). It is said that they tend to be risk-averse when off medication, and risk-seeking when taking certain medications, to the point where some patients become pathologic gamblers and incur devastating financial consequences for themselves and their families.  Current clinical tests can tell us if someone is risk-seeking or risk-averse, but do not tell us why they make decisions in a risk-prone or risk-avoiding manner. Decisions about money and risk are complex, and involve numerous cognitive operations. For example, a subject must determine how much they value the reward at stake, estimate the probability of obtaining that reward, determine how much to stake, and in certain situations determine how much value they are willing to sacrifice to take a chance on a choice where they have little or no information about the odds or the payoff.  We have created a battery of easy clinical tests that allow us to calculate each of these factors independent of the others:  probability estimation, magnitude estimation, impulsivity, and the valuation of ambiguity. Our goal is to apply these to patients with Parkinson's disease on medication and off medication, as well as Parkinson's patients with a history of a gambling disorder while on medication. By using such a comprehensive battery, we will establish which cognitive operations are anomalous in Parkinson's disease and altered by the medication, giving us insights on how dopamine alters behaviours and judgements related to reward. We will also assess whether these tests reveal any characteristics in patients off medication that determine which patients have a higher risk of developing problem gambling on medication.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of stable gene repression by the promyelocytic leukemia protein PML.
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA DAMAGE; E2F TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; GENE EXPRESSION; HETEROCHROMATIN; PML; PROTEOMICS; RETINOBLASTOMA PROTEIN; SENESCENCE; SUMOYLATION; TUMOR SUPPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer cells need to produce many cellular components for their aberrant cell division process. These components are made from instructions encoded in genes positively regulated by a family of proteins known as E2F. To stop cell growth E2Fs need to be inhibited and this process can be reversible or irreversible. The latter prevents cancer cell growth in the long term and it is of great interest to understand its detailed mechanisms so drugs can be designed. This proposal aims to identify several components of the mechanism that permanently blocks E2F-target genes including the retinoblastoma tumor suppressor protein, the promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML) and a small protein called SUMO, that we think acts as a glue keeping together stable repressor complexes on E2F genes. We will use innovative cell culture of primary cells, gene transfer with viral vectors, novel proteomic technologies and animals models to provide a new conceptual model on the mechanisms that stably turn off E2F-target genes expecting to generate reagents, biomarkers and potential drug targets for future work.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms underlying anxiety disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYGDALA; ANXIETY; ENDOCANNABINOID; LEARNING & MEMORY; POSTTRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER; PROTEIN TYROSINE PHOSPHATASE; STRESS; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Anxiety disorders affect 20% of the population worldwide. The brain has its own version of the drug found in marijuana (cannabis) and uses these endogenous cannabinoids to regulate neural activity and anxiety.  Several studies have shown that stress changes the endogenous cannabinoid signalling that leads to the development of anxiety.  By chance, we discovered that mice that lack a small protein in certain neurons of the brain become very anxious. We found that this protein inhibits the activity of a phosphatase that is important in control of endogenous cannabinoid signalling. The present application will seek to understand how the activity of this phosphatase is regulated by stress. We will determine how this phosphatase regulates endogenous cannabinoid signalling. The goal of these studies is to develop a new therapeutic strategy to treat anxiety by restoring the disrupted endogenous cannabinoid signalling caused by stress.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the mutations driving non Hodgkin lymphomas and developing plasma-based assays for tumour detection and monitoring
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; DRUG TARGETS; GENOMICS; NON HODGKIN LYMPHOMA; SEQUENCING; SOMATIC MUTATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Lymphomas are a diverse and complex collection of cancers that all arise from cells of our immune system. Some lymphomas are indolent, meaning they grow slowly and result in few symptoms, whereas others are aggressive and can lead to death in a short amount of time. It is well known that specific changes to the DNA in these cells ("mutations") contribute to the formation of these cancers. By understanding the way a cell changes to become a cancer, we can begin to determine how these cells might be efficiently destroyed and thus work towards more effective therapies. Follicular lymphoma (FL) and mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) are two lymphomas that are rarely cured. There is limited knowledge of the mutations that produce these illnesses. This study will use new approaches that can rapidly read ("sequence") the DNA to better understand how FL and MCL cancers arise. We will use similar techniques to compare the genetics of these two diseases to other lymphoma types. This information should allow us to learn how to better diagnose the different lymphoma types and thus better identify the most appropriate treatment for each patient. It has recently been observed that patients with cancer have a detectable signature in their blood from the tumour cells. This study will implement methods for detecting this signature in lymphoma patients, which may allow us to indirectly observe changes to the tumour. We will test whether these assays yield information about tumour growth and whether or not a cancer is responding to therapy. Such tests may ultimately provide clinicians with early indication of disease resistance or relapse, thus providing valuable time needed to alter treatments as necessary.

TitreApplicationTitle: SOCIAL JUSTICE and PET OWNERSHIP: A qualitative inquiry to improve population health and to advance public health ethics
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTHROPOLOGY; ANTHROZOOLOGY; HEALTH PROMOTION; HUMAN-ANIMAL STUDIES; IMPLEMENTATION SYSTEMS; POPULATION HEALTH; SOCIO-LEGAL STUDIES; URBAN STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal advances a research program on how well-being is generated and diminished in everyday life. Pets anchor our investigation of small differences to well-being that stand, through accumulation and ripple effects, to carry major consequences for health inequity. In this project, barriers to a positive experience of pet ownership among lower-income Canadians will serve as a prism for rethinking the nature of society, the basis for promoting population health, and the meaning of social justice. While previous health research on the benefits of pet ownership has focused mainly on measuring associations, our main concern is unevenness in the preconditions for a positive experience of pet ownership. By listening closely to low-income Canadians' stories about pet ownership in interviews, and by placing these stories into a broader scholarly, cultural, and political context, we will be re-examining the relationship between poverty and ill-health. We will also translate what we have learned into public debate, thereby improving public understanding of poor mental health, the role of social stressors in health outcomes, and health inequity. In terms of policy and practice, this project is relevant to animal welfare charities, poverty alleviation, housing, and human rights.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of STAT5b in the protection against diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE TRANSFER; CYTOKINES; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; JUVENILE TYPE 1 DIABETES; PATHOLOGY; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: In the past decade, childhood type 1 diabetes that is now generally referred as type 1 diabetes (T1D) has increased dramatically worldwide and has almost reached endemic proportions. However the mechanisms underlying diabetes onset remain poorly understood. Whereas basic and clinical research aim at understanding the causes that lead to diabetes, along with therapies to improve managing, are somewhat limited in human diabetic patients from several angles. Fortunately, animal models are available, and this is the case of the non-obese diabetic (NOD) mouse that has become invaluable for studies on diabetes. NOD mice spontaneously develop T1D, and many characteristics of diabetes in these mice mirror features of the chain of events that lead to development of diabetes in humans. Of significance, a large body of knowledge with respect to regulation of immune responses in NOD mice is known. Furthermore, NOD mice can be genetically modified to address specific immune aspects of diabetes. For instance, specialized cells called dendritic cells (DCs) act to dampen unwanted immune responses and promote a specialized white blood cell (named regulatory T cells: Treg) function in order to prevent diseases onset. Abnormal function of DCs has been reported to play a critical role in initiation and progression of type 1 diabetes. Many proteins influence the normal set-point of DCs. Recent research indicates that augmenting the function of a protein called Stat5b leads to increased numbers of beneficial specialized white blood cells (Treg) in mice. Our proposal seeks to determine if correcting Stat5b protein function expressed in DCs can suppress development of juvenile diabetes in a well-characterized NOD mouse model. If successful, this approach may spur the development of new therapies for patients suffering from childhood type 1 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The molecular mechanisms of exocytosis in mast cells
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY INFLAMMATION; ASTHMA; CONFOCAL AND ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; DEGRANULATION; KNOCKOUT MOUSE; LENTIVIRUS; MAST CELL; RBL-2H3 CELLS; RNA INTERFERENCE; TIRFM
Abstract-Résumé: Mast cells are types of immune cells that are responsible for quick immune responses upon invasion of pathogens to the body. They do so by releasing chemicals called immune mediators, which cause inflammations and recruitments of other members of immune systems, eventually leading to general protection of the body. However in disease state, the release by mast cells can be abnormally high, causing allergic reactions such as asthma in airway, and atopy in skins. Therefore, understanding regulations of the release from mast cells is critical in order to provide potential cures against these diseases. In our lab, we have focused on two proteins known as Munc18-2 and Munc13-4 as key regulators of the release from mast cell-line called RBL-2H3 cells. We have successfully generated cells that have low expressions of these two proteins and found the release became significantly decreased. Our future research will focus to narrow down mechanisms of the mast cell release by 1) taking detailed pictures of cells to see if locations of other release machineries are altered by low level of these proteins 2) re-introducing Munc18-2 or Munc13-4 to see if this can revert release ability back to normal 3) re-introducing Munc18-2 or Munc13-4 with mutations in certain parts of the protein to see which part of the protein is important for the function. Our approaches will provide not only insight as to basic knowledge of release mechanism from the mast cells but potential clinical solutions against allergic diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; VIEILLISSEMENT
TitreApplicationTitle: Maintenance of transcriptional networks in mature and aging neurons
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CIS REGULATORY MODULE; DIFFERENTIATION; GENE EXPRESSION; GENE MAINTENANCE; NEURODEGENERATION; NEURONAL IDENTITY; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR; TRITHORAX GROUP GENES; TRITHORAX RESPONSE ELEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: We examine how long-lived cells maintain their function for the lifetime of the organism. While relevant to many cell types, this question is particularly relevant in the nervous system. Neurons must function through life to maintain normal brain function and are mostly irreplaceable. The function of any neuron depends upon its unique repertoire of effector genes that mediates the functions of the neuron. The expression of any neuron's effector genes is initiated during development by transcription factors (TFs) expressed in that neuron. The conventional paradigm assumes that the stability of mature neurons is a default state that is disrupted only by trauma or overt pathology. However, our recent work shows that the TFs initiated during development must persist to maintain effector gene expression throughout life. Thus, a neuron's gene expression profile is not locked in to a static state, but is instructively maintained by an active, dynamic process of persistent gene activation. We propose that these dynamic, instructive processes that are required to maintain mature neuronal function represents an Achilles heal that makes mature neurons vulnerable to degeneration. Genetic evidence supporting our proposal is provided by findings that degradation of TF function in aging neurons can lead to age-related neurodegeneration, such as Parkinson's disease. In this proposal we examine the mechanisms that actively maintain TF networks in mature neurons. These studies will be the first to define the mechanisms that maintain the integrity of transcriptional networks in mature neurons and will be the first to test a novel hypothesis for why the aging brain becomes vulnerable to degeneration. By defining these dynamic instructive mechanisms, we will provide a novel paradigm for identifying the causes, and providing therapeutic avenues, for age related degeneration of the nervous system.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulatory macrophages in islet inflammation and type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; INFLAMMATION; INSULIN; ISLETS OF LANGERHANS; MACROPHAGES; PANCREATIC BETA CELL
Abstract-Résumé: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a global epidemic and an economic burden that affects more than 3 million Canadians. T2D results from malfunction of, damage, or loss of insulin-producing cells of the pancreas, called beta cells. My research focuses on how inflammation causes beta cell malfunction and loss.    The main player contributing to islet inflammation in T2D is an immune cell called the macrophage. Macrophages play both detrimental and beneficial roles. I propose to convert the detrimental macrophages found in islets of those with T2D, into beneficial healing and tissue-regenerating macrophages. Our research will facilitate this using 3 distinct approaches. First, we will make regenerative macrophages in a dish and ensure that they improve beta cell survival and function. We will then transfer these macrophages into a mouse and test whether they protect from inflammation and chemically-induced diabetes. In a second set of studies we will determine what substances beneficial macrophages produce to stimulate beta cell regeneration in a mouse. This will inform the future translation of these studies towards people with T2D. Finally, we will make regenerative macrophages in a dish using bone marrow from rodents with type 2 diabetes, and transfer them into these same rodents with type 2 diabetes to reduce inflammation and help regenerate beta cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Integrated In Vivo Multiphoton Microscopy and Confocal Raman Spectroscopy for Skin Cancer Detection and Evaluation
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHOTONICS; CONFOCAL RAMAN SPECTROSCOPY; LASER SPECTROSCOPY; MELANOMA/ SKIN CANCER DETECTION; MULTIPHOTON MICROSCOPY; NON-INVASIVE DIAGNOSIS; REFLECTANCE CONFOCAL IMAGING; SECOND HARMONIC GENERATION IMAGING; SKIN CANCER MARGIN DELINEATION; TWO PHOTON FLUORESCENCE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Currently definitive diagnosis of skin cancer requires assessment of biopsied tissue, which in turn necessitates an invasive procedure that results scarring and significant costs to the medical system. During skin cancer treatment, visual assessment is also relied upon to determine the extent of the tumor, and therefore the amount of tissue to be either excised or irradiated. It is clear that all stages in the management of skin cancer would be facilitated by techniques that could provide accurate diagnostic information without multiple expensive and disfiguring skin biopsies. Our first project goal is to develop video rate non-invasive high resolution microscopy modalities for practically acquiring skin images in vivo with quality approaching that of histology images from biopsied tissue samples. Our second goal is to combine high resolution in vivo skin imaging with targeting biochemical analysis of identified skin microstructures to create a most powerful non-invasive diagnostic tool for skin cancer detection and evaluation. Successful development of the proposed device will substantially improve the quality of life for patients with suspected and proven skin cancer by minimizing unnecessary diagnostic surgical biopsies and facilitating definitive skin cancer treatment at early curable stages.

TitreApplicationTitle: Estimating longitudinal healthcare costs for infectious diseases using administrative data
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; COST OF CARE; COST OF ILLNESS; ECONOMIC BURDEN OF ILLNESS; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTH SERVICES; INFECTIOUS DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: Over the past decade, infectious diseases have regained prominence in Canada and other jurisdictions, with outbreaks of Escherichia coli O157:H7, West Nile virus, severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and pandemic H1N1 influenza. The Ontario Burden of Infectious Disease Study (ONBOIDS) was the first comprehensive study to provide a current assessment of the mortality and morbidity of infectious disease in Canada, reporting over 7 million infectious disease episodes and nearly 4,900 deaths from infectious diseases annually in Ontario. While this study provides important estimates of infectious disease burden in terms of health outcomes, it does not evaluate the economic burden, which is an important component needed for priority setting in the healthcare system. This study will establish an overall framework and processes to estimate healthcare costs related to infectious diseases and apply the methods to three important pathogens (C. difficile, S. pneumoniae, and Hepatitis B Virus) to estimate healthcare costs for these pathogens in Ontario. All three pathogens were among the 10 most burdensome pathogens identified in ONBOIDS.  The framework will allow researchers to apply the methods to other infectious disease agents, so that a comprehensive and comparable reference set of infectious disease costs can be developed. Such information is an invaluable resource for Ministries of Health and public health agencies across the country to understand how much money is spent on infectious diseases caused by individual pathogens, and where the major burden lies (acute disease, chronic disease related to infection). Cost estimates will also be useful for policy makers to plan for future healthcare budgets, and for researchers to conduct future cost-effectiveness analyses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reversible inhibitors of the N-terminal domain of the androgen receptor
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN RECEPTOR; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; NATURAL COMPOUNDS; PROSTATE CANCER; XENOGRAFTS
Abstract-Résumé: Castration is the current treatment for advanced prostate cancer that involves the reduction of the patients' levels of testosterone (androgen). Unfortunately, castration therapies are not curative and eventually the disease will return in a form that is resistant to reduced levels of testosterone (called castration resistant disease). Two new reasons identified for castration resistance are: 1) synthesis of androgens directly by the tumor, and 2) generation of androgen receptor splice variants that act without needing androgens to activate the receptor.  Thus, even though levels of androgen are decreased in the blood of castrated patients, the tumor still activates its androgen receptor by either synthesis of androgen by the tumor, or by making androgen receptor splice variants that work without androgen. Once the disease is castration resistant, the survival time is approximately two years before the patient will succumb to his disease. Currently no therapies increase survival by more than a few months for patients with castration resistant disease.  To develop new therapies, a target must be known to create drugs that will bind to it. A drug that binds to the N-terminal domain of the androgen receptor would block both above mechanisms of resistance to current therapies. No current therapies target the N-terminal domain. Hence, we propose to identify small molecules (drugs) that bind to this target and test their feasibility for clinical development for the treatment of patients with advanced prostate cancer. We envision that upon conclusion of these studies, we will have identified important small molecules that can be used to develop new drugs that will delay or prevent lethal prostate cancer. Once a small molecule is found, usually it takes about 4-5 years to get into clinical trials depending on the ease of selection of a clinical candidate. This means that this proposed research has potential to impact the disease in a relatively short period of time.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lower GBP1 expression reduces human host defense against Listeria monocytogenes
Keywords-MotsClés: GBP; INNATE IMMUNITY; LISTERIA; NEONATE
Abstract-Résumé: Infections cause severe illness and death in newborn babies much more commonly than in adults. One of these infections is caused by a bacterium called Listeria monocytogenes (Listeria). The reason for this increased risk of newborns to suffer and die from Listeria is only partially understood. In our ongoing work aimed at finding out why newborn babies are at such high risk, we looked at 40,000 possible differences between the responses of newborns vs. adults to Listeria infection. We found that infected newborn cells made much less than the adult of one particular protein called guanylate binding protein 1, or GBP1. In adult mice this protein is known to be essential for protection from infection with Listeria, suggesting our finding with human newborn cells might be very important. The role of this and similar GBP proteins for protection from infection has never been studied at all in human newborns. We found that the level of GBP1 produced closely mimics how well the human cells infected with Listeria do, i.e. if there is more GBP1 they kill the bacteria better and resist the attack, but if there is less GBP1, they succumb to infection with Listeria and die. In this proposal we will determine the precise role played by GBP1 in protection vs. susceptibility of human cells to severe infection with Listeria. We will also identify the reason why the newborn makes less GBP1, as the first step toward finding ways to increase production of GBP1 and protect newborns better. Given the central role this type of protein is known to have for protection of mice against from other infections that are known to cause severe infection in human newborns, what we will find out will possibly be important for many of these newborn infections as well.

ClasseRechercheFR: ASTHME; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulatory dendritic cell induction of immune tolerance
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA/ALLERGY; DENDRITIC CELLS; REGULATORY T CELLS; TOLERANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma affects about 300M people globally and kills about 250,000 annually. In Canada, it affects 10-20% of us, is our primary cause of pediatric emergency visits, and it costs approximately $500-600M/yr. It is defined as reversible lung tightening and inflammation caused by exposure to things like pollen.  Its main treatments are anti-inflammatory drugs and bronchodilators, but these just treat the symptoms and do not address it real causes: errant immune responses. Healthy people are equally exposed to these same pollens, etc, but instead mount tolerant immune responses. What we need are treatments to switch off the bad immune cells, replacing them with good cells, so that the affected individual responds to pollens, etc just like healthy people.  We have discovered a cell within the body that can turn off bad immune responses, and we have shown that it works to reverse asthma in mice, and in the test tube with asthmatic people.  We will determine how these cells work, if there are better cells, and if they will work with people.  These treatments have the potential to provide a new generation treatment to cure asthma, not simply manage its symptoms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Linking laboratory and administrative data to study influenza and influenza vaccine epidemiology
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE; HEALTH ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; INFLUENZA; INFLUENZA VACCINES; LABORATORY DATA; LINKED DATABASES; SELF-CONTROLLED CASE SERIES; TEST-NEGATIVE CASE-CONTROL STUDY; VACCINE EFFECTIVENESS
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza (the flu) makes a lot of people sick each year. Young children, the elderly, and those with chronic illnesses are among the high-risk groups that are more likely to be hospitalized or die from influenza. There is also growing evidence that influenza may trigger heart attacks and strokes. However, past studies were not able to identify influenza as the specific cause of these events. Therefore, the first objective of this proposed research is to see if influenza infections that are confirmed by lab tests are related to heart attacks and strokes. We will do this by linking data from the Public Health Ontario Laboratories and several large hospitals in Ontario to health care records. We will then use statistical tests to see if people are more likely to have a heart attack or stroke shortly after having influenza (confirmed by lab testing), compared to other times. Getting a flu shot each year is the most effective way to prevent influenza infection, but we are not sure how well influenza vaccines actually work, especially for high-risk groups. The second objective of this proposed research is to use the linked data to study how well influenza vaccines work to protect these groups of people from being hospitalized or dying from influenza.  We will do this by looking at people who tested positive influenza and those that who tested negative for influenza and see how many in each group received the vaccine. These two related studies will greatly increase our understanding of how harmful influenza infections can be and how well influenza vaccines work.

TitreApplicationTitle: An Experimental Investigation of the Effects of Concrete Thinking on Worry, Problem-Solving and Cognitive Processing in Individuals with Generalized Anxiety Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ABSTRACT PROCESSING; COGNITIVE BIASES; COGNITIVE TRAINING; CONCRETENESS TRAINING; EXPERIENCE SAMPLING; EXPERIMENT; GENERALIZED ANXIETY DISORDER; PROBLEM-SOLVING; WORRY
Abstract-Résumé: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) is characterized by excessive and uncontrollable worry and anxiety, as well as irritability, physical tension, and difficulties concentrating and sleeping. GAD can make it challenging to function well at work, at school and in relationships. GAD is one of the most common anxiety disorders and is also one of the most challenging to treat. There is a pressing need to develop innovative interventions that better target factors that underpin problematic worry. Our research shows that people who experience difficulty managing their worry tend to think about problems in an abstract manner. When asked to describe how they would go about solving a hypothetical conflict involving a close other or a boss, the solutions tend to be vague, undefined and ineffective. Thinking about problems or feared situations in vague terms can interfere with problem-solving, can make it difficult to pay attention and reason, and can trigger worry and negative emotions. We will examine the effects of training a more concrete thinking style on worry, problem-solving quality, mental flexibility and negative emotions in people with GAD. We expect that with repeated practice, concreteness training can be of benefit. Adults with GAD will be allocated at random to 7 days of concreteness training, or to one of two other conditions that will help us determine that positive effects we observe with concreteness training can in fact be attributed to this training. Participants will complete assessments at Ryerson on 5 occasions, which will allow us to test the durability of training. Using an electronic diary, participants will also be asked to keep track of their thoughts, worry, and negative emotions for 7 days, which will provide us with another way to check that we have designed our concreteness training to effectively target factors in problematic worry. Our longer-range plan is to develop and test a full-scale, cost-effective concreteness treatment for GAD.
