TitreApplicationTitle: Migrant Friendly Maternity Care (MFMC) in Montreal
Keywords-MotsClés: EMERGENCY CAESAREAN BIRTH; HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH SERVICES; INTERNATIONAL MIGRANT WOMEN; MATERNITY CARE; PERINATAL HEALTH; WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: Half of all births in Montreal are to international migrant women and migrant women are responsible for over one-fifth of all Canadian births. Some migrant women are more likely to experience adverse health outcomes associated with giving birth, while being less likely to experience others. These risks are often not explained by biomedical factors and so, the role of care provided to migrant women during pregnancy, labour, birth, and afterwards comes into question. The international community has identified migrant health and care provision as a priority. Hence, we seek to know to what extent migrant-sensitive maternity care (for example, communication facilitation) is currently being provided to international migrant women who arrived in Canada less than 5 years ago and are giving birth in Montreal. We would also like to identify which factors facilitate or impinge this care from being given and further, what about this care has the greatest impact on unplanned caesarean births. We will carry out three studies within this project in the four hospitals in Montreal with the greatest number of births to international migrant women with non-English or French (i.e., 'allophone') maternal languages. First, all allophone women in Canada < 5 years, and from non-Western countries (about 2400) will be recruited in the order they give birth, their health records reviewed, and they will be asked questions about the maternity care they received and their perceptions of that care. Second, we will interview hospital staff, review policies and procedures, and observe how things function in each hospital. Third, a sub-group of women from the first study who had a caesarean birth during labour will be compared to women who had vaginal births. The results of this project will be used to improve maternity care provided to migrant women in Montreal, and elsewhere, through our partnerships with health professional associations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding patients' disease experience:  A guide to disease management in IBD
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; SURVEY STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), which includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, results in cycles of bowel inflammation, pain, diarrhea, and bleeding.  There are nearly one quarter million Canadians with these diseases, which affect people of all ages, but are especially common in young people.  IBD can impact all aspects of daily life, including work, relationships, energy and psychological health.  Our Centre has become an international leader for studying outcomes in persons with IBD, with a view to improving disease management and quality of life. The Manitoba IBD Cohort Study started in 2002. Participants have provided information to the study team every six months for almost ten years, through annual interview, blood samples, and mailed surveys.  We have recently initiated an Inception Cohort Study to follow persons with recently diagnosed disease. We  have extensive knowledge about the disease course and psychological profiles from participants in these cohorts. We will enroll participants from these cohorts into new substudies with the aim to help researchers understand the disease course, disease management issues,quality of life issues and coping approaches from the patient perspective. In one substudy we will carry out in depth interviews with participants to understand their experiences of coping with this challenging health problem over more than ten years.  In a second substudy we will track patients every 2 weeks for 1 year through computer based surveys so that we can understand their symptom experience prospectively and understand what patients view as a flare of disease. We will correlate their self-reported flares with a stool test that can measure a marker of active intestinal inflammation. The information from these studies and from other substudies of the Manitoba IBD Cohort Study will be used, in turn, to develop patient and family-centred education materials to support people in self-management of this chronic health condition

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; THERAPIE DU CANCER DU POUMON
TitreApplicationTitle: Drug resistance driven by SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers in lung cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG RESISTANCE; FUNCTIONAL GENETIC SCREENS; NSCLC; SWI/SNF CHROMATIN REMODELERS; TARGETED CANCER THERAPY; TYROSINE KINASE INHIBITORS
Abstract-Résumé: Clinical trials with targeted cancer therapeutics have demonstrated that the benefit of these agents is frequently limited to small groups of patients. Moreover, this benefit is often limited, due to the rapid development of resistance to drug actions. Thus, we need new biomarkers that can stratify patients who will respond to the therapy and ways to anticipate common resistance mechanisms. Understanding resistance mechanisms will help to optimize treatment options for patients to overcome drug resistance.   In this proposal, we will uncover the molecular pathways that confer resistance to targeted cancer therapies, using unbiased genetic tools that allow us to manipulate the expression of many different genes in cancer cells. We will focus on mechanisms of drug resistance to several current inhibitors, which are currently used to treat many cancers including several subtypes of lung cancer. Candidate genes involved in the development of resistance will be investigated in a variety of model systems, including cell culture and mouse models of cancer, to identify the mechanisms by which they drive resistance. The expression of these candidate molecules will be examined in tumor samples of cancer patients to determine whether they are predictive of clinical response. Finally, our study will also provide potential treatment strategies to overcome drug resistance and result in clinical benefit for cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Coordinating DNA deamination, double strand break and repair to prevent genomic instability during antibody gene diversification.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVATION INDUCED DEAMINASE; CHROMOSOMAL TRANSLOCATIONS; CLASS SWITCH RECOMBINATION; DNA DOUBLE STRAND BREAKS; GENOMIC INSTABILITY; NON-HOMOLOGOUS END JOINING; SOMATIC HYPERMUTATION; URACIL DNA GLYCOSYLASE
Abstract-Résumé: Antibodies can recognize and eliminate any pathogen or toxin. Since pathogens are virtually infinite, antibodies need to adapt. To do this, almost every B lymphocyte modifies the genes that encode its antibody in two regions. One is the region that binds to the antigen. The other is the region that interacts with additional components of the immune system. Both modifications are fundamental for the immune response and are initiated by the enzyme named AID. AID shapes the antibody genes by making a lesion. The imprecise repair of this lesion by genome maintenance pathways is what changes the antibody genes. This is exactly the same way in which cancer starts and therefore this is a dangerous process and must be strictly regulated to minimize the risk of collateral damage. We study the coordination between AID and the mechanisms of repair. There are many repair pathways. Some make no mistakes; hence they cannot help the immune response. Others would make too much damage and increase the risk of cancer or immunodeficiency. We are studying how the initiation of damage by AID and the subsequent repair are synchronized, most likely by AID. This is a fundamental mechanism that can explain the basis of lymphomas and other cancers that are linked to AID activity, as well as immune diseases arising from too much or too little antibody gene diversification.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of Molecular Subtypes of Preeclampsia
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CLASSIFICATION; GENE EXPRESSION; HYPERTENSION; IUGR; MICROARRAY; PLACENTA; PREECLAMPSIA; PREGNANCY; VALIDATION
Abstract-Résumé: The placenta is a vital organ of pregnancy, controlling maternal physiology and providing nutrients and oxygen to the fetus. When placenta development or function is compromised, poor maternal and fetal health outcomes follow. This situation occurs in 3-5% of all pregnancies, leading to potentially life-threatening maternal complications of hypertension and kidney dysfunction known as preeclampsia. There is no cure for this disorder. It is of tremendous importance to obtain a clear understanding of the pathological processes taking place in the placenta in order to generate effective treatments. Part of the difficulty in identifying and treating this disorder is the fact that preeclampsia can come in many different forms, with differences in: the time of onset of the disorder; the effect on fetal growth and health; and the effect on long term health complications in the mother. When a woman is diagnosed with preeclampsia we cannot tell what kind of preeclampsia she will have and therefore cannot predict what types of treatment will be effective in protecting the health of her and her unborn baby. The purpose of this study is to be able to specifically identify different subtypes of preeclampsia. We plan to take an approach that has proven to be effective in identifying and treating specific types cancers. To do this we will examine the placentae of almost 200 women with all types of preeclampsia, and screen for differences in gene expression. We speculate that differences in some genes will be specific to the different kinds of preeclampsia. These differences will provide clues as to the diverse processes within the placenta that are directly involved in promoting the different preeclampsia subtypes. Further, these genes and the proteins they make can be used as markers to help identify what type of preeclampsia a woman has and hopefully allow for tailored therapeutic treatments which will ultimately improve pregnancy outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and epigenetic control of cell physiology and metabolism during development
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; APOPTOSIS; AUTOPHAGY; CANCER; ENDOG; EPIGENETICS; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; NON-CODING TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; NUCLEUS
Abstract-Résumé: Regulated changes in cellular function underlie normal development in humans and in other organisms, and defects in these functions cause disease. For example, the biochemical mechanisms employed by proliferating cells to utilize essential nutrients (termed metabolism) contrasts with those used by non-dividing cells, and mis-regulation of metabolism causes cancerous cell growth. Moreover, the distinctive compartments that cells possess, called organelles, execute dramatic and stereotypical morphological transitions critical to human development and health. Model organisms have been utilized in the laboratory to investigate the molecular mechanisms controlling these and many other examples of cell physiology with great success. Recent work from my laboratory has described fundamental new aspects of the lifecycle of the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a powerful and widely exploited model organism. Both of these discoveries concern the gametogenesis phase of the yeast lifecycle, more commonly known as sporulation. Sporulation is a developmental program during which yeast, a single-celled microbe, exits the growth phase and produces dramatically remodeled and specialized cells called spores, which are analogous to gametes (sperm or egg) in humans. In addition to providing new insights into developmental programs employed by this widely studied model organism, the discovery of these phenomena expands the relevance of yeast to the understanding of the molecular and evolutionary underpinnings of human health and disease. Indeed, we have successfully extended some of our findings to test fundamental ideas concerning cancer using human cancer cells. Specifically, our findings illuminate unexpected and important conservation of mechanisms that govern metabolic reprogramming in human cancer cells and in yeast, highlighting yeast as a powerful model for further exploration of these mechanisms.

TitreApplicationTitle: PAX6 gene therapy rescue of mouse small eye
Keywords-MotsClés: AAV2/9; ANIRIDIA; GENE THERAPY; PAX6
Abstract-Résumé: While some illnesses, such as tuberculosis, are caused by a bacterial infection, others are inherited genetically and are caused by defects in our genes. Bacterial infections can be cured, usually by killing the bacteria that causes them, but no such cure exists for most genetic diseases. Instead, sometimes a special diet or particular medicine can reduce the symptoms, but the person lives with the disease for their entire life. One such disease is aniridia, which hinders eye development in the people affected by it, leaving them with poor vision from birth and blinding them by their mid-20s. Currently there are several treatments that help alleviate some of the symptoms of aniridia, but none of them can save the vision of a person with this disease. Gene therapy is a promising approach that attempts to cure these previously incurable diseases by providing functioning copies of the defective gene to the cells that need them. In Europe and in the United States, there have been breakthrough successes that have demonstrated the efficacy of the gene therapy approach. In most of these cases, the initial research began by testing the therapy in a mouse model, and we propose to do the same as we start developing a gene therapy for aniridia. Already a gene that causes 80% of the cases of aniridia in humans, PAX6, is known. Our research will involve testing how different viruses deliver PAX6 to any already established mouse model of aniridia. We will also explore how we can adjust the gene so that it is expressed in the right tissues and at the right levels to cure the disease in mice. Taking these first initial steps in mice will allow us to work out all of the necessary details needed before advancing towards a gene therapy in humans. By starting this project, we are working towards a gene therapy cure for aniridia in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and Characterization of Novel Type VI Secretion Effectors
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL FITNESS COMPETITION ASSAYS; BACTERIAL PATHOGENESIS; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MICROBIAL INFECTIONS; PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA; TOXIN SECRETION; TYPE VI SECRETION; VIRULENCE FACTORS; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a bacterial pathogen that is the leading cause of mortality among cystic fibrosis (CF) patients. Early in their lives, the lungs of CF patients are colonized by many different species of bacteria but in almost all instances, infection by P. aeruginosa predominates as the infection persists. Many strains of P. aeruginosa are resistant to multiple antibiotics resulting in its designation as a so-called 'super bug'. In 2000, the Center for Disease Control estimated that antibiotic resistant infections cost the United States healthcare system over $20 billion a year; by extrapolation, that indicates that they cost the Canadian system more $2 billion per year. One strategy for developing antibiotic drugs is to target the cellular processes in the bacterium that it uses to infect humans rather than the viability of the bacterium itself. The idea behind this proposal is that by targeting non-essential processes, the pressure to select for antibiotic resistance will be reduced. More specifically, my proposed research concerns the type VI secretion system (T6SS) of P. aeruginosa.  The T6SS is a molecular machine capable of killing other species of bacteria as well as the cells of the human host. In P. aeruginosa, this machine gives a competitive advantage to the bacterium during infection when it is competing with other bacteria for the nutrient rich tissue of the patient. P. aeruginosa strains which are missing a T6SS are at a significant competitive disadvantage in a laboratory model of human lung infection. My proposed research is aimed at better understanding the structure and function of the T6SS system, which in the future should facilitate the development of novel drugs that target this pathway and prevent P. aeruginosa from colonizing the lungs of CF patients while at the same time minimizing the emergence of antibiotic resistance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining executive functions as mediators of a mental and social enrichment intervention for older adults with chronic stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE AND SOCIAL ENRICHMENT; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; GERIATRICS; MEDIATION; STROKE REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Significant proportions of stroke survivors suffer long-term physical disability and are predisposed to sedentary lifestyles. This limits their performance of activities necessary for independent living in the community and contributes to increased risk for recurrent stroke and heart disease. Intervention strategies are needed to motivate stroke survivors to engage in routine physical activity and to optimize their physical and motor functions. One promising strategy targets executive functions (EFs) by engaging stroke survivors in complex mental and social activities. Broadly speaking, EFs refer to the cognitive processes that allow for adaptive behavior and self-control. The current study will evaluate the importance of improving EFs within the context of a mental and social enrichment intervention in order to have a meaningful impact on physical and motor functions, the ability to perform daily activities, and routine engagement in physical activity. The information garnered from this study will be crucial for improving stroke rehabilitation for older Canadians who suffer chronic disability from stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting future problems following mild traumatic brain injury: the role of neuroinflammation and tau accumulation
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKAEMIA; CANCER; CHEMOTHERAPY; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; LEUKAEMIA; NEUROIMAGING; NEUROPATHY; PEDIATRICS; VINCRISTINE; WHITE MATTER
Abstract-Résumé: Advances in multimodal management, including chemotherapy, in pediatric oncology patients has increased survival rates to over 80%. Children diagnosed with leukaemia often receive vincristine, a chemotherapeutic agent, during their treatment. Despite vincristine's efficacy, it is a documented neurotoxin resulting in nerve damage with consequences for sensory and motor function.  Recent studies in children with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) have shown that in addition to nerve damage, there is evidence of damage to white matter in the brain following treatment. However, children with ALL also receive the drug methotrexate which is known to cause leukoencephalopathy. Currently, no publications examine the effect of vincristine alone on white matter and how this relates to motor and sensory performance. In children, whose brains are still developing, damage may have long-term impact on balance and coordination, and may negatively impact quality of life (QOL). This pilot project will evaluate the impact of vincristine on white matter integrity in the brain through diffusion tensor imaging, an advanced MRI technique.  If the pilot results suggest children with vincristine neuropathy show changes in white matter integrity that are associated with impairments in sensory-motor function, it will be the first study to demonstrate this association.  Positive findings from this study will form the basis of an operating grant application submitted to CIHR by N. Virji-Babul, A. Rankin, R. Rassekh and J. Hukin, that aims to 1. evaluate long-term impact of vincristine on sensory-motor function and white matter integrity 2. identify genetic risk factors for developing neuropathy and 3. evaluate effectiveness of physical therapy interventions to minimize the effects of neuropathy.  As prognosis improves in childhood cancers, understanding chemotherapy-induced changes in the brain will help develop more appropriate therapeutics with fewer side effects and improve QOL.

TitreApplicationTitle: Catheter and seed delivery and localization using mechatronic applicator device and 3D-ultrasound imaging for whole-organ and focal prostate cancer brachytherapy.
Keywords-MotsClés: 3D ULTRASOUND; AUTOMATIC SEGMENTATION; BRACHYTHERAPY; FOCAL THERAPY; MECHATRONIC TRACKING; PROSTATE CANCER; SEED LOCALIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Background- Prostate cancer will affect 1 in 7 Canadian men at some point in their lives. Brachytherapy is a treatment option that involves irradiating the entire prostate by inserting radioactive seeds into the organ through the perineum. The success of treatments depends largely on seed positioning accuracy to achieve uniform coverage of the prostate while avoiding overdosing nearby organs. A template and 2D ultrasound are standardly used to position catheters for seed delivery. After catheters have been inserted, a hand-held applicator may be used to insert seeds permanently at regular intervals.  Hypothesis- Incorporating 3D ultrasound and mechatronic applicator positioning into the brachytherapy workflow will increase treatment accuracy while maintaining efficiency and will enable new focal therapies that decrease toxicity while maintaining tumour control.  Motivation- Catheters are currently imaged using 2D ultrasound sampled every 5 mm leading to an uncertainty in needle tip position. Automated 3D ultrasound and catheter segmentation have the potential to reduce this uncertainty. Permanent seed insertion results in later seeds becoming obscured by earlier ones in ultrasound images during the procedure. Our lab's mechatronic needle guidance can be extended to identify seed applicator position mechanically, providing additional spatial information at the time of seed placement while maintaining template guided needle insertion efficiency. New focal therapies that target only the tumour volume as opposed to the whole organ may decrease dose to surrounding organs but require high seed positioning accuracy.  Objectives- 1. Demonstrate an improvement in catheter position accuracy using 3D ultrasound and auto-segmentation over current 2D ultrasound techniques. 2. Demonstrate an improvement in the fraction of seeds identifiable with the addition of mechatronic applicator positioning data to images. 3. Propose and compare effective focal brachytherapy procedures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Duration of Acoustic Experience Shapes Development of Auditory Cortical Cartography
Keywords-MotsClés: CAT; CONGENITAL DEAFNESS; DEVELOPMENT; HEARING; PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: According to Statistics Canada, over one million Canadians have a hearing-related disability. Despite the tremendous value of verbal communication in today's society, auditory system research trails behind progress made in understanding the other sensory systems. Many fundamental questions remain unanswered regarding healthy acoustic processing and how it may be disrupted in deafness. In deaf individuals, areas typically involved in acoustic processing may be recruited to process other senses, like vision and touch. However, this reorganization may be maladaptive and prevent acoustic processing if hearing is restored with a cochlear implant. A recent anatomical study showed that several areas involved in auditory processing are diminished in deaf cats. Interestingly, the volume of total auditory cortex was positively correlated to the age of deafness onset, such that auditory cortex was more diminished in cats deafened earlier in life. This suggests that reduced auditory experience in early-deafened cats significantly impaired auditory cortex development. To further understand the relationship between acoustic experience and cortical development, the congenitally deaf white cat will be examined. In this strain, a genetic defect results in the degeneration of the inner ear, resulting in an animal with absolutely no hearing experience. The auditory cortex of five congenitally deaf cats will be examined and compared to hearing cats, and cats pharmacologically deafened at various ages. Examining how the brain adapts to hearing loss induced at various stages of life is vital to understanding the limitations of current prosthetics and developing more effective cochlear implants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modeling hospital intervention strategies for infectious disease control using novel contact networks
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTACT NETWORKS; HEALTH POLICY; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MATHEMATICAL MODELING; PANDEMIC PREPAREDNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Airborne, respiratory infections such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and H1N1 influenza have an incredible potential to become widespread, pandemic infections, and are often difficult to fully characterize and contain. Mathematical disease modeling has become increasingly relevant in the area of pandemic preparedness, combining the fields of mathematics, statistics, and public health in order predict the impact of outbreaks, and the efficacy of various intervention strategies.   Since many disease models are based on assumptions of contact between infected persons in a community, they are often limited in their representation of true population dynamics. With a need for more accurate and detailed contact predictions, data from radio-frequency identification (RFID), and cellular phone technologies are becoming increasingly relevant.  Hospitals, in particular, are an effective place to study contact networks, since employees have the capacity to spread an infection throughout the hospital and affect the surrounding community.   I aim to develop a detailed hospital contact network, in order to test the effectiveness of infectious disease intervention strategies in a hospital setting. My project utilizes RFID hospital contact data to create a detailed contact network. Data from the SARS epidemic, which experienced a high rate of hospital related transmissions, will be used to test my model. The dynamics of disease spread through the network model will demonstrate the relative efficacy of each infection control strategy.  This study utilizes a novel method for contact network development, and will provide a thorough and accurate assessment of infection control strategies within hospital settings. The results of this study have the potential to be expanded to infection control strategies at the provincial, national, and international level.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Immunology of the Omentum: Analysis of Omental invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) Cells in Intra-Abdominal Sepsis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; CRITICAL CARE; FLOW CYTOMETRY; INFECTION AND IMMUNITY; INTRA-ABDOMINAL SEPSIS; INVARIANT NATURAL KILLER T (INKT) CELLS; MULTIPLEX CYTOKINE ARRAY; OMENTUM; SEPSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Sepsis remains a leading cause of death in the intensive care unit, but there are few proven treatment strategies. Invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) cells are a rare group of lymphocytes that have been implicated as potent regulators of the immune system in a variety of disease states, because they produce pro- and/or anti-inflammatory cytokines. There are very few studies examining iNKT cells in human sepsis. Recent evidence shows that iNKT cells are especially enriched in the human omentum, a loose curtain of adipose tissue that drapes over the small and large bowels, and migrates towards sites of intra-abdominal injury or inflammation, including perforations, trauma, and other injuries. The immunology of the omentum and the mechanism by which it mitigates intra-abdominal sepsis (IAS) is still unknown. My project hypothesizes that omental iNKT cells will be increased in patients with IAS compared to non-septic patients, and that they will play a key role in promulgating the septic response. Omentum and venipuncture blood samples will be obtained from patients undergoing surgery for IAS and elective abdominal surgery. The proportions of iNKT cells and T cells will be determined using flow cytometry. Multiplex cytokine analysis will be used to compare levels of inflammatory markers between patients with or without IAS. A mouse model of IAS will be developed to characterize the role, function, and behaviour of iNKT cells in the early septic response.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of Cash Transfers and Micronutrient Powders on Stunting and Iron Deficiency in Children 6-23 Months in Northern Zambia, A Randomized Control Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: 24 HOUR RECALL; ANTHROPOMETRY; CASH TRANSFERS; CHILDREN; FOOD SECURITY; HEMOGLOBIN; IRON DEFICIENCY ANEMIA; MICRONUTRIENT POWDERS; SERUM FERRITIN; STUNTING
Abstract-Résumé: Child malnutrition is of major concern globally, negatively impacting the lives of millions of children. Two specific forms of malnutrition are stunting, caused by chronic undernutrition, and anemia as a result of extreme iron deficiency. In Zambia 52.9% of children under 5 years are anemic and 45% are stunted. Childhood stunting leads to impaired cognitive development, poor school achievement, and lower adult wages, while anemia in children can cause negative impacts on intellectual and physical development. In light of this, the Zambian government has initiated a Cash Transfer program, whereby households with a child under 5 years receive a stipend from the government. The purpose of the program is to increase food security and improve child health. Simultaneously, Irish Aid and UNICEF will be distributing Micronutrient Powders (MNPs) to children 0-23 months, combined with nutrition education. MNPs are single use packets of vitamins and minerals which are added to a child's food just before it is consumed. Our research will assess the impact of the cash transfers paired with MNPs in lowering rates of stunting and anemia in children. We expect that MNPs with cash transfers will prove more effective than cash transfers alone. In order to test this we will randomize 300 households in Northern Zambia who have a child 6-23 months of age to one of three groups: cash transfer only, cash transfer plus MNP, and a control. Stunting will be measured using physical measurements, as well as proxy variables such as child feeding practices, child food intake, and the incidence of disease. Iron deficiency will be measured using blood samples. The Zambian government is hoping to scale up the cash transfer program, and as such it is critical to know whether it is having the desired impact on child health. Furthermore, while MNPs have been proven effective, there is little research on their pairing with cash transfers, a gap this research will fill.

TitreApplicationTitle: The relationship between victimization, theory of mind and mental health in adolescents with autism spectrum disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER; MENTAL HEALTH; THEORY OF MIND; VICTIMIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Individuals with autism experience more mental health problems, such as anxiety and depression (Skokauskas & Gallagher, 2012) as well as higher rates of victimization than the general population (Little, 2002). However, children with autism may be unaware of their own victimization as these individuals often have difficultly understanding the intentions and mental states of others. This ability, known as theory of mind, is impaired in individuals with autism to varying degrees (Tager-Flusberg, 2007). Typically developing children who are bullied are more likely to experience mental health problems than those who are not bullied (Sesar et al., 2012). However, some children with autism may be unable to identify the malicious intentions of the perpetrators, reducing the negative impact of bullying. This suggests that victimization may not lead to mental health problems in all individuals with autism. The goal of my Master's thesis is to examine the relationship between victimization, theory of mind abilities and mental health problems in adolescents with autism. I hypothesize that victimization will not be associated with mental health problems in individuals with autism who have relatively poor theory of mind abilities. Conversely, I hypothesize that victimization will be associated with mental health problems in individuals with autism who have relatively strong theory of mind abilities. I will investigate this research question by administering questionnaires and tasks to adolescents with autism aged 12-18 and their caregivers. These measures will evaluate how often the individual with autism experienced bullying, their theory of mind abilities and their mental health. Consistent with the Canadian Institute of Health Research's mandate, this study aims to build on our knowledge of victimization and mental health problems in adolescents with autism.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of Vascular Aging by NAD Precursors
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA DAMAGE; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; NAD+ METABOLISM; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; VASCULAR AGING
Abstract-Résumé: Aging is a universal process within organisms. Over-time with advancing age, changes at the level of organs or at a cellular level will contribute to an increased chance of disease and death. Cardiovascular disease is no exception, with environmental and genetic factors contributing to coronary disease, heart failure, stroke and hypertension, but age acting as the major risk factor through life-long accumulation of damage.  Age-related changes in blood vessels, such as thickening of the arterial wall, contribute to vessel stiffness and have been observed during the aging process to precede and predict disease. Within the last decade, reducing calorie consumption has gained attention as an intervention to delay the aging process. A compound known as Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) is involved in reactions during the break-down of food. Consequently, within a low calorie diet more NAD is available to activate proteins known as sirtuins, shown to support a longer lifespan. My project will explore the role of NAD in protecting against cellular stress insults and aging on a cardiovascular model. Furthermore, I will explore the relevance and therapeutic potential of an NAD building block, nicotinamide riboside, in delaying vascular aging.  Nicotinamide riboside has recently been identified as a nutrient in milk, offering a favourable mechanism of absorption into cells of the body. In addition, it may offer therapeutic benefit over another NAD precursor, since it is not involved in a pathway that causes a painful side effect known as flushing.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANAEMIA; ANTHROPOMETRIC MEASUREMENTS; CHRONIC MALNUTRITION; CROSS SECTIONAL; HAEMOGLOBIN; HEMOCUE; NUTRITION; PUBLIC HEALTH; QUANTITATIVE RESEARCH; RANDOM CLUSTER SAMPLING
Abstract-Résumé: Malnutrition, particularly undernutrition, is the largest contributor to child mortality and ill-health globally. My research project is part of a large, ongoing nutrition intervention in Rwanda which addresses the issue of undernutrition in children 6-23 months old. The University of British Columbia with its partners The National University of Rwanda and The Rwandan Ministry of Health are examining the efficacy of a micronutrient intervention in reducing anaemia amongst children in low resource settings. Anaemia, characterized by low haemoglobin levels in the blood, is most widely associated with micronutrient deficiencies, particularly iron deficiency, and has an adverse effect on appetite which can influence food consumption and ultimately inhibit growth. My piece of this project is to research the predictors of anaemia in young children 6-12 months old and to look at the associations between anaemia and stunting which is a form of chronic undernutrition leading to the failure to reach one's genetic growth potential. Both anaemia and stunting are pervasive health concerns in Rwanda and can lead to irreparable cognitive, social and physical damage. Currently, we lack knowledge on the strength and direction of the association between the two conditions. The results that will come out of this investigation will have a substantial impact on our understanding of nutrition interventions and the interventions designed to combat chronic malnutrition. My project will guide future research in the area of using Micronutrient Powders to combat anaemia and stunting  and to provide insight on this serious public health issue. Finally, Canada has a strong commitment to global health and international development that this research supports, and there is much to gain from broadening our current network of international research partners by fostering collaboration between emerging researchers in the field of nutrition and health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Autofluorescence and Photoacoustic Imaging for Improved Lumpectomy Margin Assessment
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOFLUORESCENCE; BREAST CANCER; BREAST CONSERVATION SURGERY; IMAGING; LUMPECTOMY; PHOTOACOUSTICS
Abstract-Résumé: On average, 62 Canadian women will be diagnosed with breast cancer every day (Canadian Cancer Society). Many of these women will have breast conservation surgeries in an attempt to remove the tumour but spare the rest of the breast. In this surgery, the surgeon removes the area identified as cancer along with a small amount of normal tissue surrounding it, called the margins. After the surgery, the tissue removed from the patient undergoes testing to ensure that the margins do not contain cancer. In 20-40% of cases, the margins are positive (Pleijhuis et al., Ann. Surg. Oncol. 16, 2009), meaning that more of the tumour is inside the patient and they will need another surgery to remove it. My research goal is to develop an imaging system that can identify cancer in the margins. I plan to investigate this technique in the operating room to determine if the need for additional surgeries can be reduced.  An imaging technique called autofluorescence imaging can detect the difference between normal tissue and cancer, but it works best on flat surfaces. Like when the sun casts the sides of a mountain into light and shadow, the uneven surface of the tumour causes light to be reflected and scattered. This makes it appear to be brighter or darker in different areas. By using a second imaging technique to map out the surface of the tumour like a topographic map, I can correct for the angles reflecting and scattering the light. This will give an accurate autofluorescence image, highlighting areas of tumour. I will use this technique to image tissue samples in surgery, and then evaluate the accuracy of the imaging system by comparing my results to the results of the tests used now. This imaging technique has the potential to detect positive margins in the operating room and prevent additional surgeries. This could reduce the workload of surgeons and supporting staff, decrease wait times for patients and give patients peace of mind knowing the entire tumour was removed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Healthcare Utilization for Chronic Pelvic Pain in Women Undergoing Hysterectomy
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN; DATABASE; ENDOMETRIOSIS; HEALTHCARE USE; HYSTERECTOMY; RETROSPECTIVE COHORT
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pelvic pain is a common and costly condition that is sometimes treated with surgical removal of the uterus, or hysterectomy.  However, approximately a quarter of women have persistent or even worsening pain after hysterectomy.  We propose a study using routinely collected anonymous Ministry of Health data from hospitals and medical services billing in British Columbia to (1) compare healthcare use between women who had hysterectomy for painful and non-painful conditions of the female reproductive organs, (2) compare healthcare use before and after hysterectomy among women with chronic pelvic pain, and (3) analyze factors that predict the use of healthcare for pain after hysterectomy.  A study of the patterns of healthcare use in women with pelvic pain may help quantify the burden of this condition on both individuals and society, identify some causes for persistent pain, and provide information on the allocation of healthcare resources for chronic pelvic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Associations of Ethnicity, Social, and Behavioural Factors with Cancer Incidence and Mortality in BC Regions
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL PREDICTORS; CANCER; CANCER DISPARTIES; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; ECONOMIC FACTORS; ETHNICITY AND IMMIGRATION; HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTH STATUS; MULTIPLE REGRESSION ANALYSIS; SOCIAL PREDICTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer differentially affects populations and geographical regions. People with lower socioeconomic status (SES), from certain ethnic groups and areas are more likely to have poor health and a higher risk of cancer. A group at particular risk is immigrants in British Columbia (BC), partly due to ethnicity and unhealthy lifestyle factors adopted in Canada, such as tobacco use, poor nutrition, obesity and physical inactivity. The purpose of this study is to investigate the factors that contribute to the disparity in cancer incidence and mortality in a sample of British Columbians, specifically socioeconomic indicators (income and human economic hardship), geographical region and lifestyle factors (diet, obesity, physical activity and tobacco use). We will also examine whether differential outcomes are related to ethnic subgroups and immigrants. Analyses will be conducted using a data set of adult cancers diagnosed over a five-year period that was collected by the BC Cancer Registry, and includes follow-up for death. Data on immigration in BC will be obtained from Citizenship and Immigration Canada and linked to the Cancer Registry data. Data on the socio economic profiles and ethnicity of specific regions in BC will be obtained through BC Stats. Correlations and multiple regression analyses will be used to examine the associations between socioeconomic factors, ethnicity, place of birth, and cancer survival for common cancers, controlling for age and sex. Health related behaviours and geographic variation by region will be examined using the BC Wellness Atlas. Understanding more about the particular risk factors for vulnerable ethnic groups, immigrants and communities is important to develop targeted prevention programs and improve the health of the BC population. Recommendations will be made regarding health promotion strategies for modifying cancer-related health behaviours, and suggestions to improve social determinants of health in disadvantaged groups in BC.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulatory T Cell Accumulation in Pre-metastatic Tissues in Response to Primary Tumour Hypoxia
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; FLOW CYTOMETRY; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; HYPOXIA; IMMUNE SUPPRESSION; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; LYMPH NODES; METASTASIS; PRE-METASTATIC NICHE; REGULATORY T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that 186,400 Canadians will be diagnosed with cancer in 2012. Of those diagnosed, 90% will die when tumour cells detach from the initial tumour site and spread throughout their body (metastasize) to distant locations. When tumour cells leave the initial tumour mass and colonize distant tissues they form life-threatening tumour metastases. Tumours often contain poorly oxygenated (hypoxic) cells, and this low oxygen environment favours the development of highly aggressive tumour cells with enhanced capacity to spread throughout the body. Our lab has found that hypoxic tumour cells are linked to the accumulation of immune suppressive cells at sites of secondary tumour growth. These immune suppressive cells can mask the detection of tumour cells and promote tumour growth through a localized suppression of the immune system. The purpose of this project is to investigate the link between hypoxia within the initial tumour and the accumulation of immune suppressive regulatory T cells (Tregs) in distant tissues. The ability of accumulating Tregs to suppress the immune system and promote metastatic growth will be evaluated by isolating these immune cells from tissues and testing their immune suppressive capacity. Additionally, in an effort to translate our research into the clinic we will develop a therapeutic strategy to deplete immune suppressive Tregs by eliminating hypoxic tumour cells.  To improve the health of Canadians living with cancer, we need to advance our understanding of the leading cause of cancer-related deaths. This study will provide valuable insight into the relationship between hypoxic tumour cells and Treg accumulation and function in tissues, and the means by which Tregs influence the growth of tumour metastases. Ultimately, this project will aid in the design of new strategies to treat metastatic cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: The identification of master regulatory genes (MRGs) whose altered expression and activation play a central role in the development of metastatic prostate cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; MASTER REGULATOR; METASTASIS; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; PROSTATE CANCER; THERAPEUTIC TARGETS; XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Prostate cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in North American men. While current therapies are able to cure prostate cancer if it is discovered at the early stages, therapies for late-stage prostate cancer (i.e. prostate cancer spread) are only effective for a short term. As such, diagnosis with prostate cancer spread is considered ultimately fatal and an effective therapeutic option is crucially needed. While traditional methods of discovering potentially important changes focus on the most drastic of differences between cancer cells and normal cells, such results are often very noisy and difficult to interpret. The latest advances in computational analysis methods have allowed us to uncover causative changes that are less obvious but potentially more important to prostate cancer spread.   Research Direction: We will use the new computational methods to identify the causative changes that drive prostate cancer spread as potential therapeutic targets through the following three research goals:  1) Using a world-class tumour model that closely resembles patient cases in conjunction with new computational strategies, we will predict the underlying changes that potentially drive prostate cancer spread.  2) We will confirm the predicted changes by evaluating patient tissue samples to ensure the discovery is truly relevant to patients.  3) We will further investigate the underlying biology behind the changes in order to come up with effective treatment options for prostate cancer spread.   Significance: By identifying such driver changes and validating the discovery through further tests, we hope to uncover new and effective therapeutic targets, accordingly develop more effective therapies for treating late-stage prostate cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: National Transgender and Gender Variant School-age Youth Survey: Stigma, Resilience, and Mental Health
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT HEALTH; DEPRESSION; GENDER & HEALTH; HEALTH PROMOTION; MENTAL HEALTH; PUBLIC/POPULATION HEALTH; RISK & PROTECTIVE FACTORS; STIGMA; SUICIDALITY; TRANSGENDER
Abstract-Résumé: This project will document the mental health issues and related risk exposures of transgender and gender variant youth in Canada, and how their home, school, and community environments contribute to mental health. While limited research has documented the mental health status of trans and gender variant youth, especially younger adolescents, the evidence suggests this is an extremely vulnerable group. The National Canadian Trans Youth Survey will sample trans and gender variant youth nationwide, recruited through service providers and social networks. Survey questions will assess a broad range of physical and mental health outcomes and related behaviours, primarily drawn from existing national, provincial, and international school-based adolescent health surveys. This will allow direct comparison of trans and gender-variant youths' health and well-being to the rest of the population. I will lead the mental health component of the project. This will involve exploring the relationship between young people's social environments and mental health, including school experiences, family supports, and exposure to discrimination or violence. With a focus on specific mental health issues such as emotional distress, self-harm, suicidal ideation and suicide attempts, this research will identify both health inequities for trans and gender variant young people, as well as environments and experiences that contribute to mental health risk or resilience. Analysis of all of these factors will identify potential intervention points for school and community strategies to improve the mental health and well-being of transgender youth. The results will be taken back to trans youth themselves, as well as academic audiences, and education and public health stakeholders through a variety of knowledge-to-action strategies, and serves as the critical first step in developing policies and programs to promote the mental health of transgender adolescents.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of humanized mice to evaluate HIV vaccine candidates
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE TRANSFER; AIDS; B CELL PHYSIOLOGY; CELL SIGNALLING; HIV; IMMUNOLOGY; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: HIV has infected over 65 000 people in Canada, and 34 million worldwide. In addition to its immediate effects on health, widespread HIV infection has devastating social and economic impacts in the developing world. Some HIV infected individuals generate neutralizing antibodies that bind to HIV and prevent the virus from entering host cells. We are working to generate an HIV vaccine that works by injecting healthy people with non-infectious proteins that trick the immune system into making antibodies that will protect them from HIV; the same way that a flu shot works.  Antibodies are made by specialized cells called B cells. Everybody has millions of different B cells circulating in their blood at any given time, each one can potentially recognize anything foreign, like bacteria or viruses.  In order for an HIV vaccine to work the correct B cells must recognize the foreign protein. Once they do, they begin to undergo a number of processes that lead to the production of antibodies against HIV. Previous studies from our lab have shown that HIV proteins are generally not recognized by the correct B cells that will eventually give rise to the kind of protective neutralizing antibodies that we desire to make through vaccination. This may explain why HIV vaccines have failed so far. However, we have recently modified an HIV protein that does engage the correct B cells.  If used as part of a vaccine, this modified protein might be capable of generating neutralizing antibodies against HIV. Unfortunately, Human HIV vaccine trials are incredibly expensive and take many years to conduct. As an alternative we are working to transfer B cells found in the human immune system into laboratory mice which we can then use to rather quickly test whether our modified proteins can drive the desired antibody response upon immunization.  If this strategy works it would provide justification for moving further towards human clinical trials, and hopefully an effective HIV vaccine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of chromatin 3D organization in gene transcriptional regulation
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN ORGANIZATION; GENE REGULATION; HOX GENES; LIMB DEVELOPMENT; MOUSE GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Between 3 to 5% of births are affected by congenital malformations and 20 to 30% of infant deaths are due to genetic disorders. Understanding genetic traits associated with congenital disorders are critical for early diagnosis and improving treatments. Increasing evidence suggests that a large proportion of congenital disorders are linked to impaired regulation of gene expression. Over the years, studies have shown that transcription of a single gene or a cluster of genes is regulated by remote cis-regulatory elements. The remote cis-regulatory elements are brought in physical contact with the promoter of a given gene by chromatin looping.  However, the underlying mechanism remains poorly understood. The aim of the proposed research is to improve the understanding of the mechanism controlling long distance gene regulation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Wnt Signaling in Cardiac Pacemaker Cell Specification
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRHYTHMIA; BIOLOGICAL PACEMAKER; CARDIAC ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ION CHANNELS; PATCH-CLAMP; SOMATIC REPROGRAMMING; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: This project addresses an important health problem, heart rhythm disorders (particularly bradycardia which means low heart beating rate). Current therapy for bradycardia usually involves the implantation of an electronic pacemaker, which has many limitations. This study has the potential to identify new methods for creating a pacemaker with the patient's own heart muscle cells. The major strategy of this project is to find the signals that direct a heart progenitor cell to develop into a pacemaker cell in embryonic heart, and then to use these signals to convert ordinary heart muscle cells into pacemaker cells. The long-term biomedical significance of the project is that it can potentially yield a new method to treat cardiac rhythm disorders. If successful, this new method would have several advantages over currently used electronic pacemakers. First, it will use the patient's own cells and there would be no need to implant wires and batteries in the patient's body. Second, there would be no need to worry about hardware failure that may cause sudden death. Third, the chance of bacterial infection and bleeding due to hardware implantation would be eliminated. Finally, the biological pacemaker created with the new method would be able to adjust the patient's heart rate in response to changes of patient's physical and emotional conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the role of invariant natural killer T cells in the lung during infection, sterile inflammation, and their interplay.
Keywords-MotsClés: INTRAVITAL MICROSCOPY; INVARIANT NATURAL KILLER T CELLS; PULMONARY FIBROSIS; PULMONARY INFECTION; PULMONARY INJURY; SPINNING DISK CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Respiratory diseases will be the fourth leading cause of death worldwide by 2020. Yet our ability to visualize the lung parenchyma and vasculature at the single cell level has lagged behind most other organs.  As such what is common knowledge in some tissues remains a mystery in lung. In collaboration with Dr. Krummel at UCSF, the Kubes laboratory has recently developed a novel way of imaging the lung to have single-cell resolution.  Using this approach we will begin to elucidate some of the fundamental issues regarding the immune system in the lung. Invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells are extremely important cells in immunity because they bear characteristics of innate and adaptive lymphocytes, which allow them to dictate whether an immune response to infection or to an allergen is established.  As such they are being implicated to play important roles in many diseases including allergic asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and during lung infections. We recently uncovered that in the liver under basal conditions, iNKT cells constantly patrol the liver microvasculature, living inside the blood vessels. During infection macrophages in the liver catch the bacteria and present antigen via CD1d to iNKT cells, which activate the immune system. However, it remains completely unclear 1) where the iNKT cells reside in lung, 2) whether they can be presented with antigens and if so by which cells, and 3) what role iNKT cells play during bacterial lung infections with Streptococcus pneumoniae or during sterile lung injury like in the case of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). In this study we will use our newly developed live imaging technique to address these issues and understand the role of iNKT cells during lung disease. We believe that this work will lead to important insights into how the lung responds to injury and infection. Furthermore this work will provide potential clues for novel therapeutics against currently untreatable lung diseases such as IPF

TitreApplicationTitle: Preventing post-anesthetic memory deficits
Keywords-MotsClés: ANESTHETICS; GABAA RECEPTORS; HIPPOCAMPUS; IN VITRO; IN VIVO; MEMORY; POSTOPERATIVE COGNITIVE DYSFUNCTION; PREVENTION OF MEMORY IMPAIRMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Over 236 million anesthetics are administered worldwide each year. A major adverse effect of most general anesthetics is memory loss, which may persist for days to months, long after the anesthetic drugs have been eliminated from the patient's body. Such memory disturbance is associated with prolonged length of hospital stay, loss of independence, increased risk of death and increased costs, yet no treatments or prevention strategies are available. Our research goal is to find a safe, plausible and effective strategy to prevent postanesthetic memory loss. Our lab has previously identified a receptor in the brain that, when activated, causes memory deficits. Our preliminary results suggest that when anesthetics activate these receptors, they unexpectedly trigger a long-lasting increase in the number of these receptors, which persists long after the drugs are eliminated. Therefore, we propose that blocking these receptors before exposing the brain to anesthetic drugs, will prevent the initial anesthetic activation of the receptors and will prevent long-term memory loss. We anticipate that our results will be rapidly translated into new therapies to prevent memory loss after general anesthesia and possibly other related memory disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Therapeutic potential of stem cells in lung injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; BRONCHOPULMONARY DYSPLASIA; CELL CULTURE; CHRONIC DISEASE; LUNG; LUNG DEVELOPMENT; LUNG MORPHOMETRY; NEWBORN; OXYGEN; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a chronic lung disease that follows ventilator and oxygen treatment for acute failure to breathe in babies born very prematurely (24-28 weeks of gestation instead of 40). BPD is a major complication of prematurity with a short and long term burden for infants and their families. Damage to the still developing lung stops the normal formation of the alveoli (the air sacs in the lung that allows the uptake of oxygen and release of waste carbon dioxide). Currently there is no treatment for this disease. Our laboratory is seeking new medications to protect and potentially heal the damaged lung.  Our body contains stem cells, a pool of cells that have the ability to become any type of cell (i.e., bone, muscle, liver, or blood cells, etc.). Stem cells can be found in the bone marrow but also in the umbilical cord blood (UCB) of babies. UCB is discarded after birth, but can be safely collected and stored without risk to mother or baby. Our lab was one of the first to show that stem cells from UCB can repair lungs in a model of BPD induced in newborn rats by exposure to high oxygen concentrations. In this proposal, we will test the best way to use UCB stem cells to prepare for a safety study in humans. Our research could lead to new treatments to improve the outcomes for premature babies. Ultimately, our findings may extend to the treatment of other lung diseases that currently lack efficient treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Meningococcal Transferrin and Lactoferrin Receptors in Colonization, Infection and Disease Prevention.
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA; HUMANIZED MICE; IMMUNITY; LACTOFERRIN; MENINGITIS; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; RECEPTOR; TRANSFERRIN; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: The bacterium Neisseria meningitidis is a major cause of meningitis and invasive infection in humans, yet it may also colonize humans without causing disease. This bacterium only lives in the human upper respiratory tract, and has evolved very specific interactions with human cells and proteins during its adaptation to this environment. The inability of this bacterium to colonize and cause disease in other animals has made it impossible to assess the relative importance of different bacterial proteins to infection and disease, or to truly evaluate vaccines before testing them in humans. To overcome this problem, we have undertaken to 'humanize' mice so that they express the human form of proteins that the bacteria interact with. This has proven fruitful, since our humanized mice are the first animals other than humans that can be infected with N. meningitidis. In this study, we plan to demonstrate the importance of bacterial proteins that allow the bacteria to effectively remove iron from the human iron-binding proteins, transferrin and lactoferrin, an activity required to allow bacterial growth in the tissues. For these experiments, we will take advantage of our strains of mice that express human transferrin, human lactoferrin, or both of these proteins. We will compare the relative ability of virulent N. meningitidis strains that we have mutated to be defective in one or more of their transferrin or lactoferrin binding proteins in the expectation that the human and bacterial proteins are both essential for infection and disease. Since these bacterial proteins appear to be ideal targets for vaccines, we will also engineer them so that they can be used to protect against N. meningitidis infection and disease. The humanized mice provide us with the first opportunity to evaluate the effectiveness of these vaccines, and we expect that these studies will demonstrate that our optimized vaccines will protect against infection by all strains of Neisseria meningitidis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and validation of a new adrenergic receptor tracer
Keywords-MotsClés: ADRENERGIC RECEPTOR; HUMAN; IN VIVO IMAGING; PET; PRIMATE; TRACER DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Noradrenaline (NA), a common chemical in the brain, plays an important role in many disorders including depression and Parkinson's disease but little is known about its exact involvement in disease or treatment efficacy. It is thus important to investigate NA contributions to brain health in vivo and non-invasively in human subjects.  Positron emission tomography (PET) allows a window into a living brain by use of trace amounts of chemically specific drugs labeled with radioactive isotopes. There are to date no fully characterized tracers to label the NA receptors in the brain or to image variation in NA transmission in response to pharmacological or psychological challenges. Yohimbine, a drug used to treat hypertension and sexual dysfunction, has recently been labeled as a tracer for the alpha2 NA receptors. Direct extrapolation from the results obtained in pigs and rats to the human case are however not possible because of significant metabolic differences.  Some of the validation studies necessary to fully characterize yohimbine as a tracer in primates require several administrations of the radioligand to the same subject and pharmacological manipulations that would not be ethically feasible in humans. Thus, these studies will be performed in non-human primates, who have very similar metabolism and receptor distribution as humans. Follow-up preliminary studies will be performed in normal volunteers to evaluate the distribution of alpha 2 receptors during aging and the reproducibility of the tracer data in between studies. If successful, these studies will permit rapid translation of our data to the design of focused studies in specific patient populations and provide the field with a much needed imaging agent for the NA system. The availability of this tracer will provide new insights into disease mechanism and will help improve the design and the interpretation of future clinical studies including the characterization of potential therapeutic targets

TitreApplicationTitle: Protective mechanisms of endocannabinoids in cardiac hypertrophy
Keywords-MotsClés: 2-PHOTON LASER SCANNING MICROSCOPY; CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; CARDIAC MYOCYTES; ENDOCANNABINOIDS; MITOCHONDRIAL BIOENERGETICS; PRESSURE-OVERLOAD MODEL OF HYPERTROPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Conditions such as hypertension or heart attack increase the risk of heart failure. An intermediate step between these conditions and heart failure is cardiac hypertrophy, or abnormal growth of the heart. Finding ways to avert hypertrophy has emerged as a research priority.  The endocannabinoid system is of interest as a therapeutic target for a variety of disorders. We will focus on the cannabinoid (CB) receptors, as we found that drugs which activate CB receptors block hypertrophy. Unfortunately, these drugs also act in the brain to cause side effects such as dysphoria, memory impairment, and possibly addiction.   We will focus on CB receptor activators that are devoid of psychoactive side effects.  We hypothesize that these drugs will protect against hypertrophy.  We will study the mechanisms that mediate the ability of CB activators to inhibit hypertrophy using an established model of hypertrophy - heart muscle cells that are treated with a growth stimulus. We identified targets at which CB signaling might be interfering, and the effects of CB signaling on these targets will be pursued by genetic, biochemical, and imaging techniques.   We will next verify that findings realized in cells are relevant to intact animals. We will generate hypertrophy in  mice by placing a band on the aorta, and assess the effects of CB-activating drugs on hypertrophy and relevant signaling pathways.  The incidence of heart failure is predicted to double by 2025, so we are striving to prevent the transition from hypertrophy to heart failure. By learning how CB receptors might control this transition while avoiding adverse side effects, we may discover molecular targets that can be manipulated for therapeutic gain to treat heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Re-activation of human endogenous retrovirus-K in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: A consequence of genetic mutations in TDP43 and Optineurin.
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; FUNCTIONAL POLYMORPHISMS; HUMAN ENDOGENOUS RETROVIRUS-K; INFLAMMATORY DISEASE; INFLAMMATORY TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTERFERON RESPONSE FACTORS; NEUROVIROLOGY; NUCLEAR FACTOR-KAPPA B SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Over 8% of our DNA contains ancient retroviruses, such as human endogenous retrovirus-K (ERVK). These viruses are normally silent, but can be re-activated during inflammatory disease, such as Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). We do not understand what signals re-activate these retroviruses. Two key proteins known to be mutated in ALS patients - Optineurin and TDP43 - are known to modulate inflammatory pathways through Nuclear Factor-kappa B (NF-kB) signalling. Our preliminary results show that NF-kB can induce ERVK in human cells. The proposed study will examine how Optineurin and TDP43 might contribute to ERVK expression and neuroinflammation in ALS. We will use a combination of molecular biology and imaging techniques to address this research question. Our findings will allow us to identify potential therapeutic targets which modulate either the retrovirus or the immune system, thus preventing the development and clinical symptoms of ALS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of Endothelial Dysfunction on Hemostasis and Cardiovascular Health in Chronic Kidney Disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; BLOOD OUTGROWTH ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; ENDOTHELIUM; HEMOSTASIS; INFLAMMATION; OSTEOPROTEGERIN; THROMBOSIS; VON WILLEBRAND FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Although over 2 million Canadians have chronic kidney disease, CKD, they die from diseases of their heart and blood vessels.  This is caused by the build-up of toxins that the kidneys no longer filter out of the blood.  This causes the lining of the blood vessels to not work properly.  This makes them less to respond to the changing demands of the body leading to heart disease and death.  Additionally, CKD patients suffer from blood clotting problems.  This is because of the damage happening to the blood vessels, but how and why this happens is poorly understood. We have identified factors that can be monitored to see if we can diagnose the disease earlier and treat the underlying problem sooner by developing better treatments to better protect the blood vessels. We will use rats to model chronic kidney disease by feeding them a diet high in a substance which damages the kidneys. By changing the amount of phosphate in the diet, we will also show we can accelerate or delay the onset of the calcium build-up, and thereby alter when problems with the blood vessels occur. We will measure other substances in the blood that tell us about overall blood vessel health. Finally, when we try new treatments, we will monitor substances produced by the blood vessels to see if they can be returned to normal levels and function properly.  In parallel experiments, we will look at CKD patient blood and see how the cells in the blood are functioning, and see if we can measure the damage to these cells.  We will then see if we can treat these cells to work normally again, to become a potential treatment for these individuals blood vessels. This research will lead to a new understanding of the way this disease process works, and a starting point for new potential treatments and earlier diagnosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Protection and Informed Target Discovery for Gene and Stem Cell Therapy in Sepsis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BIOINFORMATICS; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; INFLAMMATION; MESENCHYMAL STEM CELLS; MICROARRAY; PRIMARY CELLS; SEPSIS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TRANSGENIC MICE/KNOCKOUT MICE
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, severe sepsis strikes young and old alike (~75,000 cases per year) and the mortality is 30-40%. Despite much research, no treatment for sepsis has emerged and the problem increases each year. Costs of ICU care for these patients are also enormous and post-acute care of survivors is nearly 3.5 million per year post-ICU discharge. New treatments are urgently needed.  Treatment with Mesenchymal Stem Cell (MSCs) has been shown to reduce morbidity and mortality in septic animals. How these cells work is unclear so we analysed the expression of 54,000 genes in five sepsis-target organs collected from septic mice treated with either placebo or MSCs. We rationalized that genes important in helping mice get better and surviving would be changed between the sick mice and those that received the cells. We found that a particular gene usually involved in Parkinson disease (autosomal recessive, early onset) 7 [PARK-7] or DJ-1 was markedly changed in ALL 5 organs studied. We looked at the levels of the DJ-1 protein in patients with sepsis and found that not only was it increased, but it was significantly higher in those who died from sepsis. To determine the role of DJ-1 in sepsis, we obtained the mouse that lacked the DJ-1 gene and found that these mice were much more resistant to sepsis than the normal wild type mouse. The goal of the current grant application is to study the role of DJ-1 in the knockout mice and in different cells derived from these mice to better understand the mechanisms they have developed to protected themselves from sepsis. We think these mice are better able to cope with sepsis because absence of DJ-1 makes their immune cells much more aggressive getting rid of bacteria. Moreover, we also study the option of inhibiting DJ-1 in MSCs or conditioned medium from cells - to determine if this approach can be used to improve the beneficial effects of MSC treatment or even serve as an approach in itself for the treatment of sepsis.

Abstract-Résumé: The small ubiquitin like modifier (SUMO) is an evolutionarily conserved protein that plays a number of critical roles in biology.  We and others have recently implicated SUMO function in the regulation of DNA.  Here, I propose to use a technology called mass spectrometry to better characterize the role of the human SUMO system in DNA regulation.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination on adolescent health outcomes: The Ontario Grade 8 HPV vaccine cohort study
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS VACCINE; POPULATION HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH INTERVENTION; SEX-BASED ANALYSES; VALIDATION STUDY; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: In 2007, provinces began implementing human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programs for young girls in an effort to reduce the occurrence of genital warts and cervical cancer. Although there was a great deal of hype about these programs, there was also controversy over the many unanswered questions about the real-world effects of the HPV vaccine in this young population. Even now, more than five years after the programs began, the controversy continues. This study is based in Ontario, where the HPV vaccine has been offered free-of-charge to all Grade 8 girls since September 2007. The study will include all girls in Grade 8 in 2007/08-2010/11 (eligible for free vaccination) and 2003/2004-2006/2007 (ineligible for free vaccination). We will create a similar cohort of Grade 8 boys. Data for this study will come entirely from the province's administrative health and immunization databases, which contain secure, anonymous information on all individuals covered under Ontario's Health Insurance Plan. Using this information, we will answer questions of particular public interest - for example: (1) To what extent does vaccinating girls in Grade 8 girls reduce their risk of getting genital warts? (2) Has HPV vaccination led to an increase in teen pregnancies or sexually transmitted infections (excluding warts)? and (3) Does vaccinating girls decrease the occurrence of genital warts in boys? To ensure the accuracy of our results, we will also be undertaking a re-abstraction study to validate our outcome definitions. The results of our study will help young girls and their parents make more educated decisions about HPV vaccination. The results will also provide information that policy decision makers can use for strengthening HPV vaccination programs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding effective Audit and Feedback: Identifying and prioritizing theory-informed predictions around improving a common class of knowledge translation interventions
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDIT AND FEEDBACK; DELPHI; INTERVIEWS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; THEORY
Abstract-Résumé: Researchers in health care systems around the world have identified large gaps between ideal and actual care provided to patients. Some commentators have suggested that compared to developing new treatments, there is more to gain by working to close this gap so that patients consistently receive the treatments that we already know are effective. One very common method for encouraging health care providers to improve their practice is called audit and feedback, where a summary of some aspect of current practice behaviour is fed back to individual providers, teams, or health care organizations, often with a recommendation about how to improve. While evidence says that such feedback can be effective, it often is not. This is because we do not understand how or why audit and feedback works, or the conditions that make it more likely to be effective. There is considerable theoretical work that might be used to inform our understanding of audit and feedback; so much, in fact, that there needs to be a systematic approach both for identifying relevant theoretical work, and for prioritizing which areas we should target for future research. This study will lay the foundation for a theoretical understanding of audit and feedback by identifying and prioritizing theory-informed predictions about how to improve this important class of knowledge translation interventions. We will: 1) develop a list of clear, testable predictions about how to improve audit and feedback interventions based on wide range of theoretical perspectives; 2) explore the extent to which existing audit and feedback interventions already conform to these predictions; and 3) obtain consensus within the audit and feedback research community about which predictions should be prioritized for future research. This work should improve our ability to develop consistently effective audit and feedback interventions that improve the quality of Canadian healthcare.
