TitreApplicationTitle: Régulation de la Contractilité du Myocarde par la MAPK p38 dans l'Insuffisance Cardiaque : Rôle des Phosphatases DUSPs.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOMYOCYTES; CONTRACTILITE CARDIAQUE; DUAL-SPECIFICITY PHOSPHATASES; HYPERTROPHIE COMPENSATOIRE; INSUFFISANCE CARDIAQUE; MAPK P38; MECANISMES SIGNALETIQUES
Abstract-Résumé: A l'echelle canadienne, les maladies cardiovasculaires sont responsables des taux de morbidite et de mortalite les plus eleves. En plus d'infliger un fardeau economique majeur a notre societe, la diminution graduelle de contractilite du myocarde observee chez les patients souffrant d'insuffisance cardiaque chronique est fatale. Comprendre les mecanismes moleculaires a l'origine de la perte d'integrite fonctionnelle des cardiomyocytes (cellules du coeur permettant la contraction) est donc primordial au developpement de nouvelles strategies therapeutiques pour lutter contre l'insuffisance cardiaque. Plusieurs evidences impliquent la «mitogen-activated protein kinase» (MAPK) p38 dans la perte de contractilite cardiaque venant aggraver l'evolution des cardiomyopathies. Par contre, notre comprehension des mecanismes de regulation et l'identite des cibles moleculaires de la MAPK p38 dans le coeur restent encore rudimentaires. Nous avons montre recemment que les proteines «dual-specificity phosphatases» (DUSPs) DUSP1 et DUSP4 freinent l'activite pathologique de la MAPK p38 au myocarde. Nos plus recents resultats montrent de facon inattendue que la DUSP10, elle aussi exprimee dans le coeur, exacerbe l'evolution de l'insuffisance cardiaque. Par l'utilisation d'une combinaison d'approches genetiques, biochimiques, moleculaires et pharmacologiques, nous proposons de mettre en lumiere le role des DUSPs sur la fonction cardiaque et d'identifier les cibles moleculaires de la MAPK p38 contribuant au developpement de l'insuffisance cardiaque. A l'heure ou les inhibiteurs de la MAPK p38 sont a l'etude dans differentes phases cliniques, il est important d'approfondir notre comprehension du role des DUSPs et de la MAPK p38 dans la regulation de la contractilite cardiaque.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of the WiiFit to enhance walking in older adults with Lower Limb Amputation
Keywords-MotsClés: LOWER LIMB AMPUTATION; NINTENDO WIIFIT; RANDOMIZED CONTROL TRIAL; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Many older Canadians are living with lower limb amputation (LLA). The prevalence of LLA is projected to double by 2050 primarily due to chronic systemic dysvascular diseases that are common with aging. Prosthetic rehabilitation programs are designed to enhance mobility primarily through gait retraining. An ideal rehabilitation program optimizes balance and lower limb strength which in turn enhance functional mobility. This potentially equates to a reduced risk of prosthesis abandonment, falling and fear of falling, and an increase in participation in physical and social activities. Providing a rehabilitation program that is motivating and engaging is challenging because improvement requires highly repetitious task performance.  Shrinking health care resources often make it difficult to deliver sufficient amount of therapy to achieve standard of care, and impossible to deliver more therapy. In 1994-97, the cost of surgery, rehabilitation and one year follow up post LLAs varied between $86,000 to $110,000 (US) depending on the level of amputation. Thus, novel methods which are practical, cost-effective, and well-received by clients are needed to deliver sufficient amounts of therapy. Commercially available virtual reality (VR) gaming software such as the WiiFitTM by Nintendo has the potential to be a valuable intervention for older adults with LLA.  Based on pilot and feasibility studies our team has developed a customized version of the WiiFit for individuals with LLA called WiiNWALK.  WiiNWALK is a 4-week supervised, home-oriented intervention targeted to improve walking capacity in individuals with LLA.  The purpose of our randomized controlled trial is to evaluate the effect of the WiiNWALK program in older (50+ years) community living adults who have a unilateral above or below knee amputation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of SHP-1 in poor collateral vessel formation and angiogenic response in diabetes.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; COLLATERAL VESSEL FORMATION; DIABETES; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; PDGF; PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE; PHOSPHATASE; SHP-1; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; VEGF
Abstract-Résumé: The mechanisms underlying the progression of poor collateral formation during ischemia in diabetes are not completely understood. High glucose levels have been suggested as one of the most important causal factors of impaired vessel formation characterized by deregulation of growth factor actions causing lower-extremity amputation in patients with diabetes. Our group has made very interesting findings on a new potential target that is elevated with high glucose in ischemic muscles of rodent animals called SHP-1. SHP-1 is a protein and member of the phosphatase family, that downregulates the activity of important growth factors which have crucial impact on growth factor actions and cell survival.  We propose to study the mechanism of SHP-1 activation in diabetes causing inhibition of growth factor actions in the formation new capillaries under ischemic condition. The aim of the present proposal will investigate and characterize the contribution of SHP-1 to the incapacity of diabetic animals to generate new blood vessels.  To accomplish this aim, we will use genetically modified vascular specific mice of SHP-1 to characterize its cellular mechanisms implicated in collateral vessel formation. Several molecular tools to specifically manipulate SHP-1 protein expression levels in endothelial cells and smooth muscle cells will be used to elucidate the molecular interaction of SHP-1 with vascular growth factors.  We believe that this proposal will provide new insights of the mechanisms underlying poor capillary formation in diabetes. Our research project will offer new mechanistic tools to develop new strategies to promote new blood vessels during ischemia and prevent extremity amputation in type 1 and 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of cell adhesion during separation of embryonic tissues
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL ADHESION; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL MIGRATION; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; GASTRULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Most of the cells of our body are held together by a "glue" made of special "adhesion molecules". During embryonic development, and later even in the adult, cells must modify their relative positions relative to neighbors. In extreme cases such as cancer invasion, cells can even leave the tumor of origin and penetrate through other tissues. Such rearrangements required the adhesive bonds to be dynamically formed and undone. This is a fundamental question in Cell Biology that has remained largely unsolved. We study the separation of embryonic tissues from the initial homogenous mass of embryonic cells. This is not only a key event in the organization of the future organism, but also an excellent model to investigate the mechanisms through which cells can "recognize" cells to which they should bind from the ones they should keep at bay. This property seems to be somehow lost or bypassed by invasive cancer cells. We have recently discovered that the separation of early tissues is controlled by specific cell surface "sensors" that react when they touch cells of another type. This triggers a local retraction that temporarily pulls cells part, thus preventing intermingling of the two tissues. We believe that this is a central mechanism that controls contacts between normal and cancer cells as well. We have now for the first time a model where cells naturally undergo constant cycles of attachment and detachment. This proposal aims at determining how these "repulsive reactions" are able to disrupt the tight attachments formed between the two cells: are the adhesive bonds simply ripped apart by the sheer force of the cells retracting? Or are they on the contrary "melted" by a well-controlled disengagement of the adhesion molecules? And if so, what are the signals and the genes involved? The frog embryos used in this project are uniquely suited to combine molecular manipulations and biochemical studies with direct live observation of the dynamics of adhesive bonds.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pronostic biopsychosocial des douleurs thoraciques inexpliquées suite à une consultation dans une unité d'urgence.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETE; DOULEUR THORACIQUE INEXPLIQUEE; MEDECINE D'URGENCE; PRONOSTIC; PREDICTION
Abstract-Résumé: Chaque annee, environ 400 000 Canadiens consultent dans une unite d'urgence en raison de douleurs thoraciques qui demeurent inexpliquees au moment du conge. En depit de l'origine medicale benigne des douleurs thoraciques, celles-ci limitent la capacite des patients a travailler, a veiller au bien-etre de leur famille et a faire de l'activite physique. Consequemment, les douleurs thoraciques inexpliquees sont a l'origine de multiples consultations medicales souvent infructueuses. La recherche montre qu'environ 30% des patients eprouvent toujours des douleurs thoraciques recurrentes qui affectent leur fonctionnement quotidien 2 ans apres la consultation a l'unite d'urgence. A ce jour, les facteurs impliques dans la chronicite des douleurs thoraciques inexpliquees sont meconnus. De plus, les facteurs permettant de predire si un episode de douleurs thoraciques est a risque de chronicite demeurent inconnus. Ce projet de recherche vise d'abord a quantifier de facon precise la proportion de patients pour lesquels les douleurs thoraciques vont evoluer de facon chronique et incapacitante. Un second objectif est d'identifier les facteurs medicaux, psychologiques et sociaux qui peuvent expliquer l'evolution chronique des douleurs thoraciques inexpliquees. Le dernier objectif est de developper un bref questionnaire qui permettra d'identifier precocement les patients a risque de presenter des douleurs thoraciques chroniques inexpliquees chroniques 2 ans apres la consultation a l'unite d'urgence. Cette etude ameliorera notre comprehension de ce probleme de sante important, tout en permettant de cibler les efforts pour identifier les patients les plus a risques de chronicite pour leur offrir de meilleurs soins de sante.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Molecular Targets and Mechanisms of Human Atrial Fibrillation
Keywords-MotsClés: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; GENETICS; MECHANISMS; PHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common heart arrhythmia. It presents as an irregular heart beat that is often experienced as a fluttering sensation in the chest.  The abnormal electrical activity in the atria causes the top chambers of the heart, the atria, to lose their ability to pump blood into the lower chambers of the heart (the ventricles).  This loss of pumping action can cause blood to pool in the atria which can lead to the formation of blood clots that can travel to the brain and cause a stroke.  Patients with AF suffer from a nearly 5-fold increased risk of stroke. Costs for treating AF in the U.S. have been estimated at $10 billion dollars/yr. It is projected that the number of affected Americans will surge to nearly 20 million by 2050. These trends are similar in Canada and European countries. Identifying genes that predispose individuals to AF has been a research emphasis in the last decade. The driving force for this research is the fact that an understanding of the genes (and their proteins) that may be responsible for causing AF is essential in order to develop the best medical therapies.  Genetic research now clearly indicates that individuals may be at risk of AF through very different mechanisms. Therefore, some treatments may be better targeted to individuals based on the specific genetic type they suffer with. Our research will focus on understanding the physiology and cause of AF in various genetic subtypes. Increasing our insight into the abnormal electrical physiology induced by genetic defects will allow us to devise novel medications and treatment approaches to counteract the abnormal physiology in patients prone to AF.

TitreApplicationTitle: Persons by Proxy: An Examination of the Social Construction of Person-Centred Dementia Care
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SERVICES; INSTITUTIONAL ETHNOGRAPHY; LONG TERM CARE; PERSON-CENTRED DEMENTIA CARE; SOCIAL CONSTRUCTIVISM
Abstract-Résumé: This project seeks to understand the role that social organization of dementia plays in constructing the meaning and value of person-centred care. Through institutional ethnographies of two nursing homes in Nova Scotia (one traditional and one new model of care), it will provide evidence of barriers to the implementation of person-centred approaches to residential dementia care. It is expected that the project's findings will contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between institutional policy and practice and the organization of the lived experiences of residents with dementia diagnoses. This project is unique in two ways: 1) It questions how the meaning of personhood is socially organized within the institutional context of the nursing home environment; 2) It questions how knowledge of person-centred dementia care interventions (practices and policy) within the nursing home setting are mediated by the social organization of the setting. Although the proposed research focuses on Nova Scotia its findings have relevance to other jurisdictions where person-centred dementia-specific models of care have been implemented or are currently under consideration. This research is critical to the study of quality of life for residents with dementia. It will expand understanding of how residents' relations to the setting in which their status as persons has been made into a 'problem' in need of a 'solution' called "person-centred dementia care" are organized by and within that very setting. Such understanding shifts attention from a focus on individual preferences and treatment plans and the production of a 'home-like' environment, to a focus on how the institutional objectives, ordinary orders and social organization of everyday life of the nursing home (as revealed in social interaction, personal accounts and institutional texts such as pamphlets and newsletters) may work to impede the successful implementation of person-centred dementia care.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of collaborated problem-solving in marital relationships for self-reported and objectively measured stress
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTISOL; RELATIONSHIPS; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: A plethora of research suggests that being married is associated with a variety of health benefits (e.g., Glanz et al., 2009; House et al., 1982). However, other research suggests that not all marriages are beneficial for health (Coyne et al., 2001) and very little research has been conducted to identify which specific relationship factors contribute to the health benefits of marriage for individuals. In this study, it is our goal to assess whether the ways in which couples approach problem solving (e.g., collaboratively or independently) impacts one important determinant of health: stress. In order to determine the relation between problem-solving style and stress, a community sample of couples will be asked to report the extent to which they approach their partners for help in problem solving. Additionally, participants will be asked to state their current affect quality and provide saliva samples for cortisol estimation approximately every three hours in a 1-week time-sampling assessment. Multilevel analysis will be used to determine whether problem-solving style is related to self-reported and objectively-measured stress.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the unusual effectiveness of Virus-Like Particle (VLP) vaccines made in plants
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODIES; CELLULAR IMMUNITY; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; IMMUNE RESPONSE; INNATE IMMUNITY; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; TRANSIENT TRANSFECTIONOF PLANTS; VACCINES; VIRUS-LIKE PARTICLES (VLPS); VLPS MADE IN PLANTS
Abstract-Résumé: Nanoparticle vaccines can be highly effective but are generally quite expensive to make. A small biothecnology company in Quebec City (Medicago Inc) has found a way to make tiny virus-like particles (VLP) inexpensively in plants. When one or more viral proteins are placed on the surface of these VLP, they can act as powerful vaccines. Since there is no viral genetic information in the VLPs, these candidate vaccines are also very safe. We have developed animal models (mouse and ferret) and have performed 3 clinical trials of candidate VLP vaccines bearing either the H5 hemagglutinin of the highly dangerous avian flu virus or the H1 protein of the recent pandemic flu (a forth human trial is on-going). Results from both  animal models and human trials suggest that these vaccines are unusually effective at stimulating strong immune responses. Preliminary data suggests that these vaccines work well administered by needle in either the muscle or the skin (animals. human) or inhaled into the nose (animals). For several years now, we have been working with Medicago to better understand how these plant-made vaccines work. So far, we have shown that the VLP vaccines interact rapidly with both animal and human immune cells to promote both immediate (innate) and long-lived (adaptive) immunity. We propose to continue these studies in more depth to fully understand what elements within the VLP drive this effect. We have also succeeded in making VLP vaccines with influenza HA protein on the surface and a fluorescent molecule (eGFP) on the inside. We have just begun to use these unique reagents to study how the VLP vaccines interact with individual immune cells and how they move within the immune system. The studies we propose are critical to understanding how these extraordinarily promising vaccine candidates actually work.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural Coding and Interactions for Human Brain Regions Involved in Hand Actions
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN STIMULATION; COGNITIVE NEUROSCIENCE; CONNECTIVITY; FRONTAL CORTEX; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; GRASPING; PARIETAL CORTEX; REACHING; SENSORIMOTOR CONTROL; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: Research from my lab investigates how the human brain controls hand actions like reaching, grasping and tool use. We have identified human brain networks involved in different aspects of these actions. Past theories have emphasized simple properties of single areas and differences between areas.  We want to provide a richer and more realistic understanding of how specific brain areas contribute to hand actions. Moreover we must consider how these areas interact with one another and change with different goals.   To do this research we will use two techniques. First human brain imaging (functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI) will be used to examine brain activation. Using fMRI we will apply a new analysis approach (sometimes called "brain reading") to decode brain activation patterns. Second, we will use human neurostimulation (transcranial magnetic stimulation, TMS) to examine whether briefly perturbing single brain areas affects action performance. In addition, we will apply TMS to multiple brain regions simultaneously to examine how these areas interact.   These projects will enable us to understand the processing and interactions of brain areas that control hand actions. The knowledge from normal healthy subjects will help us understand how goal-directed actions are disrupted in patients with brain damage or neurological disorders. Developments in technologies (neural prosthetics) may one day enable patients - for example amputees or patients with spinal cord injury - to use brain signals fed into a computer chip to control movements of an artificial arm. Our research will provide an important stepping stone for such technology: we are developing a richer and more realistic understanding of the brain networks involved in planning and controlling complex hand actions.  Importantly our research studies involve naturalistic actions performed on real objects - factors that are critical in bridging the gap between basic research and everyday life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Large-scale analysis of complex genetic suppression networks
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLEX GENETIC DISEASE; COMPLEX TRAITS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENETIC INTERACTIONS; SUPPRESSION; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Scientists now know that the ability of cells to grow and divide is governed by thousands of genes and that the function of genes is remarkably conserved from simple yeasts to human cells.  Our group has pioneered methods that take advantage of the experimental accessibility of the yeast model system to understand how genes work together to create healthy cells or to produce a disease state.  We have developed a unique robotics lab called GenNet that allows us to automate yeast genetic screens.  We have used GenNet to produce the first maps of genetic interactions, providing a view of the 'wiring diagram' of a cell.  We now propose to expand our GenNet platform to allow us to explore genetic interactions that are often associated with human diseases.  We are particularly interested in understanding a phenomenon called genetic suppression in which lesions in one gene compensate for the deleterious effects of mutations in another.  Suppression provides a powerful tool for identifying new relationships between genes and their corresponding pathways in the cell. Moreover, suppressors of mutations associated with a human disease gene represent potential targets for therapeutic intervention.  So far, there have been no methods developed for systematic analysis of genetic suppression, and we aim to produce the first complete 'network' of genetic suppression for any organism.  We expect that our diagram will be an invaluable tool for predicting genetic interactions relevant to many complex human diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Expanding the number of treatable intellectual disabilities through an integrated "-omics" approach
Keywords-MotsClés: DISCOVERY; GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY; INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; METABOLOMICS; WHOLE EXOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Intellectual disability (ID) affects 2-3% of children and adults, or 140-210 million people worldwide. Defined strictly as low IQ, ID can have devastating lifelong effects on all aspects of life. The health cost of ID equals that of stroke, heart disease and cancer combined. The burden on families is incalculable. In most cases of ID, we do not know the cause (the majority is genetic), and so cannot provide effective treatment. ID can be an unchangeable fate for a child.  Via our "Treatable Intellectual Disability Endeavour in British Columbia" (TIDE-BC) research, we found 81 published ID conditions that could be treated for underlying cause. These "inborn errors of metabolism" usually affect important enzymes and are treated using special diets, medications or stem cell transplants. In TIDE-BC, by careful screening, we identified treatable causes of ID in 5% of patients so far. In some cases, treatment has completely changed the child's life.   Here, our team of doctors and scientists will use a comprehensive and individual approach to discovering more treatable genetic causes of ID. We have studied 8 families so far, and found one new treatable cause and five probable causes. Next ,we expand our approach in a total of 50 families, and the results will be directly implemented it into clinical practice via TIDE-BC. Ultimately, our aim is to be able to quickly diagnose the cause of ID in our patients, so we can provide correct treatments to each child to prevent brain damage and optimize health outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Living-and-Dying with Fatal Chronic Conditions: Understanding Narratives of Liminality
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CHRONIC FATAL ILLNESS; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE LUNG DISEASE; FAMILY; HEART FAILURE; LIFE-THREATENING ILLNESS; LIMINALITY; NARRATIVE INQUIRY; QUALITATIVE
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, the leading causes of death include fatal chronic conditions such as chronic kidney disease, heart failure, chronic obstructive lung disease, and advanced cancer. Improved symptom management has created a new phase where people with these fatal chronic conditions are living longer in between relative health (with complex symptom management) and impending death. Although knowledge and understanding of chronic illness and palliative care are increasing, there is little known about peoples' experiences of living with the uncertainties of fatal chronic conditions where life may continue with surprisingly good quality of life or end suddenly with an illness event. While research has provided knowledge about the needs of informal or family caregivers during the palliative phase, it is also important to understand the perspectives of family members of those with fatal chronic conditions. Families are often critical in providing the necessary support for patients to remain independent while at the same time facing death. It is vital to understand how patients and their families want to be engaged in facing uncertainty and impending death. Through listening to the stories of people living with fatal chronic conditions and their families, this narrative study will further clarify how the disruptions, contradictions and uncertainties of living with these conditions change over time. Knowledge of peoples' needs during this liminal or in-between time can assist in avoiding over treatment, address issues in the coordination of care, and promote effective use of limited health care resources. Most importantly, a better understanding of patient and family experiences will assist in developing meaningful supports and resources to foster patient-centered care and improve quality of life for people living-and-dying with fatal chronic disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Traffic-Related Air Pollutants and the Transplanted Lung
Keywords-MotsClés: AIR POLLUTION; AIRWAY INFLAMMATION; LUNG TRANSPLANTATION; TRAFFIC-RELATED AIR POLLUTION
Abstract-Résumé: Large population studies have identified a link between the development of heart and lung diseases, and exposure to air pollutants, especially those arising from vehicle emissions. How this occurs is not well understood. In fact, the best way of assessing relevant pollutant exposures and its health impact is not clear.     We believe that the best way to understand the impact of air pollutants on lung health is to use a comprehensive set of tools that will measure pollutant levels externally (i.e. pollutants outside and at home) and internally through the analysis of lung fluid, blood and urine, while assessing the body's physiological responses at the same time. Such a tool is useful only if it is scientifically valid, cost effective and convenient to apply using routine clinical samples (e.g. blood and urine).    We have developed a comprehensive set of tools to evaluate pollutant exposures from vehicle emissions and the consequent physiological responses. We plan to apply this set of assessments in a group of lung transplant patients at the Toronto Lung Transplant Program. They are the ideal type of patient for this study as we monitor these patients closely as part of the routine post-transplant care. Therefore, we have the ability to measure the extent of pollutant exposure over time, and to identify onset and timing of disease development without placing significant additional burdens on the patients. In addition, these patients take anti-rejection medications which disrupt the normal immune responses and make them more susceptible to the harmful effects of pollutants. The new lungs are normal at the time of transplantation. However, a high risk of developing airway disease begins precisely on the date of transplantation.    Our goal in conducting this study is to develop a validated and cost-effective set of tools that can be used in future studies of more common diseases to determine the causal relationship between specific pollutants and health outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a protocol for the use of electromyography arrays in the assessment and treatment of neuromuscular impairment in those with knee osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; ELECTROMYOGRAPHY; ELECTROMYOGRAPHY ARRAY; GAIT; KNEE OSTEOARTHRITIS; MUSCLE ACTIVATION; MUSCLE STRENGTHENING; NEUROMUSCULAR CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is characterized by cartilage damage resulting in pain, stiffness and decreased function. Over 4.4 million Canadians have OA, with a yearly economic impact of $7.6 million. This will worsen due to the aging population and obesity. The knee is most often affected, and more difficulty with activities such as walking and climbing stairs is reported by those with knee OA than any other medical condition. Because economic and personal burdens of knee OA increase as the disease worsens, treatments to slow progression are needed. Non-pharmaceutical and non-surgical treatments are recommended due to low cost and treatment risk. High knee loads play a role in progression, and a main research focus in the Motion Analysis and Biofeedback laboratory is developing knee OA treatments and looking at how they affect loading, pain and function. Muscle impairments (ex. decreased strength, changes in activity patterns) are reported with knee OA. Studies have looked at how exercise improves strength, but not at how patterns of muscle activity change. This is important, because patterns of activity can increase knee loading. Our research will use a novel technique to examine muscle activity, letting us look at patterns of activity within a single muscle. This will give new information about the role of muscle activity in knee loading. This is the first time this has been done in those with knee OA, so the first objective will be to develop a standardized protocol. The protocol will be used to assess changes in muscle activity following an exercise program. Because we can get more detailed information about what is going on in different parts of each muscle, this technology will allow us to develop patient-specific programs to target muscle impairments. Combined with clinical outcomes (pain and function), this research will provide new information needed to guide conservative treatment, thus improving quality of life while minimizing healthcare costs.

OrgNm: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (Toronto)/Centre de toxicomanie et de santé mentale
TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroinflammation in Major Depressive Disorder and Treatment Resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: DEPRESSION; INFLAMMATION; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: According to the World Health Organization, clinical depression is the leading cause of death and disability in moderate to high income nations, affecting up to 5% of Canadians at any one time. While currently available treatments often help, up to 40% of clinical depressions do not adequately respond. It is likely that clinical depression involves several biological mechanisms and that present treatments miss some of these mechanisms. The current study will investigate the possibility that inflammation is one of these overlooked mechanisms that is creating clinical depression.   We think that an inflammatory response is part of this illness, as increased markers of inflammation outside the brain have been linked with depressive symptoms and exposures that create inflammation also create depressed mood. Also, a previous study found that substances that stimulate inflammation (called cytokines) are increased in the brain. However, no studies have examined whether markers of inflammation are present in the brain in people who are having clinical depression.  We propose to brain scan people with clinical depression using a new kind of brain imaging method that can detect inflammation in the brain.  Also, since we think present treatments do not affect brain inflammation, we wish to see if people with treatment resistant clinical depression have brain inflammation.  This would be the first study to look at brain inflammation in people suffering from clinical depression.  If we see increased brain inflammation in clinical depression and treatment resistant depression, then reducing brain inflammation may become a way to treat clinical depression.

TitreApplicationTitle: The neurobiology of clinical placebo in chronic pain patients
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN MARKERS; CHRONIC PAIN TREATMENT; CLINICAL PLACEBO RESPONSE; NEUROIMAGING; PAIN; RANDOMIZED DOUBLE BLIND CLINICAL TRIALS
Abstract-Résumé: This project proposes to study the brain circuitry of the placebo effect in patients suffering from chronic pain using randomized double blind clinical trials (RCT) combined with brain imaging. While previous studies have revealed the brain networks involved in the experimental placebo response in healthy individuals, the neural basis of the clinical placebo response underlying sustainable and long lasting relief of chronic pain observed in the setting of clinical studies remains unknown. It is currently very difficult, if not impossible, to dissociate the effectiveness of a treatment independently from the placebo effect in clinical trials. Recent studies conducted in Dr Apkarian's laboratory suggest that brain-imaging techniques could accurately predict the patients' propensity to respond to clinical placebo. Building on these findings, the present project aims at dissociating the neurobiological placebo response from the NSAIDs response (naproxen 500mg) in a treatment of chronic back pain utilizing the setting of a RCT. Being able to identify a priori placebo responders from non-responders will permit to dissociate the actual effect of the pharmacological response independently from the placebo response in the treatment. The overall objectives of this project are (i) identifying brain markers predicting the placebo propensity in a large sample of chronic pain patients and (ii) dissociating the placebo effect from the active treatment, and (iii) determining the importance of the placebo response in the treatment of chronic pain. This project is therefore novel and important for better assessing drug effectiveness in RCT and improving the safety of the patients by introducing the opportunity of using the placebo treatment to better manage chronic pain by reducing exposure to undesired side effects that all active treatments invariably impart to recipients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Building a Social Policy Framework for the Health and Well-being of Mi'kmaq Communities: A Two-Eyed Seeing Approach
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; SOCIAL POLICY AND HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: In many First Nation communities, a high percentage of the population depends on social assistance for some or all of their income. This makes policy and programs that set the rules for receiving assistance, and that provide supportive services, an important area of public administration. Research has shown that life on social assistance is characterized by poverty, stress, insecurity and parenting challenges, which contribute to negative outcomes in health and well-being.  The Mi'kmaq in Nova Scotia, living in 13 communities, have the opportunity to design social policies and programs related to social assistance that are suited to their culture and community conditions. This project undertakes research on how dependence has arisen historically and the forces that contribute to dependence today. In its action phase, the project supports the Mi'kmaq in developing a social policy framework that will serve them well in the future.  The project takes a "two-eyed seeing" approach, a concept developed by Mi'kmaq elders. Two-Eyed Seeing refers to looking at something with one eye that draws on Indigenous knowledge, using the other eye to draw on Western knowledge, and using both these eyes together, for the benefit of all.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of a Smartphone Intervention on Quitting Smoking in a Young Adult Population of Smokers: A Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR MODIFICATION; CANCER PREVENTION; POPULATION HEALTH; PSYCHOSOCIAL DETERMINANTS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SMARTPHONE APPLICATION; SMOKING CESSATION; SOCIAL MEDIA; TOBACCO STRATEGIES; YOUNG ADULTS
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, tobacco causes over 37,000 deaths annually & about one-third of cancers. The economic impact of tobacco related illness in Canada is also significant, with an estimated 2.2 million acute hospital stays and $4.4 billion in direct health care costs. Young adults have the highest smoking prevalence (23%) & 69% of young adult cell phone users are smartphone subscribers. While current evidence supports the effectiveness of text messaging for smoking cessation, to date no controlled trials have been done on the use of smartphone cessation apps. Smartphones provide greater functionality than mobile phones. The interactive nature of smartphones & their ability to integrate information, motivational techniques, links to support networks & collect real-time data is promising for smoking cessation. An in-depth look at existing quit smoking apps found that none were based on clinical practice guidelines for tobacco; therefore, were less likely to be effective. To address this gap, investigators developed an evidence-informed smoking cessation app that has been piloted with over 300 smokers. This study will be the first to examine a smartphone smoking cessation app for young adult smokers using a randomized controlled trial. The primary aim will be to determine the effectiveness of the app on quitting smoking. Secondary aims of this study include examining: 1) proximal outcome measures of cessation behaviour; 2) satisfaction, extent of app use, and use of NRT and other cessation services; 3) mediators of cessation outcomes between conditions; and 4) the incremental cost-effectiveness.  A usual-care, self-help guide will act as the control condition. The long-term potential of an effective smartphone-based innovation to reduce tobacco use will impact government health care spending & save the young adult population from the morbidity and mortality associated with smoking, improving the overall population health of Canadians in the process.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of a tailored virtual intervention as an instrument of prevention and therapeutic support to improve the health of PLHIV and reduce comorbidity associated with HIV
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENCE; HEALTH BEHAVIOURS; HIV COMORBIDITIES; ONLINE RCT; SELF-MANAGMENT BEHAVIOURS; TAILORED; VIRTUAL INTERVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Formerly considered a terminal illness, HIV infection is today classified as a chronic disease. The advent of a powerful antiretroviral therapy (ART) has contributed to reduce morbidity and mortality substantially among persons living with HIV (PLHIV). However, the long-term use of these drugs, the normal aging process and the presence of certain risk factors have been found in recent years to be associated with the appearance of metabolic disorders. To prevent the emergence and evolution of comorbid problems such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease, it is essential that PLHIV adopt health behaviours, namely, ceasing smoking, engaging in physical activity, and following a healthy diet. Unfortunately, the literature suggests that smoking is actually considerably more prevalent among PLHIV than in the general population (50-70%) and that physical activity levels are lower among PLHIV than in the healthy population. The fact that PLHIV are at higher risk for cardiovascular disease and diabetes owing to ART and the aging process and that they present lower levels of health behaviours will place an acute stress burden on an already taxed healthcare system, particularly in the area of chronic illness care. In addition to adopting health behaviours, PLHIV must make a constant and perpetual effort to manage their antiretroviral drug intake. Treatment adherence among PLHIV has been the focus of a good deal of research in the past decade and warrants being pursued on an ongoing basis for a simple reason: less than two-thirds of PLHIV have been found to adhere optimally to treatment. Against this background, we are proposing a clinical innovation in the domain of information and communications technologies that offers a new model of accessible care delivery for the PLHIV clientele across Canada. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of a tailored virtual intervention to support PLHIV in managing the demands inherent to their health condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sexual desire emerges from arousal: Testing a model of responsive desire in women with and without sexual difficulties.
Keywords-MotsClés: HORMONES; SEXUAL AROUSAL; SEXUAL BEHAVIOUR; SEXUAL DESIRE; SEXUAL DYSFUNCTION; SEXUAL INTEREST/AROUSAL DISORDER; SEXUAL PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGY; WOMEN'S SEXUALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Sexual health is an integral component of physical and mental quality of life. Sexual arousal and desire problems affect up to one third of women, yet effective and safe treatments do not yet exist. Recently, changes to the way sexual arousal and desire problems are conceptualized have been proposed by sexuality researchers, such that sexual arousal and desire are no longer distinct experiences where desire leads to arousal. Instead, sexual desire is triggered by, or emerges, from experiencing sexual arousal. This new model of sexual response may be beneficial to women's health because it more accurately captures women's experience of their sexuality and better explains women's experiences of sexual difficulties.  This model has not, however, been scientifically tested to determine which aspects of sexual arousal trigger sexual desire, and whether these aspects differ for women with and without sexual arousal and desire difficulties. Our primary objective is to understand the relationships among sexual arousal, sexual desire, and sexual health in women. We will assess sexual arousal in women with and without sexual arousal and desire difficulties using physiological, psychological, and hormonal measures. We will then follow women after participation and collect behavioural and self reported measures of their experience of sexual desire.  Understanding the relationship between sexual arousal and desire will create gender-specific knowledge about women's sexuality and about the causes of women's sexual dysfunctions. This outcome is vital given the unsuccessful history of applying male based models of sexual functioning to women. The proposed research will have direct implications for identifying risk factors for sexual arousal and desire problems, inform treatment decisions, and decrease the burden of sexual dysfunction and its negative impacts for Canadian women.

TitreApplicationTitle: Recurrent Somatic DICER1 Mutations:  Functional Implication and Role in Oncogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; BIOINFORMATICS; CELL CULTURE; DICER1 MUTATIONS AND CANCER; EMBRYONIC DEVELOPMENT; MICRORNA; ONCOGENESIS; RNA PROCESSING; SEQUENCING; TERATOMAS
Abstract-Résumé: Many cancers are caused by the abnormal production of normal or mutated proteins from our genes. An important means that determines which proteins are made by our cells occurs just before the last step in protein production, when the 'messenger' intermediates of genes are read by the machinery that makes proteins. We have discovered mutations in an enzyme called Dicer that normally produces cellular components that block these messengers thus reducing protein production (published in the New England Journal of Medicine, 2012). In tumours with Dicer mutations the products of Dicer are not made causing the protein building machinery to make proteins they shouldn't. This novel mechanism leads to protein changes that eventually cause cells to become cancerous. While we first found these mutations of Dicer in rare ovarian cancers we have also recently identified these Dicer mutations in uterine cancers, and Dicer is known to be involved in the development of other more common non-ovarian cancers. Therefore, studying the rare cancer mutations will help resolve the many conflicting theories about how Dicer contributes to cancer. Our research will study how Dicer mutations we found affect the behaviour of Dicer, and how Dicer helps determine which proteins are made in a cell. These studies will be performed in both cells and test tube experiments by changing the structure of Dicer and measuring changes in the protein making machinery, the gene-messenger intermediates changed by this machinery, and the proteins that are finally made. From our studies we hope to expose treatment strategies specialized for ovarian and other cancers with Dicer mutations. Our results could also have a much broader impact as changes in the amount of Dicer in a cancer cell, either too much or too little, are often reported. We hope increasing our knowledge on how Dicer controls production of specific proteins that could lead to cancer will lead to more generalisable treatment opportunities.

TitreApplicationTitle: D-dimer testing, tailored to clinical pretest probability, to reduce use of CT pulmonary angiography in suspected pulmonary embolism: A management study. (PE Graduated D-dimer [PEGeD] Study)
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL MANAGEMENT; COHORT STUDY; COST; D-DIMER; DIAGNOSIS; PULMONARY EMBOLISM; VENOUS THROMBOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: A D-dimer test is a blood test that measures proteins that are formed when the body breaks down lung or leg vein clots. If a D-dimer test is normal, it is much less likely that a patient has one of these clots. However, because other illnesses also increase D-dimer levels, an abnormal D-dimer level is unhelpful and other tests need to be performed. If there is concern about a lung clot, this test is usually a lung "CAT" (or "CT") scan.  We recently completed a study in patients with suspected leg clots that showed that, rather than labelling D-dimer results as "positive" and "negative" in the same way in all patients, it is better to use a higher D-dimer cut-off value (i.e., level that separates a negative from a positive result) if, after examining the patient, the doctor thinks that there is a "Low probability" of clots. We now want to apply this new way of using D-dimer blood testing to reduce how often lung CAT scans are needed in patients who may have lung clots.  2,000 patients in 14 hospitals will be assessed as Low, Moderate or High probability for lung clots by their doctor, and then have D-dimer measured. Lung clots will be ruled-out if D-dimer is <1,000 with Low probability, or <750 with Moderate probability. Those who do not have lung clots ruled-out in this way will have a lung CAT scan. Patients who have had lung clots excluded will then be followed for 3 months, expecting that very few will have clots (<1%), thereby confirming the safety of this diagnostic approach. We will also calculate cost savings.  This diagnostic approach will reduce lung CAT scanning by one-third. As 1.1 million North Americans are investigated for lung clots each year, and as CAT scanning is very costly and can have serious side effects, this reduction in CAT scanning is important to patients, health care providers and to society.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of cardiotrophin-like cytokine partners in the immune response
Keywords-MotsClés: APOLIPOPROTEIN E; B CELLS; CYTOKINE RECEPTORS; CYTOKINES; EAE; LEPTIN; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The phenotypes of patients deficient for the gene coding for cardiotrophin-like cytokine (CLC) indicate that this protein has multiple roles in the nervous and immune systems, suggesting that it interacts with multiple partners. We identified two of these partners that could have key roles in autoimmune and Alzheimer diseases. We will investigate the immunoregulatory roles of CLC complexed with these molecules and their functions in models of multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and evaluation of an anatomic model for advanced surgical training
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; GYNECOLOGIC MALIGNANCY; MEDICAL EDUCATION; MEDICAL SIMULATION; SURGICAL THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Introduction:   Traditionally, surgery was taught almost exclusively in the operating room using an apprenticeship system, whereby a trainee observed a master surgeon and then was granted increasing hands-on opportunities over time.  However, resources for this system of training are becoming limited due to the increased expense of operating room time and pressure to use that time with maximum efficiency, concerns about patient safety, and rapid technological advances in surgical techniques.   In this environment, basic surgical skills simulation training has thrived for simple tasks such as knot-tying.   However, there are few tools for advanced surgical simulation training.  Objective:  We propose to develop complex anatomic models for advanced surgical training in our specialty of expertise: gynecologic cancer surgery.  We will focus particularly on surgical removal of the lymph nodes surrounding the large blood vessels of the pelvis which is of importance in operations for cancer of the ovary, uterus, and cervix.  The principles of anatomic model development we develop will potentially improve training across several different surgical specialties.   Methods: To develop the anatomic model, we will use videos of surgical procedures, anatomic studies of cadavers, and the opinions of experienced gynecologic cancer surgeons about the realism of the model.   We will develop platforms by which the model can be used for training in traditional (open) surgery, laparoscopic (key-hole) surgery, and robotic surgery.   Whether practice with the model improves performance will be assessed.   Outcomes:   We hope that this model will contribute to better health outcomes by providing an important training tool for future surgeons.    By incorporating advanced simulation training, we also aim to reduce costs of surgical training by making teaching in the operating room more focused and efficient.

TitreApplicationTitle: Socio-economic status and the comprehension and Use of Nutrition Information among Adolescents in Canada.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIET; HEALTH BEHAVIOUR; HEALTH COMMUNICATION; HEALTH DISPARITIES; HEALTH POLICY; NUTRITION; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Objective: Adolescents are important populations to target for nutrition interventions in Canada given relatively high intakes of calories, fat, sodium and increasing prevalence of nutrition-related conditions within these groups. Adolescence is a period of transition, characterized by increasing independence, a growing role in food shopping for themselves and their families, and long-term eating patterns that can track through adulthood. Nutritional labelling policies, such as the Nutrition Facts table (NFt) on pre-packaged foods, represent a low-cost population-level health intervention. Research suggests nutrition labels may promote healthier food choices when read and used; however, comprehension of the nutrient amounts, serving size and how to compare food limit effectiveness of nutrition labels. In addition, comprehension and use of the NFt varies by socio-economic status. To date, there is little evidence on the effectiveness of nutrition labelling policies among young people. The proposed study will examine socio-economic differences in how young people in Canada use the NFts when choosing and comparing foods, and to test modifications to NFts.        Methods: The study will consist of an online survey with a sample of 1,000 young people (ages 16-18) from across Canada. A between-participants experiment to empirically test the efficacy of the current and modified NFts on comprehension and use of serving size and % Daily Value (% DV) information when choosing and comparing foods will be conducted. Analyses will explore potential differences in the efficacy of the NFts by socio-economic factors such as income, education, immigrant status, and ethnicity.      Potential Impact: The findings will inform regulatory changes to the NFt, and interventions for improving young people's understanding and use of NFts when choosing and comparing food products. Results will provide evidence for communicating nutrition information on NFts and other forms of labelling.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenetics of Cocaine Addiction
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; COCAINE; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; MENTAL HEALTH; SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Drug addictions create a substantial negative health impact on those who are affected by them and often have massive economic and social consequences.  Like many other complex mental health issues, there is some evidence that biological factors contribute to individual vulnerability to addiction.  For example, small changes to the sequence of certain genes may predispose some individuals to develop addiction; however, these changes are unable to explain how every addiction develops.  Scientists have shown that cocaine use is associated with epigenetic changes in animals.  These changes are chemical modifications to the DNA and surrounding proteins that affect the level that a gene is expressed without altering the sequence of the gene itself.  Using post-mortem brain tissue from the striatum, a region that is known to be altered with cocaine use, I will examine epigenetic changes associated with cocaine addiction in humans.  In particular, I will study DNA methylation patterns that mark the transition from recreational cocaine use to cocaine dependence.  Methylated DNA is associated with decreased gene expression and is a stable epigenetic mark.  To study this, I will use high-throughput sequencing on samples from individuals with a history of cocaine dependence, individuals who had cocaine in their systems at the time of death, and those with no history of cocaine use.  These techniques can identify multiple sites of DNA methylation at once and will allow me to identify subtle differences between the groups.   By understanding how biological factors, including epigenetics, influence the development of cocaine addiction, it will be possible to develop more efficient screening and prevention programs.   In addition, characterizing the molecular effects of cocaine use on the structure of DNA will enhance research into the discovery of innovative and personalized treatment options.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metabotropic Glutamate Function in a Neurodevelopmental Model of Schizophrenia.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS OF SCHIZOPHRENIA; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; METABOTROPIC GLUTAMATE RECEPTORS; NEONATAL VENTRAL HIPPOCAMPAL LESION (NVHL) MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a complex mental disorder with an estimated global prevalence of one percent. Symptoms typically appear in the second and early third decade of life at a time when most individuals are entering the most productive part of their life. These symptoms include hallucinations, delusions, social withdrawal, lack of motivation, and problems with learning, memory, and attention. This causes severe impairments in a persons ability to function in all aspects of their life. Individuals with schizophrenia are over represented in prison and homeless populations and have a higher risk of substance abuse. About forty to sixty percent of those afflicted with the condition go on to attempt suicide. The economic costs in Canada are estimated to be over six billion dollars yearly. This is due not only to the cost of healthcare, but as well as the loss of productivity of from affected individuals, and incarceration costs. The exact mechanism behind how schizophrenia develops is unknown, but current theories suggest that during early brain development the wrong connections are made, resulting in symptoms that appear in early adulthood. Researchers use animal models of the disease in order to test theories on schizophrenia, as well as to develop potential drugs. Current evidence has suggested that a specific protein called glutamate works abnormally in schizophrenia. We propose to use animal models to investigate specific details on how glutamate is functioning in these schizophrenia modelling animals, in order to gain knowledge on how the same systems may be changed in humans, and how drug treatments can be targeted towards these changes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Whole-body and muscle myofibrillar protein degradation in response to insulin: a new non-invasive technique for use in elderly and cachectic patients
Keywords-MotsClés: 3-METHYLHISTIDINE; INSULIN; PROTEIN BREAKDOWN; SKELETAL MUSCLE ATROPHY; UBIQUITIN PROTEASOME SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: The muscle loss observed during aging (sarcopenia) and in cancer-associated cachexia is detrimental as it reduces the patient's physical function, autonomy, responses to therapy, immune responses, quality and duration of life.  It could be due to impaired action of insulin in stimulating muscle protein synthesis (PS) and in suppressing breakdown (PB). Both components need to be measured to establish protein balance or net anabolism, but current in vivo techniques to measure muscle PB are too invasive to use in frail subjects. Our objectives are 1) to measure total and skeletal muscle myofibrillar PB in response to high insulin levels, using the dilution of a stable isotope, in healthy humans with the aim of validating a new approach to be used as a non-invasive technique in frail patients and 2) to relate acute changes in muscle PB to the expression of protein and genes of a major proteolytic system in the muscle cells.  This initial study will establish the validity of estimating muscle PB from a surrogate measure in plasma, which would thereafter preclude the need for muscle biopsies and thus be less invasive to use in frail patients.  We can then apply this approach in conditions of increased catabolism and/or impaired anabolism, in aging and cancer cachexia, to help unravel the mechanisms of the associated muscle loss.

TitreApplicationTitle: Highly stable trimerization of HIV-1 envelope based antigens will improve their immunogenicity and capacity to elicit a neutralizing antibody responses
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODY; ENVELOPE PROTEIN; HIV-1; IMMUNOLOGY; TRIMERIZATION; VACCINOLOGY; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Despite recent advances in antiretroviral treatments for HIV-1 infected individuals there still remains no cure or effective vaccine to prevent transmission of the virus. Recent vaccine trials, which have used monomeric HIV-1 envelope protein, have shown some optimism but have yet to induce a broadly neutralizing antibody response.  Since the HIV-1 envelope protein exists as a trimeric spike on the surface of the virus, some researchers have attempted to create a trimeric envelope vaccine, which has been recently shown to illicit a greater immune response compared to a monomeric envelope vaccine. We will attempt to create a stable trimeric HIV-1 envelope vaccine by using novel trimerization domains. This vaccine will be used to immunize a small animal model by both DNA electroporation and as purified protein. We believe this will induce a greater immune response compared to a monomeric envelope vaccine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Individual Patient Data Meta Analysis of the Diagnostic Accuracy of the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9)
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSESSMENT; DEPRESSION; INDIVIDUAL PATIENT DATA; MENTAL HEALTH; META-ANALYSIS; SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: Major depressive disorder (MDD), a disabling condition that negatively impacts quality of life, is present in 10-20% of patients with chronic diseases. Routine screening for depression has been recommended as a way to improve depression management. However, existing studies have not found that screening improves depression outcomes. For depression screening to be effective, screening tools must be able to accurately distinguish between patients with and without MDD. Typically, patients scoring above a cutoff score on a screening tool are considered likely cases of MDD, whereas patients below the cutoff are considered unlikely cases. Many studies have been conducted to attempt to identify optimal cutoff scores to maximize diagnostic accuracy for MDD across a range of screening tools. Most studies are limited, however, by small sample sizes, and do not generate precise accuracy estimates. As a result, different studies often generate different optimal cutoff scores for the same screening tool. Furthermore, published studies often do not provide the same information, making synthesizing information across these studies difficult. In order to overcome these problems, Dr. Thombs has developed a large depression screening data registry to conduct individual patient data (IPD) meta-analyses. IPD meta-analysis involves obtaining original patient data from existing studies and synthesizing the data to obtain precise, unbiased diagnostic accuracy estimates across all possible cutoffs. The registry will also allow us to analyze factors that may influence accuracy, such as gender and medical conditions. This registry is a step towards better understanding whether depression screening is likely to be an effective approach for improving depression management and, if so, will help identify the best screening tools to use. For my project, I will use data from the registry to assess the diagnostic accuracy of the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) depression screening tool.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetics of Radiation-Induced Lung Disease in Mice
Keywords-MotsClés: CONGENIC; GENETICS; MURINE; PULMONARY FIBROSIS; RADIATION; RESPIRATORY
Abstract-Résumé: Pulmonary fibrosis is a disease of the lungs that can occur in individuals who are exposed to thoracic radiation, a common therapy for several types of cancer. Previously, our laboratory has shown that C57BL/6J mice, a common laboratory strain, also develop fibrosis upon radiation treatment.  The goal of this project is to identify genes which may contribute to the development of radiation-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice.  In order to identify these genes, several lines of mice which are being bred in our laboratory will be used.  These mice contain genomic regions from the lung fibrosis-resistant strain C3H/HeJ on a C57BL/6J background.  These C3H regions were previously identified in our laboratory as areas likely to contain genes involved in the development of fibrosis.  The experimental mice will be subjected to thoracic radiation and euthanized when they become ill or 26 weeks following irradiation.  The severity of the lung disease will be investigated using various histological and molecular approaches.  Comparison of the lung disease in these mice to that of C57BL/6J mice will give further information about which regions of the genome contain genes which are involved in the pulmonary fibrosis response.  Knowledge of a patient's susceptibility to radiation-induced fibrosis would be useful in determining the appropriate radiation dosage.

TitreApplicationTitle: Search for non-coding mutations in patients with cblC and mut inborn errors of cobalamin metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMAN GENETICS; METABOLIC DISEASE; MUTATION ANALYSIS; NON-CODING MUTATIONS; PATIENT-FOCUSED RESEARCH; PCR; SEQUENCING; VITAMIN B12
Abstract-Résumé: Inborn errors of vitamin B12 metabolism are rare, recessive genetic disorders. Affected patients cannot properly metabolize vitamin B12, often leading to neurological problems, anemia, developmental delay or death. There are currently nine known classes, each caused by mutations in a specific gene. Being recessive diseases, patients must have a genetic mutation in both the maternal and paternal copies. Patients are classified by functional cell assays performed in our laboratory and the mutations are found by sequencing the patient's DNA in the gene's protein coding region. However, one or both mutations may lie outside this region. Identification of these non-coding mutations is much less common but are likely more prevalent than previously thought due to the relative difficulty in finding them. The goal of this project is to find and characterize non-coding mutations in two of the nine classes: cblC and mut. In our current patient inventory, twenty cblC and eight mut patients are ideal candidates as one or both mutations remain unidentified after DNA sequencing.  An important benefit of this research is that it will provide more knowledge in non-coding mutations' role in causing rare genetic disease. Since they are more complicated to find, their importance has likely been under-represented in research to date. Characterizing these mutations would improve health care delivery for the affected families. For most cases of inborn errors of vitamin B12 metabolism, there are no good therapies available. Since a couple with an affected child has a one in four chance of then having another sick child, family planning is the only option to avoid these diseases' severe effects. Identifying the mutations that cause a child's disease is essential for pre-implantation diagnosis, the process where early embryos are screened for genetic mutations before being implanted in the mother. It also makes prenatal diagnosis, or screening the fetus for these diseases, much easier.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nutrient sensing in the dorsal vagal complex
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN-LIVER AXIS; CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM; DORSAL VAGAL COMPLEX; GLUCOSE-SENSING; HEPATIC GLUCOSE PRODUCTION; HEPATIC LIPID METABOLISM IN VIVO; LIPID-SENSING; MEDIOBASAL HYPOTHALAMUS; PANCREATIC CLAMP; STEREOTAXIC SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: High blood glucose and lipid levels are hallmarks of diabetes, obesity, and/or cardiovascular disease. Thus, a treatment goal is to lower blood glucose and blood lipids by lowering liver secretion of both glucose and lipids. The brain, using mechanisms that sense the body's nutrient state, normally controls glucose and lipid production by the liver.  However, with metabolic conditions like diabetes and obesity, the brain mechanisms that sense nutrients are disrupted, and a dysregulation of glucose and lipid homeostasis ensues.    Our proposed experiments will be performed in rodents. Catheters surgically implanted in specific brain regions and blood vessels will enable direct administration of compounds into the brain (such as nutrients and treatments to block and/or stimulate nutrient sensing pathways) and blood sampling (to measure the production of glucose and lipids by the liver), respectively. State-of-the-art techniques in molecular biology and pharmacology will be used to define the precise components involved in specific brain pathways that control liver fuel output. Our laboratory has experience with these procedures making the proposed experiments more feasible.  This project will be the first to delineate how a specific region in the brain stem senses nutrients to control the liver's release of both glucose and lipids. These findings will reveal new therapeutic molecular candidates/strategies targeting the brain to lower blood glucose and lipids in diabetes and obesity, which will help reduce the risks of diabetic complications and cardiovascular disease. Improved management of heart disease and stroke, diabetes, and obesity will improve the quality of life of the millions of people who are affected by these conditions and reduce the collateral effects on health care and spending.

Abstract-Résumé: We have discovered a new set of proteins that are present in the heart which appear to be critical for translating the calcium signal to the contraction and relaxation machinery. These proteins belong to a well known family of protein kinases that are activated in response to changes in calcium concentration in the cell. These proteins are also important in relaying information to the genome of the heart and control activity of genes involved in the growth of the heart. We believe these proteins to be important targets in heart disease as their family members are deregulated in human heart failure.

Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; AUTOPHAGY; NEUROTOXICITY; OXIDATIVE STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Oxidative stress is a major contributing factor leading to neurotoxicity in acute and chronic neurodegenerative conditions. Apoptosis and Autophagy are triggered in neurons by oxidative stress and are key pathways regulating neuronal survival. This research proposal seeks to understand the signaling pathways that control these cellular pathways in brain cells during oxidative stress. Identification of these pathways will be an important step in the development of novel strategies to treat a variety of neurodegenerative conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Régénération de la peau humaine
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULES SOUCHES; CULTURE CUTANEE; DIFFERENCIATION ET PROLIFERATION DES CELLULES CUTANEES; GENIS TISSULAIRE; PEAU; PLAIES ET BRULES
Abstract-Résumé: Ce projet effectue au Centre LOEX de l'universite Laval s'inscrit dans le cadre de nos recherches en Cellules Souches et Genie Tissulaire qui vise a reconstruire differents organes humains in vitro a partir de cellules postnatales, dont la peau et la cornee (oeil). Il porte sur la regeneration de la peau humaine a partir des cellules souches cutanees postnatales (cellules responsables de la regeneration et du maintien des tissus tout au long de la vie). La peau est un organe fascinant pour l'analyse des cellules souches et de leurs voies de differenciation puisque l'epiderme se renouvelle a tous les 28 jours: il necessite une production continue de nouvelles cellules. Le but du projet est d'ameliorer nos connaissances sur la peau afin de reconstruire de meilleurs substituts cutanes in vitro par genie tissulaire. Nous poursuivrons nos etudes des cellules souches de l'epithelium et des conditions permettant de les preserver dans les peaux reconstruites en laboratoire. Nous analyserons egalement les signaux provenant du derme ou de l'epithelium qui favorisent le maintien des cellules souches ou leur differenciation. De plus, les signaux intermediaires impliques dans la mort des cellules epidermiques induite par la kinase DLK seront identifies. Les retombees cliniques de notre projet sur la peau se situent d'abord dans le domaine de la guerison des plaies chroniques tels les ulceres cutanes ou les blessures graves comme celles dont souffrent les grands brules. Il s'agit d'ameliorer la production de substituts cutanes vivants (epiderme autologue, peaux reconstruites) qui est effectuee par le LOEX pour le traitement des brules depuis plus de 25 ans. Une retombee de ces recherches fondamentales sur la peau est la decouverte de l'implication de DLK dans une maladie de l'oeil, le glaucome (Welsbie D.S. et al, PNAS, 2013 sous presse), grace aux outils qui ont ete elabores pour nos etudes du role de cette kinase dans la peau.

TitreApplicationTitle: Our Health Counts Toronto:  Developing a Population Based Urban Aboriginal Cohort to Assess and Enhance Individual, Family, and Community Health and Wellbeing
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; HEALTH ASESSEMENT SURVEY; HEALTH CARE UTLIZATION DATABASE LINKAGE; RESPONDENT DRIVEN SAMPLING; URBAN ABORIGINAL HEALTH CARE ACCESS; URBAN ABORIGINAL HEALTH STATUS; URBAN ABORIGINAL POPULATION HEALTH ASSESSMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Over half of the Aboriginal people in Canada now live in cities.  The number of Aboriginal people living in cities is growing rapidly.  We don't have good systems in place to understand the specific health needs of Aboriginal people living in cities.  This is a big problem for planners and health workers who want to make sure that urban health and social services meet the needs of all people in cities, including Aboriginal people. In this study we will work in partnership with Aboriginal organizations and city health planners to build a good set of information regarding the health of Aboriginal people living in the city of Toronto.  We will do this using a new way of finding Aboriginal people called respondent driven sampling.  Once we find a group of Aboriginal adults, youth and children, we will interview them and ask permission to look for their health care usage records as a group in the existing system of health information (where it is currently hidden).   Once we have organized the results of the survey interviews and health care usage records we will work with Aboriginal organizations and city health planners to put this information to use in the planning of health services.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of osteoclast formation and function in bone microenvironment
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEMIA; ARTHRITIS; BONE; CANCER METASTASES; CO-STIMULATORY RECEPTORS; OSTEOCLAST
Abstract-Résumé: Musculoskeletal disorders affect people of all ages, severely compromising their health and well-being.  The destruction of bone is characteristic of several classes of diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis, and periodontitis. Osteoclasts are the cells responsible for resorbing bone in healthy tissue (to mainain good bone quality) and abnormally in these disorders. The molecular factor RANKL has been identified as a critical stimulator for osteoclast formation and function, and was shown to play an important role in mediating bone destruction in inflammatory arthritis, periodontitis, and cancer metastasis to bone. However, we have recently found that although RANKL is necessary during initial stage of osteoclast formation, in the later stages, proliferating bone marrow cells produce factors that can substitute for RANKL and induce successful osteoclast formation.  The proposed studies will address the role of co-stimulatory receptors and their potential ligand identified during previous cycle of funding, in mediating osteoclast activation by proliferating cells in pathological situation of bone metastasis from breast cancer and physiological situation of recovery from bleeding. The results of these studies may lead to the development of novel targeted therapeutic interventions for inflammatory arthritis, metastatic bone disease and hematolytic anemias.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of microRNAs in pancreatic cancer metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: METASTASIS; MICRORNAS; PANCREATIC CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is one of the leading causes of death in North America. Almost 90% of cancer-related deaths are due to metastasis, a process whereby cancer cells spread from the primary to distant sites within the body. The latter highlights the necessity to elucidate the mechanisms and players involved in the metastatic process.        MicroRNAs are small molecules that are found inside cells. They have the ability to control the way cells function, and thereby interact with other cells. Recent studies have also implicated microRNAs with tumour progression. Intriguingly, a recent groundbreaking study by the laboratory of Dr. Douglas Hanahan has identified a number of microRNAs that are associated with pancreatic cancer metastasis in mouse models. Preliminary data suggest that several may act alone or together to promote pancreatic cancer metastasis to the liver.        The goal of the current project is to further characterize and identify which microRNAs have the ability to enhance the capability of pancreatic tumour cells to metastasize to other tissues. For this purpose, we will first use mouse models of pancreatic cancer. Once we identify the microRNAs that have the capacity to increase the metastatic ability of pancreatic tumours, we will then examine whether these microRNAs are potentially associated with pancreatic cancer metastasis in human patients. We will finally attempt to understand how they influence tumour spread, for example whether they affect the way tumour cells interact with neighboring cells or invade the surrounding tissue.        This study will further the understanding of the metastatic process, and may aid in the design of therapeutic strategies aiming to inhibit metastasis, and therefore improve survival of cancer patients.
