TitreApplicationTitle: Comparison of Magnetic Resonance and Ultrasound Elastography with Liver Biopsy for Noninvasive Staging of Liver Fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ACOUSTIC RADIATION FORCE IMPULSE (ARFI); CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE; CIRRHOSIS; DIAGNOSTIC PERFORMANCE; LIVER BIOPSY; LIVER FIBROSIS; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI); QUANTIFICATION; SENSITIVITY AND SPECIFICITY; TRANSIENT ELASTOGRAPHY (FIBROSCAN)
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic liver disease can be difficult to diagnose because symptoms can be vague. In some cases, the liver may already be damaged without any symptoms. Chronic liver disease from any cause can lead to liver fibrosis, a process of tissue scarring in response to injury. Over time, fibrosis can evolve toward cirrhosis, an advanced stage where liver function is disrupted. Once cirrhosis is established, patients have an increased risk of developing gastrointestinal bleeding, liver cancer and liver failure that may require transplantation. To obtain a diagnosis of chronic liver disease, a biopsy is currently needed. A liver biopsy involves inserting a needle inside the liver to remove a small piece of tissue which is then examined under a microscope to visually determine the amount of fibrosis. Liver biopsy is an invasive procedure with a risk of major complications such as bleeding in 0.5%. The goal of this study is to compare three noninvasive technologies called magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), acoustic radiation force impulse (ARFI), and transient elastography (Fibroscan) for the staging of liver fibrosis. If MRE superiority is demonstrated, this study will open the possibility of MRE as an adjunct tool in the diagnosis of cirrhosis. Used in combination, these methods may reduce the need for liver biopsy in the future. A clinical imaging trial will be performed to compare MRE, ARFI and Fibroscan. This study is an important step towards developing a noninvasive diagnostic method in chronic liver disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel unimolecular combination models for selective tumour targeting: A tandem approach to the enhancement of chemoselectivity and abrogation of chemoresistance
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST; EGF; EGFR; HER1; HER2; OVARIAN
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer cells are protected by several proteins that prevent them from dying. These proteins allow them to communicate with the body and particularly to receive message telling them to multiply. Cells that are normal, receive a message to stop multiplying when their job for the body is over. However many cancer cells do not have this stop signal and continue to grow unnecessarily. One class of protein responsible for this behaviour is called "growth factor receptor". In some cancer cells these growth factor receptors are at high levels and most of the time, they do not need to receive a message from the body to tell the cancer cell to divide and more importantly when they feel that the cancer cells are exposed to cancer drugs they launch a message to activate and recruit other proteins that can shield them against the action of anticancer drugs. Therefore these growth factor receptors can not only unnecessarily activate the cancer cells to multiply but also to defend themselves against cancer drugs. Despite the common knowledge that the defence against anticancer drugs is mediated by several proteins, cancer drug researchers persist in making drugs that can block one protein and these drug are classified as "single-targeted". The purpose of the current proposal is to make molecules that are multi-targeted and can hit the cells at several of these shielding proteins in order to make them more sensitive to cancer drugs and ultimately stop the proliferation of cancer cells. We will engineer molecules according to a "divide-and-conquer" trategy whereby these agents will penetrate the cells as a single molecule that will be allowed to degrade into several pieces, each of them being targeted to one of the disordered proteins. This strategy will lead to more efficacious anticancer drugs and is now called "combitargeting".

TitreApplicationTitle: Selective Translation of HIV-1 mRNAs: Mechanism and Effect on Host Innate Immune Responses
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV; INNATE IMMUNITY; RNA PROCESSING
Abstract-Résumé: Upon entry into a cell, viruses have two objectives; to maximize the production of progeny virions while minimizing the activation of innate immune sensors that will limit virus replication. Recent work by our group has demonstrated that HIV-1 inhibits host cell protein synthesis, an activity essential to the activation of the innate immune response. However, we have also determined that HIV-1 uses a novel strategy to ensure efficient expression of its own proteins. Understanding how each of these processes is regulated will provide new insights to enhance the innate immune response to HIV-1 and provide tools to selectively inhibit HIV-1 gene expression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying host genetic factors that affect the interplay between M. tuberculosis and macrophages.
Keywords-MotsClés: HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; HUMAN GENETICS; IMMUNOLOGY; MACROPHAGES; MYCOBACTERIUM TUBERCULOSIS; QUANTITATIVE TRAIT LOCI; REGULATORY NETWORKS; RNA SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) is a major public health problem. One-third of the world's population is estimated to be latently infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB), the etiological agent causing TB, and active disease kills nearly 2 million individuals world-wide every year. A striking feature of TB is that only 10% of infected individuals develop the disease. While a significant proportion of inter-individual variation in susceptibility to TB can be attributed to environmental factors such as malnutrition or poor hygienic conditions, several lines of evidence indicate that genetic factors also play a key role to inter-individual differences in susceptibility to TB. However, to date, very little is known about the underlying genetic determinants or mechanisms contributing to differences in susceptibility to TB at the population. Here, we propose to combine expertise in immunology, human and molecular genetics, and statistics, to identify genes and regulatory pathways that contribute to inter-individual variability in the immune response to infection with MTB. Specifically, we will infect macrophages (Mfs) from 100 healthy individuals with MTB, and use techniques from genomics and molecular biology to characterize: i) transcript and protein levels pre and post infection in both the host Mfs and the bacteria, ii) the percentage of Mfs that have been infected with MTB, and iii) the capability of MTB to survive and grow on genetically distinct Mfs. We will then genotype each individual at 5 million polymorphic sites, and correlate each typed locus with the molecular phenotypes described above. This work is expected to yield unprecedented insight into the genetic basis and mechanisms underlying variation in immune response to infection with MTB, as well as to increase our general understanding of inter-individual variation in immune response to infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Environmental Modifiers of Remyelination
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOCRINE DISRUPTING CHEMICALS; ENVIRONMENT; LYSOLECITHIN DEMYELINATION MODEL; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; OLIGODENDROCYTE; REMYELINATION
Abstract-Résumé: In the brain and spinal cord, together referred to as the central nervous system (CNS), oligodendrocytes form the myelin sheath, an insulating membrane wrapped around axons, that is responsible for protection of axons and facilitation of rapid conduction of electrical impulses. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory condition of the CNS where oligodendrocytes, and the myelin that they form, are destroyed. The CNS has the ability to undergo remyelination, a regenerative process where new myelin sheaths are restored to demyelinated axons.  Remyelination is important in MS because it may lead to some degree of recovery of neurological disability in patients. Both genetic and environmental factors contribute to the neurological loss in patients with MS. The study will test whether Endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs) including bisphenol A (BPA), which are found in plasticizers and as pollutants in our environment, impact remyelination.  Another aspect of the project assesses the impact of vitamin D on remyelination, and whether vitamin D prevents the potential of BPA or other EDCs to impair remyelination.  Results may provide new insights into the role of environment in modifying a recovery response in MS.   The significance of this research is emphasized by the inability of current therapies to halt the progression or reverse the long-term disability of MS.  Determining the factors that inhibit successful remyelination is a crucial step in order to design therapies that promote remyelination, and stop or reverse the chronic disabilities involved in MS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving the validity of treatment effect estimates from observational data of uncommon diseases. The scleroderma lung transplant survival model.
Keywords-MotsClés: BAYESIAN; OBSERVATIONAL COHORT DATA; PROPENSITY SCORE; RARE DISEASES; SCLERODERMA; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Scleroderma (also called Systemic Sclerosis (SSc)) is a disease that can affect the skin, joints and internal organs (heart, lungs, kidneys). There is no cure. The leading cause of death for Canadians with SSc is end-stage lung disease from high pressure in the lungs called pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) or scarring of the lungs called interstitial lung disease (ILD). Lung transplant may be a cure for SSc lung disease, but it has potential risks (infection, recurrence of SSc in the new lung or death). Whether lung transplant improves survival is not known. Using a novel research approach, this series of 3 studies will evaluate if lung transplant improves survival in SScPAH and SScILD.   Part 1 will study experts' beliefs about the benefits/risks of lung transplant for people with SSc, will study factors that determine access to lung transplant and will study factors that affect survival. Part 2 will study a computerized, internet-based method of getting experts' knowledge about lung transplant and scleroderma survival. Part 3 will study if lung transplant improves survival by comparing the survival of SScPAH and SScILD with other PAH and ILD patients after lung transplant.   This program of research will be the largest to study if lung transplant improves survival in this deadly disease, and will develop innovative research methods for all researchers who study rare diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: PURE-MIND: A Population-based Study of Covert Cerebrovascular Disease and Its Contribution to Age-Related Cognitive Decline
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; DEMENTIA; MRI; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Symptomatic strokes cause paralysis or other neurological symptoms. However, it is now recognized that for every person with a symptomatic stroke there are up to 10 people who have unrecognized small strokes in the brain. These strokes contribute to the risk of dementia (the medical term for disabling problems with memory and thinking), which affects up to 25% of Canadians during their life. Up to half of dementia is caused by strokes or blood vessel diseases, and most of the rest is caused by Alzheimer's disease, another disease of the brain. Because we have no treatments to stop Alzheimer's disease, the most promising way to prevent dementia is to test treatments to prevent small unrecognized "covert" strokes. However we have very little information on how frequently new covert strokes occur. We also have very little information on what age covert strokes begin to occur at, because most previous studies have focused on the elderly exclusively without also including persons in middle-age.   To address these limitations in our knowledge we are doing a study called PURE-MIND. Our objectives are to: a) find out how commonly covert strokes happen in mid-life, b) identify risk factors for covert strokes that might lead to new ideas for prevention beginning in middle age, before people get dementia in later life, and c) determine the consequences of covert stroke on the speed of thinking.  This is a substudy of a large international study called PURE. The PURE-MIND substudy will enroll 1,500 Canadians age 40-70 who are participating in PURE. The study participants will have a brain MRI scan and cognitive tests. At the end of the study we will have information on how many people have had covert strokes, how it affects their memory, and what the risk factors are. We and others can use this information to plan subsequent studies to test treatments to improve memory and thinking by preventing covert strokes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic analysis of Williams-Beuren syndrome: linking genes with behaviour and cognition
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE REGULATION; MOUSE MODELS; NEURONS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR; TRANSCRIPTOME; WILLIAMS SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Williams syndrome (WS) is a genetic disorder that presents with a complex set of medical and cognitive symptoms.  People with WS have a range of disabilities such as  intellectual impairment, severe anxiety and poor spatial skills, yet have relatively well preserved language abilities and a natural friendliness and empathy. WS is caused by the deletion of a small region on one copy of chromosome 7 that removes key genes involved in the development and function of the human brain. Understanding how these key genes contribute to the features of WS will further our understanding of the genetic basis of cognitive function and give insight into common problems like mental retardation and anxiety disorder. We will use brain cells made from patient blood cells, and mouse models to interrogate the role of specific genes that have been implicated in WS, and so take advantage of this unique opportunity to link genes with human behavior and brain function.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Multi-Centre 2x2 Factorial Randomized Trial Comparing Sliding Hip Screws versus Cancellous Screws AND Vitamin D versus Placebo on Patient-Important Complications and Quality of Life in the Treatment of Young Adult (Ages 18-60) Femoral Neck Fractures (FAITH-2)
Keywords-MotsClés: FEMORAL NECK FRACTURE; INTERNAL FIXATION; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: Each year, 280,000 Americans and 36,000 Canadians break (fracture) a hip. This is a significant cost to the health care system with estimated annual costs reaching a staggering $9.8 billion in the United States and $650 million in Canada. Globally, hip fractures rank in the top 10 causes of disability. While most of these fractures occur in adults over age 65, approximately 100,000 hip fractures occur in patients under age 50 each year worldwide. Hip fractures in younger adults are typically the result of car accidents and other high-energy traumas. Despite the use of modern surgical techniques, 25% of these patients will experience a major fracture healing complication. One factor that may be contributing to their high complication rate is low vitamin D levels. Approximately 75% of trauma patients have vitamin D levels that are too low to maintain adequate bone health. While there is significant research for elderly fractures, there is very little guidance for treating younger adults. We will complete a preliminary (pilot) clinical trial comparing two common surgical treatments, as well as comparing vitamin D supplementation vs placebo tablets on the rates of complications and quality of life in patients under age 60. The pilot study will enroll a total of 50 patients across 10 hospitals in Canada, USA, and India. The purpose of completing a pilot study is to demonstrate a larger definitive trial is feasible and to ensure Canadian taxpayer funding is used efficiently.  Our research group has performed extensive preliminary work to ensure we are proposing a high-impact clinical trial that will benefit the health of Canadians and those abroad. We have experience in completing similar clinical trials that have established Canadian researchers at the forefront of fracture care trials. Our research will benefit the lives of patients who suffer these devastating hip fractures and may also lead to future research that will benefit other patients with difficult fractures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Simple Bone Cysts in Kids (SBoCK)
Keywords-MotsClés: BENIGN TUMORS; BONE; BONE HEALTH; SIMPLE BONE CYST
Abstract-Résumé: Simple Bone Cysts in Kids (SBoCK) is a blinded, multi-center, randomized clinical trial comparing the effectiveness of three standard interventions for the treatment of simple bone cysts in children and adolescents.  Simple bone cysts (SBCs), also known as unicameral bone cysts, are the most common benign lesions in children.  They are often associated with significant pain and fracture and may limit patient's range of movement.  Many treatment options are available for SBCs. While some clinicians may suggest a non-interventionalist approach, current treatment practice variation is enormous ranging from no treatment to those which are highly invasive.   This randomized clinical trial will compare the effectiveness of (1) steroid injections (2) curettage with puncture or (3) curettage with puncture and injection of calcium sulfate pellets for the treatment of SBCs. Using x-rays we will assess healing rates, which patients are at risk for fracture as well as additional prognostic factors.  Patients will be assessed throughout the study to determine the extent of their pain and how this disease is affecting their activities of daily living.   The results of this trial will inform clinical practice and provide Level I evidence regarding the treatment of simple bone cysts.

TitreApplicationTitle: A systematic review and meta-analysis of depression treatment in children and adolescents
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; CHILDHOOD; DEPRESSION; META-ANALYSES; SCREENING; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a leading cause of disability among children and adolescents and is associated with problems that include poor school performance, drug and alcohol abuse, early pregnancy, and suicide. Despite the overall burden of depression, most Canadian children and adolescents with the condition do not receive treatment. Screening for depression is one possible solution. For screening to be considered, it is important to understand the degree to which different treatments are effective in treating depression for children and adolescents. Thus, an important empirical question is the degree to which different available options to treat depression are effective and the degree to which they may harm children and adolescents. The objective of my proposed project is to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy of treatments for MDD, including pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical treatments, in children and adolescents, aged 7 to 18 years. Specifically, I will investigate whether treatment of depression during (a) childhood and (b) adolescence (i) improves symptoms of depression and (ii) reduces the number of children who meet diagnostic criteria for depression. This systematic review will involve multiple sources of evidence, including multiple databases; manual journal searches; reference list reviews; citation tracking of included articles; trial registry reviews; queries of experts in the field; and non-published data from pharmaceutical companies. This study will determine the optimal methods for treating depression among children and adolescents and include an evaluation of evidence of potential harms from each treatment modality. The conclusions drawn from this systematic review and meta-analysis, once disseminated to policy-makers, healthcare providers, and researchers, will inform treatment decisions and will inform the larger review of evidence on whether screening programs are likely to benefit children and adolescents.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mitochondrial Dynamics in Adult Neural Precursor Cell Maintenance and Neurogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT NEUROGENESIS; AGING; MITOCHONDRIA; NEURAL PRECUSOR CELLS; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: It was always believed that the adult brains cannot regenerate damaged brain tissue and that brain cells (neurons) must last throughout life. Recently, it was found that the adult brain contains active stem cells and progenitor cells, which have the capacity to regenerate new neurons.  A major challenge is that most neural stem cells lie dormant in the adult brain and their numbers decline with age. It is therefore essential to identify new strategies to activate and expand the adult stem cell population. Defects in mitochondria, the energy producing powerhouse of the cells, is associated with neurodegenerative diseases. The impact of mitochondrial impairment in adult stem and progenitor cells in the adult brain remains unknown. Our preliminary data shows that adult stem and progenitor cells are highly sensitive to changes in mitochondrial dynamics and loss of mitochondrial function causes a severe impairment in the development of new neurons in the adult brain. In these studies we will manipulate mitochondrial dynamics in an effort to prevent the decline of adult neurogenesis in the aging brain or in neurodegeneration. The overall goal is develop new treatment strategies by which to regenerate damaged brain tissue.

TitreApplicationTitle: PET Imaging Monoamine Oxidase-A in Borderline and Antisocial Personality Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTISOCIAL PERSONALITY DISORDER; BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER; MONOAMINE OXIDASE A; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: People with borderline personality disorder (BPD) suffer from fluctuating mood. BPD has a 2% occurrence in the general population, and is present in approximately 10% of psychiatric outpatient cases, and 20% of psychiatric inpatient cases. The mood can get so extremely unpleasant, that people with this condition often self harm to block out the emotional pain.  Almost 70% of people with BPD will have at least one suicide attempt in their lifetime and they are more likely to complete suicide than any individuals with any other psychiatric disorder. MAO-A is a protein that has increased levels in several conditions of sad mood, and we suspect that MAO-A protein is elevated during this state of severely unpleasant mood that happens intermittently in borderline personality disorder.  Our pilot imaging data of this state shows the highest levels of MAO-A ever reported (more than 50% in 6 subjects).  If this result holds in a larger study, future treatments of borderline personality disorder, when mood is severely unpleasant, should include medications that shut down MAO-A in combination with existing treatments to improve response.  People with antisocial personality disorder are predisposed to violent aggression towards others.  In addition to influencing mood, MAO-A has a role in the developing brain and healthy people with greater levels of aggression and impulsivity are known to have lower levels of MAO-A in the part of the brain called the prefrontal cortex.  We hypothesize that people with antisocial personality disorder who have high levels of aggression and violent behaviour will have even lower levels of MAO-A.  If this is true, future work would focus on trying to reduce the environmental factors that lead to low MAO-A as a strategy to reduce risk for antisocial personality disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiac-derived stem cell therapy to treat Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC DERIVED STEM CELLS; DUCHENNE CARDIOMYOPATHY; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a devastating X-linked muscle wasting disease for which there is no specific treatment. Affecting 1 in 3,500 male births, DMD accounts for 80% of all cases of muscular dystrophy. Boys are diagnosed as toddlers and most are wheelchair bound by age 15. Death often occurs by age 20 from respiratory muscle weakness and cardiomyopathy. More patients are surviving to age 30 thanks to non-invasive home ventilation and corticosteroids, which can prolong ambulation by 2-3 years, reduce the risk of scoliosis, and temper pulmonary decline in the second decade. Corticosteroids are no panacea however, and cause much toxicity; aprroximetly 28% of boys develop intolerable side-effects. A therapeutic breakthrough is therefore urgently needed. Investigational therapies aim to: (1) increase muscle mass and regeneration, (2) decrease muscle inflammation and fibrosis, (3) correct perturbations in cellular calcium handling, or (4) correct abnormal blood flow regulation.  We postulate that stem cell derived from the heart, could simultaneously address all of these therapeutic targets. Indeed, cardiac-derived stem cells have been shown to regenerate heart muscle, reduce inflammation and fibrosis, and grow new blood vessels in common ischemic heart disease, thus restoring normal cardiac function. We now hypothesize that cardiac-derived stem cells constitute an effective novel therapy for the heart in DMD.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Mechanisms by which S. Typhi Senses and Responds to its Environment Within Human Cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL BIOLOGY; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MICROBIOLOGY; RNA-SEQ; SALMONELLA TYPHI; TRANSPOSON MUTAGENESIS; VIRULENCE FACTORS; VIRULENCE GENE REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi) is the causative agent of typhoid fever, an infection that affects 17 million people each year resulting in an estimated 200,000 deaths. Given the importance of this pathogen for global health and the emergence of S. Typhi resistance to commonly used antibiotics, it is imperative to develop more effective treatments. Unlike other Salmonella enterica serovars, which typically cause self-limiting infections of the GI tract, typhoid fever is a systemic infection that can be fatal if left untreated. While there are a number of subtle differences between S. Typhi and other serovars, its enhanced ability to cause dangerous systemic infections in humans is poorly understood. The goal of this research project is to study the unique ways in S. Typhi detects its presence within human cells and the unique responses it mounts to carry out its virulence program within this environment. Recent research by the Galan lab has uncovered a novel toxin that is produced by S. Typhi but not other serovars dubbed typhoid toxin. Typhoid toxin is only produced after S. Typhi has successfully invaded human cells, where it is secreted and taken up by neighbouring cells, often resulting in cell death. This project seeks to understand how S. Typhi ensures the correct location and timing for the production and release of this toxin. Furthermore, using this information we hope to identify and characterize other S. Typhi virulence factors that are regulated in the same manner. Finally, we seek to gain a better understanding of the host cell factors that trigger toxin production. Overall, this project aims to piece together a picture of the unique virulence program of S. Typhi and gain a better understanding of the factors that make it more dangerous than other serovars. We believe that understanding S. Typhi virulence will hold the key to developing novel strategies for the prevention and treatment of the life-threatening infections it causes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating the effectiveness of community based holistic health programming in addressing Inuit food security in Arctic Canada: A case study of The Tukisigiarvik Friendship Centre
Keywords-MotsClés: CLIMATE CHANGE; COMMUNITY FOOD PROGRAMS; COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; FOOD SECURITY; INUIT; NUNAVUT; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Food security has been identified by Arctic communities and Northern governments as a significant challenge facing Inuit communities across Arctic Canada. Accessing sufficient nutritious food is a chronic problem for many community members in Iqaluit, Nunavut and a problem which is being exacerbated by environmental and socio-cultural changes. To address this issue the Tukisigiarvik Friendship Centre (TFC) was created in 2003 by Inuit for Inuit. The TFC provides traditional foods to those in need as well as access to counseling, opportunities to learn traditional skills and a chance to go out on the land for those who may not usually be able to. As such, TFC seeks to not only provide food to those in need - and importantly traditional foods - but also seeks to address the broader socio-cultural determinants of food insecurity. This project will serve to evaluate the effectiveness of  the TFC at three levels: the programs ability to ameliorate food insecurity among those unable to obtain sufficient culturally acceptable food in the face of climatic uncertainty; to address the broader socio-cultural determinants of food insecurity; and to transmit land skills and food preparation skills essential for harvesting and consuming traditional foods (i.e. food availability, quality). This evaluative process will determine the extent to which the TFC is helping to address root causes of food insecurity, and provide potential strategies and recommendations for policy makers and community organizations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining the optimal range of vitamin D intake for cardiovascular health
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOTENSIN II; BLOOD PRESSURE TELEMETRY; CALCIFICATION; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; HYPERTENSION; RECOMMENDED DAILY ALLOWANCE; RENIN; RENIN-ANGIOTENSIN SYSTEM; VITAMIN D DEFICIENCY; VITAMIN D TOXICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Vitamin D, also known as the sunshine vitamin, is in short supply in many modern populations. In particular, a Stats Canada survey in 2010 found that one tenth of Canadians have a deficiency and two thirds may not be receiving optimal levels. Severe deficiencies manifest themselves as rickets and osteomalacia, conditions characterized by the development of soft bones. Canadians are disadvantaged in this regard because they have long winters with long nights and little sunshine. In fact, vitamin D synthesis appears to be insufficient for 5-6 months of the year in Canada. As a result, dietary sources and sometimes supplementation are necessary to maintain healthy vitamin D levels. However, the optimal levels of vitamin D are currently in question. Canada's dietary recommended intake is 600 IU/d for adults and capped at an upper limit of 4000 IU/d, but some researchers suggest these values should be higher.  Although the evidence is not conclusive, many studies have correlated low vitamin D levels with various chronic diseases. This study will help address this uncertainty by investigating the dose-response relationship between vitamin D and cardiovascular health. If this relationship is significant these results will help determine the vitamin D requirements for optimal heart health. Additionally, the safety of high therapeutic doses will be tested to see if the upper limit of vitamin D could be increased without introducing adverse effects.

TitreApplicationTitle: At the intersection of clinical ethics and harm reduction: Clinician perspectives on reducing discharges against medical advice for substance using patients living with HIV and Hepatitis C
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CARE; DECISION MAKING FRAMEWORKS; EQUITY; ETHICS; HIV/AIDS; SUBSTANCE USE
Abstract-Résumé: Existing research suggests that as many as 70% of people living with HIV/AIDs (PHAs) used illicit drugs or reported hazardous alcohol use in the previous year. These findings are concerning because substance use has a negative impact on anti-retroviral treatment (ARV) adherence, HIV disease progression, and HIV transmission. People who use illicit drugs and/or drink hazardously have very high rates of emergency room visits and hospital admissions. However, when they go to the hospital for care they often experience stigma, may receive substandard care, and leave hospital against medical advice. This is complex care and public health issue with important ethical dimensions. We propose to conduct four phase project and improve the capacity to understand and respond to these issues. First, we will complete interviews to understand how substance use among PHA/HCVs influences the care provided by physicians, nurses and social workers in acute care settings. Second, we will develop a framework to analyse the ethical challenges faced by clinicians using existing literature and empirical results. Third, we will host a consultation with key stakeholders (i.e., clinicians, policy makers, PHA/HCVs) to analyse the study findings and begin to develop a framework for ethical decision making as it relates to the care of PHA/HCVs who use substances. Fourth, we will increase our team and develop a larger program of research to test and disseminate a framework for ethical decisional making as it relates to the care of PHA/HCVs who use substances while in hospital.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Chaperone Mechanisms and Functions
Keywords-MotsClés: CYSTIC FIBROSIS; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM; HSP70; INTRACELLULAR TRAFFICKING; J DOMAIN; LONG QT SYNDROME; MOLECULAR CHAPERONES; PROTEIN BIOCHEMISTRY; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; PROTEIN FOLDING
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins are made as linear molecules which must fold into stable three-dimensional structures, and find their correct workplace within cells. Defects in protein folding are the underlying causes of neurodegenerative syndromes including Parkinson and Alzheimer diseases, and genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis. The molecular chaperones are specialized proteins which help other proteins to fold, and are critical cellular defenses against misfolding. A key chaperone is Hsp70, which has important roles in promoting folding but also in selecting proteins for degradation. Importantly, Hsp70 activity depends on co-chaperone proteins which regulate its action. My focus is on the two major co-chaperones, DnaJA1 and DnaJA2, and how they work together with Hsp70. The experimental approach follows two inter-related directions: understanding the biochemical mechanisms by which Hsp70 and its co-chaperones act on proteins, and investigating the cellular division of labour between the co-chaperones. Both of these research directions will be essential to understand and ultimately address the serious health challenges posed by protein misfolding diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chemical biology to study virus entry
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIVIRALS; CYTOMEGALOVIRUS; FUSION; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS; INFLUENZA VIRUS; MEMBRAN CURVATURE; VIRAL DISEASE; VIRAL ENTRY; VIRAL INFECTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Viral diseases continue to be a major cause of disease despite the successful development of many vaccines and 45 antiviral drugs. No vaccines exist against important viruses such as hepatitis C virus, for example. No fully protective vaccines exist against others such as influenza (flu). No treatments exist to cure some chronic viral infections either, such as hepatitis B or herpesvirus. Some viruses such as influenza are extremely variable, which makes it difficult to target them with vaccines or antiviral drugs. Viruses new to the human population continuously emerge, such as SARS and the new SARS-like coronavirus in the UK and the Arabic peninsula. There is even the possibility of the intentional release of very virulent viruses as biological or terrorist weapons. In brief, viral diseases are a continuous threat to human health, and result in a heavy burden to the Canadian health care system and its resources. Viruses have a greater impact on certain marginalized populations. Women, the elderly and the very young are particularly susceptible to viral diseases. We use small chemicals as probes to explore virus functions that are essential for the virus to gain entry into a cell, to reproduce itself within a cell, and to cause disease. A major advantage of our approach is that it provides information and lead compounds for developing novel antiviral drugs. These lead compounds often have several advantages over conventional antivirals. They tend to be effective against several viruses, and they minimize the selection for viral resistance. In the research proposed here, we will continue our studies that have already uncovered a novel family of antivirals, the RAFIs. These antivirals are active against a variety of viruses, including influenza, hepatitis C and herpesviruses. Our proposed studies will result in a better understanding of how viruses enter cells. This new knowledge, in turn, can be used to the development of better antivirals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and Functional Studies of Nonribosomal Peptide Synthetases
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTICS; BIOCHEMISTRY; CANCER DRUGS; CHEMICAL REACTION MECHANISMS; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; ENZYMES; MOLECULAR MACHINES; NATURAL PRODUCTS; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Many of the medicines on which we rely today are produced naturally by earth's flora and fauna. An important class of these compounds is made in fungi and bacteria by massive enzymes called nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs). NRPSs synthesize all sorts of antibiotics, which can kill dangerous fungi and bacteria, as well as compounds that can help us fight off viral infections and cancers. NRPS products include the antibiotic viomycin, used to treat multidrug-resistant tuberculosis; cyclosporin, widely used as an immunosuppressant in organ transplants, which can also inhibit hepatitis virus C replication; and penicillin.  The goal of this research is to expand our knowledge of NRPSs and the mechanisms they employ to synthesize important compounds. We will use biochemistry and biophysics, including techniques known as X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy, to capture three-dimensional pictures of NRPSs at different points in the process of making these natural products. We will study several NRPSs, including the penicillin synthesizing enzyme, and the results of the work will be applicable to all NRPSs and their products. We will answer a range of questions, elucidating the precise details of how building blocks are chemically assembled into the antibiotics, and explaining the large-scale rearrangements these enzymes need to perform to create drugs.  NRPSs hold a vast potential to produce new therapeutics. Because NRPSs are divided into segments, with each segment adding one building block to the compound, we can switch around the order and specific type of segment to produce variants of the compound. Our studies can help us learn how best to rearrange NRPS segments to make millions of new compounds. Among these compounds could be important drugs to fight viruses, antibiotic resistant bacteria, and cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Beyond pain subjectivity: A neuroimaging investigation of multidimensional pain-responses and their related function
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTONOMIC RESPONSE; AVOIDANCE LEARNING; BRAIN; CORTISOL; FACIAL EXPRESSION; FEAR CONDITIONING; INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES; PAIN; SPINAL REFLEX; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Pain is a fundamental experience thought to reflect the vital biological function of the nociceptive system in the protection of the body.  This experience is accompanied by a variety of physiological reflexes (e.g. withdrawal, sweating), and behavioral responses (e.g. facial expression) that vary largely between individuals.  Pain is also though to help us predict and avoid future harm through learning processes. The brain mechanisms involved in the monitoring and regulation of these physiological, behavioral, and functional (i.e. learning) responses are not well understood. The proposed project will be conducted in healthy volunteers receiving series of brief painful but safe electrical stimulations. The research methods involves brain imaging to further understand how brain responses reflect the activation of partly separate sub-systems involved in the monitoring and regulation of multiple physiological, behavioral and functional responses. This research will advance our understanding of basic brain processes involved in pain and will help explain the neural basis for the large individual differences typically observed in various pain responses. This has direct implications for the understanding of individual variability in acute clinical pain and may help understand basic brain processes that may contribute to chronic pain conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Health Impacts of Mining on Aboriginal Communities in British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; BRITISH COLUMBIA; HEALTH IMPACT ASSESSMENT; MINING; OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH; POPULATION HEALTH; SOCIAL AND CULTURAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The current mine approval process in BC and Canada has resulted in many successful applications for mining projects even though health impact assessments have often been inadequate so that impacts on community health, for the duration of a project (i.e. in some cases, over a quarter century from exploration to reclamation), are unknown. There is an urgent need to develop the research foundation, policy and knowledge translation (KT) tools to: 1) better inform the mine planning and development process, 2) improve community health monitoring and the potential to mitigate community health impacts associated with mining, and; 3) ensure economic benefits from mining specifically from provincial revenue sharing agreements and impact benefit agreements) lead to sustainable social and economic community prosperity beyond mining. The overall objective of this project is to develop; using a multi-method integrated KT approach, a collaborative framework that will serve to mitigate the impacts of mine development on the health of communities associated with mine projects and, to maximize mining-related health, social, and economic benefits.

TitreApplicationTitle: Major Determinants of Non-Adherence in Saskatchewan (MD-NAS)
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH-ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; MEDICATION NON-ADHERENCE; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; QUESTIONNAIRES
Abstract-Résumé: Medications for diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol play a critical role in the Canadian health care system because they can reduce the need for emergency hospitalizations and protect against the long term harm from these conditions.  Indeed, people who take these medications regularly tend to live longer and have fewer emergency visits to the hospital compared to those who don't.  However, only half of all people prescribed these medications take them regularly.  As a result, a great strain is place on hospitals because prescription medications are not being used correctly to keep people healthy.       Non-adherence to medications costs billions of dollars per year in Canada because of all the extra hospital visits required in people who don't take their medications.  Non-adherence is often blamed on the cost of drugs, the side-effects of drugs, or poor communication between doctors and patients.  All of these factors are important; however, most of the studies carried out previously have not been able to find out how all of these problems add-up together to cause 1 out of every 2 people to become non-adherent.  Our study will identify the most important predictors of non-adherence so we can begin to find effective ways to fix the problem.      The study will be carried out on people who start new prescription medications for diabetes, high blood pressure, or high cholesterol in Saskatchewan.  All people starting new medications will be identified and followed carefully over the next year using a survey and health records.  We will collect information about the patients, their doctors, and their drugs (including the cost).  By combining all this information in one study, we will be able to identify the most important problems that prevent people from taking their medications regulary.  Ultimately, we think this information will help keep more Canadians healthy and out of hospitals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting colorectal cancer-initiating cells and anti-EGFR therapeutic resistance by manipulating levels of the reactive aldehyde, 4-hydroxynonenal
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-EGFR THERAPY; CANCER STEM CELLS; CHEMORESISTANCE; COLORECTAL CANCER; XENOGRAFT MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the 2nd leading cause of cancer mortality in Canada, with 9,200 deaths annually. We have previously shown that CRCs are initiated and maintained by a subset of colorectal cancer-initiating cells (CC-ICs). There is also increasing evidence in a number of solid tumors that cancer-initiating cells are preferentially chemoresistant. Therefore it is important to understand the biology of these cells in order to develop methods to specifically target the CC-IC subset. In preliminary work we have shown that CC-ICs are very sensitive to level of the reactive aldehyde, 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE). Increased levels of 4-HNE results in increased CC-IC death and potentiates the response to cetuximab, an EGFR-targeted therapy commonly used in the treatment of colorectal cancer. There are existing drugs, already approved for other purposes, that increase 4-HNE levels and it is our plan to use these drugs in combination with anti-EGFR targeted therapies to develop new therapeutic strategies directed at increasing the therapeutic responsiveness of CRCs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional impact of cannabinoids on the visual system
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IMAGING; CANNABINOIDS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; NEUROANATOMY; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES; NEUROMODULATION; NEUROSCIENCE; SYSTEM PHYSIOLOGY; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: Endocannabinoids (i.e. cannabinoids synthesized by the human body) play an important role in a variety of neurobiological functions, including memory, nociception, and synapse formation. They are also present in the human retina. However, their role in vision remains unknown.  In this proposal, we will investigate the functional impact of cannabinoids on the visual properties of neurons comprising the retina and the visual brain. State-of-the-art complementary techniques will be used such as optical brain imaging and multiple recording of neurons.   This project will help us understanding the mechanisms by which endocannabinoids can modify visual perception. It will also increase our understanding on the contribution of endocannabinoids in the visual deficits observed in pathologies in which a dysfunction of the endocannabinoids system has been demonstrated (such as Huntington's and Alzheimer's diseases).

TitreApplicationTitle: Colchicine for Prevention of Peri-Operative Atrial Fibrillation in Patients Undergoing Thoracic Surgery (COP-AF) Pilot Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; COLCHICINE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; THORACIC SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Statement of health problem Patients undergoing surgery are at risk for many complications. Atrial fibrillation (fast chaotic heart beats) is one of the most common serious complications after thoracic surgery. As many as 1 in 4 patients will develop atrial fibrillation after thoracic surgery. Patients who develop atrial fibrillation after surgery often develop worse outcomes such as: death, stroke, longer hospital stay. Strokes after surgery are usualy devastating leaving most patient incapacitated or severely limited (require assistance to perform daily activities of living). Preventing atrial fibrillation resulted in less strokes and shorter hospital stay. Atrial fibrillation occurs when there is excessive inflammation in the body (such as after surgery); regulating the inflammation in the body after surgery resulted in less atrial fibrillation.  Colchicine is a safe and effective anti-inflammatory drug and we anticipate that it will prevent almost half (45%) of atrial fibrillation after surgery.  Objective of project Test if colchicine is effective in preventing atrial fibrillation after surgery. The pilot trial (50 patients) represent an initial foundation for a larger trial with hundreds of patients.  How will you undertake your work? The study is in two major hospitals in Canada; St. Joseph hospital (Hamilton, ON) and University of Manitoba Health Sciences Centre, Winnipeg. The Population Health Research Instituite in Hamilton will be the coordinating site.  Patients will receive colchicine or placebo pill for 10 days after the surgery and will be monitored to see if they develop atrial fibrillation.  What is unique/innovative about your project? The solution we are proposing will represent a safe/cheap medication to prevent a major complication. Effective prevention of atrial fibrillation will result in less strokes and shorter hospital stay.

TitreApplicationTitle: Magnesium Nebulization Utilization in Management of Pediatric Asthma - MagNUM PA Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE ASTHMA; NEBULIZED MAGNESIUM; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Acute asthma is the most common pediatric emergency and a leading cause of hospitalizations in children. Due to genetic and other factors, recommended treatment does not always produce desired results, especially in children with severe attacks. Many children are thus admitted to hospital, particularly these 'non-responders'. This high-risk population may benefit from an addition of another medication such as magnesium  which can be given intravenously or by inhalation.  The intravenous is invasive and usually used as a last resort. Factors influencing its lack of use include belief that an intravenous is usually not needed and concern about side effects of Mg.  In contrast, inhaled magnesium is non-invasive and likely much safer. The research of inhaled magnesium shows promising results but the evidence of benefit is still uncertain. In this definitive study in 8 pediatric emergency departments we plan to find out if children with acute asthma who remain in breathing distress after initial therapy with steroids and inhaled bronchodilators are more likely to be discharged home if they are subsequently arbitrarily assigned to be given 3 treatments of inhaled magnesium with salbutamol compared to those given salbutamol only. We also plan to examine the difference in asthma severity as well as hospital admissions and unplanned medical visits for asthma within one week between these two groups. If inhaled magnesium proves effective, this would decrease hospitalizations in the high-risk population with poor response to current treatment while offering numerous advantages over IV. This would also reduce burden of asthma on inpatient wards and reduce economic burden on both health care system and society.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dishonesty in Children with Severe Conduct Problems
Keywords-MotsClés: CONDUCT DISORDER; DISHONESTY; LYING; SEVERE CONDUCT PROBLEMS
Abstract-Résumé: Conduct disorder is one of the most commonly diagnosed conditions in child mental health centers in North America. While some children already meet clinical diagnostic criteria for Conduct Disorder before the age of 10, many display severe, yet subclinical, symptoms such as fighting, shoplifting, and lying that are yet to meet criteria. Left untreated in early childhood, these early conduct problems place the child at risk for developing full blown Conduct Disorder later on. The limited existing evidence regarding lying in children with conduct problems comes primarily from hearsay reports. The current research program will address this significant gap by using experimental methods to systematically investigate lying behaviors of children with severe conduct problems. We will capitalize on both our unprecedented access to a large population of children between the ages of 6 and 10 with severe conduct problems and our unique expertise and extensive knowledge of the development of lie-telling. In contrast to previous studies that have treated lying as a unitary behavior, we will examine how children with conduct problems lie for prosocial and antisocial purposes, and establish whether and how their lies differ from those of typically developing children. We will also investigate verbal and nonverbal cues associated with children's deception as well as cognitive and social factors affecting pro- and anti-social lying. We will test the hypothesis that children with conduct problems will display a developmental trajectory opposite from that of typically developing children, displaying more antisocial lies and fewer prosocial lies with increased age. Results from this five-year, large scale study will greatly enhance understanding of the development of lying in children with conduct problems, provide new insights regarding their honesty-dishonesty profiles, and help develop more comprehensive assessment and intervention tools for children with conduct problems.

TitreApplicationTitle: An RCT and economic analysis of three exercise delivery methods in men with prostate cancer on ADT
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN DEPRIVATION THERAPY; BONE MINERAL DENSITY; CANCER-RELATED FATIGUE; COST-EFFECTIVENESS; ELDERLY; EXERCISE; PHYSICAL FITNESS; PROSTATE CANCER; QUALITY OF LIFE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer affects 1 in 7 men. Half of these men will be treated with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), or hormone therapy. ADT slows disease progression and prolongs survival, but it also leads to worse quality of life (QOL), increased fatigue, loss of strength and fitness, osteoporosis, and metabolic effects. Prior research has shown that individually supervised exercise helps improve these side effects. Other forms of exercise, such as supervised group exercise or home-based independent exercise may be just as good and considerably cheaper to implement across Canada. However, these types of exercise have never been compared to individualized supervised exercise, and a formal analysis of costs and benefits has never been done.  A major challenge in implementing an exercise program is helping people to keep exercising after the formal program is done (typically 6 months). The factors that make a cancer survivor more or less likely to continue exercising are not well understood, which makes it difficult for health professionals to help a cancer survivor maximize his chances of gaining the benefits of sticking with an exercise program.  In this randomized trial, we will compare three different exercise programs for men with prostate cancer on ADT. The formal exercise program will be delivered over 6 months. We will measure QOL, physical fitness, bone strength, and metabolic effects. We will look at various psychological factors that may predict the ability to keep up with exercise, and we will monitor how much exercise men do, along with health benefits (QOL, physical fitness, bone strength, and metabolic effects) both during and after the 6-month program. Finally, we will do a formal economic analysis of each program.  These results will be enormously useful in understanding what kind of exercise program is best from both the patient and government (i.e., health funding) perspectives, as well as helping cancer survivors continue to exercise long-term.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuropsychological Functioning of Women with Prophylactic Oophorectomy
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER DISEASE; APOLIPOPROTEIN-E; CANCER GENETICS; COGNITION; ESTROGENS; MEMORY; NEUROPSYCHOLOGICAL TESTING; OOPHORECTOMY; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Women with bilateral salpingooophorectomy (BSO) prior to natural menopause (estimated at 300,000 per year in the U.S. alone) have a higher incidence of all causes of death including, Alzheimer's dementia (AD). Healthy women who carry the breast cancer gene mutations, BRCA1 and 2 are routinely counseled to have their ovaries removed in order to reduce the risk of ovarian cancer. Since one effect of BSO is to remove the body's major source of 17-B-estradiol (E2, one of three naturally occurring estrogens), these data suggest that E2 prior to natural menopause may be critical for cognition. It has been demonstrated that at up to 6 months post-BSO verbal recall declined without E2 replacement, but with replacement did not. The objectives of the present study are to determine: (1) the domains in which cognition and memory change; (2) the timeline of these changes out to 10 years; (3) whether cognitive changes correlate with the apolipoprotein-E gene (APOE) that is a risk factor for AD (APOE4); (4) whether cognitive changes correlate with levels of estrogens and progestagens, and (5) whether there are observable BSO-correlated brain changes. We will study verbal, spatial, and attentional memory using a suite of neuropsychological tests of frontal, hippocampal and parietal cortex. Performance on these neuropsychological tests will be correlated with time since BSO and APOE4. The volume, thickness and integrity of select brain regions pre- and post-BSO will be determined. The results of this study will contribute to our understanding of an important outcome of an increasingly common elective surgery undertaken in healthy women, as well as to our understanding of estrogen's role in young women's cognition and memory. It will also provide important information for women with BRCA mutations - information particularly important for those who carry the AD risk factor variant of the APOE gene. Only with this knowledge will women be able to make fully informed decisions about BSO.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic modulation of Virtual Navigational Strategies, and brain function and grey matter in Healthy Aging
Keywords-MotsClés: FMRI; GENETICS; HIPPOCAMPUS; SPATIAL MEMORY; VBM; VIRTUAL NAVIGATION
Abstract-Résumé: A brain structure called the hippocampus (HPC) degenerates with age causing memory problems to arise. Certain genes have an impact on the HPC: for example, a gene called ApoE and another called BDNF play a role in protecting the HPC or increase the risk of having cognitive (memory) deficits associated with the HPC. Cognitive factors such as navigational strategies (i.e. how we find our way in the environment), also have a modulatory effect on the HPC. Interestingly, research in our laboratory showed that ApoE and BDNF are associated with specific navigational strategies in young adults. Here, we will determine how these genes affect navigational strategies, and the function and grey matter of the HPC of healthy older adults. We will: 1)invite 253 healthy older adults, most of whom have already been previously tested in our laboratory to determine navigational strategies, on tests that further assess spatial memory and general cognition; 2)determine their ApoE and BDNF genotype, and; 3)perform MRI scans in order to assess the structure and function of the HPC. We anticipate that older adults genetically at risk for cognitive deficits will be more likely to use navigational strategies that do not engage the HPC and therefore, will suffer a volume reduction (use it or loose it) compared to the other genotype groups. Those genetically protected against cognitive deficits will be more likely to engage in navigational strategies that stimulate the HPC and will show more activity and function in the HPC. This study will have an impact on the aging population because it will explain how genetic factors contribute to navigational strategies and grey matter and function of the HPC. Certain genotypes and the use of certain navigational strategies may decrease use of the HPC, resulting in loss of grey matter. If this is the case, individuals could be identified early in order to obtain training on navigational strategies that will stimulate the HPC and promote healthy aging.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying opportunities to improve care for patients after acute kidney injury.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; END STAGE RENAL DISEASE; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH SERVICES; PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Acute kidney injury (AKI) as defined by sudden worsening of kidney function, is an important complication in hospitalized patients affecting up to 15% of all hospital admissions, and has been consistently associated with an increased risk of chronic kidney failure requiring dialysis, and death following hospital discharge.  The incidence rate of AKI has been rising by 10% annually. Recently released international guidelines for the diagnosis and management of AKI recommend that all patients with AKI be followed up three months after AKI for assessment of kidney function. This opinion-based recommendation has significant implications for the health care work force. Currently there is no specific treatment for AKI, and the benefits of specialist follow up care for all patients who experience AKI are unknown.  We will use a unique dataset from Alberta, Canada to describe how patients are cared for after a hospitalization with AKI, and to determine the impact of specialist follow up following hospital discharge. This information will identify groups of patients who may not be receiving care after hospital discharge and will help us determine how to best care for these patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization and functional analyses of incorporated HERV envelope proteins in placenta-derived exosomes
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CELLULAR BINDING; ENVV AND ENVP(B); EXOSOMES; HUMAN ENDOGENOUS RETROVIRUSES; HUMAN TROPHOBLASTS; IMMUNOSUPPRESSION; PLACENTA; PRE-ECLAMPSIA; SYNCYTIN-1 AND SYNCYTIN-2; UPTAKE AND FUSION
Abstract-Résumé: Human endogenous Viruses (HERVs) are sequences having been conserved over millions of years in our genome and produce proteins originating from former viruses. Some of these proteins are important for the normal development of the placenta. Changes in the level of these proteins in pregnant women suffering from pre eclampsia have been associated with this disorder. Recently, our team has shown that these proteins can also be present at the surface of extracellular entities known as exosomes, which have been described to play a functional role in different cell types and tissues. Herein, we are hypothesizing that these former viral proteins are important for the normal development of the placenta through their presence not only at the surface of placental cells but also at the surface of exosomes and that they differ in abundance on the surface of exosomes from preeclamptic patients. To test this, we will demonstrate that some of these proteins are indeed varying in their levels on  exosomes derived from placental cells from normal pregnant women vs patients. Next, we will determine if these proteins are involved in processes associated with exosome function, such as binding and fusion with adjacent cells or inhibition of activation of cells from the immune system. We will also test if their altered levels in exosome from pre-eclamptic patients result in changes in exosome function. The body of knowledge gained from these studies will permit to achieve a better understanding of the involvement of these HERV proteins through their association with exosomes on the function of the placenta. Furthermore, they will allow us to determine if reduction of these proteins in pre-eclamptic (PE) patients leads to altered exosome function. Finally, this project might provide indication that HERV proteins could become new and promising markers for the development of PE.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sustained ovulation-associated inflammatory signaling in fallopian tube epithelium as a predisposing factor of serous carcinoma
Keywords-MotsClés: FALLOPIAN TUBE; GLUCOCORTICOID; INFLAMMATION; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; OVARIAN CANCER; OVULATION; SEROUS CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Epithelial ovarian cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related death in Canadian women and is the most lethal cancer of the female reproductive tract. Unfortunately, there are no reliable tests for early detection of the disease, and symptoms that might alert a woman to seek medical treatment at an early disease stage are easily dismissed as being due to minor ailments. A major barrier in developing tests for early detection is our lack of knowledge of how this cancer develops. Women with a family history of breast or ovarian cancer are at very high risk of developing ovarian cancer, with much of this risk being due to a mutation within the breast cancer susceptibility gene 1, referred to as BRCA1. Promising recent studies indicate that the most common and lethal form of ovarian cancer may actually arise from cells lining the fallopian tube. The fallopian tube is a structure that carries the egg cell to the uterus following its release from the ovary. Each woman has two fallopian tubes, one for each of the two ovaries. We have identified molecular differences in the fallopian tubes from women with BRCA1 mutations relative to fallopian tubes from control patients that could contribute to cancer development. Of particular interest, these differences appear only during the period of the menstrual cycle following the release of the egg cell from the ovary (ovulation), suggesting that factors associated with ovulation may contribute to predisposition to ovarian/fallopian tube cancer development. During a typical menstrual cycle, an egg cell is released from only one of the ovaries, and thus these changes may occur in the fallopian tube near the ovulating ovary and not the fallopian tube on the other side.  Our studies are determining if this is indeed the case, and are identifying potential molecules that are likely to participate in turning cells within the fallopian tube to cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diffusion tensor imaging as an in vivo brain imaging technique to study the effects of chronic pain and its treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; IMAGING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MULTI-TENSOR TRACTOGRAPHY; PAIN; STRUCTURAL BRAIN IMAGING; TRACTOGRAPHY; TRIGEMINAL NERVE
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic neuropathic pain can be defined as long-lasting pain related to nerve injury.  Exactly how nerve injury results in chronic neuropathic pain is not entirely understood, however it is known that persistent pain can have lasting effects on the brain.  Our fundamental understanding of how the brain changes with pain has been limited.  This is in part due to the lack of objective methods to link changes in the injured nerves of patients with neuropathic pain with changes in gray and white matter areas of the brain. The trigeminal nerve is responsible for majority of neuropathic pain syndromes affecting the face. We propose to use a non-invasive brain imaging technique called diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to study how microscopic changes in the structure of the trigeminal nerve result in the different clinical presentations of facial neuropathic pain.  The technique of DTI allows for the imaging the architecture of white matter nerve fibers, and provides microscopic details about the structure of the nerves. Additionally, abnormalities in these microscopic measures can give information on mechanisms of disease. We plan to use DTI to image the architecture of the fibers of the trigeminal nerve and construct prediction models that will permit us to understand why some patients respond well to treatment while others do not.  Following this, we will attempt to understand what changes occur in the brain once chronic pain patients have been successfully treated.  This study highlights that chronic pain can be studied accurately and objectively in a non-invasive manner using novel imaging techniques.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of hepatic encephalopathy on liver transplantation outcome
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY; HEPATOLOGY; HYPOTENSION; LACTATE; LIVER DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Minimal hepatic encephalopathy (MHE) is a serious complication of liver disease characterized by cognitive, psychiatric and motor disturbances that can lead to coma and death. As much as 80% of patients with cirrhosis suffer from MHE, of which the burden is immense, considering its impact on the patients, their families and society. To date, liver transplantation (LT) is the only curative treatment that has demonstrated to prolong the lives of patients with end-stage liver disease. However, the development of neurological complications (NC) following LT is an arising problem in transplanted patients. We hypothesize that the presence of MHE at the time of LT is an important factor involved in NC observed post-LT. In addition, given that LT is a major surgical procedure associated with excessive blood loss that leads to hypotension, the latter may be responsible for the neurological impairment that develops post-LT in patients with MHE. Thus, we argue that patients with MHE may be more susceptible to cerebral damage following a hypotensive insult. In view of this, we will study the metabolism of lactate, brain edema and the newly identified lactate G-protein-coupled receptor (GPR81), and conduct a prospective study of patients with end-stage liver disease who are to receive a new liver, in order to better evaluate the impact of MHE and the pathogenic factors on neurological impairment following LT. Results of this study will clarify the respective roles of lactate, brain edema and GPR81 in the pathogenesis of MHE-sensitive neurological damage resulting from hypotension, and emphasize the importance of treating MHE before LT. Finally, as the pathogenic factors are identified, insights for new therapeutic strategies will be uncovered, not only to help improve the quality of life of liver disease patients with MHE on the LT waiting list, but also to lead to a better neurological outcome after following LT.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenetic destabilization of histone 3 by MLL5 in glioblastoma
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMOUR STEM CELLS; CHROMATIN; EPIGENETICS; EPIGENOME; GLIOBLASTOMA; HISTONES; MLL5; PATIENT-DERIVED CANCER STEM CELLS; TRITHORAX GROUP PROTEINS; TUMOUR-INITIATING CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive adult brain tumor. No cure exists for this disease.  Current treatments consist of tumor resection followed by chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Even with such aggressive treatments, patient survival is about 11-15 months. The dismal prognosis for GBM patients and the lack of effective treatments highlight the need for a deeper understanding of the biology of this cancer and for the development of new therapies.  Novel therapeutic avenues will be opened by gaining a better understanding of epigenetic events, which act globally to change the structure of a cell's DNA and turn genes on or off. Evidence exists for epigenetic differences between cancer and normal cells, but they are poorly understood. In our laboratory, we grow cells directly from tumors freshly resected from the patients. These cells represent a great system to study GBM biology because they maintain patient-specific differences in cell properties and allow for clinically relevant studies. Using these patient-derived GBM cells, we discovered that a single protein, called MLL5, is able to change the structure of the DNA throughout the genome. This finding is important because MLL5 does not seem to perform this epigenetic function in normal brain cells.  Furthermore this aberrant function of MLL5 is reversible, so that by removing MLL5 from GBM cells we were able to restore normal DNA structure. The reversibility of this epigenetic program upon removal of MLL5 suggests that by targeting this protein, one might be able to target cancer cells and stop their tumorigenic properties.  We aim at better understanding the GBM-specific epigenetic program regulated by MLL5.  Concomitantly, we are engaged in developing drugs that target MLL5 and the process it regulates.  Our work will expand our understanding of GBM biology and will make it possible to design rational therapies to improve the prognosis of patients affected by this incurable disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing the Quality of Romantic Relationships in Young Adults with Cancer Compared to their Healthy Peers
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; CANCER PATIENTS; CROSS-SECTIONAL DESIGN; DEPRESSION; FERTILITY; FINANCIAL BURDEN; MARITAL ADJUSTMENT; QUALITY OF LIFE; UNDERSERVED POPULATIONS; YOUNG ADULT CANCER SURVIVORS
Abstract-Résumé: A diagnosis of cancer is often the last thing a young adult (18-39 years old) would expect to face amidst normal concerns such as gaining independence, solidifying a career, and developing a secure romantic relationship. Because the population of young adult cancer patients and survivors is smaller compared to older adult and childhood cancer patients and survivors, young adults are often forgotten, or lumped into the larger category of being an "adult cancer survivor". As a result, researchers have understudied the unique needs of young adult cancer survivors. In particular, little is known on how cancer may affect the quality of romantic relationships in young adults. Other studies with older adults have found that cancer can bring couples closer together and may lead to a stronger relationship with a significant other. In contrast, studies have shown that cancer may put young adult couples at greater risk of divorce or separation and many young adults report that having cancer negatively impacts their relationship with their spouse. This has important implications for the health of young adults, as previous research has demonstrated that poor marital relationship quality may have a negative impact on a cancer patients' psychological health and overall quality of life. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to examine how cancer may impact the quality of romantic relationships, first by comparing the relationship satisfaction of cancer patients vs. healthy peers, and secondly by examining whether other factors, such as depression, anxiety and fertility issues, may lead to poorer relationship satisfaction. This study will be a first step in engaging the smaller young adult cancer patient and survivor population in Canada. The results of this study will provide insight on how young couples can better cope with cancer to sustain lasting and healthy romantic relationships, improved health, and a higher quality of life.
