TitreApplicationTitle: The Effects of Strengths on the Decision to Admit, Length of Stay, and Outcome for Adolescent Psychiatric Hospitalization
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; MENTAL HEALTH; PSYCHIATRIC HOSPITALIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: One in five adolescents suffer from a mental illness, with half of these developing before the age of 14 and 70% before the age of 18. Without appropriate help, such disorders are detrimental to a young person's relationships, school, and future life trajectory. In the past, the most common way to treat a mental illness was through hospitalization. However, due to concerns with the intrusiveness and cost of hospitalization the rates of psychiatric inpatient care decreased from the 1990s to 2004. More recently, research has suggested a surge in admission, with 30% of all adolescents seeking treatment being hospitalized. As a result of this surge in admissions, it is essential to understand factors that can influence the likelihood of admission into a psychiatric hospital and the length of stay and outcomes if admitted, specifically in adolescents. Research has suggested that individual's strengths impact factors related to mental health including risk behaviours, symptoms, and level of functioning in residential placement. We are interested in the impact that strengths have on the decision to admit, the length of stay, and outcomes from inpatient psychiatric hospitalization in adolescents. It is hypothesized that patients with greater strengths at the time of admission will require a shorter length of stay and exhibit better mental health outcomes. It is also hypothesized that the greater an individual's strengths are the more likely they are to divert psychiatric inpatient admission. Participants will be youth aged 13-20 who have sought psychiatric help and have been treated in a psychiatric hospital. The Child and Adolescents Strengths and Needs assessment tool will be used to evaluate the prevalence of strengths in 850 adolescents prior to admission and when first admitted. The results of this study can influence the way strengths are used to reduce the length of stay, improve treatment outcomes, and help prevent psychiatric hospitalization in youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transfusion Requirement in Cardiac Surgery III (TRICS III)
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC SURGERY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; RED CELL TRANSFUSION; RED CELL TRANSFUSION THRESHOLDS
Abstract-Résumé: There are over fifty thousand heart surgeries conducted in Canada and over one hundred thousand coronary artery bypass graft procedures in the United States yearly, and red cell transfusion rates for these patients are the highest and most variable amongst all surgical specialties. Red cells when transfused unnecessarily are associated with an increase in adverse events as are transfusions that are not administered when required as adverse events secondary to anemia may also occur. To ensure that these patients, who are at high risk of developing anemia and of receiving transfusion, receive optimal transfusion therapy, we will conduct an international multicentre controlled trial, randomizing patients having cardiac surgery to red cell transfusion using two transfusion strategies. Patients randomized to a restrictive transfusion strategy will receive red cell transfusion if their hemoglobin is less than seventy five grams per litre during and after their operation. Patients allocated to a liberal transfusion strategy will receive red cell transfusion if their hemoglobin concentration is less than ninety five grams per litre during their operation, immediately after the operation and less than eighty five grams per litre when they are transferred to the ward. Randomization will be generated by the Applied Health Research Centre at the Li KaShing Knowledge Institute of St. Michael's Hospital, the official trials unit for the University of Toronto who co-ordinated our highly successful multicentre pilot study using the same transfusion strategies. To determine if one transfusion strategy has better outcomes than the other, our primary outcome will be a combined measure of death, and major adverse events in the three vital organs that can be affected by anemia, the kidney, heart and brain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular determinants of small airway obstruction in COPD
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY FIBROSIS; CLINICAL BIOASSAYS; COPD; EPITHELIUM; FIBROBLASTS; GENE EXPRESSION; LUNG MORPHOLOGY; MICRO-COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; SMALL AIRWAY DISEASE; TRANSFORMING GROWTH FACTOR BETA
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is currently the fourth leading cause of death in Canada and is the only disease where mortality rates continue to climb. This is due to Canada's aging population being at greater risk of developing COPD, as the "Baby boomer" generation grew up when smoking rates were at their peak and smoking is the number one risk factor for COPD.  COPD patients have difficulty breathing as their airways - the tubes that carry air in and out of the lung - become partially blocked and damaged. Importantly, there are no cures for COPD, which makes the disease so deadly. The structural cells that line the airway tubes respond to smoke exposure by promoting inflammation and thickening of the airways, termed fibrosis. Our research is focused on understanding how these cells respond to smoke and promote fibrosis in the 20-30 percent of individuals who smoke.  The goal of our study is to identify the disease drivers that cause airway fibrosis in COPD patients and to identify new therapies to prevent the disease. Our work leverages a unique set of donated human lungs which will be analyzed with new computed tomography (CT) scanning methods to understand how the physical damage and airway fibrosis occurs over time within COPD lungs. We will then use lung cells isolated from smokers with and without COPD to test if the disease-drivers we identify can be modulated with new or existing therapies.  This research will allow better understanding of smoke-related airway disease, and should lead to improved measures to protect Canadians exposed directly or indirectly to smoke exposure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of centriole duplication in human cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL CYCLE; CENTROSOME; CYTOSKELETON; GENOME STABILITY; MICROSCOPY; MICROTUBULES; MITOSIS; MITOTIC SPINDLE; RNA INTERFERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Centrosomes are cellular structures composed of a centriole pair surrounded by an ordered matrix of proteins, collectively referred to as pericentriolar material. Centrioles template the formation of cilia and flagella, the cellular appendages that play a prominent role during human development. When cilia or flagella are defective, this can lead to a plethora of ciliopathies and infertility. Centrosomes also play a key role in the organization of the cytoskeleton and in the segregation of chromosomes by participating in the assembly the mitotic spindle. Without centrosomes, chromosomes would not segregate properly to each daughter cell during mitotic division, giving rise to aneuploidy, a condition that causes genetic disorders and other diseases including cancer. In order to correctly specify the assembly of a mitotic spindle, centrosomes need to duplicate once and only once per cell cycle so that only two centrosomes are present during mitosis, one at each of the two spindle poles. We have previously defined a conserved set of proteins required for centriole duplication. Recently, we have uncovered new critical roles for the proteins CEP120 and SPICE1 in the regulation of centriole duplication, more specifically, centriole length and stability. The overall goal of the work proposed in this application is to delineate the precise role of CEP120/SPICE1 in centriole duplication, as well as to use genomic approaches to identify and study with unprecedented detail, the novel regulators of this process. This work will lead to a better understanding of centrosome biogenesis and illuminate how defects in centriole function can contribute to disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Leukemia Stem Cell Activity by Signaling through PKC[theta]
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CANCER STEM CELLS; CHEMOTHERAPY; LEUKEMIA; LEUKEMIA STEM CELLS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MOUSE MODELS; NOTCH; PKCTHETA; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, or "T-ALL", is a type of blood cancer that affects children and adults worldwide, with approximately 30 new cases per million children and 10 new cases per million adults diagnosed each year. Within Canada, this adds up to about 80 new cancer patients per year in total. While current treatments cure about 80% of children, only about 40% of adults are as fortunate. Even for those who are cured, the chemotherapy they have to go through makes them very sick and can cause other, long-term health problems. Dr. Weng's team has recently shown that a molecule called "protein kinase C theta", or PKCtheta, is a critical regulator of cancer stem cells in T-ALL, which are thought to be responsible for disease relapse even after successful chemotherapy. In this study, Drs. Weng and Morin now propose to use a cutting edge technology called "mass spectrometry" to discover exactly what PKCtheta does in cancer stem cells by identifying what other molecules in the cell it interacts with. The results of this work will form the basis for design of new drugs that target PKCtheta signaling elements in hopes that they will be more effective in curing patients with leukemia than traditional chemotherapy. While the immediate goals of this research are to cure T-ALL, we predict that PKCtheta will activate common cellular pathways that control cancer stem cells more generally, and thus these studies may provide leads towards identifying cures for other cancers as well.

TitreApplicationTitle: REporting of studies Conducted using Observational Routinely-collected Data (RECORD)
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPARATIVE EFFECTIVENESS RESEARCH; HEALTH ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; REPORTING GUIDELINES; ROUTINE ELECTRONIC HEALTH DATA
Abstract-Résumé: With the entry of health care to the electronic age, routinely-collected health data (such as administrative data collected by governments, electronic medical records, and disease registries) are increasingly being used to conduct health research. These types of data are subject to various limitations because they are not being collected for research purposes. Additionally, researchers do not necessarily report the details of their research using these data adequately. Limiting the reporting of results or highlighting only those which are interesting or significant can lead users of the research, such as policy makers and health care providers, to make suboptimal or incorrect decisions that may impact patient care and policy. Reporting guidelines have been shown to improve the transparency of research studies to allow journal editors, peer reviewers and users of the research to understand the strengths and limitations of such studies.    In this application, we propose to create guidelines for the REporting of studies Conducted using Observational Routinely collected Data (RECORD). Following a survey of stakeholders who use or conduct research using routinely collected data (including researchers, policy-makers, journal editors and industry representatives), we will develop the guidelines by consensus.  Development of the RECORD guidelines will follow in conjunction with members of the STROBE initiative using rigorous methodology. They can then be applied by researchers, journal editors and research consumers to understand the strengths and limitations of research using routinely collected health data.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of Pathological Worry on Executive Functioning in Generalized Anxiety Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE FUNCTIONING; GENERALIZED ANXIETY DISORDER; MENTAL HEALTH; PATHOLOGICAL WORRY
Abstract-Résumé: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is an anxiety disorder characterized by high levels of worry. People with this disorder experience problems in their personal, social, and work lives as a result of their chronic worrying. People with GAD experience difficulty with concentration, problem solving, memory and attention. The difficulties may be due to the inability to disengage from worrying. Getting caught in a "worry loop" may prevent people from focusing on the task at hand and may make it difficult for people to focus on how they can solve problems they are encountering. This idea will be tested by measuring the memory, problem solving, and attention abilities of people with GAD who are actively worrying compared to those who are not. It is expected that people who are worrying will show worse performance on memory, problem solving, and attention tests. This study will help improve the understanding of why people with GAD experience the difficulties that they do. Understanding this will help researchers develop more effective treatments for this persistent and disabling condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immunity and Transcription Regulation of Lysosome Genes
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNITY; INFLAMATION; LYSOSOME; LYSOSOME BIOGENESIS; MACROPHAGES; MITF; PHAGOSOME; SIGNALLING LIPIDS; TFEB; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Infection by pathogens remains a global health priority because many pathogens evolved mechanisms that bypass the immune system, which otherwise protects our bodies.  Thus, we hope to better understand our immune system in order to better understand how to defeat pathogens.  Macrophages are immune cells that hunt and engulf pathogens into a new organelle called the phagosome.Phagosomes are then transformed into phagolysosomes by fusing with lysosomes, which are very acidic and hydrolytic organelles, killing and digesting the pathogen.Thus, lysosomes are intimately linked to immune clearance of pathogens.  Lysosome biogenesis is up-regulated by increased expression of lysosome genes via the TFEB-family of transcription factors. TFEB is stimulated by conditions that require more lysosome, like autophagy that degrades the compartments of its own cell during starvation.We have three hypotheses that I will test.  First, since phagosomes need lysosomes for maturation, we hypothesize that phagocytosis triggers TFEB-mediated increase in lysosome gene expression.  Second, I will show that inflammatory signals like bacterial products that activate immune cells, but not non-inflammatory signals like apoptotic bodies (dead cells) will increase lysosome gene expression to better prepare cells to fight off pathogens.To do test this, I will transfect and express fluorescent TFEB in RAW macrophages.  I will then challenge cells with inflammatory signals, like antibody-coated particles and bacterial products, and non-inflammatory signals like cellular debris, and examine the location of TFEB by microscopy. Importantly, my preliminary data already show that antibody-mediated phagocytosis leads to TFEB stimulation. We will employ pharmacological and gene silencing methods to dissect the signaling pathways that control TFEB and use qRT-PCR to show increased lysosome gene expression after phagocytosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Geometric torsion in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis(AIS): A new method in differentiating Lenke sub-types
Keywords-MotsClés: 3D; SCOLIOSIS; TORSION
Abstract-Résumé: Objectives: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS), by nature, is a three-dimensional (3D) deformity of the spine. However, the most widely accepted and used classification systems, such as the Lenke classification system, still rely on two-dimensional aspects of x-rays to describe this 3D deformity. Multiple studies have demonstrated the efficacy of evaluating AIS in 3D in order to identify the optimal surgical strategy. Yet, a 3D classification of AIS still remains elusive as the aforementioned studies propose 3D parameters that are still too qualitative in nature. Therefore, the goal of this study is to find a true global 3D parameter that quantifies the torsion effect in AIS in order to better personalize surgical strategies based on new 3D descriptors of the spine. Methods: This is an analysis of patients with Lenke classified AIS recruited at a pediatric hospital in Quebec. The Lenke classification of each patient was verified by two observers and 3D reconstructions of the spine were obtained using a stereo-reconstruction technique based on two-rays of the spine each with a different view. Torsion was estimated using a novel technique by approximating local arc lengths at the neutral vertebra in the thoraco-lumbar segment (apex to apex). Each vertebral apex was identified by a single observer. An inter and intra-group statistical analysis was performed to evaluate the torsion effect. Pertinence: AIS has long been described as a 3D deformity of the spine and many reseaerch societies have recognized the necessity of developing a 3D classification. This necessity stems from not only the literature, but also from some of the complications in deformity reduction of some patients by using standard surgical methods. Thus, by finding a true global 3D descriptor of the spine, a potential new classification can be developed and improve our current therapeutic methods for AIS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prospective memory in traumatic brain injury
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES; PROSPECTIVE MEMORY; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Prospective memory (ProM) is the ability to remember to do something in the future at the right time and place (Graf & Uttl, 2001; Uttl, 2008).  ProM abilities are vital for everyday activities and essential for rehabilitation stages in individuals with traumatic brain injury (TBI). The research investigating ProM in TBI patients is scarce, and to date, although cognitive deficits in TBI have been investigated, most of the research efforts have been concentrated in studying retrospective memory deficits (Shum, Valentine, & Cutmore, 1999). This new line of research focusing on ProM, has found individuals with TBI to perform more poorly than controls groups using several measures of ProM (Shum et al., 1999). However, ProM measures currently used suffer from several methodological issues. Consequently, the purpose of the present study is to asses ProM performance in patients TBI using a continuous measure with established reliability (Uttl & Kibread, 2011). Moreover, it will correlate ProM performance levels with executive functioning and individual differences in cognitive functions such as, verbal intelligence, retrospective memory, and working memory. Participants will be patients with TBI, between the ages of 18-40 years of age (n = 100) and a control group (n = 100). The ProM task will be embedded within a word association task designed to measure verbal intelligence. Implications of the results for neuropsychological assessment and rehabilitation strategies of individuals with mild TBI will be discussed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Motivational Interviewing for Bariatric Surgery Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: BARIATRIC SURGERY; BINGE EATING; DEPRESSION; MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING; OBESITY; PSYCHOSOCIAL FUNCTIONING; QUALITY OF LIFE; READINESS FOR CHANGE; SELF EFFICACY; WEIGHT LOSS
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is one of the leading causes of preventable mortality in Canada. Despite the critical role psychological factors play in the development and maintenance of obesity, the best treatment for extreme obesity is bariatric surgery. Although effective in reducing weight, this procedure alone does not address the underlying psychological factors and behavioural compliance issues that often lead to relapse, and as a result, up to half of patients begin to regain their weight within the first two years following the surgery. Motivational interviewing (MI), a client-centered strategy for enhancing intrinsic motivation for change, is efficacious in improving a variety of health behaviours, including eating behaviours. I am proposing to conduct the first study to examine whether MI may constitute a brief, effective intervention for improving psychosocial outcomes in obese patients who have undergone bariatric surgery. Participants will be recruited from the Bariatric Surgery Program at Toronto Western Hospital one year post-surgery. It is hypothesized that, relative to wait list controls, the MI group will report greater self-efficacy for change and improved eating behaviours with implications for subsequent improvements in weight loss and psychosocial functioning (i.e. depression, quality of life). Psychosocial intervention research in the field of bariatric care is currently listed among the CIHR research priority areas due to varied treatment response, high relapse rates, and re-emergence of medical comorbidities. The identification of cost effective psychosocial interventions, such as MI, that hold promise as adjunct treatments to bariatric surgery will become increasingly important as the prevalence rate of obesity and number of bariatric surgeries performed in Canada continues to rise.  If MI is found to be effective, the MI protocol could eventually be delivered to MI to patients registered with other centres in the Ontario Bariatric Network and perhaps beyond.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of a home visitation intervention on biological outcomes in infants exposed to psychosocial adversity: A longitudinal evaluation.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL EMBEDDING; BIOLOGICAL MECHANISMS; CHILD AND MATERNAL HEALTH; EPIGENETICS; HPA FUNCTION; PRENATAL ADVERSITY; PREVENTIVE INTERVENTIONS; PSYCHOSOCIAL ADVERSITY
Abstract-Résumé: Young, low-income mothers and their children are at high risk of suffering health and economic disparities. There is an urgent need for effective early interventions for two reasons: (1) pathways of risk are established early on and tend to be reinforced over time; and (2) the ability to change behaviour, biology and brain plasticity decreases over time, likely increasing costs of implementing successful programs. The Nurse Family Partnership (NFP) is a home visitation program that has been shown to prevent a range of child behavioural problems when evaluated in US randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Our study makes strategic use of a RCT of the NFP, funded by the British Columbia government (the BC Health Connections Project, BCHCP) which seeks to evaluate the impact of the NFP within a Canadian context. Participants for the proposed study (n = 600) will consist of a sub-sample drawn from the BCHCP.  Women aged 24 or less are enlisted at 26 weeks gestation and their infants are followed to age 2 years. Our study has three objectives: (1) to determine whether the NFP has an effect on infant biological functions; (2) to investigate whether the NFP has an impact on maternal prenatal stress and whether this is associated with alterations in infant's biology; and (3) to examine whether alterations in biological markers explain the association between the NFP and infant health. We will collect samples from mothers and infants to measure levels of stress. Infant samples will be collected to examine markers that affect the expression of our genes. These measures will be related to child health at age two. Findings will be disseminated to researchers, policy makers and practioners. These findings will inform the design of effective preventive interventions aimed at the health of children born into adverse circumstances. To this point, the biology of change has been neglected, an important oversight given the mutual influence of biological and psychological processes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering the pathobiology of Shwachman Diamond syndrome hematopoietic failure using induced pluripotent stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: DISEASE MODELS; EMBRYOGENESIS; GENE EXPRESSION; HEMATOPOIESIS; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; INHERITED BONE MARROW FAILURE SYNDROMES; SBDS; SHWACHMAN-DIAMOND SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Our goal is to advance the field of bone marrow (BM) failure and discover effective treatments. BM is the red space in bones that makes blood cells. BM failure is a life threatening state where not enough blood cells are made. Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS) is a genetic type of BM failure, which affects children from birth. The success with current treatments is limited and the life expectancy and quality are markedly reduced. To study the blood problems in SDS we need BM cells. However, patients make little BM cells. Also, since patients with SDS and other inherited BM failure syndromes are born with low number of BM cells, there is a need to study why BM cells are not formed properly before birth. Recently, scientists developed methods to generate special cells, called induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), from any people tissues (e.g. skin). It is possible to grow iPSCs in a petri dish indefinitely and produce all types of bona fide patient cells as in the embryo. We generated iPSCs from SDS patients and healthy individuals. We found that SDS iPSCs reliably mimic the patient reduced blood and BM cells. In the first part of the study we will use iPSCs to study whether the SDS defect starts during embryonic development and whether it impairs the formation of BM cells from early stem cells. We will also develop approaches to put back the gene in the iPSCs and correct the defects. In the second part of the study we will decipher how the patient mutations in the SDS gene (called SBDS) impair the formation of BM cells and whether this is through disruption of the function of other specific genes that are important for blood formation. Significance: In this research we will develop a human cell model to clarify how patient mutations affect blood development and to develop methods to correct the genetic defect. Follow-up studies will use the identified aberrant behavior of SDS cells to screen for chemicals that correct it and improve blood cell formation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gender disparities in perinatal and child health and maternal well-being associated with maternal country of birth
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD HEALTH; ETHNICITY; GENDER INEQUALITIES; HEALTH SERVICES; IMMIGRATION; INFANT MORTALITY; MATERNAL HEALTH; PERINATAL HEALTH; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Immigrants are expected to account for nearly all population growth in Canada over the next two decades. The province of Ontario is an appropriate setting to study maternal and newborn health among its immigrants, as more than half of all new immigrants to settle in Ontario. Immigrant mothers currently contribute to 25% of all births in Canada and 37% of all births in Ontario. In many nations, females are less likely to survive or to maintain health compared to males. About 4 million excess female deaths occur every year, the majority in Asia and Africa: About 35% are never born or die at birth, 15% die in early childhood and 33% in their reproductive years. Female disadvantage impairs the ability of mothers to take care of themselves and their children. Canada increasingly receives immigrants from world regions where females are disadvantaged. However, little  is known about how female immigrants and their newborns fare, or if the female disadvantage found in some countries persist after immigration to Canada. To examine these issues, we will study 2.6 million mother-newborn pairs in Ontario over the last two decades, including 535,000 births to immigrant women. Our goal is to determine if infant, child and maternal health and well-being differ according to the sex of the baby and the country of origin of the mother. With our strong research team, we will work in collaboration with immigrant community organizations to ensure that our findings translate into more equitable and improved care of mothers and their children in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving patient safety by optimizing the use of nursing human resources
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CARE HOSPITALS; ADVERSE EVENTS; NURSE STAFFING; PATIENT SAFETY
Abstract-Résumé: Each year, adverse events (AEs) are responsible of 44,000 to 98,000 deaths in acute care hospitals, and it is estimated that 30% to 40% of all AEs are preventable. Recent ecological studies have suggested that understaffing, the use of less qualified nursing staff and of high volumes of overtime hours may be important contributors to the incidence of AEs in these settings. The next step in investigation is to determine the optimal numbers and mixes of nursing staff as well as the optimal volumes of overtime hours that are needed to minimize the risk of AEs. To this end, the temporal association between nurse staffing levels and the incidence of AEs, the thresholds for safe staffing levels, and the potential modification of these relationships by patient complexity need to be determined by conducting longitudinal studies. Until recently, detailed daily patient and staffing data were not readily available to conduct such an investigation. With the advent of electronic medical records and digital capture of payroll and staffing data, an exciting opportunity has emerged to address these important questions in the management of nursing staff in acute care hospitals. Therefore, the aims of this study are to determine if: a) nurse staffing levels are associated with an increased risk of AEs, and if particular patterns of nurse staffing are of greatest risk; b) the risk of AEs in relationship to nurse staffing levels is modified by the complexity of patient requirements and, c) optimal nurse staffing levels can be established by level of patient complexity. The results of this study will likely produce evidence-based information that will assist hospital managers in making the most effective use of the scare nursing resources, and in identifying optimal models of care delivery that minimize the incidence of AEs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and fuctional characterization of novel and known proteins involved in Parkinson's disease; exome sequencing and functional genetics approach
Keywords-MotsClés: EXOME SEQUENCING; FOUNDER POPULATION; GENETICS; PARKINSON'S DISEAE
Abstract-Résumé: More than 100,000 Canadians have Parkinson's disease, a chronic, progressive and devastating disorder, which creates a huge burden on the individual, his family, and the entire society. This burden is physical, social, psychological and financial, and as the age of the population increases, more and more individuals are expected to develop Parkinson's disease.  In this proposed project, we will study the French-Canadian population for genetic alterations that either increase or decrease the risk for Parkinson's disease. We will use advanced genetic methods to identify these genetic changes, such as exome sequencing, and will follow up by studying the biology of these changes in cellular models of Parkinson's disease. In addition, we will study already known genetic changes that increase the risk for PD in the French-Canadian population, such as mutations in a gene called GBA, that are found in more than ten percent of French Canadians who have Parkinson's disease.  The proposed study will take place in one of the world's best labs that study genetics of neurological diseases, led by Dr. Guy Rouleau, the director of the Montreal Neurological Institute. This lab identified more than 20 genes that are associated to different neurological conditions. Dr. Ziv Gan-Or performed his PhD on the genetics of Parkinson's disease, and is experienced with studying a founder population, as well as with the GBA gene, which was his main target of investigation of his PhD thesis.  We are expecting that this proposed research will identify new genetic elements that cause Parkinson's disease, or affect the chances to get this disease. Identifying these elements will allow us to study the biology of Parkinson's disease, start developing new treatments, but may also have an immediate effect, as it will allow us to identify individuals that tend to have Parkinson's disease, and diagnose the disease in earlier stages, which may affect the efficiency of the treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Environmental regulation of maternal care
Keywords-MotsClés: ARGININE VASOPRESSIN (AVP); BRAIN DERIVED NEUROTROPHIC FACTOR (BDNF); CORTICOTROPHIN-RELEASING FACTOR (CRF); DNA METHYLATION/HYDROXYMETHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; HISTONES MODIFICATIONS; MATERNAL CARE; OXYTOCIN (OT); PRECONCEPTION STRESS; REGULATION OF GENE EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Chez l'humain le comportement maternel est regule par la qualite de l'environnement. Le stress environnemental influence les relations entre la mere et sa progeniture ce qui a son tour accroit le risque de developper certains desordres mentaux tel que l'anxiete et la depression. Chez les rats, il existe une variation naturelle du comportement maternel. Le comportement maternelle est stable d'une portee a l'autre pour une meme femelle, n'est pas code par le genome et se transmet de la mere a sa fille. Des etudes precedentes ont demontre un effet determinant du stress environnemental sur la qualite des soins dispenses par la mere a sa progeniture. Cependant, les mecanismes par lesquels le stress environnemental modifie le comportement maternel ne sont pas connus. Ce projet propose d'etudier cette question en dressant un portrait detaille de la relation de cause a effet entre la qualite de l'environnement et la variabilite du comportement maternel ce qui permettra d'entrevoir l'importance d'une telle interaction sur la sante mentale.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving Quantitative Research Methods in Sex, Gender and Population Health:  Theory,  Empirical Evidence, and Development of Applications for Multi-Dimensionality and Intersectionality
Keywords-MotsClés: CONSTRUCT VALIDITY; INTERSECTIONALITY; POPULATION HEALTH; RESEARCH METHODOLOGY; SEX AND GENDER; SEXUAL ORIENTATION; STATISTICAL INTERACTION
Abstract-Résumé: This project consists of a four-year program of research to better develop the ways in which researchers can account for biological sex and social gender in the research they do on the health of populations. Sex, gender and sexual orientation (which has biological and social components) are often thought of in ways that may be a bit simplistic. For example, sex is thought of as one thing, even though it has different dimensions (chromosomal sex, sexual and reproductive organs, hormones). These may or may not go together within an individual (for example, a woman may not have a uterus). This project examines how researchers can better design their research by being more specific about dimensions of sex or gender. In addition, it explores whether existing and new survey questions on sexual orientation and gender really "make sense" to research participants, especially given that younger and older generations may conceptualize their gender and sexuality differently, and that understandings can vary by cultural background. In addition to these issues, this project develops plans for how researchers can better design research and conduct statistical analysis to account for the way that different combinations of demographics or social status indicators may be associated with different health impacts. For example, the effect of living in poverty may differ based on sex/gender, and the health impacts of being a low-income woman cannot be understood by studying the effects of poverty and (separately) the effects of gender, and then just adding these together. While researchers often understand this, they are also often unsure of what to do about that when it comes to analysing data from health surveys. The ultimate goal of this project is to allow researchers in Canada and abroad to produce higher quality research that is both more scientifically valid and more directly relevant to the lives of the people under study.

TitreApplicationTitle: Microvascular remodeling of the adipose and muscle tissues in diet-induced obesity: regulation by FoxO proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CAPILLARIES; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: A sedentary lifestyle coupled with a diet high in fat has led to the current obesity epidemic.  Obesity increases the risk of developing insulin resistance and type II diabetes.  Excessive fat is linked to an increased production of factors that can alter the function of many organs, including skeletal muscle.  The blood vessels that supply oxygen and nutrients to each organ are important in maintaining the appropriate function.  Loss of these blood vessels is thought to occur in obesity, which may contribute to an increased risk of poor health outcomes.  However, the underlying causes for this are not known.  This proposal aims to examine the blood vessel networks within fat and muscle, and how they are affected by a long term high fat diet.  We propose that an inhibitory regulatory protein (FoxO)is increased by the high fat diet, and contributes to the blood vessel loss.  To test this, we will use a mouse model in which FoxO is deleted from the cells that make up blood vessels.  We will determine whether lack of FoxO protein is sufficient to reverse the negative consequences of high fat diet on the blood vessels within fat and muscle.  We also will consider whether loss of this protein in the high fat fed animals can improve their metabolism.  These investigations will provide knowledge of how a high fat diet leads to loss of blood vessels, and new insight into ways in which these negative outcomes may be reversed.  These findings may have potential clinical implications for treatment of obesity-associated complications that are linked to diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gamma(c)-dependent cytokines in CD8 T cell differentiation and exhaustion
Keywords-MotsClés: CD8 T CELLS; DIFFERENTIATION; EFFECTOR FUNCTIONS; EXHAUSTION; GAMMA (C)-DEPENDENT CYTOKINES; MEMORY GENERATION; SIGNALING PATHWAYS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TRANSGENIC MICE MODELS; VIRAL INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Lymphocytes are the critical cells involved in the elimination of viruses. Signals involved in their differentiation impact the potential for protective responses generated after an infectious event. Some of these essential signals are delivered by cytokines present at the time of infection. However, their role remains to be evaluated in the context of severe chronic viral infections. In fact, in this context, lymphocyte differentiation is altered and cells become dysfunctional and exhausted. This project will compare the impact of three cytokines, IL-2, IL-15 and IL-21, in the differentiation of CD8 T lymphocytes, during an acute and chronic viral infection. By using unique mice models, we will examine the expansion, proliferation and differentiation of CD8 T cells in the presence or absence of cytokines. The quality of the lymphocytes generated will be tested by evaluating their capacity to eliminate virally infected cells. The cellular and molecular pathways modified by the presence or absence of the cytokines will also be analyzed. Together, these results will define the mechanisms by which cytokines influence functional T cell generation. This will provide new critical information needed to promote efficient immune responses after viral infections and to improve and design new preventive and therapeutic vaccines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modifying membrane structure to promote neuronal survival and regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: AXONAL REGENERATION; CNS INJURIES; EYE; LIPID RAFTS; MEMBRANE BIOLOGY; NEURONAL SURVIVAL; OPTIC NERVE; PROTEIN RECEPTORS; REGENERATION INHIBITORS; RESTORATION
Abstract-Résumé: Nerve cell injuries lead to the loss of functions, such as vision or the ability to move. To preserve or even restore these functions it is important to maintain nerve cells alive and allow them to function normally again. To function properly, nerve cells require to be connected with each other. However, these connections are often damaged by injuries. We made the surprising discovery that changing the surface of nerve cells, by altering the levels of cholesterol, promotes survival and allows for the re-establishment of connections. In the rat, manipulating cholesterol levels allowed nerve cells from the eye to survive and reconnect after injury. Remarkably,the same treatment allowed rats to walk again after spinal cord injury. Thus, this application will study the effects of cholesterol on cell survival and during the re-establishment of connections. This will be done using the rat as an animal mode. We will also assess various drugs that modify cholesterol levels in nerve cells to restore lost functions.

TitreApplicationTitle: WrapAround Care for Youth Injured by Violence: A Randomized Control Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES; COMMUNITY BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; INJURY; INTERVENTION; PREVENTION; PUBLIC HEALTH; TRAUMA; WRAPAROUND CARE; YOUTH VIOLENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Youth injured by violence is a major public health concern in Canada. It is the fourth cause of death and the leading reason for a youth to visit an emergency department. In Winnipeg, 20% of youth who visit an emergency department with an injury due to violence have a second visit for a subsequent violent injury within the following year. This is consistent with studies in other jurisdictions that demonstrate that violent injury is a chronic condition.   Youth injured by violence are in a reflective and receptive state of mind, rendering the emergency department setting appropriate for intervention. We propose a WrapAround Care model delivered by a support worker with lived experience with violence, supported by a social worker, an addictions and mental health counsellor, a family counsellor and links to multiple community partners. Support workers will be on call 24 hours a day, 7 days a week in order to start the intervention in the ED and take advantage of the "teachable moment".   The proposed study is a pilot randomized control trial to assess the feasibility of a randomized control trial  designed to assess efficacy. For the pilot trial we will assess recruitment, treatment fidelity, participant adherence and safety. The intervention arm will receive wraparound care initiated at the time of their visit for injury due to violence. The control arm will receive standard of care (usually a list of community contacts). We will use an adapted pre-consent randomization methodology. This intervention has been developed using a community based participatory research approach. Our team includes clinicians, nurses, social workers, community youth workers, ex-gang members, elders and researchers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiac Consequences of Excessive Exercise
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRHYTHMIA; ATHLETE; CARDIAC MAGNETIC RESONANCE; CARDIAC REMODELING; CARDIOVASCULAR; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; ELECTROCARDIOGRAM; ENDURANCE; EXERCISE; INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Regular exercise is known to improve general health, quality of life and reduce the incidence of heart disease and other chronic conditions. In addition, exercise leads to improved heart function at rest and during exercise. Despite these benefits, there is increased concern that 'excessive' exercise performed over many years may lead to changes in the heart that include abnormal function after exercise and arrhythmias that require treatment. This study will examine the heart size and function at rest and during exercise, comparing responses between individuals who perform regular, recommended aerobic exercise and those with long-standing experience in intensive, endurance exercise. We will examine heart function using sophisticated techniques to determine if excessive exercise leads to changes which increase an individual's vulnerability to heart conditions, compared to regular exercise that is 'cardio-protective' and only beneficial. Males and females between the ages 45-65 will be studied and will have their hearts assessed for size and function at rest and during vigorous exercise. We will use novel measurement techniques to assess cardiac function and highly accurate imaging methods to assess the chamberss of the heart. Additional measurements will be made to assess heart rhythm, pressures within the heart and the responses to exercise. We predict that those individuals with a long-standing history of 'excessive' exercise and larger hearts, will have unusual patterns of heart function that can increase their vulnerability to certain heart problems. This research will help to clarify what the appropriate limits to exercise should be, and will aid clinicians who use exercise to assess cardiac health in various disease conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Systematic screening of engineered microenvironments for improved heart valve tissue regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIAL DESIGN; BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; CELLULAR MICROENVIRONMENT; HEART VALVE; MECHANOBIOLOGY; MICROTECHNOLOGIES; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Heart valve diseases are increasingly common but currently can only be treated by replacing the diseased valve with a synthetic valve. Synthetic valves are poorly suited for children and younger patients who increasingly are afflicted with the disease. This has motivated efforts to make living replacement heart valves that can grow, adapt, and repair themselves. Generally, engineered valves are produced by placing cells in biomaterials that are designed to guide the cells to produce valve tissue. This process is aided by bioreactors, devices that exercise and nourish the tissue. Selection of biomaterials and bioreactor conditions has been largely based on "best guesses", which may explain why no one has been able to engineer a functional aortic valve (the most commonly replaced valve) yet. We believe that improved heart valve tissue engineering requires systematic testing of combinations of biomaterial and bioreactor conditions. In the current proposal, we will apply novel microtechnologies we have developed and advanced statistical methods to widely screen cell sources, biomaterial designs, and bioreactors. From these screens, we will select biomaterial and bioreactor conditions that promote the growth of mechanically-robust heart valve tissue. We will then implant the most promising engineered tissues in rats to test whether they calcify, as this is the way synthetic valves fail. We expect this systematic and innovative approach to identify design criteria for next generation tissue engineered heart valves with improved function and resistance to calcification.

TitreApplicationTitle: Antimicrobial peptides and M2 macrophages as new targets for intervention in type 1 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNITY; DIET; GASTROINTESTINAL TRACT; HIGH THROUGHPUT ANALYSES; MICROBIOME; NUTRITION; TYPE 1 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) develops when a patient's immune cells destroy the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas, resulting in lifelong insulin injections and decreased lifespan. T1D arises from complex interactions between a patient's genes and the environment. The gut is the major site of interaction between the immune system and environment. Environmental factors encountered in the gut such as microbes and diet play an important role in T1D development and feeding an antigen-free diet prevents T1D in diabetes-prone rats. We have found that cathelicidin (CAMP), an antimicrobial protein, was increased in the gut of rats fed a protective antigen-free diet vs. a wheat-based, T1D-promoting diet. CAMP was also identified in the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. Thus, CAMP is a common factor in both the gut and the pancreas. After injecting CAMP, treated diabetes-prone rats displayed increased regeneration of beta-cells and increased beneficial, probiotic gut bacteria. Additionally, our research has shown that injection of a chemical called CoPP protected diabetes-prone rats from T1D, increased antimicrobial proteins in pancreas and induced  anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages. The action of CAMP and CoPP likely occurs through activation of protective immune responses in the gut and pancreas. We expect that antimicrobial proteins and M2 macrophages are key players in regulating the immune system and beta-cells to prevent T1D.  In this grant, we propose to investigate the involvement of antimicrobial proteins, M2 anti-inflammatory macrophages and gut microbiota in T1D development in diabetes-prone rats fed a protective or diabetes-promoting diet to understand the sequence of events that links environment to beta-cell destruction. Insight into the function of antimicrobial peptides and anti-inflammatory immune cells could provide insight into T1D development, prevention, and treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preventing Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) infection with a novel antigen-adjuvant platform
Keywords-MotsClés: PHASE 1; RESPIRATORY SYNCYTIAL VIRUS; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is the most common cause of lower respiratory tract infection in young children worldwide, and re-infections occur throughout life. In persons older than 65, those with underlying cardiac or lung disease and in the immune compromised RSV causes a serious illness like influenza. Despite this burden of illness no vaccine is currently available to prevent RSV. In this study we will test a novel RSV antigen combined with a new adjuvant (immune booster) to see if it is safe in healthy people age 50 to 64, and if they make antibodies to the vaccine. If the vaccine is safe and antibodies are made, the RSV vaccine would have the potential to be a future vaccine to prevent this common infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cognitive Insight, Metacognition and Structural Neuroimaging in Youth at Clinical High Risk of Psychosis
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING (DTI); DTI-TRACTOGRAPHY; INSIGHT; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI); METACOGNITION; PSYCHOSIS; SCHIZOPHRENIA; YOUTH AT RISK OF PSYCHOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders strike 3% of the population worldwide, causing a loss of contact with reality. The course of these disorders is predominantly chronic with recurrences and relapses of symptoms requiring frequent hospitalizations. Deficits in cognitive insight (self-reflectiveness, overconfidence) and metacognition (the ability to self-monitor and self-regulate which ultimately allow people to expand the meaning of their experiences and adapt to a changing environment) may be vulnerability markers of psychosis. An understanding of the brain systems that underlie cognitive insight and metacognition in individuals at clinical high risk (CHR) of developing a psychosis may allow more precise early detection of impending psychosis and/or relapse.  Signs of CHR for developing a psychosis include sub-threshold psychotic symptoms, brief intermittent psychotic symptoms or a recent decline in functioning, and a family history of psychosis. Approximately 22% of CHR individuals will develop a psychosis within a year. The aim of the present research in individuals at CHR of psychosis is to map the brain systems involved in poor cognitive insight and metacognition by way of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and diffusion tensor imaging tractography.  An understanding of the brain systems that lead to impaired cognitive insight and metacognition and is critical to influence illness trajectories early in the disease process. For example, this research may help to identify individuals who may benefit from adjunctive therapies known to ameliorate cognitive insight and metacognitive distortions, such as cognitive behavioural therapy. Individuals suffering from psychosis and society will benefit because of an expected improvement in cognitive insight, metacognition and symptoms, ultimately enhancing the quality of life of people with psychosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vigorous Physical Activity for Glycaemic Control in Type 1 Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: AEROBIC EXERCISE; ANAEROBIC EXERCISE; BLOOD GLUCOSE; CONTINUOUS GLUCOSE MONITORING; HBA1C; INSULIN; NOCTURNAL HYPOGLYCEMIA; TYPE 1 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Exercise increases the chance of a longer and healthier life for people with type 1 diabetes, but can also cause low blood glucose. It is unknown which kind of exercise provides the greatest benefit and smallest risk of low blood glucose. Short bursts of vigorous exercise may protect against low blood glucose during and shortly after activity. How vigorous interval training affects long-term blood glucose control is also unknown.  Objective: This research examines the immediate and long-term effects of short, vigorous exercise bouts on blood glucose levels in people with type 1 diabetes.  Methodology: We will assign 175 volunteers with type 1 diabetes to one of three 16-week treatments:  (1) moderate intensity exercise (150-200 minutes/week), (2) moderate intensity + vigorous intensity exercise (150-200 minutes/week of moderate intensity exercise with repeated bouts of high intensity exercise lasting 30-60 seconds with 2-4 minutes of moderate-intensity activity in between) and (3) control (standard diabetes education). We will measure blood glucose control at baseline and weeks 8, 16, and 52 after receiving the intervention. We will also measure how often blood glucose goes low overnight and how long it stays low by using continuous glucose monitoring during and after exercise.  Relevance: Fear of low blood glucose prevents many individuals with type 1 diabetes from exercising. This research will provide information so that people with type 1 diabetes can exercise more safely and effectively.

TitreApplicationTitle: Large-scale identification of suppressors of human disease genes in yeast
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETIC DISEASES; GENETIC SUPPRESSION; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; SYNTHETIC GENETIC ARRAY MAPPING; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Mistakes ("mutations") in DNA can cause damage to cells. Often additional DNA mutations can compensate for the harm caused by the first mutation. This process is referred to as genetic suppression. If the initial mutation occurred in a gene involved in human disease, the site of the second mutation (the "suppressor") indicates a potential target for novel drugs. In this research project, we will map these compensation-relations for human disease genes on a large scale. To do this, we will use baker's yeast as a model organism. On a microscopic level, yeast cells provide a model for human cells and, indeed, many genes involved in human diseases have an equivalent yeast gene. After the suppressor genes have been identified in yeast, we will screen a collection of chemicals to identify compounds that mediate a chemical suppression phenotype and therefore likely target the suppressor gene product. Identification of such compounds might lead to the development of new drugs and disease therapies. This type of large-scale suppressor analysis will gain us new insight into compensatory relationships between genes. Additionally, this project should identify possible drug-targets for specific genetic diseases and provide valuable information on the molecular mechanisms underlying these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation into the role of antioxidants in breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIOXIDANTS; BREAST CANCER; CELL PROLIFERATION; CELL SURVIVAL; GENOMIC MINING; GLUTATHIONE (GSH); MCF10A CELLS; PIK3CA; PTEN; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES (ROS)
Abstract-Résumé: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) is produced as a byproduct during generation of energy and production of proteins. At low levels, ROS can promote cell growth and DNA damage, which can benefit a cancer cell. Yet, if it is allowed to accumulate, ROS can become a stress which can lead to cell death. Due to the rapid growth of cancer cells, a high level of energy generation and protein production is required, leading to a high level of ROS generation. In order to quench the buildup of ROS, cancer cells upregulate the synthesis of antioxidants, which convert ROS into non-reactive species, such as water. It was recently shown that by reducing oxidative stress, antioxidants are able to promote cancer cell survival and growth Advancements in biochemical technology have uncovered numerous changes in genes which are specific to cancer. Interestingly, many of the genes found to be modulated in breast cancer have powerful roles in promoting antioxidant synthesis. Three of the genes found to be changed were glutaminase 2 (GLS2), cystathionase (CTH) and glutamate dehydrogenase 1 (GLUD1). GLS2 and CTH both promote synthesis of glutathione (GSH), the most abundant antioxidant within the cell, while GLUD1 decreases GSH synthesis. Interestingly, expression of both GLS2 and CTH was found to be increased in cancers and GLUD1 expression decreased in cancers My role in the project will be to elucidate the roles of GLS2, CTH and GLUD1 in breast cancer. It is hypothesized that GLS2 and CTH promote cancer, and GLUD1 prevents it. The significance of this project is enormous as we have the potential discover novel genes which control the growth and survival of breast tumors. Finally, the present proposal has the potential to lead to better treatments for cancer patients. The proteins that I have chosen to investigate are enzymes and considered 'druggable' targets; therefore, this proposal can lead to novel drug targets and improved therapies for cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring how the process of genetic counselling influences outcomes for individuals with serious mental illnesses.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIPOLAR DISORDER; GENETIC COUNSELLING; PATIENT OUTCOMES; PSYCHOSOCIAL ISSUES; QUALITATIVE METHODOLOGY; SCHIZOAFFECTIVE DISORDER; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SERIOUS MENTAL ILLNESS; TREATMENT ADHERENCE; UNCERTAINTY
Abstract-Résumé: Serious mental illnesses (SMIs), like schizophrenia, schizoaffective, and bipolar disorder, impact almost one million Canadians. The cause of SMIs are extremely complex. While research clearly demonstrates a genetic component, multiple genes are thought interact with environmental factors to cause the illnesses. Until recently, knowledge on the genetic and environmental causes of SMIs have not been addressed in standard medical care for patients and families. But it seems that genetic counselling, an established clinical service, can provide important and far-reaching benefits for patients. These benefits may include decreased feelings of stigma, increased feelings of control, and improved medication adherence. Despite these potential benefits, little is known about how genetic counselling actually influences patient outcomes. In this qualitative interview study I will explore how the process of genetic counselling influences outcomes, particularly treatment adherence, for individuals with SMIs. The data generated will be used to inform the development of genetic counselling guidelines for SMIs. Increasing our understanding of how the process of genetic counselling influences patient outcomes will facilitate improvements to this health service and support standardized care for patients with SMIs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phosphatase Regulation of Mitosis: A Systems Biology Approach
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL CYCLE; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; INTERACTOME; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MITOSIS; PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN PHOSPHATASE; PROTEOMICS; RNA INTERFERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: A major strategic advantage of cancer cells is an abnormally high rate of cell division, and accordingly, many of the chemotherapies used today target the process. However, because healthy cells also divide, these drugs have unfortunate side effects that impact the quality of life of the cancer patient. In healthy cells, cell division is tightly regulated, in large part though temporary, reversible modification of proteins involved in the process. This is achieved by two sets of enzymes - kinases and phosphatases - that are frequently disrupted in cancer cells. Several targeted therapies are currently being developed to interfere with specific kinases important for cell division, and as phosphatases balance the activities of kinases, phosphatases may also represent promising targets for new cancer therapies. However, very little is known about the phosphatases involved in cell division, and in fact, the roles of the majority of the ~150 distinct protein phosphatases in human cells remain unknown. To identify phosphatases with important roles in cell division, we are conducting two independent screens, in which we a) express each phosphatase in human cells and identify the interactions it makes with other proteins; and b) remove each phosphatase from human cells and look for negative effects on various stages of cell division. By combining the results of these two datasets, we can not only identify which phosphatases may be regulating certain processes, but also how the phosphatase is acting within various protein complexes. Through this work, we will gain insight into the roles of protein phosphatases in cell division, revealing new targets for cancer therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-term use of proton pump inhibitors: an overlooked risk factor of vitamin B12 deficiency?
Keywords-MotsClés: GASTRIC ACID-LOWERING AGENTS; NUTRITIONAL DEFICIENCY; PROTON PUMP INHIBITORS; VITAMIN B12
Abstract-Résumé: Vitamin B12 deficiency is common in Canada. It causes anemia and neurological symptoms (ex. foot numbness). Undiagnosed vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to severe and irreversible damage to the nervous system. It is thus important to know who is at risk of vitamin B12 deficiency in order to periodically evaluate their status and ensure early treatment. Vitamin B12 deficiency is primarily caused by the malabsorption of vitamin B12. Most often, it is the lack of gastric acid that alters absorption. Given that, gastric acid-lowering drugs (ex: Nexium®, Pantoloc®) are increasingly thought to be a risk factor of vitamin B12 deficiency, especially in older adults to whom these drugs are the most frequently prescribed. To date, seven studies have been published on this topic. However, their results are equivocal because of important biases in their methods. A major concern is that none of them took into consideration vitamin B12 intake, either from food (ex. meat, dairy products) or supplements (ex. multivitamins). Because it is not yet a well-established risk factor, physicians do not routinely screen their patients treated with gastric acid-lowering agents for vitamin B12 deficiency. Accordingly, our main objective is to unequivocally determine whether users of gastric acid-lowering agents are more at risk of vitamin B12 deficiency over time while taking into account the amount of vitamin B12 they consumed through foods or supplements. In the present application, we propose to conduct a study based on a sample of >1000 older adults whose were followed during four years. More than 18% are taking gastric acid-lowering drugs. The results will allow determining whether patients treated with gastric acid-lowering drugs should be periodically screened for vitamin B12 deficiency. A better understanding of this potential risk factor will help preventing serious and costly conditions such as anemia and irreversible neurological damages.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using optogenetics to identify and regulate cortical circuits that lead to interhemispheric inhibition after stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; CHRONIC WINDOW; INTERHEMISPHERIC INHIBITION; MOTOR CORTEX; MOTOR MAPPING; OPTOGENETICS; PLASTICITY; RECOVERY; STROKE; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: A stroke is caused by a rapid disruption in blood flow to a certain brain region, thus causing brain cells to die. The burden of this disease is significant. With 50,000 new cases occurring each year it is the leading cause of disability in Canada. One potential way for decreasing the impact of stroke is to develop treatment strategies that enhance the brain's inherent capacity to reorganize and recover some of the lost functions. Recent work suggests that transcranial magnetic brain stimulation (which can be applied non-invasively) can enhance the beneficial effects of rehabilitation by transiently reversing some of the brain abnormalities caused by the stroke. In the current experiments we will use a mouse model of stroke to further optimize brain stimulation parameters and also examine the mechanisms of action for effective brain stimulation. Our experiments will utilize a recently developed technology, which allows for light stimulation delivered to the brain to activate selective brain regions. Using this approach we will first identify the specific brain regions that enhance recovery when stimulated by light. In addition, we will also identify optimal stimulation parameters, such as the timing and duration of stimulation. Lastly, we will evaluate the effects of modulating a specific sub-population of neurons within the brain. This population of cells normally sends out inhibitory messages, acting to keep brain activity in check. A stroke may induce over-activity in these cells, thus producing too much inhibition. We will examine the effects of inhibiting these overactive cells with the hope of improving brain function after a stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: A supervisor training program for work disability prevention: a Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: MUSCULOSKELETAL DISORDERS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SUPERVISOR; TRAINING PROGRAM; WORK DISABILITY PREVENTION; WORK-RELATED INJURY; WORKPLACE ACCOMMODATION
Abstract-Résumé: Supervisors of injured workers play a key role in preventing prolonged work absences. Providing supervisors with tools to improve their response to musculoskeletal and other workplace injuries may improve worker health and disability outcomes. The purpose of the proposed study is to determine if a supervisor training program can improve work disability outcomes for injured workers. The project will involve at least one large employer in Canada and one in the US. Work units within the companies will be randomized to either receive the training or not. All supervisors within those work units randomized to receive the training will be given 2 two-hour sessions of supervisor training. The goals of the training program consist of increasing opportunity for problem solving to reduce injury rates, improving supervisor response to prevent or decrease work disability, and improving communication between supervisors, employees and health care providers. Worker outcomes, to be determined from workplace records, include number of lost-time injuries, duration of lost-time injuries in days, and number of days of sick leave. Results from this study will provide a strong conceptual basis for the inclusion of supervisor training in the implementation of future workplace intervention trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: A trial of labour or repeat Cesarean section? A mixed methods study examining women's preferences and providers' counsel
Keywords-MotsClés: CESAREAN SECTION; CONJOINT ANALYSIS; DECISION MAKING; MATERNITY CARE PROVIDERS; MATERNITY CARE SYSTEM; MIXED METHODS; PATIENT CHOICE; TRIAL OF LABOUR; WOMEN'S PREFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Repeat cesarean sections (c-section) are a major contributor to the high rate of c-sections in Canada. Planned repeat c-sections that are not medically indicated are associated with increased risks to maternal and newborn health, increased cost to the health care system and added strain on the already existent shortage of maternity care providers. The majority of women with a previous c-section are eligible for a trial of labour leading to a vaginal birth; yet the number of women opting for this choice has dropped by half over the last decade (CIHI, 2011). Our study examines the factors pregnant women who have had a previous c-section consider when deciding on delivery method. We will also examine issues maternity care providers consider in counseling pregnant women on method of delivery. The study will implement in-depth interviews with pregnant women who have had a previous cesarean section to explore factors they consider when deciding their preferred delivery method. Similarly, we will interview maternity care providers about issues they consider when counseling pregnant women about method of delivery. Two surveys will be developed based on the interview findings. The first survey will be distributed to a representative sample of pregnant women with previous c-sections to evaluate under what circumstances they would decide to have a trial of labour over an elective repeat c-section. The second survey will be delivered to a representative sample of maternity care providers to examine under what circumstances they would counsel women to attempt a trial of labour or an elective repeat c-section. The study findings will provide important new knowledge for policy makers, maternity care planners and providers to inform the ongoing development of safe and effective strategies to address the high rates of c-section in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reducing the risk of serious adverse events and improving quality of life for patients with kidney disease: the role of arteriovenous fistula creation in hemodialysis patients
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HEMODIALYSIS; VASCULAR ACCESS
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with kidney failure have a high risk of adverse health outcomes and are very expensive to care for. Most patients are treated with hemodialysis, which requires access to the bloodstream, or vascular access. While vascular access is a lifeline, it is also the cause of many complications and invasive procedures.  The two most common forms of vascular access are fistulas and catheters. Many physician consider fistulas the preferred form of vascular access and actively promote them, but this is based on low quality evidence that has important limitations. There is the potential that we are promoting a therapy that may be harmful to some patients and could lead to increased resource use and costs.  We plan to compare the risk of complications in patients who use a fistula for vascular access to those who use a catheter. Our study will address many of the shortcomings of previous studies in an attempt to take a more objective look at the relative merits of catheters and fistulas. We will also look at special groups of patients where the benefits of having a fistula created may not be clear.  We have taken a number of steps to prepare for this research project, have access to unique data holdings that allow us to answer this question, are experts in the care of dialysis patients, and have a strong track record of research in this area. In addition, we have already secured funding to cover a portion of this project.    Our findings will have important implications for patients, doctors, and decision-makers. The information gathered will allow us to better educate patients about the likely consequences of choosing a particular form of vascular access and we will ensure that that efforts to increase fistula use do not have unintended consequences for patients and do not lead to increased resource use and costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: AMSTAR-NRS: helping decision makers distinguish high and low quality systematic reviews of non-randomized studies
Keywords-MotsClés: KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MEASUREMENT; META-ANALYSIS; METHODS DEVELOPMENT; SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS
Abstract-Résumé: Systematic reviews (SRs) are the standard way of summarizing multiple studies on the effects of new health care interventions, and decision makers have come to rely heavily on their results. Where the individual research studies are randomized clinical trials, well-conducted SRs provide reliable summaries that are a good basis for policy decisions. Many research studies are not randomized but are 'observational' studies that can give inaccurate impressions of the effects of an intervention. We have found that almost 70 percent of published SRs include observational studies that address important topics in policy development. But how do policy makers judge whether a SR of observational studies can be trusted? There is no guide to the quality of such reviews. We have developed an instrument for assessing the quality of SRs of randomized trials and have found that it is also being used to assess reviews of observational studies for which it is not suited, leading to misleading results and bad decision making. A new instrument, AMSTAR-NRS will be developed to enable users of such reviews to make rapid and accurate assessments of their validity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanosensitive ion channels contribute to mechanical hypersensitivity in a mouse model of osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HYPERALGESIA; ION CHANNEL; MECHANOTRANSDUCTION; NOCICEPTOR; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PAIN; PATCH CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: Over 4.6 million Canadians suffer from arthritis. This disease is a major cause of morbidity, disability and health care utilization, with an economic impact of about $33 billion annually. Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and affects more than 10 percent of Canadians. The most prominent yet least studied feature of OA is joint pain, characterized by spontaneous pain as well as pain during movements in the working range of the joint and during gentle pressure such as palpation. The mechanisms responsible for these symptoms are not fully understood, and current pain therapies have only limited effectiveness and their long-term use is precluded by unwanted negative side effects. There is therefore a need, from a health and economic standpoint, to identify new therapeutic targets in the treatment of arthritic pain. OA pain emanates from nerve fibers in the joint, termed articular afferents. It is now accepted that during OA, these fibers become hypersensitive to mechanical stimuli such as palpation and movement, yet the underlying mechanisms are unclear. Increasing our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying the sensitization of articular afferents could lead to the identification of new targets for therapeutic intervention in OA pain. Our project aims at defining the mechanisms underlying the sensitization of articular afferents in a mouse model of OA pain, with an emphasis on the role played by a subset of membrane proteins, termed mechanosensitive ion channels, specialized in sensing mechanical forces. We will use a combination of techniques including biology, electrophysiology, and behavioral testing of pain thresholds in a mouse model of OA pain. In addition to clarifying the role of these channels in physiology and pathology of articular afferents, our program will create new knowledge about fundamental aspects of sensory physiology, including pain transmission and how neurons sense mechanical forces.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulatory mechanisms in oocyte meiosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM SIGNALING; CHROMOSOME SEGREGATION; CYCLIN B AND CDK1; LIVE CELL IMAGING; OOCYTE MATURATION; POLAR BODY; RHO FAMILY G PROTEINS; SPINDLE ASSEMBLY CHECKPOINT; XENOPUS
Abstract-Résumé: Generation of a haploid female germ cell, the egg, is essential for animal and human reproduction.  Aberrations in this process cause infertility, miscarriages, congenital birth defects (e.g. Down syndrome), as well as cancers (ovarian teratoma). This process, called meiosis, consists of two rounds of asymmetric cell division (meiosis I and meiosis II), yielding two diminutive and non-viable polar bodies and a large haploid egg.   My lab has been at the forefront of studying animal egg meiosis, using the Xenopus frog model, discovering fundamental mechanisms that are important for egg meiosis in all vertebrates including mice and humans. For example, based on our earlier work on the metabolic enzyme ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) in frog oocytes (Zhou et al. 2009. Mol. Cell Biol. 29:1786-95), we have recently discovered that deficiency of the same enzyme, and its product putrescine, is a causal factor of aging-related infertility in mammals (Tao and Liu. 2013. Aging Cell 12:42-49; Liu and Tao. 2012. Aging 4:1-3). These studies may lead to a fertility treatment for older women (see a feature story in Science Update:  http://www.scienceupdate.com/2012/12/egg/).   We propose to continue our studies in the frog system to elucidate fundamental mechanisms important for animal egg meiosis. Unraveling these mechanisms will help understand animal and reproduction and reproductive abnormalities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Building a Rock to Stand On:Health, Life Style Choices, and Social Determinants of Health in Young Adulthood
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; ADOLESCENT HEALTH; ECONOMIC CAPITAL; EMERGING ADULTHOOD; INJURIES; MENTAL HEALTH; PHYSICAL HEALTH; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; TRANSITIONS TO YOUNG ADULTHOOD
Abstract-Résumé: Young adulthood is a critical stage of life when healthy life styles, social supports, and economic futures are established. However, research shows that this age group is at higher risk than either adolescents (under age 18) or adults (over age 29) for substance abuse, suicide, deaths due to injuries and homicides, and relationship violence. Youth transitioning into young adulthood across the recent period of economic downturn are being described by the media as the "lost generation" who are "mired in debt and working in dead end jobs" and deferring long term relationships and child rearing (see DOC ZONE's Generation Jobless). Yet, there is little empirical research on the predictors of health, healthy life styles, and social determinants of health in Canadian young adults. Research informed guidelines for preventive health care are not available for this age group, and access to medical care by a regular family doctor is limited. The proposed study of predictors of young adult health trajectories builds on five waves of data from the Victoria Healthy Youth Survey (V-HYS), collected every two years (2003 to 2011) from 664 Canadian youth (ages 12 to 18 in 2003). Our past V-HYS research focused on whether and how adolescents' characteristics and experiences influence differences in health trajectories in emerging adulthood (the early twenties). Our findings show that injuries, self-harm, alcohol and substance use, dating violence, bullying, and mental illnesses in adolescence affect health, education, and romantic relationships do have consequences for their health and well-being as young adults. In this next phase of our research, we contribute to a much needed understanding of the determinants of health outcomes in young adulthood (the late twenties) when the majority of our sample is leaving school, entering the labour market, and making lasting decisions about social support networks, romantic relationships, family formation, and life styles.
