TitreApplicationTitle: Neural Basis of the Sleep-Waking Cycle
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYCHOLINE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GABA; GLUTAMATE; HISTOCHEMISTRY; PARADOXICAL SLEEP; REM SLEEP; SLEEP DISORDERS; SLEEP-WAKE STATES; SLOW-WAVE SLEEP
Abstract-Résumé: The sleep-waking cycle in mammals is comprised of three distinct states: waking (W), slow wave sleep (SWS) and rapid eye movement sleep (REMS) or paradoxical sleep (PS).  These states are generated by neuronal systems distributed through the core of the brain and by the chemicals utilized by these neurons as neurotransmitters.  To understand how these neurons generate sleep-wake states, we must learn how they discharge and thus release their chemicals across the sleep-waking cycle.  With this aim (1) and by applying optogenetics in mice, we propose to record while manipulating during natural sleep-wake states and labeling for subsequent histochemical identification, neurons which utilize acetylcholine (ACh), GABA or glutamate as neurotransmitters.  We can thus distinguish and study how specific neurons promote cortical activation or behavioral arousal of wakefulness versus those which dampen cortical activation or behavioral arousal.  The sleep-waking cycle is also regulated in a homeostatic manner such that an imbalance created by deprivation of sleep will be compensated for by a subsequent increase in sleep.  Understanding how this homeostatic regulation occurs necessitates learning how the responsiveness of specific neuronal groups to the neurotransmitters released might be altered following sleep deprivation and recovery.  With this aim (2), we propose to examine using histochemical staining following sleep deprivation versus sleep recovery, levels of receptors for excitatory (glutamate) and inhibitory (GABA) neurotransmitters, along with levels of regulatory proteins.  We can thus determine how homeostatic scaling of excitability in specific neuronal groups can promote recovery of sleep.  Collectively, these studies will illuminate the way in which normal sleeping and waking are generated and regulated and how disorders like narcolepsy and insomnia can result from neural-chemical imbalances in these systems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of rTMS treatment on brain structure using advanced neuroimaging approaches
Keywords-MotsClés: MRI; NEUROIMAGING; SCHIZOPHRENIA; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Working memory deficits are a significant cognitive impairment in schizophrenia, and predict disability and functional outcome. There are currently no satisfactory treatments for working memory deficits in schizophrenia. Results from our just published randomized sham-controlled pilot study suggest that four weeks of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation applied bilaterally to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex significantly improves working memory performance in patients with schizophrenia. We are now funded to conduct a larger, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled study to confirm the efficacy of transcranial magnetic stimulation treatment for working memory deficits in patients with schizophrenia. This clinical trial provides the opportunity to leverage our controlled study design to improve our understanding of the biological mechanisms of transcranial magnetic stimulation treatment. This project proposes to conduct high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging immediately before the treatment trial, and immediately after the completion of treatment to comprehensively assess how transcranial magnetic stimulation affects brain structures that are important for working memory performance. Using advanced neuroimaging approaches, we will assess changes in: a) dorsolateral prefrontal cortex gray matter morphology and b) microstructure of white matter tracts connecting to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex using diffusion tensor imaging. Our sham-controlled study design and our sophisticated neuroimaging will determine the effects of transcranial magnetic stimulation treatment on brain structure, and provide us with knowledge regarding how this treatment affects brain structures important for working memory performance. Furthermore, our study design provides us with the opportunity to discover mechanisms of this treatment that improve working memory performance, and identify biomarkers of treatment response.

TitreApplicationTitle: Allele-Specific Suppression of Mutant Huntingtin
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLELE-SPECIFIC GENE SILENCING; ANTI-SENSE OLIGONUCLEOTIDES; GENE EXPRESSION ANALYSIS; GENE SILENCING; GENE THERAPY; HAPLOTYPING; HUNTINGTONS DISEASE; NEURODEGENERATION; OLIGO CHEMISTRY; PRIMARY NEURONAL CULTURES
Abstract-Résumé: Huntington disease (HD) is a fatal, genetic neurodegenerative disorder caused by a mutation in the huntingtin gene, which codes for a protein called huntingtin (Htt). The pathogenesis of HD is complicated and multiple cellular mechanisms and functions are compromised leading to loss of motor control, dementia and psychiatric disturbance. Death usually occurs 15-20 years after onset of symptoms, and there is currently no effective therapy. Therefore attacking the problem at its root by reducing mutant huntingtin (mHtt) expression is a promising therapeutic strategy to prevent pathology and delay or prevent the onset of disease.   Most HD patients have one normal copy and one mutant copy of the Htt gene (one copy from their mother and one copy from their father). Normal Htt is essential for brain function and therefore selectively and specifically reducing mutant and sparing normal Htt is ideal, especially when considering the fact that treatment will mostly begin early and continue throughout life. To achieve this goal we target DNA sequence variations, which are associated with the mutant gene and are not present in the normal gene.   HD can be found everywhere in the world, but the genetic background of HD patients differs between ethnic populations and therefore a personalized approach is required for a successful therapy. We have previously found reagents targeting one of these DNA sequence variations in half of the Caucasian HD population. However, we need to identify DNA sequence variants present in the remaining population including other ethnicities across the world with HD and design new reagents targeting these sites. The main goal of this project is to design and evaluate new reagents for the ability to selectively reduce mHtt expression in the remaining Caucasian HD population as well as in HD patient populations of other ethnic origins allowing a treatment option for every HD patient.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural Mechanisms of Cognitive and Behavioural Rehabilitation in Chronic Stroke Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL MRI; MAGNETOENCEPHALOGRAPHY; MEMORY; REHABILITATION; STROKE; VIRTUAL BRAIN PROJECT
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is the third leading cause of death in Canada, and despite successful advancements in treatments, only 10% of stroke patients recover completely. The majority of stroke patients continue to live with disabilities, and despite some recovery in the first 3-6 months post-stroke, rehabilitation typically plateaus after that initial period. Given the large population of individuals that continue to be affected by stroke, it is important to understand, develop, and promote effective methods of rehabilitation for these patients.  In the last few years, a new cognitive-based approach to rehabilitation has been successfully applied to rehabilitate chronic stroke patients after the supposed recovery plateau. The Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance (Co-Op) approach helps chronic stroke patients develop problem-solving skills to achieve goals using a unique guided discovery process. In order to understand why this approach is particularly effective, I plan to use my expertise in implicit motor learning to examine changes in neural activity that relate to the cognitive and behavioural outcomes associated with the Co-Op method. Specifically, I will examine how rehabilitation with the Co-Op method affects functional neural activity in brain regions important for problem solving, learning, and memory. My work will bring us closer to understanding how cognitive-based rehabilitation can lead to changes in neural activities that result in positive cognitive and behavioural outcomes. Furthermore, by understanding the neural networks that are reorganized in chronic stroke patients undergoing Co-Op treatment, it may be possible to identify patients based on their brain profiles using the virtual brain project. With these brain profiles we may be able to maximize treatment outcomes by tailoring treatment to the individual patients. Therefore, my work will create new knowledge that will be translated to clinical practice in rehabilitating chronic stroke patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Experience shapes connectivity of new neurons in the infant and adult hippocampus
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT NEUROGENESIS IN SUBGRANULAR ZONE; ANTEROGRADE CRE DEPENDENT VIRAL TRACING; CELL FATE MAPPING; CONNECTOME; DEPRESSION AND RESILIENCE RELATED BEHAVIOUR; MICROSCOPY; POSTNATAL NEUROGENESIS IN SUBGRANULAR ZONE; RETROGRADE CRE DEPENDENT VIRAL TRACING; STEREOTAXIC SURGERY; STRESSFUL AND ENRICHING EXPERIENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a pervasive disease that impedes social relationships and professional success to consequently render enormous emotional and financial costs to affected individuals, their families and society. Current treatments for depressive disorders, such as anti-depressant medication and therapy, can be inadequate at relieving symptoms in many affected individuals and new treatments are necessary. Although depression has a genetic component, experience plays an important role in the development of disease. Stress in early life and adulthood can induce lifelong changes in brain function to dramatically increase vulnerability to depression, while enriching experience can lead to resilience. The mechanisms in the brain involved in integrating experience to produce sustained changes in emotional behaviour are poorly understood and investigation into these processes will be crucial for developing novel treatments.  The hippocampus is a brain region that is highly susceptible to experience. Throughout life new neurons are produced in the hippocampus and integrate into circuits in the brain. Studies in mice show that stress reduces the number of new neurons in the hippocampus and induces depression related behavior. Whereas antidepressants and enrichment increase the number of new neurons in the hippocampus and promote resilience. Consequently new neurons are expected to connect to brain areas that regulate depression and resilience behavior, but the connectivity of new neurons has not yet been studied. This project will investigate how new neurons integrate into existing circuits in the brain and determine if experience changes connectivity. Infant and adult mice will experience stress and enrichment and connectivity of new neurons will be observed. By identifying connections of new neurons we will better understand the effects of experience in the brain which will assist in the development of better treatments for depression in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting Seizure Onset
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTATIONAL ANALYSIS; COMPUTER SCIENCE; EEG; EPILEPSY; HFOS; HIGH FREQUENCY OSCILLATIONS; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; SEIZURE DETECTION; SEIZURE LOCALIZATION; SIGNAL PROCESSING
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is one of the most common and serious neurological conditions, affecting up to 300,000 Canadians. About 30% of these patients have seizures that cannot be controlled by any available therapy. One devastating aspect of seizures is their seemingly unpredictable nature, which precludes driving and many types of employment. If it was possible to predict seizures before they occur, then preventative action could be taken to avoid them, thereby opening new treatment options. For example, patients could have implantable devices (e.g., deep brain stimulators or drug delivery devices) that would be activated during the transitional period leading into seizures, known as the pre-ictal period. In this proposal, I plan to identify and characterize a marker of the pre-ictal period in persons with epilepsy.  Increasing evidence suggests that seizures are preceded by changes in overall brain activity, increased blood flow, and changes in the activity rate of cells in different brain regions. We hypothesize that these changes are reliable predictive markers for seizure onset. We will test this hypothesis further by identifying pre-ictal changes in synchronization of brain activity by measuring high frequency oscillations by electroencephalography.  Overall, the proposed research will lead to a better understanding of how seizures begin and how to predict them. It is important to note that the technology is currently available to monitor some of these markers in freely moving patients who have measuring devices of these markers surgically implanted. Because our centre uses this technology, we will be uniquely positioned to begin clinical trials using these markers to predict seizures and deliver therapies to prevent the onset of seizures.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC; BACTERIAL TRANSPEPTIDASE; BETA-LACTAM RESISTANCE; BETA-LACTAMASE; STRUCTURE BASED INHIBITOR DESIGN; STRYNADKA; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Bacterial resistance to the beta-lactam class of antibiotics, which includes penicillin, is an extremely relevant and important field of health research. Pathogens have developed a variety of strategies to render antibiotic treatment ineffective, including employing proteins that degrade the antibiotics and enzymes that do not bind and therefore are not inhibited by beta-lactams. To address this problem, novel drugs must be designed or modifications to existing antibiotics must be made. Either of these strategies can be greatly aided through the availability of detailed three-dimensional molecular structures of the pathogen proteins. X-ray crystallography is capable of providing such structures. This technique acts through computer analysis of the diffraction pattern generated when X-rays pass through a protein crystal. The resulting structures can be used to determine the structure of the protein when it interacts with antibiotics. This knowledge can in turn be used to elucidate the mechanism through which the protein acts. Overall, the information gained from these techniques can be used to improve the effectiveness of new or existing antibiotics. Since bacteria are constantly evolving to counter existing antibiotic treatments, research to develop new inhibitors of their growth is critically important.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of intestinal microbiota, short-chain fatty acids, and endotoxemia in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
Keywords-MotsClés: 16S RNA SEQUENCING; BIFIDOBACTERIA; ENDOTOXIN; GAS-CHROMATOGRAPHY; INTESTINAL MICROBIOTA; LIMULUS AMEBOCYTE LYSATE ASSAY; NON-ALCOHOLIC FATTY LIVER DISEASE; REAL-TIME PCR; SHORT-CHAIN FATTY ACIDS; STEATOHEPATITIS
Abstract-Résumé: About 20-30% of Canadians have non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which is a fat buildup in the liver with or without inflammation. The disease can damage the liver and sometimes patients require a liver transplantation. It is not clear why some patients develop inflammation and therefore more severe disease. Scientists think that a number of factors can play a role, including diet and a person's genetic makeup. Very recently it has been discovered, that the kind of bacteria in the gut could also influence the course of fatty liver disease. Dr. Johane Allard, the candidate's supervisor, has recently received a grant from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) to examine this. The goal of the project is to describe the bacteria in the stool and to measure bacterial products in stool and blood of patients with fatty liver compared to healthy controls. The candidate will collect stool samples and blood from 60 patients with fatty liver disease (30 with fat only, 30 with fat plus inflammation in their liver) and 30 healthy living liver donors as healthy controls. In addition, patients will write down their food intake and their physical activity for one week, and they will fill out a questionnaire to assess other factors that can influence the gut microflora, including country of origin and use of antibiotics.  This study is new and important, as it could lead to new treatments for patients with fatty liver disease. If the gut bacteria are different in patients with fatty liver, we might in the future try to treat fatty liver with beneficial bacteria (probiotics) or carbohydrates that promote the growth of these "good" bacteria (prebiotics).

TitreApplicationTitle: A qualitative exploration of prenatal care utilization among low-income women in Calgary
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLEMENTARY AND ALTERNATIVE MEDICINE; HEALTH CARE UTILIZATION; LOW-INCOME; PRENATAL CARE; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Maternity care is publicly funded in Canada, but it is not equally accessed by all. In particular, women living at or below the low-income cut-off are less likely to initiate prenatal care in their first trimester and to attend regular prenatal classes. This is of concern because prenatal classes have been shown to be beneficial, resulting in more positive outcomes for mothers and babies (ex. higher birth weights for children of mothers who attended prenatal classes, and fewer emergency Caesarean sections performed on women who attended prenatal classes). Apart from conventional maternity care options (i.e. physicians, obstetricians, hospital deliveries), there is also an increasing number of alternative options available such as home birthing, doulas (non-medical birthing assistants), midwifery, and complementary and alternative medicines (CAM) such as yoga, massage, and acupuncture. While these practices can be beneficial to pregnant women, they are not accessible to all, as most are not covered by public health insurance. Little is known about low-income women's knowledge and use of CAMs, and about the factors which influence women's decision-making around these options when it comes to pregnancy and birth. Utilization factors and barriers are complex phenomena and should be studies as such. Therefore, this project will use in-depth interviews to explore low-income women's use and knowledge of conventional and alternative maternity care. This research will add to our understanding of women's views of their care needs and preferences, the barriers and facilitators that exist to accessing maternity care, and the social contexts within which women make decisions about their care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Anatomical Correlates of Kinesthesia in the Human Brain
Keywords-MotsClés: KINESTHESIA; PROPRIOCEPTION; REHABILITATION; ROBOTIC TECHNOLOGY; SOMATOSENSORY; STROKE; VOXEL-BASED LESION SYMPTOM MAPPING
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is the third leading cause of death in Canada and costs the Canadian economy approximately $3.6 billion every year. People who survive a stroke are often left with severe disabilities.  Almost 50% of stroke survivors lose the ability to sense when a body part is moving. Sensing when and where our limbs are moving without seeing them is known as kinesthesia.  Kinesthesia is vital to performing activities such as picking up a coffee cup, washing our hair, and even walking.  Stroke survivors with poor kinesthesia require more care and assistance to do their daily activities. Little is known about which areas in the brain are responsible for kinesthesia.  Unfortunately, the bedside assessment of kinesthesia has significant limitations and depends on a doctor's or therapist's judgement. Therefore, the goal of this research is to 1) use reliable robotic technologies to measure kinesthesia in people who have suffered a stroke, and 2) determine which areas in the brain are responsible for this sense by using brain images taken from an MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) machine. By knowing where in the brain kinesthesia is processed, doctors may be able to make more accurate predictions on how someone will recover following a stroke and rehabilitation specialists may be able to provide more specific exercises based on a persons disability. Ultimately, this research will increase our knowledge about the areas of the brain responsible for kinesthesia and should lead to improved recovery after stroke by providing better guidance around treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Monitoring quality of care for joint replacements: Assessing novel statistical techniques to recommend standardized, unbiased measures of revision rates
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPETING RISKS ANALYSIS; HIP REPLACEMENT SURGERY; KNEE REPLACEMENT SURGERY; MUSCULOSKELETAL; OSTEOARTHRITIS; REVISION RATE; SURVIVAL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a complex, chronic, progressive joint disease expected to affect 1 in 4 Canadians by the year 2040 [1]. With no known cure, joint replacement is the only treatment. Although a highly successful procedure, about 10% of patients require a revision surgery to repair or modify the original prosthesis. Revisions are expensive, difficult to perform, and result in additional pain. Canada does not have an accurate method for estimating revision rates, which are necessary to measure the safety and effectiveness of joint replacement surgery and plan future health services. The top national joint replacement registries in the world (Australia and Sweden) use statistical methods that overestimate revision rates, since they do not account for deaths among the elderly population receiving joint replacements. OBJECTIVE: To identify an accurate method for estimating and projecting future revision rates for hip and knee replacement surgery. DATA: Time to revision for all patients that received a primary joint replacement from 1994 to 2011 will be measured using the Alberta Health Discharge Abstract Database and operating room data, linked to deaths registered in Alberta. Data from Australia and Sweden will be used to inform estimates and projections, and compare alternative methods to those currently used. METHODS: 1) Assess methods currently used to estimate rates in Alberta, Canada, Australia and Sweden; 2) identify and compare all alternative statistical methods available to date; 3) apply all methods and examine variations in estimates; 4) select an accurate method to estimate and project rates. IMPACT: Accurate revision rates estimates will allow health care providers to make evidence-based decisions and enable decision-makers to maintain a sustainable level of quality care.   [1] Arthritis Alliance of Canada. The Impact of Arthritis in Canada: Today and Over the Next 30 Years. 2011.

TitreApplicationTitle: Macrophage lipotoxic inflammation: Its mechanism, impact on insulin delivery and interplay with muscle
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL-CELL COMMUNICATION; INSULIN TRANSCYTOSIS; LIPOTOXICITY; MACROPHAGE ACTIVATION; MICROVASCULAR ENDOTHELIUM; MUSCLE INSULIN RESISTANCE; OBESITY-INDUCED INFLAMMATION; VESICULAR TRAFFIC
Abstract-Résumé: Six million Canadian are obese and 2 million have type 2 diabetes. The obesity-diabetes epidemic is dismal to health budgets and quality of life. Insulin is an important hormone that controls the use of sugar by body tissues.  A key feature of obesity is insulin resistance, i.e., slow insulin delivery from blood capillaries to muscle and poor insulin action in muscle. Although experiments preventing insulin resistance in mice stop the development of diabetes, none of the existing anti-diabetic medications directly target insulin arrival or action in muscle.  Muscle is the major user of blood sugar, controlled by insulin. Notably, under this grant, we discovered that muscle is inflamed in obesity: i.e., inflammatory cells (macrophages) increase within muscle in obese diabetic humans, and in mice by one week of high fat feeding. 'Good' macrophages usually help muscle repair, whereas 'bad' inflammatory macrophages cause insulin resistance. Why do muscle macrophages become inflammatory? Our recent studies show a link between high amounts of saturated fat and inflammation; specifically, saturated fat as well as fat-challenged muscle cells made macrophages inflammatory. In return, factors released from inflamed macrophages made muscle cells resistant to insulin. This suggests the critical possibility that, in obesity or high fat feeding, a vicious cycle keeps muscle macrophages inflamed and lowers insulin action in muscle.  Here we ask: How can macrophages react to saturated fats, which are normally nutrients? Can inflammatory macrophages also affect the key step of insulin delivery to muscles across capillary cells? Using novel techniques in cells and mice, we will investigate the molecules involved in these fundamental functions. Blocking the negative effects initiated by saturated fats should lead to developing much needed, targeted treatments to prevent diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mitochondrial Redox State Modulation to Improve Human Cardiac Arrest Outcome.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ARREST
Abstract-Résumé: Sudden cardiac death is an important health problem. Ventricular fibrillation is a common cause of sudden cardiac death. Electrical defibrillation is successful in restoring regular rhythm, however it does not ensure survival of the victim. Survival to discharge  after initial successful resuscitation is limited by decreased cardiac pumping function and arrhythmias. Effective treatment strategies and exploring new mechanistic pathways are needed to address the loss of cardiac pumping function following resuscitation. During and after heart attack, in the heart glucose is not properly oxidized and produces harmful by products. Concurrently most of the energy for cardiac activity during and after heart attack is produced from fat oxidation. Under ischemic condition fat oxidation is energetically inefficient and this leads to decreased cardiac pumping activity and arrhythmia. The effect of the modulation of cardiac energy sources following cardiac arrest for regulation of cardiac pumping activity and arrhythmia has not been studied. The drug dichloroacetate (DCA) is a metabolic modulator that can increase glucose oxidation and decrease fat oxidation which could prove to be beneficial following cardiac arrest. We have found that DCA can improve cardiac pumping activity following cardiac arrest. Our preliminary findings suggest that fat oxidation during and after ischemia is deleterious for heart function. We propose that simultaneous stimulation of glucose oxidation and inhibition of fat oxidation during resuscitation from cardiac arrest synergistically will improve cardiac pumping activity and decrease cardiac arrhythmia. We have proposed experiments in the under explored paradigm of altering cardiac energy sources to improve both the cardiac pumping activity and arrhythmias following cardiac arrest. The findings of this research work will have significant impact in improving the mortality and will lead to significant improvement in survival to discharge from hospital.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modeling hypertrophic cardiomyopathy using human iPS cell-derived cardiomyocytes
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR GENETICS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PHARMACOLOGY; STEM CELL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young adults and athletes. HCM is a condition with familial patterns of inheritance that result in left ventricular and/or septal hypertrophy, leading to reduced cardiac output and arrhythmias. It is also the most common inherited form of cardiovascular disease, with a prevalence estimated to be as high as 1 in 500 people. The majority of mutations that cause HCM have been identified in sarcomeric proteins that are required for cardiomyocyte contraction. However, the molecular mechanisms that lead to the development of HCM remain unknown. Due to fundamental differences in physiology and genetic makeup between humans and animal models, the study of HCM in the most physiologically relevant human cellular model to date (induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes) will provide new mechanistic insights into disease pathology that is not attainable using animal models. This study will improve our understanding of the pathological mechanisms underlying HCM and could eventually lead to improved treatment options for HCM patients. Future efforts will be aimed at establishing high-throughput cellular platforms for analysis and compound testing to screen drugs for safety and efficacy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Orchestration of Architectural Cues from the Extracellular Environment in Breast Cancer Initiation and Malignant Progression.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; CHROMOSOMAL TERRITORIES; GENE EXPRESSION; GENE REGULATION; SPATIAL ORGANIZATION; TELOMERE
Abstract-Résumé: Telomeres are specialized structures at the ends of our chromosomes. Telomere length has long been believed to limit the number of times a cell can divide in our bodies, thereby representing a major regulator of the aging process. The Karlseder laboratory has recently discovered that the role of the telomere in controlling aging is much more complex. Despite decades of research, no organized pattern of telomere distribution has been discovered in human cells up to now. Using state of the art microscopy, they found a specific enrichment of telomeres at the nuclear periphery during a short time window at the end of the cell division process. Furthermore, this localization changes with age and is much less pronounced in old cells.  This discovery is of profound importance for cellular organization, gene expression patterns and chromosome function. Based on this breakthrough, I am suggesting the new hypothesis that telomere localization directly affects chromosome organization, and in turn regulates genome-wide gene expression programs that could alter cell fate during aging, cellular responses to external and internal stress, as well as age-associated disease. It has long been suggested that the onset of many age-associated diseases, such as progeria, Alzheimer's, cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, metabolism dysfunction, cataracts and inflammation is coordinated. I am now suggesting that telomere localization and the resulting changes in cellular gene expression programs could be the driver of this coordination, representing a unifying explanation for aging and age-associated diseases.  I expect to learn from these experiments how telomere-driven changes in chromosome localization affect gene expression programs during aging, how this drives the onset of age-associated disease and most importantly, how age-associated diseases are linked to each other and whether their cumulative onset can be suppressed by keeping telomere localization in a youthful state.

TitreApplicationTitle: Revisiting the computational and theoretical frameworks currently defining our understanding of different protein structures and folds in the context of neurodegenerative disease-related proteins.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BIOINFORMATICS; HIGH-THROUGHPUT SCREENING; INTERACTOME NETWORK; IPS CELLS; NEURODEGENERATION; PROTEIN AGGREGATION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; SACCHAROMYCES CEREVISIAE; YEAST TWO-HYBRID
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a degenerative neuronal disease with increasing prevalence in the population. Although the aggregation of a few proteins has been implicated in the disease, AD's exact mechanism of emergence remains elusive and no therapies exist to stop or reverse the loss of neurons. Using a yeast model of Alzheimer's disease developed in our laboratory, we will screen thousands of chemicals to determine compounds that reduce toxicity in AD yeasts. The effective compounds will then be used to uncover which protein interactions have been altered in yeasts alleviated of toxicity. This discovery-based approach will lead to a list of compounds which could be further studied as potential therapeutics, while at the same time identifying protein interactions which could shed light on the cellular mechanism(s) underlying AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Variabilité cérébrale comme marqueur de conversion vers une maladie neurodégénérative dans le trouble comportemental en sommeil paradoxale idiopathique
Keywords-MotsClés: MALADIE DE PARKINSON; MALADIE NEURODEGENERATIVE; MARQUEUR NEURODEGENERATIF; TROUBLE DU SOMMEIL; VARIABILITE CEREBRALE; ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHIE
Abstract-Résumé: La maladie de Parkinson (MP) et la demence a corps de Lewy (DCL) sont deux maladies neurodegeneratives frequentes et tres devastatrices. Les traitements actuels permettent de controler temporairement les symptomes, mais ils ne guerissent pas ces maladies. Au moment du diagnostic, la degenerescence des neurones est souvent deja trop avancee. Il semble que la maladie soit deja en cours avant meme que la personne ne ressente les premiers symptomes. Les etudes tentent actuellement de cibler des indices nous permettant de predire le developpement de ces maladies. Un de ces indices est la presence d'un trouble comportemental en sommeil paradoxal (TCSP), caracterise par la survenue de mouvements souvent violents et indesirables pendant le sommeil et qui occasionnent regulierement des blessures a la personne atteinte et au partenaire de lit. On observe le TCSP dans la MP et la DCL, mais tres rarement dans d'autres maladies neurodegeneratives telles que la maladie d'Alzheimer. Le TCSP peut egalement etre observe chez des adultes agees n'ayant pas d'autres maladies. De recentes etudes montrent que les personnes atteintes d'un TCSP sont davantage a risque de developper une MP ou une DCL. Une technique d'analyse de l'activite cerebrale a recemment ete developpee; l'analyse de la variabilite du signal cerebral (VSC). Cette technique permet de mesurer l'efficacite des connexions entre les regions cerebrales; la VSC serait petite chez les enfants, augmenterait graduellement jusqu'a l'age adulte et diminuerait alors qu'on devient age. La presente etude vise a utiliser la technique de la VSC chez des personnes avec un TCSP puisque nous croyons qu'elle permettra de predire avec plus de precision les individus qui sont davantage a risque de developper une MP ou une DCL (la VSC sera reduite chez les patients a risque). Cette etude nous aidera a mieux comprendre la pathologie sous-jacente aux maladies neurodegeneratives et permettra peut-etre le developpement de traitements preventifs.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Early Visual Input in Shaping Visual Development
Keywords-MotsClés: BILATERAL CONGENITAL CATARACTS; FACE PERCEPTION; VISUAL DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Adult patients who have missed visual experience in early infancy as a result of bilateral congenital cataracts have difficulty remembering recently encountered faces. However, the mechanisms underlying this deficit are not well understood. My recent work suggests that adults with normal visual experience automatically learn the average and major variation of newly encountered faces. Could this process of automatic learning be missing in patients treated for bilateral congenital cataracts? In the proposed research, I will develop a comprehensive set of paradigms to measure memory performance, eye-scanning patterns, and brain response patterns related to the learning of the average and major variation of newly encountered faces. By comparing adult patients treated for bilateral congenital cataracts and typical adults using these new assessments, I will be able to gain a deeper understanding of the deficit in remembering faces. Results from this program of research will facilitate the design of training programs aimed at improving patients' abilities to remember faces. The assessments developed in this research have the potential for application among other populations with impaired face processing abilities, such as individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder and the elderly.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development of safer oncolytic poxviruses dependent on cellular dNTP synthesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BLADDER CANCER; BREAST CANCER; CHICK EMBRYOS; CYTOTOXICITY; GEMCITABINE; ONCOLYTIC VIRUSES; RIBONUCLEOTIDE REDUCTASE; VACCINIA VIRUS; XENOGRAFTED TUMORS
Abstract-Résumé: During the process of transformation, a cancer cell acquires many different mutations. However, these mutations can sometimes create an "Achilles heel" in that they often render cancer cells sensitive to virus infection. Oncolytic virus therapies try to exploit these deficiencies by using viruses as tools for killing cancer cells. This project examines whether the poxvirus once used as a smallpox vaccine, vaccinia virus, can be used to safely and selectively kill cancer cells. We have been studying a virus-encoded protein called ribonucleotide reductase (RR). RRs play a key role in making the deoxyribonucleotides (dNTPs) that are used as building blocks for DNA synthesis. We have discovered that if one mutates the virus RR gene, the virus becomes dependent upon the host cell to provide the dNTPs that are needed for virus replication. This is important, because the levels of dNTPs fluctuate with the growth of the cell and are elevated in rapidly dividing cancer cells. Because these mutant viruses grow poorly in non-dividing cells, but grow well in tumor cells, we hypothesize that they would be safer and more selective oncolytic agents. Because cancer cells require dNTPs for growth, the biochemical pathways that produce dNTPs are important targets for chemotherapeutic drugs. Cellular RR is one of the most important of these drug targets, and many cancers are treated with RR inhibitors. Unfortunately, these treatments can select for drug resistant cells due to increased RR activity. Since these drugs may be the last line of therapy for some patients, the consequences are often fatal. We also hypothesize that RR-deficient poxviruses might offer special advantages for treating such drug-resistant cancers. This project will test whether RR-defective vaccinia viruses are safe and effective oncolytic agents in preclinical models for breast cancer and bladder cancer, and whether these viruses would offer an effective treatment for drug-resistant cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Healthy Mind, Healthy Mobility: Combined Dual-task Gait Training and Aerobic Exercise for Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment
Keywords-MotsClés: AEROBIC EXERCISE; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; DUAL-TASK TRAINING; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; FMRI OF PREFRONTAL CORTEX; GAIT VARIABILITY; MOBILITY IMPAIRMENT; OLDER ADULTS; VASCULAR FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Prevention and management of cognitive and functional impairments are essential to healthy aging. Although declining cognitive function is a normal part of aging, some older adults experience accelerated rates of decline. These older adults are pre-disposed to develop more debilitating forms of cognitive impairment, such as Alzheimer's disease. Cognition plays a role in controlling gait in older adults. In particular, reduced ability to divide attention and co-ordinate actions can lead to increased step-to-step variability when performing a secondary task during gait (e.g., talking while walking). Increased gait variability predisposes older adults to missteps and increases the risk for falls, which have important implications for safety, morbidity, and health services utilization. Older adults with cognitive impairment but not dementia (CIND), present an opportunity for health care providers to intervene before irreversible changes in cognition and mobility occur.   Cardiovascular risk factors underlie many chronic conditions in aging. Improved cognition observed in older adults following aerobic exercise may be due to altered vascular function, such as improved blood flow to vulnerable brain regions. Recently, dual-task training, which combines motor tasks with cognitive stressors, has been shown to improve cognition and balance in older adults, by training older adults to multi-task effectively during daily activities. We will investigate the effect of a community-based, combined aerobic exercise and dual-task training program in older adults with CIND, compared to aerobic exercise alone. Our proposed research will determine whether combining aerobic exercise with dual-task training is feasible and effective in improving cognition and mobility in community-dwelling older adults with CIND. Furthermore, we will examine whether this type of intervention can lead to beneficial changes in both brain structure and functioning.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of endogenous Stem/Progenitor cells in spinal cord injury and cellular transplantation
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL TRANSPLANTATION; OLIGODENDROCYTES; PROGENITOR CELLS; SCHWANN CELLS; SPINAL CORD INJURY; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Cellular transplantation is deemed a viable approach to repair spinal cord injuries (SCI), however, the optimal cell for transplantation is still debated, and the mechanisms how transplanted cells improve function of the injured spinal cord are not well understood. In our previous work with transplantation of progenitor cells derived from the skin we observed that these stimulate the presence of more cells of their own kind from the host within the spinal cord injury site.  Here we determine the origin of these host cells, their role in the repair process and the mechanisms how they become involved. We are focussing on the most frequently encountered stem cell/progenitor in the injured spinal cord and determine their role in the repair process.  Ultimately the understanding of this process will open the door to better exploit this endogenous stem/progenitor cell response for a treatment of spinal cord injuries in humans that may not require the actual transplantation of stem/progenitor cells themselves but rather targets the host stem/progenitor cells with drugs.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES A VIRUS
TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of Newly Discovered Proteins that Inhibit the CRISPR/Cas Adaptive Immunity Systems of Bacteria
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL IMMUNITY; BACTERIOPHAGE; CRISPR/CAS SYSTEM; CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; EVOLUTION; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; PROPHAGE; RNA INTERFERENCE; SITE-DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: In recent years it has become abundantly clear that microorganisms living within and on humans, also referred to as the 'human microbiome', play a crucial role in human physiology, immunity and nutrition. Although bacteria are by far the most numerous cellular components of the human microbiome, with bacterial cells outnumbering human cells in the body by approximately 10 to 1, bacteriophages (phages), the viruses that infect bacteria, are likely present in even greater numbers. Phages are the major predators of bacteria in most ecological niches on earth and the battle for survival between bacteria and phages is one of the major drivers of bacterial evolution. Furthermore, complete phage genomes, or fragments thereof, are found within the genomes of most bacterial strains and genes expressed from these 'prophages' can profoundly influence bacterial behaviours, particularly pathogenicity. Due to the importance of phages in the ecology of bacteria, understanding the factors that modulate the interactions between bacteria and phages is crucial. Our research is focused on the CRISPR/Cas system of bacteria, which functions as an immune system protecting bacteria against infection by phages and other foreign DNA elements. The CRISPR/Cas system is found in approximately 50% of bacteria and, thus, has a widespread effect on the survival of diverse bacterial species. In our laboratory, we have recently discovered a novel group of  proteins that inhibit some types of CRISPR/Cas systems. Our future research is aimed at understanding how these proteins function, determining how widespread these proteins are, and gauging the overall impact of these proteins on the survival and behaviour of bacterial populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing the care for rheumatoid arthritis at a population level
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE HEALTH DATA; ARTHRITIS; EPIDEMIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Rheumatoid arthritis is the most severe form of inflammatory arthritis, leading, if left untreated, to progressive joint damage, loss of physical function and premature mortality. New treatment approaches in the last decade have drastically changed treatment. New medications, called biologic agents, are very effective at stopping inflammation and preventing joint damage, even in treatment resistant cases. But high costs and potential side-effects are concerns to patients, physicians and health policy planners. We propose to use information from administrative health databases on everyone with RA in BC to evaluate, in real life, the risks and benefits of biologics. We will assess how treatment with different biologics affects the risk of infections and malignancies compared to treatment with traditional RA medications and to the general population. We will also evaluate whether the benefits from biologics prevents the need  for future joint replacement. We will also look at comorbidities that are linked to having chronic inflammation, such as cardiovascular disease (which is responsible for most of the excess deaths observed in RA), osteoporosis, diabetes, and will assess how to predict who will get these comorbidities.

TitreApplicationTitle: . Leukocyte Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs) in Arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; CHEMOKINES; CLINICALLY RELEVANT STUDIES IN ARTHRITIS; COMPLEMENT; CONNECTIVE TISSUE; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; INFLAMMATION; MACROPHAGE; MMPS; MURINE MODELS OF ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Arthritis is a serious and debilitating disease that affects joints, bones and ligaments in 4 million Canadians. Arthritis is one of the major causes of pain and disability in Canada with an economic burden ~$5 billion, i.e. over 10% of the total economic burden of all illnesses. A lack of clinical tests impedes early and clear diagnosis of active vs. remission phases of disease resulting in an inability to provide the best and early treatment.  In patients with arthritis, excessive inflammation in an overactive immune system mistakenly attacks healthy joint tissues. This attack leads to inflammation, pain and joint damage where the tissue components are cut by enzymes termed proteases. In arthritis the joint tissue cells and white blood cells make important proteases known as MMPs. MMPs dissolve critical proteins that add strength to joints and tendons. In addition we found in skin that MMP2 removes a block allowing inflammation to proceed. This inflammation pathway, termed complement, is overactive in patients with arthritis. In contrast, we found that MMP8 and MMP12 from the white blood cells dampen inflammation, improving healing and so are beneficial in arthritis. This is a new concept for MMPs that are usually presumed to be destructive.  We suggest that inflammatory proteins in arthritis form a diagnostic (biomarker) signature that can be used to predict whether joint destruction is present and active, or in remission. We have developed techniques to identify key inflammatory signature proteins in tissues. Thereby we aim to understand the mechanisms of inflammation in arthritis by comparing healthy joints with arthritic joints from mice lacking MMP2 or white blood cell MMPs.  The biomarkers will be developed as a new way to test for arthritis and to assess treatment options. The mechanisms by which some MMPs are protective or destructive will provide clues to develop drugs to treat arthritis, improve the health of Canadians and reduce health care costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: An Evaluation of the Organizational Process of Developing a Provincial Acute Care Discharge Model in Alberta Hospitals
Keywords-MotsClés: HOSPITAL DISCHARGE; ORGANIZATIONAL CASE STUDIES; QUALITATIVE METHODS; QUALITY IMPROVEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Overcrowding is a significant problem in Canadian hospitals, and has negative effects on both the quality of care received by patients and on the costs to the healthcare system. Research has shown that improving the efficiency of hospital care by standardizing the way in which patient care is delivered can help to reduce hospital overcrowding. On the other hand, allowing smaller subgroups within an organization to customize processes to suit local practices can also be beneficial. Between 2013 and 2015, a provincial initiative to improve the efficiency of hospital care, including planning for patient discharges, will be implemented in seven Alberta hospitals; these hospitals are organized in geographic zones. The purpose of this study is to explore the factors related to implementation that lead to greater use of this discharge process. The results of this study will be useful for future similar projects in Alberta hospitals, and may inform other healthcare organizations that are undertaking large scale improvement initiatives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Amniotic Fluid Virome and Preterm Birth
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE CONTROL STUDY; INFLAMMATION; INTRA-AMNIOTIC INFECTION; METAGENOMICS; MICROBIOME; PRETERM BIRTH; PRETERM LABOR; VIROME
Abstract-Résumé: Preterm birth causes 30% of all deaths among newborn babies and is the leading cause of infant death and illness worldwide. Because the basic reason for preterm birth in at least half of pregnancies is still unknown, scientists have not been able to develop effective tools that can predict if a baby will be born too early.  Inflammation (swelling of tissue, often caused by infection) is the biggest known cause of preterm birth. However, we do not know how inflammation relates to infections of the amniotic fluid that surrounds the unborn baby. It is hard to learn more about the role of amniotic fluid infections because current tests can only detect about 1% of existing germs.  We have developed a broad approach to infection testing based on metagenomics, which means we can detect almost all the viruses and bacteria in a sample by looking for their unique genetic signature. This test will tell us, for the first time, how common amniotic fluid infections are in preterm birth and how these infections relate to the inflammation often seen in amniotic fluid prior to preterm birth. If confirmed in larger studies, these results may lead to better clinical tests for women at risk of preterm birth or preventative measures to reduce the rates of preterm birth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Multiple Sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: 3 TESLA; 7 TESLA; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; CORTICAL LESIONS; DISABILITY; GREY MATTER; MAGNETIZATION TRANSFER RATIO; MRI; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; SUBPIAL DEMYELINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is the most common neurological disorder affecting young adults in Canada, with about 1000 new cases diagnosed in Canada each year. Current treatments can reduce the number of relapses and slow the disease, but there is no cure.  While magnetic resonance images can show MS lesions in the white matter of the brain, current techniques do not show many of the lesions in the grey matter that covers the surface of the brain (cerebral cortex). The ability to see MS lesions involving the grey matter is arguably the greatest challenge at present for the clinical application of MRI to multiple sclerosis (MS). A number of autopsy studies have demonstrated that MS lesions involving the cerebral cortex are common in MS, despite the fact that these lesions do not show up on standard MRI examinations. We have developed methods that use advanced image processing of magnetization transfer ratio (MTR) images to address this unmet need at clinically-accessible field strengths (i.e., 3 Tesla or less) by calculating the MTR on a calculated surface mid-way between the outside of the brain and the junction of the cortex and the white matter just below the cortex. We propose to validate our clinically feasible method against images obtained at the ultra-high field strength of 7 Tesla. Scanning at 7T is not generally accessible in the clinic, but appears to provide the best available technique for detection of cortical lesions in MS patients. We then will be in a position to use our validated methods to answer basic questions about the development of cortical lesions in MS, such as when in the course of the disease they develop, how they relate to physical and cognitive disability, and at what rate do they develop in different phases of the disease. Answers to these questions are vital to increase our understanding of cortical lesions, and to guide development of new therapies that are effective against this component of MS pathology.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predictors and consequences of trajectories of mental illness among prisoners
Keywords-MotsClés: DISTRESS; MENTAL ILLNESS; PRISON; RISK FACTORS; SCREENING; TRAJECTORIES
Abstract-Résumé: Rates of mental illness are high among incarcerated populations. This research will explore rates of change in mental health problems over the first year of incarceration among prisoners serving sentences of two years or longer. We will explore factors and events that occur during imprisonment that may lead to either improved or deteriorating mental health. We will also consider individual characteristics and experiences prior to incarceration to identify vulnerable sub-groups of prisoners for mental health issues. We will look at the relationship between mental health and engaging in institutional incidents such as rule breaking, assaulting other inmates or staff and self-injurious and suicidal behaviour. This research will lead to an increased understanding of factors that contribute to positive and negative mental health, and inform strategies to improve the prevention, detection and treatment of mental illness among prison populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: A phase II study to investigate combination of chemo-radiotherapy with metformin in patients with Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (LA-NSCLC).
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; CANCER BIOLOGY; CHEMOTHERAPY; CLINICAL TRIAL; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; LUNG CANCER; METFORMIN; RADIOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that in 2012 in Canada 25,600 people were diagnosed with lung cancer and more than 20,000 died from it. More than 80% of lung cancer patients are diagnosed with NSCLC which often presents at advanced stages in patients with poor health who cannot tolerate surgical treatment. Such patients are treated with radiotherapy (RT) and Chemotherapy (CT) (CRT). Unfortunately, NSCLC exhibits resistance to CRT, which leads to poor tumour control and less than 17% 5 year survival.  Metformin is an economical and well tolerated anti-diabetic medication. It is used by more than 120 million patients worldwide and it is well tolerated by non-diabetic individuals also. Metformin is associated with decreased cancer risk, improved chemotherapy responses in breast cancer and now it is investigated in breast cancer patients.  We have completed pre-clinical laboratory research which showed that NSCLC cells show high sensitivity to metformin. We observed that metformin, used at doses that can be achieved safely in humans, sensitizes NSCLC to RT and inhibits the growth of human NSCLC tumours in animals.  Here we propose to examine whether addition of metfomrin to CRT can improve treatment results in patients with NSCLC compared to those treated with CRT alone. Patients with advanced NSCLC who will be treated with CRT will receive additional oral treatment with metformin or not. Survival free of disease progression and side effects of treatment will be monitored. Blood glucose and insulin levels will be monitored during the treatment and blood samples will be taken to examine drug levels and biological activity of MET.  This study provides a valuable opportunity to examine whether an economical, well tolerate and promising medication can improve the results of standard therapy in patients with advanced lung cancer who otherwise have a poor prognosis. If positive this study will provide the first clinical evidence of a new therapeutic option for lung cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Corneal transplantation: the traditional paradigm revisited
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CORNEAL GRAFT FAILURE; CORNEAL GRAFT REJECTION; CORNEAL TRANSPLANTATION; EYE DISEASES; FUCHS CORNEAL ENDOTHELIAL DYSTROPHY; OPHTHALMOLOGY; TISSUE ENGINEERING - CORNEAL ENDOTHELIAL CELL CULTURE
Abstract-Résumé: The cornea is the transparent protective layer in front of the colored (blue, brown, etc.) iris. Irreversible loss of corneal transparency results in permanent vision loss and blindness. The World Health Organization estimates that 50 million people worldwide are bilaterally blind, and at least 150 million people have impaired vision in both eyes, corneal diseases being the second largest cause. Surgical replacement of the cornea, or corneal transplantation, is currently the only treatment to restore sight in these eyes. However, severe shortage of donor corneas remains the fundamental obstacle to corneal transplantation around the world.   Our goal is to improve significantly the outcome of corneal transplantation. Thanks to leading advances in tissue engineering technology and ophthalmology, highly functional corneas will be produced from the patient's own natural cells, thus eliminating the risk for rejection by the body. Tissue engineering also holds the promise of solving the issue of corneal tissue shortage. Finally, we propose an entirely new concept, which consists in treating the cornea early in the course of the disease, in order to avoid the necessity for corneal transplantation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Randomized controlled trial of the efficacy of pre-emptive tenofovir to prevent hepatitis B reactivation in patients who are anti-HBc antibody positive receiving curative intent rituximab-based chemotherapy for non-Hodgkin's lympohma
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMOTHERAPY; HEPATITIS B; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; REACTIVATION; REVERSE SEROCONVERSION; RITUXIMAB; TENOFOVIR
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis B virus infection is a major global public health problem with over 350 million people chronically infected and up to 2 billion with previous exposure to the virus worldwide. With the large foreign-born population in Canada, many individuals have a history of hepatitis B but may be unaware because most people have no symptoms. Anyone who has ever been exposed to hepatitis B continues to have traces of the virus in the liver. The virus can become active again if the immune system is suppressed such as with cancer chemotherapy. This is particularly common with a chemotherapy drug called rituximab. If the virus reactivates, people can suffer from severe and even fatal hepatitis. This study will determine whether it would be beneficial to start a medication for hepatitis B called tenofovir in people with a history of exposure to hepatitis B before starting rituximab-based chemotherapy for lymphoma (a blood cancer) to prevent hepatitis B reactivation.  The study will determine whether it is better to start tenofovir before starting chemotherapy or only if hepatitis B reactivation occurs. The study will also determine which of these approaches is most cost-effective.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Sex and Social Support Preferences in Predicting Psychological Distress Among Patients with Cutaneous Melanoma
Keywords-MotsClés: MELANOMA; PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS; SEX; SOCIAL SUPPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Cutaneous melanoma is the most fatal type of skin cancer and a growing component of cancer burden worldwide. Clinically relevant levels of psychological distress affects thirty percent of cutaneous melanoma patients. Social support has been associated with lower distress in cancer patients. Sex differences and preferences for support must be identified because these could influence the types of support that patients are most likely to utilize and benefit from. Whether there are psychological health benefits for cancer patients who receive a type of support that matches their preferences has not been investigated to date. The primary objective of the present study is to test the hypothesis that cutaneous melanoma patients who obtain the type of support that matches their preferences will demonstrate lower psychological distress than patients who do not. The secondary objective is to investigate whether sex moderates this relationship. The present study will be a part of an ongoing project within the McGill Health Psychology Research Group under the supervision of Dr. Koerner. An equal number of men and women diagnosed with cutaneous melanoma within the last year will be recruited. Participants will complete the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, a measure of psychological distress, and the Information and Support Needs Questionnaire, a measure of patient preferences for type of support and support received. A new continuous variable will be created assessing the degree of match between preferences for and type of support received. Moderated multiple regression analyses will be conducted to test whether a match for preferred and received support predicts lower psychological distress and whether sex moderates this relationship.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genital Pain and Disordered Eating in Women: A Mixed Methods Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ANOREXIA NERVOSA; EATING DISORDER; GENITAL PAIN; MIXED METHODS DESIGN; PROVOKED VESTIBULODYNIA; SEXUAL BODY ESTEEM; SEXUAL DISTRESS; SEXUAL DYSFUNCTION; VULVALGESIOMETER
Abstract-Résumé: Background: There has long been a proposed clinical link between sexuality and eating disorders; however, little empirical evidence exists concerning this relationship. The extant literature suggests women with anorexia nervosa (AN) experience decreased sexual desire, activity, and satisfaction, and heightened sexual anxiety. In addition, the personality profiles of women suffering from provoked vestibulodynia (PVD), the most common form of genital pain affecting up to 20% of women, and women with AN are similar. Despite the compelling clinical rationale, empirical evidence supporting the important connection between these two areas of study remains entirely uninformed.  Aims: The primary goal of this study is investigate etiological similarities between genital pain and disordered eating in women, and establish a critical empirical foundation for bridging the psychological and physiological mechanisms underlying these disorders.  Procedure: Three samples of women will be recruited: 30 women diagnosed with PVD from the BC Centre for Sexual Medicine, 30 women diagnosed with AN from the Vancouver Coastal Health's Eating Disorder Facility, and 400 female undergraduates from the University of British Columbia. Each group will complete a battery of questionnaires focused on genital pain, sexual distress, disordered eating, negative affect, and personality. Women diagnosed with PVD will undergo a vulvar pain assessment. Quantitative findings will inform the creation of a detailed qualitative interview to explore some of the emerging themes in women with PVD and AN.  Implications: This study will be the first to examine a possible etiological link that may account for both AN and PVD. Such knowledge would represent a meaningful contribution that would facilitate the creation of therapeutic interventions and advancements in clinical assessment tools, and ultimately improve the lives of Canadian women.

TitreApplicationTitle: Allosteric states of the MRN complex in double strand break repair
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE; DNA REPAIR; DOUBLE STRAND BREAK; MRE11; MRN; RAD50; SMALL ANGLE X-RAY SCATTERING; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: DNA contains the genetic information necessary for cell growth, maintenance and proliferation. These functions can be altered by mutations of the DNA resulting from the effects of different agents (UV sunlight, tobacco smoke, carcinogens, etc.). Some of these mutations can cause serious disease such as cancer. Fortunately, cells have developed different systems to repair damaged DNA in order to avoid mutations.  One of the most harmful forms of DNA damage is the double strand break (DSB). In this instance, the double helix is cleaved, leaving two unprotected ends. MRN proteins (Mre11, Rad50, Nbs1) detect these severed ends and activate one of four different types of repair. These types of repair are well known, but how MRN chooses between them is still a mystery. This choice is important since some of the types of repair are more prone to create mistakes and mutations that lead to disease.  In my project, I will determine and characterize the 3-D structures of the MRN complex in order to decipher what mechanism it uses to direct the actions leading to DNA repair. I hypothesize that different structural conformations of MRN, called allosteric states, are responsible for signalling to different types of repair of the DSB. To determine these 3-D structures, I will use X-ray crystallography and small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS). X-ray crystallography is a powerful structural biology technique that allows one to find the exact position of all the atoms of a molecule. SAXS determines the overall shape of molecules and complexes. By combining these two complementary techniques, one can better understand the structure, functions and mechanisms of the MRN complex.  These mechanisms are crucial for the cell's health. Understanding them will help us discover the cause of different diseases. Furthermore, this knowledge is essential for the development of new cancer therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The neurophysiology of spontaneous recovery post-stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: HEMIPARESIS; KINEMATICS; MOTOR LEARNING; RECOVERY; STROKE; TMS
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke affects thousands of Canadians each year. Despite its prevalence, very little is known about the naturally occurring changes and recovery after stroke. Research from animal studies seem to indicate that there is a brief window of time post stroke where changes in the brain result in an improvement of function. The purpose of this work is to explore for the first time how changes in the brain relate to the ability of patients to move their arm over a prolonged period after they have had a stroke. Many times over the course of one year (within first 2 weeks, and at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months), we will be looking at a group of 25 people who have had a first-time stroke. Our purpose is to study how neurophysiological changes in the brain relate to changes in the control and strength of hand movements. We will be using a technique called transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), where safe and painless magnetic pulses are applied over the head,  which causes the brain areas responsible for movement to be come excitable. Effectively, it will cause a small muscle twitch in the hand of the patient. We use this harmless stimulus to measure how well the brain is connected to the muscles of the body. We will then relate the changes and improvements in the brain-muscle connection to the changes in the ability to move the hand. The proposed research will improve our understanding of the brain physiology that relates to recovery after stroke. This knowledge is crucial to the development of better rehabilitation strategies that that truly help improve the quality of life of Canadians with stroke, which will ease the burden on the stroke patients as well as their families who care for them. In addition, if we can ground our rehabilitation strategies in evidence-based mechanism research, we improve our chances of reducing impairment early during rehabilitation, which will reduce the overall cost to the already overstrained health-care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of necroptosis, a novel cell death pathway to overcome drug resistance in childhood leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA; APOPTOSIS; CANCER DRUG RESISTANCE; CELL DEATH; CHEMOSENSITIZATION; NECROPTOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) accounts for almost 40% of childhood cancers diagnosed in Canada each year. Despite impressive survival rates of upwards of 90%, the sheer numbers of cases still makes leukemia the most likely cause of cancer related death in Canadian children. In ALL patients where current generation chemotherapies fail, cancer cells become resistant to cell death, which is normally induced by these drugs. Understanding what factors determine susceptibility to cell death is key to understanding drug resistance in ALL, and cancer at large.   The leukemia research group at the University Children's Hospital Zurich, has for the first time established a biobank of primary human ALL cells for laboratory study, which reflects the cross-section of ALL cancers from drug-susceptible to drug-resistant cases. Using this biobank, they have discovered that a new cancer drug (obatoclax) can resensitize aggressive drug resistant ALL cells to a standard chemotherapy drug (dexamethasone). Fascinatingly, this double drug treatment caused ALL cells to die through an only recently discovered pathway of cell death, known as necroptosis. Unlike apoptosis, a much better known form of programmed cell death, necroptosis occurs rapidly in what has been likened to cell explosion.  Necroptosis is known to be activated by the assembly of a large complex of proteins termed the necrosome. This research project aims at understanding the regulation and function of the necrosome in ALL cells. Through various advanced techniques, we will examine how the necrosome is formed, what signals are needed, and how cancer cells avoid this type of death normally. By studying necroptosis in ALL cells upon drug treatment, we may also be able to identify how it is regulated in other cancers as well. Ultimately, the hope of this type of research is that necroptosis could represent a new Achille's heel for aggressive drug resistant cancers, opening the door to new approaches for treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing the global patient experience in inflammatory bowel disease: Understanding fluctuations in symptoms, stress, mood and daily functioning
Keywords-MotsClés: COPING; DAILY FUNCTIONING; DISEASE ACTIVITY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; LONGITUDINAL ASSESSMENT; MOOD; PERCEIVED STRESS; QUALITY OF LIFE; SYMPTOM MONITORING; WELL-BEING
Abstract-Résumé: The inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), pose a significant health problem for many adults. Individuals with these chronic illnesses suffer spontaneous relapses, hospitalizations, surgery, and regular use of costly medications. IBD therefore has the potential for severe health-related consequences. Community surveys conducted in the Manitoba IBD population have found that many persons with IBD (70%) identify stress as a contributor to disease symptoms. Previous research by the University of Manitoba IBD Clinical and Research Centre has identified perceived stress as a significant predictor of IBD symptom flares when tracked at 3 month intervals. Persons with frequent IBD symptoms also report the experience of disease to be a source of stress in their lives. However, the disease experience of persons with IBD varies widely both between individuals and for each individual over time, making it difficult to assess the precise role of stress and other risks for symptom flares. The development of methods that can sample IBD symptoms and risk factors more frequently and in real time will allow research to precisely investigate these fluctuations in symptoms and predictors of these changes over shorter periods. This study aims to develop experience sampling methods for IBD and to follow a community sample of Manitobans with IBD each week for a year. Changes in IBD symptoms and in potential risk factors such as perceived stress, mood, coping, disability, and well-being will be assessed. Clinical variables such as disease type (CD or UC), phenotype characteristics, disease duration, history of surgery, smoking, and personal characteristics such as age and sex will also be explored. It will then be possible to closely examine how fluctuations in disease symptoms and risk factors may relate over time. With this information, we can develop effective ways to help persons with IBD manage symptoms and risk factors for disease flares.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of FGF9 in angiogenic remodeling and tissue regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD VESSEL NETWORK; FIBROBLAST GROWTH FACTOR 9; HINDLIMB ISCHEMIA; MURAL CELL; PERIVASCULAR STEM/PROGENITOR CELL; REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Rebuilding a blood vessel network is critical to the recovery of blood supply and tissue regeneration in ischemic (lack of blood supply) diseases, such as low extremity ischemia, heart attack and stroke. Our laboratory have identified that delivery of fibroblast growth factor 9 (FGF9) makes small-diameter vessels stronger and more functional, which in turn promotes recovery of skeletal muscle function in a mouse model of hindlimb ischemia. FGF9 is essential to maintain the supply pool of tissue stem cells in various organs. Stem cells surrounding blood vessels help rebuild blood vessels in multiple animal models of ischemia diseases. We are going to test if FGF9 delivery mobilizes stem cells surrounding blood vessels so as to rebuild a functional blood vessel network and improve blood supply during ischemic diseases. Specifically, we will delete Fgf9 gene in mice and then induce ischemia in mouse hindlimb by surgically removing an artery in thigh. We will first examine the role of FGF9 during reconstruction of blood vessel network and tissue architecture after ischemia. The structure and function of regenerative blood vessel network will be examined by state-of-the-art vascular imaging and histology. Stem cells surrounding blood vessels will be isolated from normal and FGF9 deficient mouse hindlimb. The behaviors of isolated stem cells will be compared in terms of their capacity to construct blood vessels. The mechanism for FGF9 to regulate stem cells will be explored by high throughput screening. Our project will generate novel knowledge on rebuilding a blood vessel network in ischemic diseases. Specifically, we anticipate that FGF9 will be a potential therapeutic target for improving blood supply and rescuing tissue functions in ischemic diseases. Overall, our research will make significant benefits for Canadian health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relating memory encoding success to transient changes in brain network modularity
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN LESION; BRAIN NETWORKS; ENCODING; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MEDIAL TEMPORAL LOBE; MEMORY; PREFRONTAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Human cognition requires the coordinated activity of a distributed set of brain areas that form networks. A very challenging problem is characterizing these networks both in healthy individuals and in individuals that have undergone various types of brain damage. Recent research has employed mathematical tools based on graph theory, developed for analyzing a wide variety of networks (e.g., social networks), to precisely quantify brain networks with data acquired from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Using these tools, a recent study documented systematic changes in brain network organization that take place in patients who underwent focal brain lesions as a result of stroke or traumatic brain injury, suggesting such measures are a marker of overall brain functioning (Gratton et al., 2012, Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 24:6, 1275:1285). An additional growing area of interest relates to how brain networks change when subjects perform cognitively demanding tasks, such as holding information in mind across a delay, or learning new information. In my study, I am aiming to examine whether certain types of changes in network organization appear to be related to whether environmental stimuli are successfully learned or forgotten. I will present participants with common scenes while they are being scanned with fMRI; subsequently, they will be asked to recognize these scenes outside the brain scanner. Our hypothesis is that there will be greater changes in network organization for scenes that are later remembered as compared to later forgotten. As many neurological diseases have been found to involve systematic alterations in brain network connectivity, and at the same time are associated with memory impairments (e.g., Alzheimer's disease, Schizophrenia), this study promises to yield important new knowledge that could directly inform novel efforts to provide rehabilitation for individuals with various types of learning disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Opiate reinforcement in a chronic pain model
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC PAIN; CONDITIONED PLACE PREFERENCE; GLIAL ACTIVATION; NEUROPATHY; OPIOIDS; PAIN AFFECT; PHARMACOLOGY; REWARD
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain is a significant clinical and societal burden that remains poorly managed in the clinic. Most basic science research has focused on describing mechanisms involved in the sensory abnormalities driving this condition, and consequently most pharmacological interventions deal with minimizing the sensory aspect of pain. Pain, however, has an important affective or emotional component that contributes to the severity of the chronic pain condition and subsequent loss of quality of life. Opioids represent a gold standard in acute pain management, and their high analgesic efficacy is partly related to their ability to target both sensory and affective aspects of pain. Part of the challenge in treating chronic pain is that opioids are less effective analgesics of chronic pain. While the exact mechanisms of why this may be remain debated, alterations in the affective limbic system resulting from a chronic pain state is a logical possibility. The main goal of this research project is to describe changes in affective brain regions under chronic pain conditions and examine how these changes affect opioid analgesia and reward.  To investigate this problem, we will induce a chronic pain state in the mouse by ligating the sciatic nerve that innervates the hind paw. This produces a persistent pain condition that mimics the human chronic pain state.  The rewarding and analgesic properties of opioids in a chronic pain animal will be described, and genetic and molecular changes within affective brain regions will be explored. These results will further expand our understanding of how chronic pain changes the brain, particularly as it relates to affect, and will potentially identify novel therapeutic targets to improve the analgesic efficacy of the ubiquitous opioids.
