TitreApplicationTitle: Solution Processed Carbon Based Electrodes for all Carbon Solar Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CARBON-BASED NANOMATERIALS; CARRIER INJECTION; DEVICE ENGINEERING; FULLERENE; GRAPHENE; HETEROJUNCTION; LOWCOST FLEXIBLE LIGHT-WEIGHT SOLAR CELL; NANOSYSTEMS; SINGLE WALLED CARBON NANOTUBES; SOLUTION PROCESSING
Abstract-Résumé: Carbon, the basis of all known life on earth, is one of the oldest discovered elements and is evidently widely abundant. It exists in various forms: spread as a 2D graphene sheet which could be easily obtained from a thin flake  one layer of atoms thick - of ordinary graphite (pencil lead), wrapped cylindrically as a 1D nanotube, or enclosed as a 3D buckyball sphere. In recent years, carbon based materials have attracted worldwide research focus because of their potential to allow smaller, faster and much cheaper devices. Carbon based materials possess unique and fascinating physical, chemical, and electronic properties that make them attractive for next generation electronic applications. A number of these carbon materials exhibit excellent conductive properties; graphene, for instance, is not only transparent, thin and extremely robust, it also conducts electricity better than most conductors. It also shows unprecedented thermal conductivity and stability. On the other hand, carbon nanotubes behave as semiconductors and can harness the infrared portion of the solar spectrum, long wavelength sunlight unknot captured by conventional photovoltaic materials. Combining those different graphitic components, with their respective unique properties, would allow the realization of low-cost, durable, thermally-resistant, flexible, and entirely innovative electronic devices. We want to revolutionize the photovoltaics industry by developing the first all-carbon solar cell in which all its constituents  top to bottom- are carbon based. Realizing this structure would be transformative for the world and Canadian energy landscape. It would aid in building Canada's competitive edge and position Canada as a pioneer in renewable energy research. Besides photovoltaic applications, the research could greatly impact the field of electronics and circuit design, as well as biomedical sensing applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery and Development of Protein-Like DNAzymes that Cleave Target RNA with High Efficiency
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCATALYSIS; DRUG DESIGN; KINETICS,; MOLECULAR MIMICRY; NUCLEIC ACID CONFORMATION; SELEX
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins account for most disease states represented in cancer and viral infection. Consequently, proteins have been the primary targets of most drugs. Messenger RNA (mRNA) represents an important alternative target because a drug that destroys a specific mRNA molecule prevents the production of hundreds of protein molecules translated from the mRNA. Thus the ability to catalyze the destruction of specific mRNA represents a broad and enabling approach to treating a diversity of diseases. In this proposal, we present our plan to discover DNAzymes, i.e. DNA strands with catalytic properties, that would efficiently cleave a target mRNA. To this end, we shall use modified DNAzyles, built from modified DNA bases bearing functionalities usually found in proteins, that will greatly enhance the catalysis of the RNA cleaving reaction. This work will be conducted in order to obtain DNAzymes fully active under physiological conditions, to afford applications for targeting mRNA for medical needs (HIV, hepatitis, cancer).

Keywords-MotsClés: BORON SUB PHTHALOCYANINE; ENERGY; NEW MATERIALS; NITROXIDE MEDIATED POLYMERIZATION (NMP); ORGANIC ELECTRONICS; ORGANIC LIGHT EMITTING DIODES (OLEDS); ORGANIC PHOTOVOLTAICS (OPVS); ORGANIC THIN FILM TRANSISTOR (OTFTS)
Abstract-Résumé: Plastic electronics, also known as organic electronics, are polymers or small molecules with conductive properties. Unlike traditional semiconductors such as silicon, plastic electronics are flexible and have a very low manufacturing cost. Accordingly, they represent a rapidly expanding market. Plastic electronics can range from radio-frequency identification tags (RFID) for smart ID cards, to lightemitting diodes (OLEDs) for flexible television displays, to inexpensive solar cells, or photovoltaic cells (OPVs), which can be used to recharge batteries or improve fuel consumption of road vehicles. While some of these applications are starting to be commercialized, their ability to be competitive on the market is hindered by elevated production costs and poor efficiencies. This research is focused on utilizing new polymers (plastics) with bound boron species, which have been known to be good light absorbers and charge conductors. Using industrially relevant synthesis techniques, we will be synthesizing conductive plastics that can be realistically manufactured on a large scale. The synthesis and characterization of these novel polymers as well as their implementation into lab scale OLEDs and OPVs will allow us to study whether these classes of polymers can produce cost-effective and sufficiently efficient materials to be used in nextgeneration plastic electronics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Brain-cranium interactions in the origin of tetrapod cranial diversity
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPHIBIAN; BRAIN EVOLUTION; CRANIAL EVOLUTION; DIVERSITY; EVOLUTION; EVOLUTIONARY DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; FOSSIL RECORD; GEOMETRIC MORPHOMETRICS; MICRO-COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; MORPHOLOGICAL TRANSITIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The fossil record is unique in its ability to capture events critical to understanding the origin and maintenance of animal diversity through time. However, many questions remain, such as the origin of modern amphibians. Inferences about the origin of modern amphibians, based on fossils alone, are woefully incomplete. My proposed research takes an integrative approach to understanding the role of the brain in the evolution of amphibian cranial form through the incorporation of new fossil material and novel developmental experiments. Application of modern developmental and genetic approaches is needed to reveal insights into the mechanisms that influence the production of cranial diversity. Over the course of this program of research, I will analyze the fossil record in new ways to understand the mechanistic basis of the origin of amphibian form. Evolutionary conservation of these mechanisms across animals is unknown, but can be elucidated by examining amphibians, as they represent the other major lineage of animals next to amniotes, e.g., mammals. Identification of shared mechanisms of cranial evolution implicate common genetic programs and selective pressures, which can be applied to topics such as the origin of developmental abnormalities and the evolution of functional aspects of the brain. As well, elucidation of such mechanisms, with reference to the fossil record over time, contributes to understanding what influences the duration of form across fluctuating environments and its subsequent diversification, simply because diversity provides the raw materials upon which natural selection operates. Together, this research contributes to understanding fundamental aspects of evolution theory. My proposed fieldwork promises to fill critical gaps in the amphibian record, and with sites in the Arctic, Alberta and Nova Scotia this study will highlight the natural heritage of Canada, and will draw attention to Canada as a centre of paleontological discovery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Local adaptation versus plant plasticity: Global climate change, evolutionary game theory and resilience in the boreal forest
Keywords-MotsClés: BLACK SPRUCE; BOREAL FOREST; CLIMATE CHANGE; DENDROCHRONOLOGY; EVOLUTIONARY GAME THEORY; FOREST DYNAMICS; FREQUENCY DEPENDENCE,; PLANT PLASTICITY; RECIPROCAL TRANSPLANT; WHITE SPRUCE
Abstract-Résumé: The boreal forest is the largest ecosystem in Canada, covering ~60% of Canada's land area. Economically, the boreal forest is an important resource and the harvest of pulp wood from Canada's boreal is a 60 billion dollar a year industry. Globally, the boreal is second only to tropical forests in terms of ecosystem services such as atmospheric carbon capture and sequestration. However, northern areas are expected to be hardest hit by shifts in global climate, and it is critical that we better understand the potential changes to the boreal forest. The proposed research will contribute to our understanding of the variability in the responses of boreal trees to environmental variation across the latitudinal extent of the boreal using two ecologically and commercially important tree species. I approach this from three angles. First, I will develop a predictive model of forest dynamics to help forecast potential changes into the future. Second, I will perform a reciprocal-transplant experiment to understand the flexibility of boreal forest species to respond to changes in climate. This involves taking seeds from the southern range of the boreal and planting them in the northern range, and vice versa. By comparing the performance of trees in this transplant experiment I will gain critical insights into how the boreal system might respond to a warming climate. Third, I will examine a long-term data set of annual growth rates of trees in the north and south regions of the boreal obtained from tree rings. By comparing annual growth rates to long term climate data from Environment Canada I can also understand how climatic variables will impact the performance of trees across the extent of the boreal biome. This work will be done under a formal partnership between Wilfrid Laurier University and the Government of the NWT. There is substantial potential for impact both from a basic scientific understanding of this important ecosystem, but also for real world management practices.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Genetic Architecture of Antibiotic Resistance: Measuring and Predicting Evolution in Natural Populations of Bacteria.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE; ECOLOGY; ENVIRONMENTAL MICROBIOLOGY; EVOLUTION; EVOLUTIONARY MICROBIOLOGY; GENETIC ARCHITECTURE; PATHOGENIC BATERIA; PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA; STREPTOCOCCUS PNEUMONIAE,
Abstract-Résumé: The introduction of antibiotics to treat bacterial infections in the 1950s revolutionized modern medicine. At last, physicians had a reliable way to combat many of the most common threats to human health in a matter of days. However, as more and more quantities of antibiotics were used in medical practice, bacteria capable to resist medical treatments emerged in most hospitals around the world. Now, antibiotic-resistant bacteria can be found in most environments affected by human activity such as soil and rivers. The presence of antibiotic resistance in natural environments can contribute to the burden of infectious diseases in hospitals and the broader populations. Predicting the distribution of antibiotic resistance in natural populations of microbes is therefore crucial if we are to reduce the number of resistant infections in humans. Important genetic factors could contribute to the distribution of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in the environment. For example, the presence of antibiotic resistance in a bacterium can affect the bacterium's ability to compete against bacteria that do not harbour resistance or the bacterium's capability to resist new stresses. The objective of this study is to discover whether genetic factors such as those described above shape the evolution and distribution of antibiotic resistance in populations of pathogens. Using state-of-the-art genomics techniques and real-time evolution experiments, this work will identify the cause and consequences of antibiotic resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Streptococcus pneumoniae, two of the most important pathogenic bacteria in Canadian hospitals. Understanding the general effect of genetic factors on evolution in natural populations is a key step in predicting microbial evolution and therefore controlling the spread of antibiotic resistance.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Development and Evolution of the Sexually Dimorphic Transcriptome of Drosophila melanogaster
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENT; DROSOPHILA MELANOGASTER; EVOLUTION; EXPERIMENTAL EVOLUTION; FRUIT FLY; GENE EXPRESSION; RNA SEQUENCING; SEXUAL DIMORPHISM; SEXUAL SELECTION; TRANSCRIPTOME
Abstract-Résumé: In most species, males and females are very different in many ways: in behaviour, size, colour, and lifespan. Why do these differences evolve? How do the sexes develop different traits? Answering these questions is an important challenge because sex differences in growth, disease and lifespan are important for livestock management and human health. Studies to date suggest that the sexes evolve different traits because they differ in how much competition they face for the opposite sex (sexual selection), and in the resources they require for reproduction (natural selection). In recent years, genetic sequencing technology has revolutionized biology, and we now have the opportunity to take a fresh and comprehensive look at the evolution and development of differences between the sexes. Using these new technologies, we can now measure how the sexes express all of their genes, and thus start to understand the genetic basis of differences between the sexes. I will use this approach to address two questions about differences between the sexes at the level of gene expression: how do these differences develop from juveniles to adults? And do sexual selection and resource abundance influence gene expression as we currently expect? To answer these questions, I will use fruit flies, a classic model organism. To address the first question, I will examine how the sexes express genes differently throughout development, from egg to adult. To address the second question, I will conduct an experimental evolution study in which flies evolve under weak or strong sexual selection with low or high resources. The key prediction to be tested is that sexual selection increases sex differences in gene expression, especially at high resource levels. Because fruit flies share many genes with mammals, including humans, the results will be relevant for applied topics in agriculture and human health. These studies as a whole will help us understand why the sexes differ in so many ways.

TitreApplicationTitle: A vestibulocentric visual channel for image stabilization
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESSORY OPTIC SYSTEM; DIRECTION SELECTIVE GANGLION CELLS; IMAGE STABILIZATION; OPTOKINETIC NYSTAGMUS; RETINAL PHYSIOLOGY; SEMICIRCULAR CANALS; VESTIBULAR SYSTEM; VESTIBULO-OCULAR REFLEX
Abstract-Résumé: As animals interact with their environment, their heads are frequently in motion. The brain has thus evolved dedicated circuits that detect self-motion through comparison of visual signals arriving from the retina against head rotation signals arriving from the inner ear. Comparison of these signals drives reflex eye movements that serve to stabilize the image of the outside world on the retina. Without these eye movements, image stabilization and visual performance deteriorate. Visual input to this image-stabilization system arrives from direction-selective cells in the retina - cells that are activated only when the image of the outside world moves along a specific direction across the retina. These direction-selective cells send information to a brainstem target - the accessory optic system - which in turn integrates these motion signals and routes them to higher brain processing areas, where they are compared with inner-ear head rotation signals. The objective of this study is to explore how the accessory optic system assembles signals from direction-selective cells to allow their efficient comparison with inner-ear head rotation signals. I will test two conflicting models that place the key computation underlying the assembly of motion information in fundamentally different locations - the accessory optic system versus the retina. I will use a new mouse genetic model, in which the direction-selective cells are marked by a fluorescent protein and are easy to detect, as well as various electrophysiological and morphological techniques. This proposal introduces a fundamentally new model of how visual signals are assembled and compared against head rotation signals. If confirmed, this would have profound implications for studies of the developmental mechanisms by which direction selectivity is implemented in the retina, and for the mechanistic basis of reflex eye movements that are highly conserved among vertebrates and essential for normal visual acuity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interactions between Sensory, Emotional, Cognitive, and Reward Networks in the Brain that make Music Rewarding
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IMAGING; CONNECTIVITY; DOPAMINE; EMOTIONAL PROCESSING; MUSIC; NETWORK ANALYSIS; NEUROAESTHETICS; PARTIAL LEAST SQUARES; REWARD SYSTEM; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: It makes us smile, it makes us cry, and it warms our heart. It brings us together and lets us feel what the other person's feeling, moves us in ways we never imagined possible. Sometimes it can make us really sad, but it's a good kind of sad: comforting, somehow. One thing is for sure; the emotions can be intense. Amazingly, it all happens in our heads. Nothing concrete is left behind to remind us of what a good time we had. Listening to or producing music seems to be a part of human nature. Music is ubiquitous in society and has been around in every culture for at least as long as history has been recorded. Importantly, it was not created in one place and passed on, but appears to have developed independently in each culture, perhaps it is innate to some form of human behaviour. But it does not seem to have a clear survival value (Darwin, 1871), so why has it lasted this long? What has made music so reinforcing? We investigate this question by examining the complex interactions between cognitive expectations and sensory systems in the brain, and how these interact with the emotion and reward systems to make us feel pleasure. We use functional magnetic resonance imaging to acquire brain images while people are listening to music and apply cutting-edge brain analysis techniques that allow causal inferences and examinations of changes within brain networks to be able to answer these questions: how do we start to appreciate a piece of music, and how do brain systems interact to make this happen? Why do different people like different types of music and how does previous experience with musical sounds contribute to this? What role do expectations and anticipation play in the way that we listen to music? Why do we get tired of some music after we hear it a few times, but can listen to other music repeatedly and continue to enjoy it? And finally, how do the 'intellectual' parts of our brains interact with the dopaminergic reward systems to induce pleasurable responses?

TitreApplicationTitle: Elevated temperature lithium batteries
Keywords-MotsClés: BATTERIES, LITHIUM; ELECTROLYTES; ENERGY STORAGE
Abstract-Résumé: Energy storage devices are an integral part of sustainable energy delivery as we move to rely less on fossil-fuel based resources to harness renewable energy resources such as solar and wind power. These are fundamentally intermittent energy sources that require load leveling systems to become viable. Lithium batteries are very attractive candidates to fulfill that role because of their environmental compatibility, high efficiency, high energy density and long lifetime. Nonetheless, their current temperature and safety limitations limit their applications to portable electronic equipment and range-restricted vehicular transport. This project aims to develop advanced lithium battery based on novel concepts including ionic liquid salts embedded into solid matrix electrolytes together with high voltage lithium cathode compounds which enables the safe and robust operation of lithium batteries at slightly elevated temperatures (~80C). Successful completion of the project will make available devices featuring high capacity, energy density and rate capability as well as heat integration capability. These features will allow the realization of improved low cost energy storage technologies required for electric vehicles and large scale stationary energy storage facilities in Canada. The project will also contribute to knowledge creation in this important technological sector.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nanoparticle adhesion at soft interfaces
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL IMAGING; BROWNIAN DYNAMICS; COLLOIDAL ADHESION; COMPLEX FLUIDS; DRUG DELIVERY; INTERFACIAL MICRORHEOLOGY; MATHEMATICAL MODELLING; NANOPARTICLES; POROELASTIC DYNAMICS; SOFT INTERFACES
Abstract-Résumé: Nanoparticle adhesion to and transport within soft materials arises in the active lining of biological organs, including the respiratory, digestive, and productive tracts. The fundamental mechanisms involved are extraordinarily complex, and it is only recently that research has begun to tackle the challenges of developing rigorous mathematical models to understand nanoparticle dynamics at soft interfaces and how these mechanisms impact targeted drug delivery, microrheology, and sensing applications. In this research program, we will address the adhesion of colloidal spheres to soft planar interfaces using a balance of theoretical, computational, and experimental methods. Mathematical models will be developed, drawing on fluid mechanics, elasticity, poroelasticity, and statistical thermodynamics, and these models will be solved using a combination of analytical and numerical methods. The results will be tested by comparison to experiments, which will be undertaken using state-of-the-art interfacial micro-rheological tools. From this research, our goal is to establish a clear set of guiding principles to specify the size and surface functionality of nanoparticles for targeted drug delivery and imaging, accounting for the specific chemical and physical characteristics of the tissues that the particles must adhere to and transport through.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development of single cell microfluidic technologies for analysis of microRNA expression and epigenetic state with application to hematopoietic stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; HEMATOPOIESIS; MICROFLUIDICS; MOLECULAR BARCODING; MRNA EXPRESSION; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; SINGLE CELL ANALYSIS; STEM CELL; TRANSCRIPTOME
Abstract-Résumé: Cells differ from one to the other, although the information stored within their DNA may be the same. This heterogeneity in, for example, the genes that are active or modifications to proteins may change their behavior. Stem cells can divide many times and differentiate to create various cell types and tissues, but if things go wrong they can also lead to cancer. Compelling evidence suggests that differences in the state of stem cells affect their fate and development. There is thus an urgent need to understand cell-to-cell differences and develop techniques to assess the heterogeneity between individual cells. In spite of many advances in biological and genetic techniques we are still incapable of determining cell-to-cell differences. Current techniques are not sensitive enough to measure single cells and rely on the average of many cells, thereby obscuring individual differences. If we can identify individual stem cells and determine differences in their state this would greatly improve our understanding of their development. It would also enable the detection and quantification of cancer stem cells that are responsible for perpetuating the disease. The goal of this proposal is to develop techniques to interrogate individual stem cells and determine their state. This will be accomplished by using large-scale microfluidic integration, a technique that creates devices with thousands of valves and reaction chambers to manipulate and interrogate individual cells. We will combine this technique with modern high-throughput genetic methods to measure differences between individual cells in protein modifications and RNA levels. By these techniques, we expect to determine the state of individual stem cells and uncover the mechanisms that drive them to differentiate into different cell types. This information will be invaluable to create methods to control stem cells and to develop new tools for diagnosis and treatment of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Nature of Exciton Dynamics in Organic Photovoltaics: Insight from Theory and Simulations
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTER SIMULATION; ELECTRONIC STRUCTURE; EXCITONS; NON-ADIABATIC QUANTUM MOLECULAR DYNAMICS; ORGANIC CONJUGATED SYSTEMS; ORGANIC PHOTOVOLTAICS; ORGANIC SOLAR CELLS; PATH-INTEGRAL MOLECULAR DYNAMICS; QUANTUM CHEMISTRY; SINGLET FISSION
Abstract-Résumé: Solar energy is an inexhaustible natural resource, and the invention of solar cells to harness this energy was a major step forward in our search for renewable energy sources. Recently, organic solar cells have become an important alternative to traditional inorganic devices, offering the advantages of low cost, high volume, versatility of chemical synthesis, ease of processing, flexibility, and being environmentally friendly. They have been under intense investigation for more than a decade now, but despite the significant progress in their syntheses, their efficiency remains relatively low. Since the mechanism by which solar energy is turned into electricity in organic photovoltaics is still far from being completely understood at the molecular level, overcoming this bottleneck is increasingly urgent to further advance this field. Specifically, we seek to understand the lifetime of an organic photovoltaic exciton: an excited electronic state generated upon impact of a solar photon and characterized by a locally bound electron-hole pair. The exciton can undergo fission, diffusion, dissociation, annihilation, charge separation, and charge recombination. New, accurate theoretical methods are needed to describe all these competing processes and the factors that determine the fate of an exciton. In the proposed research, we will endeavor to develop a general theoretical framework, and apply it to simulate and understand exciton dynamics in representative systems. The use of cutting-edge techniques in quantum chemistry and quantum molecular dynamics will make it possible to shed some light on the atomistic details of the organic photovoltaic mechanism. Successful completion of this research will thus lead to testable design suggestions for manufacturing high-efficiency organic solar cells that are the future of both the Canadian and world-wide solar energy industry.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the quark-gluon plasma: Towards a more realistic kinetic description of ultrarelativistic heavy ion collisions
Keywords-MotsClés: MANY-BODY QUANTUM CHROMODYNAMICS; PHYSICS; QUARK-GLUON PLASMA; RELATIVISTIC BOLTZMANN EQUATION; RELATIVISTIC DISSIPATIVE FLUID DYNAMICS; ULTRARELATIVISTIC HEAVY ION COLLISIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Ultrarelativistic heavy ion collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and the Large Hadron Collider(LHC) create a hot and dense system of strongly interacting nuclear matter that only existed in nature a few microseconds after the Big Bang. At such temperatures, one million times hotter than the core of the sun, quarks and gluons are deconfined and a new state of matter is formed, the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP). One of the most surprising results obtained at RHIC, and later confirmed at the LHC, is that this novel state of nuclear matter behaves as an almost prefect fluid, with the smallest viscosity ever observed in nature. Understanding the thermodynamic and transport properties of the QGP and explaining the striking observations made at RHIC and LHC became one of the main challenges in nuclear physics, serving to further develop our understanding of the QCD phase diagram and transport properties. In this project I will derive from multi-component kinetic theory the most complete theory of relativistic fluid dynamics, including all possible nonlinear terms up to second order in Knudsen and inverse Reynolds numbers. This sophisticated formalism will be implemented in MUSIC, a relativistic fluid dynamics simulation used and developed by the nuclear theory group in McGill, and will be used to model the dynamics of the QGP with a precision never obtained before. Several fundamental issues in heavy ion physics will be addressed: the effect of bulk viscosity on flow, the description of the hadron gas formed at the end of the collision, and the emission of thermal photons from the QGP. By tackling such problems simultaneously and within the same framework, it will finally be possible to extract the thermodynamic and transport properties of strongly interacting QCD matter: a challenge that is around since the discovery of QCD as the fundamental theory behind the strong force.

TitreApplicationTitle: Susceptibility to Dento-Gingival Attachment Loss in Amelotin-deficient Mice
Keywords-MotsClés: AMELOTIN; GUM DISEASE; LIGATURE; PERIODONTAL DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Gum disease, or periodontitis is the most prevalent disease affecting oral soft tissues. One of the earliest signs of periodontitis is the loss of attachment between the teeth and the oral soft tissues that encase them.  We have recently discovered that amelotin - a novel enamel protein that is crucial in the proper formation of tooth enamel - is also found exclusively at this interface between gums and teeth after tooth eruption. We have preliminary evidence from our laboratory that amelotin is involved in binding the cells of the gum surface to the mineralized tooth. In this research project we will use a unique mouse model developed in our lab that is deficient in amelotin. These amelotin-deficient mice, and normal mice for comparison, will be treated to induce periodontal disease. After a certain period of time we will use several analytical methods to determine whether the detachment of gingiva from teeth is worse in mice lacking amelotin. This work will potentially identify novel components of the tooth-to-gum attachment apparatus.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development of an educational module for oral mucosal screening within a high-risk community setting
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO CARE; HEALTH PROMOTION; HIV+; HPV; ORAL AND OROPHARYNGEAL CANCER; ORAL HEALTH; ORAL MUCOSAL LESIONS; REFERRAL PATHWAYS
Abstract-Résumé: Persons living with HIV/AIDS are at a high risk of experiencing negative changes in their oral health.  Viral, fungal, and bacterial oral infections are prevalent and affect approximately 40-50% of individuals who are HIV-positive.  Oral lesions that are strongly associated with HIV infection (such as pseudo-membranous candidiasis, oral hairy leukoplakia, Kaposi's sarcoma, and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma) are prominent and can progress undetected, especially in individuals who do not have access to oral health care.  An increased risk of HPV may also increase the risk of oropharyngeal cancer in a segment of this population.  Barriers to oral care for this segment of society can be great and are often associated with financial limitations, stigma, discrimination, and fear.  Among those who face barriers to care, lack of oral health education is problematic, and the ability to find care providers who can attend to them is even more difficult.  While there is an extensive amount of research dedicated to the identification, diagnosis, and treatment of oral conditions related to HIV/AIDS, little attention has been paid to the development of educational material and resources that will help these individuals become informed about their oral health.  The student will: (1) collect and assess current educational oral health resources aimed at the HIV+ population as background to the development of future educational resources; and (2) initiate the development of referral pathways for lesion follow-up.  Findings will be presented to the Positive Living Society of British Columbia, and oral health and medical professionals to raise awareness of HIV individuals who do not receive regular oral health care and oral mucosal screening.  Results of this research will educate non-oral health personnel to screen HIV+ individuals who do not access regular oral health care about oral lesions and aid in the referral of individuals with lesions which may require further follow-up.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of exercise training and ibuprofen on bone in older women
Keywords-MotsClés: BALANCE; BONE; IBUPROFEN; INFLAMMATION; MUSCLE; OSTEOPOROSIS; SARCOPENIA; SENIORS; WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis is a disease involving bone loss and risk of breaks or fractures. It is particularly common in older women, causing physical and social challenges for those with this chronic condition, and costing our health care system billions of dollars each year. One possible contributing factor to the development of osteoporosis is increased inflammation with aging. Inflammation is linked to the breakdown of bone. One way to treat inflammation is to take over the counter, non-steroid anti-inflammatory medication like ibuprofen. Research has shown that young women who take ibuprofen after exercise training sessions increase bone mineral density in their hips. Our study will be the first to investigate the effect of taking ibuprofen after regular exercise sessions (done 3 times per week for 9 months) on bone mineral density at the hip in older women (i.e. women aged 65y or greater). It will provide new evidence about possible ways to reduce the sometimes devastating impacts of osteoporosis, and will be useful to health care practitioners.

Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MICROSTRUCTURE; ESTROGEN; MECHANOBIOLOGY; OSTEOCTYES
Abstract-Résumé: Cells embedded within bone tissue, known as osteocytes, form an interconnected network which serves several functions including adaptation to mechanical stimuli (e.g. activity-induced loading) and the storage/mobilization of calcium.  Women face increased physiological demands for calcium associated with reproduction and also face an increased risk of age-related bone loss and fractures. It is well established that Estrogen plays a key role in bone health but it is unclear how this hormone affects the organization of bone at the cellular level.  The proposed study will examine the inter-relationship of estrogen and loading on the cellular organization of growing bone using advanced 3D imaging.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adjunctive nutritional strategies to overcome sarcopenic muscle loss in aging
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CITRULLINE; SARCOPENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Aging is accompanied by a progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass known as sarcopenia. Although the physiological mechanisms of sarcopenia have yet to be determined, declining muscle mass is inevitable, and the consequences are profound regarding reduced mobility, increased risk of falls and metabolic diseases such as type II diabetes. The differences in muscle protein breakdown and muscle protein synthesis with age are related to this net muscle loss, and as a result, efforts are being made to find nutritional rather than pharmaceutical solutions to maintaining skeletal muscle and functional independence of elderly adults. Exercise has been proven to be an effective measure to reduce the rate at which muscle is lost in elderly adults, but the synthesis of integral muscle proteins is 'blunted' in the elderly when responding to normal stimuli for protein synthesis such as doses of protein, which may be due to the inactive lifestyles of older adults. In order to answer fundamental questions regarding the underlying mechanisms of sarcopenia, the effects of citrulline, a natural precursor to agents which increase muscle blood flow, is to be investigated. Varying doses of citrulline will be ingested in conjunction with whey protein, and short bouts of resistance exercise will be performed prior to isotopic tracer and muscle biopsy analysis. Citrulline has been linked to an increase in muscle protein synthesis and we predict that its combined effects with exercise will serve to increase the delivery of nutrients to skeletal muscle and preserve muscle in the face of aging and inactivity. It is hypothesized that citrulline's effects, when added to a dose of whey protein and subsequently ingested, enhance the effects of a less than optimal dosage of protein, especially in the elderly, through stimulation of muscle protein synthesis with no change in the breakdown of protein.

TitreApplicationTitle: effet d'une supplémentation en protéine combinée à un programme d'activité physique sur la fonction musculaire chez des hommes âgés de 70 ans et plus sains ou pré-frêles; étude randomisée à double insu
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTONOMIE; CAPACITE FONCTIONNELLE; EXERCICE; FONCTION MUSCULAIRE; FORCE MUSCULAIRE; METABOLISM MUSCULAIRE; MOBILITE; NUTRITION; PROTEINE; VIEILLISSEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: INTRODUCTION : Les personnes freles sont considerees comme celles ayant le plus grand risque de devenir dependant. Or, la perte de force musculaire, qui est un de ces criteres, semble etre un facteur important dans la perte de mobilite, de chute et de fragilite. Selon Statistique Canada, l'esperance de vie sans handicap est de 67 ans pour les hommes. Le cout total des soins d'un adulte age dans la communaute et dans les institutions est respectivement de $ 9.600 et $ 30.000 par an. Il est donc crucial de trouver des strategies non pharmacologiques pour prevenir ce processus physiologique lie au vieillissement normal et contrer la perte d'autonomie et de mobilite. Il a ete demontre que l'activite physique et plus specifiquement l'exercice en resistance semble une strategie efficace pour contrer la perte de capacites fonctionnelles. Une autre intervention a considerer pour ameliorer la fonction musculaire chez les adultes ages est le supplement proteique. Toutefois, l'impact de la combinaison de ces deux interventions, ainsi que les facteurs impliques dans les adaptations musculaires chez des personnes agees en bonne sante ou pre-freles sont encore mal compris.  OBJECTIFS: Cette etude interventionnelle (exercice + proteine/placebo) randomisee a double insu de 12 semaines a pour objectif de :1) Comparer l'effet d'un programme de 12 semaines d'entrainement en force, avec ou sans supplementation en proteines, sur la fonction musculaire chez des hommes ages en bonne sante et pre-freles; 2) Quantifier la contribution des facteurs neuronaux et musculaires sur les adaptations de la force musculaire.  RETOMBEES: Definir des strategies pour ameliorer la force musculaire chez les personnes agees pre-freles est une necessite absolue pour reduire le fardeau de notre systeme de sante. Cette recherche permettra: 1) de mettre au point une intervention adaptee et efficace pour prevenir la perte de mobilite liee au vieillissement.

ClasseRechercheFR: ETATS MORBIDES MAL DEFINIS; TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX
TitreApplicationTitle: Development of biomarker profile and rapid screening tool for mild traumatic brain injury due to subclinical primary blast.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; AXONAL INJURY; BEHAVIOUR; BIOMARKERS; MILD TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY; PRIMARY BLAST TRAUMA; THERAPY; WHITE MATTER INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is highly prevalent in civilian and military populations yet is frequently undiagnosed and untreated.  The symptoms associated with mTBI manifest as neurological disorders including insomnia, anxiety, poor concentration and coping skills. These symptoms have significant impact on quality of life.  In military populations, the potential for mTBI is high due to occupational hazards.  There have been increasing reports of veterans with mTBI symptoms.  It has been suggested that shock waves (also referred to as primary blast) from explosions, such as those occurring from improvised explosive devices, may have potential to cause brain injury in the absence of blunt physical trauma. We have demonstrated that the brain is in fact far more susceptible to primary blasts than other organs (lungs and ear drums) that have previously been used as indicators of blast exposure. One of the leading challenges to treat mTBI is the ability to accurately diagnose its occurrence. We are currently developing a blood-based test to determine whether an individual exposed to a primary blast has endured mTBI. The sensitivity of this test would rival current imaging tests, such as MRIs, which do not have the sensitivity to detect subtle molecular changes in the brain. We have demonstrated that specific regions in the brain are preferentially injured when exposed to primary blasts. We have proposed to examine a group of blood biomarkers (protein fragments from the brain that end up in the blood)to determine whether they reliably predict brain injury from primary blasts. We have also proposed experiments that will demonstrate whether biomarkers can predict outcome after primary blast exposure. The development of a biomarker test for mTBI would be of tremendous value in the clinical setting to diagnose and prioritize treatments to those patients who are most likely to have a poor outcome.

Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD FLOW; FIBROMYALGIA; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PAIN; SKIN TEMPERATURE; THERMAL AGENTS; TIVI
Abstract-Résumé: People with bone and joint injuries or arthritis often use heat or cold to manage their pain, reduce swelling and allow them to move more easily. Although this treatment is commonly used, we do not know enough about how it affects pain, blood flow in the area and ability to move. If not used properly, these treatments can cause tissue injury or be ineffective. This study will determine that in people with no problems, or that have arthritis or fibromyalgia, people will apply the heat or cold in the same way they would do at home, but we will monitor all of these effects with precise equipment. This will allow us to provide guidelines to patients in the future about how to use heat or cold in a way that is both safe and effective. We will also determine whether these effects are different in patients with arthritis compared to people without arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Combinatorial Hopf Algebra of polytopes and structure constants
Keywords-MotsClés: ALGEBRAIC COMBINATORICS; CLUSTER ALGEBRAS; COMPUTER SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT; CONVEX POLYTOPES; DISCRETE GEOMETRY; HOPF ALGEBRAS
Abstract-Résumé: Our research project consists of two strands. In one direction we will use high dimensional geometric objects to construct algebraic structures and, in the other direction we will use our knowledge of algebra to better understand the structure behind the geometry. This process of connecting seemingly disparate fields increases our understanding of each area and pushes the boundary of scientific knowledge. The study of geometric objects in a higher dimensional space is a wide research area with enormous technological and scientific impact. A remarkable application is the use of optimization problem models applied to industries including transportation, energy and telecommunications. An example from the scientific side is the physical model of the universe as a 10-dimensional space. Understanding geometry in a high dimensional space is not trivial. Simple questions such as "How many corners does a four dimensional cube have?" seem to be complicated to solve. This project presents an innovative idea of using algebraic methods as a tool to analyze the geometry of higher-dimensional objects. We will study algebraic structures whose elements are geometric objects together with algebraic operations. Roughly speaking, we are able to multiply and decompose geometric objects into new geometric objects. In each direction of this project, from geometry to algebra and from algebra to geometry, we will investigate a selection of open problems. Our inquiries will involve extensive use of powerful computers to gain a better understanding of the objects under study. The complexities that we will encounter in our analyses will require the implementation of new algorithms that will contribute to the development of free open source computer software. In addition to increasing basic knowledge of mathematics and developing algorithms in computer science, we expect to have an impact in mathematical physics as well. Algebraic Structures of High Dimensional Geometric Objects

NomDuProgrammeFR: Programme de bourses postdoctorales Banting CRSNG/CRSH
TitreApplicationTitle: Plasmonic Nanoswitches for Rewritable Materials
Keywords-MotsClés: FLUORESCENCE MODULATION; MOLECULAR SWITCHES; NANOPARTICLES; NANOSCALE RESOLUTION; REVERSIBLE PATTERNING; SURFACE PLASMON
Abstract-Résumé: The miniaturization race in the computer industry leads scientists to investigate the possibility of designing and constructing materials at the nanometer scale. In the last fifty years, progressive miniaturization of electronic components has resulted in outstanding achievements in the field of information and communication development, moving us into the nanotechnology era. Further progress in miniaturization will not only decrease the size and increase the power of computers, but will enable new technologies in the fields of medicine, environment and energy. The chemists of the 21st century can manipulate atoms and molecules in a way that past generations could not even dream about. Today we can construct devices for the processing of information at the molecular level. Like their macroscopic counterparts, molecularlevel devices need energy to operate, and signals to communicate with the operator. Light is the most ecological, most abundant and most attractive tool to read and write information, allowing us to do this locally or remotely, noninvasively and with relatively inexpensive experimental setups, ultimately with the possibility of major scale ups in production. This project describes the realization of molecular devices able to switch their properties in response of an optical stimulus. Their light driven switchable character, in combination with an exciting new nanotechnology, called plasmon electronics, can be exploited for the fabrication of high-performance reusable systems for communications and computer industry, in a world that uses nanotechnology to invent energy efficient, recyclable materials.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Programme de bourses postdoctorales Banting CRSNG/CRSH
TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing physiological and behavioural mechanisms of arctic-nesting birds to mitigate the effects of climate change.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARCTIC; ARTHROPODS; BEHAVIOUR; CLIMATE CHANGE; ENERGETICS; GROWTH; SHOREBIRDS
Abstract-Résumé: In seasonal environments, maximizing the growth of offspring requires that adults synchronize reproduction with peaks in resource availability. In temperate breeding birds, a lack of synchrony between hatch and peaks in resources (mismatch) mostly attributed to recent climate changes, has led to decreases in reproductive success and even population declines in some species. These population level effects of mismatch are thought to occur because food peaks on the breeding grounds are occurring earlier as temperatures increase, yet in some species of birds, timing of breeding has either not changed, or not advanced enough to meet these peaks, leading to reduced growth and survival of young. Recent studies have indicated that arctic-nesting shorebirds may be particularly vulnerable to a mismatch between hatch and food resource peaks due to the short arctic breeding season and climate driven peaks in food availability. Though there is some evidence that growth rates of chicks can be hindered by a mismatch between hatch and food resource peaks, fewer studies have investigated whether the same temperature increases that may drive this asynchrony, could actually decrease energetic requirements of chicks, and thus compensate for the potential negative effects of reduced food availability. The purpose of this research is to investigate whether arctic-nesting shorebirds possess the behavioural and physiological mechanisms necessary to mitigate trophic constraints hypothesized by current climate change scenarios. By collecting detailed ecological and physiological data on juvenile growth and survival of shorebirds, the proposed research will test key hypotheses regarding both the direct and indirect effects of climate change on arctic wildlife, as well as provide valuable information for the management of wildlife in the Canadian Arctic.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Programme de bourses postdoctorales Banting CRSNG/CRSH
TitreApplicationTitle: Caractérisation thermique du bassin sédimentaire des Basses-Terres Saint-Laurent pour systèmes géothermiques profonds et superficiels
Keywords-MotsClés: CHAUFFAGE; CLIMATISATION; CONDUCTIVITE THERMIQUE; EAU SOUTERRAINE; ESSAIS DE TERRAIN; MODELISATION; TRANSFER DE CHALEUR; ELECTRICITE, CHAUFFAGE; ENERGIE, GEOTHERMIE
Abstract-Résumé: L'energie geothermique est une ressource renouvelable qui provient de la chaleur accumulee dans la croute terrestre. Elle est utilisee pour produire de l'electricite ou chauffer des batiments et diminue les emissions de gaz a effet de serre. La production d'electricite s'effectue avec des centrales operees avec de l'eau souterraine a plus de 80 °C et captee par des puits ayant quelques kilometres de profondeur. Le chauffage de batiments est realise avec des thermopompes liees a des echangeurs de chaleur amenages dans des forages a quelques centaines de metres de profondeur. L'utilisation de ces technologies reduit la dependance aux combustibles fossiles. Le cout d'installation des systemes geothermiques est par contre dispendieux puisque des forages sont necessaires. L'evaluation des proprietes thermiques du sous-sol permet de cibler les environnements geologiques favorables et ainsi reduire le cout d'installation. L'objectif du projet propose est de caracteriser les proprietes thermiques des unites rocheuses du bassin sedimentaire des Basses- Terres du Saint-Laurent afin de contribuer au developpement de systemes geothermiques de toutes sortes. Des echantillons de roc seront analyses en laboratoire pour connaitre les proprietes thermiques qui serviront a definir le potentiel geothermique des sources profondes et superficielles a l'aide de modeles mathematiques. Des essais seront effectues dans des forages pour mesurer de facon in situ ces memes proprietes et comparer les resultats aux analyses de laboratoire. Une technologie novatrice en voie d'etre brevetee sera utilisee pour effectuer les essais de terrain. Le projet servira a valider cette nouvelle technologie d'un potentiel commercial pour les systemes geothermiques superficiels. Les resultats valideront egalement la faisabilite de produire de l'electricite avec des centrales geothermiques hybrides fonctionnant en partie avec des biocombustibles, une technologie prometteuse encore inexploitee au Canada.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Programme de bourses postdoctorales Banting CRSNG/CRSH
TitreApplicationTitle: Geoarchaeology in the Southern Levant: the macroscopic, petrographic, and geochemical characterisation of chert from archaeological and geological contexts
Keywords-MotsClés: ARCHAEOLOGY; EPIPALAEOLITHIC; GEOARCHAEOLOGY; GEOLOGY; HUNTER-GATHERERS; LITHICS; MOBILITY; RAW MATERIAL PROVENANCING; SEDENTISM; SOUTHERN LEVANT
Abstract-Résumé: This project will investigate the sourcing of stone tool raw materials in the Southern Levantine (modern-day Israel and Jordan) Epipalaeolithic, which dates to about 8,000-18,000 BC. This time period and region are critically important in global human history, as they cover the complex transition from hunter-gatherers to farmers in what is often referred to as the 'Neolithic revolution', with concomitant research questions regarding sedentism and social change. Raw material sourcing studies are a vital part of archaeological considerations: they help us understand human behaviour and the relationships between people and the environment, allowing us to reconstruct the movement of peoples and objects in the landscape, including seasonal mobility, social boundaries, exchange systems, and trade routes. They also provide evidence for the territory, location, and size of resources that relate to the social and technical organisation of crafts and industries. While the Southern Levant is a region with a rich archaeological heritage, there is a significant gap in the region's raw material sourcing research. This project will begin to fill this gap, and therefore deepen our understandings of the prehistoric communities there. Dr. Killian Driscoll will research with an interdisciplinary team of archaeologists and geologists at the Universite de Montreal. He will analyse the archaeological and geological material, using a range of research methods from the fields of geology and archaeology, to answer the research questions regarding the prehistoric hunter-gatherers in the region. A critical part of the project is the formulation of a research framework for other researchers to follow as best practice in raw material sourcing studies. A web-based, multilingual, raw material provenance database will be constructed, and open to researchers to upload and download data, therefore creating an important Canada-based portal for worldwide raw material sourcing studies.

Abstract-Résumé: CBRAIN is a national platform that provides brain researchers across the country with easy access to the Canadian supercomputing network. We now propose to build upon this IT network by creating a layer of (i) online databasing, (ii) neurological/neuropsychological testi instruments, (iii) software tools for analysis of imaging/clinical/genetic data, and (iv)  management staff customized for research into neurodegenerative diseases. We will focus on Alzheimer's disease but the technology will have general application in all areas of research into neurodegenerative diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: AD ontological architecture for neuroimaging datawarehouse: merging and establishing anatomical normative data from 17 datasets
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; ANATOMICAL STRUCTURES; BIOMARKERS; DATAWAREHOUSE; DOMAIN ONTOLOGY; METABOLIC INFORMATION; MULTIMODALITY; ONTOLOGICAL PROCESSING; POPULATION NORMS; RELATED DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: No single neuroimaging dataset is sufficiently large to provide a comprehensive understanding of the AD disease process, propose accurate diagnostic and prognostic, and evaluate response to therapy. Yet, federating databases remains an arduous task, as we cannot rely on any domain-specific interoperability framework. We propose an ontology-based strategy to alleviate this situation. We will use ontologies to merge 17 neuroimaging-centric datasets, process them identically, and establish population norms for anatomical structures and metabolic information. We will implement the system locally, and disseminate the ontology nationally and internationally.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transformation of Indigenous Primary Healthcare Delivery (FORGE AHEAD): Community-driven Innovations and Strategic Scale-up Toolkits
Keywords-MotsClés: CAPACITY BUILDING; CHRONIC DISEASE; COMMUNITY READINESS; DIABETES MELLITUS; FIRST NATONS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PARTICIPATORY ACTION RESEARCH; POLICY; PRIMARY HEALTHCARE DELIVERY; QUALITY IMPROVEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, significant disparities between the health status of Indigenous peoples and the general population exist, particularly for chronic diseases such as diabetes. There is a pressing need to shift the present episodic care focus common to most First Nations communities, to one that integrates prevention and management of chronic disease care.  The overarching goal of the TransFORmation of IndiGEnous PrimAry HEAlthcare Delivery (FORGE AHEAD) research program is to develop and evaluate community-driven primary healthcare delivery models that enhance chronic disease management with appropriate access to available services in First Nations communities. The program will use a participatory research approach that honors and reflects the communities' involvement as full partners. Type 2 diabetes mellitus will be the chronic disease targeted. The activities in FORGE AHEAD are linked to the Expanded Chronic Care Model which describes the inter-relationships of individual, community, population and health system factors in chronic disease prevention and care. The projects within FORGE AHEAD include measuring community and healthcare provider readiness to change, supporting and integrating prevention activities within the community, developing community capacity for quality improvement activities and evaluating community-driven strategies to improve the quality of diabetes care. The program will produce a tool-kit of tested strategies that can be successfully implemented, sustained and used for other chronic diseases in First Nations communities in Canada.

Abstract-Résumé: People with chronic conditions are likely to have more than one condition. But the healthcare system is mostly designed for one condition at a time. This 5-year proposal is for a Team whose goal will be to change primary health care and community-based chronic disease prevention and management programs: to reorient care from single disease focus to a multiple disease focus; to centre on not only disease but also the patient; and to change the health care system from separate to coordinated components in care. After the Team has changed care, it will study the improvements. The Team will pay close attention to what works and does not work. When a change has led to better results, the Team will spread the word and improve care for more and more Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Team to Improve Community-Based Cancer Care along the Continuum (CanIMPACT)
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; PRIMARY CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer patients rely on good coordination of care between their primary healthcare providers and their cancer specialist providers throughout their cancer journey from diagnosis to survivorship. However, there are often problems of communication, continuity, and coordination of care that can lead to suboptimal care and anxiety for patients and their families, as well as inefficiency within the healthcare system. We are a pan-Canadian team of healthcare providers, researchers, and policy makers who are committed to improving care for cancer patients. We will also engage patients and their families through a Patient Advisory Committee. We will tackle the problems of continuity and coordination of care through a program of research involving an interrelated sequence of research steps that involve seven provinces will span five years. First, we will comprehensively study the factors associated with poor continuity and coordination of care. Second, we will listen to the perspectives of patients and their families on these aspects of their cancer journey. Third, we will examine the existing medical literature as well as examples of best practices across Canada. Based on what we learn from these steps, we will develop an approach to help primary healthcare providers, cancer specialists, and patients and their families to work together to improve continuity and coordination of care throughout the cancer journey. We will test the approach by the most rigorous scientific standards for clinical trials. At the conclusion of this program of research we will make clear and actionable recommendations on how to improve care for cancer patients and efficiency within the healthcare system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innovation in Community Based Primary Healthcare Supporting Transformation in the Health of First Nations and Rural/remote Manitoba Communities: iPHIT
Keywords-MotsClés: FIRST NATIONS HEALTH; GOVERNANCE; MIXED METHODS; PARTICIPATORY; PRIMARY CARE; RURAL AND REMOTE; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: It is well known that the health outcomes of First Nations are considerably worse than other Canadians.  This is due to many factors, some of which have been studied extensively.  The role of Community Based Primary Healthcare (CBPHC) in determining the health of First Nations and other rural/remote communities is not well understood.  This program of research uses both qualitative and quantitative methods to understand the current state of CBPHC in First Nations and rural and remote Manitoba.  We will engage community members to understand their perspective on their health and needs.  We will compare communities with different governance models of CBPHC (federal, provincial and self-governance models) and we will compare communities with better health outcomes to those with worse outcomes.  We will then work with the participating communities and our advisory groups of elders and experts to propose innovative local models of care that can improve the health of the communities.  The final stage will include an evaluation of the implementation of some of these new models of care. A key component of this team is the collaboration and full integration of the First Nations communities and partnership with the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs and our commitment to helping train a new generation of First Nations primary care researchers.

Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; ECONOMIC EVALUATION; HEALTH CARE ARCHITECTURE AND DESIGN; HEALTH PROFESSIONS; NORTHERN HEALTH; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; RURAL AND REMOTE HEALTH CARE; TELEHEALTH TECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Health care in Canada's North faces many challenges due to geographic isolation, harsh climate, and inadequate staffing. Despite spending a lot more on a per person basis than the rest of Canada, there is still a large gap in the health of the people of the North compared to other Canadians, and within the North, between Aboriginal and non-aboriginal residents. Our proposed Circumpolar Health System Innovation Team brings together an international team of researchers, health professionals, managers, and policy makers to try to design, implement and evaluate strategies to improve access to primary health care. There are three major components: (1) to explore what policies exist and compare how health systems in circumpolar regions are performing; (2)to develop innovations that improve health care at different point of the patients' pathway: before they reache care, while they are receiving care, and afterwards when they may be needed to bereferred out of the community for further care; (3) to increase the capacity for health care research based in the North. The suite of projects within our research program will provide health care agencies the evidence and tools to improve the level of health and patient satisfaction while reducing costs

TitreApplicationTitle: Advancing Primary Healthcare for persons living with HIV in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO CARE; CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT; COHORT STUDY; COMPLEX CHRONIC CONDITIONS; ELECTRONIC HEALTH TOOLS; HIV; INTEGRATED CARE; PRIMARY CARE; PRIMARY HEALTHCARE; SELF-MANAGEMENT SUPPORT
Abstract-Résumé: People living with HIV have traditionally been seen by specialists because the focus of their care has been to prolong their life through complex HIV treatment. With improved treatment, people with HIV are now living longer and developing other chronic conditions associated with aging and specific HIV- and treatment-associated disorders.  These multiple chronic conditions need to be managed, but our current system is not equipped to deliver this kind of comprehensive care. We need to shift HIV care into the primary care setting of teams of family doctors and other primary care providers, who are experienced in working with people with multiple chronic conditions, while still linking to needed specialist HIV expertise (i.e. provide integrated care). The goal of our research program is to create an integrated care delivery model for people living with HIV in Canada. We will use data to understand how people with HIV access care, what their healthcare needs are, and what kind of care leads to better outcomes, such as improved access to HIV treatment and chronic disease management. We will change how care is delivered by using innovative strategies to connect family doctors and specialists. We will develop tools for providers to understand what ethical issues affect how people receive care and will test strategies for patients to be involved in managing their own care.  Our team brings together partners across 3 provinces (MB, ON, NL) including researchers; front-line providers who work in a variety of primary care and HIV-specific care and medical ethics settings; people with living with HIV; and key policy makers and organizations in order to improve care for this population.

Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; HEALTH SERVICE UTILIZATION; MENTAL HEALTH; OPERATIONS RESEARCH; PATIENT JOURNEYS; PATIENT OUTCOMES
Abstract-Résumé: A team of researchers from Memorial University of Newfoundland (MUN), University of New Brunswick (UNB), University of Prince Edward Island (UPEI) and Saint Mary's University (SMU) in collaboration with a wide-range of government and NGOs propose to conduct research on children and young adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder, Eating Disorders, Conduct Disorder, Anxiety, and Depression.  These conditions, like other mental health disorders affecting children, involve a myriad of service providers and from health, education and in more serious cases justice and social services.   Our approach to studying each of these conditions is to explore them through multiple lenses in each Atlantic Province to identify crucial gaps in service delivery across the health, education and other public agencies that interact with children and youth.   If funded, we will use both qualitative and quantitative methods to examine access to services and health improvement as well as leading edge Operations Research techniques.  Our intention is to examine how each of these conditions is managed in all four Atlantic Provinces, allowing for inter-jurisdictional comparison. The compiled evidence will be used to  recommend ways in which care can be better coordinated to improve health, educational and social outcomes.  Research Questions: 1)   What health services are these patient populations currently accessing? 2)   What services are they accessing through other agencies (education, social work, private sector providers)? 3)   What are the significant barriers/facilitators to accessing these services? 4)   What services are effective/ ineffective and why? 5)   In what ways can services for children with mental health conditions be better coordinated to improve outcomes and increase efficiencies?  We will identify key service gaps and best practices across the region and through an integrated Knowledge Translation strategy, share the findings with the wider stakeholder community.

TitreApplicationTitle: Wnt signaling: biomarker and target evaluation in Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMERS DISEASE; BIOMARKERS; CANONICAL; CELL BIOLOGY; MOUSE MODELS; NEURODEGENERATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; WNT SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease has thus far proven refractive to effective treatments and early detection. This pathfinding proposal from three collaborating research teams in Canada, England and Spain is investigating the role of a signaling system that they have found is frequently active in patients and animal models of Alzheimer's disease. They will use cells and mouse models to determine which parts of this pathway (which has two distinct arms) are important for disease progression and will use an extensive blood and patient data set to then validate the state of these elements in patients with the disease (as well as healthy controls). The two year project is intended to yield strong supportive information to then collaborate with companies that are interested in developing new tests and treatments for this terrible disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transfusion of Red cells In Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation: The TRIST Study
Keywords-MotsClés: HEMATOPOEITIC STEM CELL TRANSPLANTATION; RED CELLS; TRANSFUSION; TRIGGER
Abstract-Résumé: Transfusion of red blood cells (RBCs) is important for the care of patients undergoing stem cell transplantation. Stem cell transplants are used to treat blood cancers and bone marrow disorders. This involves the use of high doses of chemotherapy and/or radiation to kill cancer cells; but this damages the marrow and blood system.  Blood stem cells are transplanted by infusing into the recipient and blood counts recover over 2-3 weeks. Before bone marrow recovery, RBCs are needed to support the patient. Higher hemoglobin in these high risk patients may have benefits such as better energy and organ function. However, research in other areas of medicine suggests that a higher red cell count may be dangerous. Taken together, it is unclear whether having a lower or higher red cell count is better for patients having a blood stem cell transplant. I plan to study this by randomly assigning patients having a transplant to be transfused with RBCs either at a higher or lower hemoglobin level. In this way, we will be able to accurately find out if there are any benefits or harms in having a lower or higher red cell count during the recovery period after blood stem cell transplantation. This training ward from CIHR will allow me have the full resources of the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute and the University of Ottawa to successfully carry out this vital research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of Expertise in Surgical RCTs:  An opportunity for International Impact in Orthopaedic Fracture Care
Keywords-MotsClés: FRACTURE; ORTHOPAEDIC TRAUMA; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Orthopaedic (bone and joint) injuries are common in Canada and throughout the world.  In Canada, 73% of patients hospitalized for a major injury have an orthopaedic injury. Up to 40 million people worldwide are permanently disabled as a result of trauma each year, and many more are temporarily disabled.  Research is needed to improve patient care and treatment outcomes in these patients.  Clinical trials play a vital role in improving patient care and treatment outcomes.  Performing clinical trials in surgical disciplines is challenging. Specialized training is necessary to learn to perform successful clinical trials, and few orthopaedic surgeons have this training.  The funding from this grant will pair a new researcher, Dr. Slobogean, with a researcher who is highly experienced in performing pivotal clinical trials, Dr. Bhandari.  Both Dr. Slobogean and Dr. Bhandari are orthopaedic surgeons whose clinical and research interests center around improving the the care and outcomes of patients with bone and joint injuries.  Dr. Slobogean will be integrated into Dr. Bhandari's team and will have the opportunity to work on several of his ongoing clinical trials.  Under the mentorship of Dr. Bhandari, Dr. Slobogean will also design and implement a new trial related to the treatment of hip fractures in younger adults (ages 18-60) and the effect of vitamin D on complications and quality of life related to these fractures.  Hip fractures in younger adults are challenging to treat, and despite the use of modern surgical techniques, 25% of these patients will experience a major fracture healing complication.  Improving these patients' outcomes has the potential to make a significant difference in the lives of these patients. The experience gained by Dr. Slobogean in designing and implementing this trial will give him the necessary skills to carry out large clinical trials in the future that will have the potential to improve bone and joint injury care throughout the world.

Keywords-MotsClés: AMYLOID BETA; BLOOD-BRAIN BARRIER; IMAGING; INFLAMMATION; TRANSPORTERS; VASCULAR DEMENTIA
Abstract-Résumé: In the aging brain two major events contribute to loss of memory and dementia: disease of brain vessels and accumulation of a protein, amyloid, that causes brain inflammation. This project will study how these processes work together to cause cognitive decline. The project will also test effects of new molecules designed to speed up the elimination of toxic amyloid from the brain.  This will be evaluated in animal models using strong expertise of German and Canadian researchers and their advanced imaging techniques.  Should the treatments prove effective, the project will proceed to more rigorous evaluation of these molecules for their application in human patients.

Keywords-MotsClés: MENTORSHIP; RCT
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a serious health problem affects 850 million people worldwide and is the third leading cause of disability. Depression is also associated with high risk of suicide leading to premature loss of life. One in five Canadians is currently suffering form depression. Depression treatment is mostly focused on antidepressants medications. Despite the usefulness of antidepressants for some people, many individuals do not respond to medications, suffer from serious side effects including weight gain, risk of diabetes, heart disease and with some antidepressants there is also an increased risk of suicidal behaviour. Therefore there is an urgent need to identify safe and effective treatment for depression. One such treatment is the use of light therapy, where an individual with depression uses a special lamp with bright light every morning for half an hour and the exposure to this bright light will help to improve the symptoms of depression without the need for medications. This light therapy has been shown useful in insomnia and seasonal affective disorder (SAD) however its use in depression is not well studied. It has also been seen that people response to treatment may be impacted by their genetic profile. We propose to study the usefulness of light therapy as a depression treatment taking into account the person's genetic profile. To be able to conduct this study, the applicant, a psychiatrist with experience in depression treatment and genetics, will required an in-depth training on the conduct of special research projects called randomised controlled trials or RCTs, supported by two leaders in the field. The CIHR RCT mentorship program will offer invaluable opportunity to train the applicant in the conduct of the study of light therapy in depression thus leading to the development of a solid independent researcher and the development of a research program dedicated to study treatment options for depression aside form the commonly used medications.

Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMERS DISEASE; AUTOMATED IMAGE ANALYSIS; BIOMARKERS; BRAIN; DEMENTIA; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; DTI; INTEGRATED SOFTWARE; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MRI; WHITE MATTER
Abstract-Résumé: Multi-centre studies of Alzheimer's Disease and dementia include magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain. MRI can provide a window to the status of the brain and make quantitative measurements that can then be compared to clinical data such as cognitive tests (e.g. memory), genetic anomalies, and biochemical markers to evaluate the relationships with brain structure and function. Major goals for imaging are to assess which brain regions are selectively involved in the progression of dementia, to enable early diagnosis, and to provide predictive biomarkers. Much of the previous efforts of the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI-1) has been on images that assess lesions and volumes of substructures. However, follow-up studies (ADNI-2) have incorporated diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), an advanced and promising MRI method that can identify and measure white matter tracts and their connectivity in the brain. However, current DTI software packages have marked limitations for white matter tract-based analyses in large populations.  This proposal builds upon our expertise as the leading DTI site in Canada and one of the top sites world-wide. Our group has developed novel DTI analysis methods to measure key white matter tracts in large numbers of patients; however, these have not been made widely available yet. Our methods have shown insight into white matter changes with aging over the lifespan, but they have not yet been applied to Alzheimer's Disease. The goal of this grant is to fund a research associate to develop integrated software modules to make these sophisticated DTI analyses usable by the community. We have been working for several years with the developers of two free publicly downloadable DTI software packages (ExploreDTI, A. Leemans, Utrecht, Netherlands and DTI-TK, H. Zhang, London, UK) where we will integrate our methods. Another goal is to show that these new methods detect unique white matter differences in Alzheimer's Disease.

Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) affect over 1.3 million Canadians and account for 29% of all deaths in Canada each year. Most CVDs have a strong genetic component, however current estimates suggest that many of the specific genetic contributors to CVDs remain unidentified. I propose to leverage maps of functional activity across the human genome at different stages of development and in different tissues to improve our ability to find specific genetic changes that important in CVDs. My proposed research plan would provide a novel methodology for identifying previously unknown genetic contributions to CVD predisposition by considering not just the effects of individual polymorphisms, but the contributions of entire mis-regulated networks to CVD. Successful results could lead to more accurate clinical tests for CVD susceptibility, and also would identify novel genes as candidates for therapeutic interventions.
