TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular targets and circuit mechanisms of basal ganglia opioid signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; BASAL GANGLIA; CALCIUM IMAGING; DOPAMINE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; OPIOIDS; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; STRIATUM
Abstract-Résumé: Addiction to drugs of abuse is a devastating and debilitating disease that afflicts many Canadian individuals and their families in addition to negatively impacting crime and violence in communities. Understanding how these drugs act in the brain to powerfully influence behavior is paramount for developing optimal therapies to treat addiction. Within the brain, the basal ganglia is known to play an important role in fine motor control, habit formation, and addiction to certain drugs including heroin, codeine and morphine. These drugs are known as opioids - molecules that bind opioid receptors in the basal ganglia to modulate activity and ultimately affect behavior; in excess, this causes what we recognize as addiction. How opioid signaling influences basal ganglia activity in this profound manner is not understood. Here, I propose to employ a combination of new tools to investigate how opioids modulate basal ganglia information processing. The research will be conducted using mice as a model organism, and comprise two complimentary approaches. Firstly, I will determine the cellular mechanisms of opioid signaling in the basal ganglia. These results will allow us to construct a map of which cell types within the basal ganglia are modulated by opioids. Secondly, I will probe the circuit mechanisms of opioid signaling in the basal ganglia. These results will illuminate how opioids act to change the overall output of the basal ganglia, ultimately influencing behavior. While this research will most directly benefit future development of therapies for addiction, the data will also instruct our understanding of neurodegenerative motor diseases, such as Huntington's and Parkinson's Disease, which arise from dysfunctional basal ganglia activity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interactions among coding and non-coding functional genetic variants in asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; GENE-GENE INTERACTIONS; GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENETICS; GWAS
Abstract-Résumé: BACKGROUND: Asthma is a common respiratory illness in Canada, having a prevalence of over 8%, and its costs of care exceed $600 million per year. A key challenge in tackling this problem is in understanding asthma's genetic basis, which remains poorly understood.  Most studies of asthma genetics have focused on identifying genes that independently increase the risk of developing asthma. However, genes can interact with one another to increase risk in ways not predictable from their independent effects. The few asthma studies of these "gene-gene interactions" that have been conducted to date have focused on analyzing genetic variants located in regions of the genome that code for proteins. While it is becoming increasingly clear that a subset of non-coding genome regions can also strongly affect biological function and thereby cause disease, they have been difficult to study due to, until recently, a lack of knowledge about which non-coding regions do and do not have function.  Recently, the ENCODE project released a catalogue of functional DNA elements, and this has made it possible to identify coding and non-coding functional genetic regions throughout the genome. PURPOSE:   We aim to identify gene-gene interactions that increase the risk of developing asthma, by examining coding and non-coding functional regions of the genome.  METHOD:  We will first identify all functional coding and non-coding genetic variants located within genomic regions that are likely to be involved in asthma. We will then search for interactions among these variants, using data from GABRIEL, a large asthma study involving 10,365 subjects with asthma and 16,110 subjects without the disease. We will attempt to confirm any interactions that we find using an independent sample. SIGNIFICANCE: the finding of gene-gene interactions associated with asthma may provide insight into the biological causes of the disease, and thus hold the potential to inform the development of new treatments.

Abstract-Résumé: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disease that affects most critically the lungs, but also the pancreas, the liver, and the intestine. It is the most common lethal inherited disease of Caucasian populations, affecting ~80,000 individuals worldwide with a median life expectancy of only ~36 years. Typically, CF individuals suffer from repeated bacterial infections of the airways eventually leading to respiratory failure. Current treatments are focused on providing symptomatic relief and fighting infections; for patients this is an important treatment burden, requiring several hours of self-administered therapy daily. To date, no treatment that targets directly the genetic defect is available, despite its identification in 1989. It is anticipated that correction of the genetic defect through gene therapy could be an effective therapy in the future. Although monthly administration of non-viral gene therapy is currently being investigated for Cystic Fibrosis in the clinical setting, it is anticipated that viral gene transfer might be more efficient and might persist longer. The project will therefore aim at producing a virus specifically adapted to enter airway cells to transfer the correct gene to these cells in affected patients. We hypothesise that this viral induced gene transfer into the airways will provide an effective treatment for Cystic Fibrosis' lung disease. There will also be an exciting opportunity to exploit these vectors as a delivery platform to treat other lung diseases in the future such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and emphysema.

TitreApplicationTitle: A prospective cohort of direct-to-consumer genetic testing customers: Consumer motivations, behavioral responses, and the impact on the health care system
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL UTILITY; DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER; ETHICAL; GENETIC TESTING; GENOMICS; HEALTH LITERACY; LEGAL AND SOCIAL ISSUES; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; PSYCHOSOCIAL; RISK ASSESSMENT; SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: Direct-to-consumer genetic testing (DTC-GT) - purchased through private genomics companies without the involvement of one's physician - is increasingly popular. Today, DTC-GT refers to the analysis of specific genetic variants associated with an increased or decreased disease risk. Soon, DTC-GT companies will expand their offerings to include whole genome sequencing, permitting analysis of an individual's complete genetic code. Little empirical data exists regarding the motivations of consumers, the ability of DTC-GT to improve health, or its impact on the health system; however, the Canadian College of Medical Geneticists has warned of the potential for DTC-GT to drain public resources without improving patient care. The Impact of Personal Genomes study at Brigham & Women's Hospital (Boston MA) has compiled, in cooperation with two commercial genomics companies, a sample of 1 740 DTC-GT customers. Study participants have completed 3 surveys: one prior to testing, another shortly after receiving their results, and a third 6 months later. Data has been collected regarding motivations, health/family history, health behaviors, genetic knowledge, risk perception, emotional impact, and health service use. My research will investigate why customers choose to undergo DTC-GT, the impact of DTC-GT on personal health and the health system, and the role of genetic literacy (functional genetic knowledge) on these outcomes. I will also define factors that predict whether or not, after testing, consumers: (1) discuss their results with a physician, (2) modify health behaviors, and (3) receive additional screening or specialist health services. An understanding of consumer motivations, the role of genetic literacy, and the impact of DTC-GT on the health care system will facilitate the development of informed and appropriate practice guidelines and regulatory policies in the United States and Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Peer Victimization and Adolescent Substance Use: Prospective Associations and Preliminary Impact of a Preventive PEERS Intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT SUBSTANCE USE; CYBER VICTIMIZATION; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; OPEN TRIAL; PEER VICTIMIZATION; PILOT RANDOMIZED-CONTROLLED TRIAL; SCHOOL-BASED PREVENTIVE INTERVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Peer victimization is a significant stressor affecting many youth in Canada, the United States, and countries worldwide. Emerging evidence suggests that adolescents who experience peer victimization are at increased risk for substance use (e.g., cigarette and alcohol use). A better understanding of this peer victimization-substance use relationship over time and the specific role of cyber victimization is needed and can inform interventions to reduce adolescent substance use.  The proposed research includes two studies that will address important research gaps.  Study 1 will examine whether peer victimization experiences (including cyber victimization) lead to increases in adolescent cigarette and alcohol use over time. Participants are 1170 high school students who completed various measures at three time points.  This study will also examine how gender, social support, social anxiety, and depressive symptoms may potentially affect the relationship between peer victimization and substance use.  Study 2 will examine whether a school-based preventive intervention for peer victimized youth, that addresses cyber victimization, will lead to reductions in adolescent substance use. Specifically, an Open Trial will first test the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of a 12-session PEERS intervention. A pilot randomized-controlled trial of the PEERS intervention will then be conducted with 48 adolescents. The proposed studies hold significant implications for adolescent health, as they will elucidate the relationships between types of peer victimization (including cyber victimization) and youth's substance use and also examine the potential impact of a peer victimization-related intervention on youth's substance use.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of health literacy in cancer prevention among the ageing population
Keywords-MotsClés: AGEING; CANCER PREVENTION; CANCER SCREENING; COHORT; HEALTH LITERACY; LONGITUDINAL; SURVEY
Abstract-Résumé: Ageing involves rising challenges for health and well-being. Because age is the strongest risk factor for many cancers, cancer screening and prevention are an important part of healthy ageing. At the same time, risk for reduced health literacy increases with age. Health literacy is essential for comprehension of the complex information that people need when making decisions about cancer preventive behaviours. However, recent studies show that many Canadians do not possess the health literacy skills required to successfully navigate issues related to cancer prevention. This is an important and understudied topic of research. Using data from a large study of the ageing experience in England, I will examine how the social and cognitive changes that occur with ageing influence health literacy among older adults. Next, I will use data from a new survey titled "Attitudes, Behaviour, and Cancer-UK" (ABACUS) to determine whether health literacy influences cancer preventative behaviours, and how this relationship may work. I will test whether cancer fears, fatalism, and knowledge are important in the relationship between health literacy and participation in cancer preventative behaviours. I will also look at barriers to access of health information, such internet access. I am undertaking this research in England because of the rich data sources and scientific expertise available. Results are directly applicable to England and to Canada, where our health care systems communicate information to the public about cancer screening and prevention. Results will identify social and cognitive changes in the ageing process that may be associated with risk of low health literacy. Through identifying potential intervention targets (e.g. improving cancer knowledge, reducing fatalism, providing internet services), results will also be important for health education strategies to ensure that literacy is not a barrier to cancer prevention among older adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparing how disability income support is designed in Australia and Ontario for people with mental illness
Keywords-MotsClés: AUSTRALIA; CANADA; COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS; GROUNDED THEORY; MENTAL ILLNESS AND DISABILITY; MODELS OF DISABILITY; MULTIDISCIPLINARY RESEARCH; POLICY TRANSFER; QUALITATIVE INTERVIEWS; SOCIAL POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: Over the past 20 years, there has been a change in thinking about people who receive disability-related income support in many high-income countries including Australia and Canada. The view has changed from considering these recipients as permanently unemployable to seeing them as employable. As with any policy that has eligibility criteria, there are boundaries drawn between who can and cannot receive government support. However, there has been little analysis about how this line is drawn and more importantly the impact this line has on those with episodic conditions such as mental illness, because many of the regulations assume that disability is stable.  By 2030, mental illness will be the leading cause of disability in high-income countries and the associated costs will be immense.  Current estimates of the cost of mental illness now are about $200 billion in Canada alone. As mental illnesses become more 'common', how do we determine who can and cannot work as a result of their illness and who needs publicly-funded support?   In order to address this vital question, a comparative multiple-case study will be undertaken in Australia and Ontario (Canada), jurisdictions that have foundational similarities, but differ in their models of disability welfare, making them of interest for policy evaluation and improvement.    This project will first engage with key policy-makers to gain knowledge from them about the policy design process and identify their perceptions of the main areas for improvement. Second this knowledge will be used to provide evidence on how to address those areas that need improvement. This project has the potential to reduce the risk of marginalisation among those with mental illness by facilitating knowledge translation between those who work with people with mental illness and those who create the policies that affect them.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Effect of a Mobile Health Intervention on Pre-Antiretroviral Therapy Retention in HIV Care
Keywords-MotsClés: GLOBAL HEALTH; HIV/AIDS; MOBILE HEALTH; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; RETENTION IN CARE; SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA; TEXT MESSAGING
Abstract-Résumé: As access to HIV care and treatment programs continues to expand throughout sub-Saharan Africa, treatment adherence and patient retention in care are widely becoming recognized as imperative to the success of these programs. Yet, among patients who test positive for HIV, less than one-third remain continuously in care until they start treatment. Retaining patients not yet eligible for HIV treatment is critical to ensure they start treatment on time and thereby have a reduced risk of HIV-related illness and mortality.  In a ground-breaking Canadian-led study in Kenya (WelTel Kenya1), Dr. Lester and his colleagues demonstrated that a weekly cell phone text message improved patient outcomes, including treatment adherence. This study aims to determine whether the text-messaging service is effective in promoting retention of HIV-infected individuals not yet eligible for treatment in an informal urban settlement in Nairobi, Kenya. In the study, half of the individuals will receive weekly text messages for one year. The other half will not be sent the messages but will receive their usual medical care. At the end of one year, we will compare the two groups to determine whether the text messages improved retention in care. Data will also be collected to enable us to evaluate whether the service is cost-effective.  This study will contribute important information on the effectiveness of a mobile health program to engage patients in care during the first year of HIV care. In addition to furthering our understanding of retention among individuals not yet eligible for treatment, this research has the potential to demonstrate that the WelTel text-messaging service is an effective, feasible retention strategy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the interactions between Registered Nurses and industry in clinical practice.
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFLICT OF INTEREST; ETHICS; HEALTH POLICY; INDUSTRY RELATIONS; NURSING PRACTICE; QUALITATIVE METHODS; REGISTERED NURSES
Abstract-Résumé: Conflicts of interest arising from relationships between health professionals and industry in clinical practice are receiving increased attention due to their potential for negative impacts on the integrity of professions, public trust in health professionals, the quality and safety of care, transparency of decision-making and informed consent, and healthcare costs. For physicians, an association exists between industry interactions and harmful changes in prescribing practice, including increased prescription volume and cost. Interactions between Registered Nurses (RNs) and industry have been little studied, yet RNs frequently influence treatment and purchasing decision-making, and thus are likely marketing targets. As policies restrict industry access to prescribers, RNs are likely to encounter more marketing in their clinical practice. Research is required to understand RNs' interactions with industry so that relevant and effective policy can be developed to ensure the quality and safety of patient care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of store-operated calcium entry in cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM IMAGING; CALCIUM SIGNALING; CALPAIN; CANCER METASTASIS; STIM1
Abstract-Résumé: Calcium is important for many cellular functions, including a pathway known as store-operated calcium entry, or SOCE. SOCE is controlled by a protein called stromal interaction molecule 1, or STIM1. STIM1 has been implicated in a variety of diseases, including immunodeficiencies and the ability of breast cancer cells to move to other locations in the body. For these reasons, STIM1 is an important research target for the development of therapeutics to treat several different diseases. While most research has looked at SOCE is turned on, our research instead looks at how SOCE is turned off. We have identified a unique role for a family of proteins known as calpains in the control of STIM1 and SOCE. Calpains have previously been identified to play a role in breast cancer, and so we propose that the relationship between STIM1 and SOCE may affect the development of breast cancer. By investigating this relationship in greater detail, we hope to understand how these pathways can be externally controlled. This research may contribute to the development of novel therapeutics to treat breast cancer and prevent its migration to other parts of the body.

TitreApplicationTitle: Entre médecine personnalisée et déterminants sociaux de la santé: Interprétation et intégration de l'épigénétique moléculaire à la sphère publique - politiques de santé, recherche et médias
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOETHIQUE; DETERMINANTS SOCIAUX DE LA SANTE; EVIDENCE-BASED PUBLIC HEALTH; GENETIQUE; JUSTICE; MEDECINE PERSONNALISEE; POLITIQUES DE SANTE; RISQUES ET VULNERABILITES; TRANSMISSION ET APPLICATION DES CONNAISSANCES; EPIGENETIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: Le developpement des connaissances en epigenetique moleculaire (EM) suscite un interet grandissant dans le monde biomedical et celui des sciences sociales. L'objectif de cette these est de mettre en evidence une diffusion incomplete et desequilibree des interpretations academiques de l'EM dans la sphere publique canadienne (politiques de sante, recherche et medias). Nous croyons et desirons demontrer que l'interpretation sociale de l'EM est sous-representee par rapport a son interpretation biomedicale dans la sphere publique. Pour nous, un desequilibre indu en faveur de l'interpretation biomedicale de l'EM peut avoir pour effet d'entretenir injustement le mythe du 'tout genetique' et de favoriser l'allocation preferentielle de ressources a la medecine personnalisee, au detriment de l'allocation de ressources a la gestion des determinants sociaux de la sante. Pour verifier notre hypothese, nous procederons en trois phases. La premiere phase consistera a caracteriser la tension ethique au niveau de l'allocation de ressources limitees en sante. Les principaux reperes conceptuels qui nous permettront de decrire et d'analyser cette tension sont : l'origine des susceptibilites-vulnerabilites, la gestion des risques, l'attribution des responsabilites et la justice. La seconde phase consistera a rassembler les diverses interpretations qui sont faites de l'EM dans la litterature issue du domaine biomedicale et des sciences sociales. La troisieme phase consistera en une analyse documentaire de l'integration de l'EM au sein des politiques de sante, a l'orientation de la recherche et dans les medias ecrits au Canada. Les documents a l'etude seront les politiques de sante, les resumes de consultations, les plans strategiques, les annonces de priorites et les communiques faisant reference a l'EM. Une analyse qualitative du contenu des medias ecrits sera conduite.

TitreApplicationTitle: Imaging structural brain abnormalities in Parkinson's disease with rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder.
Keywords-MotsClés: MALADIE DE PARKINSON; NEUROIMAGERIE; NEUROPSYCHOLOGIE; POLYSOMNOGRAPHIE; SOMMEIL ET TROUBLES DU SOMMEIL; TROUBLES COGNITIFS; ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHIE
Abstract-Résumé: La maladie de Parkinson est une maladie neurodegenerative qui touche plus de 100 000 canadiens. Pres de la moitie des patients avec la maladie de Parkinson presentent un trouble comportemental en sommeil paradoxal (TCSP), qui se caracterise par la manifestation de comportements indesirables et souvent violents au cours du sommeil paradoxal. Les individus affectes par ce trouble du sommeil actent en quelque sorte le contenu de leurs reves. Plusieurs etudes de notre laboratoire ont demontre que les patients avec la maladie de Parkinson qui ont egalement un TCSP presentent plusieurs anomalies cerebrales fonctionnelles comparativement aux patients qui n'ont pas de TCSP, entre autres au niveau de l'activite electroencephalographique a l'eveil et des potentiels evoques dans les regions corticales posterieures. Egalement, les patients avec TCSP ont plus souvent des troubles cognitifs visuospatiaux et sont plus a risque de developper une demence. L'identification de facteurs de risque cliniques du developpement de la demence dans la maladie de Parkinson apparait donc essentielle pour permettre un diagnostic precoce. Le but de ce projet est de detecter des anomalies dans la structure des regions cerebrales des individus avec la maladie de Parkinson associee a un TCSP en utilisant des methodes innovatrices d'imagerie par resonance magnetique (epaisseur corticale, imagerie par diffusion de tension). Nous croyons que les patients avec la maladie de Parkinson qui ont un TCSP presenteront des anomalies cerebrales (regions corticales posterieures) comparativement a ceux qui ne presentent pas de TCSP et les sujets controles. Ce projet de recherche aura des retombees majeures pour l'etude des maladies neurodegeneratives. En effet, il sera possible de mieux comprendre les mecanismes pathophysiologiques impliques dans le developpement de la maladie de Parkinson ainsi que le role potentiel du TCSP comme facteur de risque clinique au developpement de la demence.

TitreApplicationTitle: Expensive Orphan Drugs and Translational Research in Rare Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTHROPOLOGY OF PHARMACEUTICALS; ECONOMIC ANTHROPOLOGY; ETHNOGRAPHY; HEALTH POLICY; INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM; LEGAL ANTHROPOLOGY; MEDICAL INDUSTRY ETHICS; ORPHAN DRUGS; RARE DISEASES; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding pharmaceutical development is vitally important to understanding the current state and future directions of our medical system. Through an ethnographic, multi-sited project, I intend to explore the dynamics of research and development of what are called 'orphan drugs': pharmaceuticals developed to treat rare and/or neglected diseases, many of which are priced between $100,000.00 and $850,000.00 per person per year. The high prices of these drugs have become the subject of much debate, especially vis-a-vis publicly funded prescription drug programs like the ones in place in Canada.  Historically, rare diseases were seen as 'orphans' of the pharmaceutical industry as the patient population was seen as too small to be profitable. Treatments for some of these diseases are now becoming available as a result of international incentivizing legislations like the United States' 1983 Orphan Drug Act. Rare disease research is becoming increasingly popular with big pharmaceutical companies as their patents for drugs for more common diseases run out.  This means that we may see an expansion in the availability of orphan drugs for rare diseases, but lowered costs are not anticipated. This project will examine how different institutional, legislative, and cultural dynamics and relationships are shaping orphan drug development.  It will also investigate the forces that shape the translation of rare disease research in to marketable pharmaceutical therapies.   The research will provide a better understanding of how knowledge about rare genetic diseases gets translated in to therapeutic practice. It will also illuminate the ways that orphan drugs are creating, mediating, and transforming discussions of the ethics surrounding the accessibility of health care technology. This research is timely, as the cost and sustainability of therapeutic development is a key aspect of debates surrounding the viability of universal health care coverage in Canada and internationally.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of a Brazilian conditional cash transfer program on infant mortality and child health at different ages and levels of household poverty
Keywords-MotsClés: CAUSAL INFERENCE; CHILD NUTRITION; CONDITIONAL CASH TRANFERS; GLOBAL HEALTH; INFANT MORTALITY; MATERNAL HEALTH; MILLENIUM DEVELOPMENT GOALS; REGRESSION DISCONTINUITY
Abstract-Résumé: Conditional cash transfer (CCT) programs provide additional income to poor families with children if the mother and children meet specific criteria. Examples of these criteria currently being used in CCT program are attending pre- and post-natal checkups for the mother and regular health checkups, vaccines and maintaining satisfactory school attendance for children.       By 2009, CCT programs had been implemented in 27 developing countries serving 25 million families and had a total budget of C$12 billion. These programs have a strong potential to help meet at least three maternal and child health Millennium Development Goals (MDG) that the Canadian Federal Government has prioritized: to halve the proportion of people who suffer from hunger (Goal 1C), to reduce by two-thirds the under five mortality rate (Goal 4) and to improve maternal health (Goal 5). While the economic benefits of CCTs have been well documented, a recent review of the evidence of CCTs impact on child and maternal health is less clear.      Data from two birth cohorts (groups of people whose health is periodically monitored from birth) in Brazil are ideal for analyzing the child and maternal health benefits of the Brazilian CCT program. This thesis will be the first to evaluate a CCT program in children in two age groups (two and eleven) and in households at two levels of poverty. This will be done using a statistical method called regression discontinuity that is arguably the best able to replicate results from randomized trials without the important costs of running a trial.      This thesis will simultaneously provide strong evidence for whether CCTs are effective tools to reach MDGs and will also strengthen the quality of global health research by using methods that are straightforward and ideally suited to evaluate global health policy, yet remain largely underused.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular structure of the Staphylococcal antibiotic resistance protein AAC(6')-Ie/APH(2'')-Ia: structural analysis as a starting point in combating clinical resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; ANTIMICROBIAL DEVELOPMENT; BIOCHEMISTRY; DRUG DESIGN; ENZYMOLOGY; PROTEIN CRYSTALLIZATION; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; X-RAY SCATTERING (SAXS)
Abstract-Résumé: Antibiotic resistance is one of the most serious problems affecting the future of medicine, in Canada and worldwide. Resistance exists for every antibiotic used in the clinic, and multiple drug-resistant bacteria such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and vancomycin-resistant Enterococci (VRE) continue to spread through hospitals and the community. In order to stay ahead of the spread of resistance, it is essential to improve our understanding of the mechanisms of antibiotic resistance, and to use this understanding to combat and counteract resistance.  The aminoglycosides are one class of antibiotics commonly used to treat serious bacterial infections, but unfortunately widespread resistance limits their usefulness. Aminoglycoside resistance is primarily caused by enzymes that chemically modify the antibiotic. These enzymes are spread throughout pathogenic bacteria, including the "superbugs" MRSA and VRE. A particularly troublesome enzyme is AAC(6')/APH(2''), which inactivates almost every aminoglycoside. There is currently no effective way to inhibit this enzyme, and so bacteria that carry the enzyme cannot be treated with aminoglycosides at all. This project will address this problem by studying the molecular structure of AAC(6')/APH(2''). AAC(6')/APH(2'') is also unique, as it is bifunctional - two enzymes in one. Study of the molecular structure of the enzyme will give us a better understanding of the resistance caused by this enzyme.  I will examine the molecular structure of this enzyme using X-ray crystallography. By generating crystals of the purified enzyme, I will be able to use X-ray diffraction to construct an atomic model of the enzyme. From this atomic model, chemical compounds that can block or bypass the enzyme can be designed, which could restore effectiveness of aminoglycosides against bacteria carrying AAC(6')/APH(2''). These compounds could become useful anti-resistance drugs for use in the clinic.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuropeptides in Depression: A Focus on Oxytocin
Keywords-MotsClés: ABUSE; CYTOKINE; DEPRESSION; IMMUNE; NEUROENDOCRINE; OXYTOCIN; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISM; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the prevalence of depression and its impact, our understanding of the mechanisms underlying this disorder is rudimentary in comparison to other chronic conditions. Current treatments of depressive disorders have met limited success, and the poor understanding of this illness has prevented the development of novel antidepressant agents. Although most views of depression have centered around serotonin processes, recent evidence has also suggested a role of neuropeptides, such as oxytocin, in the development of depression. For instance, patients with major depression display low plasma oxytocin levels. Furthermore women who experienced childhood abuse also have lower oxytocin concentrations. Early-life stress such as experiencing abuse is known to be a potent risk factor for developing depression. In addition to stressful experiences, environment/gene interactions, for example genetic variants seem to be important in the likelihood of an individual developing depression following a stressor such as abuse. In this regard genetic variants of the oxytocin receptor may play an important role in sensitivity to stressors and furthermore vulnerability to depression. I plan to examine the role of oxytocin on biological responses to a stressor (i.e. cortisol and immune signaling molecules such as pro-inflammatory cytokines), and further determine how genetic variants of the oxytocin receptor gene may be differentially responsive to the stressor. We predict that intranasal oxytocin administration will attenuate levels of cortisol and pro-inflammatory cytokines following a stressor and that certain oxytocin genetic variants will be associated with greater sensitivity to oxytocin administration. The findings may provide important insight into the underlying mechanisms of depression by further explaining the involvement of oxytocin, thus offering new targets for the development of novel antidepressants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effets du stress aigu chez les asthmatiques avec ou sans trouble dépressif majeur
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHME; EXPECTORATION INDUITE; REPONSES BRONCHIQUES; REPONSES CARDIOVASCULAIRES; REPONSES IMMUNITAIRES; REPONSES PARASYMPATHIQUES; STRESS PSYCHOLOGIQUE AIGU; STRESS PSYCHOLOGIQUE CHRONIQUE; TEST A LA METACHOLINE; TROUBLE DEPRESSIF MAJEUR
Abstract-Résumé: L'asthme figure parmi les quatre maladies chroniques les plus communes chez les adultes, affectant environ 8,5% des Canadiens. Malgre que des traitements efficaces soient disponibles, plus de la moitie des asthmatiques au Canada (53%) continuent d'avoir des symptomes qui interferent grandement avec leurs activites quotidiennes et qui sont associes a une qualite de vie moindre. Par ailleurs, il semble que le stress psychologique puisse influencer la frequence et la severite des symptomes de l'asthme. Toutefois, les mecanismes physiologiques pouvant expliquer la relation entre le stress psychologique et le taux eleve de symptomes de l'asthme ne sont pas encore bien connus. Ainsi, cette etude vise a mieux comprendre l'impact du stress psychologique sur quatre grands systemes biologiques impliques dans l'asthme, soit le systeme respiratoire, le systeme immunitaire, le systeme nerveux autonome et le systeme cardiovasculaire. Il est attendu que les resultats de cette etude permettront (1) de determiner comment le stress psychologique affecte les systemes biologiques qui sont impliques dans l'asthme; (2) de sensibiliser les professionnels de la sante, tels que les medecins, les psychologues et les infirmiers a l'importance de considerer le stress psychologique en tant que facteur pouvant influencer la maitrise de l'asthme; (3) de mieux cibler les asthmatiques pouvant etre a plus grand risque d'avoir une faible maitrise de leur asthme; (4) et de mettre en evidence le besoin de traitements adaptes aux asthmatiques vivant des stress psychologiques importants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of hyperglycemia and glucose fluctuations on inflammation in Cystic Fibrosis-related diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; CYSTIC FIBROSIS-RELATED DIABETES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GLUCOSE FLUCTUATIONS; HYPERGLYCEMIA; INFLAMMATION; LYMPHOCYTES; NUTRITION
Abstract-Résumé: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is one of the most common genetic diseases in Canada. People with CF often suffer from repeated pulmonary infections and, in most cases, ultimately die from respiratory failure. However, with recent advances in their treatment, the median life expectancy of CF patients has risen to 47 years old and a number of new complications have emerged. One of these complications is CF-related diabetes (CFRD). CFRD is an important co-morbidity of CF because it increases mortality and affects between 20 to 40% of CF adults. We still fail to understand why people with CFRD show increased loss of lung function in the years preceding their diagnosis of CFRD. We have previously demonstrated that adults with CF metabolize glucose differently than healthy peers and have increased glucose excursions even if they are not yet diabetic. An animal model of CF shows that such glucose excess affects the immune system and worsens the clinical course of the disease. Therefore, we hypothesize that increased glucose excursions might affect the immune system which would negatively affect the lung functions of CF patients in the years preceding their diagnosis of CFRD. To test this hypothesis, we will recruit 75 adults with CF either with or without CFRD as well as 25 healthy subjects. We will measure glucose excursions over a three-day period and then the association of these excursions with specific immune cells implicated in lung infections. We will then culture these cells in milieu reproducing these glucose excursions and investigate the impact of high glucose on their ability to protect from infections. We want to determine if glucose excursion could be a new target to improve health of CF adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: pRedictivE Value of artEriAl stiffness in the development of pre-ecLampsia (REVEAL)
Keywords-MotsClés: APPLANATION TONOMETRY; ARTERIAL STIFFNESS; BIOMARKERS; HYPERTENSION; MIRNA; PRE-ECLAMPSIA; UTERINE ARTERY DOPPLER
Abstract-Résumé: Pre-eclampsia is a common problem in pregnancy. Pregnant women who get pre-eclampsia have high blood pressure and a substance in their urine that should not be there. Pre-eclampsia can be fatal for the mother and the baby. It affects 8 million women in the world. Women who are pregnant for the first time have higher risk of having pre-eclampsia. Other risks for pre-eclampsia are being older than 40 years, overweight, or having high blood sugar, high blood pressure or kidney problems before pregnancy. Some specialists found that the arteries are harder when a person has pre-eclampsia. On top of that, based on past research, we think the arteries start getting harder a long time before pre-eclampsia happens. The goal of REVEAL is to find out if measuring hardness of the arteries early on in pregnancy can predict if pre-eclampsia will happen later. We will test women who are pregnant for the first time and are at high risk for pre-eclampsia (older than 40 years, overweight, high sugar, high blood pressure or kidney problems before pregnancy). We will also check some chemicals in their blood and do an ultrasound test. These other tests have not proven very reliable in identifying women at high risk for pre-eclampsia. We want to compare all three tests (hardness of the arteries, blood chemicals, and ultrasound) to see which one can predict pre-eclampsia best. To do this, we will measure hardening of the arteries with a safe, easy, and comfortable test. We will start measuring the hardness of the arteries in the first three months of pregnancy and then every 4 weeks until 12 weeks after the birth. Women will give a little bit of blood every 3 months during pregnancy to check the blood chemicals. We will also do ultrasounds at 18-22 weeks. To summarize, right now there is no very good way to tell in advance who will get pre-eclampsia. We will try to find a safe, comfortable, and easy way to do that, and hopefully help save millions of lives in the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular determinants of early and dual asthmatic responses
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGEN INHALATION CHALLENGE; ALLERGIC ASTHMA; BIOMARKERS; DATA INTEGRATION; DATA MINING; IN-SILICO ANALYSIS; MACHINE LEARNING; OMICS; PERIPHERAL BLOOD
Abstract-Résumé: Individuals with allergic asthma that exhibit an immediate drop in lung function (measured through spirometry) that resolves 1-3 hours after allergen inhalation are called isolated early responders. In some allergic asthmatic individuals called dual responders, the early response is followed by a more severe late phase response.  The early phase is characterized mainly through the narrowing of the airways whereas the late response is characterized by mucus hypersecretion, increased lung tissue permeability, and the infiltration of immune cells into the airways.  Since it is the consequences of the late allergic response that are believed to contribute to chronic airway inflammation and uncontrolled disease it is important to identify molecular markers that can predict this fundamentally different response.

TitreApplicationTitle: Self-Talk about Exercise in People with COPD: An Observational and Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL HEALTH OUTCOMES; EXERCISE; EXPERIMENTAL; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; RESPIRATORY PATIENTS; SELF-TALK
Abstract-Résumé: Lung diseases are a significant burden on individual quality of life, and on the Canadian Health Care system. Participating in exercise-based rehabilitation has been shown to improve the quality of life of people with lung diseases, and reduce health care costs. Unfortunately, many people do not continue to exercise once rehabilitation is over, losing the health benefits accrued during rehabilitation. This research uses practices developed in clinical psychology applied to health-enhancing exercise behaviour. Self-talk is a technique used in clinical psychology to understand and change people's thought processes and behaviours. Self-talk has demonstrated to be effective in improving athletic and educational performance, and it may also be suitable for changing people's thoughts about exercise, and increasing their exercise behaviour.  The purpose of this research is to: 1) understand the relationships between self-talk, exercise, and quality of life in people with lung diseases participating in rehabilitation; and 2) test the effectiveness of a self-talk intervention aimed at changing perceptions associated with exercise on post-rehabilitation exercise adherence. If the self-talk intervention helps people continue to exercise once rehabilitation ends, it will offer an easy and inexpensive approach to more successfully changing long-term behaviour in programs with limited scope and funds. Furthermore, if a self-talk intervention successfully produces long-term behaviour change in lung rehabilitation patients, it may also be successful in many other groups of people, potentially leading to substantial improvements in functional capacity, quality of life, and reduced health-care costs. Self-talk is an appealing intervention technique because it is something that people already use and requires few resources to deliver.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of gait biomechanical patterns in patients with knee osteoarthritis using a single tri-axial accelerometer
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCELEROMETRY; BIOMECHANICS; KNEE; OSTEOARTHRITIS; WALKING
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis is the most common disease affecting our muscle and skeletal systems. It occurs as the tissues and bones of our joints breakdown, causing pain and disability in more than 4.4 million Canadians. Osteoarthritis costs the Canadian health care system over $10 billion annually and with our aging population, this number will only continue to grow. The knee joint is most often affected by this disease and is a major source of disability for older adults.   Specific walking patterns have been linked to the development and progression of knee osteoarthritis. Unfortunately, the motion capture equipment used to measure these patterns is expensive and not readily available to many health clinics. For this reason, there is a need for a simple and affordable device to measure walking patterns in adults with, or at risk of, knee osteoarthritis.  A tri-axial accelerometer is a small device that can measure changes of movement occurring in three dimensions. This device has the ability to pattern walking similar to the more expensive motion capture equipment, but is more readily available to health clinics. There has been no research using this device to aid in the diagnosis and treatment of knee osteoarthritis. The purpose of the current research will be to test and develop an acceleration-based device for measuring walking patterns of adults with, or at risk of developing, knee osteoarthritis.  Knee osteoarthritis patients will be tested with both conventional motion capture equipment and a tri-axial accelerometer at the University of Calgary's Running Injury Clinic. This will provide a better understand of the walking patterns associated with knee osteoarthritis and demonstrate the predictive capabilities of the tri-axial accelerometer. The final output from this project will be an acceleration-based tool to help predict and treat knee osteoarthritis, thereby improving the long-term health of older adults and reducing the economic burden of this disea

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of in vivo regulation of Ribosome Biogenesis via Transcription Initiation Factor IA (TIF-IA/TIF1A/Rrn3) and Upstream Binding Factor (UBF).
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CHROMATIN REMODELLING; GENE KNOCKOUT AND TRANSGENESIS; GROWTH REGULATION; HUMAN; MOUSE; RIBOSOMAL RNA GENES; RIBOSOME BIOGENESIS; RNA POLYMERASES I AND II; TRANSCRIPTION REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: The form that cancers take can be extremely varied, ranging from solid tumours that can affect almost any part of the body, to the overgrowth of blood cells. These differences are related mainly to the origins of the cancer cells. However, regardless of its origin cancer is fundamentally the result of unrestricted growth. It was recognized many years ago that, to improve the effectiveness of cancer treatments, we need to understand how cells regulate their growth and what exactly goes wrong with this process in cancer. Each cell uses a complex network of signals in order to decide how rapidly it should grow. Our work aims to understand this growth network and how it is changed in cancer cells. The ribosome, the large and complex "machine" that makes all the proteins of the cell, is at the heart of this network. Manufacture of the ribosome requires many hundreds of components and is an endeavour that occupies between 50 and 80% of the cell's efforts. We have found that growth factors, oncogenes and tumor suppressors directly control ribosome manufacture. Further, bottle-necks in production of ribosomes cause a range of degenerative diseases, but have been also been correlated with an inability to activate the most important tumour suppressors. Our aim is to understand how the earliest steps of the manufacture of ribosomes occur and how this relates to cancer and other diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Les substrats cérébraux du déclin de la mémoire sémantique dans la maladie d'Alzheimer
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; MAGNETOENCEPHALOGRAPHIE (MEG); MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER; MALADIES NEURODEGENERATIVES; MEMOIRE SEMANTIQUE; NEUROPSYCHOLOGIE; NEUROSCIENCES; TRAITEMENT SEMANTIQUE; TROUBLE COGNITIF LEGER (TCL); VIEILLISSEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: La memoire semantique represente l'ensemble des connaissances sur le monde exterieur que nous accumulons tout au long de la vie. Elle regroupe les connaissances sur les objets et les personnes, ainsi que les connaissances historiques, geographiques, scientifiques et artistiques qui sont partagees par un meme groupe culturel. Ce type de memoire ne decline pas dans le vieillissement normal. Toutefois, la memoire semantique represente l'un des aspects de la cognition les plus precocement touches dans certains types de maladies neurodegeneratives du cerveau telles que la maladie d'Alzheimer et la demence semantique.   Certaines etudes recentes ont demontre que les personnes agees qui souffrent d'un trouble cognitif leger (TCL) sans demence presentent egalement un risque important de developper une maladie d'Alzheimer. Par ailleurs, tres peu d'etudes se sont interessees a savoir si ce declin precoce de la memoire semantique etait associe a une atteinte de regions cerebrales specifiques. En effet, aucune etude in vivo en neuroimagerie n'a ete realisee a ce jour aupres d'une population d'individus ages a risque de developper une maladie d'Alzheimer dans le but de mieux connaitre les bases cerebrales de ce declin semantique.   L'objectif de la presente etude sera donc d'identifier des marqueurs neuropsychologiques et neurobiologiques du declin de la memoire semantique. L'identification de tels marqueurs pourrait permettre d'ameliorer le depistage precoce de la maladie d'Alzheimer, et permettra l'elaboration de strategies d'intervention efficaces visant a ameliorer la qualite de vie des gens atteints et celle de leur entourage.

Abstract-Résumé: Personal social media use is popular among health professionals and has both benefits and risks. Clients or patients may not be able to discriminate between the personal and the professional when viewing content on social media sites, so the line between the two may become blurred for them. Further, without clear, accepted etiquette for social media, some content posted by health professionals could be considered unprofessional and reputation damaging. Finding out how health professionals and clients perceive this content and how it affects the doctor/client relationship and client health outcomes is the goal of this project.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deep Brain Stimulation for the Treatment of Negative Symptoms in Schizophrenia: Clinical Outcomes and Mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; EEG; GAMMA OSCILLATORY ACTIVITY; NEGATIVE SYMPTOMS; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a serious mental disorder that affects about 1% of the Canadian population and incurs enormous personal and national health care costs. SCZ is characterized by positive symptoms (i.e., delusions and hallucinations) and negative symptoms (i.e., amotivation and apathy). While current medications are effective against positive symptoms, treatments for negative symptoms are lacking even though these symptoms account for the greatest proportion of functional impairment in SCZ. Given the desperate need for an effective treatment against negative symptoms, deep brain stimulation (DBS) represents a novel therapeutic approach that can target pathological regions of the brain though focal stimulation. DBS is highly effective in treating late stage Parkinson's disease and has been shown to be safe and effective for treatment-resistant depression. Given the neurosurgical and psychiatric expertise at the University of Toronto, a phase I, pilot trial of DBS for SCZ patients with treatment-resistant negative symptoms has recently been approved. While the main purpose of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of DBS for negative symptoms, better understanding of the mechanisms through which the treatment works will lead to more effective and personalized treatments in the future. Our group has recently reported that SCZ patients demonstrate excessive high frequency (30-50 Hz) brain activity during cognitive tasks. We also have data from severe depression patients suggesting that DBS selectively suppresses pathological high frequency activity and that such suppression was related to symptom response. Building upon our existing knowledge, we aim to evaluate the efficacy of DBS treatment for negative symptoms and whether or not excessive high frequency activity is suppressed by the treatment. Completion of this pilot study may lead to the first bona fide treatment for negative symptoms and shed light on the mechanisms and brain structures mediating them.

TitreApplicationTitle: Importation of infectious diseases through travel and immigration in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH CARE; IMMIGRANT; INCIDENCE; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; RISK ASSESSMENT; TRAVEL
Abstract-Résumé: Growing airline travel and immigration have led to an increase in the numbers of travel-related infections and outbreaks, at a high cost to the health care system. With over 60 million passengers travelling through Canada's three major airports and 200,000 new immigrants each year, the relationship between travel and health is critical for Canada.  Despite the clear value of this information to doctors, decision-makers and Canadian travelers, there are no studies in Canada that estimate the burden of these imported infections. To address this issue, I propose to: (1) count the number of travel-related gastrointestinal and vaccine preventable disease infections and associated health care use in Ontario; (2) measure the riskiest places to travel based on airline travel patterns of Ontario passengers; and (3) create and test an intervention to prevent infection for those travelling to these risky locations. To measure burden (e.g. number of infections and health care use) of travel-related infections, existing health data on infectious disease cases, health care utilization, such as doctor's visits and hospitalizations, and immigration will be linked and analyzed.  A mathematical model will be used to understand which locations are the riskiest, based on the burden of travel-related infections and travel patterns of Ontarians.  Lastly, best practices from the literature, expert opinions from doctors and health promotion theory will be used to create an intervention targeted at Ontario travelers.  Identifying riskiest travel destinations and potentially effective interventions to help travelers protect themselves against infection can be used to reduce the burden of imported infections and outbreaks in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Synaptotagmin XI, a regulator of cytokine secretion and phagocytosis, is targeted by leishmanolysin.
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINE SECRETION; GP63 METALLOPROTEASE; INNATE IMMUNITY; LEISHMANIA-MACROPHAGE INTERACTIONS; MACROPHAGE BIOLOGY; PARASITOLOGY; PHAGOSOME MATURATION; SYNAPTOTAGMIN XI
Abstract-Résumé: Leishmania parasites are responsible for ~70000 deaths per year and can cause cutaneous, mucocutaneous, and fatal visceral illness. Although treatments exist, anti-Leishmania drugs are toxic and very expensive. Leishmania infects macrophages, which are cells of the immune system that destroy pathogens and foreign particles. Macrophages also secrete cytokines, which are chemical messengers that mediate parasite clearance. In order to invade the same cells that are supposed to destroy this parasite, Leishmania disrupts phagocytosis and cytokine release in order to build a safe niche inside macrophages. Synaptotagmins (Syts) are proteins that regulate processes such as cell communication, secretion, and phagocytosis. Among Syts, we chose to study Syt XI because recent data suggests that it may control trafficking inside cells. This project aims to investigate the roles of Syt XI in phagocytosis and cytokine release. In addition, the impact of Leishmania on Syt XI integrity and function will be investigated in the context of macrophage biology disruption. Due to the structure of the Syt XI protein, we hypothesize that it suppresses cytokine release and phagocytosis. We will demonstrate this by assessing the impact of Syt XI deletion or overexpression on cytokine release and particle ingestion. Degradation of Syt XI by Leishmania proteins such as leishmanolysin could result in amplified cytokine secretion and parasite uptake. This will be demonstrated by quantifying Syt XI degradation, cytokine secretion and phagocytosis post-Leishmania infection. Increased cytokine release post-infection could attract more macrophages to the infection site and hence help propagate the infection. In sum, this project will improve our current understanding of macrophage biology and Leishmania pathogenesis. This research can lead to the identification of novel therapeutic targets for the battle against this neglected disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of drivers of metastasis in Ewing sarcoma using next-generation sequencing technologies
Keywords-MotsClés: EWING SARCOMA; EXOME SEQUENCING; METASTASIS; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; TRANSCRIPTOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Ewing sarcoma is the second most common bone/soft tissue cancer in children and adolescents. Besides a few genetic mutations known to cause the primary tumour, little is known about what promotes the aggressive progression of Ewing sarcoma. Indeed, mutations that cause metastasis in Ewing sarcoma have remained utterly elusive. Children with metastatic Ewing sarcoma have a very poor outlook, with less than 20% survival rate. Sadly, this survival rate is further reduced to about 14% for patients with combined lung and bone/bone marrow metastases. Hence, there is an urgent need to identify the genetic causes of metastasis and to find and evaluate novel therapeutics that specifically target metastases in Ewing sarcoma. The principal aim of the proposed research is to discover the causes of metastasis in Ewing sarcoma using high-throughput DNA and RNA sequencing technologies and thereby to reveal new therapeutic options for fighting this grim childhood malignancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissection of signaling roles of motility-associated ciliary genes in Caenorhabditis elegans
Keywords-MotsClés: CAENORHABDITIS ELEGANS; CILIA; HUMAN DISEASE; MOTILITY; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Ciliopathies are a group of genetic disorders resulting from dysfunction of cilia, which are tail-like projections found on most cells, and exist as both motile and non-motile (sensory) forms. Roles of motile cilia in clearing mucus and propelling sperm are well established, where loss can result in respiratory dysfunction and sterility. Conversely, non-motile cilia have only recently been recognized as being clinically important since several disorders with overlapping features, including blindness, abnormal kidneys, liver disease, brain malformations, skeletal bone defects and obesity, are caused by mutations in genes required for non-motile cilia function. It is now generally accepted that non-motile cilia enable proper cellular communication and development. Although a strong distinction is often made between the roles of motile versus non-motile cilia, both require the action of shared genes, and at least some genes important for cilia motility may also have significant roles in ciliary signaling. To investigate this, we are studying motility-associated genes conserved in C. elegans, which lacks motile cilia, such that any signaling roles can be isolated. We identified three such genes: EFHC1, mutated in a common form of epilepsy, PACRG, whose production is in common with a gene mutated in inherited Parkinson's disease, and Tektin genes known to be important for sperm motility. Both C. elegans PACRG and EFHC1 are present in cilia responding to mechanical stimuli, and are required for longevity, pointing to important roles in cellular communication. Studying these proteins in C. elegans will provide key insight into their potential signaling roles, and as they are abundant in the human brain, these roles may be conserved and essential for proper neuronal communication. A better understanding of these proteins, in particular EFHC1, may provide important clues for understanding and ultimately providing novel avenues for intervention of disorders such as epilepsy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immune recognition of the Streptococcus milleri Group at sites of natural colonization and infection
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY INFECTIONS; INNATE IMMUNITY; MICROBIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The Streptococcus milleri Group (SMG) is a group of bacteria that colonize the upper respiratory, gastrointestinal, and urogenital tract in 15-30% of the healthy population. If the SMG breach these barriers, they are able to access underlying tissue where they cause serious infections, including purulent infections, abscesses in the head, neck, brain and liver, and pulmonary exacerbations in patients with Cystic Fibrosis. Why the SMG go unrecognized by the immune system at certain sites, but are recognized and cause infection at other sites is not known. Our laboratory contains a collection of over 300 clinical isolates of SMG cultured from both healthy individuals and invasive infections. This collection will be surveyed for interactions with the host immune response. We expect that SMG will induce a harmful pro-inflammatory response by cells present at sites of infection, and prevent the pro-inflammatory response from cells present at sites colonization. Strains of SMG will vary in the magnitude of the pro-inflammatory response, falling along a spectrum of less harmful to more-harmful. We will investigate this variation in order to identify microbial and human immune factors that distinguish strains more prone to causing infection. A mouse model of SMG infection will confirm the importance of these factors in causing disease. This research may help understand the mechanisms that the human immune response uses to distinguish colonizing bacteria from infecting bacteria and may identify potential pathways to target with therapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gating Deficiency in Schizophrenia: Nicotinic Treatment Effects and Clinical and Neural Correlates
Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHA 7 NICOTINIC RECEPTOR GENE; ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY; EVENT RELATED POTENTIALS; NICOTINIC RECEPTOR AGONIST AND POSITIVE ALLOSTERIC MODULATOR; NICOTINIC RECEPTORS; PSYCHO-PHARMACOLOGY; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SENSORY GATING; SENSORY MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: People who are diagnosed with schizophrenia tend to have difficulties with attention and concentration. Studies found that patients with schizophrenia are unable to block out or filter irrelevant, distracting information (e.g., noises). This may lead to overloading the brain and may worsen symptoms like hallucinations and delusions. The ability to filter sensory information has been linked to a gene that affects the way nicotine acts in the brain. 60-90% of patients with schizophrenia are cigarette smokers compared to 25% of the general population. Some experts suggested that patients with schizophrenia may use nicotine to improve the ability of the brain to block or filter out distracting information. Also, brain imaging studies revealed reductions in brain regions that may lead to hallucinations and brain dysfunctions. One method of laboratory research examined brain electrical activity (EEG) in response to sounds and has been useful in our attempt to understand this gating problem in schizophrenia. The present study uses EEG measures and brain imaging to achieve these goals: 1) to determine how patients with schizophrenia differ from non-patients in their response to sounds; 2) to see whether gating defects are related to both the subjective experiences and the EEG activity associated with hallucinations; 3) to find out the effects of novel nicotine-like drug treatment on gating and hallucinations; 4) to look at reduced brain regions and how they might affect gating and response to treatment. The study will also compare those with and without the nicotine regulating gene. This research will improve our understanding of the way in which schizophrenia patients process information in their environment and how smoking/nicotine affects their attention and concentration. We hope that the nicotine-like treatment will help improve attention and concentration deficits to ameliorate the lives of those suffering from schizophrenia and their families.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the monocytic origins of fibroblast progenitor cells and how we can use this information for myocardial therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; CELL SORTING; FIBROCYTES; FIBROSIS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HEART FAILURE; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; LIPOSOMES; MONOCYTES
Abstract-Résumé: Scar tissue is a common feature in many types of heart disease and can lead to the reduced ability of the heart to pump blood, called heart failure. Heart failure continues to carry a 3-year mortality of up to 50% and as such, is an important target for novel, effective therapies. In this proposal, we outline how our knowledge of scar tissue development can potentially be used in therapies to prevent or treat heart failure. The primary focus of our research is a type of cell called fibrocytes. Fibrocytes are important in the development of heart failure because they move from blood into injured tissues, where they deposit scar tissue. Some scientists have tried to target fibrocytes for therapies, but the results to date have not showed much promise. We are using a different approach than those previously tested: we believe that by targeting the cells that become fibrocytes, we can reduce or even prevent the development of scar tissue in the heart. Fibrocytes develop from a cell type called monocytes, which can be specifically targeted by changing the way certain drugs are delivered to the body. Monocytes circulate in the blood and take up virtually any objects they identify as foreign (e.g. bacteria). By packaging drugs as foreign objects, we are able to deliver them specifically to monocytes. We use drugs that kill monocytes with minimal to no toxic effects on other cells. In doing so, we are able to kill the cells that give rise to fibrocytes. Studies that use this method of monocyte targeting have being effective in reducing scar tissue in other organs like the kidneys; however, they have never been tested in heart failure. Using an animal model of heart failure, we will be testing how killing monocytes affects the development of scar tissue in the heart. We will specifically be looking at how getting rid of monocytes affects fibrocytes and whether this therapy can be used as a treatment for already established scar tissue as well as a preventative therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Distinguishing double-strand DNA breaks from telomeres
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER DEVELOPMENT; DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE; GENOME INSTABILITY; TELOMERES
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer affects the lives of many Canadians and can arise due to adverse changes in a cell's DNA. The goal of my work is to understand how cells protect their DNA from these changes and what happens when they are no longer able to do so. Our DNA is divided into numerous chromosomes which are linear strands and contain two ends called telomeres. When damaged these DNA strands can also break into pieces which pose a problem to the cell as they need to be accurately put back together. To do this, cells must be able to distinguish ends generated by the break from the natural telomeric ends of the chromosome. The goal of my research is to understand how cells make this distinction. When an end of DNA is found, how does the cell know if it is a break which needs to be repaired, or if it is a telomere which needs to be protected from repair and instead elongated with telomerase? To do this I use the simple model organism budding yeast to study how different DNA ends are dealt with by the cell. I am investigating a key protein in this process, Pif1, which acts at DNA breaks and inhibits telomerase. Interestingly, once DNA ends begin to resemble telomeres, Pif1 is no longer active. My project will characterize and investigate the mechanism of this observation with the hope of identifying similar mechanisms in human cells. This work will help our understanding of a key chromosome biology question and reveal how cells normally prevent certain errors which can lead to cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Circulating endocannabinoids, female sexual arousal, and depression
Keywords-MotsClés: DEPRESSION; ENDOCANNABINOID SYSTEM; FEMALE SEXUAL AROUSAL; FEMALE SEXUAL FUNCTIONING; SEXUAL DYSFUNCTION TREATMENT; SEXUAL PSYCHOPHYIOLOGY; VAGINAL PHOTOPLETHYSMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Research into the physiological mechanisms underlying female sexual functioning is in its infancy, especially compared to male sexual physiology. This knowledge deficit has manifested in an absence of effective pharmacological treatments for female sexual dysfunctions, while several are available for treating male sexual dysfunctions. Given the high prevalence rate of female sexual dysfunctions and their negative impact on mental health, better treatment and knowledge regarding female sexual functioning are required. A promising way to achieve these goals is to study the endocannabinoid system. My colleagues and I conducted the first study employing physiological measures to examine the relationship between circulating endocannabinoid levels and female sexual arousal. All previous human data on this relationship had been indirect, i.e., from self-reports on sexual functioning and cannabis use. Although our study was the first to find a relationship between endocannabinoid levels and female physiological sexual arousal, it cannot inform whether or how the endocannabinoid system is involved in female sexual dysfunction, as it analyzed only sexually healthy women. The purpose of the first proposed study is to assess whether endocannabinoid activity is abnormal in women diagnosed with female sexual arousal disorder (FSAD). If this is found, pharmacological manipulation of the endocannabinoid system would be a promising treatment for FSAD. The aim of the second study is to determine whether irregularities in endocannabinoid activity can explain the well-documented but generally inexplicable link between depression and diminished sexual arousal. If supporting evidence is found, pharmacological treatment for depression that targets endocannabinoid signaling may concurrently restore sexual arousal and thus be superior to existing anti-depressants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Harnessing the Communication between Multipotent Stromal Cells and Endothelial Cells to Improve Modular Tissue Engineering
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIALS; BIOMECHANICS; ENDOTHELIAL CELL BIOLOGY; MESENCHYMAL STROMAL CELLS; MICROFLUIDICS; STEM CELL BIOLOGY; TISSUE ENGINEERING; VASCULARIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Engineering tissue for implantation is one of the most promising avenues of research to effectively deliver regenerative stem cells and to help meet the need for organ transplantation. One of the main challenges in this line of research is the issue of blood vessel formation to permit oxygen and nutrient delivery to these engineered tissues. The proposed study takes advantage of a newly-developed approach in which a specified cell type is encapsulated in collagen-based modules, coated with blood vessel cells, and then implanted. With time, due to the presence of blood vessel coating cells, the artificial tissue will develop its own capillary network consisting of cells from both the modules and the recipient.   Improvement to this system has been noted with the encapsulation of bone marrow-derived mutipotent stem cells (MSCs) which speed the rate of vessel formation and reduce the leakiness of the resulting vessels. The aim of this study is to better understand this phenomena at the molecular level so it may be better exploited. More specifically, the means by which blood vessel cells and MSCs communicate to produce vessels that are stable and coated with smooth-muscle cells will be elucidated. This will be undertaken using ex vivo cell culturing systems, such as microfluidic devices which mimic the vascular microenvironment. Insights gained from these studies will contribute to the design of improved modules that may produce blood vessels faster and with increased stability compared to the current system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adolescent Depression in Early and Late Conduct Disorder: Gendered Risk Factors and Outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; CONDUCT DISORDER; DEPRESSION; HIGH RISK POPULATION; LATENT GROWTH CURVE MODELLING; MENTAL HEALTH OUTCOMES
Abstract-Résumé: Conduct disorder and depression occur frequently in teens and disrupt healthy adjustment as teens move into young adulthood. Previous research has shown that when youth experience both disorders at the same time, they are at increased risk for poor outcomes risk such as poor academic achievement, mental health (e.g., suicide) and physical health (e.g., unplanned pregnancies). However, researchers do not yet fully understand how these disorders increase and interact across the teenage years and into early adulthood and whether symptoms develop the same way for males and females.  Researchers have also neglected to examine the relationship between depression and conduct disorder in youth who began their conduct problems as a child (i.e., early onset) or as a teenager (i.e., late onset).  Such research is essential to the development of effective intervention.  This research aims to address how depression and conduct disorder increase and interact the same way for males and females over adolescence and into young adulthood by using data from a high-risk sample collected at three time points from mid-adolescence to early adulthood.  This research will also look at whether having early onset conduct disorder or late onset conduct disorder affects these symptoms.  Finally, this research will look at whether gender and early or late conduct disorder increases the risk for poor outcomes such as poor academic achievement, mental health (e.g., suicide) and physical health (e.g., unplanned pregnancies). Results from this study will help in the development of intervention programs in order to help youths contribute positively to society.

TitreApplicationTitle: Les inégalités sociales d'accès aux soins de santé des indigents au Burkina Faso et les effets de l'exemption du paiement des soins.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCES AUX SOINS DE SANTE; INEGALITES SOCIALES DE SANTE; SANTE DES FEMMES ET DES HOMMES; SANTE DES POPULATIONS; SANTE MONDIALE; SYSTEME DE SANTE; UTILISATION DES SERVICES DE SANTE; ETUDE LONGITUDINALE; EVALUATION
Abstract-Résumé: En Afrique, il existe des inegalites d'acces aux soins de sante. Les indigents, incapables de payer les soins sont les plus affectes par la barriere financiere a l'acces aux soins. Des etudes ont montre que la gratuite des soins favorise l'utilisation des services de sante. Mais ces etudes ne se sont pas interessees aux indigents. Premierement, les methodes disponibles pour identifier les indigents ont une faible efficacite et devraient etre ameliorees. Deuxiemement, les facteurs determinant l'utilisation des services par les personnes indigentes sont peu connus. A cause de leurs besoins importants en sante, les indigents pourraient avoir une utilisation tres accrue des services apres que les soins soient rendus gratuits. Par ailleurs, d'autres facteurs lies a leur indigence tels que l'age, le genre, et leurs incapacites physiques ou mentales, pourraient constituer un frein a leur recours aux soins de sante, meme dans un contexte ou les soins seraient gratuits. En Afrique, les personnes agees sont sujettes a des besoins croissants en soins de sante et a une diminution de leurs revenus. Les femmes ont un faible pouvoir decisionnel et des ressources financieres limitees. Au Burkina Faso, une intervention communautaire a permis la selection d'indigents dans le but de leur rendre les soins de sante gratuits. Ces indigents sont composes a 60% de personnes de plus de 50 ans et a 49% de femmes. Cette intervention permettra de tester le ciblage et d'observer les effets de la gratuite sur l'utilisation des services de sante. Objectifs : 1-Mesurer l'impact de l'exemption du paiement des soins sur l'utilisation des services de sante par les indigents.2-Examiner les inegalites d'utilisation des soins de sante des indigents selon le sexe, les limites fonctionnelles physiques ou  mentales.3-Identifier les facteurs qui determinent la selection des indigents.

TitreApplicationTitle: Healthcare and Rehabilitation Needs of Disabled Children in Immigrant Families: A Digital Ethnography
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTS-BASED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; HEALTH SERVICES; IMMIGRANT HEALTH; PEDIATRIC DISABILITY; QUALITATIVE METHODS; REHABILITATION; SOCIAL THEORY; SOCIO-CULTURAL DIMENSIONS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Disabled children in immigrant families remain marginalized in Canada, and their needs, perspectives, and capacities have been overlooked. As immigrants, these children face barriers (e.g., language, location, discrimination) to health services, which contribute to their vulnerability to poor physical (under treatment, pain, fitness) and psychosocial (stress, depression, exclusion) health outcomes. With rising immigration rates and the increasing prevalence of pediatric health needs, it is critical to understand the health and rehabilitation needs of disabled children in immigrant families. In response to this gap in knowledge, I will conduct an in-depth exploratory study on children with chronic physical conditions in immigrant families. My aims are to: 1) understand how children and parents manage and perceive disability, health and rehabilitation and 2) identify needs, barriers and solutions to optimal health and rehabilitation care.   I will focus on South Asian families in this study, as they comprise the largest immigrant group in Toronto (12%). As a result of this work, I will formulate a conceptual framework and methodology for future health research with other immigrant populations.  I will design and conduct a critical ethnographic study with 20 families (with children aged 10 to 14). Parents and children will participate in sessions using interactive digital and visual data collection methods. These methods produce multi-layered digital recordings that facilitate in-depth analysis. They also provide the basis to create Integrated Arts-based Knowledge Translation videos, which can be edited and framed by knowledge users for dissemination. Findings from this study have the potential to minimize barriers to optimal health and rehabilitation care, enhance client and family-centered care, and tailor rehabilitation and support strategies, ultimately improving physical and psychosocial health outcomes of disabled children and their families.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; BIOINFORMATICS; FACS; IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; INFLAMMATION; INTERLEUKIN-10; MACROPHAGE; MASS SPECTROMETRY; REAL TIME QPCR; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: When our bodies are attached by pathogens, inflammation is an important host-defense mechanism that protects us. However, excessive inflammation leads to diseases such as arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and cancer therefore it must be tightly controlled. Our lab is interested in one of the natural inflammation mediators that our body produce called interleukin-10 (IL-10), which is a type of hormone.  IL-10 is a regulator that binds to immune cells to inhibit inflammatory response. Understanding the mechanisms by which IL-10 use to regulate immune cells will provide insight development of novel therapeutics mimicking the beneficial anti-inflammatory effects of IL-10.  The best studied pathway used by IL-10 to inhibit inflammation involves the transcription factor STAT3.  However, we have recently found that IL-10 also activates the SHIP1 pathway and that this pathway cooperates with the STAT3 pathway.  I propose to study in greater detail the mechanism by which the SHIP1 pathway mediates the immediate ant-inflammatory action of IL-10 and how the SHIP1 pathway cooperates with the STAT3 pathway.  These studies will lead to a better understanding of how IL-10 functions and may aid in developing new methods for treating inflammatory diseases.
