TitreApplicationTitle: Human complementation of yeast mutations to identify candidate cancer therapeutic targets
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER PREDISPOSING GENES; CHROMOSOME INSTABILITY (CIN) GENES; COMPLEMENTATION; SACCHAROMYCES CEREVISIAE; SYNTHETIC GENETIC ANALYSIS; SYNTHETIC LETHALITY; TUMOR-SPECIFIC MUTATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: DNA instability plays an important role in the initiation and progression of cancer. Sequencing of DNA in cancer patients has identified many tumor-specific mutations that are not found in normal cells. These tumor-specific mutations were predominantly found in genes that function in DNA stability. To assess the role of these mutations and their impact on cancer initiation/progression, we will introduce the human genes that are mutated in cancer into a model organism to facilitate the systematic study of these tumor-specific mutations. In this study, the budding yeast is used as the model organism because the genes and proteins that are involved in cellular division and DNA stability are essentially the same between yeast and human cells. Further, genetic manipulations, genomic engineering, and high-throughput experiments are easier, quicker, and cheaper to carry out in the budding yeast. Once we introduce the human genes into yeast, we will insert the tumor-specific mutations into the genes and follow it with a synthetic-lethal screen. Synthetic lethality occurs when a mutation in either gene A or B has no effect on the cell, but mutations in genes A and B simultaneously cause the cell to die. The synthetic-lethal screen will allow us to examine on a genome-wide level whether there are secondary sites that when mutated will specifically be lethal with the mutated human gene and not the normal gene. The synthetic lethal interaction will then be confirmed in other model organisms and mammalian cells. These secondary sites would serve as potential anti-cancer targets thereby setting up the basis for the development of anti-cancer therapeutics that specifically target the killing of cancer cells and not normal cells in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mutational and Functional Analysis of PPP2R1A in High Risk Endometrial Carcinomas
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; ENDOMETRIAL CARCINOMA; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; MOLECULAR CLASSIFICATION; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; PATHOLOGY; PROTEIN PHOSPHATASES; PROTEOMICS; SOMATIC MUTATIONS; TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: Endometrial, or uterine cancer, is the most common gynaecological cancer and affects mostly post-menopausal women. The population of women in Canada is aging, therefore the occurrence of uterine cancer will likely increase over the next few decades. The majority of low-risk uterine cancers are generally cured by hysterectomy with no additional chemotherapy needed. High-risk uterine cancers are often difficult to diagnose, and will require additional treatment after hysterectomy. These women tend to have metastatic disease and do not respond well to standard chemotherapy, thus leading to a low chance of survival. Therefore these types of aggressive diseases need to be thoroughly studied to understand the molecular differences to improve diagnoses and develop more effective treatments.       In our research, we have used sequencing technology to discover a gene with a high frequency of mutations found in high risk endometrial cancers. This gene is part of an important enzyme complex, which is involved in directing many cellular processes. We will study the function of this enzyme complex and determine how these mutations can affect the growth of uterine cancer cells. This work will help improve diagnoses and potentially develop novel treatments to target this gene. In some cancer types, tumour DNA can be detected in the blood of cancer patients, and used as a non-invasive method to diagnose and monitor disease. We propose to isolate circulating tumour DNA from the plasma of high-risk endometrial patients, and then use sequencing technology to find specific gene mutations. The presence or absence of plasma circulating tumour DNA may be used as a biomarker to determine if treatments are effective and if alternative patient-specific treatment is needed. This cutting edge genomics research has major implications for Canadian women's health, as it will be used to improve and develop much needed translational research for an often lethal uterine cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of an in vivo mass screen for chemicals linked to Parkinson's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR ANALYSIS; MASS SCREEN; NEUROBIOLOGY; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease is a neurological disorder classified by a clinical diagnosis of movement difficulty, tremor at rest, and other fine motor control loss because of neurodegeneration in the brain. Parkinson's disease is the second most common neurological disorder, affecting 12% of all Canadians. A small percentage of patients who have Parkinson's disease have an associated genetic link, however, the vast majority of Parkinson's disease tends to affect patients over the age of 50 with no discernible cause.  The zebrafish (Danio rerio) is a small freshwater fish that is commonly used in molecular biology, and as a model for human disease. Zebrafish embryos posses transparent bodies, allowing internal processes such as blood flow and brain development to be imaged externally in a convenient manner. These features make the zebrafish a strong model for performing screens of functional and anatomical changes from chemical exposures.  This project will use zebrafish in a mass chemical screen for environmental and drug compounds that cause neurological damage, and cause observable motor deficiencies that could be related to Parkinson's disease. This model can also be used as a tool to screen for chemicals that can alleviate the symptoms of parkinsonism in zebrafish that have been pre-treated with neurotoxins to have deficits associated with Parkinson's disease. Changes in behavior and neuroanatomy can then be assayed, with associated investigations into the mechanism of action of each candidate compound on its effects on the progression of Parkinson's disease in affected zebrafish embryos.   The end goal of this project is to establish the zebrafish as a cost-effective live animal platform for mass screening drug discovery and environmental toxicology studies, and to develop this platform into an efficient assay of neurodegeneration. With the findings from this project, we can identify potential chemicals that could help treat Parkinson's disease in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic Dissection of Phenotypes Defining Susceptibility to Allergic Asthma: Airway Hyperresponsiveness and Atopy
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY HYPERRESPONSIVENESS; ALLERGY; ASTHMA; ATOPY; COMPUTATIONAL BIOLOGY; GENETIC MAPPING; HYPERSENSITIVITY; LINKAGE; RECOMBINANT CONGENIC STRAINS
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is a complex respiratory and immune disease. The environment and its interaction with the genetic make-up of the host determine the onset, progression and severity of the lung inflammatory response associated with asthma. The limited success in identifying genes regulating asthma is not only due to the inherent genetic complexity of the disease, but also to the very limited number of genetic models suitable for studying this complex disease. By taking advantage of a new mouse model of asthma together with a unique genetic platform, we have shown that genes conferring susceptibility to asthma are tractable. We have identified several mouse candidate chromosomal regions that coincide with asthma susceptibility loci identified in humans, indicating that our approach will yield genes with a high probability of being relevant to the development of asthma. In this proposal our initial efforts will be directed to identify asthma susceptibility genes within a chromosome region, which has gone undetected in previous studies, because 1) the region shows the stronger effect and therefore will be more easily amenable to gene identification, 2) the region harbors several candidate genes that may point to new insight into the mechanisms of asthma susceptibility. A second aspect of the proposal involves an understanding of the various aspects of asthma and will aim to address the question of whether the same genes and pathways underlie allergic asthma and atopy, a heritable trait that results in higher than average expression of immunoglobulin E (a protein involved in allergy). We anticipate that the proposed studies will provide us a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying asthma and will enable the identification of new treatments and targets for new drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Impact of Psychotropic Medication on Health, Public Safety and Costs in a Canadian Correctional Population
Keywords-MotsClés: CORRECTIONAL POPULATIONS; EFFECTIVENESS OF PSYCHOTROPIC MEDICATION; HEALTH AND SOCIAL POLICY; HEALTH ECONOMICS; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; MENTAL HEALTH; PHARMACO-EPIDEMIOLOGY; POPULATION-BASED LONGITUDINAL ANALYSIS; PUBLIC HEALTH AND SAFETY; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Due to low effect sizes & high placebo response rates, previous research questions the efficacy of psychopharmacological treatments. Nonetheless, Canadians are the highest per capita users of psychiatric medications in the world. In correctional centres, these medications dominate drug utilization, yet little research has examined their impact on improved health among mentally ill offenders & improved public safety mediated by greater psychosocial rehabilitation. Current research is also restricted by small sample sizes, limited follow-up, lack of diagnostics, commercial conflicts of interest & incomplete understanding of drug action & disease aetiology. Additional research is needed, especially in Canada, where maintenance of public safety & societal reintegration of inmates are the two primary mandates of correctional services.   The purpose of my PhD research is to build on existing knowledge concerning the safety & effectiveness of psychiatric medication & to extend this research into the realm of the justice system by focusing on a population of offenders in BC. In particular, I will use linked administrative data from the BC Ministries of Health, Justice, & Social Development to compare behavioural & occupational functioning outcomes (i.e., recidivism, mental health-related hospitalizations, dependence on income assistance & aggregate service-related costs) between physician-diagnosed offenders prescribed psychotropic medications & those who are not. Propensity score matching will be used to establish group comparability.   Given substantially higher documented prevalence of mental disorder & correspondingly higher prescription of psychotropics among female offenders, outcomes will be examined by sex & adjusted models will control for key socio-demographic variables.   Results will be relevant to further development of evidence-based policy & services addressing the interaction between the prescription of psychiatric drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transition of adolescents with chronic health conditions from pediatric to adult health care: Exploring the experiences of youth, families and health professionals.
Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS; HEALTH CARE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MIXED METHODS; PARTNERSHIPS; TRANSITION; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: Today, one in five Canadian children, adolescents, and young adults live with a chronic physical, developmental, behavioural or emotional condition. Better medical technology and health care means that more youth and young adults with chronic health conditions are now surviving into adulthood. These youth and their families and health care providers find it hard to go from pediatric to adult health care because of barriers in the adult system (e.g., adapting to a different health care system and changes in services).   So far, there are no studies that explain how the youth feel about their transition experience in their day-to-day environment. But also how people like their friends, family, teachers, and health care providers impact this experience. For example, we know little about how youth interact with their health care providers. This study will develop knowledge in this area to make transition a smooth process. The study uses a step-by-step guide for creating and sharing knowledge. The first step will look at the literature (i.e., what people have researched and written) to find gaps in what we know about transition. In the next step, we will invite youth, families and clinicians from McMaster Children's Hospital to tell us about what they feel is important to know about their transition experiences. We will collect many stories through interviews to get a bigger picture of the things that make transition easier or harder. The last step will combine what we find from the literature with the interviews to create new strategies that youth, their families, and their health care providers can use to make transition to adult care easier. This study will help us to understand how youth and those around them experience transition. Results of this study will help us learn about how we can make transition services better to allow youth to live healthy lives and enjoy their transition experience.

TitreApplicationTitle: Auditory electrophysiological evaluation and assessment of attention and language development in children born prematurely and at term.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTION; CHILD DEVELOPMENT; COGNITIVE DEVELOPMENT; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; PERINATALITY; PREMATURITY
Abstract-Résumé: Recent advancements in neonatal and perinatal care have had a significant impact in reducing the infant mortality rates related to preterm birth (less than 37 gestationnal weeks). However, the last weeks of gestation are particularly important for the development of the central nervous system of the child and the effects of a premature delivery on cognitive, language and attentional developments are substantial. To date, very few programs are available to detect early on the neurocognitive and functional impairments associated with a premature birth. Therefore, this study aims to identify the markers predictive of the cognitive development of preterm infants using a sensitive and specific methodology that evaluates auditory and cognitive functioning. The mismatch negativity (MMN) is an auditory event-related potential (AERP) corresponding to the automatic detection of a change in the acoustic environment that can be measured in infants and children as it does not require active participation or a sustained response from the child. Pre-attentional and automatic processes that detect changes in the acoustic environment, such as those reflected in the MMN, can serve as early markers predictive of cognitive deficits. Moreover, the use of both verbal and non-verbal stimuli can help to better qualify and quantify the type of cognitive deficit (attentional and/or linguistic) often associated with a premature birth. Improvement in assessments could help to further clarify normal and abnormal development of these children in the hope of detecting potential problems earlier and more precisely. Early referrals to specialists (e.g. neurologists, speech pathologists) could better prepare children during the pre-school years for the early and later academic challenges they will face.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse au doctorat - Bourse d'études supérieures du Canada Frederick Banting et Charles Best (BESC-D)
NomDuComitéFR: Bourses de recherche au doctorat - A
TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring the impact of the induction of a massive systemic inflammatory response on a developing mouse brain having undergone a prior perinatal insult with or without underlying immunodeficiency.
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE DISORDERS; GENETIC MAPPING; HISTOLOGY; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY ON TISSUE; INFLAMMATION AND INFECTION; IVH ANIMAL MODEL; MICROSURGERY; NEUROIMMUNOLOGY; NEUROSCIENCES; PREMATURITY
Abstract-Résumé: The extreme preterm infants, born at 28 weeks old or less, have been a new population reality for about three decades. As a medical community we strive to increase their survival rate, but what do we do for their quality of life? These children are here, they have survived and now they are a stratum of society in need of help to live a normal life, a life with full physical and mental capacities.  To do this, as researchers we must understand everything that can influence their future neurodevelopment.  It is well known that the fact of getting an infection following childbirth or during the ICU stay in neonatalogy unit induces widespread inflammation in these infants and increases their risk of suffering long-term cognitive or motor sequelae.  In addition, it has recently been demonstrated that premature infants have certain immune deficiencies making them more susceptible to severe infections. But how does this infection modulate their developing brain? Are some children are more fragile than others? Does gestational age influence their risk? Through this project, we want to answer these questions using animal models to demonstrate how brain gene expression is modulated by inflammation. Furthermore, we want to replicate in mice the immune deficiency seen in premature infants and expose them to infection in order to better understand the susceptibility of this population. This research will thus develop new therapeutic targets to help premature infants fight infections with more success and improve their neurological and motor outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Of Health and Home: Mixed Methods Outcomes of a Housing First Intervention for Homeless Adults who Use Volatile Solvents
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH SERVICE UTILIZATION; HOMELESSNESS; HOUSING; MENTAL HEALTH; MIXED METHODS; PHYSICAL HEALTH; QUALITATIVE NARRATIVES; VOLATILE SOLVENT USE
Abstract-Résumé: Using mixed methodology, this project will look at the health and housing outcomes for homeless adults (n=504) who use volatile solvents in a randomized controlled trial of a Housing First intervention. Study 1: Using regression analyses, comparison of groups of individuals who use solvents and those who do not will be made across five outcome measures over a two year follow up period. The variables of interest include housing stability, physical and mental health status, social functioning, community integration and quality of life. Additionally, administrative health data (i.e., physician diagnosis, emergency service use, etc.) will be compared across the solvent use and non-solvent use groups.  Study 2: Using Narrative methodology and photovoice techniques, semi-structured, in-depth interviews will be conducted with 15-20 participants of the solvent use group in order to answer the question: How do individuals who use volatile solvents articulate their experience of health in the context of a Housing First intervention?  Implications: The findings of this study will provide direction for policy makers and service providers in terms of health service need and utilization by a marginalized sub-group of the urban homeless population.  As well, information about the trajectory into and maintenance of volatile solvent use,  homelessness, and aspirations for recovery may be uncovered in the qualitative findings adding to a scarce body of literature on adult solvent use.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effets de l'exposition prénatale aux contaminants environnementaux sur l'intégrité des fonctions sensorielles chez le très jeune enfant
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTAMINANTS ENVIRONNEMENTAUX; DEVELOPPEMENT; EXPOSITION PRENATALE; JEUNES ENFANTS; POTENTIELS EVOQUES VISUEL; SANTE; SYSTEMES SENSORIELS (VISUEL ET AUDITIF); ELECTROPHYSIOLOGIE
Abstract-Résumé: Ce projet de recherche vise a etudier les effets des contaminants environnementaux (CE) sur la sante et le developpement du jeune enfant. En effet, plusieurs etudes scientifiques rapportent que les fonctions cognitives (p. ex. intellectuelles, attentionnelles, etc.) des enfants peuvent etre affectees par l'exposition a certain CE, tels que le plomb, le mercure ou les biphenyles polychlores. Par contre, la majorite de ces etudes ont ete effectuees aupres de populations fortement et/ou chroniquement exposees, par exemple, lors d'incidents de contamination. Aussi, de nouvelles toxines ont vu le jour au Canada, communement appele les polluants emergents (p. ex. bisphenol-A) et leurs taux ne cessent d'augmenter dans les echantillons biologiques de la population. Cependant, aucune etude canadienne n'a encore evalue les effets de ceux-ci sur la sante de l'enfant. Il est important de s'y attarder puisque cette population est tres vulnerable etant donne l'exposition prenatale aux CE et certaines caracteristiques physiologiques (p. ex. systeme nerveux et cerveau en developpement). Aussi, l'etude vise a etudier les effets des CE en lien avec une exposition a des taux communs de contamination, c'est-a-dire l'exposition a laquelle nous sommes quotidiennement confrontes. En nous interessant aux fonctions visuelles et auditives, nous sommes en mesure d'evaluer les effets des CE sur les systemes sensoriels, lesquels peuvent etre precurseurs de dysfonctions cognitives. Ainsi, les taux d'exposition des Canadiens pourront etre documentes et des recommandations necessaires seront elaborees en lien avec les effets des CE sur la sante. De plus, un suivi longitudinal sera effectue aupres des enfants participant a la recherche.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oncogenic collaboration between RUNX and Notch in T-cell leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER RELAPSE; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; LEUKEMIA STEM CELLS; MOUSE MODELS OF LEUKEMIA; T-CELL ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA; THERAPEUTIC TESTING
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer cells arise when normal cells lose control of proteins that regulate their growth and survival. Mutations in DNA may cause proteins to change or lose their normal functions and malfunctioning regulation systems may cause altered protein levels. Proteins interact with each other within cells to form networks that function to relay signals for growth and survival among many others. Although commonly we aim to target these mutated proteins in cancer, cooperating pathways may support cells in evading treatment from traditional therapies. In T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (T-ALL), Notch signaling is known to drive leukemia cell development and growth. Research also shows that pathways other than Notch signaling are needed to generate leukemia. Recent experiments suggest that RUNX proteins may assist Notch in making leukemias. However, mutations in RUNX1 have been recently described that are predicted to inhibit normal RUNX signals in this disease. The effects of these mutations have yet to be rigorously tested. We propose to manipulate the RUNX pathway to determine the contexts in which it is primarily supportive or detrimental to cancer growth. We will use a genetic approach to generate leukemias with different types of RUNX proteins: mutated and normal, to see if they generate leukemias faster, or delay and possibly prevent their onset. Additionally, we will attempt to generate leukemias in mice without any RUNX signaling to see if the pathway is absolutely necessary to make leukemia. Once we establish a role for RUNX mutations, we can begin further studies to see if we can better treat patients with T-ALL by targeting this pathway to reduce the likelihood that the disease will come back after treatment, and reduce the need for high-dose chemotherapy and its associated toxicities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure and Function of E. coli Tyrosine Kinase: a Regulator of Capsule Development and Antibiotic Resistance in Gram-Negative Bacterial Pathogens
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; BACTERIAL PATHOGENS; COMPUTATIONAL MODELLING; IN VIVO FUNCTIONAL ASSAYS; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; PHARMACEUTICAL DESIGN; PROKARYOTIC TYROSINE KINASES; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEIN STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Most E. coli strains are not harmful, but some have acquired genes that make them a serious health concern. These virulence genes encode different traits, such as the ability to produce toxins, protect pathogens from the immune system, or provide antibiotic resistance. The most serious pathogens emerge when multiple virulence genes are combined. An example of a particularity dangerous E. coli strain recently emerged in Germany (May 2011). Over 4000 people were infected and at least 50 died. Smaller outbreaks, like the contaminated beef from a slaughter house in Alberta (September 2012) continue to occur. In addition to causing severe illnesses, these incidents can have a significant economic impact. When outbreaks of bacterial disease occur, rapid containment is essential and antibiotic treatment may be required. Further, the emergence of multi-drug resistant bacteria, including the German E. coli strain, highlights the need for novel antibiotic research. My work focuses on the protein Etk (E. coli Tyrosine Kinase), a potential target for antibiotic development. Within E. coli, Etk confers resistance to the antibiotic polymyxin B and regulates assembly of the capsule, an outer layer which protects bacteria from the human immune system. Proteins with a high degree of similarity to Etk also control capsule formation in other pathogens, including pneumonia and "superbugs", which cause serious hospital outbreaks. My research will yield a thorough understanding of Etk's structure and function. This knowledge will be applied to the design of new antibiotics with a unique mechanism of action. Inhibiting Etk could prevent formation of the capsule, thereby increasing the effectiveness of the immune system and current antibiotics. The inhibitors developed in this project may lead to new drugs with the potential to treat a broad range of bacterial infections, including serious pathogens that continue to evolve.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implication of the endocannabinoid system during development of the primate visual system
Keywords-MotsClés: CANNABINOIDES; DEVELOPPEMENT; IMMUNOHISTOCHIMIE; MATURATION; MICROSCOPIE; NEUROLOGIE; PHYSIOLOGIE; PRIMATES; RETINE; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: There are several causes of visual deficiencies; they could be congenital, post-trauma, degenerative or secondary to other pathologies. Fundamentally, the endocannabinoid system plays a crucial modulatory role in a variety of neurobiological functions such as memory, nociception, plasticity, and several other cell signalling processes. This system is also important in several physiological mechanisms such as axon guidance, synaptogenesis and plasticity of the central nervous system. Only recently, the laboratory of endocannabinoids (Drs Bouchard, Ptito, and Casanova) showed that the endocannabinoid system is present during postnatal development of rat and mouse retinas. In fact, they observed that some components of the endocannabinoid system have different temporal expression profiles in neurons of the retina. This reinforces the hypothesis that endocannabinoids are involved in the development and maturation of the retina. These results are very promising and interesting but difficult to extrapolate to humans. Thus, it is necessary to go through similar studies on the non-human primate visual system. By targeting key antigens involved in the development of the monkey visual system, it will be possible to identify pharmacological targets that may treat blindness, a disease that is still incurable today. Undoubtedly, this project will have a direct impact not only on the health and quality of life of patients with visual disorders, but also on their families and the population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Kinase control of Bax-mediated neuronal apoptosis
Keywords-MotsClés: AXOTOMY; BCL-2 FAMILY PROTEINS; CEREBELLAR GRANULE NEURONS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NEURONAL APOPTOSIS; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; TRANSCRIPTIONAL CONTROL; TROPHIC FACTOR WITHDRAWAL
Abstract-Résumé: When cells are exposed to stress, they often undergo a process of programmed cell death called apoptosis.  When this type of cell death occurs in brain cells it can contribute to neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Huntington's disease.  Furthermore, apoptosis is responsible for much of the brain damage that occurs after stroke.  Therefore knowledge about how this process occurs will help in the development of treatments and intervention strategies for these disease states.  In our research we have found that a pro-death protein, Puma, is essential for neuronal programmed cell death in response to many different stressors.  Due to its importance, the research in this project focuses on identifying how Puma activity is regulated.  More specifically, we have recently published data showing that certain kinase pathways (proteins that control the activity of other proteins through phosphorylation), namely JNK, GSK3 and AKT, mediate apoptosis in a Puma-dependent manner.  The aim of my project is to establish the mechanism by which these pathways mediate production and activity of Puma and subsequent cell death.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse au doctorat - Bourse d'études supérieures du Canada Frederick Banting et Charles Best (BESC-D)

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the role of DJ-1 in metabolism via regulation of mitochondrial homeostasis and autophagy
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; DIABETES MELLITUS; DJ-1; ENERGY HOMEOSTASIS; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; OBESITY; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is a serious chronic illness that is becoming increasingly common worldwide, and there are significant limitations to current treatment strategies. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are highly active molecules containing oxygen and, when generated in excess, are thought to play a causal role in the development of type 2 diabetes. However, emerging evidence suggests that ROS at normal physiological levels are in fact required to maintain essential functions within the cell. DJ-1 is a protein that can sense cellular ROS levels and quench excessive ROS. Its effects on metabolism and on diabetes outcome are not yet known.  Using mice genetically engineered to lack DJ-1 in the whole body, we have recently shown that DJ-1 deficiency protected against obesity and diabetes induced by a chronic high fat diet. This metabolic protection was due to increased ROS levels in skeletal muscle as it could be abrogated by treatment with N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC), a chemical that lowers ROS levels. We wish to further study how ROS regulates glucose metabolism in the setting of DJ-1 deficiency. We propose to assess for the turnover and function of mitochondria, the energy producers of the cell. In addition, we wish to examine the contribution of autophagy, a process that degrades a cell's own components including damaged mitochondria, to the metabolic protection seen in DJ-1 deficient mice. To accomplish this, we will render DJ-1 null mice deficient in autophagy. Our proposed experiments will allow us to determine the role of DJ-1 in metabolism by regulating ROS levels, which will help identify potential therapeutic strategies for diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of the Human Growth Hormone Synthesis During Development of Obesity in a Novel Humanized Transgenic Mouse Model
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN IMMUNOPERCIPITATION (CHIP); CHROMOSOME CONFORMATION CAPTURE (3C) ASSAY; DIET-INDUCED HYPERINSULINEMIA; ENZYME-LINKED IMMUNOSORBENT ASSAY; HUMAN GROWTH HORMONE GENE; OBESITY; PRIMARY PITUITARY CULTURE; REAL TIME POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION; TRANSGENIC MICE; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is a serious global health challenge. Understanding obesity as a progressive disease and the factors involved in its development will help with management and even prevention. One of the factors that is severely reduced in obesity is growth hormone (GH), which plays an essential role in maintaining a healthy balance of the body's fat supply. Normally another hormone, insulin, is highly elevated in obesity and favors use of sugar over stored fat, however GH offers balance by increased use of fat. So, the more GH you make, the less you tend to be obese. Recently, a study showed that GH is rapidly lowered in healthy non-obese individuals who overate for three days, suggesting GH production is affected at the very early stages of developing obesity. Interestingly, the increase in insulin seen with overeating is believed to be responsible for low GH levels. I am interested to study when, how and why GH is reduced in individuals who are on their way to become obese. We believe that the fundamental changes in GH production are happening at the level of the gene, but until recently there have been difficulties in studying human GH gene regulation. These include: (i) a lack of normal human pituitary samples availability until after death; and (ii) that human GH is distinct from mouse, rat or pig GH, so animal pituitaries are likely to represent a partial solution. Thus, we generated a mouse containing the human GH gene and enough DNA information for it to be made specifically in GH-producing pituitary cells. Using pituitary cells from these mice we observed that the human GH gene switches off in response to insulin excess. My proposed project is to use these humanized mice, to model overeating and obesity in humans. Specifically I will examine the effect of high fat diet-induced obesity on GH levels at progressive stages of obesity. My hope is to increase our knowledge of the causes and consequences of abnormal GH levels, a hormone with strong anti-obesity function.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse au doctorat - Bourse d'études supérieures du Canada Frederick Banting et Charles Best (BESC-D)

TitreApplicationTitle: Musical training as a rehabilitation program in children with congenital amusia
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY PERCEPTION; BRAIN PLASTICITY; CONGENITAL AMUSIA; ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY; MUSIC COGNITION; PITCH PERCEPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Music is universal and is a source of pleasure for the vast majority of people. Infants show impressive abilities to perceive and appreciate music, and many researchers believe we have a predisposition for music processing. However, some people are not able to develop those musical skills and are impaired in music perception, despite normal intelligence and normal audition. This disorder is named congenital amusia and affects about 5% of the population. Brain abnormalities have been identified in amusic individuals in areas that are related to auditory perception. Recent findings suggest that the same pattern of difficulties documented in amusic adults can be found in children afflicted with the disorder. Our research project aims to further explore congenital amusia and to focus on a possible way to rehabilitate music perception through music training. We focus on young individuals (children), since it is known that their brain has a great potential for plasticity (the ability to change). Our intervention has the potential to benefit amusic children socially and cognitively and will help us to better understand this disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Flooring for Injury Prevention (FLIP) Trial: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Compliant Flooring to Reduce Fall-Related Injuries in Long-Term Care
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCIDENTAL FALLS; AGING; CLINICAL TRIAL; COMPLIANT FLOORING; COST-BENEFIT ANALYSIS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIP FRACTURE PREVENTION; INJURY RATES; LONG-TERM CARE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Falls are the leading cause of unintentional injury among older adults in Canada, including over 90% of hip and wrist fractures, and a large percentage of head and spine injuries. Long-term care (LTC) is a particularly high-risk setting - approximately 60% of LTC residents will fall at least once each year, and 30% of falls in LTC cause injury. Despite these disturbing statistics, little attention has been directed to fall injury prevention in LTC settings. A promising strategy for reducing fall-related injuries in LTC is to decrease ground surface stiffness and the subsequent force applied to the body at impact. Laboratory studies have demonstrated that purpose-designed compliant ("safety") flooring can reduce the force applied to the hip during a fall by ~35 % and to the head by ~70%, without impairing balance. However, no studies have tested the effect of compliant flooring on fall-related injuries in LTC or evaluated the cost-effectiveness or acceptability of compliant flooring in LTC. The objectives of the proposed randomized double-blinded controlled trial are to (1) determine the effect of compliant flooring relative to control flooring on the incidence of fall-related injuries; (2) determine the cost-effectiveness of compliant flooring; and (3) assess perceptions about compliant flooring among key stakeholders. We will randomly assign 150 resident rooms at a LTC facility to receive installation of either compliant or control flooring, and then track fall-related injuries (e.g., fractures) in these rooms and their associated health care costs for 3 years. We will also conduct semi-structured focus groups with LTC staff and resident families before, during, and after the intervention to assess perceptions about injury prevention and flooring. Results will help guide programs and policies for fall injury prevention in older adults, and will inform the design and retrofitting of buildings for vulnerable older adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physician Payment Programs and the Administrative Health Data: Data Quality Assessment and Policy for Preventing Data Loss
Keywords-MotsClés: DATA QUALITY; HEALTH INFORMATICS; SYSTEM PERFORMANCE
Abstract-Résumé: When a person goes to visit their doctor or to the emergency room, this visit and most of their information is recorded by their doctor. Doctors write down your symptoms, the reason you came to see them and many other details. This is done to keep track of all the different types people and illnesses that exist in Canada. Doctors also record this information so they can send a bill to their provincial government in order to be paid for the service they provide. In the past, doctors in Canada have submitted bills for every service they provide. As a result,all these records are placed into a database called physician claims data. This database captures complete and comprehensive information on health care services for all specialties. It is very important that all the information that goes into this database is correct, since health care leaders use it for planning and management of the health care system. Recently, the billing process doctors usually go by has changed. The introduction of different payment models across Canada has changed the way that many doctors are paid and the process of physician billing. Unfortunately, with this new payment program, they are not compensated for the time spent recording the service they deliver. Under-reporting of shadow billing may be occurring and the erosion of data due to shadow billing may be a possible explanation of underestimates of disease burden and differences of illness levels across different places in Canada. When doctors claims are being lost because they do not send this information and those that are sent are potentially of poor quality, the usefulness of the data becomes limited for health services research, and thus for health care planning and decision. This project will address what the current state of physician funding looks, assess the quality of the information in the billing database and finally look at how physicians have changed their billing behaviors and current policy initiatives across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of de-N-acetylation of the biofilm polysaccharide poly-ß-1,6-N-acetylglucosamine
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIOLOGY; BIOFILMS; DEACETYLATION; ENZYMOLOGY; GLYCOBIOLOGY; POLYSACCHARIDES; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Since the discovery of modern antibiotics bacterial infections have not been a major concern to human health. But with the emergence of antibiotic resistant 'super bugs' there is a growing concern in today's health care system. It is estimated that 65-80% of human bacterial infections are from bacteria establishing persistent infections from the adherence to surfaces. In the United States of America alone, infections caused by the adherence of Staphylococcus epidermidis to medical devices cost the health care system upwards to 1 billion dollars a year. This is because when bacteria adhere to surfaces they become more resistant to antibiotics and the host's immune system. These bacterial adherences, known as biofilms, from a number of human pathogenic bacteria all form from a common mechanism. The biofilm is primarily composed of exopolysaccharides, but specifically a conserved polysaccharide known as Polysaccharide Intercellular Adhesin (PIA). PIA undergoes a modification that allows for surface association to the bacteria and subsequently biofilm formation. If this modification is prevented the bacteria are unable to form biofilms and establish infection. We are currently investigating this modification in gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria using a structure-function approach. This will allow for the synthesis of small molecules that can inhibit the modification of PIA and allow for the development of novel therapies against biofilm related infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Viability of an Online Program for Equipping Caregivers to Support Youth Who Self-Injure
Keywords-MotsClés: CAREGIVER; INTERNET; KNOWLEDGE UPTAKE; MENTAL HEALTH LITERACY; NONSUICIDAL SELF-INJURY; PARENT; SELF-INJURIOUS BEHAVIOR
Abstract-Résumé: Self-injury not only affects the wellbeing of youth, but can also have a significant impact on parents/caregivers who play a vital supportive role through the recovery process. Caregivers of youth who self-injure want more information about self-injury and resources to help them support their youth; however, to date, there are no programs providing this support to caregivers. Research shows that parents use the Internet to find information about issues experienced by their children, including health information. This study will look at the effectiveness of the Internet as a way to provide caregivers with more accurate and useful information about self-injury and increasing their confidence in their ability to support youth who self-injure. The proposed program will be developed based on current guidelines for caregivers as well as focus groups consisting of caregivers of youth who self-injure. The effectiveness of this online program will also be tested. Successfully using an online program to increase caregiver knowledge about self-injury and confidence in supporting youth who self-injure may have a positive effect on treatment and recovery for youth. Furthermore, this study has implications for the use of the Internet as a way to provide caregivers with information on both self-injury and more general mental health issues.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adapting vulnerable populations to health impacts linked to changing water dynamics and climate sensitive diseases.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTATION; CLIMATE CHANGE; CLIMATE SENSITIVE DISEASES; DECISION-SUPPORT SYSTEM; VULNERABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: IPCC assessments have linked climate change (CC) with widespread health consequences. Population health is dependent on external biophysical, political, and social structures as they impact individual and group behaviour. Biophysically, ongoing CC has led to observable changes in water availability (e.g. droughts) and changes in water cycle dynamics (changing frequency and intensity of rainfall). Beyond the availability of safe water for drinking and sanitation, changes in water cycle dynamics have important implications on human activities impacting in turn agriculture, environment, economy and mental well-being.  Decreased agricultural production, revenue and food security can decrease nutritional status of individuals while insect and animal life cycles changes can impact disease dynamics including waterborne and vector-borne diseases. Anticipating the impacts and contributing to the adaptive capacity of populations in the face of CC is a public health priority. One of the current challenges is identifying and characterizing geographical and population vulnerabilities to CC, and generating appropriate data for integrated adaptation measures.  This project aims to understand the physical factors and social determinants linked to vulnerability and adaptation to climate sensitive diseases and develop a customized multicriteria decision analysis tool to prioritize local adaptation. A review of health impacts related to changing water resources dynamics and related climate sensitive diseases affecting Quebec will be produced, along with a tool for integrating vulnerability indicators and maps of vulnerable areas, based on scientific information, administered surveys and consultations with local stakeholders. A comparison study will be conducted in Niger to identify generalizable elements of vulnerability from context specific ones. This will enable a general approach to be established, in order to improve planning for public health hazards related to CC.

TitreApplicationTitle: Concrete Processing Training: Impact on Generalized Anxiety Disorder Symptoms and Related Cognitive Processes
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE PROCESSING STYLE; COGNITIVE TRAINING; GENERALIZED ANXIETY DISORDER; INTOLERANCE OF UNCERTAINTY; NEGATIVE INTERPRETATION BIAS; PROBLEM SOLVING; WORRY
Abstract-Résumé: Over the course of their lifetime, 5.7 percent of Canadians will suffer from Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), a condition characterized by excessive worry and anxiety. GAD has a chronic and debilitating course and is associated with significant economic costs (e.g., overuse of the health care system), social and occupational impairments (e.g., strained relationships and lost work productivity), and serious health concerns (e.g., fatigue and cardiac conditions). Moreover, up to 40% of individuals with GAD do not experience a reduction in worry or anxiety following existing treatment interventions. Thus, it is necessary to investigate ways to improve the treatment of this chronic disorder. Research indicates that people with GAD tend to think about their problems in an abstract and fuzzy way. This type of thinking hinders problem solving, impairs information processing, and interferes with people's ability to effectively handle uncertain situations. Previous findings indicate that cognitive training in concrete thinking resulted in improved problem solving. The proposed studies will extend this line of research by examining the effects of repeated cognitive training sessions on GAD symptoms and related cognitive biases. Cognitive training interventions have the potential to enhance existing psychological treatments for Canadians who suffer from GAD and in turn, reduce the social and personal costs of this disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact d'un programme d'entraînement physique et de stimulation cognitive chez une population présentant des troubles cognitifs légers d'origine vasculaire.
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; NEUROPSYCHOLOGIE; PREVENTION; VIEILLISSEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Selon l'Organisation mondial de la sante (OMS, 2009), pres de deux milliards de personnes seront agees de 60 ans et plus en 2050. Le vieillissement de la population entrainera des couts substantiels en raison de la prise en charge des personnes affectees et du traitement des maladies associees. Une meilleure comprehension des facteurs pouvant retarder l'apparition ou l'evolution de condition pathologique est donc primordiale. Les troubles cognitifs legers (TCL) sont un stade souvent precurseur a un vieillissement pathologique. Le diagnostic de TCL implique un declin cognitif plus important qu'attendu pour un individu en considerant son age et son niveau d'education. Un corpus croissant de recherches indique que des mecanismes de compensation et des facteurs individuels comme le style de vie, pourraient reduire l'impact de certains deficits cognitifs. Afin de capitaliser sur la plasticite du cerveau qui serait preservee meme a un age avance un entrainement cognitif visant a ameliorer la memoire, l'attention et la resolution de problemes a ete propose par plusieurs etudes. De plus, des etudes suggerent que des programmes favorisant l'activite physique chez les personnes agees peuvent egalement ameliorer leurs performances cognitives et physiques. L'objectif du present projet est de combiner ces deux types d'entrainement et d'evaluer leurs impacts sur la capacite cardiorespiratoire, ainsi que la cognition et la qualite de vie chez une population presentant des TLC d'origine vasculaire.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-Term Outcomes and Corresponding Vulnerability and Protective Factors in Adolescents With Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; DEVELOPMENTAL TRAJECTORY; FETAL ALCOHOL SPECTRUM DISORDER; LONG-TERM OUTCOMES; MENTAL HEALTH; PSYCHOSOCIAL FUNCTIONING; RESILIENCE; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) is an umbrella term used to describe a range of physical and mental disabilities that may result from prenatal alcohol exposure. FASD is a leading cause of developmental disability in North America, yet few researchers have investigated predictors of long-term outcomes. Findings from the first follow-up study of Canadian adolescents with FASD have revealed adverse long-term outcomes including problems with the law, school and mental health. However, a group of adolescents have displayed resilience, achieving near average functioning. The individual and environmental factors that differentiate these two groups are not clearly understood. The study's objective is to identify the long-term outcomes and related risk and protective factors in Canadian adolescents with FASD. Adolescents, who were previously diagnosed with FASD at the Motherisk Clinic at The Hospital for Sick Children, will be contacted for follow-up 2 to 7 years post-diagnosis. Long-term outcomes will be examined using standardized questionnaires and semi-structured interviews, aimed at caregivers and adolescents. Adverse long-term outcomes will be defined as deficits in specific domains of functioning, as well as documented trouble with the law, substance abuse, school drop-out and mental health disorders. Standardized psychological test results and life history data, gathered during the initial diagnostic assessment, will be used to examine potential risk and protective factors for long-term outcomes. We will investigate individual factors such as level of childhood functioning across various domains (e.g., IQ, behaviour), and environmental factors such as early intervention, history of abuse and stability of home placements. FASD is a major public health concern. Identifying risk and protective factors that can serve as evidence-based targets for mental health interventions is particularly critical considering the current lack of available FASD-specific services.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting Neuronal Calcium Sensor-1 to treat cognitive deficits in schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL NEUROSCIENCE; BIOCHEMISTRY; DOPAMINE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; MOLECULAR GENETICS; NEURONAL CALCIUM SENSOR-1; NEUROPSYCHOPHARMACOLOGY; SCHIZOPHRENIA; VIRAL-MEDIATED GENE THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a chronic mental disorder affecting 1% of people worldwide and cost Canadians an estimated $6.85 billion in 2004. Schizophrenia involves not only psychotic symptoms like hallucinations and delusions but also depressed mood, and impaired cognitive abilities like attention, learning and problem solving. Current drugs reduce the psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia, but they do not treat patient's cognitive deficits, making it difficult for patients with schizophrenia to make full functional recoveries and hold onto jobs. Cognitive deficits account for much of the long-term disability of schizophrenia and often appear before the psychotic phase of the disorder. Thus finding treatments for the cognitive deficits is crucial for the functional recovery of people with schizophrenia and may allow earlier treatments before the first psychotic episode. Cognitive abilities such as planning, abstract thinking and flexible switching of attention, are thought to depend on a brain area called the prefrontal cortex. Studies show that levels of the protein Neuronal Calcium Sensor-1 (NCS-1) are higher in the prefrontal cortex of people with schizophrenia, perhaps contributing to cognitive deficits. Therefore, I will test if there is a causal link between higher NCS-1 levels and schizophrenia and test if NCS-1 can be targeted to treat cognitive deficits. I hypothesize since schizophrenia is associated with increased NCS-1 in the prefrontal cortex, increasing NCS-1 in the analogous brain region in mice will cause them to exhibit behaviours relevant to schizophrenia and impaired cognition. Moreover, I expect decreasing NCS -1 will correct such behaviours or impaired cognition in these mice and other models of schizophrenia. Results from testing these hypotheses will pave the way to new treatment strategies for schizophrenia. Indeed, modeling cognitive deficits and finding novel ways to treat them is also relevant to other diseases with cognitive decline like Alzheimer's.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relationship between healthcare service utilization, costs and highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) uptake among HIV-positive persons in British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH CARE COST; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTHCARE SERVICE UTILIZATION; HIGHLY ACTIVE ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; HIV/AIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Although not a cure, present-day HIV medicines commonly referred to as highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) has been established globally as an effective therapy for reducing HIV/AIDS-related morbidity and mortality. An emerging body of research suggests that expanding access to HAART may be a powerful strategy for reducing new HIV infections. Despite this evidence, British Columbia (BC), which has the highest HIV prevalence rate in Canada, has one of the lowest rates of HAART uptake. HAART's use among HIV-positive individuals clinically indicated for treatment remains suboptimal in BC where access to HAART is free via its universal health care system. It is unclear how HAART uptake affects healthcare service utilization and cost in BC. This proposal includes a set of inter-related objectives employing epidemiologic and health economics methodologies, and seeks to understand the relationship between healthcare service utilization, costs and HAART uptake. It aims to explore how clinical and socio-demographic characteristics of a BC cohort of HIV-positive individuals and their uptake of HAART impact healthcare service utilization and cost over time. It is hypothesized that HIV-positive individuals receiving HAART will have lower healthcare service needs compared to those not receiving HAART, and thus will present an overall lower economic burden to society. This research will benefit the Canadian public by helping them understand how the proportion of HIV-positive people receiving treatment has changed (increased, decreased, or remain constant) over time. This knowledge is necessary to understand the impact of HIV on healthcare service utilization and associated costs. For policy makers, this understanding will be useful in informing resource-allocation decisions regarding how best to target underserved HIV-positive individuals, potentially reduce new HIV infections, improve overall HIV health outcomes and ultimately reduce healthcare cost in the long-term.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Physical Activity and Muscle Properties in Determining Bone Strength
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MICROARCHITECTURE; CLINICAL FUNCTIONAL TESTING; FINITE ELEMENT MODELING; FRACTURE; HIGH-RESOLUTION PERIPHERAL QUANTITATIVE COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; MUSCLE CROSS SECTIONAL AREA; MUSCLE DENSITY; MUSCULOSKELETAL STRENGTH; PERIPHERAL QUANTITATIVE COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY AND ACCELEROMETER
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis is a complex disease in which bones become fragile and are more likely to break. Approximately 2 million Canadians live with osteoporosis, costing our health care system $3.9 billion each year. We do not have a complete understanding of what makes a bone strong; therefore, we are unable to predict if someone is going to suffer a fracture when they fall. Muscles and bones can gain strength from physical activity because they both increase in cross sectional size (girth) and density. The small architecture inside the bone can also increase bone strength, but we do not know if more physical activity or bigger, denser muscles can affect this aspect of bone strength. The role of physical activity, muscle size, strength, and density on bone structure is poorly understood in both men and women, especially in older adults. Our study will examine the roles of physical activity and muscle properties in bone strength in 66 young adult men and women around the age of 30, as well as 147 healthy men and women around 75 years of age. Muscle and bone properties will be measured using state-of-the-art high resolution imaging technologies, mechanical engineering computer models, and various movement tests often used by physical therapists. Physical activity will be assessed by having participants wear a small accelerometer and answer questions about their regular activity. We will focus our predictions about bone micro-architecture on the wrist, a common site for fall related fractures, and the ankle, a weight-bearing bone site. This work will provide new evidence about physical activity and muscle-bone health in both men and women at different ages and will contribute in making better tools for predicting bone strength and risk of fractures. Importantly, these results will guide new fracture prevention and rehabilitation programs to help improve the quality of life and physical functioning of Canadians who suffer with osteoporosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modelling Self-Regulation in Women Suffering from IC/BPS: Results and Knowledge Translation
Keywords-MotsClés: CATASTROPHIZING; COPING; DISABILITY; ILLNESS REPRESENTATIONS; INTESTITIAL CYSTITIS /BLADDER PAIN SYNDROME; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NEGATIVE AFFECT; PAIN; SELF-REGULATION; SOCIAL SUPPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Interstitial Cystitis / Bladder Pain Syndrome (IC/BPS) is a debilitating and chronic pelvic pain condition affecting up to 6.5 percent of North American women (Clemens et al., 2009). Comparing patients with IC/BPS to age matched controls, patients reported poorer mental and physical QoL, more pain, depression, anxiety, catastrophizing, sexual dysfunction and less social support (Nickel et al., 2010). There is no standard etiology or medical treatment for IC/BPS, and pain is often palliative relying on symptom management. As such, IC/BPS is a disease associated with significant pain-related disability that incurs large costs to the medical system (inpatient / outpatient care, medications), costs to society (lost work productivity, unemployment) as well as costs to the self (diminished relationships and QoL) (Clemens et al., 2007).   My Master's research showed that in women with IC/BPS, symptoms become disabling through negative affect (e.g., depression and anxiety) and catastrophizing (Katz et al., 2011). The next step in my line of research is to expand this model to include illness representations and cognitive behavioural coping to better understand how pain and symptoms may lead to disability. My plan has two primary objectives: 1) To develop a comprehensive self-regulatory cognitive behavioural model of IC/BPS. This study will collect questionnaire data from international collaborators (e.g., Canada, US, India, Germany, Taiwan). 2) Secondly, to disseminate these findings in a brief educational intervention to the community as well as health care professionals to improve knowledge on IC/BPS pain and management. This international multi-centre study will expand the literature by connecting research on pain, IC/BPS, self-regulation and cognitive behavioural theory. These results can be used to develop brief knowledge translation interventions in communities as well as clinical therapies to improve outcomes and decrease IC/BPS patient related disability.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studying The Evolution Of Cancer Genomes
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CANCER; COMPUTATIONAL BIOLOGY; EVOLUTION; GENOMICS; MACHINE LEARNING
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is a disease caused by healthy cells which have acquired genomic mutations enabling these cells to uncontrollably proliferate. As the disease progresses, the population of cancer cells rapidly expands causing tumours. During this expansion the cancer cells also acquire new mutations which lead to genetically distinct sub-populations within tumours. These sub-populations of cells can have different proliferative potential, ability to metastasize and susceptibilities to treatments. Clinically this is a very important issue as treatment strategies need to be tailored to target and eliminate all of these sub-populations, otherwise relapse will occur when new tumours are formed by the remaining cancer cell sub-populations.  My research is primarily focused on using high throughput genome sequencing technologies to quantify the diversity of these sub-populations and study their dynamics across time and space. The current generation of genome sequencing technologies allow us to simultaneously sequence the genomes of thousands or millions of cells in a single sample. Unfortunately it is very difficult to use this data to directly infer the sub-population structure as we cannot identify which fragments of DNA came from which cells.  I will be developing statistical and computational models to solve this problem. I will then be applying these tools to study tissue samples taken from different regions of tumours or from metastasis and recurrence events, with the goal of understanding how cancers evolve. This work will provide novel insights into the basic biology of cancer which ultimately will be useful in the development of personalized treatment strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Misregulation of microRNAs in multiple sclerosis - impacts on oligodendrocytes and their ability to differentiate, mature and myelinate axons in the central nervous system
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOSKELETAL ORGANIZATION; EXPERIMENTAL AUTOIMMUNE ENCEPHALITIS; LENTIVIRAL TRANSDUCTION; MICRORNA; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; OLIGODENDROCYTES; REMYELINATION; STEM-LOOP QPCR
Abstract-Résumé: MicroRNAs are small regulatory molecules that control gene expression. Mammalian systems use them to regulate important aspects of growth, development, tissue differentiation and cell survival throughout the life of an organism. Because of the significance of microRNAs in fundamental aspects of biology, it follows that errors in their regulation can lead to disease. Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is one such disease. Misregulation of many microRNAs is found in tissue samples from MS patients. However, the implications of their misregulation - i.e., what specific cell types and/or pathways are negatively affected - remain unknown. This project focuses on a small subset of microRNAs consistently found at unusual levels in tissues from patients with MS. They are predicted to target genes that may affect the ability of specific brain cells, called oligodendrocytes, to mature and function properly. Oligodendrocyte function is crucial to nerve signal conduction in the central nervous system. MS is characterized by a progressive loss of this nerve signal conduction, which leads to the physical and cognitive disabilities associated with the disease. Normally, oligodendrocytes are able to repair some of this damage, but this ability appears to be lessened in MS. Should the misregulation of the microRNAs in question prove to cause the decreased repair function in oligodendrocytes, then manipulating their regulation may in turn induce repair by oligodendrocytes and reverse some of the damage caused by MS. These theories are being tested by controlling the levels of these microRNAs in oligodendrocytes in cell model systems. This research will reveal the impact of these microRNAs specifically on oligodendrocytes and their ability to repair damage in the central nervous system, thus providing possible therapeutic targets for animal model and clinical MS research in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of hyperosmotic stress survival in the diarrheal pathogen Campylobacter jejuni
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL PHYSIOLOGY; CAMPYLOBACTER; DNA MICROARRAY GENE EXPRESSION; FOOD-BORNE PATHOGEN; HYPEROSMOTIC STRESS; MICROBIOLOGY; MICROSCOPY AND FLOW CYTOMETRY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PATHOGENESIS; VIRULENCE FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Campylobacter jejuni is the leading cause of bacterial gastrointestinal disease in Canada, with symptoms including watery to bloody inflammatory diarrhea. Infection may also lead to autoimmune disorders such as reactive arthritis, and the neuromuscular paralysis Guillain-Barre Syndrome. The majority of human infections are acquired from agricultural sources because C. jejuni harmlessly inhabits fowl, cattle and pigs. Despite intensive efforts to eliminate the bacterium during food processing, it is found on up to 95% of fresh poultry meat. Adaptation to hostile environments of high osmotic concentration, found in animal hosts and the human body, is a critical feature of the C. jejuni lifecycle, and is necessary for transmission of the disease to humans. We identified a gene for a regulatory protein called Cj1533c that is over-produced under conditions of high osmotic stress. If Cj1533c is absent from C. jejuni, the pathogen is unable to survive osmotic stress. We also discovered that Cj1533c has two functions, the first function may be to control the expression of genes important for stress survival, and the second function may modify important stress proteins to control their activity. Identifying (I) which genes Cj1533c regulates, (II) the proteins that interact with Cj1533c, and (III) genetic mutations that confer osmotic stress tolerance in the absence of Cj1533c, will provide insight into new stress survival mechanisms. Increasing antibiotic resistance, and the high number of C. jejuni infections reported worldwide, necessitates a mechanistic understanding of stress responses for the discovery of next-generation drug or vaccine candidates and pathogen control strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Delineating the genomic differences between primary and recurrent medulloblastoma
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER GENOMICS; CANCER RECURRENCE; COPY NUMBER PROFILING; MEDULLOBLASTOMA; PEDIATRIC ONCOLOGY; WHOLE GENOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Medulloblastoma is the most common solid malignant tumour in children. Current standard treatment, which consists of radiation and chemotherapy, can cure most medulloblastoma patients of the disease with adverse life-long side-effects. A substantial portion of patients, however, suffer from recurrent or progressive disease, for which no treatment options are available. Recurrent medulloblastoma is poorly understood, and its differences from the primary disease are not well defined. In fact, clinicians have largely assumed that recurrent medulloblastoma tumours are identical to primary tumours, and patients are enrolled in clinical trials based on molecular tests of the primary tumours. The present study aims to define the genetic and biological distinctions between primary and recurrent medulloblastoma, in order to improve the enrolment criteria for clinical trials and to facilitate the development of effective targeted therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of borderline personality features in positive affect-driven impulsive behaviours
Keywords-MotsClés: BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER; EMOTION; EMOTION REGULATION; IMPULSIVITY; POSITIVE AFFECT; PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) comprise a population at risk for suicide, deliberate self-harm, and psychiatric hospitalization. This project assesses impulsive behaviours characteristic of this population following positive (excitement), negative (rejection), and neutral emotion states. Participants high and low in BPD features listen to audio recordings designed to elicit positive and negative emotions. Following each emotion induction, participants complete a computerized task assessing risk-taking. Extending research in other populations, it is expected that experienced positive emotion will lead to significantly more risk-taking behaviours in the computer task in participants high in BPD features than those low in BPD features.   Impulsivity is a core dimension of BPD, but the role of positive emotion in precipitating certain impulsive behaviours has been largely overlooked. This research should contribute to an understanding of which specific emotional states in high risk BPD populations are uniquely associated with various harmful behavours related to impulsivity (including suicidal behaviour, self-harm, and substance use). TitreApplicationTitle: Validation of a cold pressor test protocol for the identification of complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) and concurrent psychometric testing of a condition-specific outcome measure for CRPS.
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLEX REGIONAL PAIN SYNDROME; DIAGNOSIS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MULTIDISCIPLINARY ASSESSMENT; OUTCOME MEASUREMENT; SOMATOSENSORY REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS) is a painful condition of the nervous system that sometimes develops after a trauma i.e. in about five percent of persons after a wrist fracture.  Symptoms can include: swelling; pain; abnormal sweating; changes to the skin, hair, and nails in the area of the injury; and difficulty in moving.  These symptoms can combine to create devastating impacts on the person's ability to participate in their daily activities. At present, there is no diagnostic test for this condition, and many of the assessments used by health care professionals to monitor their patients only look at a single symptom, and do not consider the impact of the syndrome as a whole.  This makes it difficult for patients to get the correct diagnosis and treatment, and for health care providers and researchers to evaluate new treatments and make treatment decisions.   This doctoral research will look at two key issues: 1) Can a cold stress test (that identifies abnormal responses to immersing a foot in cold water) help front-line health professionals detect CRPS by magnifying any temperature differences between their hands (as measured by an inexpensive infra-red thermometer), and 2) to test two new assessment tools developed to monitor the specific signs and symptoms experienced by people with CRPS. One tool is for health professionals to fill out, and the other is for the patients themselves to complete. We will make comparisons between these new tools as well as to other existing assessments for pain and disability in general to evaluate if they can help us to monitor changes in the symptoms and how the person with CRPS is managing those.   Results from this research will assist health care professionals in identifying persons with CRPS quickly, so they can get the necessary treatment.  It should also assist in testing new treatments for this condition, as well as assisting care providers and their patients in monitoring their journey towards recovery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Associations between amyloid-beta, white matter lesions, and cognitive function - Implications for future therapeutic approaches
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYLOID BETA; COGNITIVE FUNCTION; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; WHITE MATTER LESIONS
Abstract-Résumé: As Canada's population ages, dementia will become a significant health care burden. In 2008 approximately half a million Canadians suffered from dementia. By 2038, over a million Canadians will have dementia and their care will cost over $150 billion. Alzheimer's disease (AD) and vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) are the two most common forms of dementia. AD is characterized by the accumulation of amyloid-beta (A-beta) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. VCI is caused by hemorrhagic brain lesions or diffuse ischemia in the brain and is characterized by subcortical lesions such as white matter lesions (WMLs). Traditionally, these pathogenic mechanisms were considered to be distinct and unrelated. However, we now know that AD and VCI can and do co-exist (i.e., mixed dementia). Currently, little is known about how WMLs and A-beta plaques interact to affect cognitive function. Furthermore, it is unknown whether the presence of both WMLs and A-beta plaques attenuates the effect of interventions such as exercise. Yet, the answers to these questions are important towards ensuring optimal care for those exhibiting mixed dementia-related changes. Our objective is to 1) To compare cognitive function between those with WMLs and those with A-beta+WMLs and 2) To determine whether A-beta+WMLs attenuates the effect of targeted aerobic exercise training on cognitive function.  Gaining a deeper understanding of the interplay between WMLs, A-beta, and targeted exercise training will facilitate the development of effective prevention strategies for cognitive decline. Strategies to slow down the rate of cognitive decline could preserve independent functioning and quality of life in this population. This, in turn, could lead to reduced health care utilization costs and avoidance of early institutional care.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse au doctorat - Bourse d'études supérieures du Canada Frederick Banting et Charles Best (BESC-D)
NomDuComitéFR: Bourses de recherche au doctorat - A
TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a Novel Class of Anti-HIV-1 Inhibitors Targeting Viral RNA Processing
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; ELISA; GENE EXPRESSION; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING; HIV-1; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; MAMMALIAN CELL CULTURE; QRT-PCR; RNA SPLICING; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: The increasing cases of resistant HIV-1 to current drugs are an alarming concern. New tactics are necessary for continued success in combating HIV-1 infection. Previous studies established that viral growth can be affected by manipulating cellular host factors involved in viral RNA processing. We have advanced these studies by demonstrating that compounds can inhibit HIV-1 growth, establishing that targeting viral RNA processing with compounds/drugs is effective at impairing viral expansion. We have previously identified two FDA-approved drugs, chlorohexidine and digoxin, as novel inhibitors of this stage of the virus lifecycle. Unfortunately, chlorhexidine is not suitable for systemic use. However, doses of digoxin required to suppress HIV-1 replication (in clinical isolates) are suitable for human use, demonstrating the potential of RNA processing inhibitors in becoming novel ARTs. To expand on our approach, I searched and identified five more inhibitors within the digoxin family of drugs (cardiac glycosides, CGs) and six more splice modulators. Of these, three CGs are even more potent and closer to clinical doses in use than digoxin.  In this proposal, I will (1) complete the characterization of lead compounds in our HIV-1 cell line. Next, I will (2) investigate the mechanisms by how these compounds influence host cells to specifically inhibit HIV-1 replication. Lastly, I will (3) confirm the effectiveness of our best inhibitors against viral replication using HIV-1 clinical isolates.  In summary, this research will develop a novel class of antiretroviral drugs that alters HIV-1 RNA processing-a stage of the virus lifecycle not targeted by current antiretroviral therapies. Since these inhibitors target host processes and a subset are already in clinical use, they show great promise in becoming broad spectrum inhibitors of multiple HIV-1 strains, reducing chances of virus resistance, and allow rapid re-purposing into novel HIV-1 antiretroviral therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Informatic discovery of small molecules targeting human biology from Legionella pneumophila
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOACTIVE SMALL MOLECULES; DRUG DISCOVERY; GENOME MINING; IMMUNOMODULATORY; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; LEGIONELLA PNEUMOPHILA; MACROPHAGE; NONRIBOSOMAL PEPTIDE; PATHOGENIC METABOLITES; POLYKETIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Bacteria are known to produce a variety of biologically active compounds to affect their environment; an observation that has lead to the discovery of many successful antibiotics. Some human pathogens also use bioactive molecules to advance disease, indicating that these compounds may be adapted for affecting human systems. Among bacterial pathogens that manipulate human processes, Legionella pneumophila is perhaps the most adept, converting hostile cells into complacent food sources within a few hours of infection. Extensive DNA sequencing has revealed that Legionella possesses several genes that may produce small molecules to control host cells during infection. Our laboratory has developed new methods of finding molecules from bacteria, and I intend to use these unique tools to identify the predicted drug-like molecules from Legionella. Initially, I have inactivated each of the genes responsible for producing these drug-like molecules, and have used these mutant bacteria to assess the role these chemicals may play in disease. Early results indicate that Legionella produces at least two complex new chemicals and that one of these plays an important role early in infection. Our laboratory is currently working to isolate these new chemicals to understand their structure and what component of human cells they might target. Further investigation of these initial results will explain how Legionella uses small molecules during infection, and may reveal novel human-targeted compounds that might be useful as chemical probes or as drugs for diseases of malfunctioning human systems, like cancer.
