TitreApplicationTitle: A Longitudinal Study of Risk Factors, Correlates, Course and Treatment Outcomes of Adults who Engage in Non-suicidal Self-injury.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULTS; DELIBERATE SELF-HARM; LONGITUDINAL; MENTAL DISORDERS; NON-SUICIDAL SELF-INJURY; RISK FACTORS; SUICIDE ATTEMPTS; TREATMENT OUTCOMES
Abstract-Résumé: Studies of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) have primarily focused on adolescents who engage in this behaviour. In adolescent research comparing different types of deliberate self-harm (DSH), NSSI was associated with borderline personality features, while major depression and posttraumatic stress disorder were associated with suicide attempts (SA). In addition, NSSI was associated with higher incidents of DSH during treatment and childhood abuse and neglect. The study of NSSI, however, has been widely neglected in adults. The current research aims to investigate the relationship between different types of DSH (i.e., SA only, NSSI only, both SA and NSSI, and no DSH) among adults and risk factors, mental disorders, and treatment outcomes in three separate studies. Study 1 will determine which mental disorders are associated with each DSH group and whether different DSH groups are associated with different risk factors. Study 2 will investigate these relationships longitudinally, to determine the course of different types of DSH. Study 3 will compare treatment outcomes in the different groups of DSH. Participants will be selected from Suicide Assessment Form in Emergency Psychiatry (SAFE) database. The SAFE database is comprised of all consecutive adults who are assessed by psychiatric services at two Manitoba hospitals. Data collection is ongoing, with a sample size of 6,918 as of December, 2011.  The SAFE database will also be linked to the Manitoba Centre for Health Policy (MCHP) databases which will enable examination of the relationship between DSH groups and suicide outcome measures, psychiatric diagnoses, medication prescription and treatment utilization. This research will play a crucial role in understanding the prevalence, course and treatment of DSH and help to prevent suicide among North American adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: A switch from nicotinic to muscarinic excitation alters neurons necessary for attention
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE; ATTENTION; CALCIUM IMAGING; DENDRITIC MORPHOLOGY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MUSCARINIC ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTORS; NICOTINE; NICOTINIC ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTORS; PHARMACOLOGY; PREFRONTAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: The ability to concentrate depends on stimulation of the prefrontal cortex in the brain by the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.  The neurons in this region that play a critical role in attention are normally stimulated by the nicotinic subtype of acetylcholine receptors.  In cases where this subtype is abnormally weak (either because of a common genetic variation or because of exposure to the drug nicotine), we have found that a different subtype of acetylcholine receptor, the muscarinic receptor, can become stronger and take its place.  However, very little is known about how these important neurons affect the development of attention circuitry under these circumstances.    In this study, we will investigate ways in which changes to nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptor balance can alter normal development of neurons critical to the development of attention circuitry.  We aim to examine: (1) neuron shape and structure, (2) neuronal signaling, (3) the effects of early nicotine exposure on the normal development of these neurons.  Up to 10% of children in Canada are exposed to nicotine at an early stage of development.  Better understanding the role of acetylcholine receptors in the development attention circuitry in normal and abnormal conditions will help uncover novel treatment approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Functional Balance in Knee Osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: BALANCE; BIOMECHANICS; FALLS; GAIT; OSTEOARTHRITIS; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Falling is the leading cause of injury among those 65 and older accounting for over 80% of all injury admissions to hospital, and nearly 50% of those with knee osteoarthritis (OA) have experienced a fall. The risk of falling is related to an individual's level of balance control. Balance treatment programs for those with knee OA have had limited success, even though targeted balance interventions in other populations have seen positive results. This may be because there is no validated tool to measure balance in the knee OA population, and the risk factors specifically related to balance in people with knee OA are unknown. The purpose of this project is to better understand the role of functional balance and risk factors for balance control in people with knee OA, and to develop a targeted functional balance intervention to treat balance impairments in this population. Study 1: Validity and reliability of a measure of functional balance will be assessed in individuals with knee OA, by comparing to scores on other measures of balance and function including the gold standard for balance assessment in the elderly. Study 2: Potential factors that contribute to functional balance impairments will be explored. Muscle strength, knee pain, joint proprioception (body awareness), and disease severity will be measured and results of those with knee OA and healthy adults will be compared. Study 3: A 12-week targeted functional balance intervention will be developed, with exercises that specifically target the balance factors identified in Study 2. Functional balance and physical function will be evaluated before and after the intervention. The creation of an effective, evidence-based balance intervention for those with knee OA represents a new, innovative approach to balance treatment in OA and should improve balance and physical function, while simultaneously reducing the risk of falls for those with OA. This will decrease the long term personal and economic burden of OA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Behaviour is in the practice: Locating excessive behaviours in social practices
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL PATTERNS; COUPLE RELATIONSHIPS; EXCESSIVE BEHAVIOURS; FAMILY RELATIONSHIPS; INTERACTIONAL PATTERNS; SOCIAL PRACTICE
Abstract-Résumé: While working at a family therapy centre as a Counselling Psychology doctoral trainee, I increasingly came to see family conflicts arising from concerns about family members' over-engagement in certain behavioural practices. For young men it was often video games; for young women, it was the Internet; for mothers, shopping or work; and for fathers, pornography use or work. Interactions with others (including family members about these behaviours) also became patterned in problematic ways, possibly exacerbating excessive behavioural patterns. While there is evidence from brain imagining research showing the repetitive or patterned nature of these behaviours, there is a lack of research examining the social practices (such as family interactions) that sustain or impede these behaviours. I am interested in understanding these behaviours in an additional way, by examining how these behaviours are influenced by interactions, practices, and cultural messages surrounding these behaviours.   The objective of my research is to develop an additional way of understanding excessive patterned behaviours (gambling, internet use, video game playing, shopping, working, eating, and sex) by examining how individuals engage in these behaviours, how their interactions with their family members influence and are influenced by the behaviours, and the cultural messages influencing these behaviours. My findings should yield alternative options for Canadians to understand and address these behaviours for themselves and others, with more possibilities for change. Furthermore, results from this project may have implications for policy and economic decisions, by treating aspects of excessive behaviours socially rather than relying exclusively on the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Access to Residential and End-of-Life Care: Exploring South Asian Older Adults' and Family Caregivers' Perspectives
Keywords-MotsClés: END OF LIFE; ETHNO-CULTURAL; OLDER ADULTS; PALLIATIVE SERVICES/CARE; POLICY; QUALITATIVE; RESIDENTIAL LONG-TERM CARE; SERVICE DELIVERY
Abstract-Résumé: By 2031, approximately one third of the Canadian population will belong to a visible minority group and the South Asian (SA) population will comprise the largest visible minority group in Canada and the second largest in British Columbia (BC). Between 2006 and 2031, the proportion of the population belonging to a visible minority group in the 65+ age category will double from 9% to 18%. These shifts in the aging Canadian population prompt important questions as to whether the current organization of residential long-term care (LTC) and end-of-life services are designed to meet the needs of increasingly diverse ethno-cultural older adults. This study will explore: (1) to what extent are existing residential LTC services prepared to provide culturally responsive and competent care to older adults from diverse ethno-cultural backgrounds? (2) what are the unique needs and preferences of older adults from diverse ethno-cultural backgrounds regarding residential LTC and end-of-life care? (3) what challenges do these older adults and their family caregivers face in accessing these services? The questions will be examined from the perspective of SA older adults and their family caregivers, a focus which is appropriate given their increasing numbers and the fact that despite their growing presence in the population, the volume of research on SAs has not kept pace and the diversity among the population is seldom acknowledged leaving gaps in the understanding of their needs.  The intended outcomes of this proposed area of research are to inform the planning and delivery of residential long-term care and end-of-life services for the growing ethno-cultural population of Canada and inform policy decision-making related to these service delivery areas.

TitreApplicationTitle: The roles of parkin and PINK1 in mitochondria-derived vesicle biogenesis and mitochondrial quality control
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CELL CULTURE; CELL-BASED ASSAYS; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; MITOCHONDRIAL DYNAMICS; MITOCHONDRIAL QUALITY CONTROL; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASE; TRAFFICKING AND CELL SIGNALING; UBIQUITINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second-most common neurodegenerative disease, affecting roughly 1% of the population over 65 years of age. Over the next few decades, population demographics predict a higher proportion of elderly Canadians, and therefore a higher percentage of the population at risk for PD. This emphasizes a growing need for more basic research into the pathology of PD. Although the exact cause of PD remains unknown, genetic evidence from inheritable forms of PD points to a role for the dysfunction of mitochondria; the parts of a cell responsible for energy production. Two of these PD-linked genes, parkin and PINK1, have been recently shown to regulate the health or "quality control" of mitochondria. We aim to further elucidate their roles regarding mitochondria quality control, focusing specifically on a recently-discovered cellular pathway involving the specific transport of damaged mitochondrial components away from otherwise-healthy mitochondria. We will use both cell and animal models to investigate the function of these genes, and our findings may shed light on how exactly mitochondrial dysfunction is involved in PD. These findings may also point to novel therapeutic avenues, which will ultimately benefit the aging Canadian population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating Vaccination Strategies to Contain the Spread of Pertussis in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: COST-EFFECTIVENESS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; IMMUNIZATION POLICY; MATHEMATICAL MODELING; PERTUSSIS; TRANSMISSION MODELING; VACCINATION PROGRAMS; VACCINE-PREVENTABLE DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: Pertussis (whooping cough) is a highly contagious respiratory infection that is currently making a major resurgence in North America. While vaccination against pertussis has become routine among infants and school age children, current immunization strategies may not be sufficient to control the spread of the disease: new evidence has suggested that immunity after vaccination wanes after a short period of time. Thus, there seem to be a number of underimmunized adults who are able to pass the infection on to young children, who are at highest risk of severe complications and even death. The purpose of my research is to evaluate competing immunization strategies for adults in Canada: a one-time only vaccination and a booster vaccination every ten years. I will examine relative effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of these strategies, in order to identify optimal immunization strategies for pertussis in the Canadian context.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery of molecular factors that increase the risk of facial clefting
Keywords-MotsClés: AVIAN EMBRYO; CLEFT LIP; MORPHOMETRICS; WNT SIGNALLING
Abstract-Résumé: Cleft lip with or without cleft palate is one of the most common birth defects affecting 1 in 700 newborns. In most cases, these clefts are not associated with other health problems and for this reason patients can have a normal life. However, treatment of these defects involves high costs and complicated surgery in order to re-establish normal esthetics and function.  Multiple genetic and environmental factors contribute to increased risk of clefting. Although some of the genes that produce clefts were studied previously, there is no clear explanation of how they interfere in normal face formation. The goal of my research is to identify the risk factors and to explain the molecular mechanisms that lead to abnormal development in the face.  In my investigation I will be using the chicken embryo because it is a suitable model where we have direct access to the growing face. Previously, novel methods to induce unilateral clefts were developed in our lab, while allowing the other side to continue normal development. I will produce and inject a specific virus that generates a cleft and then I will investigate how face changes during growing.  Thus, by comparing normal and abnormal development of the face we can assess the risk factors that produce the cleft. Furthermore, I will develop innovative methods to make real-time movies by marking facial cells with fluorescent dye during face formation. My research will clarify how fine tuning of cell signaling during embryogenesis may shape facial development and increase the risk of forming clefts and other birth defects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multiple social and built environments and physical activity among youth in the QUALITY Cohort
Keywords-MotsClés: BUILT ENVIRONMENT TYPOLOGIES; CLUSTER ANALYSIS; HOME; NEIGHBOURHOOD AND SCHOOL ENVIRONMENT; PHOTOVOICE METHODOLOGY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; QUALITY COHORT; SOCIAL AND BUILT ENVIRONMENT; YOUTH OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Canadian youth are increasingly overweight and very few children, ages 5-17 years, are meeting the recommended guidelines of 60 minutes daily of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. It is known that features of the social and built environments may either promote or hinder youth physical activity. However little is known about how together, social environments, such as attitudes towards physical activity or perceptions of access to places that promote physical activity, and built environments, such as how well connected streets are or availability of play equipment, can influence physical activity among youth. This research project aims to characterize the home, neighbourhood and school social and built environments for physical activity of Montreal youth at high risk of obesity from the QUALITY (Quebec Adipose and Lifestyle Investigation in Youth) Cohort. It will then look at possible associations between social and built environmental characteristics and physical activity outcomes among these same youth. This project will also ask a subsample of the youth to take photos of and describe where and how they spend their leisure time, to better understand why, where, how and with whom these youth spend time being physically active or inactive and how this might be different according to their weight status. The results of this project may help to improve recommendations, interventions, and policies relating to physical activity among youth and describe optimal design of built environment features to improve access to physical activity among youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: OHTN 2013 Annual Research Conference
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH RESEARCH; HIV RESEARCH; HIV/AIDS CONFERENCE; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: The OHTN Annual Research Conference is a dynamic event that attracts over 600 participants every year, and showcases Canadian HIV research findings in basic and clinical science, epidemiology, socio-behavioural, prevention, intervention, and community-based research. This year's conference theme is 'The Prevention and Treatment Cascade', and will take place from November 17-20, 2013. The goals of this year's conference are to: identify current gaps in the HIV Prevention and Treatment Cascade in Ontario and Canada; showcase research and interventions that have the potential to close those gaps; highlight research that is relevant to populations in Ontario most affected by HIV; reinforce the role of implementation science in putting research findings into action; create an interactive environment where researchers, clinicians, community-based organizations, policy makers, and people living with HIV can network, share knowledge and experience, and discuss emerging and potentially controversial issues; give participants an opportunity to hear from leading researchers from Ontario, Canada and other jurisdictions with comparable epidemics; and demonstrate innovative KTE methodologies that make research findings accessible to frontline workers and those most affected by HIV. The OHTN is requesting $25,000 to support ten scholarships for community members and researchers who are early in their careers from outside Ontario to attend the conference; to contribute to costs associated with innovative KTE initiatives at the conference, including open space technology and social media, challenge panels, and policy round-tables; and to support honoraria for experts who will make keynote presentations and participate in challenge panels and policy roundtables.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of blood transfusion strategies in neurocritically ill patients
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEMIA; BLOOD PRODUCTS; CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; CRITICAL CARE MEDICINE; NEUROCRITICAL CARE; TRANSFUSION
Abstract-Résumé: Blood transfusions to correct anemia (low level of red blood cells) in critically ill patients have been of major importance in critical care over the last decades. Restrictive transfusion strategies (low red blood cells levels) have shown potential benefits over more liberal strategies (high red blood cell levels by transfusions) in critically ill patients. Restrictive strategies are therefore recommended in order to reduce complications arising from blood transfusions. Critically ill patients with brain lesions are vulnerable to secondary injuries such as those from hypoxemia (a lack of oxygen in the blood), which can results from anemia. It has been postulated that patients with acute brain conditions might benefit from liberal transfusion strategies, being transfused when red blood cell levels falls below 9 g/dl, in order to increase the oxygen supply to the brain. However, a recent systematic review of the literature highlighted the paucity of data on the clinical impact of transfusions in this specific population. Considering the financial burden and risks associated with the use of blood products, research addressing these questions is urgently needed. Therefore, we aim to evaluate the impact of anemia and transfusion strategies on mortality and morbidities in critically ill patients with brain lesions. First, we will systematically review the literature to synthetize the current knowledge on transfusion practices. Second, we will conduct a multicenter cohort study to evaluate characteristics associated with transfusions, the clinical impact of anemia and the transfusion strategies used. Third, we will survey Canadian physicians to determine their attitudes toward blood transfusions in critically ill patients with brain lesions.

TitreApplicationTitle: New Science, New Directions in HIV and Hepatitis C

Abstract-Résumé: We are at a pivotal point in our response to HIV, one which is filled with tremendous optimism. In recent years there has been a rapid acceleration of research findings in HIV prevention, transmission, testing and treatment. TitreApplicationTitle: Men and Workplace Health: Establishing a Research Agenda to Advance Workplace Health and Safety
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH PROMOTION; INJURY PREVENTION; MASCULINITY; MEN'S HEALTH; RETURN TO WORK; SEX AND GENDER ANALYSIS; WORK; WORKPLACE CULTURE; WORKPLACE HEALTH AND SAFETY
Abstract-Résumé: We can gain a better understanding of differences between men and women's health by examining how the concepts of "sex" and "gender" interact with and influence various aspects of health, such as health promotion, risk taking behaviour, chronic disease and occupational injuries. For example, men are more likely to die from cardiovascular disease, diabetes and occupational injuries. In fact the majority of workplace fatalities in Canada occur among men.   The World Health Organization indicates that there is a limited understanding of how socially proscribed male ideals and values such as competitiveness, strength, control and independence may influence men's behaviour, expectations, and daily practices. The workplace is a key setting where gender-typical behaviour can influence health and safety and it is often within worker roles that men are exposed to the greatest dangers, health risks and potential for death. The enactment of dominant masculine behaviours, particularly in high-risk occupations, presents significant challenges related to health and safety practices in the workplace.    To increase our understanding of men's physical and mental health in relation to workplace safety practices we will bring together researchers from varied disciplines (e.g. occupational science, sociology, men's health, occupational health and safety) and workplace stakeholders (e.g. occupational health and safety personnel, workers, employers) for a two-day workshop in Toronto. The goals of this workshop are to: 1) identify research gaps in the areas of men's health, work, and workplace safety; 2) develop a research strategy; 3) develop research projects to enhance men's safety at work.

TitreApplicationTitle: Outil Web interactif de sensibilisation sur la violence au travail vécue par les femmes et les hommes
Keywords-MotsClés: APPLICATION DES CONNAISSANCES; GENRE; SANTE MENTALE; SENSIBILISATION; VIOLENCE AU TRAVAIL
Abstract-Résumé: La violence en milieu de travail est un phenomene peu reconnu par les travailleurs et les organisations qui les emploient. De plus, il reste beaucoup a faire pour comprendre et reconnaitre ses effets differentiels sur la sante mentale des femmes et des hommes. Notre equipe, qui mene un programme de recherche visant a ameliorer la prise en charge des travailleurs victimes de violence, a constate recemment aupres de ses partenaires et utilisateurs des connaissances un besoin urgent et immediat d'accroitre les activites de sensibilisation dans les milieux de travail a ce qu'est la violence au travail, a ses impacts et a l'importance de la declarer. Ainsi, dans le but d'atteindre trois publics cibles, soit les agents de la paix, le personnel de soins et celui des transports publics, notre equipe souhaite developper un outil Web de sensibilisation interactif qui s'integrerait dans notre site Internet. Pour creer cet outil, nous priorisons une strategie de co-construction qui implique un processus continu d'echanges avec nos partenaires permettant la mise en commun des connaissances/expertises avec nos chercheurs. Sous une forme ludique, l'outil axe surtout sur du contenu visuel permettra aux travailleurs d'acceder a des informations vulgarisees basees sur les resultats de nos etudes. Les retombees attendues: susciter un changement de vision au sein de ces milieux de travail au travers de l'acquisition de nouvelles connaissances, pour qu'a terme des changements de pratiques soient possibles grace notamment a la declaration des actes de violence par les travailleurs et a la mise en place de politiques et d'une meilleure prise en charge de ce probleme par les organisations.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Surviving Opioid Overdose with Naloxone (SOON) Project and Roundtable
Keywords-MotsClés: BASIC LIFE SUPPORT; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GUIDELINE DEVELOPMENT; HARM REDUCTION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MEDICAL DEVICES; NALOXONE; OPIOIDS; PUBLIC HEALTH; RESUSCITATION
Abstract-Résumé: In response to an alarming increase in opioid overdose deaths over the last decade, many public health programs worldwide now distribute naloxone, a drug that reverses the effects of opioids, and teach overdose first aid to at-risk opioid users.  Like epinephrine for anaphylaxis, naloxone is a potentially life-saving rescue medication, however, few tools exist outside of a hospital setting to effectively deliver or evaluate this intervention. In the United States, nearly 200 local opioid overdose prevention programs distribute roughly 39,000 vials of naloxone per year, with over 10,000 reports of naloxone use since 1996. In Canada, similar programs are operating in Edmonton, Toronto, Ottawa, and throughout British Columbia.    Program evaluations suggest that teaching bystanders to respond to overdoses may reduce risky drug use behaviours and improve responses to emergency situations, but no standardized protocols for the implementation and delivery of this intervention have been developed.  Additionally, no high-quality trials have been completed to determine the effects of this intervention on opioid-associated injuries and deaths.  We propose a national interdisciplinary collaboration of community stakeholders, patient leaders, and knowledge users, along with content experts from diverse clinical fields, methodologists, and industry to review the state of the art in overdose rescue and develop standardized protocols, optimize implementation strategies and identify best means to evaluate outcomes. This approach will enable public health strategies that are evidence driven and effective.

TitreApplicationTitle: Telling our Stories, Sharing our Successes: The Second Metis Knowledge Exchange
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY AND HEALTH SYSTEM RELATIONSHIPS; COMMUNITY RESEARCH PRIORITIES; INDIGENOUS CULTURE; INDIGNEOUS KNOWLEDGE; KNOWLEDGE DISSEMINATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; METIS HEALTH; PROGRAM EVALUATION
Abstract-Résumé: The Health & Wellness Department of the Manitoba Metis Federation is committed to helping improve the health of Metis in Manitoba.  We are applying for funding to hold a two-day meeting in Winnipeg in the fall of 2013. At this meeting we want to bring together policy and decision makers from Regional Health Authorities and community representatives from the Manitoba Metis Federation Regional Offices and who have been working together in teams over the past few years. At the meeting, we will hear about the work that all of the teams have been doing so that they can learn from each other. The Health & Wellness Department, in partnership with the University of Manitoba, is the only research team devoted to studying the health of Metis in Manitoba.   That puts the department in a unique position to be able to disseminate research findings that have the potential to influence program and policy making to improve the health of Metis. At the meeting we will present findings from all the research projects the Health & Wellness Department and the University has been working on. Finally, there will be an open panel discussion where people can ask questions about how the teams are going to identify future research needs and how they are going to use the research findings to adapt program and policy.  Using this new information the teams will go back to their regions and continue working together to improve Metis health. Funding will cover the costs of this meeting including travel, hotel, meeting room, sound and equipment rental.

Abstract-Résumé: An HIV epidemic is disproportionately affecting indigenous men and women over non-indigenous migrants in Papua and West Papua, the easternmost provinces of Indonesia. There continues to be no HIV prevention strategy that focuses on the needs and experiences of indigenous Papuans, despite clear recommendations produced a decade ago. Our project, based on partnerships with three indigenous-run non-governmental organizations in Manokwari, West Papua, aims to engage local community members and non-local stakeholders working in the field of HIV prevention in a three day consensus-building activity to define an Indigenous HIV Strategy for Tanah Papua, as well as to establish priorities for research, training and capacity-building that will enable this Strategy to be operationalized.

TitreApplicationTitle: A longitudinal examination of the relationships between early immunization pain and future needle fear
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNIZATIONS; INFANT PAIN; NEEDLE FEAR; PEDIATRIC PAIN
Abstract-Résumé: Negative experiences with immunizations in childhood have been related to the development of needle fears that continue into adulthood and can contribute to avoiding the use of the health care system. No research has examined whether negative experiences during immunizations in the first year of life (the period in which most Canadians receive the greatest amount of immunizations) play a role in setting the stage for the development of needle fears. The proposed study will invite parents and children who have already been videotaped during routine immunizations at 2, 4, 6, and 12 months of age to again be videotaped at the routine immunization that takes place at preschool. These videotapes will be coded for child needle fear behaviours as well as child pain behaviours. Children and parents will also be asked to provide a verbal report of the child's fear of needles. This study will help us to better understand how negative experiences during immunizations in the first year of life can influence a child's development of needle fears. This research has implications for interventions and best practices used by parents during immunizations. Findings from this research will help us to implement strategies to better soothe the child during immunizations, reduce the development of needle fears, and ensure greater Canadian use of the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innovations in gynaecologic specialties: Translating science into improved health for Canadian women
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOMETRIOSIS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PELVIC FLOOR HEALTH; PELVIC/GENITAL PAIN; SEXUAL MEDICINE; SPECIALIZED GYNAECOLOGY; URINARY INCONTINENCE; UROGYNAECOLOGY; VULVODYNIA; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The study of women's health issues is increasingly receiving the sophisticated scientific attention that has been lacking in past decades. New discoveries in the identification, diagnosis, and treatment of various women's health topics has led to improvements in the life span and quality of life of Canadian women. Within specialized areas of gynaecology, however, barriers exist in translating scientific findings into clinical practice, and into a language that is accessible by consumers. The Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at UBC is at the forefront of creating new discoveries in many areas of women's health. Our Division of Gynaecologic Specialties is a new divisional home to researchers who are carrying out their work on highly specialized populations of women-groups that have received relatively less focus in terms of knowledge translation activities. Research within this division spans from incontinence to pelvic/genital pain to family planning and sexual health to Hepatitis B vaccination in pregnant women to personalized medicine. Collectively this team of researchers has garnered several million dollars in grant funding to successfully lead to new discoveries. In this Dissemination Grant, members of the Division of Gynaecologic Specialties will translate their recent scientific findings, first-hand, to the public consumers who will benefit from it directly. Six monthly public talks will be given, and opportunities for interactive dialogue will be presented. Sessions will be video-recorded and later made available freely to the public. The six talks will then be summarized and captured in an informational booklet (3,000 copies produced) which will then be disseminated to Vancouver-area family physicians. The long-term expected outcome is to provide the public with important information about new discoveries in women's health which will empower them to take control of their own reproductive and sexual health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comprendre l'absentéisme des patients aux rendez-vous opératoires en chirurgie élective : explorer le rôle du conflit décisionnel et identifier les lacunes du processus d'obtention du consentement libre et éclairé des patients.
Keywords-MotsClés: APPROCHE COMPARATIVE; CONSENTEMENT AUX SOINS; POLITIQUES PUBLIQUES EN SANTE; PRISE DE DECISION PARTAGEE
Abstract-Résumé: Parmi les chirurgies electives planifiees qui sont annulees, 14% le sont parce que les patients ne se presentent pas a leur rendez-vous operatoire et ce, malgre les procedures de rappel mises en place par les etablissements hospitaliers. Cette situation entraine des couts importants pour le systeme de sante. Les patients qui ne se presentent pas a leur operation ont pourtant signe un formulaire de consentement, mais ces formulaires ne temoignent pas d'un reel consentement eclaire de la part des patients. Le patient qui consent a un traitement devrait theoriquement le faire en toute connaissance des risques et des benefices associes a ce traitement, mais egalement en connaissant les autre options qui s'offraient a lui. Ce pourrait-il alors que le taux d'absenteisme des patients aux rendez-vous operatoires reflete un conflit decisionnel important vecu par ces patients? Le conflit decisionnel se definit comme l'incertitude personnelle ressentie face au choix d'une option au depend d'autres options offertes presentant des risques ou des resultats incertains et des enjeux importants en termes de benefices potentiels et de pertes. Ce projet de doctorat a pour principal objectif d'evaluer dans quelle mesure le conflit decisionnel permet d'identifier si des lacunes sont presentes dans le processus de consentement libre et eclaire des patients aux chirurgies electives. Deux questions secondaires en decoulent, a savoir 1) le conflit decisionnel est-il associe a l'absenteisme des patients aux rendez-vous operatoires des chirurgies electives, et 2) comment les processus normatifs mis en place par les etablissements hospitaliers dans le but d'assurer un consentement libre et eclaire des patients peuvent-ils etre ameliores? Cette etude fournira aux professionnels de la sante et aux decideurs des outils pratiques et concrets en vue d'ameliorer les processus normatifs mis en place pour obtenir le consentement eclaire des patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Engagement matters: a pan-Canadian e-learning resource supporting health services planners to engage marginalized women in planning
Keywords-MotsClés: DISSEMINATION EVENT; ELEARNING TOOL; HEALTH SERVICES PLANNING; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; PATIENT ENGAGEMENT; SEX AND GENDER-BASED ANALYSIS; WEB-BASED TECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed project will develop web-based educational modules to give Canadian health service planners access to a newly developed tool - the AWESOME model - which supports planners to include diverse groups of women in planning for health services, a process referred to as patient engagement. Patient engagement helps health service planners learn about how to make health services work best for patients. However, the engagement methods that are commonly used, which assume that 'one-size fits all', might make it challenging for some women, particularly those with the most complex healthcare needs or poor health, to be involved in patient engagement. This limits the voices that are heard in health service planning. The AWESOME model supports health service planners to widen the group of people that are included in health service planning. The proposed e-Learning tool will make this model available on an existing, high-traffic web-based platform (www.sgba-resource.ca). In addition to explaining the AWESOME model content, the modules will have tutorial videos and other interactive learning components. We anticipate that making these web-based modules available to health service planners across Canada will increase their ability to engage women, which will support improvements to the health delivery system by bringing diverse women's voices into the conversation about planning health services.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of Personalized Feedback Intervention with Physicians to Reduce Inappropriate Antibiotic Use
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; ANTIBIOTIC UTILIZATION; PROGRAM EVALUATION; RANDOMIZED DESIGN; TIME SERIES ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The inappropriate use of antibiotics contributes to the problem of antibiotic resistance, where some bacteria that cause infections are becoming resistant to the medications we use to treat them. In an effort to improve appropriate antibiotic use, we mailed out personalized feedback to physicians in BC describing their use of antibiotics to treat patients diagnosed with certain kinds of infections. The feedback included a comparison to their peers, and to guidelines. This feedback was anonymous, so that only the physician saw his or her own information. The project proposed here will evaluate the effect of this feedback on improving antibiotic use in BC, using rigorous statistical methods that allow us to understand the short and long-term impact of this intervention. Understanding how this program impacted antibiotic use will help us to design effective interventions in this and other areas in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of action of complex molecules rationally designed to target multiple adverse signaling pathways in tumor cells
Keywords-MotsClés: C-MET; C-SRC; CANCER; COMBI-TARGETING DRUGS; EPIDERMAL GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR; RECEPTOR TYROSINE KINASES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION PATHWAYS
Abstract-Résumé: With a better understanding of signaling pathways functionally deregulated in human cancers, a lot of progress has been made in the field of targeted therapy. Cancer, especially in its advanced stages is extremely heterogenous and is controlled by a complex network of signaling molecules involved in synergistic cross-talk and redundancy. In trying to address this challenging issue, we designed and synthesized drugs capable of releasing potent inhibitors of tyrosine kinases (EGFR, c-Src, c-MET) often overexpressed in cancers. The aim of my project is to assess the ability of these drugs in blocking proliferation, invasion, migration as well as inducing apoptosis in tumor cell lines. Through this approach, we wish to develop single molecules that are capable of potently inhibiting two or more kinases, thereby eliminating the need to use multiple drugs, to achieve similar outcome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Integrating Traditional Ecological Knowledge and Local Resources with Agroforestry Stewardship Practices to Enhance Food Security in Sub-arctic First Nations
Keywords-MotsClés: AGROFORESTRY; FOOD LOCALIZATION; FOOD SECURITY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LOCAL ECOLOGICAL FERTILIZERS; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; REMOTE FIRST NATIONS; SUB-ARCTIC HEALTH; SUSTAINABLE FOOD SECURITY INTERVENTION; TRADITIONAL ECOLOGICAL KNOWLEDGE
Abstract-Résumé: Canada's First Nation (FN) people are known to have a disproportionately high prevalence of health conditions linked to poor diet, including obesity, tooth decay, heart disease, Type 2 diabetes and hearing impairments. Poor dietary habits ubiquitous to FN communities are related to their high risk of experiencing food insecurity.  Food Security can be defined as "access by all people at all times to enough food for an active, healthy life, including availability of nutritionally adequate and safe foods that can be acquired in socially acceptable ways".  Food security in remote FN communities of northern Canada is challenged by a modern dependence on an unreliable, import-based food system that often lacks nutritional quality, bears high transportation costs and results in loss of traditional food systems and associated knowledge, ultimately degrading individual and community health. Our innovative intervention strategy using agroforestry stewardship practices, traditional ecological knowledge and local "wastes" as soil fertilizers, will foster adaptive capacity and resilience in the face of global warming and rising food transpiration costs.  Agroforestry is an alternative land-use system to conventional agriculture that has been utilized as a socioeconomically and ecologically sustainable means to establish long-term food security in impoverished areas, mainly within the sub-tropic and tropic regions.  Ecological wastes from the northern lifestyle, such as fish guts and wood ash, are full of essential nutrients for agricultural crops and can be integrated into this agroforestry system.  Preservation of traditional culture and foods has shown to be a vital component of indigenous well-being and community health.  By integrating these three components into one local food system,  we predict that this  intervention strategy will partially substitute unhealthy food imports, reduce costs of healthy diet and empower remote FN's to gain autonomy over their health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Community and research partnerships to strengthen labour market access for persons living with or at risk of acquiring HIV/AIDS who use illicit drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY PARTNERSHIP DEVELOPMENT; EMPLOYMENT; HIV/AIDS; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; LABOUR MARKET ACCESS; RESEARCH PLANNING; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SOCIAL ENTERPRISE; SUBSTANCE USE; VOCATIONAL SERVICES
Abstract-Résumé: Employment has long been identified as intrinsically linked to individual health. Among persons living with HIV/AIDS who use illicit drugs (PHAUD), employment may be a key influence on disease progression and individual health outcomes. Given potential health benefits and high barriers to labour market participation for PHAUD and people who use drugs (PUD) at risk for HIV infection, alternative labour market participation models appropriate to this population are urgently needed. While many organizations currently provide vocational services (VS), employment or social enterprise-based opportunities for low-income individuals, there is a dearth of opportunities for PHAUD and PUD. It is unclear whether current service and opportunity providers are aware of research on the income generating patterns and barriers to employment among these populations, or whether this research supports their ongoing operations. Additionally, little research examines the socio-economic and health impacts of VS provision, alternative employment or social enterprise-based opportunities. Finally, current gaps warrant the exploration of alternative labour market access models. The activities outlined in this proposal aim to (1) develop partnerships between researchers and local vocational service providing organizations (VSPO), employers and social enterprises serving PHAUD/PUD; (2) draw on these partnerships to conduct need and feasibility assessments for social and structural interventions targeted at improving access to the labour market for PHAUD; and (3) leverage the outcomes of these assessments to inform research plans to develop, pilot and evaluate such interventions. We propose to meet these objectives through the development of research briefs, an environmental scan of VSPO, employers and social enterprises serving PHAUD and PUD, the planning and conducting of partnership development meetings, and collaborative research planning activities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing a Multidimensional Theory of Suicide Among Middle-Aged and Older Men
Keywords-MotsClés: EMOTIONAL REGULATION; GENDER AND HEALTH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION AND EXCHANGE; MEN AND MASCULINITY; MULTIDIMENSIONAL THEORY DEVELOPMENT; PERSONALITY THEORY; SOCIO-CULTURAL PERSPECTIVES; SUICIDE; SUICIDE PREVENTION AND INTERVENTIONS; TEAM BUILDING AND DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Suicide is a significant public health issue in Canada and throughout much of the world. Men represent the vast majority of those who die by suicide.  The 2009 suicide rate for men and boys in Canada was three times higher than that for women and girls (17.9 versus 5.3 per 100,000); and accounted for nearly 80% of the 3,890 deaths by suicide in that year.  The overarching goals of the proposed research planning meeting are to: 1. Convene a North American interdisciplinary team of suicide prevention researchers, theorists on masculinity and personality, experts in health systems, and knowledge users; 2.  Formulate and test a novel multidimensional theory of suicide  incorporating sociocultural norms of masculinity relevant to middle-age and older men; 3. Examine the effectiveness of theory-driven outreach in helping to overcome major barriers inherent in identifying and intervening with men at risk for suicide. The following planning activities are proposed: 1. A literature review and synthesis of current multidimensional models of suicide and input from key stakeholders and knowledge leaders; 2. A face-to-face meeting of project experts and knowledge users with the goal of establishing an interdisciplinary team, formulating team roles, creating an administrative structure,  and  consolidating  specific research proposals.  The planning meeting will include plenary presentations, small group discussions, planning for specific research proposals and formulating team role functions and governance. 3.  Within 45 days,  a video-conferencing team meeting to finalize the team's proposed research agenda and confirm the team's governance and structure; 4. Within 90 days from the video-conference, we will undertake a teleconference to finalize operating grant submission(s) to CIHR and to finalize our deliverables from the planning meeting process. This planning meeting process will lead to the first known interdisciplinary team in Canada focused on suicide among men.

TitreApplicationTitle: Planning for an HIV PrEP Demonstration Project among Toronto Men Who Have Sex with Men
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV; PLANNING MEETING; PRE-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS; SCOPING REVIEWS; STAKEHOLDER CONSULTATION; WORKING GROUP MEETINGS
Abstract-Résumé: Men who have sex with men (MSM) continue to bear a major burden of HIV infections in Canada.  Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a new approach to HIV prevention involving daily use of an HIV medication, and has been shown to reduce the risk of HIV in clinical trials. There are now urgent global calls for PrEP pilot or Demonstration projects that could study how best to deliver PrEP in the real world.  However, in contrast to the United States, where PrEP has received formal FDA approval and where pilot projects are already underway, there has little effort to prepare for PrEP in Canada.  We are thus planning a PrEP Demonstration Project for Toronto MSM that will study how best to implement this proven HIV prevention strategy in the Canadian context.  Because there is a risk that PrEP users may be stigmatized (eg. as promiscuous or dangerous), with negative effects on PrEP uptake and adherence, we are also planning community-based efforts to address stigma and related issues in a pro-active fashion.  This planning grant will address these issues through a careful, consultative process.  Our interdisciplinary team will first conduct two brief scoping reviews about existing PrEP projects and related community efforts, to clarify how our work can best contribute to the global PrEP knowledge base.  We will then host a two-day in-person meeting, including speakers from ongoing PrEP projects in other jurisdictions, to articulate the key operations research questions for our Demonstration Project, initiate a community-based anti-stigma effort, and develop substudy plans that will maximize the research output of our project.  Working groups will mature these ideas into full substudy protocols, and we will synthesize our findings into a formal project proposal to be submitted to CIHR and other funding agencies.  Ultimately, this work has the potential to translate recent research findings into tangible HIV prevention benefits for this important, vulnerable population.

Abstract-Résumé: Our growing understanding of brain function not only opens the door to new avenues of treatment for major diseases, but also provides substantial insights into the ways in which our brains function in everyday life. As these technologies move from concept to implementation, substantive questions arise about their impact upon society. To promote ethically sound applications of neuroscience and a dynamic research culture that supports neuroscience literacy, it is important to focus on multidirectional engagement -the inclusion of knowledge and attitudes from, and dissemination of information to stakeholders upstream of the scientific research. The conference Brain Science and Social Responsibility addresses this challenge directly by engaging not only traditional scholars but also by integrating perspectives from diverse publics in a healthy dialogue about the social responsibility that accrues with discoveries in the brain sciences.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Association for HIV Research (CAHR) New HIV Researcher Workshop 2014: Practical Advice on Planning a Pathway to Career Success in HIV Research
Keywords-MotsClés: CAREER DEVELOPEMENT; CONTINUING EDUCATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MENTORING; NETWORKING; NEW RESEARCHERS; RESPONSIVE PROGRAMMING
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Association for HIV Research (CAHR) is the professional organization for HIV and AIDS research in Canada or by Canadians. CAHR includes all researchers and all disciplines of the scientific approaches to HIV and AIDS, for the purpose of its better prevention and treatment and ultimately for its eradication and cure. The annual CAHR Conference is the premier gathering in Canada for those working in the field of HIV, as well as policy makers, persons living with HIV and other individuals committed to ending the pandemic.  The 2014 CAHR Conference programme will present new scientific knowledge and offer many opportunities for structured dialogue on the major issues facing the global response to HIV.  A variety of session types, from abstract-driven presentations to symposia, bridging and plenary sessions, will meet the needs of various participants. Other related activities, including ancillary meetings and exhibitions will contribute to an exceptional opportunity for professional development and networking. Of specific note, CAHR will once again offer its annual New HIV Researcher Workshop which brings together mentors and trainees in a day long learning session.  As part of its mission, CAHR promotes education and the development of new researchers. Each year at the Conference approximately 60 graduate students, doctoral students, postdoctoral fellows, medical trainees and other new HIV researchers attend the CAHR New HIV Researcher Workshop. This skills-based workshop is designed to focus on all four CAHR research tracks (Basic Sciences, Clinical Sciences, Epidemiology and Public Health, Social Sciences) and includes such sessions as: CIHR 101; Getting Funding for your Research; Grantscrafting; Mentorship; and Career Development. Sessions are led by leading Canadian HIV researchers and representatives from research funding organizations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evidence based planning of an optimal triaging strategy for arthritis care in Alberta
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; CENTRALIZED REFERRAL; MODELING; OPTIMIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Alberta Health Service (AHS) is seeking to improve outcomes and reduce wait times for arthritis care in Alberta.  To achieve this goal, the Bone and Joint Strategic Clinical Network (BJSCN) within AHS, and the Alberta Bone and Joint Institute (ABJHI), has proposed using centralized referral as a triaging strategy for arthritis care in Alberta.  Centralized referral involves pooling individual wait lists to create a single first-come first-served but severity-prioritised queue from which patients are scheduled to see a specialist.   The purpose of this planning grant is for the research team and members from AHS, BJSCN and ABJHI to meet, with the objective of producing a joint submission to the CIHR Partnership for Health System Improvement (PHSI) grant competition. The scope is the use of modelling to develop and implement a new evidence-informed centralized referral process for arthritis care. Its purpose is to improve access, while ensuring patients receive appropriate, safe and effective care and are treated with respect through their healthcare journey.   The meeting will be held at the University of Calgary in August 2013. A number of objectives will be met. First, to delineate the priority knowledge translation (KT) objectives of the partner organizations as they relate to the design and management of the central referral strategy for arthritis care in Alberta. Second, to outline research deliverables, the methodology needed to conduct the research and corresponding timelines. Third, to outline the methods and processes of knowledge translation that will be employed in the proposed research.   We are ready to begin development of this collaborative research program now.  This meeting will reinforce the strong partnership between our research team and partner organizations (AHS, BJSCN, ABJHI) by ensuring the development of an innovative research program that is focused on the needs of AHS health system managers, decision makers and policy makers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying the Health and Mental Health Impacts of Social Exclusion for Young Gender Non-Conforming Males and Transgender Boys in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN AND FAMILIES; GENDER NON-CONFORMITY; MALES AND BOYS; PLANNING MEETING; SOCIAL EXCLUSION
Abstract-Résumé: American and European research has revealed high levels of social exclusion and associated poor health outcomes among gender non-conforming children (children who do not conform to social gender norms). Two identified sub-groups of this population are: young gender non-conforming (GNC) males (natal males who behave in ways deemed to be feminine); and transgender boys (young natal females who transition to live as boys). Currently we lack research to understand the impact of social exclusion on the health of these populations in the Canadian context.  Rainbow Health Ontario, together with Co-Applicants and Collaborators, proposes a two-day planning meeting to bring together researchers, knowledge users and families to develop new research partnerships to advance research into the health and mental health impacts of social exclusion for young GNC males and transgender boys in Canada. Our research agenda will focus on four key areas:  Health and Social Services; Mental Health Services; Health and Wellbeing in Educational Settings; and Health and Wellbeing in Sport & Recreational Settings. We will engage researchers with a wide range of methodological expertise, knowledge users working in health and social services, and families of young GNC males and transgender boys in a two-day meeting on September 26th and 27th, 2013 in Toronto. The goals are to: 1) Gain a thorough understanding of the expertise of researchers and service providers collaborating on the grant; 2) Identify priority research questions related to health and mental health impacts of social exclusion for GNC males and transgender boys; 3) Identify knowledge translation and exchange (KTE) needs among health and social service providers working with these populations across Canada; 4) Initiate and support the development of new research partnerships to study the health and mental health impacts of social exclusion for these populations; and 5) Submit an operating grant proposal to CIHR in 2014.

Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; EDUCATION; HIV/AIDS; KNOWLEDGE DISSEMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal people experience poorer health and socio-economic conditions than the general population in Canada. Epidemiological data also suggest that Aboriginal people continue to be over-represented in the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Canada. Proportionally, Aboriginal people who self identified in the 2006 census represented 3.8% of the general Canadian population, and yet they accounted for an estimated 8% of all prevalent HIV infections and 12.5% of all new HIV infections in 2008 (PHAC, 2009). Further, Aboriginal people are one of the eight target populations identified in the Federal Initiative to Address HIV/AIDS in Canada. The Canadian Association for HIV Research (CAHR) is the leading organization of HIV/AIDS researchers in Canada. CAHR includes all researchers and all disciplines of the scientific approaches to HIV and AIDS, for the purpose of its better prevention and treatment and ultimately for its eradication and cure. As part of CAHRs mission is to promote education and the development of new researchers, CAHR runs several new researcher workshops (NRW) each year. These skills-based workshops are designed to focus on all four CAHR research tracks (Basic Sciences, Clinical Sciences, Epidemiology and Public Health, Social Sciences) as well as Community-Based Research. These workshops include such sessions as: CIHR 101; Getting Funding for your Research; Grantscrafting; Mentorship; and Career Development. Sessions are conducted by leading Canadian HIV researchers and representatives from research funding organizations. With this background, CAHR is supporting efforts to address the needs of the Aboriginal community, and to play a role in building a cadre of First Nations, Inuit and Metis HIV/AIDS researchers in Canada. Of central importance to this effort, CAHR will utilize new funding to promote these workshops and to offer travel incentives to aspiring First Nations, Inuit and Metis HIV/AIDS researchers in Canada to attend a CAHR NRW in Fall/Winter 2013-14.

TitreApplicationTitle: Building intersectoral partnerships to improve the health services response to elder abuse
Keywords-MotsClés: ELDER ABUSE; HEALTH SERVICES; INTEGRATED AND COORDINATED CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Worldwide elder abuse is recognized as a significant public health issue, affecting as many as one in three older adults depending on type of abuse and specific population group.  In Canada, the larger of two national surveys on EA conducted in 1999 found a rate of 7% for at least one type of abuse, although maltreatment and neglect were not examined.  This health and social problem will proportionately increase as the number of older adults more than triples over the next 50 years. The physical, psychological, and social consequences of abuse in later life can be considerable and include physical injuries, depression, anxiety, isolation, and death. However, in Canada there is no integrated health-based service that assesses for elder abuse and addresses the wide range of needs of older adults who have been victimized. Our goal is to improve health services and policy for older people by developing a comprehensive, multidisciplinary hospital-based elder abuse intervention with links to relevant community, financial, interfaith, law enforcement and legal sectors. This will be accomplished by working with these other sectors to address the complex functional, social, forensic, and medical needs of elder abuse victims in a coordinated and collaborative manner. Over the period July 2013-June 2014, this planning grant will bring together academic, community, healthcare, and government leaders and citizens:  a) to determine the key components of the proposed elder abuse intervention and associated training curriculum and b) to develop a programmatic elder abuse health services research agenda that includes the future piloting of the intervention. These activities will be achieved by building a strong, collaborative, interdisciplinary, intersectoral research team of elder abuse experts.

Abstract-Résumé: First Nations youth and elders on Vancouver Island have worked in collaboration to create digital stories focused on the preservation of cultural knowledge and community histories. In addition, these stories contain prevention messages (healthy eating, healthy living, respect for land, connections to community and cultural values).  These stories were generated by and produced by community members based on the values and concerns of each community but have relevance for many communities. Disseminating these stories as well as lessons learned in the application of the digital story method for engaging First Nations youth will support the preservation of cultural knowledge and the dissemination of health promoting information in culturally relevant ways. This will also continue the capacity building objectives of the research by supporting youth and community members to do presentations and attend symposia in their communities and other jurisdictions. In addition, the knowledge of the outcome research that indicates the value of the collaborative digital story methodology for the youth and elders will be shared with appropriate audiences (academic and policy and practice).

TitreApplicationTitle: Échange de connaissances suite à deux synthèses sur les meilleures politiques pour réduire les inégalités sociales de santé : «Synthèse de connaissances sur les politiques des pays nordiques qui contribuent à réduire les inégalités sociales de santé» et «Synthèse de recherche sur les collectivités viables nordiques et leurs caractéristiques favorisant la santé dans l'équité»
Keywords-MotsClés: APPROPRIATION DES CONNAISSANCES; CAFE SCIENTIFIQUE; GRAND PUBLIC; INEGALITES SOCIALES; INEGALITES SOCIALES DE SANTE; MILIEUX CITOYENS; PAYS NORDIQUES; POLITIQUES PUBLIQUES; EQUITE EN SANTE
Abstract-Résumé: Selon l'OCDE, les ecarts entre riches et pauvres ne cessent de croitre dans ses pays membres et les mecanismes de repartition de la richesse sont de moins en moins efficaces, en particulier au Canada. Aujourd'hui, le Canada compense moins les inegalites que la majorite des pays de l'OCDE. Ces dernieres annees, de nombreux ecrits scientifiques ont fait etat des effets sanitaires de ces inegalites. Les inegalites sociales de sante (ISS) sont des differences de sante systematiques entre les groupes socio-economiques, ecarts socialement construits et donc, evitables. Les pays nordiques (Suede, Norvege, Finlande, Danemark) se distinguent par de faibles taux d'inegalites et d'ISS. Notre projet consiste a disseminer les resultats de deux recherches portant sur les politiques sociales et les politiques de developpement durable de ces pays et sur leur impact potentiel sur la sante. Nous prevoyons: 1- organiser un cafe scientifique bilingue pour presenter au grand public ces politiques, exposer ensuite nos resultats de recherches,  et terminer sur les implications pour la pratique de la sante publique au Canada;  2- diffuser l'enregistrement de ce cafe sur plusieurs plateformes; 3- Comme notre travail initial ete realise en francais, nous prevoyons aussi le rendre accessible en anglais. Il importe que soient discutees les meilleures pratiques, non seulement au niveau des decideurs qui ont la responsabilite de faconner l'intervention de l'etat dans la reduction des inegalites sociales, mais aussi au niveau du public en general, dont la sensibilisation aux politiques favorables a la sante est cruciale pour leur adoption ainsi que pour leur mise en application. Le cafe scientifique est une formule etablie, permettant de rejoindre les citoyens interesses par une problematique dans un cadre convivial et de leur permettre d'interagir directement avec les chercheurs et les parties prenantes de l'appropriation des resultats de la recherche.

Abstract-Résumé: The Gordon Research Conference (GRC) and the Gordon Research Seminar (GRS) on "Elastin, Elastic Fibers and Microfibrils" will be held in conjunction from July 20th - 21st (GRS) and July 21st - 26th 2013 (GRC) at the University of New England. This biennial conference represents the leading international forum for the knowledge exchange and dissemination of research on elastic fiber systems in health and disease. The conference will provide the scientific community and non-academic stakeholders with new basic mechanisms of elastic fiber systems, as well as with new and improved diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for genetic and acquired connective tissue disorders originating from derailed functions of the elastic fiber system. The oral presentations at the GRC feature distinguished scientists as well as selected students and post-doctoral fellows. In addition, poster sessions will expose trainees to the scientific community for constructive feedback. For the first time in 2011, the GRC was preceded by the Gordon Research Seminar. This GRS was extremely successful so that the scientific community and other stakeholders decided to continue it. The GRS is uniquely designed to foster and enhance career development for students, postdoctoral fellows, and early stage independent researchers. An invited keynote speaker from a Canadian institution will give an introductory overview while all other oral presentations will be selected from the submitted abstracts. A mentorship component will feature a panel of scientists with different backgrounds providing insights in successful career development. The overarching goal of both, the GRS and GRC, is to disseminate innovative research and to foster new research networks. Funds requested from CIHR will be used to cover travel and presentation awards for trainees and to contribute to travel expenses for invited participants.

Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CONFERENCE; INTERNATIONAL; PRIMARY CARE
Abstract-Résumé: This application is asking for funding for a meeting of a group of cancer researchers called "Ca-PRI" or the Cancer in Primary Care Research International Network. These researchers from Canada, the USA and Europe will be meeting in Winnipeg, Manitoba on June 10-13, 2014 to discuss how cancer patients receive care from their family physicians and other health providers who work in primary care.  Important topics include cancer screening and prevention, diagnosing patients quickly, and supporting patients after cancer treatment. Ca-PRI is especially interested in encouraging research projects that involve international comparisons of how cancer patients are treated in primary care.  This meeting will involve 80 researchers and their students from ten countries who will present research findings to an audience of other researchers, cancer patients, family physicians (FPs), nurse practitioners (NPs) and government health system leaders.  This will increase the chance of the research being improved by good discussion with people who will use the information when the research is done. As well, special "patient partners" and "policy partners" will provide their viewpoints during research discussions. The meeting will include a special education day for FPs and NPs where some of the best international Ca-PRI researchers will be presenting and facilitating a two-way exchange of information that will help improve both medical practice and research. A special meeting between these international experts and the leaders of the "Manitoba Cancer Journey Initiative" will take place to discuss the work of speeding up the testing and referral process for cancer diagnosis in Manitoba.  The conference will be a success because of the strong and experienced team of doctors, researchers, and educators who are organizing it, with the support of the University of Manitoba, CancerCare Manitoba and Ca-PRI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Re-Tracing the African, Caribbean, and European (ACE)Pathways to Care in First-Episode Psychosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNO-RACIAL GROUPS; HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH SERVICES; MENTAL HEALTH; PATHWAYS TO CARE; PSYCHOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The sooner an individual gets treatment for psychotic illnesses, such as schizophrenia, the better the treatment outcome is. In an effort to assist this goal, early intervention services have been set up across Ontario. However, studies of these services suggest that there is a greater delay between developing symptoms of psychosis and getting treatment for people of African and Caribbean origin than European Canadians. These delays may lead to more severe illness with worse outcomes and more involvement of emergency services and the criminal justice system.  The ACE Pathways to Care project documented and compared the pathways taken to early intervention services for African, Caribbean and European origin Canadians living in Toronto and Hamilton. Furthermore, it looked at the different routes these ethnic groups took to getting care and why they took particular routes over others. The study results are now ready to be shared with healthcare providers, community agencies and policy makers in order to promote early treatment and better outcomes.   By bringing together different stakeholders, this project will provide an opportunity for communities, clinicians and policy makers to learn about the key findings of the ACE Pathways to Care study and to engage in the subject in a public setting. To ensure the maximum impact of the study findings, knowledge will shared using two activities: A. Digital-Storytelling Workshops, where 3 minute digital movies will be created by study participants (e.g., clients and their family) as well as staff working in early intervention services. These digital stories will be used as a discussion tool during the forum, and; B. Abstract-Résumé: Le Colloque des programmes de bioethique de l'Universite de Montreal est un evenement annuel ayant pour objectif d'apporter un eclairage theorique et pratique sur une problematique touchant de pres l'ensemble des acteurs lies a la sante,au systeme de sante, a la recherche et a l'etablissement des politiques de sante. En favorisant les echanges, ce colloque est un vecteur de dissemination des connaissances, des resultats de recherche, des experiences et des expertises aupres des professionnels de la sante, des chercheurs, des gestionnaires et des decideurs, tant au niveau micro-ethique que macro-ethique. Il aura lieu les 14 et 15 novembre 2013 et il porte sur un probleme ethique central: l'impact de la limite des ressources sur le systeme de sante.Quatre tables rondes regroupant des chercheurs, des praticiens et des decideurs ont pour theme:  1) l'acces aux services de sante,  2) les professionnels comme gardiens du systeme,  3) la pertinence et les couts des technologies,  4) des pistes de solution.  Le colloque contribuera ainsi a l'avancement des connaissances theoriques et pratiques et produira un effet catalyseur qui donnera lieu a de nouvelles initiatives pour l'etablissement de collaborations interdisciplinaires fructueuses entre les milieux de recherche et de pratique, de maniere a eclairer les decideurs dans la recherche de solutions pour l'amelioration du systeme de soins et de la sante populationnelle.

Abstract-Résumé: The Visioning Health Project is strengths-based, arts-informed, and culturally-grounded community-based participatory research project that explored the meaning and experience of health and wellness from the perspective of Positive Aboriginal Women (PAW). It also explored the role of culture and gender in creating, supporting and maintaining PAWs health and wellness. Guided by a decolonizing and Indigenous approach to research, this project responded to the community-identified need for research that focused on PAWs strengths and assets instead of their weaknesses and deficits as is more commonly the case with health research. To share our process and preliminary findings throughout the project, we engaged in numerous integrated KTE activities, including workshops, conference posters and presentations, and innovative and culturally-relevant photo exhibitions. Now at the end of our CIHR-IAPH AK-NEAHR funded project, we are seeking new funds to share our final results and recommendations with a multidisciplinary and multi-sectoral audience and to engage new and existing partners in discussions to develop a Visioning Health II Operating Grant submission for CIHR.

TitreApplicationTitle: Santé sexuelle des jeunes femmes et hommes du Québec - Des pistes pour l'action
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCES AUX SERVICES DE SANTE SEXUELLE; APPLICATION DES CONNAISSANCES; CONTRACEPTION; GENRE; INFECTION TRANSMISSIBLE SEXUELLEMENT; SANTE DES POPULATIONS; SANTE SEXUELLE; TECHNOLOGIE DE L'INFORMATION ET DES COMMUNICATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Dans le cadre de PIXEL, une etude sur la sante sexuelle des femmes et des hommes de 16 a 24 ans au Quebec, une serie d'activites de transfert et d'application des connaissances est proposee, notamment un atelier d'echange, un module interactif a partir du site Internet de PIXEL et des outils de partage de resultats et de soutien. PIXEL combine des prelevements biologiques (chlamydia, gonorrhee, VPH) et un questionnaire dont les themes sont varies (conduites, bien-etre sexuel, acces aux services de sante, etc.). Grace a un echantillon de 9 000 jeunes, des analyses seront menees afin de mieux comprendre l'influence du genre et du sexe sur la sante sexuelle et sur l'acces aux services de sante sexuelle, par exemple en lien avec le depistage des infections transmissibles sexuellement (ITS) et l'acces a la contraception. La demarche proposee permettra de mobiliser divers professionnel-le-s implique-e-s dans la mise en uvre d'actions educatives et preventives liees a la sante sexuelle, mais egalement des responsables de politiques, des gestionnaires de programmes et des chercheurs afin de discuter des resultats de PIXEL et de leur implication dans l'action. Cette approche collaborative favorisera la consolidation, l'adaptation, voire le developpement de pratiques fondees sur des resultats de recherche, tout en etant equitables et adaptees en fonction du genre et du sexe.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissemination of evidence-informed care for chronic pain
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC PAIN MANAGEMENT; INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY; INTERGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: More than half of all Canadians suffer from some form of chronic pain during their lives and only 50% of those describe their pain as "controlled". Findings from several studies suggest that the model of health professionals with different expertise working together to provide care has the potential to provide the best care and improved outcomes for individuals with chronic pain and this approach is supported by the Canadian clinical practice guidelines. The Centre of Expertise in Chronic Pain (CECP) in collaboration with several Agences de sante et de services sociaux (ASSS) and Centres de sante et de services sociaux (CSSS) and the Ministry of Health and Social Services (MSSS) of Quebec is implementing and evaluating an integrated and interdisciplinary primary care program for patients suffering from sub-acute low back pain  as part of a larger strategic initiative aimed at building continuums of care for chronic pain. The program is being implemented in the CSSS west-island in Montreal region and will be replicated in three other CSSS.   The purpose of this dissemination grant is to develop a web-based platform that will allow members of the CECP, collaborating clinical sites, clinicians, patients and decision makers interested in chronic pain management to interact and share common tools that can be used to implement evidence-informed care for chronic pain; to expand the knowledge gained and tools developed to other regions; to allow the creation of online communities of practice on chronic pain. We will gradually build on the website the CECP at the MUHC has just started to develop to provide the community with online resources on chronic pain, guided by feedback from end users of the site including clinicians, decision makers, and patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Obesity and Mental Health Workshop
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL FRAMEWORK; CLINICAL PRACTICE; EVIDENCE-BASED CARE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: One in five Canadians will experience a mental illness in their lifetime.  As the second leading cause of human disability and premature death, mental illness constitutes a significant burden of disease in Canada. A parallel epidemic of obesity, currently affecting one in four adult Canadians and as many as one in ten Canadian children is estimated to cost Canadians more than ninety-five billion dollars per year, including health-related productivity losses from absenteeism, foregone taxation revenues, welfare and other payments . The link between these two major health problems affecting millions of Canadians is significant but is often missed. Both obesity and mental illness are highly stigmatized conditions and patients living with these conditions face multiple forms of prejudice and discrimination. This translates into inequities in employment settings, healthcare facilities, and educational institutions, often due to widespread negative stereotypes. The workshop will disseminate research in area of obesity and mental health. The goal of this workshop is to link health professionals working in the field bariatrics with practitioners from the mental illness community as well as practitioners working in primary care. Practitioners will learn the latest evidence based approaches for weight management in individuals with mental illness. They will also have a broader understanding of the link between obesity and mental health and will have practical take-away resources to use in their practice.
