TitreApplicationTitle: Prison Health Now: Protecting Prisoners from HIV and HCV through Prison-Based Needle and Syringe Programs
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; COMMUNITY-BASED COLLABORATION; EFFECTS OF CRIMINALIZATION; EVIDENCE-BASED RESEARCH UP-TAKE; HARM REDUCTION; HIV/AIDS PREVENTION AND REDUCTION; NEEDLE AND SYRINGE PROGRAMS; OVER-INCARCERATION OF ABORIGINAL PEOPLES; PRISONER HEALTH AND HUMAN RIGHTS; WOMEN IN PRISON
Abstract-Résumé: According to the Correctional Service of Canada, approximately 80% of federal prisoners have substance use issues and over 1 in 7 inject drugs behind bars, where sterile injection equipment is not available. As a result, estimates of HIV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) prevalence among federal prisoners are, respectively, 10 and 30 times the population as a whole - with rates considerably higher for women and Aboriginal people. Among Aboriginal women in federal prisons, for example, over 1 in 10 is reported to be living with HIV and almost 1 in 2 is living with HCV. Whereas Aboriginal people make up only 3.8% of the total Canadian population, they represent approximately 20% of federal prisoners, and are thus disproportionately affected by HIV and the lack of access to clean needles.   While the Canadian government has thus far been resistant to prison-based needle and syringe programs (PNSPs), a lawsuit undertaken by four HIV organizations and a former prisoner might result in the courts compelling the prison service to make PNSPs available as a public health measure. In order to be effective, however, PNSPs need to be developed and implemented on the basis of scientific research and practice-based evidence. Evaluations of PNSPs have found them to be an important means of reducing the risk of HIV and HCV infection. Outside of Canada, these programs currently work in a variety of institutions (e.g., men's and women's prisons of differing security levels) and have employed different methods of needle distribution (e.g., peer distribution, automatic dispensing machines, distribution by prison staff or outside agencies).   Prison Health Now, held January 23-25, 2014 at Ryerson University, will bring together national and international stakeholders in the fields of HIV, Aboriginal health, harm reduction, women's health, and prisoner rights to disseminate research, dispel common misconceptions of PNSPs, build new partnerships, and develop practical PNSP guidelines.

Abstract-Résumé: For the first time, the Society for Integrative Oncology (SIO) will be hosting it's international conference outside of the United States. From October 20-22, 2013, over 400 researchers, health professionals, cancer survivors and patient advocates will attend the 10th International Conference in Vancouver, British Columbia. This three day meeting will include keynote speakers, plenaries, oral and poster presentations as well as experiential workshops that will focus on the latest biomedical and clinical research on the efficacy, safety and integration of complementary and supportive care into conventional oncology care settings. Special programming for patient advocates from the US and Canada will also be provided to support translation of evidence into cancer survivorship communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Recognizing World Sepsis Day: An Opportunity to Foster Collaboration and Disseminate Knowledge
Keywords-MotsClés: CITIZEN ENGAGEMENT; INFECTION; KNOWLEDGE DISSEMINATION; SEPSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Sepsis is a systemic inflammatory response of the body to a suspected or proven infection. The Global Sepsis Alliance has recently declared sepsis a global medical emergency. It is estimated that 20,000,000-30,000,000 people suffer from sepsis annually, with 6 million of these being children. In Canada, more than 90,000 people develop sepsis on an annual basis. The mortality rate for septic shock ranges from 25-50 percent for adults and 15-70 percent for children, making this condition both common and deadly.  Sepsis rates are on the rise, particularly in developed countries where people now often survive serious illnesses and live with chronic medical conditions. Sepsis also represents a significant financial burden to the health care system. In 2012, September 13th was declared World Sepsis Day with the goals of increasing public knowledge about sepsis and improving knowledge dissemination and outcomes.  As a group of interdisciplinary and interprofessional pediatric researchers and health care providers we witness the effects of sepsis every day. The CIHR Knowledge Dissemination funding opportunity offers us the chance to take significant action.  Our activity includes 2 components: 1) a Researcher and Knowledge User Engagement Component, and 2) a Citizen Engagement Component. We will conduct a World Sepsis Day Symposium on September 13, 2013 to enhance knowledge exchange among researchers and knowledge users at McMaster Children's Hospital to catalyze development of a collaborative pediatric sepsis research agenda.  The Citizen Engagement Component of our activity consists of a public promotional campaign, which will include a poster contest for children and use of a communications strategy to disseminate knowledge about what sepsis is, how to prevent it, and how to treat it.  Anticipated outcomes include increased research related to pediatric sepsis, enhanced public and knowledge user awareness, and improved uptake of preventative strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Knowledge Translation in Dementia Care: It Takes a Community
Keywords-MotsClés: CAREGIVING; COMMUNITY CARE; DEMENTIA; HEALTH CARE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; POLICY DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Despite a growing commitment to support individuals with dementia and their caregivers to age in place, the need to improve the capacity of health care resources to meet the growing demands of persons with dementia and their families living in the community is a challenge. Now is the time to refine and optimize community dementia care in Canada by investing in knowledge translation (KT) strategies that will promote an evidence-based partnership approach that addresses this challenge. Working collaboratively with dementia care experts across the country, the overall goals of this KT grant proposal are to:  (1) identify specific changes needed in dementia care practices and policies that promote system navigation and partnering in community care; (2) develop a plan for facilitating needed refinements and /or changes in community dementia care; and (3) create opportunities for advocacy and mobilization of practice and policy changes to support the transformation of community dementia care in Canada. By examining the challenges and opportunities within community dementia care, the ultimate aim of this KT Initiative is to enhance community care experiences for persons living with dementia, their family members and formal caregivers.  In order to meet these project goals, the project team plan to host a Transformative Knowledge Translation Workshop to promote dialogue, awareness and knowledge exchange among people with dementia, family caregivers, practitioners, educators, administrators, policy makers and researchers interested in addressing common issues in community dementia care.  Through a socially interactive, inclusive, and action-oriented dialogue, invited workshop participants will use their deepened understanding of the challenges and opportunities in community dementia care to develop or refine policy recommendations and to create successful research and community partnerships that integrate dementia care evidence into policy and practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Needs Assessment to Action: Community participation in KTE of findings from an Ottawa Harm Reduction Community Needs Assessment
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY NEEDS ASSESSMENT; COMMUNITY PARTICIPATION; GAP ANALYSIS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER AND EXCHANGE; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH METHODS; QUANTITATIVE RESEARCH METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: The rates of HIV and hepatitis C among people who inject drugs in Ottawa are 15.8% and 72.5% compared with 5.6% and 62.2% respectively, in the rest of Canada. Ottawa Public Health (OPH) conducted a needs assessment to identify current needs of people who use drugs; existing local capacities and gaps in service provision; and opportunities for expansion and/or increased coordination of services across the city. A range of stakeholders were consulted during design of the study. Ethics approval was received, a literature review of best practices in harm reduction and needs assessments was conducted, and mixed methods were employed to conduct 100 client surveys and 35 key informant interviews and focus groups with a range of key community stakeholders, e.g. harm reduction agencies, police, community associations, housing, addictions. To optimize uptake of needs assessment findings to inform policy and practice, OPH will engage a comprehensive knowledge transfer and exhange (KTE) process, where key stakeholders will be invited to discuss findings, and to identify solutions to fill current gaps in services. Guided by a peer advisory committee comprised of people who use drugs, the research team is proposing: to host a one-day Needs Assessment to Action KTE event to brainstorm solutions and identify recommendations to improve serivces and prevent HIV among people who use drugs; to produce one-page research summaries outlining recommended changes in practice or policy resulting from the needs assessment findings; to present at local, regional and national conferences; and, to submit manuscripts to peer-reviewed journals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing Cardiovascular Quality Indicators for Rheumatoid Arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; QUALITY INDICATORS; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Rheumatoid arthritis affects 1 in 100 people causing joint destruction and disability if untreated. The inflammation from the arthritis also has another important consequence: an increased risk of premature heart attacks and strokes. This risk is 50% higher than in the general population and is a major cause of premature death in patients with RA. Current RA treatment guidelines emphasize early diagnosis and aggressive management of the symptoms from the joints, but do not address who should be screened for heart disease or how. Our goal is to bring together medical experts in heart disease and RA as well as RA patients to develop a set of measures by which we can determine the quality of healthcare being provided to manage heart disease risk in RA. This allows us to also identify where the care being provided needs to be improved. This will be done using state of the art consensus methodology online. This work will also be applicable to other chronic inflammatory conditions associated with increased heart disease risk.

TitreApplicationTitle: Community forum on fathers' involvement in caring for children in South Africa
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN'S WELLBEING; COMMUNITY FORUM; FATHER INVOLVEMENT; HIV/AIDS; SOUTH AFRICA
Abstract-Résumé: In South Africa there is a common perception that men are failing to fulfill their responsibilities to women and children. Statistics that may contribute to this perception include the fact that fewer than half of all children under the age of five live with their biological fathers and nearly one-in-four women have been abused by a male partner in their lifetimes. Yet, we have very limited information on how much (or how little) men are actually involved in caring for children and in supporting their children's mothers. Without these types of it is difficult to turn negative public perceptions into more constructive interventions to improve men's contributions to child and family well-being. Since June 2012, we have been studying the involvement of a group of fathers in caring for their young children in the Western Cape province of South Africa. In this proposal we are asking for funds to host an event to engage the people participating in the study and their families, governmental and non-governmental organizations, and researchers in a discussion of our study findings and the implications they have for future research and advocacy on fatherhood in South Africa.

TitreApplicationTitle: Visualizing Survey Data: Disseminating Results from a Population Health Survey on HIV and AIDS in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADIAN POPULATION HEALTH SURVEY DATA; DATA VISUALIZATION; HIV/AIDS; INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGIES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; RESEARCH DISSEMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: The challenge with disseminating research data is that many people may have great difficulty fully understanding and applying statistical information. The use of data visualization is increasingly recognized as a key knowledge transfer tool to assist in moving this research into action. Instead of searching through pages of tables and graphs, large amounts of information can be understood quickly in a single visual. In 2011, The CIHR Social Research Centre in HIV Prevention (SRC) and the Canadian Foundation for AIDS Research (CANFAR) conducted a survey to gain a better understanding of Canadians' behaviours, attitudes, knowledge and perceptions of HIV and AIDS. This project proposes the creation, piloting and evaluation of a prototype for an online, interactive data visualization tool to disseminate results from the survey. Users will be able to select a research question and view a static image of the data displayed in a map, chart or table format. The target knowledge user for this dissemination activity will be staff of non-governmental organizations (NGOs) working in the field of HIV and AIDS. This project will provide the tools and resources necessary to enable NGOs to understand and use the survey data appropriately to better inform service delivery, grant writing, and program and policy development. This application is also responding to a current gap in community knowledge, by building capacity in non-academic individuals to make sense of the research data. Training materials such as online videos will be used to explain concepts related to interpreting the data. The effectiveness of both the training and dissemination prototype to build capacity and disseminate results will be measured and used to inform further development and research into effective methods of knowledge translation and exchange and research uptake.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding Ethical Responsibility for the Impacts of Medical Tourism in the Caribbean
Keywords-MotsClés: CARIBBEAN; CAYMAN ISLANDS; ETHICS; HEALTH PLANNING; MEDICAL TOURISM; TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
Abstract-Résumé: Medical tourism occurs when patients leave their home countries to intentionally access nonemergency medical care abroad. A number of ethical concerns are associated with medical tourism, including shifts in resources from the public to private health sector in destination countries and undermining health equity. This Planning Grant proposes activities in the Cayman Islands and Trinidad & Tobago to lay the foundation for a new Operating Grant. We focus on these two Caribbean countries because they are actively pursuing medical tourism development, want to attract Canadian patients as consumers, and complement our existing research in the Caribbean. The Operating Grant will focus on developing a model of ethical responsibility of medical tourism stakeholders (e.g., workers, patients, policy-makers) in Anglophone Caribbean destination countries for the potential negative impacts of medical tourism. Working with collaborators, we will undertake on-site research development activities in Nov/13 that will include holding meetings with medical tourism stakeholders and touring public and private health care facilities. In undertaking these activities we will create a network of collaborators to enable the successful development of an Operating Grant examining ethical responsibilities of stakeholders over multiple Caribbean sites. We will also write an article for BMC Health Ethics and prepare a short report, to be circulated widely through our own and our collaborators' networks.  Medical tourism development in the Anglophone Caribbean holds important implications for Canada. Canadian patients are traveling to the Caribbean for private medical care, Canadian companies are investing in the medical tourism sector in the region, and Canada is a signatory to global declarations that work to ensure health equity globally. This Planning Grant will exchange knowledge and ideas across sectors through engagement with medical tourism stakeholders, including our collaborators.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vers la mise en place d'une équipe de recherche sur la santé des hommes.
Keywords-MotsClés: CLIENTELES MARGINALISEES; MASCULINITES; PREVENTION; SANTE DES HOMMES; TRAVAIL SOCIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Les hommes se retrouvent en surnombre pour 14 des 15 principales causes de deces au Canada. C'est bien connu, ils utilisent moins les services preventifs, ils attendent plus tardivement pour demander de l'aide ou faire appel au medecin. Pourtant, ce n'est que recemment que les chercheurs et les intervenants commencent a se preoccuper de la sante des garcons et des hommes. Il n'y a encore aucune structure de recherche (equipe ou centre) clairement dediee a cette question. Nous desirons pallier a ce manque en travaillant a la mise sur pied d'une equipe de recherche canadienne sur la sante des garcons et des hommes. Dans l'objectif de parfaire et d'ameliorer les connaissances sur la relation qu'ont les garcons et les hommes avec leur sante, ce projet souhaite jeter les bases d'une equipe de recherche canadienne orientee sur la sante des hommes. Trois objectifs sont principalement vises par ce projet : 1) Solidifier un partenariat concret entre differents chercheurs francophones de trois provinces canadiennes travaillant sur la sante des garcons et des hommes; 2) Mettre en commun leur expertise et connaissances a ce jour concernant cette population; et partant de la, 3) Definir une programmation de recherche pour les prochaines annees. C'est a partir d'echanges sur les connaissances a ce jour que pourra se definir une programmation visant a mettre en place une equipe formelle de recherche sur la sante des garcons et des hommes. Celle-ci pourra ainsi se fonder sur la reconnaissance des elements prioritaires en matiere de sante et bien-etre des garcons et des hommes, des questions de recherche rigoureusement definies et repondant aux besoins actuels, autant des milieux de pratique que du monde de la recherche.

TitreApplicationTitle: Emerging research and clinical priorities in the detection and management of frailty in older patients across acute care settings.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CARE; CONSENSUS; CRITICAL CARE; FRAILTY; HEALTH OUTCOMES; OLDER ADULTS; OPERATIONAL DEFINITIONS; PREDICTIVE ACCURACY
Abstract-Résumé: Frailty, although often recognized in an older person, is difficult to define. Apparently frail persons are more likely to encounter health problems, particularly during periods of stress (e.g., when hospitalized or receiving complicated treatment and/or surgery). A better understanding of how to detect frailty in older hospitalized patients might help physicians and other health professionals to identify different or new ways to care for such vulnerable patients that would lead to improved health outcomes and quality of life. Our proposed meeting and forum aims to explore opportunities and identify priorities for research on frailty relevant to older Canadians being cared for within acute and critical care settings. We will review the literature to better understand ways to measure frailty in older patients and to see how well the different measures predict important health outcomes. We will bring national research and health experts together for a 2-day meeting to present and discuss the latest research on frailty and to identify the key questions and measures to be included in a new study of older frail patients in acute and critical care. Our 2-day meeting will be held in Calgary, Alberta on September 27-28, 2013. The evening before, our team of research and health experts will host an open public forum with a presentation and discussion on frailty and the care of vulnerable patients in hospital settings. We will announce this forum to all local hospitals and continuing care facilities, post-secondary educational institutions, provincial Aging Centres, and to the Seniors Health division of Alberta Health Services. Our findings may help to identify the pathways that lead to frailty and possible treatment approaches to prevent or slow functional decline and improve quality of life for vulnerable seniors receiving care in the hospital.

TitreApplicationTitle: Weight Bias and Primary Health Care: Creating a Provincial Research Strategy
Keywords-MotsClés: INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; OBESITY; OVERWEIGHT; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT; WEIGHT BIAS; WEIGHT-RELATED ISSUES
Abstract-Résumé: In the face of the urgency associated with the obesity epidemic, it is vital that programs and services aiming to prevent or manage overweight and obesity be systematically assessed for ethical pitfalls such as unintended stigmatization and blame of people who carry extra weight (ten Have et al., 2012). Health care professionals have been found to endorse negative weight-related stereotypes, which in turn affect their weight management practices, contributes to biased treatment of overweight and obese patients, and impacts obese patients utilization of health care services (Puhl & Huer, 2009). However, recommendations to include weight bias awareness and training in the field of obesity have been largely ignored.  Experts in the field of weight bias have made a call to action for future research to focus on the most effective ways to provide training to health care providers about weight bias in order to dispel negative stereotypes and improve client care (Puhl & Heuer, 2010).  Education about appropriate use of language, increasing awareness about the complex etiology of obesity and discussion about effective approaches to weight management are the strategies for training that have shown some promise (Puhl & Heuer, 2009).   Since the implementation of the Alberta Obesity Strategy, consensus has been reached that professional development about weight bias in primary health care will address a high priority and policy-relevant health care service problem. The planning grant will provide the necessary foundation to develop an evidence-informed provincial strategy through the establishment of a research network related to weight bias. The provincial strategy will (a) facilitate interdisciplinary and collaborative research in the area of weight bias, (b) act as a provincial resource for weight bias training to optimize limited resources and reduce duplication, and (c) transfer co-created knowledge to practice by engaging providers in the training and research process.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health outcomes in male survivors of interpersonal violence
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD MALTREATMENT; INTERPERSONAL VIOLENCE; MEN AND BOYS; MENTAL HEALTH; PHYSICAL HEALTH; RELATIONAL ADJUSTMENT; SEXUAL HEATLH
Abstract-Résumé: Exposure to interpersonal violence is a risk factor highly associated with psychological difficulties (anxiety, depression, impulsivity), relational problems (maritalconflict, intimate partner violence), and physical health (cancer, heart disease). Survivors may experience a variety of traumatic events in childhood (neglect, physical, psychological, or sexual abuse, bullying, exposure to domestic violence) and adulthood (revictimization, assault, intimate partner violence). Beginning in childhood and extending across the lifespan, men are more likely than women to experience violence inside and outside the home. Although sexual victimization is more prevalent in women, men are less likely to disclose victimization, thus depriving themselves of health services. Consequently, untreated effects of violence may contribute to the greater health difficulties found in men. Despite an extensive literature relating interpersonal violence to a broad variety of health problems, the precise mechanisms linking violence and the development of health issues remain largely unknown. By what process might exposure to violence lead to health problems in men? How does sex and gender contribute to these outcomes? What bio-psycho-social factors explain the health effects of violence among men and boys? What predicts positive adaptation and resilience among survivors? Building on our previous and current research, we plan to produce a detailed review of the literature and to organize meetings to foster collaborations among researchers from different scholarly domains and universities, identify key research priorities, and provide knowledge translation on the health-related effects and treatment of interpersonal violence in men and boys. This planning grant not only seeks to identify current knowledge gaps in Canadian research, but will also set the stage for the development of ongoing research collaborations that guide health services offered to male survivors.

Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE CHILDHOOD EXPERIENCES; BLENDED RESEARCH METHODS; GEOGRAPHICAL INFORMATION SYSTEMS; HEALTH INFORMATICS; RESIDENTIAL SCHOOLS; SOCIAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: In the USA adverse childhood experiences (ACE) have been demonstrated to have an incredibly detrimental impact on health, social and economic risk. Given that Canadian First Nations communities have been greatly impacted by Residential Schools this study will explore the impact of these schools in a large First Nations community in Northern Ontario. We will adapt the methodology used in the USA study (ACE) and make use of current technology (Electronic Medical Records) to collect data in partnership with the North Shore Tribal Council. Further we will use Geographical Information Systems to portray and analyse the results of our exploration allowing up to visually represent the impact. This research will allow us to better target programs to help communities work towards reconciliation and healing; reducing long term risks and the impact of previous adverse events on future generations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diabetes Management and Education in Older Adults:  The development of a national network and consensus of key clinical and research priorities.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES EDUCATION; DIABETES MANAGEMENT; OLDER ADULTS; TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS
Abstract-Résumé: As the prevalence of diabetes continues to climb along with an aging population, the management of diabetes in older adults will increasingly become an important focus of care.  Several studies have also identified that as diabetes treatment is complex, coupled with functional decline as part of the aging process, older adults often receive less optimal care.  Diabetes management in older adults is even more challenging when there are other medical problems, such as cognitive decline or cardiovascular disease.  This proposal outlines a workshop which aims to engage key stakeholders in discussion to identify priority areas for future development related to improving the clinical management of diabetes in older adults, with the emphasis being on community dwelling older adults.  Additionally, the proposed workshop will serve as a launch for a network of researchers, clinicians and decision makers to share current evidence and to develop national, provincial and local diabetes management and education initiatives for the older population.  The workshop will take place over two days and will comprise individual and panel presentations, as well as small and large group discussions.  Approximately thirty participants, including international leaders in the area of diabetes management and gerontology will be invited to attend.  Other participants will include clinicians, decision-makers, and researchers.  The workshop recommendations and conclusions for future research related to diabetes management in older adults will position Canada as leaders in this area and provide a catalyst for further collaborative work, both nationally and internationally.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and Validation of Sexual Quality of Life Questionnaire for Men-Who-Have-Sex-with-Men with Prostate Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: MEN-WHO-HAVE-SEX-WITH-MEN; PROSTATE CANCER; QUALITY OF LIFE; QUESTIONNAIRE; SEMI-STRUCTURED QUALITATIVE INTERVIEW; SEX; VALIDATION
Abstract-Résumé: Sexual health is an integral part of overall well-being. For prostate cancer patients, the impact of treatments on sexual function is ranked consistently as a major cause of diminished quality of life. There are multiple established assessment tools on sexual well-being for heterosexual men, which have led to scientific knowledge that guides treatment decision. On the other hand, no such assessment tool has been developed for men-who-have-sex-with-men (MSM). Therefore, prostate patients in this group and their physicians are often forced to make important decision without knowing the impact of treatments on sexual well-being.  Our team consists of multiple quality of life experts and oncologists specialized in prostate cancer, and we hope to develop a standardized assessment tool for sexual well-being in the MSM prostate cancer population. This tool will cover all areas of sexual quality of life, from emotional well-being, relationship, desire, and satisfaction, to erectile function, frequency, and physical comfort during sexual activity.  According to Statistics Canada, Prostate Cancer Canada, and Cancer Statistics Canada, over 25,000 men were diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2012 and over 150,000 men were living with a prostate cancer diagnosis in the last 10 year. Assuming 5% of the Canadian male population is MSM, each year over 1,200 MSM are newly diagnosed with prostate cancer and over 7,500 are living with this disease.   The assessment tool developed in our proposed study should become the essential instrument on which all future sexual quality of life studies in the MSM prostate cancer population will be based.

TitreApplicationTitle: Augmentative and Alternative Communication Outcomes for Kids Workshop (AAC OK Workshop)
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY; AUGMENTATIVE AND ALTERNATIVE COMMUNICATION; CHILDHOOD DISABILITY; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HEALTH SERVICES; INTERDISCIPLINARY
Abstract-Résumé: Some 12,000 Canadian children with disabilities between the ages of 5 and 14 years need assistive devices to communicate. However, 51% of these children had none of their communication device needs met, while another 20% had only some of their needs met. This is worrying because unmet communication needs can severely hinder a child's ability to participate meaningfully in everyday activities. Neglecting communication needs can lead to marked delays in school achievement, and foster social isolation in young people with disabilities. Yet, the effectiveness of special communication devices and services on the lives of children is unclear. It is critical that research priorities be set now to improve access to effective communication products and services for this young, diverse, and vulnerable segment of the Canadian population. A 2-day research planning workshop will be held with expert clinicians and researchers at Holland Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital in Toronto - Canada's largest rehabilitation hospital for children. The purpose of the workshop is to: 1, share the latest research evidence relating to the effects of special communication interventions for children with complex communication needs; 2, gather clinical service perspectives on related AAC research priorities; and, 3, engage clinicians and researchers in future applied research to address one or more the priorities identified. This crucial, integrated knowledge translation event will identify pressing research questions to address the most vexing and least understood areas of assistive technology outcomes in children and youth with chronic disabilities. The proposed activity will yield new clinician-researcher collaborations and catalyze a clinically-rooted program of applied research in augmentative and alternative communication.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimizing Adverse Drug Event Reporting within a Provincial Medication Information System to Improve Pharmacovigilence and Inform Pharmaceutical Policy
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE DRUG EVENTS; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; ETHNOGRAPHY; FOCUS GROUPS; HEALTH INFORMATION SYSTEMS; HIERARCHIAL TASK ANALYSIS; IMPLEMENTATION SCIENCE; PHARMACOVIGILANCE; SEMI-STRUCTURED INTERVIEWS; WORKFLOW ANALYTICS
Abstract-Résumé: An adverse drug event (ADE) is an injury which results from the use of drugs. Every year ADEs cause around 700,000 visits to emergency departments (EDs) and are one of the main reasons for unplanned hospital admissions and death in Canada. A large number of ADEs which are potentially avoidable require hospitalisation and could be due to poor recording by clinicians and communication about ADEs between care providers and also they result in high costs to the Canadian healthcare system. The main goal of proposed post-doctoral research is to support the development of a new electronic system for reporting ADEs which will be integrated into PharmaNet, which is an electronic medication usage system for British Columbia. I will conduct this research project in 3 phases. Phase 1 will examine the reasons why ADEs in EDs are not being recorded and reported in a draft electronic system currently used by clinicians. This will enable me to prepare for Phase 2 of this research project which is to examine the workflow patterns in EDs and directly observe the ways that ADEs are identified, recorded and reported by ED healthcare personnel. These results will be used to further develop the ADE reporting system and an ADE reporting framework for ED settings that will be applied to this research project, and could be applied to other medication usage systems and other jurisdictions. Phase 3 will identify and develop the data fields required for ADEs to be reported accurately in PharmaNet and this will result in an updated version of the ADE reporting system. Therefore, I will evaluate this updated version with clinicians and pharmacists in order to determine if it is appropriate for ADE reporting and if any further modifications are required. Once optimized, the ADE data can be linked to Canadian administrative health databases and used by stakeholders such as health researchers to support research into drug safety and effectiveness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Planning the implementation and evaluation of an ECHO project (Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes) to improve primary care provider management of chronic pain and reduction of prescription opioid misuse in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; ARTHRITIS; CHRONIC PAIN; FIBROMYALGIA; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; PRESCRIPTION OPIOID MISUSE; PRIMARY CARE; STRATEGIC PLANNING
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain affects one in five adult Canadians. It consists of conditions like back pain, arthritis and fibromyalgia. Chronic pain is usually managed by primary care physicians with very little access to pain clinics and addiction medicine. There is a need for education and networking of primary care providers to better manage chronic pain.  This grant is to support a group of primary care providers, pain specialists, addiction medicine, educators and policy makers to organize a plan for implementation of an innovative model to manage chronic pain in Ontario. The Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes (ECHO) model was developed by the University of New Mexico (UNM) Health Sciences Center as a platform for both delivery of services and outcomes research. The main objective of the ECHO program is to improve the access of minorities and other underserved populations to best-practice care for chronic health conditions. The ECHO program increases the accessibility of populations outside urban areas to the specialized medical resources of academic medical centers. Using state-of-the-art telehealth technology and clinical management tools, ECHO trains and supports primary care providers in the community to develop knowledge and self-efficacy on a variety of diseases not usually considered within their scope of practice.  This grant will enable members of the core team in Ontario to travel to UNM to attend the orientation on the ECHO model. It will also allow the strategic planning for activities and workflows for the implementation of the ECHO model in Ontario. Lastly, our group will potentially apply to a funding opportunity to assess the effectiveness and efficiency of the ECHO model to manage chronic pain in Ontario.

TitreApplicationTitle: Resuscitation in Motion 2014: Building networks of excellence to advance resuscitation science research,development and practice
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATIVE RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MENTORING; NETWORKING; RESUSCITATION SCIENCE; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Resuscitation science is concerned with saving the lives of people who suffer cardiac arrest, shock and other life-threatening and time-sensitive emergencies. More than 45,000 Canadians suffer a cardiac arrest each year. Rates of survival are still very low, despite advances in medicine. Resuscitation science is a continually changing field of study, across disciplines, level of research and practice. Yet, there are only three senior and two young clinician scientists with dedicated research programs in Canada. It is important to advance the science by improving the spread of knowledge and developing more highly skilled resuscitation researchers. These are people who can, for example, conduct large clinical trials to develop solid evidence. To this end, the Collaborative Program in Resuscitation Sciences (CPRS) was launched at University of Toronto in 2011. The program contributes to improving health systems, resuscitation strategies and care in prehospital and in-hospital settings. It trains graduate students and supports young investigators to conduct quality research in respect of these outcomes.The CPRS held its first scientific meeting, Resuscitation in Motion (RiM), in May 2012 at the Li Ka Shing Knowledge Institute in Toronto. The one-day gathering was attended by 85 delegates from Canada, the US and Australia. These included clinician scientists, research fellows, young investigators, graduate students, and public and private stakeholders. A persistant challenge identified by participants was the lack of networks of excellence to make resuscitation science competitive for large operating grants.  The CPRS intends to make this the main focus of the next RiM meeting, planned for May 2014. About 100 participants from a variety of sectors and disciplines will attend the meeting. The aim is to develop productive networks of excellence that can identify and take forward resuscitation research projects with strong potential for success.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gaining Insight to Brain-Behaviour Relationships: Developing a Neuroepidemiology Study Using the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITIVE FUNCTION; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; MOBILITY; NEUROIMAGING; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) is the largest, national, long-term study of adult development and aging in Canada. The goal of the CLSA is to assemble a cohort of 50,000 Canadians aged 45 to 85 years to be followed for at least 20 years. The longitudinal design and extended follow-up will provide a unique opportunity to examine health transitions and trajectories over time, with the goal of better understanding the complex interplay among the vast array of determinants of health. The CLSA provides an exceptional platform for research on aging, especially since it allows embedded ancillary studies.   Of the 10 comprehensive CLSA data collection sites across Canada, two will be in Greater Vancouver, BC. Specifically, starting in 2013, the Brain Research Centre (BRC) located on the University of British Columbia (UBC) campus will be a data collection site for 1,500 participants who will be tracked at three-year intervals. This provides a unique opportunity for BC researchers to collaborate nationally and internationally to develop and initiate embedded ancillary CLSA studies.  Our core research team, which includes researchers and clinician-scientists from both Canada and United States, has a strong background and long-term interest in defining brain-behaviour relationships. Hence, we propose a series of specific activities to promote ongoing collaboration over the next 12 months with the aim to develop an ancillary CLSA study to gain novel insight into longitudinal changes in brain-behaviour relationships in adult development and aging. We will collectively aim to submit an operating grant to CIHR in 2014. Critically, the application of neuroimaging markers to the CLSA will provide an unparalleled model of translational neuroepidemiology in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Moving Mountains: Addressing HIV/AIDS in Northern BC through Community Based Research
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; HIV/AIDS; NORTHERN BRITISH COLUMBIA
Abstract-Résumé: Northern British Columbia (BC) has had limited success in addressing HIV/AIDS. The region lacks suitable human and financial resources to engage the social determinants of health that underlie such a persistent, communicable disease. This circumstance is not new for a northern, rural and remote region. Many regions face similar resource issues, including limited human and financial means, reflected in a gap between needs and adequate programming and research. Prince George, the largest urban centre in northern BC, has been host to many researchers and research projects. However, the region, and similar northern, predominantly rural areas, have not directly benefited from these projects. Many research projects are not inclusive of the region, as many researchers do not attempt to incorporate issues of community engagement indicative of northern, rural and remote regions. As a result, we propose to create greater collaboration among regional participants, researchers, knowledge users (KUs) and those located in urban centres. The purpose of the planning meeting is to assemble leaders in HIV/AIDS research and service delivery, policy-makers, and PHAs in northern BC, with the specific intent, to map current research projects and established collaborations with in Northern BC.  Further, we aim to plan the next steps for future collaboration through knowledge exchange and the identification of research questions and emerging issues among people living with HIV/AIDS (PHAs), researchers, and knowledge-users involved in HIV research, while keeping the coordination and provision of HIV health services in northern BC paramount in our focus.

TitreApplicationTitle: Caractérisation expérimentale du liquide interstitiel d'une tumeur mammaire et rôle des facteurs angiogéniques dans le micro-environnement
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESE; BEVACIZUMAB; IRM; LIQUIDE INTERSTITIEL; MICRO-ENVIRONNEMENT; METASTASE; VASCULARISATION; VEGF
Abstract-Résumé: Le cancer demeure une des maladies les plus complexes connues de l'homme. En plus des cellules cancereuses elles-memes, l'environnement tumoral joue un role crucial dans la croissance et la reponse au traitement, mais reste peu etudie. Encore moins connu, mais pourtant critique pour la tumeur, est le liquide interstitiel (LI). Ce liquide dans lequel baignent les cellules de la tumeur contient plusieurs molecules importantes qui vont regir tous les aspects de son developpement, croissance, etendue et reponse au traitement. Nous croyons qu'une meilleure comprehension du LI nous permettra d'ameliorer les traitements disponibles, particulierement ceux visant la croissance des vaisseaux sanguins, qui sont associes au transport du LI. Nous proposons donc, a l'aide de technique d'imagerie medicale non-invasives, de caracteriser le LI dans un modele de cancer mammaire chez la souris ainsi que son role dans le developpement des vaisseaux sanguins associes a la tumeur. Nous allons egalement recolter ce fluide dans la tumeur a l'aide de chambres de drainage miniatures implantees dans l'animal. Nous pourrons ainsi en determiner le contenu en plusieurs facteurs interessants pour notre etude tels que le facteur de croissance vasculaire epithelial (VEGF). VEGF est une cible therapeutique tres interessante dans plusieurs cancers et nous nous promettons d'evaluer dans quelle mesure son role passe par son transport dans le LI.  Nous allons egalement administrer des traitements aux animaux cancereux visant specifiquement le VEGF. Ces medicaments nous permettrons d'associer ou non les changements de concentration en VEGF du LI avec les effets anti-cancereux du traitement. Cette etude promet de jeter un regard nouveau sur une composante sous-etudiee du developpement d'une tumeur, le liquide interstitiel. Les parametres que nous tirerons de notre etude nous permettront de mieux comprendre la maladie et paveront la voie a de meilleurs traitements contre le cancer chez l'humain.

Abstract-Résumé: This application requests funding for planning activities required to prepare a submission for Partnerships for Health Systems Improvement (PHSI).  The proposed PHSI will address pregnancy risk in Aboriginal women from Labrador and Nunavut and identify solutions to strengthen the local health care system. Using the determinants of health such as her physical and social environments, we will develop a comprehensive model of risk for each community and overlay it with geographic mapping to visualize pockets of communities with good and bad outcomes. In preparation for the PHSI submission, we require funds for literature review, costing for technological requirements for geographic mapping, consensus on analytic framework and meetings to build partnerships with key stakeholders, local academics and community members.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Subventions de planification - Annonce de priorités : maladies infectieuses et immunitaires

TitreApplicationTitle: Supporting PHA service providers at the individual, organizational, and systemic levels
Keywords-MotsClés: KNOWLEDGE SYNTHESIS; PARTNERSHIP DEVELOPMENT; PEER AND PROFESSIONAL SUPPORT; PHA EMPLOYMENT SUPPORT; PHA EMPOWERMENT; RESEARCH DEVELOPMENT; STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT AND CONSULTATION
Abstract-Résumé: The advance of effective anti-retroviral treatment for people living with HIV/AIDS (PHAs) has enabled significant improvement in health status and outcomes, and PHAs are now increasingly engaged in the workforce. In these roles, PHAs undergo a shift along the continuum of service recipient to service provider. This shift can have psychosocial consequences and identity implications that are often overlooked or misunderstood. We propose to bring together key stakeholders from across Canada to share knowledge and regional priorities in addressing the needs of PHA service providers and to form a national knowledge exchange network. Our objectives are to: 1) Synthesize knowledge on regional research and practice issues and share the experiences of PHAs to build capacity on the issues affecting self-care and access to support for PHAs in service provider roles; 2) Identify the gaps in knowledge and establish priorities for regional and national research agendas, programming, and policy development to support PHA service providers; 3) Develop a national knowledge exchange network to engage a broad range of stakeholders to share learning about current regional research and projects aiming to address support for PHAs in service provider roles; and 4) Bring researchers, community members, and service providers together at a face-to-face Think Tank to develop a national collaborative intervention research initiative and to establish a plan to disseminate the findings. This planning grant would support a review of the current literature and a program scan; development of a national knowledge exchange network; a two day face-to-face research Think Tank to consolidate current knowledge and to develop a collaborative intervention research initiative; and dissemination of a final project report and submission of a process paper and research synthesis paper for publication in peer reviewed journals.

TitreApplicationTitle: CLSA-TECH:  Extending the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging Platform Through Environmental and Person-based Technologies
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CLSA; CONSENSUS WORKSHOP; DATA; LONGITUDINAL; PLANNING; SENSORS; TECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Aging populations in Canada and worldwide demand innovative approaches to ensure people can live and age well across and within societies. Information and communications technologies (ICTs) have recently emerged as a potential solution to improve the health, safety and social participation of seniors. These technologies utilize environmental and person-based (i.e. body-worn) sensors, and communications networks to provide important information on the health and care needs of seniors. As well as clinical applications, ICTs offer huge opportunities for gerontological research, particularly in respect to the collection of real-time data on the daily lives and health behaviours of older individuals.  The goal of CLSA-TECH will be to exploit the research opportunities afforded by ICTs through a partnership with the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) to collect a longitudinal real-time data set that will include both sensor and health data from the homes and communities of older people.  This data set will be collected, developed, and stored with the intention of it becoming part of the CLSA platform that researchers can use in their own research programs.    Preliminary discussions with various groups and researchers involved in the ICT field, gerontology researchers, and current members of the CLSA have indicated strong interest and support for the idea of CLSA-TECH.  The aim of this Planning Grant will be to formally extend these initial consultations and to begin concrete planning of a major new Canada-wide research initiative that will have a global impact.  Our planning activities will comprise consultation with key stakeholders and members of the current research community on technology and aging in order to identify and reach a consensus on an optimum pathway for future research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Levelling the playing fields: Will the provision of risk and natural play opportunities provide more equitable playgrounds?
Keywords-MotsClés: BOYS HEALTH; DESIGNING FOR PLAY; GENDERED PLAY; NATURAL PLAY ENVIRONMENTS; RISKY PLAY
Abstract-Résumé: There are detrimental effects on child development when too many restrictions are placed on children's outdoor risky play and access to natural environments. Despite this, recent generations of children have seen their natural play environments substituted with pre-fabricated play spaces that optimize safety and risk reduction with little regard for children's develop¬mental and play needs. Furthermore, evidence indicates that if children, especially boys, do not have sufficient outdoor risky play opportunities, they will seek them elsewhere, potentially in more dangerous environments. Thus, the current dominant approach to playground design-which is intended to minimize risk-eliminates healthy and supervised risky play opportunities, paradoxically placing children at increased risk of injury.    We are developing a new interdisciplinary research initiative called CHILD'S Play (Creating Healthy Inspiring Landscape Designed Spaces for Play), which ultimately aims to develop recommendations for playground design that incorporate developmentally-necessary and gender-neutral risky play in natural environments. The first aspect of the collaboration is this planning grant, Levelling the playing fields, which examines whether risky play opportunities with natural elements provide (i) more equitable playgrounds for all genders overall and (ii) more developmental opportunities for boys, in particular. Our proposal for this CIHR planning grant will seek to understand the existing body of work in this area and develop intersectoral partnerships and international collaborations to develop a research proposal for CHILD'S Play.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités : Epigénétique
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the BTB/POZ domain protein Miz-1 in the development of B-cell lymphoma
Keywords-MotsClés: B-CELL LYMPHOMA; C-MYC; EPIGENETIC REGULATION; GENE REGULATION; MIZ-1
Abstract-Résumé: More than 7,500 Canadians suffer from B-cell lymphoma (Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma; NHL), a disease which affects particularly the lymphatic and the immune system. One subtype of NHL is the B-cell Burkitt-type lymphoma (BL), which is very aggressive and affects several tissues. In North America, this type of cancer accounts for 1-2% of all lymphoma. In Africa, BL is the most common childhood cancer. Patients with this malignancy show abnormal rearrangements in their chromosomes inducing the overexpression of the protein c-Myc. This protein is involved in cell growth and is associated with the development of several cancers. The protein Miz-1 that is under investigation in the present proposal binds to c-Myc and regulates its function. We hypothesize that Miz-1 is required for the development of BL. In our study, we will use mouse models which develop tumors similar to those observed in patients with BL. We will ablate the function of Miz-1 in these mice to verify if this protein is important for the development of the disease and whether the ablation could influence the development or progression of the disease. Since abnormal regulation of chromatin is often associated with cancer development, we will also assess the ability of Miz-1 to modulate the structure of chromatin in normal and malignant B cells. The identification of Miz-1 as an important collaborator of c-Myc in the development of BL will be an important step in the development of new, targeted therapies. In fact, if Miz-1, as our preliminary data suggest, is required for the emergence of c-Myc dependent B-cell lymphoma, it could be possible in the future to target this protein with small molecules to favor regression of these tumors in lymphoma patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genomic regulation of hippocampal postnatal development and neuron activity by H2A histone variants and their post-translational modifications is influenced by early maternal care
Keywords-MotsClés: CHIP-SEQUENCING; CHROMATIN; EPIGENETICS; HIPPOCAMPUS; HISTONE VARIANTS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; NEURODEVELOPMENT; QRT-PCR; STRANDED RNA-SEQUENCING; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: Fetal and early child development is marked by profound changes in brain structure and organization. As a child matures, the brain undergoes dramatic growth as neurons form new connections and eliminate superfluous ones. Such alterations in brain physiology result from a 'programmed' maturation or in response to environmental stimulation. If errors occur during this process, developmental disorders can result. What drives this brain maturation during early development is of great interest. Scientists have found that variations in gene expression can influence the brain's malleability. Genes are a 'blueprint' that contains all of the information needed for the body's proper development and function. Genetic information is contained within a 'code' known as DNA. DNA is located in virtually every cell of the body. During development, it is critically important for genetic information to be accessed at precise times and places. How is genetic information controlled? Proteins, known as histones, organize the DNA and control how genetic information is 'read' or 'turned off'. The aim of this research is to understand how a subset of histone proteins, known as variants, control genetic information and brain maturation during early development. It is of interest to understand how histone variants and chemical modifications of the variants regulate neuron activity in response to stimulation. I have shown that the amount of histone variants varies during early development, which may reflect their unique roles in regulating brain function. Histone variants are also responsive to activity-dependent stimulation of neurons. If we understand the fundamental processes that govern healthy development, we will better know how the early childhood environment can impact positive brain development. Such knowledge will facilitate the delivery of therapeutic interventions to ameliorate the effects of adverse early childhood conditions or neurodevelopmental disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Age-Related Cognitive Decline in Indigenous Peoples: Developing International Strategies to Improve Diagnosis and Care
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; ACCESS TO HEALTH SERVICES; COGNITIVE ASSESSMENT; CULTURALLY APPROPRIATE HEALTH SERVICES; INDIGENOUS AGING; INTERVENTION; NEURODEGENERATION IN AGING; RESEARCH PLANNING
Abstract-Résumé: Our planning grant will bring together researchers and knowledge users who work with Indigenous populations in Canada, the United States and Australia, and who are active in the field of aging, dementia and cognitive impairment research. The grant will facilitate meetings, discussion and knowledge translation concerning priorities for research, early lessons learned in each country, and the development of best practice research models to address health service needs for age-related dementias in Indigenous peoples. Discussions to take place in the winter of 2014 will focus on the process of developing culturally appropriate screening and clinical care interventions for cognitive impairment in Indigenous peoples. This international meeting will lead to the development of an international collaborative research partnership between Indigenous health researchers and health workers focused on age-related cognitive decline in Canada, Australia and the United States. Information shared at this meeting and the early stages of research planning will subsequently be shared with Indigenous communities and a wider circle of knowledge users in each of the three countries in order to further develop a feasible research strategy.  Our goal is to develop funding proposals to be submitted to foundations such as the Alzheimer's Societies and Associations in each country and to national granting agencies to support  research for international intervention research aimed at improving diagnosis, care and outcomes for Indigenous populations affected by age-related dementias.

TitreApplicationTitle: Framework for Action to Create Social Support Networks for 60+ Gay Men in BC
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; AIDS; HIV; INFORMAL CAREGIVING; OLDER GAY MEN; SOCIAL CAPITAL; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS; SOCIAL SUPPORT; SOCIAL SUPPORT NETWORK; TRANSGENDER MEN
Abstract-Résumé: A team of health researchers, health service providers, and others experienced in senior gay men's health will meet to review new data about health challenges faced by senior gay men in BC. Focusing on social support networks and the health benefits that belonging to such networks fosters, the team will pool their expertise to develop a Framework for Action outlining the best ways for the public health community to proceed in creating new social support network options for senior gay men. BC organizations that promote health, provide health services, and partipate in health policy production have expressed interest in applying the knowledge from such a framework for action. Their interest stems from recognition of unique challenges senior gay men face in creating and belonging to such networks, and no other undertaking in BC at present to bolster social support network options for senior gay men. The proposed Framework for Action is essential in BC to senior gay men's increased access to and belonging in social support networks, their experiencing the health benefits that result from belonging to such networks, and their improved maintenance of functional autonomy and reduced reliance on formal BC healthcare services.

Abstract-Résumé: The main activity support by this planning grant is a 2-day planning meeting to be held in Toronto on November 21-22, 2013. This meeting will include an estimate of 30 invited participants representing various stakeholder groups (e.g. fathers, institutions) as well as international researchers in the area of fathers' mental health. Prior to this event collaborators have been identified through a literature review of fathers' mental health or through a consultation process with initial applicants and knowledge users. Selected participants will be informed of the participant list as well as receive the necessary documentation in advance of the meeting.   The 2-day meetings will consist of a series of large and small group discussions including keynote addresses from top international researchers. Knowledge and ideas will be exchanged so that all participants can appreciate the potential opportunities for further research in paternal mental health in Canada.   In order to prioritize these research questions, a discussion of clinical needs and feasibility will address the strengths and limitations with each category of research questions. A computerized ranking process will be explained to all participants and will be used in order to prioritize these questions for further research.   The primary objective of this activity is to produce a detailed strategy of Men's Mental Health: Fathers - Phase 2. In order to meet this objective the planning meeting will establish the Fathers' Mental Health Research Network; prioritize the research questions and make a clear Action Plan to advance this project onto its next phase.  This project is designed to identify the mental health risks, illnesses and treatments required to advance the care of fathers with mental illness. In doing so, innovative models of screening, assessing and treating fathers will not only improve their quality of lives, but also significantly affect the health of children and families.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités : maladie de Huntington
TitreApplicationTitle: Implication de miR-132 dans la pathogénèse de la maladie de Huntington
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BLOOD BRAIN BARRIER; HIGH SENSITIVITY FLOW CYTOMETRY; HUMAN BLOOD SAMPLES; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; IMMUNITY; IN VITRO STUDIES; LEUKOCYTES; MICROVESICLES; MUTANT HUNTINGTIN
Abstract-Résumé: To date, the problem in Huntington's disease (HD) has been thought to be due to nerve cells producing their own, genetically coded for, abnormal mutant huntingtin protein (mHtt), which then causes them to dysfunction and die. In recent years, there has been evidence to suggest that other cells, such as those involved in inflammation, may also contribute to the loss of neuronal cells. However, such cells have only been thought of as having indirect effects and not central to the disease process. Recently, though, we have found in HD patients - who were transplanted with fetal tissue designed to replace cells lost to the disease process - that the abnormal mHtt could be seen in the transplant. This mHtt could only have got into the transplant from the patient as the grafted tissue was from unaffected donors. This unique observation forms the basis of this application as we now investigate the theory that mHtt can be transferred between cells from circulating immune cells that can get into the brain via leaky blood vessels. If true, this new theory would have wide ranging implications for HD, and similar diseases, and bring with it a totally new therapeutic approach to this currently incurable condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Redesigning the management of responsive behaviours for persons living with dementia
Keywords-MotsClés: DEMENTIA; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; RESPONSIVE BEHAVIOURS; SELF-MANAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The current proposal is designed to request funding for activities that would ultimately result in the identification of key elements to be incorporated into a CIHR grant application by a multi-disciplinary, inter-sector team working on better management of behaviours for persons living with dementia. We propose an in-depth review of relevant literature, best practices, and programs to consolidate the evidence and gain a better understanding of the triggers and management of behaviours for persons with dementia.  We also propose regional/national meetings that would bring together a multidisciplinary team of investigators, clinicians, persons with dementia, caregivers, care providers in long-term care, policy makers, and members of dementia-related organizations. The purpose of these proposed meetings would be to (1)capitalize on each team member's expertise to redefine self-management that focuses on change at various levels (intrapersonal, interpersonal, institutional, community, policy) rather than solely within the individual, (2)explore the potential for further national and international collaborators, (3)promote knowledge exchange, and (4)draft an application to a funding opportunity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Les maladies chroniques chez les aînés: un portrait du domaine scientifique au Québec pour la planification stratégique du Centre d'Excellence sur le Vieillissement et les Maladies Chroniques du RUIS McGill (Réseau Universitaire Intégré de Santé McGill).
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYSE BIBLIOMETRIQUE; ANALYSE DES RESEAUX; GERIATRIE; MALADIES CHRONIQUES; PLANIFICATION STRATEGIQUE; SCAN ENVIRONNEMENTAL
Abstract-Résumé: Le Centre d'Excellence sur le Vieillissement et les Maladies Chroniques (CEVMC) a ete cree en 2012 pour apporter un soutien clinique concret aux etablissements et aux cliniciens du RUIS McGill (Reseau Universitaire Integre de Sante de l'universite McGill). Le RUIS McGill a la responsabilite clinique de 63% du territoire du Quebec et dessert 1,8 million d'habitants.  Le CEVMC compte jouer un role cle dans l'implantation des meilleurs modeles de prise en charge medicale au sein des hopitaux de courte duree, en lien avec la premiere ligne et les autres partenaires du reseau, dans le domaine conjoint des Syndromes Geriatriques et des maladies chroniques. Dans le cadre de sa planification strategique, le CEVMC aimerait mieux apprecier l'activite scientifique qui se deroule dans son champ d'interet et les experts qui y evoluent, dans le RUIS McGill et au Quebec. L'activite proposee se deroule en deux parties. La premiere consiste a dresser une cartographie du domaine scientifique conjoint de la geriatrie et des maladies chroniques au Quebec par le biais d'une analyse bibliometrique de la litterature scientifique pour identifier les experts, les reseaux d'acteurs et les themes majeurs de recherche qui forment les ressources dont le CEVMC pourra disposer pour remplir son mandat. La deuxieme consiste en une serie de rencontres ou le Comite strategique pourra confronter l'offre de ressources (les resultats de l'analyse bibliometrique) a al demande du milieu (les resultats de l'analyse des besoins en cours au niveau du CEVMC)de facon a disposer d'options strategiques pour mieux orienter son action, definir ses activites de formation et de recherche et optimiser la mise en place d'equipe de projets d'intervention. Le projet propose contribuera a aider le CEVMC et le RUIS McGill a catalyser les ressources disponibles au Quebec pour developper des interventions innovantes et de qualite pour les aines souffrant de maladies chroniques.

TitreApplicationTitle: Supporting Older Adults and Caregivers in Transitions Between Health Services: Planning Grant
Keywords-MotsClés: CAREGIVERS; HEALTH SYSTEM; HEALTHCARE UTILIZATION; OBSTACLES; OLDER ADULTS; STRATEGIES
Abstract-Résumé: As we age, we are more likely to face health challenges that require the use of various types of health services including home and community-based services, physician and hospital-based services, and residential housing and care services. Our long-term research plan is to examine strategies that older adults and their caregivers use to navigate between these three types of health services and identifying obstacles that they face in doing this. We want to learn how these strategies and obstacles influence what services are used, how they are accessed and how easy access to services influences quality of life. We will spend a year conducting activities that will help us develop a research proposal. We will first review and summarize research already completed on our topic. This summary will be shared in consultation sessions with older adults and their caregivers, healthcare providers, and policymakers. These people will provide input into what research questions are most urgent to ask and how best to do this research. After receiving and processing this input, our research team will write a research proposal, primarily during a two-day grant writing meeting where we will refine the research questions and methods that we will use, identify how to recruit research participants, create a plan to analyze the data we will collect, develop a timeline for the research, and create a budget. We will mentor undergraduate students and graduate students/postdoctoral fellows as employees and as part of their academic programs. The results of our research will help identity how to help older adults and their caregivers in accessing and navigating appropriate health services. This can help to keep older adults healthier by helping them use the right services at the right time and place, while supporting their transitions from one service to another. This can reduce healthcare costs by reducing the number of admissions and re-admissions to services like hospitals and nursing homes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relevance of vascular adaptations to exercise training in improving quality of life in aging populations: transitioning from the laboratory to the community
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATIVE GRANT PROPOSAL; EXERCISE TRAINING; OLDER ADULTS; VASCULAR CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular fitness is one of the best predictors of independent living in the elderly. Thus, ensuring higher levels of fitness is critical in the aging population. Several studies have demonstrated improvements in cardiovascular fitness subsequent to exercise training interventions in older individuals. However, the vascular aspect and the sex-specific component of these positive adaptations remain poorly understood. Our laboratory at Western University is a leader in the study of the cardiovascular benefits of exercise training in the elderly. Recently, we have established a close working relationship with a group at the University of Verona, who are also research and exercise prescription leaders in their community. Both laboratories are producing some of the most relevant data related to exercise training adaptations in the elderly and the use of these interventions to prevent or mitigate the detrimental effects of aging. Additionally, both laboratories run their own outreach exercise training programs so that research is immediately translated into action in the community. This collaboration resulted in shared supervision of students, visiting scholars to both centres, and dissemination of scientific work.  Although we are proud of what we have attained thus far, these accomplishments are just the foundation of a long-lasting collaboration, which needs the planning and execution of grant proposals to obtain the financial support to complete our work together. To move to this next step, we need to organize "face to face" meetings including the leading members of each team to design a complete research project and submit grant proposals. This project will focus on the beneficial effects of exercise training interventions (exercise as "medicine") on vascular responses in the aging population. The goal of this group is to "bring" the scientific knowledge generated through research to the community that will eventually benefit for this advancement in knowledge.

TitreApplicationTitle: Establishing a Durham Region Resuscitation Research Collaborative
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ARREST; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PUBLIC HEALTH; RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE; RESUSCITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Sudden cardiac arrest is a common but potentially reversible cause of death.  Understanding factors that contribute to improved survival from cardiac arrest can lead to a revised research agenda and more effective knowledge translation (KT).  Multicentre KT  projects have attempted to focus on various links in the 'chain of survival' beyond the actual cardiac arrest event however; knowledge gaps remain and represent an important area of inquiry. This project intends to explore the creation of a community-based resuscitation research collaborative that lengthens the chain of survival beyond the scope traditionally considered, incorporating broad stakeholder representation to establish research priorities and leverage regional health care and academic strengths. The Collaborative will also explore factors earlier in the chain of survival, such as primary prevention incorporating public health strategies.  Key is the inclusion of patient and family member representation during the formation and lifespan of the collaborative. With a strong tie to KT science, the proposed collaborative will attempt to directly improve outcomes from cardiac arrest in the Ontario Durham Region, and share lessons learned with other jurisdictions in Canada.   This grant proposal aims to secure funding to support a one-day meeting in early Fall 2013 to establish the resuscitation collaborative network, linking researchers, knowledge users and community stakeholders.  Funding will support meeting activities and environmental scans.  At the meeting experts with demonstrated success in establishing resuscitation collaborative networks will be asked to share best practices and contribute to the network development plan.  The meeting is intended to be a working, constructive experience that will generate collaborative groups, identify research/KT issues, prioritize potential projects, identify gaps/resources, and lead to relevant and impactful work to improved patient outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing Interdisciplinary Knowledge Exchange Capacity between Canada and China on Imaging Outcomes for Hemophilic Joints
Keywords-MotsClés: ANKLES; CHILDREN; ELBOWS; HEMOPHILIA; INTERNATIONAL RESEARC; JOINTS; KNEES; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; ULTRASOUND
Abstract-Résumé: In hemophilia recurrent joint bleeds result in progressive arthropathy which leads to long-term physical impairments. To avoid arthropathy the clinician must have sensitive tools to detect minimal joint changes. Imaging techniques such as ultrasound (US) and MRI can play a critical role in the diagnosis of joint bleeds in hemophiliacs. There are currently no standards on how to acquire and interpret imaging findings on hemophilic joints. In order to effectively treat hemophilic joints we need to develop standardized imaging protocols and reading methods to support shared decision making between hemophilic patients and health care providers. The SickKids (Toronto, Canada) group has previously developed imaging protocols and scales for assessment of hemophilic joints. The next steps are to develop: (1) Consensus with another hemophilia care centre regarding imaging protocols and methods to be used as guidelines in clinical practice and research across the world. (2) A plan of research to evaluate the feasibility of using ultrasound and MRI as outcome measures in hemophilic arthropathy followed by a validation research project, preferentially conducted in countries with different health care systems such as Canada and China. (3) A knowledge translation strategy to disseminate results from consensus conferences and educational materials. The Toronto group plans to conduct the 3 aforementioned steps conjointly with the Beijing Children's Hospital, China group through this project which has the ultimate goal of improving clinical management of hemophilic patients across the world. This can be accomplished once the results of a larger research project to validate the proposed imaging tools become available. The Toronto and Beijing groups plan to conduct such validation study in the future upon successful completion of this project which will assess the feasibility of this endeavour and will generate consensus guidelines for future clinical and research applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assurer la sécurité et l'autonomie à domicile des personnes âgées atteintes de démence suivant un séjour en milieu hospitalier
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTINUUM DE SOINS ET SERVICES EN SANTE; DEMENCE DE TYPE ALZHEIMER ET AUTRES MALADIES APPARENTEES; MAINTIEN A DOMICILE; TRANSFERT DE CONNAISSANCES
Abstract-Résumé: Au cours d'une hospitalisation, les personnes atteintes de demence sont souvent evaluees pour connaitre leur capacite a realiser certaines taches de la vie courante (par exemple, preparer un dejeuner). Cette evaluation aide a identifier les services necessaires, une fois a domicile. Les personnes atteintes de demence risquent toutefois d'eprouver plus de difficultes a realiser des taches dans un milieu qu'elles ne connaissent pas. Inversement, les risques de se blesser ou de se perdre peuvent etre sous-estimes lors de l'evaluation a l'hopital. Par consequent, il est essentiel de preciser a quel point les evaluations realisees en milieu hospitalier permettent d'estimer adequatement les risques et l'aide dont les personnes atteintes de demence ont reellement besoin a domicile. La presente proposition donc vise a reunir dans le cadre d'un symposium une trentaine de participants concernes par cette problematique (chercheurs canadiens et internationaux, gestionnaires, decideurs, cliniciens, representants d'organismes communautaires, de proches-aidants et de personnes atteintes de demence en debut d'evolution). La tenue de cet evenement permettra de: 1) construire une equipe representative ralliant des intervenants issus de disciplines et de milieux diversifies; 2) faire etat des connaissances relatives a cette problematique afin de mieux comprendre la complexite des enjeux qui y sont associes; 3) preciser des objectifs de recherche prioritaires et atteignables; 4) faciliter l'echange de connaissances entre les producteurs et les utilisateurs de connaissances. Ce symposium sera precede d'une serie de consultations preliminaires menees par le chercheur principal aupres d'utilisateurs de connaissances des regions de Montreal, Sherbrooke, Quebec et Ottawa. Ces echanges meneront a l'elaboration et a l'implantation d'un programme de recherche visant a s'assurer que les services offerts aux personnes agees atteintes de demence correspondent davantage a leurs besoins a domicile.
