TitreApplicationTitle: Testing the feasibility, acceptability, and effectiveness of HORYZONS: A new on-line intervention to prevent relapses in youth diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL HEALTH INFORMATICS; E-MENTAL HEALTH; FIRST EPISODE PSYCHOSIS; IMPOVING ACCESS AND QUALITY OF CARE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MENTAL HEALTH SERVICE DELIVERY; MIXED-METHODS RESEARCH; PARTICIPATORY APPROACHES; PSYCHOSOCIAL INTERVENTIONS; RELAPSE PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Youth diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis are at high risk of relapse, even when they are receiving specialized care. Relapse involves a worsening of symptoms (e.g., hallucinations, disorganized thinking), a decline in daily functioning, and often hospital admission (83% hospitalized at 7.5 years). These relapses contribute to the development of chronic disability which is of serious concern as psychosis is associated with schizophrenia, one of the top five leading causes of disability in the world for individuals aged 15 to 44. Relapses are preventable. There is strong evidence that relapse prevention therapy, which involves education and support, can significantly reduce relapse in this population. However, this treatment is rarely provided because it is resource intensive (e.g., requires therapist time and training), and also because it is challenging to maintain face-to-face engagement of youth in treatment. Thus, it is important to find ways to provide this therapy in accessible and cost-effective formats. Using information and communication technologies is one promising avenue to address this challenge. Our research involves testing the benefits of a new, on-line, interactive, and clinician-supervised intervention that aims to reduce relapse and improve recovery of youth diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis. The intervention is also accessible through smartphones and tablets. This is a first Canadian study on the use of web-based and mobile technologies to support the provision of specialized services for youth with psychosis. It brings together an international group of researchers with expertise on the use of technology in health care, youth mental health, and relapse prevention. The results will improve our understanding of the usefulness, challenges, and benefits of delivering relapse prevention therapy through an on-line format, and provide important information on whether this type of intervention warrants wider implementation in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: From Embers to Flames: Identifying strategies of resilience and mental health among inner-city Aboriginal children and youth
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL MENTAL HEALTH; CHILD AND YOUTH HEALTH; COMMUNITY HEALTH PSYCHOLOGY; CULTURAL PSYCHOLOGY; INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE; MEDICAL ANTHROPOLOGY; QUALITATIVE METHODOLOGIES; QUANTITATIVE METHODOLOGIES; RESILIENCE; SOCIAL ACTION
Abstract-Résumé: Mental illness and distress enact a significant toll on Canadian children and youth, yet are unevenly distributed throughout the country. Current estimates suggest that 15% of young Canadians between the ages of 10 and 19 cope with anxiety, depression, addictions or other disorders, while estimates among Aboriginal populations are twice the national average (35%), with addictions and suicide being five to six times the national average. Additionally, the Saskatchewan 2010/2011 Student Health Survey found that First Nations and Metis children and youth from low-income, inner-city neighbourhoods of Saskatoon were significantly more likely (17.2%) than city averages to report poor mental health status, depressed mood symptoms, and suicide ideation in the past 12 months. These mental illness and addictions inequities signal a crucial need for focused research among Aboriginal children and youth. The operating principle behind this study is that the resources, knowledge, and capabilities required to address the mental illness and addictions inequalities of Aboriginal children and youth are already present within inner-city contexts and young people themselves. Hidden resources of resilience represent small embers that can, through the intervention of informed strategies, be fanned into flames. These resources need to be identified for the benefit of this population. A mixed-methods approach will be employed. The Child and Youth Resilience Measure (CYRM-28) will be administered to quantitatively identify sources of stress, risk, and resilience. Qualitative stories will also be generated from the most resilient children and youth to determine their successful coping strategies. The results of this research will identify sources of resilience and positive mental health strategies that can inform early intervention theory and policy to promote the mental health and wellness of Aboriginal children and youth in Saskatoon and other Canadian urban contexts.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Psychosocial Approach to Fostering Improved Mental Health Among Aboriginal Canadians
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL CANADIANS; COLONIALISM; CULTURAL CONTINUITY; EXPLICIT ATTITUDES; IMPLICIT ATTITUDES; MATERIAL CIRCUMSTANCES; MENTAL HEALTH; SOCIAL SUPPORT; STEREOTYPES; SUBJECTIVE WELL-BEING
Abstract-Résumé: The determinants of Aboriginal people's mental health are complex and multi-faceted and research on these topics must take an inter-disciplinary and multi-method approach that acknowledges that forced assimilation and oppression have hindered cultural continuity and fostered in some Aboriginal people negative stereotypes about their own group. Recent psychological studies show that the gut automatic associations we have and our deliberately expressed attitudes are predictive of mental health indicators and a range of health behaviours. The objective of the proposed research is to gather qualitative and quantitative data from Aboriginal Canadians on the automatic associations and deliberately expressed attitudes they have about their own group, their sense of cultural continuity and social support, and a variety of measures of mental health. The research aims to examine the interaction between these variables and to create, and administer, training tasks aimed at ameliorating automatic associations and deliberately expressed attitudes Aboriginal Canadians have about their own group, and, as a result, foster improved mental health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating the Impact of Moral Arguments on Societal Values for Orphan Drug Coverage
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNICATION; DISCRETE CHOICE EXPERIMENT; DRUG COVERAGE; HEALTH POLICY; MORAL DILEMMA; ORPHAN DRUGS; PRESCRIPTION DRUGS POLICY; RARE DISEASES; SOCIETAL VALUES; SURVEY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Orphan drugs for rare diseases are often very expensive, with the cost of treating a single patient reaching up to $1 million per year. These drugs rarely meet the usual thresholds for efficacy or cost-effectiveness used in health technology assessment, however, which poses a moral dilemma for policy-makers, since the same funds used to treat one individual with a rare disease could provide less costly medications for many more Canadians.  Since taxpayers must ultimately bear the costs of funding these treatments through the public insurance system, empirically estimating society's willingness to pay for expensive treatments for rare diseases, despite the significant opportunity costs, is a key element of democratic decision-making in this area.  Using an online survey of 3,000 Canadians, we will explore societal preferences for orphan drug funding by presenting respondents with different scenarios in which provincial health authorities must decide whether or not to fund a specific treatment through the provincial insurance system.  The scenarios will vary based on characteristics like the cost of the treatment, the severity and prevalence of the disease it targets, and, crucially, the types of arguments used by proponents and opponents of funding that particular treatment.  This survey will provide an estimate of societal willingness to pay for the treatment of rare diseases under conditions that approximate the real-world context in which Canadians might learn about the policy challenge posed by orphan drugs.  Knowledge generated will facilitate more informed orphan drug policy decisions consistent with the value that society places on the treatment of rare diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interactions between food security, traditional food consumption, nutrients, contaminant exposure and anemia among Canadian Inuit
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEMIA; ECOSYSTEM APPROACH TO HUMAN HEALTH; FOOD SECURITY; INTERNATIONAL POLAR YEAR INUIT HEALTH SURVEY; INUIT; LEAD; MERCURY; NUTRITION
Abstract-Résumé: Inuit in the Canadian Arctic disproportionately experience food insecurity compared to the general Canadian population. Moreover, this food insecurity is associated with poorer nutrient status and health. The Inuit are going through a nutrition transition, reflected by a decrease in traditional foods consumption and an increase in the consumption of market foods. While traditional foods are important sources of energy, protein and nutrients, environmental contaminants (eg. heavy metals and persistent organic pollutants) have been identified in these foods and in human blood. Nutrient deficiencies and heavy metal exposure have been associated with anemia, an important public health concern among Inuit. A recent study suggested that the dietary sources of heavy metals may also be major sources of iron. This project will investigate the interactions between food security, traditional food consumption, nutrients and contaminants, as well as their impacts on anemia in the Canadian Inuit. This project will explore regional, community and household vulnerability to food insecurity, describe mercury and lead exposure and nutritional status according to the food security status, and describe the prevalence of anemia and its determinants, looking at nutrients and lead exposure. The data is from the International Polar Year Inuit Health Survey, a cross-sectional survey of Inuit adults living in the Arctic. This research will further our knowledge on the dynamics between the environmental and socio-economic determinants of food security, traditional food consumption, nutrients and contaminants exposure, and provide further knowledge on how these interrelations are associated with anemia. The results will contribute to the development of strategies to reduce food insecurity, maximize nutrient intake and minimize exposure to contaminants, in order to guide stakeholders and governments in their discussion of policies and programs to improve health in the Arctic.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inuit Knowledge Translation: Community-controlled, culturally-sensitive research with Inuit youth on experiences of violence, health effects and coping mechanisms, engaging Inuit youth in developing a research-based, health promotion campaign on issues of violence using social media
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL METHODOLOGIES; CULTURALLY-SENSITIVE HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTH PROMOTION OUTREACH USING SOCIAL MEDIA; INUIT YOUTH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MENTAL AND PHYSICAL HEALTH EFFECTS OF VIOLENCE; PARTICIPATORY ACTION RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Violence is a common experience for many Inuit youth, and so is self-violence/self-harm (such as cutting, binge drinking, suicide). Research shows that physical or sexual abuse in childhood is a risk factor for self-harm later in life. The experience or witnessing of ongoing sexual and physical violence can predispose individuals to substance abuse, low self-esteem, mental and physical health issues, and to themselves becoming perpetrators of violence.   Pauktuutit Inuit Women of Canada is the national organization representing Inuit women in Canada. Pauktuutit chose Inuit youth, violence and health as a research priority, with a view to use the research results to create a health promotion outreach campaign to Inuit youth on this issue. The project is guided by an Inuit advisory team from beginning to end. This means Inuit organizations, elders and youth will have substantial input into the research plan, research instruments, recruitment of participants, interview techniques, analysis and dissemination of results, and the use of the results in designing a health promotion outreach campaign. Forty male and female Inuit in Ottawa between the ages of 18 and 21 will be interviewed to document past experience of violence; health and other effects of violence; family history; awareness of messages about violence; social networks; awareness of help available; experience of help available; coping mechanisms for experiencing and witnessing violence; use of social media; and ideas about what kinds of social media messages could get positive messages to Inuit youth, specifically about ending violence and seeking help for violence. Sex and gender differences in responses will be noted and this information used in designing different social media strategies to reach females and males if necessary.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Kahnawake School Diabetes Prevention Project as a community 'social movement'. Taking into account the community level outcome of a health promotion program in an Indigenous community.
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY HEALTH; COMMUNITY-BASED; DIABETES PREVENTION; EVALUATION; HEALTH PROMOTION; INDIGENOUS HEALTH; INTERVENTION RESEARCH; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: The Kahnawake Schools Diabetes Prevention Project (KSDPP) was created in 1994 by a team of Kahnawake community members (a Mohawk community located near Montreal) and university academics to promote healthy lifestyles and prevent type 2 diabetes in Kahnawake. Since the start of KSDPP, many studies have attempted to evaluate the effects of the project on diabetes and on the lifestyles of the targeted population. These evaluations have shown modest or no improvements on physical activity, diet, weight and diabetes. Changing behaviors leading to better health is a complex and long-term task that needs a variety of efforts directed not only at individuals, but also at their social and physical environments. For this reason, health promotion projects do not always translate directly into lifestyle and health improvements. Some researchers believe that health promotion projects targeting communities have to become social movements in order to properly succeed in changing people's behaviors. A social movement permeates a society's organizations, institutions, and policies (also named 'structures'), and conveys a particular message (also called the 'framing discourse') hinging on values to mobilize people. My hypothesis is that KSDPP has evolved into a community mobilizing movement, which is a first step in the path leading toward health improvement. During my project, I want to explore which kind of structures (organizations, institutions, policies) KSDPP has penetrated and what is the particular message that KSDPP uses to mobilize people. This study is important because it encourages reflection on health promotion effects in terms of community mobilization. Results will be helpful to the community by pinpointing structures, messages, arguments and values that could be used to further mobilize the actors and the community toward diabetes prevention. Knowledge emerging from these results will be relevant to other health promotion projects as well as their evaluations.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de Recherche - Annonce de priorités : lésions cérébrales traumatiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Environmental enrichment for minimizing neurodegeneration and improving memory outcomes in chronic moderate-severe traumatic brain injury in young and older adults
Keywords-MotsClés: MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI); MEMORY INTERVENTION; MODERATE TO SEVERE TBI; SPATIAL MEMORY; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY; VERBAL MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, more than 16, 000 people suffer a traumatic brain injury each year. These people must cope with the social isolation, poor employability, and chronic memory deficits that result from this injury. Recent studies have found that even after people with traumatic brain injury leave the hospital, parts of their brain may continue to deteriorate. One area of the brain that is vulnerable to this progressive deterioration is the hippocampus, a brain structure involved in memory. Recent research suggests that patients who engage in more cognitive activities show less deterioration of the hippocampus. It is unknown, however, whether the prevention of this deterioration leads to better memory function. The purpose of the proposed study is to examine whether regular and intensive mental stimulation can offset the progressive deterioration of the brain and improve memory function in these patients. In the proposed study, there will be three groups of patients. One group will receive a cognitive training program in which they must engage in several hours/week of challenging but enjoyable cognitive activities, including memory exercises. We will examine whether the brains of these individuals are healthier (i.e., less brain shrinkage; better memory) than individuals with similarly severe brain injuries who did not go through the intervention. Given the growing evidence that progressive brain deterioration as a result of traumatic brain injury may be contributing to poor long-term outcomes, this study aims to offset these problems in order to reduce the suffering of patients and their families, and decrease the enormous economic costs of TBI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Methods of Cognitive Assessment in a Preclinical Model of Frontal Traumatic Brain Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; COCAINE SELF ADMINISTRATION; OPERANT BEHAVIOURAL ANALYSIS; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major problem worldwide. Each year, more than 10 million people suffer a TBI. Sadly, despite over 25 years of research and many clinical trials, to date, there are no pharmaceutical treatments for TBI. This has been attributed in part to a lack of preclinical assessment in animal models. Surprisingly, although impaired cognitive function and memory are some of the most pervasive deficits following a TBI, only one type of task is typically used to measure cognition in animals (a test of spatial learning known as the Morris water maze). This leads to a simplistic view of the multifaceted phenomenon of cognition. To address this concern, the current series of studies seeks to develop improved methods for assessing cognition after TBI in rats. After delivering a frontal TBI, we will first assess the most basic type of learning that occurs as rats are rewarded for the learned behavior of pressing a lever according to different schedules of reward delivery. Once performance on these basic schedules has been established, more complex tasks will be evaluated in which we measure how motivation, temporal judgment, attention and impulsivity are affected by TBI. The final portion of this study will utilize these tasks to evaluate the relationship between substance abuse and brain injury by examining how injured rats self-administer cocaine, followed by what happens during forced abstinence and finally look at reacquisition of self-administration (a model of relapse). The outcome of this research could influence how pharmaceutical agents are evaluated before going to clinical trials. Expansion of testing into these domains for pharmaceutical evaluation, could help reduce the potential of an ineffective drug proceeding on to clinical trials. Ultimately, research of this kind - on cognitive behavioral processes after frontal TBI- could make the drug-discovery process more cost-efficient and lead to better outcomes for patients who suffer from TBI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Pharmacology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disorder in the world. As old age is the major risk factor, a dramatic rise in the incidence of AD is anticipated. The pathogenic amyloid beta 42 generation is a promising target for a causal therapy. The research of the applicant is geared towards amyloid beta 42-lowering gamma-secretase modulators (GSMs), which are a subclass of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and to unravel their exact mechanism of action. The goal is to generate mechanistic, pharmacological and methodological knowledge that will foster the development of novel, more specific and effective strategies for prevention, diagnosis and therapy.

Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Social medicine
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of the Canada Research Chair in Approches communautaires et inégalités de santé is to improve public health systems capacity to address social health inequalities by fostering the sustainable development of Population Health Intervention Research (PHIR), a science of solution. The program consists in: 1) conducting participatory research to contribute evidence on process and outcomes concerning the public health strategy to support community development to reduce social health inequalities; 2) creating a global community of practice of university-community partnerships to study innovations in governance and practice of PHIR; and 3) developing the science of PHIR for the study of complex interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chaire de recherche du canada en neurophysiopharmacologie de la douleur chronique
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: La douleur chronique est une douleur qui ne sen va pas. On estime cependant quaujourdhui 20 à 30% des Canadiens souffrent de douleur chronique. Une meilleure connaissance des mécanismes physiopathologiques à l'origine de ces douleurs rebelles est donc essentielle pour pallier la souffrance de ces millions de personnes en attente dun traitement efficace. Le programme de recherche du Dr. Philippe Sarret met lemphase sur la découverte de nouvelles classes danalgésiques non morphiniques pour une prise en charge plus efficace et personnalisée de la douleur chronique. En particulier, nous essayons de mieux comprendre le mode de fonctionnement dune famille de récepteurs membranaires, les Récepteurs Couplés aux Protéines G (RCPGs) dans le contrôle de la douleur.

TitreApplicationTitle: RNA Biology and Cancer Genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: What causes cancer? Attempts to answer this question by studying gene sequence were faced with limited success. This research program is taking a different approach to understand cancer biology by focusing on RNA processing and degradation. We use yeast as a model system to understand how changes in RNA processing and stability influences cell growth and study human tissues to define the contribution of RNA splicing to cancer outcome and drug resistance. In the coming years we will determine how splicing and RNA degradation regulate gene function and how this regulation influence cancer outcome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intestinal Immunophysiology in Health and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: The inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), Crohns disease and ulcerative colitis, are life-long, incurable disorders affecting 1/160 Canadians: the cause of IBD is unknown.  Dr. McKays research is aimed at advancing knowledge of the process of IBD that will result in improved therapies and ultimately contribute to a cure.  He focuses on interactions between immune cells, epithelial cells and bacteria in normal gut function and how perturbations of this association can cause injury and disease.  Specific projects: affects of inflammatory mediators on epithelial barrier function; the role of macrophages in IBD; and use of parasitic helminths to explore anti-inflammatory pathways and mechanisms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Cardiolipin Metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiolipin is an important fat found in cells and is required to produce energy. In the hearts of children with Barth Syndrome and in heart failure patients the amount and type of cardiolipin is altered.  Dr. Hatch proposes to examine if restoring the proper amount and type of cardiolipin will reverse the pathology associated with these diseases. In addition, he proposes to examine if changes in cardiolipin serve as a marker for the development of Type 2 diabetes in children. Finally, he proposes that cardiolipin may play an important role in transport of compounds across the blood brain barrier.

Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Howell is a pioneer in the area of the molecular mechanisms associated with chronic bacterial infections. As a Canada Research Chair in Structural Biology and Biochemistry, she has provided new insights into how bacteria manufacture the device they require to attach to a surface and the molecules they use to communicate with each other, as well as how they produce the matrix material that encapsulates them and protects them from antibiotics and detergents. She has obtained significant funding for these studies and her discoveries have appeared in prestigious international peer-reviewed journals and have helped train highly skilled, next generation investigators.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiac Regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Following a heart attack, damaged heart tissue is replaced with scar tissue. The result is compromised heart function that often leads to heart failurea major cause of death in North America. Led by Dr. Ren-Ke Li, the current research proposal is focused on the development of promising new technologies including cardiac stem cell implantation, a bio-engineered cardiac patch and new enhanced biomaterials for the repair and regeneration of damaged heart tissue. In addition, Dr. Li has identified age as a factor in cardiac repair, and will combine his pioneering cell transplantation techniques with new gene therapy techniques to improve outcomes for aged patients.

Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Like computers, our cells depend on operating systems to drive normal functions. Thegene expression programs are the source code our cells rely on to play theirbiological functions. Corrupted programs trigger diseases. This research proposaluses embryonic stem cells to study how cellular operating systems are regulated.We recently discovered that SMC complexes connect the chromosome architecturewith regulation of the gene expression program. SMC complexes subunits aremutated in cancers and developmental syndromes including the Cornelia de LangeSyndrome (CdLS), an autosomal dominant syndrome. Defining how the cellularoperating system is regulated is crucial to understanding defective gene expressionprograms in diseases such as CdLS.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Statistical Genomics: Integrating genomics and proteomics data through the use of instrumental variables estimators
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Novel technologies that can measure genes and proteins in the blood open new venues for biomedical investigations that can result in minimally-invasive clinical tests to diagnose and monitor various diseases. The proposed research plan offers appropriate computational approaches to find genes and proteins that indicate the progression of a disease (biomarkers). The identified blood-based biomarkers can be used to develop new clinical tests to improve patients care and decrease costs in the Canadian health system. Dr. Cohen Freue has been working in the development of proteomic clinical tests that can replace biopsies to monitor organ rejection in transplantation.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Placental development and maternal-foetal health
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The placenta is the essential organ of pregnancy that feeds the baby and regulates pregnancy related changes in the mother's body. Diseases of the placenta affect up to 10% of all pregnancies and have no treatments other than the often premature delivery of the baby. My work will explore the origins of these diseases by developing stem cell based models. I will identify the changes in gene expression and cell types that occur in placenta disease. I will make mathematical models to identify the causes of these diseases to develop new treatments resulting in healthier mothers and children.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Lung Transplantation
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: A shortage of healthy donor lungs combined with post-surgery complications has contributed to lower success rates of lung transplantation when compared to other organs. Dr. Marcelo Cypel has played a large role in the development of the normothermic Ex vivo Lung Perfusion (EVLP) system, in which donor lungs are kept at normal body temperatures outside the body and evaluated for function before transplantation. Cypel proposes to use EVLP to simultaneously treat lungs for specific injuries and identify gene signatures that will help clinicians better assess injured donor lungs and ultimately increase the donor pool available for this life-saving procedure.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Vascular Cell and Molecular Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Blood vessels are lined by endothelial cells. These cells play a vital role in maintaining a healthy cardiovascular system. For example, in response to tissue injury, endothelial cells promote blood vessel growth (i.e. angiogenesis) to promote tissue repair. However, endothelial cells also contribute to disease. Angiogenesis can feed a growing tumour and dysfunction of endothelial cells can lead to heart disease. The research program of Dr. Fish will identify the molecular mechanisms that control endothelial cell biology. The long-term goal is to identify novel ways to manipulate endothelial cells as a means to prevent and treat human disease.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Diabetes and Vascular Complications.
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Vascular complications are the major causes of morbidity and mortality in patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. However, the mechanisms underlying the progression of vascular complications are not completely understood. Toxic glucose and lipid metabolites are the most important causal factors of vascular cell death. My research program is interested in finding new therapeutic targets that inactivate survival signals in vascular tissues affected by diabetes such as the kidney, lower limb and heart. I believe that my research will be essential to develop new strategies to prevent and treat vascular complications in type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: biomodélisation et traitement des maladies neurodégénératives
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: Les causes et le processus de développement des maladies neurodégénératives demeurent largement inconnus, car il nexiste que peu de modèles pour les étudier efficacement.  En comprendre les causes serait une étape essentielle pour aider à trouver de nouvelles stratégies thérapeutiques pour les traiter et les guérir.  Ma recherche vise le développement de modèles cellulaires et animaux dont le but est de mieux comprendre ces maladies.  Une approche multidisciplinaire combinant le génie tissulaire, lutilisation de différents modèles animaux (souris et poisson zébré) et létude déchantillons de tissus humains sera idéal pour caractériser et modéliser les mécanismes physiopathologiques de ces maladies.  Cela ouvrira de nouvelles perspectives thérapeutiques pour le traitement de ces maladies incurables.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Natural Product Drug Discovery
Keywords-MotsClés: Pharmaceutical products, Health
Abstract-Résumé: This research program will identify novel bioactive compounds with enormous potential for medical and economic benefits to Canada. A cutting-edge strategy will identify natural small molecules, polyketide and nonribosomal peptides, known for their therapeutic utility. This research will diverge from what is known and apply powerful strategies to identify new natural products with unprecedented structures and actions. New infrastructure, along with prior investments at McMaster University in chemical biology, high-throughput and high-content screening, are the necessary components to identify new medicines.  These discoveries may lead to spin-off companies focused on discovering novel, cost-effective therapeutic agents of great need to Canadians.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Pharmaco-Epidemiology and Vaccine Evaluation
Keywords-MotsClés: Preventive medicine, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: The ultimate goal of Dr. Mahmuds research is to find effective ways to prevent disease. He will be studying whether certain widely used medications (e.g., aspirin, cholesterol lowering drugs, and anti-depressants) could prevent major cancers, such as prostate, colon and cervical cancer. The results of this research could improve our understanding of how cancers develop, which in turn could lead to the development of more effective drugs. He will also carry out studies to assess the effectiveness and safety of vaccines against diseases caused by the human papillomavirus such as cervical cancer.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Aging, Chronic Disease and Health Promotion Interventions
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Identifying effective interventions to improve quality of life for older adults is a public health priority because of the unprecedented aging of the population. Most likely to benefit from such interventions are older adults with multiple chronic conditions (MCC) like diabetes and arthritis, representing 33% of community-living adults aged 65 or older. Seniors with MCCs make up 40% of reported health care use among seniors in Canada. This research programs objective is to develop and evaluate the effectiveness of new, innovative interprofessional nurse-led health promotion interventions aimed to reduce the burden of chronic conditions among community-living older adults with MCC.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: culture collaborative en droit et politiques de la santé
Keywords-MotsClés: Social structures and relationships, Hospital structure and organization of medical care
Abstract-Résumé: Lobjectif de la Chaire est de mieux comprendre et de modéliser le défi de la collaboration au sein des systèmes de santé, un enjeu ayant des retombées concrètes et notables sur leur viabilité. En mettant laccent sur la nécessité de saisir les impératifs et les facteurs de coopération afin datteindre des objectifs de justice, defficience, dadaptabilité et de réactivité des systèmes de santé, la Chaire modélisera une culture collaborative originale qui guidera les professionnels de la santé, les acteurs corporatifs, les administrateurs et les décideurs publics dans leur compréhension des interactions interpersonnelles et institutionnelles au sein du système de santé. La Chaire explorera le rôle du droit et des politiques publiques dans latteinte dobjectifs de collaboration. La dialectique de la collaboration fédére les acteurs autour dun enjeu commun positif plutôt que de mettre laccent sur les ratés, les antagonismes et la régulation punitive dun système; la cohérence et la mobilisation sont des outils fondamentaux en politiques publiques.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Ergonomics and Musculoskeletal Health
Keywords-MotsClés: Agriculture, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Musculoskeletal disorders are the most common work-related injuries in many industries. Despite agriculture being identified as highly dangerous, injury prevention strategies for these workers are relatively undeveloped. The objectives of this program are to identify, measure, and reduce workplace exposures that contribute to musculoskeletal disorders in high-risk agriculture occupations such as commodity farming and animal production. This program will provide enhanced understanding of the mechanisms that result in musculoskeletal disorders; create opportunities for injury prevention; incorporate participation with industry, clinical, and policy stakeholders; and contribute significantly to the health of working Canadians in agriculture and other industries with similar exposures.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Characterization of Neurological Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: Preventive medicine, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis is a highly prevalent disease which affects over two million people worldwide. This research is particularly important to Canadians, since Canada has one of the highest rates of multiple sclerosis in the world. The main aim of this project is to implement the latest scientific technologies to define this disease at a molecular level. The identification of genes and mutations implicated in the development of multiple sclerosis will lead to a better understanding of the biology of the disease which will result in novel therapeutic avenues to better treat, halt and potentially cure multiple sclerosis.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Comparative Genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Preventive medicine, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Transcription factor-DNA binding controls the specificity and timing of gene expression. However, the impact of disrupting transcription factor-DNA interactions in human disease is largely unknown. Starting with hemostasis and cardiac-related diseases, we will ask whether disease-related genes and pathways harbour pathological regulatory variants. Our novel approach will identify and functionally characterize regulatory variants by combining high throughput targeted human DNA sequencing, reporter gene assays, and evolutionary comparisons of experimentally determined transcription factor-DNA interactions. Identifying pathological alterations in human regulatory DNA will lead to new diagnostic tools for pediatric diseases and address outstanding questions in human gene regulation and epigenetics.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Signal Transduction in Diabetes Pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes affects more than 3 million people in Canada and significantly increases the risk of developing cardiovascular diseases and cancers, which together account for more than 60% of all deaths in Canada. Therefore, there is an urgent need for increased research in type 2 diabetes and its long-term complications. The proposed studies will provide insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of insulin resistance and its associated complications. Findings from these studies may facilitate development of effective prevention and therapeutic strategies, which will ultimately improve public health.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: the Genetics of Obesity and Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: We are currently facing epidemics of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Once thought to be adult diseases, these are now being seen in children. Inherited (genetic) factors strongly affect the risk of an individual developing these diseases, but we do not yet know what most of these genes are. This research program seeks to identify these genetic factors. By determining what these genes are, we can understand how they affect the development of obesity or diabetes. This will help us uncover new means of treating these diseases to improve human health and lessen their impact on the health care system.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Environment and Health Risk Communication
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: When situations arise that could lead to potential losses or risks to public health and safety, government, industry, and scientists must communicate those risks to the public. Dr. Driedgers research is about understanding how these risks can be better communicated when they are uncertain, and how stakeholders can better communicate with each other in risk situations. In practice, for example, this research can help policy-makers when deciding what treatments to pay for to maximize positive health outcomes for Canadians, or it can help clarify what information the public needs to make informed decisions about health risk situations and protective behaviours.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Ethnicity and Health
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: The foreign-born population of Canada may total 28% of the population by 2031. The resulting super diversity presents challenges for public health policy and health care provision. The wider socioeconomic determinants of health significantly shape access to and navigation of health services.  Understanding these influences is central to Dr. Gina Higginbottoms research program in Ethnicity and Health, through which she collaborates with researchers, government and immigrant support agencies, community organizations, and community members. She currently leads five research projects related to ethnicity, immigration and maternal health and plans several collaborative projects of high relevance to priority areas of governmental and funding agencies.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Cardiovascular Physiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Age-specific incidence rates for cardiovascular disease have fallen by half over the past 30 years, as the result of better prevention and treatments based on growing knowledge of vascular biology. However, an additional dramatic effect on cardiovascular disease incidence and mortality is unlikely to be achieved without the development of entirely new therapeutic and preventive strategies. My research will deepen our understanding of the molecular basis for cardiovascular disease. I will investigate the pathways whereby blood flow confers its atheroprotective effects, which is important to better appreciate the therapeutic potential of currently available drugs and to identify new target molecules.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Genetics of Stem Cell Hematopoiesis
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: Increasing evidence indicates that global chromatin remodeling events underlie normal and leukemic hemopoiesis but the mechanisms involved have been unclear. Dr Lessard is a young principal investigator at Institut de Recherche en Immunologie et en Cancerologie (IRIC). Her Tier II Chair in Molecular Genetics of Stem Cell Hematopoiesis was created in 2007, based on a program aimed at deciphering the role of SWI/SNF-like BAF chromatin remodeling complexes in the developing hemopoietic system and in leukemia. Her most recent work indicates that subunit exchange within a novel family of hemopoietic BAF complexes orchestrates normal and leukemic hemopoiesis. Strikingly, she finds that some subunits are essential for HSC function, while others are required later in the hemopoietic hierarchy for the development of specific lineages. Perhaps most provocatively, her studies indicate that BAF subunits are combinatorially assembled into functionally specialized complexes in the developing hemopoietic system and in leukemia and that adroit targeting of subunits specifically expressed in leukemic stem cells (LSCs) may have potent and specific therapeutic effects.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Health Services and Systems Research
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Increasing economic efficiency and competitiveness
Abstract-Résumé: During my CRC tenure starting in July 2008, I have: a) developed a specialised program of health services and systems research including system decision analysis modeling and preferences measurement methods, b) applied these methods to generate new translational and transformative knowledge to inform stakeholder organizations and healthcare professionals about how to improve access, effectiveness and efficiency for a sustainable healthcare system, c) created and established a strong research program with a successful track record of Tri-Council peer-reviewed funding, a strong international research network, and excellent opportunities for highly qualified personnel and trainees at the graduate and postdoctoral level.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Neurochemistry of Major Depressive Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: This chair will focus on investigating treatment resistant depression and preventing major depressive disorder (MDD).  Treatment resistance and prevention are important because MDD is now the leading cause of death and disability in moderate to high income nations, according to the world health organization.  Key directions are identifying biological subtypes of clinical depression, facilitating treatment development to target the specific biological subtypes, determining environmental mechanisms that lead to brain changes of clinical depression and initiating development of protective natural health products.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Centrosome biogenesis and Function
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Centrosomes are important for chromosome segregation during cell division and in theformation of cilia and flagella. Without centrosomes, chromosomes would not segregate properly to each daughter cell during division, giving rise to aneuploidy, a condition that causes diseases such as cancer. Furthermore, cilia would not form leading to many pathologies including polycystic kidney disease. The goal of our work is to understand how centrosome duplicate, grow and participate in the formation of mitotic spindles and cilia. This work will lead to a better understanding of centrosome biogenesis and how centrosome defects can lead to cancer formation and cilia-related diseases.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Health Services Research
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Reducing wait times and increasing the use of electronic medical records (EMRs) are two challenges faced by the health care system today. Dr. Thind will lead an international multidisciplinary team to with the twin aims of (a) developing the knowledge base to optimize the use EMRs in primary health care in order to improve disease outcomes in Canada; and (b) using clinical, mathematical and operational research techniques and tools to develop reproducible methods to reduce wait times across Canada, thus improving access to care.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Children's Health Policy
Keywords-MotsClés: Preventive medicine, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Mental disorders are the leading health problems currently facing Canadian children from infancy onwards  with marked social disparities in how children experience both the causes and the consequences of these disorders. But Canadian policy-making has yet to widely adopt the population health ideas that could address these disparities. This CRC will therefore investigate: 1) the landmark primary prevention program, Nurse-Family Partnership, and its potential for improving mental health and life chances for some of Canadas most vulnerable children; 2) new approaches for addressing health disparities in Aboriginal communities; and 3) new means of supporting policy-makers to adopt population health ideas.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: DNA Repair and Chromatin Dynamics
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: DNA damaging ionizing radiation (IR) is everywhere, in the form of atmosphere-penetrating cosmic rays, environmentally prevalent radioisotopes such as radon gas and radiation-based military, medical and energy technologies. There is no biological mechanism to prevent the damage caused to cells by IR ; instead, life has evolved exquisite mechanisms to resolve it once it has formed. The most deleterious lesion caused by IR is a break in both strands of our DNA, a DNA double-strand break (DSB). Unless accurately repaired by the molecular machinery of our cells, DSBs can lead to genome instability  a fundamental driver of cancer and ageing. We now know that DSBs occurring within regions of complex DNA arrangement are much more difficult to repair and require substantially more multifaceted (but as yet unclear) processes to resolve. My research endeavors to understand the molecular pathways underlying DSB repair in these regions and, in doing so, improve our knowledge of cancer formation, human ageing and radiation protection.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités : lésions cérébrales traumatiques - Fondation ontarienne de neurotraumatologie

TitreApplicationTitle: Promoting Financial Management Independence after Traumatic Brain Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ACQUIRED BRAIN INJURY; ASSESSMENT; COGNITION; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT; INSTRUMENTAL ACTIVITIES OF DAILY LIVING; NEUROSCIENCE; REHABILITATION; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Many survivors of a traumatic brain injury (TBI) have significant thinking and planning impairments that affect their judgment, awareness and decision-making.  As a consequence, TBI-survivors can have difficulties in managing their finances.  Depending on the extent of these issues, family or the public guardian may be given the legal right to manage the survivor's finances or family members may informally take on the survivor's financial management responsibilities.  This represents a significant loss of independence for the TBI-survivor.  Surprisingly, decisions regarding the financial management abilities of people living with a TBI are made in the absence of evidence-based assessments.  Furthermore, there are no guidelines to assist clinicians and families in helping survivors to keep decision-making power when they are able based on assessment results, thereby maximizing independence.  For example, some survivors may be able to participate in general banking tasks but may need help with budgeting.  This research aims to review assessments of financial management abilities and to determine which assessment tools can best evaluate TBI-survivors' skills.  This research will also provide guidelines for the assessment of TBI-survivors' financial management abilities with the view to maximizing independence in survivors thereby promoting their quality of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Minority Stress and HIV Risk Behaviour in South Asian-Canadian men who have sex with men
Keywords-MotsClés: HETEROSEXISM; HIV PREVENTION; HIV RISK FACTORS; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; MINORITY STRESS; PROTECTIVE FACTORS; RACE/ETHNICITY; RACISM; SEXUAL HEALTH PROMOTION; SOUTH ASIAN
Abstract-Résumé: Gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (MSM) are at an increased risk for HIV infection. Research suggests that the stress associated with being a stigmatized sexual minority (minority stress) is related to HIV risk behaviours (e.g., unprotected anal intercourse). However, these studies have predominantly focused on White populations while largely ignoring the impact of minority stress on HIV risk behaviours in racial/ethnic communities. The present study will address this gap in the literature by investigating the impact of three minority stressors (racism, internalized homophobia, and experiences of heterosexism) on HIV risk behaviours (unprotected anal intercourse and substance use) among South Asian-Canadian MSM. This study is significant because it will be first in its kind to provide data on HIV risk behaviour in a major Canadian ethnic minority group that has been previously neglected in HIV prevention research . Thus, this study will inform future Canadian HIV prevention research and sexual health promotion programs among South-Asian Canadian MSM, which can be expanded to target other MSM of colour. Consequently, this research will contribute to the overall health and well-being of populations at risk for HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the Effect of Anti-latency Agents on HIV Epitope Presentation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-LATENCY AGENTS; EPITOPE PRESENTATION; HIV REACTIVATION; HIV-1; HIV-1 GAG
Abstract-Résumé: Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) can effectively treat HIV; however, it must be maintained for life due to HIV's ability to establish reservoirs of latently infected cells that are not affected by antiviral drugs. Recent studies have identified drugs that are capable of reactivating latent HIV. These are now being tested in "shock and kill" strategies to potentially eradicate the virus in treated individuals.  In this approach, anti-latency drugs reveal hidden HIV+ cells in the body, which then become targets for killing by host cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL). Though it is possible to reactivate infected cells, their elimination by CTL appears ineffective. Poor recognition of these cells by CTL could be due to inadvertent effects of anti-latency drugs on the immune system. It is important to clarify the role of CTL following reactivation and to examine the impact of anti-latency drugs on CTL in order to enhance strategies to eliminate HIV. This study has two aims. First, we will measure the kinetics of HIV epitope presentation by reactivating cells. Latent HIV+ T cells will be stimulated and presentation of viral epitopes (small peptide sequences) will be detected on reactivating cells by co-culture using a sensitive luciferase reporter cell assay. Second, we will examine the effect of anti-latency drug candidates on the ability of reactivating cells to present HIV epitopes using the same assay. Reduced epitope presentation kinetics or frequency in the presence of an anti-latency drug will be explored as a potential limitation to its clinical utility. The results of this work could have important implications for HIV therapy, since potential adverse effects of anti-latency drugs may be identified.  As such, data will contribute to the choice and optimal use of anti-latency therapeutics for HIV. In addition, the proposed experimental methods are broadly applicable to examine HIV epitope presentation using different stimulation conditions and cell types.

ProgramNameEN: Master's Award - Priority Announcement: HIV Research (SHOPP)
NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse à la maitrise - Annonce de priorités : recherche VIH (PPPOS)

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the role of rectal mucosal fluid in HIV infection and susceptibility in HIV-exposed men who have sex with men
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; MICROBICIDE; MSM; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; PROTEOMICS; TRANSMISSION; URAI
Abstract-Résumé: Men who have sex with men (MSM) are one of the highest risk groups for HIV acquisition, and are a major contributor to the global HIV/AIDS epidemic. Risk of HIV-acquisition is greatest through unprotected anal intercourse (URAI); thus, developing related prevention technologies (microbicides) remains a priority. The rectum produces mucosa as the first line of defense against HIV; but the properties of rectal mucosa (RM) that block HIV infection are understudied and are a major gap in knowledge. Our published studies investigating HIV-exposed seronegative (HESN) individuals-those repeatedly exposed to HIV, but remain uninfected-have associated antiviral proteins bPRP2 and Serpins with the protected HESN phenotype in the oral and vaginal mucosa, respectively, and are helping to guide microbicide research. These finding strongly support the need to study protein factors within mucosa, and defining these proteins in the RM of HESN MSM would help advance microbicides that prevent high-risk HIV transmission through URAI.   Our preliminary proteomics data has characterized >300 proteins within RM, including proteins associated with HIV-susceptibility, and identified RM as unique from vaginal/oral mucusa. Our comparison of HESN MSM to control individuals revealed that HESN MSM overexpress the anti-HIV protein DMBT1. We have also shown that RM can inhibit HIV infection in vitro by 40%. Thus, my hypothesis is that DMBT1 and other protein factors of the rectal mucosa are associated with HIV-protection. This hypothesis will be tested with further proteomic characterization of HESN MSM vs. non-exposed MSM controls to validate DMBT1 and find other correlated proteins, evaluation of the antiviral properties of RM during mock infections of human cells, and by testing the antiviral properties of DMBT1 in cell culture.  This novel, comprehensive study will significantly increase our understanding of the immunobiology of the rectal tract and will shape microbicide research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Risk and protective factors for HIV infection among Canadian First Nations people living off reserve, Métis and Inuit.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES; ABORIGINAL PEOPLES SURVEY; CANADA; HIV PREVALENCE; HIV TESTING; INDIGENOUS POPULATIONS; LINEAR REGRESSION; LOGISTIC REGRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: According to the Public Health Agency of Canada, there were an estimated 65000 people in Canada living with HIV in 2008, an increase of 12.3% from 2005. The total number of Canadian Aboriginal people living with HIV (including AIDS patients) in 2005 was 3500, which by 2008 increased by 24% to 4900. The 2006 Census reported that Aboriginal people represented only 3.8% of the Canadian population, but in 2008 accounted for 8.0% of the country's prevalent infections. The disparities in HIV prevalence between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginals must be considered when evaluating the HIV epidemic in Canada. The objective of this project is to develop an informed epidemiological analysis of HIV status and testing in Aboriginal populations using information from the 2001 and 2006 Aboriginal Peoples Survey. The analysis will include all three main Aboriginal groups (North American Indian, Metis and Inuit identity or ancestry), excluding people living in settlements or on reserves. We also plan to analyze the unique characteristics of the HIV epidemic among female Aboriginal people, as compared to male. Factors associated with HIV positive and HIV negative people will be statistically compared, and changes between 2001 and 2006 survey periods will be analyzed. This research is being conducted in a contributing effort to that which is necessary to characterize the unique needs of the First Nations, Inuit and Metis populations, in order to identify and analyze culturally appropriate and effective approaches to HIV prevention, care, treatment and support.

TitreApplicationTitle: Propriétés des muscles du plancher pelvien et fonction urogénitale de femmes ayant reçu un traitement de radiothérapie adjuvante suite à un cancer de l'endomètre
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DYNAMOMETRIE; FORCE MUSCULAIRE; INCONTINENCE; PLANCHER PELVIEN; RADIOTHERAPIE; READAPTATION; SANTE DES FEMMES; UROGENITAL
Abstract-Résumé: On estime qu'entre 1997 et 2007, plus de 48 000 femmes ont recu un diagnostic de cancer genital au Canada. Le cancer du corps de l'uterus a represente a lui seul 7 % de tous les cancers chez la femme, devenant ainsi un des plus importants pour cette population. Une detection plus rapide du cancer et le perfectionnement du traitement medical expliqueraient l'encourageante baisse de mortalite et le plus grand nombre de survivantes de ce cancer. La radiotherapie est communement utilisee comme traitement chez les femmes avec un risque plus eleve de recidive ou un stade avance de cancer. Il est reconnu toutefois que ce traitement laisse des dysfonctions physiques importantes qui perdurent de nombreuses annees apres la fin du traitement. Parmi ces dysfonctions physiques, on note l'incontinence urinaire et fecale. Ce serait pres de 70% des survivantes de ce cancer qui souffrirait d'un probleme d'incontinence, tous types confondus. A son tour, l'incontinence serait associee a de la detresse psychologique de meme qu'a une baisse de participation aux activites de la vie quotidienne et aux activites sociales. L'incontinence pourrait s'expliquer par un mauvais fonctionnement des muscles internes du bassin, soit du plancher pelvien. Ceci demeure toutefois a etre demontre. Ce projet de recherche vise donc a mesurer les proprietes musculaires du plancher pelvien chez des survivantes d'un cancer de l'endometre qui ont recu un traitement de radiotherapie. Ceci permettra de caracteriser d'abord les dysfonctions musculaires de ces femmes puis de verifier si elles sont associees aux symptomes d'incontinence urinaire ou fecale qu'elles vivent. Mieux comprendre les dysfonctions musculaires du plancher pelvien et leur association avec l'incontinence urinaire et fecale permettra de proposer des interventions de reeducation ciblant les dysfonctions specifiques de ces femmes et de reduire les dysfonctions urogenitales tout en ameliorant leur participation et leur qualite de vie.

TitreApplicationTitle: Working with Parents to Prevent and Manage Childhood Obesity in a Primary Care Setting
Keywords-MotsClés: MANAGEMENT; OBESITY; PEDIATRICS; PREVENTION; PRIMARE CARE; SCREENING AND BRIEF INTERVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood obesity is an urgent public health issue. Roughly one-quarter of Canadian children are overweight, putting them at risk for chronic diseases. Because most families access health services in primary care, it is an ideal venue for obesity prevention. Specifically, programs in primary care can prevent unhealthy weight gain in healthy weight children (primary prevention) AND reduce unhealthy weight gain in children who are already overweight (secondary prevention). Parents play a key role in children's health, so it is vital to include parents in strategies to prevent childhood obesity.  Our team will work with the Edmonton Oliver Primary Care Network (EOPCN) to prevent childhood obesity through the following objectives:  1. Develop a web-based, brief (10-15 minutes long) program for parents as an educational tool to (i) motivate parents to support healthy lifestyles in children, and (ii) access community resources and health services that can prevent childhood obesity; 2. Assess the acceptability of the program using focus group interviews with parents (n=15) and health professionals (n=12); 3. Determine family recruitment (n=140) and retention rates at baseline, 1-, and 6-months follow-up; 4. With the same sample (n=140), collect preliminary data at baseline, 1-, and 6-months follow-up to explore if the program led to changes in (i) parents' motivation to support their children's lifestyle habits, and (ii) families' use of resources and health services to prevent childhood obesity.  Findings from this developmental study will inform a future clinical trial to test intervention efficacy. The collaborations we will develop between our researchers, decision-makers, and the EOPCN are very important. These partnerships will help us to develop a novel program for parents as well as share our results with professionals and families dedicated to preventing childhood obesity in Alberta and across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intervenir face aux inégalités sociales pour la santé de la population : point de vue d'un professionnel de la santé
Keywords-MotsClés: ENTREVUES; GROUPES DE DISCUSSION; INTERVENTIONS DE SANTE; INEGALITES SOCIALES; SANTE DES POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: L'education en nutrition n'est pas suffisante pour aider nos patients a pratiquer de saines habitudes de vie. Plusieurs conditions favorables sont en effet necessaires, bien au-dela de l'education en nutrition, afin que nos patients puissent aisement pratiquer de saines habitudes de vie et ce, pour leur mieux-etre. Ce projet de recherche s'interesse donc a l'approche que les professionnels de la sante peuvent developper pour approcher les inegalites sociales, sachant que celles-ci limitent la capacite des individus a pratiquer de saines habitudes de vie et menent ainsi au developpement de problemes de sante chroniques. Nous determinerons d'abord les conditions defavorables a la pratique de saines habitudes de vie (bien manger, etre actif, bien dormir) et nous proposerons ensuite des interventions que les professionnels de la sante pourront mettre en pratique face aux inegalites sociales de leurs patients afin d'ameliorer et de promouvoir la sante. Puisque ce projet de recherche nait d'un probleme social et de sante bien reel, les interventions proposees apporteront des pistes de solutions qui seront benefiques pour l'ensemble de la population canadienne.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pain among elderly South Asian immigrant women
Keywords-MotsClés: ELDERLY; IMMIGRANT; MIXED-METHODS; PAIN PERCEPTIONS; SOMALI
Abstract-Résumé: The research project proposed will examine pain among elderly South Asian women in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA), one of the most diverse areas in the world. Pain is a complex bio-psycho-social experience, and therefore it deserves a broader understanding, rather than simply attributing it to biological factors. At the present moment there is no literature on pain among elderly immigrant populations.  The current literature on pain demonstrates that minority populations remain at risk for inadequate pain control, and the reasons may be due to lack of awareness of how these populations experience pain. As the population of those 65-years of age and over is increasing, there are going to many older immigrants in Canada. There needs to be an understanding of the intersectionality between gender, age, and culture in relation to pain. This is essential for primary care providers to know, because it may affect how they deliver care and how they determine the best treatment options. It is also important for those who work at community-based organizations focused on immigrant and/or elderly populations when planning health-related programs. This is a mixed-methods study that will include 20-25 participants. Interviews will be conducted and participants will complete the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire-2. Pain is a public health problem as it affects 1 in 5 adults globally. It truly affects the well-being of individuals, and based on the literature, there is no reason elderly people should be suffering from pain in Canada, because there are various treatments available for them.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Program of RCT Research on Developmental Care Interventions to Enhance Preterm Infants and Mothers Health Outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: RCT
Abstract-Résumé: After birth, the physical environment of the hospital may influence the growth and development of preterm infants. In addition to the physical environment, it appears that the psychological health of mothers may influence the preterm infants' optimal growth and development. Some interventions are identified as reducing the preterm infants' stress, improving the stability of vital signs, and promoting sleep as well as enhancing mothers' well-being in this environment. These interventions consist of reducing the light and noise in the hospital environment along with encouraging skin-to-skin contact between preterm infants and their mothers. The goal of this mentoring program is to get expertise in conducting experimental research evaluating these interventions that are aimed at promoting preterm infants' and mothers' health outcomes. Ultimately, the goal is to allow premature infants to grow in an environment adapted to their physiological systems and encouraging periods of rest long enough to allow their optimal growth and development as well as enhancing mothers' well-being.

TitreApplicationTitle: Harnessing the SLAM-SAP pathways to improve immune surveillance against cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-TUMOR IMMUNITY; IMMUNOLOGY; NK CELLS; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Cytotoxic lymphocytes, namely natural killer (NK) cells and CD8+ T cells, play a key role in the ability of the host to control the growth of cancer cells. However, though a multitude of mechanisms, cancer cells frequently escape immune surveillance and produce clinically-apparent cancers that have devastating effects. Considering these notions, much effort has been devoted over the past decades towards understanding and, hopefully, improving immune surveillance against cancer cells, in order to halt or reverse tumor progression in humans.  Previously, we showed that the SLAM-SAP pathways play a key role in the ability of NK cells to kill malignant hematopoietic cells, but not non-hematopoietic cells, in vitro. This feature relates to the fact that hematopoietic cells, but not non-hematopoietic cells, express ligands for the SLAM family receptors, which trigger the functions of SAP family adaptors. In a related way, others subsequently demonstrated that the SLAM-SAP pathways are necessary for the capacity of CD8+ T cells to kill abnormal hematopoietic cells, but not non-hematopoietic cells, in vitro. Thus, as a result of their roles in NK cells and CD8+ T cells, the SLAM-SAP pathways seem to have pivotal functions in the ability of immune cells to prevent hematopoietic cell-derived tumors.  To validate the physiological importance of this mechanism, it is important to examine the effects of the SLAM-SAP pathways on tumorigenesis in vivo. Here, we will elucidate the role and potential therapeutic usefulness of the SLAM-SAP pathways in anti-tumor immunity in vivo. Using mouse models, we will: 1) evaluate the role of the SLAM-SAP pathways in immune surveillance against hematopoietic cancers in vivo. 2) Test the possibility that enforced expression of the SLAM family ligand, CRACC, on hematopoietic tumors could improve anti-tumor immunity in vivo. And 3) examine the therapeutic usefulness of ectopically expressing SLAM family ligands on non-hematopoietic cancers.

Abstract-Résumé: Blood cells called phagocytes are key components of the immune system; however, when dysregulated, they contribute to inflammatory and autoimmune diseases as well as cancer.  My research program is focused on identifying genes and regulatory pathways governing the development and activity of phagocytes, to better understand and manipulate them in an effort to control disease.  My laboratory uses models of lupus, inflammatory bowel disease, breast cancer and colitis-associated cancer, which mimic the complex physiology observed in human diseases. Our aim is to translate our improving understanding of phagocyte biochemistry into strategies to control autoimmunity, chronic inflammation or elicit anti-tumour immunity.

TitreApplicationTitle: The functional relevance of bile acids in childhood cholestasis caused by ABCB11 and ABCB4 mutations
Keywords-MotsClés: BILE ACID; BILE SALT EXPORT PUMP (BSEP); CHOLESTASIS; LIVER; MDR3; MUTATION; PHOSPHOLIPIDS; PROGRESSIVE FAMILIAL INTRAHEPATIC CHOLESTASIS (PFIC); TRANSPORTER
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic defects in bile formation are found in children with Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis types 2 and 3 (PFIC2 and PFIC3). PFIC is a devastating liver disease, the most severe form of cholestasis, often resulting in jaundice, growth retardation, cirrhosis, liver failure, and death. Bile acids are one of the main constituents of bile and BSEP is a bile acid pump responsible for driving bile flow. MDR3 is a similar protein that transports lipids to protect liver cells from the toxic detergent effects of bile acids. These two genes work together to produce healthy bile. PFIC2 and PFIC3 are associated with mutated BSEP and MDR3 genes, respectively. Mouse models with mutations similar to PFIC2 and PFIC3 have been created. They show that the mouse liver has the amazing ability to alleviate the toxic effects of cholestasis by making use of genes not normally involved in bile flow.  The goal of this application is to determine if the livers of PFIC patients also have similar compensatory mechanisms to alleviate cholestasis in people. We will use the mouse models as a guide to investigate compensatory bile forming-genes in patients. Any new bile acids found in patients will be studied using the mouse models of cholestasis to determine how they might protect liver cells. We expect that findings from this study will result in the identification of diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers to improve clinical management of patients with severe PFIC-like liver diseases.   This proposed research is synergistic because of collaboration between the Fudan University Pediatric Liver Diseases Centre, headed by Dr Jian She Wang in Shanghai, with the laboratory of Dr Victor Ling in Vancouver. Dr Wang's centre is a major referral centre for PFIC patients in China and clinical material can be obtained readily for this study. Dr Ling's lab is recognized as the world authority on the experimental mouse models of PFIC.

Abstract-Résumé: The overarching purpose of the research program is to develop fundamental understanding of the cortical control of the human hand.  The unique emphasis is on higher-order somatic area 5 and the secondary somatosensory cortex. Cutting-edge techniques in Functional magnetic resonance imaging and Transcranial magnetic stimulation will be used to examine the representation of the hand in high-order somatic loci and determine the neural mechanisms by which each area influences the primary motor cortex to modify hand control.  The information obtained is essential for developing effective therapeutic interventions that aim to improve hand control in patient populations.

Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Nutrition and food hygiene
Abstract-Résumé: People who are overweight or obese are at a higher risk of developing serious health problems.  The metabolic and cellular mechanisms of why some of these individuals develop diseases while others do not are not fully understood. Furthermore, we lack effective ways to treat obesity, as most people who lose weight eventually regain it.  The goal of this novel research program is to identify the long-term effects of obesity, from the cell to the entire body, that contribute to disease development and weight regain.  Results will promote the development of better public health interventions at both ends of the prevention-treatment spectrum.
