TitreApplicationTitle: Injectable Hydrogels Encapsulating Living Cells for Myocardial Infarction Repair
Keywords-MotsClés: ALGINATE HYDROGEL; CARDIOMYOCYTE REGENERATION; CELL ENCAPSULATION; CELL TRACKING; CELL VIABILITY; ENGINEERING CARDIAC CONSTRUCTS; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; SCAFFOLD VISUALIZATION; SYNCHROTRON BIOMEDICAL IMAGING; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Myocardial infarction (MI), commonly known as heart attack, is one leading cause of death worldwide, including both Canada and China. The myocardium has extremely limited regeneration potential. With advances in tissue engineering, implantation or injection of tissue engineering cardiac constructs made from biomaterials and/or living cells into the affected myocardium shows promise for improving MI repair. This therapy is still being conducted in animal trials, and we believe significant advances can be made by creating cardiac scaffolds or constructs with carefully controlled composition and properties.  In this project, we will develop novel injectable cardiac scaffolds that encapsulate living cells for use in MI repair. Our central hypothesis is that alginate hydrogels can be engineered with controlled composition (including living cells and locally-delivered molecular agents) and properties for optimal cardiomyocyte regeneration and functional recovery after MI. Our specific objectives are to: (1) synthesize self-cross-linked alginate hydrogels to optimize cell viability during cell injection; (2) examine the ability of hydrogels encapsulating living cells to promote cardiomyocyte regeneration in vitro; (3) integrate strategies for promoting cardiomyocyte regeneration and antagonizing the effects of matrix metalproteases to achieve combined or synergistic effects for MI repair in vivo; and (4) develop synchrotron biomedical imaging technologies to track the success of the strategies developed. This work will significantly advance the theoretical and practical basis of developing injectable hydrogels encapsulating living cells to foster MI repair in animal models, and eventually in humans. As such, this project is well aligned with research on "treatment and ultimate cure of cardiovascular diseases, including MI" within the "cardiovascular system" research area of the 2013 China-Canada Joint Health Research Initiative funding opportunity announcement.

TitreApplicationTitle: Systematic identification of dynamic epigenetic modifications in DNA damage repair for novel cancer therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CHROMATIN BINDING MODULE; DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE; DYNAMICS; EPIGENETICS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MULTIPLE REACTION MONITORING; PEPTIDE ARRAY; PROTEIN METHYLATION; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Epigenetics refers mainly to the study of DNA and histone modifications and their role in regulating the gene transcriptional program in cells. Aberrant epigenetic changes have been associated with a plethora of human diseases, including cancer. Histones around which the DNA is wrapped in chromatin is subject to numerous modifications on specific types of amino acids, including lysine and arginine, by histone modifying enzymes. Interestingly, a number of recent studies indicate that non-histone proteins are also substrates of these enzymes. These studies therefore expand epigenetic modifications to non-histone proteins and call for further research into this new area in order to understand the role of protein methylation in general as well as their functions in specific cellular processes. The Li lab has recently shown that epigenetic modifications on histone and non-histone proteins are highly dynamic and that these modifications play an important role in regulating DNA damage response, a key cellular process for maintaining genome stability. Because cancer cells are characterized with a highly unstable genome and targeting the DNA damage response signaling pathways is an important strategy in chemotherapy, these studies have far-reaching implications to cancer research and treatment. In the proposed project, Dr. Li and his collaborator, Dr. Ye in China, will employ an integral approach that combines two powerful proteomic techniques, peptide arrays and mass spectrometry, to systematically identify the methylated lysine and arginine residues in proteins and characterize how these modifications change in response to DNA damage induced by chemicals. This work will provide valuable insights into the epigenetic mechanism of cancer and at the same time, identify novel targets for cancer treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: MicroRNAs as biomarkers and therapeutic targets of preeclampsia
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; MICRORNA; PLACENTA DEVELOPMENT; PREECLAMPSIA
Abstract-Résumé: Preeclampsia (PE) is a major disorder of pregnancy and a leading cause of maternal death and stillbirth.  Currently, there are no early diagnostic markers to predict PE and the only effective intervention is delivery. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small RNAs that play important roles in controlling gene expression. In 2009, we received a China-CIHR joint health initiative grant to study miRNAs in PE.  This seed grant has allowed us to establish a highly productive collaboration and let to the identification of key miRNAs that have abnormal levels in PE patients.   We discovered several miRNAs that are up- or down-regulated, in the placenta and plasma of pregnant women before they developed symptoms of PE, raising the exciting possibility of using them as predictive biomarker. We also found that these miRNAs regulate placental cell invasion.  We propose that abnormal levels of these miRNAs (miR-210, -18a, -19b, and -92a) lead to the development of PE.  In this study, we will investigate how these miRNAs are involved in PE and if they can be used as predictive biomarkers and therapeutic targets for this disease.   We have collected thousand of blood samples from pregnant women and will determine if miR-210, miR-18a, miR-19b, and miR-92a levels in early pregnancy can predict the onset of PE later on.  We will also use human placental cells and tissues to determine the function of these miRNAs.  Finally, we will generate mice that either have more miR-210 or have no mir-17-92 in the placenta and determine if these will induce PE like symptoms.  We will then develop strategies to manipulate the level of these miRNAs and test if they can prevent or reverse PE.   This joint grant will allow us to combine expertise and valuable resources to conduct cutting edge research, which will result in the development of novel strategies for diagnosis, prevention and treatment of PE.  Therefore, the proposed study will be beneficial not only to China and Canada, but also around the world.

Abstract-Résumé: The mission of the MScPH program at McGill is to train outstanding public health professionals, by offering a rigorous academic program in methods, research and practice. Other areas that have already been identified are public health policy and program planning and evaluation.

TitreApplicationTitle: MPH Practicums for Future Public Health Practitioners
Keywords-MotsClés: MPH; PRACTICUM; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The Masters in Public Health (MPH) program at the University of Manitoba was developed to educate and train graduate level students with a background in training and/or experience in health/health care to better prepare for work as public health practitioners. The primary intent is to increase the number of competent public health practitioners in Canada. Our program attempts to balance public health theory and practice, preparing our graduates to work at many levels in the public health system, including decision-making, policy advice, program development, implementation and evaluation.  The MPH program has been designed with a balance of didactic courses - some of which are mandatory (e.g. biostatistics and epidemiology) and some elective (e.g. economic evaluation, program evaluation) - and practical experience and training. Unlike our Masters of Community Health Sciences which requires the completion of a master-level thesis and is intended for researchers, the MPH program requires the completion of a three month (full-time equivalent) practicum. This practicum is located off site from the university in a public health practice setting (e.g. regional health authority public health unit, provincial government program unit) and is jointly overseen by a local supervisor and a University faculty member. These practicums are taken after all courses have been completed. It is anticipated that there will be between five and ten practicums per year, based on the current number of students that have applied and been accepted, with anticipated future growth. With no stipends for students, the program and these practicums can be a significant financial burden for the students, especially if there are additional expenses (e.g. equipment, travel). Vouchers to support these practicums would be very helpful to our mission to attract the best MPH students and provide them with a very useful and practical training to strengthen public health practice in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Study the role of SAMHD1 in HIV-1 transmission
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV; RESTING CD4+ T CELLS; SAMHD1; TRANSMISSION; TRANSMITTED/FOUNDER VIRUSES
Abstract-Résumé: This research project is aimed at advancing our understanding of HIV-1 transmission. The knowledge can be translated into the novel strategies to intervene HIV-1 infection. HIV-1 transmission cannot be captured in clinics due to the absence of HIV-1 molecules and the HIV-1 specific antibodies in the subject's blood. Therefore, there is still a large knowledge gap in comprehending HIV-1 transmission, and this has hampered the development of effective prevention and cure strategies. This study is proposed to use human primary CD4+ T cells and human mucosa tissue explant as models to determine the role of SAMHD1 in modulating HIV-1 transmission. SAMHD1 is a recently discovered HIV-1 restriction factor. It is highly expressed in HIV-1 target cells during transmission including resting CD4+ T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells. It is expected that modulating the activity of SAMHD1 will provide one strategy to prevent HIV-1 transmission.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aberrant Handling of Neutrophil Extracellular Traps as an Origin of Chronic Inflammation in Obesity Related Insulin Resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE IMMUNE SYSTEM; ADIPOSE TISSUE; DENDRITIC CELLS; INNATE IMMUNE SYSTEM; INSULIN RESISTANCE; NEUTROPHIL EXTRACELLULAR TRAPS; NEUTROPHILS; OBESITY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity and type 2 diabetes are major global health concerns. When people become obese, their hormone, insulin, does not properly control blood sugar levels, leading to type 2 diabetes.  This inability of insulin action is related to the body's organs becoming less responsive to insulin, but the underlying causes are not known. Normal mice that are placed on high fat diets become obese and develop disease that is similar to type 2 diabetes in humans. Fatty tissues in these mice contain a high amount of immune cells, including macrophages, neutrophils, T and B cells that produce inflammation. By neutralizing this inflammation, the metabolic disease is relieved. Thus, diabetes induced by high fat diet is caused, at least partly, by an abnormal immune response, or inflammation in the body's fat. Our recent work on T cells and B cells in fat, which identified a new immune component to type 2 diabetes was recently featured in hundreds of news media as one of the pre-eminent new findings in medicine. The objective here is to build on this work, and investigate how another immune cell, the neutrophil, functions to start the entire process of inflammation in diabetes. When neutrophils fight bacteria they release an entangling web called a neutrophil extracellular trap (NET), made up of proteins and DNA.  These NETs kill bacteria but if they are not cleared from the body, the immune system recognizes them as foreign and leads to inflammation. This has been shown to cause diseases like lupus and type 1 diabetes, and here we show a similar problem happens in type 2 diabetes in mice.  Thus, we will first find out how the handling of NETs varies in type 2 diabetes in humans.  We will then figure out how NETs promote high blood sugar in mice by studying inflammation in fat. Finally we will figure out what part of the NET the immune system is attacking to contribute to disease. The results of these experiments could lead to new effective ways to diagnose and treat diabetes.

Abstract-Résumé: Imagine having hands and feet constantly dripping with sweat whether it is in the summer or in the winter. This devastating genetic condition is called hyperhidrosis palmaris et plantaris (HHPP). There are about 300,000 Canadians and 15 million Chinese with this condition. These individuals often experience difficulties at home, in school and at work due to sweating interfering with normal activities that require the use of dry hands. As a result, their school and work performance is often judged negatively, and they often have difficulties developing interpersonal relationships. The cause of this condition has not been investigated. Our international collaborative team will use cutting edge techniques such as next generation sequencing, whole genome linkage analysis and functional genomics to determine the causes of HHPP. This study will help us find a cure for this disease that does not have a satisfactory treatment at present.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Contribution of Individual Muscles to Knee Joint Stability and Joint Contact Mechanics in Healthy and Osteoarthritic Populations
Keywords-MotsClés: AGEING; ELECTROMYOGRAPHY; ISOMETRIC EXERCISE; JOINT LOADS; KNEE; KNEE JOINT INJURY; MUSCLE ACTIVATIONS; OSTEOARTHRITIS; SEX DIFFERENCES; WEIGHT-BEARING
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most debilitating condition among older adults in Canada. Irregular forces acting on the knee are thought to cause OA. Knee forces can be regulated by muscular contractions. Deficits in muscle function are linked to the development and progression of OA. This study will investigate the differences in muscle activation strategies of younger healthy adults, older healthy adults and individuals with OA and how these differences affect the forces acting on the knee joint's cartilage.   It is hypothesized that the OA group will (1) activate their muscles more, (2) produce less muscle force, and (3) have decreased knee joint stability than the older and younger healthy groups. To test the hypotheses, a force-matching procedure will be used. Subjects will stand on a force plate and push against the ground in various directions without moving their bodies. Muscle activities will be measured with sensors placed on the dominant leg. The data collected will be processed and used to calculate how much force each muscle produced. Then, a cadaver knee testing jig will measure how these muscle forces distribute loads across the knee joint's surface. For each variable of interest, comparisons will be made between: (1) younger and older adults, (2) individuals with and without OA, and (3) male and female subjects. A direct link between actual muscle activations and internal forces acting on the knee can be made. Results from this study will contribute to a research program aimed to develop an exercise program for those with, or at risk of developing, OA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Protecting delayed neuronal death in ischemic stroke by targeting the BNIP3 pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: BNIP3; DELAYED NEURONAL DEATH; ISCHEMIC STROKE; MITOCHONDRIA; VDAC
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is a leading cause of disability and death worldwide. It affects about 50,000 Canadians each year, and about 1% of Canadians are living with the effects of stroke. About 80% of strokes are ischemic, which is caused by the interruption of blood flow to the brain and often results in massive death of brain cells (neurons) and consequently loss of neurological functions. There are two types of cell death in ischemic stroke: acute neuronal death that occurs quickly after a stroke and delayed neuronal death that occurs hours to days after a stroke. The delayed neuronal death is a hallmark feature of ischemic stroke and the primary target for neuroprotective strategies. Previously, others and we have shown that a death-inducing gene called BNIP3 plays an important role in causing the delayed neuronal death. Recently, we have obtained evidence that BNIP3 selectively causes damage to mitochondria, the chemical plant of the cell, leading to cell death. Blocking the BNIP3 cell-death pathway, therefore, is a new strategy for rescuing these neurons and improving the recovery of neurological functions following strokes. The experiments proposed here are built on our previous studies to further understand how BNIP3 induces neuronal cell death following stroke and to develop and test new approaches to protect neurons from death by inhibiting the activity of the death-inducing gene BNIP3. The outcome of the project will provide important insights into mechanisms of delayed neuronal death and new strategies for neuroprotection that can be translated to bedside care of stroke

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the basal ganglia in inhibiting and promoting voluntary movements
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; DYSTONIA; LOCAL FIELD POTENTIALS; MOVEMENT INHIBITION; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; STOP SIGNAL; VOLUNTARY MOVEMENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) or causing a injury to specific parts of the brain know as the basal ganglia nuclei are accepted treatments for movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease (PD), and dystonia.  Impulse control disorder (ICD) such excessive gambling, eating, shopping or sexual activities occurs in a significant proportion of PD patients and is a source of severe disability.  The basal ganglia play an important role in producing and stopping movements. Very few studies examined how the basal ganglia stop movement although it is an important everyday function and relates to ICD.  The proposed study is a new collaborative effort between Xuanwu Hospital of Capital Medical University (XHCMU) and the Toronto Western Hospital (TWH). Both hospitals are centers of excellence in brain surgery for movement disorders. Patients with PD or dystonia scheduled to undergo brain surgery will be recruited.  The team at XHCMU will perform recordings of single brain cell activities during surgery and the team at TWH will record brain signals that reflect activities of a large group of brain cells at 1-5 days after surgery.   The subjects will perform the same "conditional stop-signal paradigm" to allow researchers to examine activities of different parts of the basal ganglia that are associated with movement and stopping of movement.  The studies at the two sites nicely complement each other as the recordings at each site obtain different information.  The study will address a fundamental question in neuroscience of the role of the basal ganglia in mediating wanted movements and stopping of unwanted movements.  It may lead to a new way of treating PD patients with ICD and other movement disorders using DBS.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; AUTOIMMUNITY; B CELLS; CLINICAL RESEARCH; COPD; FLOW CYTOMETRY; TOBACCO SMOKE
Abstract-Résumé: The devastating impact of cigarette smoking on human health is well known. Despite this, over 1.1 billion people continue to smoke, representing one-sixth of the world's population. About half of these smokers will develop severe smoking-related illnesses, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), stroke, and cancer. The proposed research focuses on mechanisms that contribute to the pathogenesis of COPD; a chronic inflammatory lung disease. We will investigate the role of autoantibodies in inflammatory processes associated with COPD. The proposed research will provide novel biomarkers for early diagnosis of COPD and provide a framework for experimental interventions to control inflammatory processes associated with this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeted delivery of antisense-mediated exon skipping therapy in transgenic pig model of DMD
Keywords-MotsClés: MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is one of the most common lethal genetic disorders worldwide. Currently, a most promising therapeutic option for DMD is exon skipping therapy. Exon skipping employs short DNA-like molecules like "Band-Aids" and target the mutated part of the gene. However, exon skipping faces three major challenges; 1) limited efficacy in the heart, 2) limited applicability (only 10% of DMD patients can be treated with exon skipping), 3) unknown stability and function of resulting proteins produced by the DNA Band-Aids. We will address all three challenges. Our research team in China (Dr. Haifang Yin) has developed novel DNA-like molecules that efficiently target both muscle and heart. Our research team in Canada (Dr. Toshifumi Yokota) has developed a cocktail of DNA Band-Aids that is applicable to majority of DMD patients and that can optimize the resulting proteins. In addition, the Canada team has developed a novel pig model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy for development of new drugs for DMD. The efficacy and safety of these novel molecules will be tested in our pig model. Our study will eventually lead to novel clinical trials for DMD.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Chloride Channel ClC-3 in Cerebral Ischemia and Its Therapeutic Potential in Stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CEREBRAL ISCHEMIA; CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASES; CLC-3 CHLORIDE CHANNELS; IN-VIVO; ION CHANNELS; NEUROPROTECTION; STROKE; TREATMENT; VOLUME-REGULATED AION CHANNELS
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is the second leading cause of death in both China and Canada and the leading cause of adult disability in both countries. Its occurrence is expected to triple by 2050, and our aging population is especially vulnerable. The disabilities in afflicted survivors of stroke have created significant social and economic impacts for our society in both countries. For example, with more than 50,000 new strokes occurring each year in Canada, stroke and its related illnesses cost the Canadian healthcare system about $2.5 billion each year according to the 2010 Canadian Stroke Congress. The situation is similar in China, with significant and growing costs to the economy.   While stroke poses major health concerns, the mechanisms (causes) leading to brain damage in stroke are not well understood. Our collaborative project focuses on understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying stroke-related brain injury, particularly the role of anion channel, ClC-3 chloride channel. This channel plays an important role in cell damage during heart ischemia, but its role in brain stroke has not yet been studied. We will study the fundamental role of the ClC-3 chloride channel in brain stroke, and consider new drug development for treating stroke, using a variety of approaches, including molecular biology, biochemistry, in vivo stroke models, histology, advanced imaging, electrophysiology, and functional and behavioural assessments. Our goal is to develop novel therapeutic strategies to prevent brain damage and to promote brain cell survival, regeneration, and functional recovery in the injured brain after stroke, thereby reducing the burden of disease on stroke victims and their families and providing long-term economic, social, and healthcare benefits for both of our countries.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechnisms of ventilator-induced lung injury and remodeling
Keywords-MotsClés: EPITHELIAL CELL; INFLAMMATION; LUNG INJURY; MECHANICAL VENTILATION; NEUTROPHILS
Abstract-Résumé: Patients who develop a disease known as Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) have a very high mortality. Mortality is particularly high in the subset of patients with ARDS who develop fibrosis (scarring) in their lungs while they are on a breathing machine (called a ventilator) in the intensive care unit. Our hypothesis is that the ventilator which helps saves the patient's life by taking over the breathing function while they are ill, may actually contribute to the development of the scarring (fibrosis). Our studies will use animal models to see whether our hypothesis is correct, and willalso try various therapies to prevent and/or treat the fibrosis. If our hypothesis is true that the ventilator can cause lungfibrosis, the increased understanding generated our studies may lead to new therapies that can be tested in patients withacute lung injury to decrease the high mortality of this deadly syndrome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of androgen receptor splice variants in PCOS-associated ovarian follicular dysfunction
Keywords-MotsClés: FERTILITY; HORMONE RECEPTORS; HORMONES; OVARY; SEX STEROID HORMONES
Abstract-Résumé: Androgen excess is one of the most well characterized clinical features of the female-specific disease known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) that affects about 1 in 15 women of reproductive age. Yet, the etiology of PCOS is still largely unknown and no single factor or gene fully accounts for the spectrum of abnormalities associated with this disease. In collaboration with our Chinese partners at Zhejiang University, we have recently discovered a novel and important role for the male sex hormone receptor (androgen receptor, AR) and its splice variants in PCOS women. Our exciting preliminary results demonstrate the expression of two AR splice variant mRNAs in human ovarian granulosa cells from PCOS patients, but not control women. The AR variants are expressed in 65% of PCOS women examined and are associated with higher serum total testosterone and follicular fluid free androgen index. The studies outlined in this proposal are designed to test the novel hypothesis that androgen excess induces epigenetic alterations in the AR gene which promote the expression of AR splice variants in human granulosa cells. Expression of dysfunctional AR variants alters the regulation of downstream target genes such as aromatase, contributing to androgen excess in PCOS. The proposal to understand the role of specific splice variants of the male sex hormone receptor in the pathogenesis of PCOS (a female-specific disease) is highly original. Achieving this goal will represent a significant advancement in the promotion of women's reproductive health.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Program of RCT Research on Developmental Care Interventions to Enhance Preterm Infants and Mothers Health Outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: RCT
Abstract-Résumé: After birth, the physical environment of the hospital may influence the growth and development of preterm infants. In addition to the physical environment, it appears that the psychological health of mothers may influence the preterm infants' optimal growth and development. Some interventions are identified as reducing the preterm infants' stress, improving the stability of vital signs, and promoting sleep as well as enhancing mothers' well-being in this environment. These interventions consist of reducing the light and noise in the hospital environment along with encouraging skin-to-skin contact between preterm infants and their mothers. The goal of this mentoring program is to get expertise in conducting experimental research evaluating these interventions that are aimed at promoting preterm infants' and mothers' health outcomes. Ultimately, the goal is to allow premature infants to grow in an environment adapted to their physiological systems and encouraging periods of rest long enough to allow their optimal growth and development as well as enhancing mothers' well-being.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transfusion of Red cells In Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation: The TRIST Study
Keywords-MotsClés: TRANSFUSION
Abstract-Résumé: Transfusion of red blood cells (RBCs) is important for the care of patients undergoing stem cell transplantation. Stem cell transplants are used to treat blood cancers and bone marrow disorders. This involves the use of high doses of chemotherapy and/or radiation to kill cancer cells; but this damages the marrow and blood system.  Blood stem cells are transplanted by infusing into the recipient and blood counts recover over 2-3 weeks. Before bone marrow recovery, RBCs are needed to support the patient. Higher hemoglobin in these high risk patients may have benefits such as better energy and organ function. However, research in other areas of medicine suggests that a higher red cell count may be dangerous. Taken together, it is unclear whether having a lower or higher red cell count is better for patients having a blood stem cell transplant. I plan to study this by randomly assigning patients having a transplant to be transfused with RBCs either at a higher or lower hemoglobin level. In this way, we will be able to accurately find out if there are any benefits or harms in having a lower or higher red cell count during the recovery period after blood stem cell transplantation. This training ward from CIHR will allow me have the full resources of the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute and the University of Ottawa to successfully carry out this vital research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of Expertise in Surgical RCTs:  An opportunity for International Impact in Orthopaedic Fracture Care
Keywords-MotsClés: RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Orthopaedic (bone and joint) injuries are common in Canada and throughout the world.  In Canada, 73% of patients hospitalized for a major injury have an orthopaedic injury. Up to 40 million people worldwide are permanently disabled as a result of trauma each year, and many more are temporarily disabled.  Research is needed to improve patient care and treatment outcomes in these patients.  Clinical trials play a vital role in improving patient care and treatment outcomes.  Performing clinical trials in surgical disciplines is challenging. Specialized training is necessary to learn to perform successful clinical trials, and few orthopaedic surgeons have this training.  The funding from this grant will pair a new researcher, Dr. Slobogean, with a researcher who is highly experienced in performing pivotal clinical trials, Dr. Bhandari.  Both Dr. Slobogean and Dr. Bhandari are orthopaedic surgeons whose clinical and research interests center around improving the the care and outcomes of patients with bone and joint injuries.  Dr. Slobogean will be integrated into Dr. Bhandari's team and will have the opportunity to work on several of his ongoing clinical trials.  Under the mentorship of Dr. Bhandari, Dr. Slobogean will also design and implement a new trial related to the treatment of hip fractures in younger adults (ages 18-60) and the effect of vitamin D on complications and quality of life related to these fractures.  Hip fractures in younger adults are challenging to treat, and despite the use of modern surgical techniques, 25% of these patients will experience a major fracture healing complication.  Improving these patients' outcomes has the potential to make a significant difference in the lives of these patients. The experience gained by Dr. Slobogean in designing and implementing this trial will give him the necessary skills to carry out large clinical trials in the future that will have the potential to improve bone and joint injury care throughout the world.

Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a serious health problem affects 850 million people worldwide and is the third leading cause of disability. Depression is also associated with high risk of suicide leading to premature loss of life. One in five Canadians is currently suffering form depression. Depression treatment is mostly focused on antidepressants medications. Despite the usefulness of antidepressants for some people, many individuals do not respond to medications, suffer from serious side effects including weight gain, risk of diabetes, heart disease and with some antidepressants there is also an increased risk of suicidal behaviour. Therefore there is an urgent need to identify safe and effective treatment for depression. One such treatment is the use of light therapy, where an individual with depression uses a special lamp with bright light every morning for half an hour and the exposure to this bright light will help to improve the symptoms of depression without the need for medications. This light therapy has been shown useful in insomnia and seasonal affective disorder (SAD) however its use in depression is not well studied. It has also been seen that people response to treatment may be impacted by their genetic profile. We propose to study the usefulness of light therapy as a depression treatment taking into account the person's genetic profile. To be able to conduct this study, the applicant, a psychiatrist with experience in depression treatment and genetics, will required an in-depth training on the conduct of special research projects called randomised controlled trials or RCTs, supported by two leaders in the field. The CIHR RCT mentorship program will offer invaluable opportunity to train the applicant in the conduct of the study of light therapy in depression thus leading to the development of a solid independent researcher and the development of a research program dedicated to study treatment options for depression aside form the commonly used medications.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Intracellular Calcium Overload in Donor Hearts Following Circulatory Death
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM FLUORESCENCE IMAGING; DONATION AFTER CIRCULATORY DEATH; EX VIVO HEART PERFUSION; HEART FAILURE; HEART TRANSPLANT; ISCHEMIA REPERFUSION INJURY; ORGAN PRESERVATION; PATCH CLAMP; SODIUM CALCIUM EXCHANGE
Abstract-Résumé: Heart transplant is a life saving treatment for patients with end-stage heart failure; however, because of a critical shortage of donor organs many patients die while waiting for a heart transplant. There are two categories of organ donors: brain dead donors and donors after circulatory death (DCD). Currently only hearts from brain dead donors are used for transplant. DCD hearts are without blood flow and oxygen for a period of time (ischemia) before they can be harvested. Restoring blood flow (reperfusion) triggers calcium buildup inside heart cells and causes heart muscle to die (ischemia-reperfusion injury). DCD hearts are not used because of concern that ischemia-reperfusion injury causes the heart to be too weak for transplant; however, a drug called SEA-0400 has been shown to reduce the accumulation of calcium inside heart cells and minimize ischemia-reperfusion injury in mice and rat hearts.  The objective of this project is to determine if SEA-0400 can reduce the accumulation of calcium inside pig heart cells, minimize ischemia-reperfusion injury, and facilitate transplantation of DCD pig hearts. We will achieve this objective with two experiments.  Experiment 1) We will isolate individual cells from pig hearts and determine what dose of SEA-0400 minimizes calcium build-up during ischemia and reperfusion. These results will be used to inform the following transplant experiments. Experiment 2) We have developed a pig model of DCD that closely resembles what happens in human patients. We will administer SEA-0400 to DCD pig hearts and transplant them into a recipient pig. We will determine if SEA-0400 can minimize ischemia-reperfusion injury and improve heart function after transplant. Very few research projects have studied if DCD hearts can be used for transplant. SEA-0400 could minimize ischemia-reperfusion injury in DCD hearts, increase the number of donor hearts, and save the lives of patients waiting for a heart transplant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Donor Lymphocyte Infusion for the Treatment of Disease Relapse after Umbilical Cord Blood Transplantation
Keywords-MotsClés: DISEASE RELAPSE; DONOR LYMPHOCYTE INFUSION; HEMATOLOGIC MALIGNANCIES; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELL TRANSPLANT; UMBILICAL CORD BLOOD
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with blood cancers often require a bone marrow transplant from a healthy donor to provide them with a chance of cure from their disease.  This donor can be a related or unrelated healthy volunteer who matches the patient.  Although many patients will be cured, there is always a risk of relapse of the cancer after transplant.  In this circumstance, patients have the opportunity to undergo a transfusion of specific white blood cells from the healthy donor in order to try and kill the relapsed cancer cells.  This process is called donor lymphocyte infusion and provides a hope for cure in patients who have cancer recurrence after transplant.  In certain cases, if there is no available donor for a patient, doctors will use umbilical cord blood that has been frozen and stored from healthy volunteers.  In this setting, the patient still has the potential of cure from their disease, but does not have the option of donor lymphocyte infusion at the time of relapse.  We are seeking to address the use of donor lymphocyte infusion from a healthy adult donor who matches the cord blood unit in order to treat relapse in this special group of patients.  This study will analyze the safety and efficacy of this strategy with the hopes that this will cure patients who otherwise have no option when they relapse after umbilical cord blood transplant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effet de la douleur sur l'acquisition et la rétention d'un apprentissage moteur
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTATION MOTRICE; APPRENTISSAGE MOTEUR; CHAMP DE FORCE; CONTROLE MOTEUR; DOULEUR; DOULEUR EXPERIMENTALE; LOCOMOTION; MARCHE; ROBOTIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: La douleur est une problematique vecue par environ une personne sur cinq dans la population canadienne. La prevalence de la douleur est d'autant plus importante chez plusieurs populations cliniques vues en readaptation physique. Plusieurs evidences suggerent que le pronostique fonctionnel des patients vivant avec de la douleur est plus sombre que celui d'individus ayant des deficiences semblables mais ne presentant pas de douleur. Un des facteurs pouvant expliquer cette situation serait une interference de la douleur avec le potentiel du systeme nerveux a effectuer les apprentissages moteurs necessaires a la readaptation. Les seules etudes ayant evalue l'effet de la douleur sur l'apprentissage moteur se sont interessees uniquement a l'amelioration de la performance lors d'une seule seance d'entrainement. Par contre, un apprentissage moteur implique une retention des capacites acquises au dela de la periode d'entrainement. L'objectif de l'etude proposee dans cette demande de bourse est d'evalue l'effet de la douleur experimentale et clinique sur l'acquisition d'un apprentissage moteur et sa retention 24 heure apres l'entrainement.  Trente sujets sains mois participeront a cette etude. La moitie de ces sujets recevront une stimulation douleureuse lors de l'acquisition de l'apprentissage moteur. Par ailleurs, trente patients ayant subi une fracture de la cheville depuis au moins trois, dont la moitie ressentira encore de la douleur au moment de l'etude. L'ensemble des sujets effectueront une tache d'adaptation a une perturbation durant la marche lors de deux journees consecutives. Des variables decrivant le mouvement de la cheville et l'activation des muscles impliques dans la tache seront mesurees afin de documenter l'effet de la douleur sur l'acquisition (jour 1) et la retention (jour 2) de l'apprentissage. Ce projet de recherche nous permettra d'adapter les pratiques de readaptation offertes aux Canadiens presentant des deficiences motrices et de la douleur.

TitreApplicationTitle: Validity, reliability and usability of a tool for appraising the methodological quality of qualitative, quantitative and mixed studies
Keywords-MotsClés: CRITICAL ASSESSMENT TOOL; E-DELPHI; MIXED METHODS; RELIABILITY; SYSTEMATIC MIXED STUDIES REVIEW; UMBRELLA REVIEW; USABILITY; VALIDITY
Abstract-Résumé: Systematic reviews of the scientific literature are an important source on which clinicians and decision makers can rely to get reliable and valid information. Systematic reviews follow a rigorous process in which research studies are identified, selected, appraised, and synthesized. Typically, these reviews have given preference to combining similar quantitative research methods. However, more and more researchers are interested in a new form of literature review known as Mixed Studies Review (MSR). MSR combines different types of research (qualitative, quantitative, and/or mixed studies) and allows reviewers to obtain in-depth answers to complex research questions. For example, whilst looking for evidence of effectiveness of an intervention from quantitative research, evidence from qualitative research can provide insight into internal and external factors that may explain why and how an intervention works. One challenge of MSRs is the difficulty to critically appraise the quality of studies since they are of different types. To overcome this challenge, an appraisal tool was developed: the Mixed Method Appraisal Tool (MMAT). The MMAT proposes criteria for appraising the methodological quality of different types of studies. The present project will pursue the development of the MMAT, and ensures that it has enough items and that they adequately covers the methodological quality of studies included in MSRs (content validity), that similar measures are obtained if used by different raters (inter-rater reliability), and that it is usable in practice. To pursue this tool's development and validation, a review of the literature will be conducted, a panel of international experts will be mobilized, and raters will be recruited. Also, a web-application of the MMAT will be created for usability testing and dissemination. The MMAT may become a standard critical appraisal tool that will be used to improve the quality of information in MSRs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deliberative Justice: Ethical, Evidence-informed Policy on Pediatric Cancer Care in Low-and Middle-income Countries
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD CANCER; DELIBERATIVE PROCESS; ETHICS OF PRIORITY SETTING; EVIDENCE; GLOBAL HEALTH; HEALTH POLICY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LOW-INCOME COUNTRIES; QUALITATIVE METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: Life expectancy in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) has not kept pace with the steady advances in scientific knowledge and technology witnessed over the past half century.  Even so, many countries have achieved impressive reductions in maternal and infant mortality.  Paradoxically, worsening LMIC mortality from chronic, non-communicable diseases (NCDs) - cancer foremost among them - has paralleled these gains. The resultant double burden of infectious and non-communicable disease is placing enormous strain on many LMIC health systems, and provoking difficult questions about how to allocate scarce resources amongst competing health system priorities.  This research will examine the intersection of these three crucial global health problems: the gaps between scientific knowledge and health policies, fundamental ethical questions about how to allocate scarce health care resources, and the mounting global toll of NCDs. It will take childhood cancer - one of the prime killers of children in high- and low-income countries alike, and a mounting problem in LMICs specifically - as its lens, both due to the gravity of the problem and the unconscionable gulf in outcomes between high- and low-income countries.  The research aims to facilitate and evaluate a unique process for ethically sound, evidence-informed policymaking on pediatric cancer care, in the hopes of strengthening both policy on pediatric cancer care and processes for fair and effective allocation of resources in LMICs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Food addiction: studies of bio-behavioural links between nutrition and obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; GENE EXPRESSION; HIGH FRUCTOSE CORN SYRUP; INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES; MICROARRAY; OBESITY; SELF-ADMINISTRATION
Abstract-Résumé: High caloric diets are primary causes of overweight and obesity, conditions that increase risk of type 2 diabetes. Biological factors play an important role in excessive consumption of unhealthy foods and there is evidence that some foods can act on the brain and body in ways comparable to those of addictive drugs. The "food addiction and obesity" hypothesis leads to two predictions. First, as in the case of drugs of abuse, individual differences/susceptibilities must play a key role in the development of excessive behaviors. Second, alterations in hypothalamic genes involved in the regulation of motivation as well as food intake and energy balance can predict the development of individual differences in escalation of caloric intake leading to obesity. Laboratory rats will be employed to investigate these predictions. More specifically, behavioural, physiological, and gene expression (candidate and global) studies will be conducted in animals trained to self- administer high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener associated to human obesity. The results of these studies will improve our understanding of critical bio-behavioural links between nutrition and obesity. Understanding the addictive nature of behaviours reinforced by sweets, and the underlying neurobiology of fructose addiction, are two important steps in reducing risk of obesity and obesity-related comordibities like cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: What components matter most in secondary prevention interventions for coronary heart disease?: Better data for better knowledge usage
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS; CARDIAC; DISEASE MANAGEMENT; EVIDENCE USAGE; EXERCISE; HEART; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PREVENTION; REHABILITATION; TAXONOMY
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding which characteristics of health services interventions most influence the effectiveness of these interventions is useful for health professionals. It allows them to ensure that the interventions they provide incorporate some or all of these characteristics.   This synthesis focuses on interventions that seek to improve health behaviours in people with heart disease. This is vital for the future of Canada's health system because heart disease is the country's biggest cause of death and disability.  In particular, it aims to identify what interventions characteristics are associated with better outcomes. To do this we will use a taxonomy (INSPECT) we have developed and systematic review methodology (meta-analysis).   We will search for published trials of different kinds of interventions - such as those provided in hospitals, homes or community settings. We will then classify the characteristics using our taxonomy. Where needed we will survey paper authors to find out what the characteristics are of interventions they have evaluated. This will help us identify which characteristics are linked to better outcomes.  We will then disseminate this knowledge across Canada to program providers from different health disciplines via a variety of means, including workshops, YouTube videos, presentations and summaries. We will harness influential knowledge users on the team to do this.

TitreApplicationTitle: Scoping Review of Food Insecurity in the Health Care Setting
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE; FOOD INSECURITY; HEALTH CARE; SCOPING REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Adults living in food insecure households (i.e., those with insecure access to adequate food due to financial constraints) are more likely to report poor/fair health, physical limitations, mental health problems, diabetes mellitus, heart disease, and other chronic conditions. Health care practitioners caring for individuals of lower socioeconomic status are likely to encounter food insecure clients, yet with the exception of practices that focus on the most vulnerable populations such as the homeless, little attention is paid to the food access issues of those served. The implications of such a lack of attention are not merely a gap in information that might assist the care plan, but may add costs to the health system. The purpose of this scoping review is to identify the extent, range, and nature of research activity in the food insecurity area as it relates to practice in the health care setting. The scoping review will inform practitioner practices and a health care intervention study that seeks to address food insecurity in adult clients with chronic disease.  The team undertaking the scoping review has collaborated since 2007 on a variety of educational and applied research initiatives and the need for a scoping review arose from a major stakeholder consultation held in March 2012. Three research questions are posed to meet the purpose and intended use of the scoping review: 1) What studies have explored the prevalence of food insecurity in adults with chronic disease in a health care setting?; 2) What food insecurity assessment/screening tools have been utilized or tested in a health care setting?; and 3) What intervention strategies have been identified to provide clinical care, including therapeutic counselling, for food insecure adults with chronic disease accessing the health care system? Our methodology will consist of literature mapping using Levac et al's (2010) scoping review framework, based on Arskey and O'Malley's (2005) approach.

TitreApplicationTitle: Thiopurine S-methyltransferase testing for averting drug toxicity in pediatric patients receiving thiopurines: An application of enhanced meta-analysis of diagnostic tests
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA; COST-EFFECTIVENESS ANALYSIS; DIAGNOSTIC TESTING; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; META-ANALYSIS; PHARMACOGENETIC TESTING; SENSITIVITY AND SPECIFICITY; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW; THIOPURINE S-METHYLTRANSFERASE; THIOPURINES
Abstract-Résumé: Thiopurine drugs are used to treat children with severe chronic diseases, such as leukemia and inflammatory bowel disease. Approximately 11 percent of the population have an alteration in their genes that causes a defect in the enzyme TPMT which does not allow them to break down these drugs. Unless thiopurine doses are reduced in these patients, they are at greater risk of severe and potentially life-threatening bone marrow toxicity, anemia, bleeding, and infection. Therefore, it is important to identify patients with this enzyme deficiency. Laboratory tests that measure drug metabolizing enzyme activity have traditionally been used. With advances in genomic research, it is now possible to use genetic testing to identify patients with TPMT deficiencies. First-line testing with either strategy is costly compared to a 'dose and monitor for symptoms' approach. Clinical and policy decision-makers have asked for guidance regarding which diagnostic test strategy is most appropriate and cost-effective.  The study objectives are to:  1.Systematically review the literature on the performance characteristics of enzyme activity and genetic testing approaches. 2.To perform an enhanced analysis of the performance characteristics of these tests by addressing issues that hampered previous work. 3.To determine the cost-effectiveness of various approaches to testing and to use this information to interpret test results in a more meaningful way  The results of this study will be incorporated in clinical practice guidelines for clinicians to guide practice as to which testing approach is more effective. Findings will also be shared with provincial policy makers and laboratories requiring evidence of relative cost-effectiveness. Finally, the findings will also be important for researchers in health technology assessment who require guidance on the most appropriate methods for synthesizing evidence of diagnostic test performance characteristics.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Management of Bone Disease in Chronic Kidney Disease: A Systematic Review
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINE; KNOWLEDGE SYNTHESIS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAM; OSTEOPOROSIS; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Aging is associated with decreases in bone health and worsening kidney function. As a result, osteoporosis or "thinning of the bones" and kidney disease are common conditions in older men and women. Even though there are a large number of Canadians with both conditions there is a knowledge gap - patients and doctors do not have published recommendations on how to best manage these conditions. Our project will fill-in this knowledge gap by summarizing the research that has been published on men and women with kidney disease at high risk for having a broken bone and review the treatments that can be used to prevent other broken bones. This project will provide guidance to men and women with kidney disease and bone disease as well as doctors taking care of these patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Crohn's Disease genetic variants predispose to commensal-driven autoinflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOINFLAMMATION; AUTOPHAGY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INNATE IMMUNE RESPONSE; SHIP; SINGLE NUCLOETIDE POLYMORPHISMS; SUSCEPTIBILITY SNPS
Abstract-Résumé: Crohn's Disease  is an incurable chronic disease cause by inflammation along the gastrointestinal tract.  The inflammation leads to life-long symptoms that include abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea.  Disease is managed in people with Crohn's Disease by blocking inflammatory responses.  However, drugs currently available are not effective in about 10% of people with Crohn's Disease and we predict that they will eventually stop working for up to 30% of people with Crohn's Disease.  New treatments are urgently needed.      For most people, one gene does not cause disease, but genetic studies have taught us that small changes in many different genes can cause changes in gene functions that make some people more likely to develop disease.  Even though we have identified 71 different genes associated with Crohn's Disease, we do not know how they contribute to inflammation.  Stuart Turvey's and Laura Sly's research laboratories at BC Children's Hospital, University of British Columbia, have joined forces to investigate the role of specific Crohn's Disease genes in inflammation.  We have identified one gene that leads to increased inflammatory responses and key proteins that regulate that response.  In our next steps, we are going to examine all of the genes in that gene family that have been associated with Crohn's Disease (6 in total) to see if they also lead to the same inflammatory response.  These studies will allow us to identify a group of people with Crohn's Disease that have a specific inflammatory signature.  Excitingly, these people may be treatable with a drug that is already used in the clinic to treat people with inflammatory diseases, but which has never been used to treat Crohn's Disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Depression and Multiple Sclerosis: A Systematic Review
Keywords-MotsClés: DEPRESSION; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is common in multiple sclerosis (MS).  Fully half of MS patients can expect to be depressed at some point in their lives.  This compares with 10-15% in the general population, and 15-25% in other serious diseases such as heart disease and cancer.  Although depression in MS has received a good deal of attention in the published literature, findings and conclusions of studies are often conflicting.  Uncertainty remains about why rates of depression are so high in this population.  Questions also remain about the relative importance of physical, psychological and social/environmental factors in the cause and prognosis of depression in MS.  Thus, to clarify the existing evidence on depression in MS and to appraise and synthesize our current knowledge in this area, we are proposing a systematic review of the literature in this area to answer the following questions.  How common is depression in persons with MS and what are the physical, psychological and social/environmental risk factors for becoming depressed?  How does depression affect health and well-being outcomes in persons with MS?  We also want to identify gaps in our knowledge about depression in MS.  By systematically searching for the available studies, critically appraising those studies and drawing conclusions based on the best evidence, researchers can move forward purposefully by filling in the gaps in knowledge.  At the same time, clinicians can use what is known to identify those most likely to develop depression, and to work towards successful prevention and management of depression in MS.  Finally, those with MS will better understand whether they are at risk of developing depression, and they and their families will have better knowledge of how to prevent and or manage depression.

Abstract-Résumé: It has been shown that brain injuries could contribute to neuronal cell death and learning and memory deficits. Our preliminary study indicates that the expression of a subset of genes was altered after head injuries and the changes might contributes to the development of Alzheimer's disease. This proposal is to define epigenetic modification effect of brain injuries on gene expression leading to dementia and its underlying mechanism. The results could provide insights into the role of traumatic brain injuries in neurodegeneration and learning and memory dysfunction, which is fundamentally important to develop novel ways to prevent and treat brain injury-associated Alzheimer's disease-related dementia.

Keywords-MotsClés: AMBIENT AIR POLLUTANTS; BIOMARKERS OF ENVIRONMENTAL EXPOSURE; CADMIUM; CHRONIC METABOLIC BONE DISORDERS; GENE EXPRESSION; GENE METHYLATION; GEOGRAPHIC VARIATIONS IN INCIDENCE; HEAVY METALS; PAGET'S DISEASE OF BONE; SQSTM1 MUTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Paget's disease of bone (PDB) is the second most frequent bone disorder after osteoporosis, affecting approximately 3% of people over 55 years of age. Disabling complications of PDB, such as bone deformity, bone pain and fractures, occur in about 30% of PDB patients. PDB is caused by over-activity of osteoclasts, bone cells that remove bone tissue. In one-third of cases, PDB is a genetic disorder with a 50% risk of developing the disease for direct relatives of an affected individual. Genetic research in the French-Canadian population allowed us to identify the first mutation, called P392L, within a gene termed the SQSTM1 gene, in more than 40% of families with PDB. Nevertheless, experiments in cell cultures and in mice models have shown that this SQSTM1/P392L mutation may predispose a person to PDB, although possible environmental factors may be required for the complete development of the disease. In this study, we will determine how environmental factors may modulate the expression of the SQSTM1/P392L mutation and the disease severity in patients with PDB, using molecular biology experiments and a questionnaire. In addition, using Quebec Health Care administrative databases, we will determine the geographic variation of PDB incidence in the province of Quebec and correlate geographic variations in the occurrence of PDB new cases to long-term exposure to ambient air pollutants. The identification of interactions of genes with environmental factors will have a significant impact on the understanding of molecular mechanisms of PDB, of bone remodelling in general, and of other increasingly common metabolic bone diseases in our aging population, such as osteoporosis and bone cancers. The detection of environmental factors with significant impact on bone remodelling should also give rise to primary prevention recommendations in common late-onset bone diseases, such as osteoporosis, and should contribute to decrease the economic burden of these chronic disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: A systematic review of process evaluations in knowledge translation
Keywords-MotsClés: BLACK BOX; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PROCESS EVALUATIONS; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Knowledge translation is taking knowledge from research and using it in real-world practice. This is a vital strategy to improve health outcomes and strengthen our health care system for the benefit of all Canadians. Knowledge translation (KT) strategies are often used to help put research knowledge into daily practice. Traditional methods of studying KT strategies have provided some insight into their effectiveness, but these approaches offer little understanding of how the KT strategy was put into practice, if the strategy worked or not, or how different factors may have influenced this process. This means that applying these strategies to new settings, organizations or clinical problems is difficult. As a result, researchers are now exploring and evaluating the features of KT strategies and the process of putting them into practice through process evaluation studies. This is necessary to identify the most effective KT strategies and overcome the barriers to practice change in health care. Currently there are no standards to guide process evaluations. Thus, a better understanding and standardized process evaluation design is urgently needed. We aim to 'take stock' of current research approaches by conducting a systematic review of completed process evaluations. The goal of our systematic review is to develop recommendations for designing future process evaluations in knowledge translation.

TitreApplicationTitle: The endogenous microbiota and Th17 cells in abdominal aortic aneurysm
Keywords-MotsClés: ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM; GENOMICS; IL-17; MICROBIOTA; T CELL; VASCULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) are a major cause of sudden death in North America.  This disease is caused by immune-mediated damage and resultant rupture of the aorta, a large artery that runs from the heart down the abdominal cavity.  The bacteria that colonize the intestine are collectively referred to as the gut microbiota and they are known to control immune responses.  In this catalyst grant, we will study how the gut microbiota controls a type of immune response, termed Th17, and whether this plays a role in the development of AAA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interactions between dietary n-3 fatty acids and genetic variations on cardiovascular disease risk factors.
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSOCIATION STUDIES; GENE-DIET INTERACTIONS; METABOLOMICS; OMEGA-3 FATTY ACIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Several of the major chronic diseases, such as cardiovascular disease (CVD), hypertension, diabetes, obesity, and cancer have hereditary and environmental causes. Therefore, preventive measures may help to reduce the prevalence of these diseases. Diet is a major aspect of environment that could be targeted in the prevention of these diseases. Among dietary factors, PUFAs of the n-3 (or omega-3) family have multiple beneficial effects on CVD risks. The omega-3 of particular interest with respect to CVD are found in fatty fish and other marine sources. A large body of literature has evolved over the past several years demonstrating the beneficial effects of omega-3 on CVD risk factors. However, there are still discrepancies between study conclusions. Beside methodological differences between studies, genetic factors may play a role. This has been the topic of a systematic review into which the authors came to the conclusion that the effect of omega-3 on CVD risk factors is highly variable depending on genetic factors. We have been interested in this phenomenon since many years and in the present research program we propose to pursue the investigation of gene-diet interaction effects on CVD risk factors in the INFOGENE Study by studying a new list of candidate genes derived from expression profiling experiments performed by our group.

TitreApplicationTitle: Early life nutrition, antibiotics, infection and bacterial sensing regulate diabesity
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSE TISSUE; ANTIBIOTICS; BACTERIA; DIABESITY; DIABETES; INFECTION; INFLAMMATION; INSULIN RESISTANCE; MICROBIOTA; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Over one quarter of Canadian children are obese. Over half of Canadian children are prescribed antibiotics. Antibiotic use has recently been implicated in obesity later in life.   Obesity significantly reduces the quality of life in childhood and increases the risk of diabetes and life threatening cardiovascular disease in adulthood. Inflammation and the huge number of bacteria that always live on us have emerged as important factors in causing these diseases during obesity. However, we know very little about the how environmental factors (such as drugs and bacteria) could contribute to obesity. The job of some of our genes is to control the bacteria that live of us and make sure it is not harmful. Bacterial infection still occurs and we often use antibiotics as a treatment. These factors change the bacteria that live in our gut and may contribute to metabolic disease.   We were the first to show that immune sensors for specific parts of bacterial cell wall regulate inflammation and metabolism during obesity. We have now discovered that deletion of a bacterial sensor (NOD2) allows bacteria to escape the gut and invade fat tissue. This contributes to inflammation, obesity, and pre-diabetes. We also have discovered that obesity reduces a type of (Th17-mediated) immunity in the gut. Without this immune response, we cannot properly control the type of bacteria that grows in the gut. These are 2 ways bacteria in our gut play a role in metabolic disease. However, we need to understand how early life bacterial infection and the antibiotics used to treat these infections may interact to promote obesity and diabetes.  This research sets the stage for testing how childhood antibiotic use and eating high fat diet work together to promote obesity-related disease, such as diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Needle Fears in Children undergoing Medical Procedures: Knowledge Synthesis, Practice Guidelines, and Dissemination Strategies
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINE; EVIDENCE-BASED MEDICINE; KNOWLEDGE SYNTHESIS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MANAGEMENT; MEDICAL PROCEDURES; NEEDLE FEAR; PREVENTION; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Painful medical procedures involving needles such as immunizations and blood draws are common in childhood and a sources of immense fear. By the time a child is school-age, he/she will have experienced upwards of 2 dozen immunization injections alone. About 2/3 of childrne and 1/4 of adults have needle fears. Needle fears usually develop in childhood and are associated with health care avoidance behaviours in childhood and throughout the lifespan (e.g., avoidance of immunization, dental visits,, insulin injections for diabetes). This results in an increassed burden of disease and disease-related complications, including death, in people affected by needle fear. The genereal public may also be affected; for instance, there may be outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases due to redued herd immunity. Preventing and managing needle fear is therefore highly relevant to clinical practice and long-term health outcomes. There are no published summaries to guide clinical practice. It is unknown which interventions reduce fear in children and if fear can be prevented through consistent fear and/or pain management. The current project with address this important issue by: 1) performing a series of systematic reviews for interventions aimed at preventing and managing needle fears in chihldren, 2) developing a clinical practice guideline on this topic, and 3) developing evidence-based educational tools for widespread dissemination and implementation in collaboration with stakeholders across the country. This project builds on our Help ELiminate Pain in KIDs (HELPinKIDS) Team's previously successful CIHR-funded work in the area of immunizaiton pain management in children.

TitreApplicationTitle: A realist synthesis addressing early childhood programs combining a social determinants and community based public health approach with an individuals' clinical primary care.
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PRIMARY CARE; COMMUNITY BASED; EARLY CHILDHOOD DEVELOPMENT; INTEGRATION; PROGRAM FACTORS; PUBLIC HEALTH; REALIST SYNTHESIS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SOCIAL PEDIATRICS; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Background:The conditions in which early childhood development occurs affect both physical & psychosocial aspects of health and can damage a developing brain, leading to life-long problems in learning, behavior, physical & mental health. A social paediatrics approach integrates clinical primary care (CPC) programs with public health (PH), through a community-based, determinants of health lens. Objectives:This realist synthesis will identify program theory(s) and associated mechanisms that lead to successful integration between CPC,  PH and community resources in child health. We will 1) identify integrated PH-CPC programs focused on integration with a determinants of health lens 2) understand the local context in which these projects are being developed & implemented 3) determine facilitators and barriers to the program 4) produce an explanatory program model to aid decision makers to develop & plan integrated approaches to child public health. Methods & Analysis:With a realist-informed approach to systematic review, we will develop and test program theories using an iterative approach, incl. mapping an explanatory model, establishing conceptual definitions, searching for program theory(s), and evidence to test them. Quality appraisal will include methodology of chosen studies, & quality of program description (thick or thin). Data extraction & synthesis will be iterative and support, weaken, modify the preliminary theory. Impact:This research will inform an explanatory program model that will allow PH practitioners, community leaders and policy makers to better understand PH-CPC programs for planning and implementation of early childhood programs and policies.  This could improve the health care experience for children through increased comprehensiveness, inclusiveness and engagement, and improve the conditions in which early childhood development occurs, by ameliorating risk factors that damage a developing brain, leading to a healthier, more successful generation

TitreApplicationTitle: Environmental Microbe-Gene Interactions: Role of Host Epigenetics in Chronic Urinary Tract Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA; CHRONIC DISEASE; E.COLI; EPIGENETICS; FACS; METHYLTRANSFERASE; MOUSE; PREDICTION; PROGENITOR CELLS; RECURRENT URINARY TRACT INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is the most common non-communicable human bacterial infection, affecting over 9 million patients annually in North America, accounting for 1.2% of all physician office visits. After initial UTI, 25% of patients experience recurrent urinary tract infection (rUTI), creating a significant burden of chronic disease. No underlying pathogenic mechanisms have been defined for rUTI. While the high prevalence of rUTI suggests a non-genetic process may be at play, the predilection for chronic UTI in a specific minority of patients suggests host tissues undergo unique and lasting biological changes that promote infection recurrence. Our goal is to provide new knowledge on how the bacterial environment interacts with the biological gene machinery of the host to promote recurrent infection.  Our lab is the first to identify that bacteria can incite lasting changes in the genetic machinery --termed epigenetic changes--in the host uro-epithelial cells lining the urinary tract. These cells are the first line of defense to infection. These exciting experiments were done in cultured cells, and now motivate the major question of whether this process occurs in living animals or in patients. In this proposal, we will use E. coli. to create urinary tract infection in mice. After infection, we will a use a novel approach to isolate specific uroepithelial cell types from the mouse bladder to assess whether epigenetic changes occur that  have lasting effects in uroepithelial cell defences mechanisms. We will also genetically breed mice so that we may selectively turn off the epigenetic machienryu in their uroeputhelial cells before or during a first UTI. Any change in how the mice respond to re-infection will suggest that infect-induced epigenetic mechanisms play a role in re-infection. We are exploiting a novel concept that host cell-specific mechanisms may predict rUTI, and may be targeted as an alternative to antibiotics to treat rUTI in patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stroke Rehabilitation and Patients with Multimorbidity: A Scoping Review
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES; LITERATURE MAPPING; MULTIMORBIDITY; SCOPING REVIEW; STROKE REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is a complex health event due to the wide range of possible resulting physical and cognitive impairments. Stroke care presents challenges for rehabilitation clinicians, as most strokes occur with other serious medical diagnoses. A recent assessment of organizational strengths and weaknesses for implementing best practice stroke care found that clinicians reported a strong need for education and training regarding patient and system complexity and multimorbidity (two or more chronic conditions).   Preliminary data from a study conducted at Bridgepoint found that rehabilitation clinicians question the applicability of the best practices to their patients and rely on their sound clinical judgment, teamwork and creativity to develop care plans for multimorbid patients. The purpose of this proposed scoping review is to assess and document how multimorbidity is addressed in stroke rehabilitation research and identify the associated gaps in research. The proposed review is part of a stroke rehabilitation and multimorbidity research program that began at Bridgepoint in 2011.   This project is being undertaken in collaboration with the Ontario Stroke Network and the Stroke Rehabilitation Evidence Based Review, two organizations involved in the development and dissemination of the Canadian Stroke Care Best Practice Recommendations. The results from this review will be valuable for researchers, clinicians, and policy makers concerned with stroke rehabilitation by expanding the understanding of the current evidence, identifying where evidence pertaining to stroke rehabilitation and multimorbid patients exists, and noting where further research is needed. Although this study is designed to assess the stroke rehabilitation intervention evidence specifically, the project methodology and study findings will be applicable to other clinical programs that provide care to patients with multiple chronic conditions (ie. geriatrics, primary health care, diabetes).

TitreApplicationTitle: Translating the pathophysiological details of diabetes mellitus, including the molecular function of Sulfonylureas drugs in the treatment of the disease state,  into accessible visualizations for patients and non-patients to increase disease understanding and motivate citizens to adopt improved diets, exercise regimens and better prescription drug adherence practices.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; DIABETES MELLITUS; HEALTH COMMUNICATION; HEALTH EDUCATION; INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY; MOLECULAR IMAGING; PUBLIC HEALTH AND OUTREACH; SULFONYLUREAS; VISUALIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes mellitus is a life-threatening disease that is unfortunately often dismissed as a minor health issue by many Canadians. Our population needs to be informed about the harmful consequences that diabetes, a disease affecting glucose metabolism, can have on the body. Furthermore, citizens must understand that this disease, which is a major burden to health care, can be readily managed or circumvented altogether through healthy living practices. Communications presenting the biological details about diabetes, how drugs treat the disease, and the importance of healthy living could positively alter the way Canadian citizens view this deadly disease. My project focuses on producing medically accurate communications describing the biological causes of diabetes. Given the many unanswered questions about how to best communicate complex ideas to lay audiences, these communications will vary in their content and will be surveyed for their effectiveness at conveying the severity of diabetes. Furthermore, I will utilize Maya 3D animation software and incorporate feedback received from initial communications to properly visualize the consequences of allowing diabetes to run rampant. In particular, I will produce vivid, step-by-step animations on how diabetes causes cardiovascular disease, particularly atherosclerosis. These new communications will also be evaluated for their efficiency. Furthermore, reluctant patients may be more inclined to take appropriate medications if they knew how the drug works on a biological level. Animations will supplement previous work by detailing how drugs treat the disease state at both molecular and biological levels. Sulfonylureas, drugs that stimulate the release of insulin from the pancreas, will serve as the example drug. The results from this study could help inform the public and may lessen the burden diabetes will have on the Canadian health care system.
