TitreApplicationTitle: Cryobiology and Preservation of Cells and Tissues
Keywords-MotsClés: AMNIOTIC MEMBRANE; CELLS AND TISSUES FOR TRANSPLANT; COMPUTER MODELLING; CORNEA; CRYOBIOLOGY; CRYOPRESERVATION; ENDOTHELIAL MONOLAYERS; EYE AND SKIN SURGERY; NON-LINEAR COOLING; THERMODYNAMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Cryobiology is the study of the effects of extremely low temperatures on biological systems. A major application is the low-temperature storage (cryopreservation) of cells and tissues for transplantation to treat injury and disease, and for research. While many cell types have been successfully cryopreserved and used clinically for decades, some cells and the vast majority of tissues encounter significant problems during cryopreservation. For example, a widely transplanted tissue is cornea, the clear tissue of the eye through which people see. The endothelial monolayer is a layer of cells on the inner surface of the cornea that is critical to the health of the cornea and understood to be a limitation for cryopreservation techniques. Individual corneal endothelial cells can be cryopreserved in suspension. However, the endothelial monolayer of cells in the cornea cannot be adequately cryopreserved without considerable cell loss resulting in loss of cornea function. This prevents the routine transplantation of cryopreserved corneas. Similarly, amniotic membrane is a tissue discarded after childbirth. While amniotic membrane is currently cryopreserved and used in surgeries of the eye and skin, an understanding of the cryobiology of this tissue is required to effectively cryopreserve larger pieces of this tissue for expanded clinical use. As cellular therapies and transplant of both natural and engineered tissue are increasingly used in modern medicine, there is an urgent need for effective cryopreservation strategies. The objective of this proposal is to combine advanced engineering modeling, cryobiological expertise, and biological experimentation to develop key understanding of identified issues in cell and tissue cryopreservation with immediate application to corneas and amniotic membrane. Proposed experiments will use cultured cells, animal tissue that is normally discarded during meat production, and human tissue that is normally discarded after childbirth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Human rights, post-2015 health development goals and universal health coverage: Defining the minimum core of the right to health to advance essential global health needs
Keywords-MotsClés: ESSENTIAL HEALTH NEEDS; GLOBAL HEALTH; HEALTH EQUITY; HUMAN RIGHTS; INTERNATIONAL LAW; LOW AND MIDDLE INCOME COUNTRIES; MILLENNIUM DEVELOPMENT GOALS; POST-2015 HEALTH DEVELOPMENT; RIGHT TO HEALTH; UNIVERSAL HEALTH COVERAGE
Abstract-Résumé: The right to health is recognized as providing key principles for developing health goals to replace the Millennium Development Goals that expire in 2015. However the right to health has a loophole that permits states to deny any level of health care on the basis of limited resources, including for the poorest and most vulnerable populations. International lawyers have tried to fix this problem by developing the idea of "minimum core obligations" to meet essential health needs that cannot be denied under any circumstances. Lawyers and policy-makers around the world have adopted this idea. However the use of this concept remains limited because the  definition of minimum core obligations fails to specify the health needs it covers. It  also fails to specify the obligations of wealthier countries to assist poor countries to meet core obligations. These gaps in the definition limit the ability of the right to health to protect people's health against government inaction and cuts in international health funding.   We propose filling this gap by analyzing how courts and scholars around the world have interpreted this concept, and using this analysis to strengthen the definition of minimum core obligations.This research will help support the development of rights-based health development goals to replace the Millennium Development Goals. It will also help judges assess whether governments are fulfilling the right to health, policy-makers to implement equitable health policy, and social groups to claim their rights more effectively.

Abstract-Résumé: Clinical trials involve exposing patients to drugs that have uncertain therapeutic value.  They are also very expensive and complicated to run.  Protecting patients in trials, and using limited research resources wisely, requires that researchers have realistic expectations about outcomes in their trials.  This study will determine whether researchers and experts who review trials are able to predict favorable trial outcomes, and whether they are good at anticipating logistical challenges. We will further explore how researchers anticipate outcomes and logistic challenges, and use our findings to develop recommendations for improving human protections.

TitreApplicationTitle: A shared understanding? Attitudes and experiences of stakeholders to newborn screening consent practices and implications for policy and practice
Keywords-MotsClés: EQUITY; EXPERIENCE; HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS; INFORMED CONSENT; INTERVIEWS; LATENT CLASS ANALYSIS; MIXED METHODS; NEWBORN SCREENING; PARENTS; POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: Newborn screening (NBS) is the program through which babies are screened for a variety of conditions shortly after birth. In Canada, NBS generally proceeds on an implied consent basis,  yet to date there has been little research assessing the impact of attitudes to consent practices on stakeholder experiences of the consent process. Do individuals, and particular groups of individuals, view and experience the consent process for NBS differently? If so, where are the differences and how do individuals or groups differ? This is important as NBS is not without the potential for harm - such as distress or impaired parent child bonding. Research suggests that these harms may be worsened if parents do not feel informed or do not understand NBS. If consent practices to screening are experienced inequitably, these harms may also be born unfairly. The overall aim of this project is to inform NBS policy and practice regarding consent processes for newborn screening in Canada by exploring the attitudes and experiences of parents, healthcare professionals, and policy decision-makers. This research is arranged in two parts. The first stage involves interviews to explore stakeholder views and experiences of consent practices for newborn screening. The second stage involves a survey based on stage one that will be sent to parents and healthcare professionals. We will analyze responses to look for groups with shared attitudes towards consent and experiences of participating in newborn screening. This study will present the first empirical data comparing stakeholder attitudes and experiences of consent to NBS. This is highly relevant with the expansion of screening panels and initiatives to introduce whole genome/exome sequencing technologies to NBS. The results will also inform the development of interventions to mitigate any inequities in parent decision-making about NBS.

TitreApplicationTitle: The roles of MBNL proteins in the pathogenesis of myotonic dystrophy
Keywords-MotsClés: MBNL1; MRNA LOCALIZATION; MYOTONIC DYSTROPHY; PATHOGENESIS; RNA AGGREGATION
Abstract-Résumé: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is caused by an expansion of CUG-triplet repeats in the DMPK mRNA. The RNA-binding protein Muscleblind-like 1 (MBNL1) binds the UGCU motif in RNA and it is involved in the aggregation of mutant CUG-repeat RNA into nuclear foci. MBNL1 also has several normal functions in the cell; as an alternative splicing factor, and as a regulator of the cytoplasmic localization of mRNA. Non-disease mRNA bound by MBNL1 do not form nuclear foci, and it is not understood why MBNL1 causes the nuclear retention and aggregation of CUG-repeat mRNA. In this project, a team of three investigators will use live-cell microscopy, purification of RNA aggregates and biochemical approaches to elucidate the mechanism of MBNL1 and CUG-repeat RNA aggregate formation in DM1, and also define the role of MBNL1 in cytoplasmic mRNA localization. This work will provide important insights into the mechanisms of toxic RNA aggregate formation, the process through which they perturb the functions of MBNL factors, as well as the ensuing impact on the intracellular trafficking of key MBNL1 target mRNAs. Understanding these pathways will allow the development of new drugs to inhibit the nuclear retention of the mutant DMPK mRNA in DM1 patients or that help to restore the normal localization properties of mistargeted cellular mRNAs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulating Disease-Associated Repeat Instability
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA MUTATIONS; DNA REPAIR; DNA REPLICATION; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; MISMATCH REPAIR; MYOTONIC DYSTROPHY; TRINUCLETOIDE REPEAT INSTABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Modulating disease-associated repeat instability 40 human diseases, including myotonic dystrophy & Huntington's disease are inherited in a manner that the symptoms become more evident through family generations. These diseases also become worse as the individual ages.  These diseases are caused by mutations in repeated DNAs. If one considers a gene as though it were a sentence such as THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT RAT, typical mutations would be spelling errors, like THE GAT ATE THE FAT FAT RAT. This mutation would be the same in all family members, all with the same symptoms. However, in repeat-associated diseases the mutation would be THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT RAT, and their children would inherit a further mutation; THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT RAT and have more severe disease than their parents. Importantly, these mutations can also continue through the life of the patient in affected tissues; progressively getting larger making symptoms worse as they age.  My research focuses on understanding this mutation with the long-term goal of being able to modulate this mutation to treat affected families. Being able to arrest or reverse this repeat mutation (reducing or preventing the expansion of the number of "FAT" repeat units) presents a therapeutic pathway to reduce disease progression and severity. The mutation of DNA repeats in these diseases occurs by mistakes during repair of damaged DNA.  We identified a set of proteins that are required to drive the expansions of the disease-causing repeats.  Blocking these proteins should block the expansion of the repeats. Specifically with regard to myotonic dystrophy we will identify drugs that can beneficially modulate this disease causing mutation which highlights novel avenues aimed at therapeutic treatment by arresting or reversing the expansion mutations (THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT RAT.....down to.... THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT RAT.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aboriginal youth living with HIV: From diagnosis to learning to manage their health and lives
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL YOUTH  WITH HIV/AIDS; ECOMAPS; EXPERIENCES AND NEEDS; FOCUS GROUP INTERVIEWS; HEALTH AND SOCIAL SERVICE CARE PROVIDERS; HEALTH SERVICES; INTERVIEWS; PHENOMENOLOGY; PHOTOVOICE; SUPPORT PERSON(S)
Abstract-Résumé: Receiving a diagnosis of HIV changes your life; learning to cope and adjust to the diagnosis and the early years following can be challenging. Moreover, Aboriginal youth often face these challenges alone due to fear of stigma and discrimination, and they are less likely to access services. If we hope to provide both timely and appropriate interventions for Aboriginal youth living with HIV from diagnosis to the early years of living with HIV, research is needed that details their experiences and perspectives during the critical period of HIV diagnosis and early years following. The purpose of this study is to arrive at an increased understanding of the experiences and needs of Aboriginal youth living with HIV from diagnosis to the first five years of living with HIV. Primary participants are Aboriginal youth who have been have been living with HIV from one to up to six years following the diagnosis. Some of the ways we will collect information include interviews combined with photovoice, which is a process that involves Aboriginal youth taking photographs to document their experiences. Aboriginal youth's support person(s) and health and social service care providers will provide additional insights about the experiences and needs of Aboriginal youth living with HIV, and recommendations about services and programs offered to Aboriginal youth. The significance of this study is fourfold. First, new knowledge will emerge about the experiences and needs of Aboriginal youth living with HIV from diagnosis to the first five years of living with HIV. Second, this study will give a voice to those Aboriginal youth participating in the study. Third, the knowledge gleaned from this study may be used to improve quality and access to existing services and programs that are meant to enhance how Aboriginal youth manage and deal with HIV. Fourth, this study will provide a basis for future community-based intervention research directed at helping Aboriginal youth living with HIV.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CELL BIOLOGY; GENE FUNCTION; INTRAHEPATIC CHOLESTASIS; LIVER DISEASE OF FIRST NATIONS CHILDREN
Abstract-Résumé: We are a unique group that studies North American Indian childhood cirrhosis NAIC, a serious liver disease of First Nations children from NW Quebec. For this genetic disease, we mapped the gene Cirh1a, identified the mutation and developed a mutation test. Patients have a mutation that changes a single amino acid on both copies of the Cirh1a gene. Our current efforts are focused on the development of animal models to understand the function of the gene and the encoded protein, cirhin.  We have established that the gene is active during development and that in mouse, embryos lacking both copies of this recessive gene, die very early in gestation. Here we propose to develop a mouse with the same mutation as in the patients to shed light on the NAIC disease process and gene function. Our efforts have already brought tangible benefits to the health of First Nations, and we continue our efforts to understand this disease, with the focus of developing therapies to replace liver transplantation, the only treatment currently available

TitreApplicationTitle: Engaging Aboriginal Youth in Tobacco Prevention Using Social Media
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; EVALUATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; RISK COMMUNICATION; SMOKING; SOCIAL MEDIA; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: Smoking continues to be a serious health issue amongst Aboriginal peoples in Canada, and is of particular concern in youth.  Tobacco intervention programs targeted towards youth must be guided by youth to be effective.  Aboriginal youth are known to require different tobacco control strategies compared to non-Aboriginal youth. This research will explore if a social media intervention developed by Aboriginal youth (specifically videos to be available through YouTube) can be an effective means for encouraging smoking prevention and/or cessation amongst youth and others in Aboriginal communities.  Aboriginal students from a remote school in the Northwest Territories and an urban school in Edmonton will develop and produce videos on smoking.  The videos will be uploaded to YouTube, and the best video from each school determined through YouTube voting and a contest in their schools and other Aboriginal schools. Through using a participatory approach for intervention development, and targeting the types of media most accessed by youth, the outcomes of this project have the potential to significantly impact smoking prevention and/or cessation for Aboriginal youth. The longer-term impacts on the youth and their communities will be evaluated. Broad dissemination of the videos and process documentaries provides the opportunity to extend this impact from a local to national/global level.  It will also facilitate knowledge translation about the approach and outcomes that will help improve future programs and policies for Aboriginal youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Application of novel assays to quantify mucosal susceptibility to HIV and to define key mucosal targets during HIV transmission.
Keywords-MotsClés: ECTOCERVICAL BIOPSY; ENDOCERVICAL CYTOBRUSH SAMPLE; FEMALE GENITAL TRACT; GENITAL EXPLANTS; HIV PSEUDOVIRUS; HIV SUSCEPTIBILITY; KENYA
Abstract-Résumé: There is great variability in susceptibility from one person to another, and less than one in a hundred sexual exposures to HIV results in infection. In addition, some recent trial of methods to prevent HIV - including vaccines and microbicides - have actually increased HIV acquisition among trial participants for reasons that we do not fully understand. While we know that immune differences in the genital lining are an important determinant of whether a person is infected after a sexual HIV exposure, we don't know enough about these differences to be able to accurately assess a person's HIV risk. Therefore, the development of safe and non-invasive laboratory tests to estimate a person's susceptibility in the genital tract would be useful in clinical studies of new HIV prevention tools. We have developed a tool that we hope will be useful for this purpose,that only requires the collection of a genital sample similar to that used for a PAP test, and that can be run in a few hours. We aim to demonstrate that this new assay works, and to use the test to assess whether certain types of cell in the genital lining are preferred "targets" for HIV during sexual transmission. If so, then a microbicide or vaccine that specifically protects these cells could be a useful way to prevent HIV transmission.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of APOBEC-induced mutations of viral genomes on adaptive immunity in HIV+ individuals
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; HIV; IMMUNE RESPONSE; MUTATIONS; VIRAL EVOLUTION
Abstract-Résumé: APOBEC3 enzymes are expressed in cells that are targets of HIV infection.  These enzymes attack the DNA copy of HIV after it infects the cell.  Consequently, they restrict the replication of HIV in experimental systems that measure infection of cultured cells outside the body.   Therefore, APOBEC3s have been perceived as a first line of defense against viral replication, whilst more specific anti-HIV immunity takes weeks-months to develop. The discovery of these enzymes less than a decade ago led to the promise of new anti-viral therapies based on manipulating their activities.  On the other hand, it has recently become appreciated that the activity of APOBEC3s is actually subverted to a large extent by HIV towards its own benefit.  Thus, the role of A3G/F in HIV infection is more complex than heretofore appreciated.  We are interested in the impact of APOBEC3 activity on the recognition of HIV-infected helper T cells by anti-viral cytotoxic T cells, which is one of the most important facets of the anti-viral immune response.  To date, two studies have examine this role: One utilized a bioinformatics approach and reported that APOBEC3-induced mutations help HIV escape from the immune system, whist another study using mice found the opposite result. Because of their experimental design, both studies have inherent biases: the first towards detection of the pro-virus activities of APOBEC3s and the second towards the detection of their pro-immune system activities.  Importantly, the impact of APOBEC3-induced mutations on cytotoxic T cells in human patients has not been examined.  In this proposal, we aim to examine the extent and mechanisms through which APOBEC3-induced mutations modulate the immune response in HIV+ individuals.  Our results will inform us and other researchers whether modulating APOBEC3 activity can be an effective approach of HIV therapy, and if so, how to  modify their activity such that optimal gain goes to the immune system rather than the virus.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic determinants of HIV-1 acquisition in Kenyan men who have sex with men
Keywords-MotsClés: AFRICA; CORRELATES OF PROTECTION; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENETICS; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNE ACTIVATION; MARPS; MSM; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; SUSCEPTIBILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Certain groups of individuals are more at risk of acquiring and transmitting HIV than others, and evidence suggests that public health interventions that cater to these groups can be most effective at preventing HIV in a population. Marginalized groups include female sex workers, intravenous drug users, and men who have sex with men (MSM). MSM have been particularly neglected in sub-Saharan Africa; these men experience stigma due to the illegality of homosexuality in kenya and high rates of HIV infection. The subset of MSM who sell sex are even further marginalized. For this reason, we aim to understand the epidemiology, immunology, and genetics of HIV risk in this understudied population. We make use of a large HIV prevention and care program in Nairobi that has already made contact with and provided services to nearly 800 MSM. In preliminary studies we have high rates of HIV infection, and high rates of acquiring HIV, and a diversity of HIV risk taking behavior (approximately 1/3 use condoms all the time; more than 1/3 also have sex with women). This opportunity represents an important first step to the design of better HIV prevention strategies like vaccines or microbicides for this important population.

TitreApplicationTitle: A HIV Vaccine Targeting Protease Cleavage Sites
Keywords-MotsClés: A HIV VACCINE TARTING PROTEASE CLEAVAGE SITES; LOW DOSE VAGINAL SIVMAC251 CHALLENGE; MICE AND GUINEA PIGS; NANODELIVERY OF IMMUNOGENS; NONHUMAN PRIMATE AND SIVMAC239/251 MODEL; VESICULAR STOMATITIS VIRUS (VSV) VECTOR SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Currently, >25 million people have died of HIV/AIDS and 34 million are living with HIV/AIDS in the world. Medications have improved the quality of life and life expectancy of HIV-infected. However, for each person getting treatment, 2 or 3 become newly infected. A safe, effective and affordable vaccine is the only way to prevent new infections, save resources for prevention and treatment, and get control of the HIV epidemic. However, the normal vaccine approach has not worked for the HIV, which infects key cells in the immune system (the CD4 T cells) and new approaches are needed to develop a vaccine to prevent HIV infection. There are sex workers in Kenya who have been exposed to HIV but did not become infected. The information we learned from these people leads us to propose that an effective HIV vaccine should target key places in HIV instead of targeting the full HIV proteins. We have identified these key places as the sites where HIV generates infectious viral particles, the protease cleavage sites(PCS). The PCS are important because the enzyme that cuts proteins for the HIV virus, the protease, is responsible to produce HIV particles that can infect people. The protease has to bind 12 specific places in the HIV virus and conduct 12 separate cutting reactions to generate an infectious virus. If it can't bind to these places, the virus generated cannot infect the CD4 T cells. A vaccine that targets the 12 PCS could generate immune responses to force the virus to change itself, which would change these special cutting sites to result in a virus that can't infect people. In this study, we will compare the effect of a vaccine targeting the PCS in the HIV virus to a vaccine targeting two special proteins. We will test the protection that the vaccine provides against HIV infection and disease progression using a model system that includes Cynomolgus macaques and SIVmac251, a virus that is similar to HIV. This vaccine could be effective to prevent HIV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effets d'un programme préopératoire d'activité physique supervisée sur l'état de santé des personnes obèses en attente d'une chirurgie bariatrique
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITE PHYSIQUE; CHIRURGIE BARIATRIQUE; OBESITE
Abstract-Résumé: La chirurgie de l'obesite est la modalite la plus efficace de prevention et de traitement de l'obesite severe et de ses complications. Cependant, ces interventions pourraient etre optimisees par une prise en charge preoperatoire. L'objectif de cette etude est d'evaluer les effets d'un Programme d'Activite Physique  PreOperatoire (PAPPO) sur la sante des personnes en attente d'une chirurgie de l'obesite. Nous inclurons 70 sujets obeses candidats a cette chirurgie, qui seront randomises dans le groupe PAPPO et soins usuels, ou dans le groupe controle recevant uniquement les soins usuels de la Clinique medico-chirurgicale du traitement de l'obesite du CHUS (rencontres aux 8 semaines avec la dietetiste et la kinesiologue). Le groupe PAPPO realisera durant les 3 mois precedent l'operation des seances d'activite physique (AP) supervisees d'endurance et de renforcement musculaire (3 fois 80 min/sem.). La condition physique, la qualite de vie, l'anthropometrie, la composition corporelle, les barrieres percues a l'AP et la pratique d'AP seront evalues dans les 2 groupes, avant et apres le PAPPO puis tous les 3 mois apres l'operation durant une annee. De plus, la satisfaction quant a la prise en charge en AP sera evaluee. Le suivi des complications peri-operatoires, la duree de la chirurgie et d'hospitalisation suite a la chirurgie,  ainsi que de la medication et les comorbidites se feront a partir des dossiers medicaux des sujets jusqu'a un an apres la chirurgie de l'obesite. Le PAPPO, associe a l'intervention chirurgicale devrait permettre d'optimiser la prevention et le traitement de l'obesite et de ses complications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of poly(ADP-ribose)polymerase-1 in cellular responses to ultraviolet radiations
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DEATH; DNA PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; DNA REPAIR; GENE EXPRESSION; HAIRLESS MOUSE SKIN MODEL; HUMAN SKIN CELLS; NER: NUCLEOTIDE EXCISION REPAIR; PARP: POLY(ADP-RIBOSE) POLYMERASE-1; SKIN CANCER; ULTRAVIOLET RADIATION (UV)
Abstract-Résumé: The exposure of skin to solar ultraviolet radiation (UV) is associated with development of skin cancers. The UV-induced damage to DNA of skin cells plays a key role in this process. The repair of UV-damaged DNA is the first mechanism by which skin cells protect themselves, and the second mechanism is death of cells that are highly damaged by UV. Together these two responses to DNA damage play an important role in preventing UV-induced skin cancer. Our team has been trying to understand how these two responses are controlled and executed in higher organisms.   Our team has been studying roles of a nuclear enzyme of higher eukaryotes called poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase-1 (PARP-1) to different responses to UV-induced  DNA damage. Our previously published series of work has already given us a strong indication about the role of this protein in repair of UV-damaged DNA by a process called nucleotide excision repair (NER). Our unpublished work also suggests its role in causing death of skin cells highly damaged by UV.   In the present project, we will use different types of human skin cells or mouse models in which PARP-1 function has been compromised by pharmacological or genetic methods. Using these models, we will examine the exact molecular mechanism by which PARP-1 participates in the repair of UV-damaged DNA specifically by rapidly alerting and recruiting repair machinery to the site of DNA damage. We will also examine how PARP-1 helps in killing skin cells that are highly damaged by UV. Finally, using specially created PARP-1 albino hairless knockout mice, we will determine whether absence of PARP-1 will make these mice more susceptible to develop UV-induced non-melanoma skin cancers.  Our project will have the translational implication in designing ways to augment activity of PARP-1 to prevent sunlight induced skin cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: The lipid peroxidation product 4-hydroxynonenal in the pathophysiology of osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: 4-HYDROXYNONENAL; ACETYLATION; CARTILAGE; DH404; GLUTATHIONE-S-TRANSFERASE; NRF2; OSTEOARTHRITIS; SIRT2; SRT1720
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common age-related chronic disorders affecting articular cartilage, joint and bone tissues. It is commonly assumed that multiple factors, including genetic and developmental, metabolic and traumatic factors can trigger OA, but the causes of this disease remain unclear. We have discovered that cartilage forming cells from OA patients produced high level of lipid-derived reactive molecule termed 4-hydroxynonenal (HNE). HNE is generated during extensive tissue damage in various tissues including cartilage. The team leads by Dr Mohamed Benderdour has identified a specific role of HNE in OA through its ability to induce different factors involved in the inflammation and cartilage degradation. Search of the mechanisms regulating HNE production in OA led this team to identify the involvement of an enzyme namely glutathione-s-transferase (GST) that detoxify HNE. Thus, preventing the generation of HNE or increasing the detoxification of HNE is an effective means to treat OA. This discovery provides for the first time a clear functional link between HNE production and GST since OA patients showed low level of this enzyme. In addition, they discovered that loss of GST in cartilage from OA patients could be caused by aberrant production of Nrf2, an essential factor that regulate GST production. Elucidation of these mechanisms could be useful to identify individuals at risk of developing OA and to the development of therapeutic compounds to maintain the level of Nrf2 and consequently GST production in cartilage to prevent OA or to stop its progression.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of anti-homocitrullinated protein/peptide immune responses in Rheumatoid Arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-CITRULLINATED PROTEIN/PEPTIDE ANTIBODIES (ACPA); ANTI-HOMOCITRULLINATED PROTEIN/PEPTIDE ANTIBODIES (HCPA); ARTHRITIS ANIMAL MODELS; AUTOIMMUNE DISEASE; B CELLS; DR4 (SE) TRANSGENIC MICE; MHC CLASS II; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS (RA); SHARED EPITOPE (SE); T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: It has been recent dogma that Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), the most common inflammatory and crippling type of arthritis is characterized by the presence of a serum factor called anti-citrullinated protein/peptide antibody or ACPA. The presence of ACPA helps in the diagnosis of this form of arthritis since its presence is highly specific for RA. The immune response to citrullinated protein/peptide, which we showed is influenced by genetic factors, is also believed to be significantly involved in causing the inflammation characteristic of this disease. Recent work in several laboratories including our own have revealed in RA the presence of another antibody to a molecule called homocitrulline, which is closely related in its structure to citrulline. We showed that homocitrulline is also immunologically related to citrulline and antibodies to homocitrullinated proteins occur as frequently in the serum of RA as ACPA. Further these antibodies are also highly diagnostic of RA.    Since these antibodies always occur in RA patients that also have ACPA our research is designed to determine whether they are necessary for the disease causing effects of ACPA. Thus we seek to determine whether their appearance is also genetically determined and whether these antibodies to homocitrullinated proteins could be responsible for the arthritic inflammation and damage which has so far been attributed to ACPA acting alone. Our studies are designed to determine whether these antibodies act alone or with ACPA. This fundamental information will help us to determine not only how the damage in RA occurs but will allow us to develop new forms of treatment to prevent this crippling disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Kitinikewin misiwanacihisowin: Researching arts-based wellness promotion for suicide prevention among Aboriginal youth
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; ABORIGINAL YOUTH HEALTH; ARTS-BASED HEALTH RESEARCH; COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; MIXED RESEARCH METHODS; SUICIDE PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Youth suicide is one of the most conspicuous examples of the inequalities that exist between the health of Aboriginal peoples and of other Canadians. Not only are suicide rates among Aboriginal youth much higher than those of their non-Aboriginal peers, Aboriginal youth in Canada have the highest suicide rate among all Indigenous groups in the world. Since youth comprise more than half of the Aboriginal population in Canada, youth suicide is a serious health issue that must be addressed. This research project seeks to fill gaps in our knowledge about Aboriginal youth suicide by building on work done in an existing arts-based research project in partnership with the File Hills Qu'Appelle Tribal Council (FHQTC) Health Services in southern Saskatchewan. Our team is composed FHQTC health professionals and a diverse group of researchers with expertise in Aboriginal youth health, arts-based methods, pubic policy, and quantitative research. The project will build the capacity of Aboriginal youth, community members, knowledge users, and researchers to investigate, identify, and address conditions leading to Aboriginal youth suicide and other self-harming behaviors through the development of culturally appropriate arts-based methods of research. The team will also study the short and long-term effectiveness of arts-based approaches in supporting Aboriginal youth wellness. Lastly, this study will formulate policy recommendations on Aboriginal youth suicide that are culturally appropriate and have the potential to increase the health and well-being of Aboriginal peoples over the coming generations. Using what Mi'kmaw Elder Albert Marshall deems "two-eyed seeing," we will bring together statistically-based epidemiological techniques and Indigenous ways of knowing. This research project has the potential to significantly and positively impact the health of Aboriginal peoples in Canada by increasing the health and well-being of Aboriginal youth, thereby decreasing suicide rates.

TitreApplicationTitle: WormMap: Mapping a High-Quality Protein Complex 'Interactome' in C. elegans
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMALS; COMPUTATION; CONSERVATION; DATA MINING; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; NETWORK; PROTEIN COMPLEXES; PROTEOMICS; WORM
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how all the proteins encoded by the genome of an animal work together to form a living organism requires a complete description of the 'wiring circuits' that underlie fundamental cellular processes. A key feature is the tendency of proteins to interact physically to form complexes that serve as molecular 'machines'. Proteins with similar or overlapping biological roles generally belong to the same complex. Here, we propose to map and explore the physical interaction architecture of protein complexes present in the classical model nematode worm (Caenorhabditis elegans) using powerful technology developed by our group. Our experimental approach will enable us to generate a high quality circuit diagram for all the essential proteins involved in important biological processes required for animal cell growth, development and survival.  Since many worm genes are conserved across animal evolution, the identification of the overall physical and functional architecture of C. elegans should inform on protein complexes in other species, including humans. The data generated in this project will lead to a deeper understanding of animal cell biology and therefore will serve as a valuable resource for the entire biomedical research community, including human geneticists trying to track down the molecular basis of important human disorders to spur on the development of new clinical therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: What Social Determinants Contribute to High Allostatic Load among Aboriginal Adults?
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; ALLOSTATIC LOAD; ENCULTURATION; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; STRESS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal populations experience high levels of health disparities. The purpose of this study is to examine the extent to which stress associated with social and economic adversity may 'get under the skin' to disrupt the biological health of Aboriginal adults. We will also examine the ways in which Aboriginal and western approaches to wellness and healing may promote resiliency in this population. An Aboriginal Advisory Committee made up of key members of the Aboriginal community will be assembled to provide input into this project as it unfolds. Quantitative, qualitative, and biomarker data will be collected from 150 adults, 18-35 years of age, who attend the University of Lethbridge and self-identify as First Nations, Metis, or Inuit over a 24-month period. This study may improve the health of Aboriginal peoples by examining the ways in which social experiences may contribute to or protect against disease at a biological level. This information can then be used to develop optimal interventions designed to reduce health disparities among Aboriginal adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tehtsitehwa:kenrotka:we (together we pull it from the earth again) - The Ohero:kon Youth Health Intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: COMING OF AGE; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; HEALTH INTERVENTION; IDENTITY; INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE; INDIGENOUS METHODOLOGIES; PUBERTY; RITES OF PASSAGE; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: There is a lack of health intervention programs for Indigenous youth and many that exist are delivered in culturally inappropriate ways. A four-year study on sexual health in the Six Nations Haudenosaunee community identified the need for cultural teachings and understanding of cultural values and protocol, and advocated the need for culture based interventions to promote sexual health. The Ohero:kon intervention in the Mohawk community of Akwesasne supports the need for youth health interventions based on Indigenous knowledge. Ohero:kon restores cultural knowledge of coming of age as a preparatory process for youth as they transition to adulthood. Through a series of teachings and ceremonies, Ohero:kon connects youth with their cultural knowledge and traditions to develop understandings of identity, life, and creation. Youth learn cultural understandings of puberty, healthy behaviours, and roles and responsibilities. Positive understandings of identity, relationships, communication and behaviours are created fostering resilience and community health. A shared desire to promote the health of Haudenosaunee youth through the restoration of Indigenous knowledge and practice has led to a Six Nations and Akwesasne community-based research partnership. Utilizing Indigenous methodologies, our objective is to evaluate and document Ohero:kon and use it as the foundation to develop a Ohero:kon ritual health intervention at Six Nations. Community Elders, Clan Mothers and the traditional mentorship system of the aunties and uncles will guide the project. Information gathered will be used to create a Ohero:kon framework and curriculum to support the development of Ohero:kon in other Indigenous communities. The project will contribute to the ongoing restoration of cultural health knowledge in Akwesasne and Six Nations. The evaluation will also provide important information about the community impacts and benefits of Ohero:kon to support and promote Indigenous health approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pattern recognition and scene analysis in older adults.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; EVENT-RELATED POTENTIALS; PERCEPTION; PSYCHOPHYSICS; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: Most people know that visual acuity - our ability to see fine details - gets worse as we age. However, many other aspects of vision also deteriorate with age. For example, older adults are less able to perceive complex patterns of motion, or the shapes of contours embedded in clutter. The changes in vision that occur during normal healthy aging can restrict the mobility and independence of older adults, and affect behaviour in many everyday tasks. Importantly, many of these changes are not linked to the optical qualities of our eyes. Instead, they are linked to subtle changes in the way the brain processes visual information, and therefore cannot be corrected by wearing glasses or having cataract surgery. Furthermore, these changes often are not detected by standard clinical tests, which often underestimate the true extent of visual deficits in elderly people. The ultimate goals of our research are to i) provide better descriptions of the effects of normal aging on vision; ii) link behavioural deficits with changes in the brain; and iii) clarify how vision affects behaviour in everyday tasks.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strengthening the rapid Health Equity Impact Assessment process: Actions toward improving health outcomes for seniors
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CRITICAL APPRAISAL; EQUITY; EVIDENCE-BASED DECISIONMAKING; HEALTH EQUITY IMPACT ASSESSMENT; HEALTH IMPACT ASSESSMENT; HEALTH POLICY; SENIORS; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The health impacts of a given intervention can vary widely within a general population.  Where differential health impacts are considered avoidable and unfair, they are considered health inequities. In an effort to reduce these inequities and ultimately improve health outcomes for vulnerable population groups, various Canadian and international organizations have created tools to assist in developing and implementing health intervention strategies.  Termed Health Equity Impact Assessments (HEIAs), these tools are currently variable in their quality, consistency, utility, and ease of use.  With an initial focus on improving the health equity impacts of health interventions (policies and programs) targeted toward seniors, we plan to strengthen an existing HEIA process, that belonging to Ontario's Ministry of Health and Long Term Care, by creating supplementary tools to improve its quality.  The tools will assess the process by which evidence of health inequities is gathered while conducting the HEIA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transitions Across the Continuum of Care for Older People with Complex Needs: A Program of Research
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; FUNCTIONAL IMPAIRMENT; GERIATRICS; INTEGRATED CARE; OLDER ADULTS; RESEARCH METHODS; TRANSITIONS OF CARE
Abstract-Résumé: This is a proposal for a five year Program of Research to study transitions across the continuum of care for older people. The common focus is to better understand the transitions of care experienced by older people, and explore the impact of dementia on care transitions. We will bring together an interdisciplinary research team of health services researchers with extensive experience caring for vulnerable older adults along with methodologists experienced in using advanced statistical methods. We provide a broad overview of transitions to study the association between transitions, safety, and quality of care, and the impact of different trajectories across the continuum on the costs of care. This Program of Research recognizes the heterogeneous nature of the older population and incorporates the fundamental importance of dementia. Building on a foundation of funded research projects, we have developed a series of new projects that are divided into complementary clinical or methodological theme areas. Our research will use linked population-based data held at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES) that includes three data sources that provide detailed information on cognitive and functional status. ICES data provides information on all older adults receiving health care in the province of Ontario. We will support trainees and improve research capacity. We will work with knowledge users in an integrated knowledge translation process. We will add value beyond having a set of independent researchers working on independent projects. Working together will allow us to leverage our joint expertise to support a higher level of research productivity, capacity development for trainees and new scientists, and engagement with knowledge users. Our overall goal is to contribute to health system solutions that target the growing older population in Canada by informing strategies to optimize outcomes for older adults across their individualized journeys of care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translating Research in Elder Care
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; FACILITY-BASED LONG-TERM CARE; INTERVENTION; KNOWLEDGE UTILIZATION; LONGITUDINAL DATA COLLECTION; MDS-RAI; RESIDENT OUTCOMES; SOCIAL NETWORK ANALYSIS; SUSTAINABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: The most rapidly expanding group of Canadians is those >85 years - the age when complex chronic diseases, in particular dementias, begin to take their greatest toll on ability to live independently. Currently 1 in 5 men >85 and 1 in 3 women >85 reside in long term care (LTC) facilities designed to provide care when family and community no longer can. With our many successes in keeping seniors healthier and in the community longer, residents are admitted later in their decline, with more complex needs and in a much greater state of vulnerability. Within these facilities, the majority of care is provided by unregulated care aides who have low incomes, are most often women with high school education or less, some with little proficiency in either official language. They constitute another at-risk group. To ensure the best possible quality of life for these two vulnerable populations, the Translating Research in Elder Care (TREC) research program will examine how the work environment in nursing homes affects staff members and residents. Like links in a chain, we believe that favourable work environments lead to enhanced use of research information, provision of better care, and ultimately better outcomes for residents (e.g. fewer pressure sores, less pain, etc). Improved staff well-being is also a link in the chain. We will be testing the strength of each link to determine where changes can be most effective. We will also test a program aimed at helping staff design and run their own care improvement projects, once again, measuring the associations with the links of the chain. A third component of our work is aimed at understanding how LTC facilities are connected to each other, which ones are the innovators and leaders, and which ones learn from the others. The TREC research will be carried out in nursing homes across the 4 western provinces. The information developed will contribute to better care for Canadian seniors who spend their final years in a nursing home.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing and Validating a Screen for Autism Spectrum Disorders in Later Life (SALL)
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; MEASUREMENT; OLDER ADULTS; QUESIONNAIRE; RELIABILITY; VALIDITY
Abstract-Résumé: Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs) are one of the most common brain development disorders in childhood. Although ASDs are a lifelong condition, little research exists that examines ASDs in later life, particularly among those aged 50 and over. Our study plans to develop and test a new screening tool, composed of a series of questions, to identify individuals who may have an ASD in later life. Currently, there are no scales to identify ASDs in later life. Scales that exist have been tested in younger groups, and may not contain age-appropriate content for older adults with an ASD. The screening tool will be developed from a review of existing scales used with younger groups, interviews with older adults with an ASD, focus groups with health professionals working with those with an ASD and/or who are aging, and from consulting experts in this area. The screening tool will be given to different groups of older people to see how well it can identify individuals with an ASD in later life. This research is the first step needed to study ASDs in later life. This work is important for three reasons. First, we do not know much about adults aged 50 and over with an ASD, and this group is expected to increase in size. Second, older adults with an ASD may have different health and social needs compared to older adults without an ASD, which need to be understood. For example, those with an ASD may: a) have higher rates of co-existing conditions (e.g. depression, dementia); b) require different treatment standards (e.g. medication guidelines) and c) experience more social isolation. This information is needed to provide appropriate care and services to older adults with ASDs. Third, older adults with an ASD may have either been undiagnosed in childhood or misdiagnosed. Identifying ASDs in later life may help older adults better understand their behaviours and difficulties (e.g. sustaining relationships/maintaining employment), and provide access to needed programs and funding.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sodium, Claudin-14 and the (Patho)Physiology of (Hyper)Calciuria and Kidney Stone Formation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CALCIUM; CELL BIOLOGY; GENE EXPRESSION; GENETICS; HYPERCALCIRUIA; KIDNEY STONES; TIGHT JUNCTION/PARACELLULAR
Abstract-Résumé: One in ten people in Canada will pass a kidney stone in their lifetime. Passing a stone is painful and the numerous emergency and operating room visits required for treatment is expensive. Moreover, emerging evidence from my research program and others has identified an increased risk of chronic kidney disease, dialysis and heart disease in people with kidney stones. The risk is greatest for women under the age of 50. Therapies aimed at preventing and/or dissolving kidney stones already present in the kidney are lacking. The main therapy is to increase water ingestion and decrease sodium intake. In some individuals a water pill can be used, but it is poorly effective and has significant side effects. The main risk factor for developing kidney stones is having a urine with a high calcium content. A large majority of people with kidney stones display this attribute. We do not know why this is. The purpose of the proposed research is to try and understand why and how people excrete too much calcium in their urine. We know that sodium intake increases calcium excretion in normal people and people with kidney stones. Our work will identify the molecules and pathways responsible for this association such that new therapies can be developed targeting this pathway. We have recently described part of a novel pathway in the kidney whereby higher levels of calcium in the blood cause increased calcium excretion in the urine, in normal people. Our research will attempt to identify all the molecules in this new pathway. Finally, we have found a genetic alteration in a gene central to this latter pathway in people who form kidney stones. We wish to understand how this mutation affects calcium excretion in these kidney stone formers such that targeted therapies can be designed for them. Together, these studies will delineate molecules and mechanisms that increase urinary calcium excretion, providing novel targets for much needed new kidney stone therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Macrophages in intestinal disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVELY ACTIVATED MACROPHAGES; ANIMAL MODELING; CROHN'S DISEASE; IL-1; IL-18; INFLAMMASOMES; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INTESTINAL FIBROSIS; INTESTINAL INFLAMMATION; MACROPHAGES
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), which includes Crohn's Disease and ulcerative colitis, is caused by inflammation along the gastrointestinal tract.  This leads to symptoms that include pain, nausea, and diarrhea.  The cause of disease is not known and so current treatments rely on non-specific immune suppression to try to block the inflammatory response.  These treatments are not effective in about 10% of people with IBD and it is predicted that up to 40% of people with IBD will stop responding to these treatments eventually.  A better understanding of the cause(s) of IBD is necessary so that we can develop new and more effective treatments for people living with disease.  My laboratory has developed a new genetic model of IBD that mimics  several features of disease that are not seen in other models.  Using our new model, we have found that a type of white blood cell, called a macrophage, is critical in intestinal disease.  Macrophages play a key role in our bodies' defense against infections but they can also contribute to inflammation in diseases, like IBD.  In the studies proposed here, we will investigate which features of macrophages contribute to intestinal disease and target those features to see if we can prevent or block disease.  These studies will provide critical information about fundamental causes of IBD and our strategies to target macrophages and their functions may provide new therapeutic options that we can use to treat people with IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Causes and Implications of Metabolically Healthy Obese
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CLINICAL WEIGHT MANAGEMENT; DIABETES; EPIDEMIOLOGY; METABOLIC SYNDROME; OBESITY; POPULATION HEALTH; WEIGHT LOSS
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is a known risk factor for diabetes and cardiovascular disease (CVD), but the risk may not be the same for all obese people. Some obese individuals may actually be at lower risk for diabetes and CVD than lean people. Recent work also suggests that many people may gain weight due to factors that do not directly contribute to the "energy in" and "energy out" equation (diet and exercise). These reasons include sleep duration, environmental toxins, or that age at which your mother gave birth to you and may account for some of the differences in health seen in obese people and may influence their ability to lose weight. The first aim of this project is to determine whether there truly is a healthy obese person. If there is, what factors protect these people from the health problems commonly seen with obesity? Do these healthy obese people benefit from weight loss? If so, how do the presence of traditional or non-traditional risk factors for obesity impact on health and the weight loss achieved? This work will be done using two approaches. First, use of existing large datasets will allow us to answer our research questions more quickly than if we had to collect all new data. We will also be able to look at repeat visits so that we can assess changes over time, to see how different groups of people with obesity develop health conditions. Some datasets have information on causes of death so that we can also determine how different factors relate with this important outcome. Second, working with the Wharton Weight Management Centre will give us a chance to apply our research findings within an existing clinic that has a better-rounded sample than typical research weight loss studies. If there are differences in health and weight loss potential between obese people, this work will help physicians more accurately identify high-risk patients and focus care. It will allow public health officials to improve resource planning and health care cost estimates of obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: MicroRNA-Dependent Regulation in Early Prion-Related Neurodegenerative Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: GENOMICS; HIPPOCAMPUS; IN VIVO IMAGING; MICRORNA; NEURODEGENERATION; NMDA RECEPTORS; PRION
Abstract-Résumé: Intense laboratory and clinical research have failed to discover effective treatments to delay the onset or progression of any neurodegenerative conditions, including those caused by infectious prions. Although prion diseases are rare and uniquely infectious, they share many common features on a sub-cellular level with other neurodegenerative diseases that are much more prevalent in the population such as Alzheimer's disease.  The most obvious similarity is the strong association with the accumulation of misfolded and insoluble forms of normal host proteins in the brains of patients. This process triggers progressive genetic changes that eventually lead to profound neuronal damage or death, however, the molecular mechanism that underlies neurotoxicity remains unresolved. It has become clear that profound changes in the brains of patients are evident long before clinical symptoms and it is at this stage at which the disease is reversible, and therefore presents 'druggable' targets. Our research effort is focused on understanding the molecular underpinnings of these early steps in disease pathogenesis. We have established methods to dissect individual neurons from the brains of rodent models of neurodegenerative disease and study alterations using a variety of techniques.  Our unique observation is that small genetic regulators, called microRNAs, are induced in neurons at very early stages of prion disease. Evidence suggests that these play roles in neuron regeneration and or survival. Understanding their functions in greater detail will determine whether these molecules can be manipulated to induce regeneration as a therapeutic strategy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inhibitory effects and mechanisms of innate defence regulator peptides in inflammatory arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; CELL SIGNALLING; CHRONIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASES; COLLAGEN INDUCED ARTHRITIS MURINE MODEL; IMMUNE MODULATION; INFLAMMATION; INNATE DEFENCE REGULATOR PEPTIDES; PROTEIN PHOSPHORYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Arthritis is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by cartilage and bone destruction. Current treatment options for inflammatory arthritis inhibit critical molecules that are important in both inflammation and in efficient immune functioning. Thus, these therapies often result in patients becoming vulnerable to increased risk of infections and sometimes development of cancers. Therefore, alternate strategies are needed to overcome the limitations of current immunosuppressive therapies for chronic inflammatory diseases.  We have shown that small peptides known as innate defence regulator (IDR) peptides have the potential to suppress inflammation in arthritis without compromising the immune responses required for resolution of infections. We have demonstrated the ability of one such IDR peptide in an animal model of arthritis. We have established screening tools and animal models for examining the activity of IDR peptides in arthritis. In this project, we will comprehensively study the biological effects of the IDR peptide in a mouse model of arthritis. We will also identify the specific cellular proteins that are involved in the IDR peptide activity to control the disease process in arthritis. In addition, this study will potentially identify new targets for anti-inflammatory therapeutics to interfere in the complex process of chronic inflammation. Overall, this study will strongly support future research into alternate therapeutics for inflammatory arthritis and other chronic inflammatory diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innate signaling in the role of interleukin-10 in heart health and repair
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOMYOCYTE CELL DEATH; CELL SIGNALING; CYTOKINES; HEART FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: Occurrence of heart failure in the survivors of heart attack (Myocardial Infarction, MI) is a common clinical syndrome with a grave prognosis.  Because of the loss of the contractile elements due to MI, the heart responds by an increase in its muscle mass as well as by an activation of other neurohumoral compensatory processes to maintain perfusion pressure.  In rats subjected to coronary ligation (myocardial infarction), we and others have shown that the activity of the protein called Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) increases and plays a causative role in the pathogenesis of heart failure.  Yet, clinical trials employing anti TNF-alpha therapy were a failure indicating that our understanding of the molecular mechanisms is not complete.  Thus the undertaking of clinical trials turned out to be a "premature" step.  In the same experimental model, we have now shown that another protein, Interleukin-10 (IL-10), known for its cell survival effects decreases during heart failure.  Therefore, we suggested that it may in fact be the ratio of IL-10/TNF-alpha, rather than TNF-alpha alone, which may have a critical role in heart failure.  Furthermore, in isolated cardiomyocytes, we showed that IL-10 antagonized almost all of the deleterious effect of TNF-alpha in a very intricate manner.  The present study, therefore, is designed to understand the molecular basis of the beneficial effects of IL-10, its innate signaling processes and to identify the molecular targets to promote its cardiomyocyte cell survival effects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of dietary essential fatty acids on octadecanoid production and biological actions in obesity-induced inflammation: implications for dietary requirements
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLS; DIETARY LIPIDS; EICOSANOIDS; HUMAN SUBJECTS; INFLAMMATION; OBESITY; OCTADECANOIDS; OXYLIPINS
Abstract-Résumé: There is much controversy surrounding the health effects and requirements for essential dietary fats.  One of the most important ways that fats affect health and disease is by being converted in the body to molecules called oxylipins.  The oxylipins are made from essential fats consumed in the diet. However, information on the levels, as well as the biological effects, of the most common oxylipins is lacking largely because of difficulties in analyzing them.  However, the development of appropriate analytical equipment and techniques now makes this possible.  This proposal will examine the effects of essential dietary fats on these novel oxylipins, specifically the ones called octadecanoids.  While octadecanoids likely influence many aspects of health and disease, this proposal will focus on their ability to affect inflammation caused by obesity.  In the first study, obese and non-obese humans will be given capsules containing different types of dietary oils.  The effects of these oils on octadecanoid and oxylipin levels, and markers of inflammation will be assessed.  The second study will use cell culture to examine the effects of adding purified oxylipins to immune cells, specifically peripheral blood mononuclear cells and human macrophages.  This will allow us to determine the modes of action and relative biopotencies of the different oxylipins in relation to markers of inflammation in immune cells.  Overall, this research will provide new information on which oxylipins are produced, how their levels are affected by obesity, how their levels are affected by different dietary fats, and whether changes in oxylipins reduce or enhance inflammation associated with obesity.  This research also will help to address questions regarding dietary fat requirements, and provide the basis for further human studies in this area.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding youths' attitudes and practices with regard to high-risk behaviors while skiing and snowboarding
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTITUDES AND BEHAVIORS; INJURY; RISK-TAKING; SKI; SNOWBOARD; SURVEY; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: Skiing and snowboarding are popular winter sports that have a high rate of injury.  There are additional high-risk behaviors that may increase the risk of injury, such as drinking alcohol or consuming drugs, not wearing a helmet or other protective equipment, or choosing to ski or snowboard in terrain parks.  Currently, it is unknown what proportion of youth engage in these high-risk behaviors and what influences their decision to do so. The choice to engage in high-risk behaviors can be influenced by many factors, such as whether youth think they are at increased risk of an injury, if their parents or friends engage in high-risk behavior, or if they think they will get caught.  Girls and boys may make different choices about high-risk behavior and factors that influence their decisions may change as they get older.  This suggests that promotion strategies to encourage safe skiing and snowboarding may need to be different for various groups of people.   The purpose of this study is to understand high-risk taking attitudes and behaviors among skiing and snowboarding youth.  Skiers and snowboarders will be interviewed at a ski resort and asked if they partake in high-risk behaviors (drinking alcohol, consuming drugs, not wearing protective equipment, and using the terrain park), why they chose to engage in these behaviors, who and what influences their decision.  They will also be asked their age, sex, activity (skiing or snowboarding), experience, previous skiing or snowboarding injury, and other sport participation.  The results will allow for more effective strategies to promote safe skiing and snowboarding that can be targeted towards those skiers and snowboarders who engage in high-risk behaviors.  By understanding youth's attitudes towards these behaviors, policy makers can intervene to reduce unsafe behavior.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mental Disorders and Treatment Needs among Parents Bereaved by Offspring Sudden Death
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; BEREAVEMENT; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH SERVICE USE; MENTAL DISORDERS; PERCEIVED NEED; SUDDEN DEATH; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Bereavement following the death of a loved one is a phase of life experienced by almost everyone. It is also a period of vulnerability, with some bereaved persons experiencing considerable emotional difficulties. Our previous study showed that parents who lose a child to suicide are at risk for depression, anxiety, and marital separation in the two years following the death. However, a deeper understanding of the effects of bereavement remains unknown. The current study will examine the effects of sudden death on bereaved relatives in the Manitoba population. Parents who have lost a child to suicide or other sudden accidental cause of death will be invited to complete a telephone survey. The survey will explore their experiences of emotional problems, depression, grief, and support from others. The survey will also ask bereaved parents what treatment they feel they need, and whether they have seen a doctor or other professional. Their responses will be compared to people in the general population to see how the emotional difficulties, treatment needs, and health service use of bereaved parents compares to others. This will provide much needed answers about the health and treatment needs of bereaved people, a group that in the past has not received appropriate treatment services. The findings from this study will therefore help to develop effective treatments for bereaved family members, and thus improve the lives of people who have suffered the sudden death of a loved one.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phospholipid Receptors as Targets for Enhancing Drug Permeability to the Brain
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD-BRAIN BARRIER; BRAIN TUMORS; DRUG DELIVERY; ENDOTHELIAL PERMEABILITY; IN VIVO IMAGING; LYSOPHOSPHATIDIC ACID; RECEPTOR EXPRESSION; SPHINGOSINE 1-PHOSPHATE
Abstract-Résumé: The treatment of brain related disorders is often hampered by the inability to achieve sufficient concentrations of the drug within the brain.  This is due in large part to the restrictive nature of the brain microvessel endothelial cells that form the blood-brain barrier (BBB).  My laboratory is interested in ways to modulate BBB permeability to more effectively delivery therapeutic agents to the brain.  One method we are pursuing involves the activation of varoius phospholipid receptors expressed on the brain endothelial cells to temporarily enhance BBB permeability to a wide variety of compounds.  Our preliminary work using the naturally occurring activators of these receptors, lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) and sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P)has proven the utility of this approach.  We propose the creation and refinement of this drug delivery platform through (1) identification of the crucial phospholipid receptors responsible for the permeability responses to LPA and S1P.  (2) Selection of more specific and "drugable" activators of these receptors by screening for responses in a series of LPA and S1P analog compounds.  (3)Proof-of-principle for brain drug delivery platform using a mouse brain tumor model. Together these studies will establish a foundation for use of this approach to improve for the treatment of various CNS disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Adenylyl Cyclase Signalling in Pulmonary Artery and Right Ventricle in Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENYLYL CYCLASE; CAMP; HYPOXIA; PERSISTENT PULMONARY HYPERTENSION OF THE NEWBORN; PROSTACYCLIN RECEPTOR; PULMONARY ARTERIAL HYPERTENSION; REGULATION OF RECEPTOR-G-PROTEIN COUPLING; RIGHT VENTRICULAR FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The newborn lung is very sensitive to low levels of oxygen. In infants who do not receive enough oxygen at birth, the low oxygen level causes lung blood vessels to go into spasm. Then blood cannot flow through the lung for gas exchange. This causes the heart to fail. This deadly disease, persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) accounts for 10% of all admissions to newborn intensive care.  Heart muscle and lung blood vessel muscles have opposite jobs at birth. The heart needs to contract harder, and lung blood vessels need to relax. These opposite events happen through a single system of signals inside the cell, called the adenylyl cyclase pathway. We studied the effects of low oxygen levels on the function of the heart, and on muscle lining the blood vessels of the newborn lung. In low oxygen, muscles in the heart and blood vessels do not respond properly to medications. We now find that the adenylyl cyclase pathway does not work in low oxygen.   Prostacyclin is a powerful molecule produced during labour and delivery, which uses the adenylyl cyclase signal system. In healthy newborns, prostacyclin protects blood vessels from excessive contraction. However in low oxygen, the signals that connect prostacyclin to blood vessel relaxation are lost. Prostacyclin cannot do its protective job. Other important drugs use the adenylyl cyclase signal system, including those we use in the ICU to make a baby's heart pump better. These drugs also stop working in low oxygen.   We plan to study the adenylyl cyclase signal system in muscle from lung blood vessels and in heart muscle from PPHN animals, to see why low oxygen stops it from working. We will look at the mechanisms for switching adenylyl cyclase on and off, and see how they are affected by low oxygen. Finally we will try to reactivate adenylyl cyclase in the heart and lung blood vessels of PPHN animals, using new selective drugs. These reactivating drugs may help us treat babies with PPHN.

TitreApplicationTitle: Semaphorin3E as a novel  therapeutic target in allergic asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: AHR; AIRWAY REMODELING; ALLERGIC ASTHMA; ASM CELLS; DENDRITIC CELLS; INFLAMMATION; SEMA3E  KNOCK OUT; SEMAPHORIN3E
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is chronic inflammation of airways which is widespread worldwide. The most common chronic disease among children, it currently affects 300 million people worldwide with 250,000 annual deaths attributed to the disease. It is also estimated that there may be an additional 100 million more asthmatics by 2025. About 12% of Canadian children and 8% of the population aged 12 or older have been diagnosed with asthma    We have recently discovered a new protein called semaphorin3E to be significantly reduced in asthmatics airways.    We found also that semaphorin 3E have tremendous effect on cell involved in the formation of airway scar tissue. In this work, we want to investigate how semaphorin 3E  inhibits asthmatic manifestation  and evaluate its therapeutic potential in asthma.   Determining the functional outcome of semaphorin3E in vivo will expand our understanding of asthma inception and evolution   and may lead to develop novel anti-asthmatic strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional changes in host cell regulatory pathways induced by reovirus infection
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; PROTEOMICS; VIRUS INFECTION; VIRUS PATHOLOGY; VIRUS UNCOATING
Abstract-Résumé: We have previously measured several thousand host proteins and determined that a few hundred are up-regulated or down-regulated after cells are infected by reovirus. Our goals in this continuing project are to now determine the functional importance of these proteins. We will also focus more detailed follow-up studies on those few proteins (approximately 10) which are known to play key roles in a few critically important cellular pathways. This will provide us important information about how viruses manipulate cells and kill them, which should move us closer to using this virus as a beneficial anti-cancer treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Contribution of Dynein light chain-1 for efficient HIV-1 reverse transcription and the underlying molecular mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: DYNEIN LIGHT CHAIN-1; HIV-1 ENVELOPE GLYCOPROTEIN; HIV-1 INTEGRASE; HIV-1 REPLICATION; HIV-1 REVERSE TRANSCRIPTION; HOST/VIRUS INTERACTION; MACROPHAGES; P21-ACTIVATED KINASES 1; RESTING T CELLS; REVERSE TRANSCRIPTION COMPLEX
Abstract-Résumé: The human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) pandemic is a major health problem worldwide. During virus infection, the HIV-1 virus must convert its own RNA into double stranded DNA (a process called reverse transcription) before HIV-1 can replicate in the cell. The HIV-1 has its own protein, called reverse transciptase, for the DNA synthesis, but it also has to use the cell's machinery for effective reverse transcription to occur. However, the cell's proteins that are used by HIV-1 to help the virus perform reverse transcription are not known. Recently, we identified a cellular protein, Dynein light chain-1 (DYNLL1), which works together with another viral protein, integrase, to allow efficient reverse transcription. We also found that an HIV-1 envelope protein (gp120) stimulated the reverse transcriptase process. We think that gp120 acts through a signaling pathway that includes Pak1, which regulates the DYNLL1 protein. In this proposal, we will continue to study how HIV-1 uses cell proteins to help with its own replication. We also want to study how gp120 stimulates HIV-1 reverse transcription. The results of this study will help us to discover the new mechanism/s underlying HIV-1 reverse transcription and may provide information to develop novel strategies to control HIV-1 infection through blocking reverse transcription.  This study is relevant to the CIHR HIV/AIDS Research Initiative research priority area: HIV Pathogenesis, and Prevention, Technologies and Interventions. Finding new interactions between HIV-1 and host signaling pathways that favor HIV-1 reverse transcription will help us to better understand how HIV works. Also, results of this project may reveal new ways to control HIV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of Kidney Development by Sox4 and Sox11 Transcription Factors
Keywords-MotsClés: GLOMERULAR DISEASE; KIDNEY DEVELOPMENT; NEPHROGENESIS; NEPHRON PROGENITOR SURVIVAL AND SELF-RENEWAL; SOX11; SRY-RELATED HMG BOX 4 (SOX4); TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR SIGNALING; WILMS' TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR-1 (WT1)
Abstract-Résumé: The childhood kidney diseases Frasier Syndrome and Denys Drash Syndrome are associated with a poorer quality of life, the need for dialysis, and in severe cases, end-stage kidney failure requiring kidney replacement. Both of these diseases are linked to genetic mutations in Wilms' Tumour Suppressor-1 (WT1). WT1 mutations also cause the paediatric cancer Wilms' tumour (nephroblastoma), the most common solid tumour of childhood. WT1 encodes a DNA-binding protein that controls gene expression during kidney development, but its gene targets are largely unknown. Neither is it understood how mutations in WT1 cause kidney disease.   As first underscored in Dr. Edith Potter's landmark book "Normal and Abnormal Development of the Kidney" (1972), understanding how WT1 controls normal kidney development is the first step toward understanding how abnormal WT1 function can cause human kidney disease.   We have recently identified SOX4 and SOX11 as novel WT1 target genes in the developing kidney. Previous studies have shown that SOX4 and SOX11 are essential for development of the nervous system, heart and brain, and are abnormally expressed in several human cancers. However, SOX genes have not been previously studied in the kidney. We generated mice with SOX4 deficiency in the kidney. These mice develop severe kidney disease leading to end-stage kidney failure. Our new work in SOX4- and SOX11-deficient mouse models will clarify how these two genes control kidney development, and will provide a foundation for designing new strategies to treat and ultimately reverse childhood kidney disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Eukaryotic organelles, parasites and multicellularity: comparative genomic and proteomic approaches.
Keywords-MotsClés: EVOLUTION OF EUKARYOTE CELLS; GENOMIC SURVEY; IMMUNOLOCALIZATION; LATERAL GENE TRANSFER; MULTICELLULARITY; NEXT GENERATION DNA SEQUENCING; ORGANELLE FUNCTION; PROTEOMICS; PROTOZOAN PARASITES; TRANSCRIPTOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how complex single-celled organisms evolved into the super-kingdoms of Life over the last 2 billion years is a fundamental question in biology.  We propose to use advanced genomic sequencing, microscopy, computation, cell biology and proteomics to reveal the mechanisms behind some major evolutionary transitions of biomedical significance:  We will address how many groups of single-celled organisms have independently adapted to life without oxygen. These include forms that are free-living in the environment, and many that parasitize humans or other animals, especially parasites of the gut. We will explore how these species have modified their cell compartments and genomes to acquire new biochemical pathways suited to low-oxygen habitats, such as the human gut, and investigate other ways in which the genomes of single-celled parasites have changed to allow them to live within their hosts.  We will also examine how single celled organisms first evolved into primitive animals.  We will target a protein complex that is involved in holding groups of animal cells together, but is also present in some single-celled microbes, where it must have a different role. This will allow us to better understand the functions of proteins important to our own multicellular bodies and develop new model systems in which to study them.  There are several of potential practical benefits of the proposed research. The species examined include close relatives of serious human pathogens; revealing unique aspects of their biology could help identify new drug targets. Further, by understanding the mechanisms by which free-living organisms become disease-causing parasites we may better evaluate risks associated with the emergence of new pathogens. Also, our genomic data can be used to detect parasites in samples of microbe DNA from human guts; we aim to use this to determine whether common human parasites are associated with complex conditions like irritable bowel syndrome.
