TitreApplicationTitle: Design, Synthesis and Evaluation of Prodigiosin Analogues as Chemotherapeutic Agents
Keywords-MotsClés: CHLORIDE TRANSPORT; COLLABORATIVE AND INTERACTIVE EVALUATION; DRUG DELIVERY; FOLATE RECEPTOR ALPHA; IN VITRO SCREENING; INTRACELLULAR PH; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; MOUSE XENOGRAFT MODELS; NATURAL PRODUCT-DRIVEN; ZEBRAFISH MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: We are developing new drugs for breast cancer based on a naturally occurring molecule called prodigiosin found in bacteria in our homes and workplaces. Extracts containing prodigiosin were used in the USA from 1893 to 1963 to treat various cancers. However, prodigiosin was too toxic and was withdrawn from the market by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 1963. We have now decreased toxicity 100-fold while maintaining broad anti-cancer activity by chemically modifying prodigiosin.  Our goal is to develop prodigiosin-based drugs that have specific selectivity for breast cancer, while reducing general toxicity and side-effects. About 50% of breast cancers have a much greater ability to take in an essential vitamin called folic acid, compared to healthy cells. We will attach a compound similar to prodigiosin to a molecule that looks like folic acid: we expect that the resultant folate-prodigiosin drugs will target breast cancer cells rather than healthy cells. Ideally, this approach should reduce toxicity (side-effects) elsewhere in the body, while killing breast cancer cells more effectively. We will evaluate the compounds using cells from breast cancers, and other cancers, and we will also evaluate how well the compounds penetrate into solid tumours.  Funding of this work will pave the way for a completely new avenue for cancer treatment. We anticipate that novel folate-prodigiosin drugs will fill an urgent need for new treatments for so-called triple negative breast cancers, which currently have limited treatment options and poor prognosis. Our continued ownership of our molecules and their applications will be secured (patents) so that clinical potential can be pursued.

TitreApplicationTitle: Age- and sex-related changes in cortical bone cellular organization across the human lifespan
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BONE; CONFOCAL; LACUNO-CANALICULAR NETWORK; MICRO-CT; OSTEOCYTES; OSTEOPOROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Bones are dynamic and living structures which undergo continuous change throughout life. When balanced, the continual destruction and formation of tissue enables bones to meet the physiological and mechanical demands placed upon them. Imbalance in these processes leads to disease - the most significant of which is osteoporosis. This disease, known as the 'silent thief', is an increasing burden (human and economic) on developed and developing nations around the globe. In this context it is imperative that we develop a better understanding of how bones age. Ultimately, it is cells embedded directly within bone tissue (osteocytes) which give it life and enable change across the lifespan. Despite being surrounded by solid bone, these cells are able to survive due to a vast network of interconnections which transports nutrients and wastes. This network, similar to that of neurons in the brain, also provides a means by which the cells communicate with each other and coordinate the activities of other cells which form (osteoblasts) and breakdown (osteoclasts) bone tissue. Thus understanding the structure and function of this network is a critical step in combatting osteoporotic disease. The current project brings together an international team (Canadian and Australian) to study the cellular-level organization of human bone. Cutting-edge 3D imaging technology and computer simulation will be combined with one of the best human bone tissue banks in the world - the Melbourne Femur Collection. A key target of the research will be to investigate differences in how the bones of men and women age and related functional consequences. Differences in structural organization of the osteocyte network could, in part, explain the increased prevalence of osteoporotic disease in women. In broader terms, the knowledge obtained will provide an unprecedented perspective on the aging of human bone and has the potential to identify novel targets for prevention and intervention in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: The molecular mechanisms of mercury toxicity
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC VS ACUTE MERCURY EXPOSURE; COMPUTATIONAL CHEMISTRY; X-RAY ABSORPTION SPECTROSCOPY; X-RAY FLUORESCENCE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Mercury is the most toxic element to which human populations are exposed. Certain forms of mercury are highly toxic, causing severe neurological and other problems, while other forms of mercury are relatively benign. Most Canadians are exposed to mercury at some level, with major sources being dental amalgam and edible marine fish. The question of whether mercury in fish is harmful to humans, especially unborn children, has particular global significance as much of the world's population depends on fish as a primary source of protein. However, despite the potential problems and prevalence of mercury, much is still unknown about how it exerts its toxicity in humans. Furthermore, no particularly effective drugs for treatment of mercury exposure are clinically available.   We will use synchrotron X-ray techniques, such as are available at the Canadian Light Source, to investigate the chemical form and microscopic distribution of mercury in biological tissues. These techniques will allow us to investigate the chemistry of how mercury is released from dental amalgams and fish, how mercury may be chemically modified in the body, and how it can influence vertebrate development. We will also continue to investigate new molecules as potential drugs to treat chronic mercury poisoning, either by changing mercury to a less toxic form or by binding mercury strongly and effectively to remove it from the body. Such studies, which will help to clarify the risk of exposure to mercury and to develop new treatments for poisoning, should have widespread impacts in Canadian and global human health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating Human G Protein-Coupled Receptor Function through Protein and Genetic Interaction Maps
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFINITY PURIFICATION; MAMMALIAN NETWORKS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MEMBRANE BIOLOGY; MEMBRANE GENETIC INTERACTIONS; MEMBRANE PROTEIN COMPLEX; NETWORK BIOLOGY; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEOMICS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: In eukaryotes, the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) superfamily comprises a large number of cell membrane receptors which influence a myriad of essential physiological functions by mediating signals to diverse stimuli such as drugs, neurotransmitters, and hormones. The execution of these responses critically depends on networks of protein-protein interactions (PPIs) organized into biochemical pathways, where GPCRs play a central role. Due to their integrative role in various physiological processes, GPCR dysfunction is emerging as a causative factor in a variety of human diseases including cancers, neurodegenerative disorders, and retinal degeneration. Yet despite decades of extensive research on GPCR complexes and pathways in isolation, how these components interact and function at a global level and the role of GPCR dysfunction in human disease remains poorly understood. The proposed research addresses this knowledge gap by comprehensively mapping PPIs among GPCRs. Optimized proteomics procedures will be used to identify the PPIs and multiprotein complexes among GPCRs in human cell lines. Higher-level functional dependencies between proteins and complexes are often obscured in such PPI networks, and we will therefore estimate these dependencies directly for all GPCR pairs by mapping their genetic interactions - defined for each pair whenever the phenotypic fitness of cells with both GPCRs knocked down significantly differs from expected given the corresponding single-knockdown fitnesses. Combining this with the PPI network will reveal the overall pathway architecture of GPCR protein complexes, and enable the discovery of new GPCR therapeutic targets for the treatment of diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Supporting a Greater Role for Patients in Assessing the Quality of Care
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSESSMENT; PATIENTS; QUALITY OF CARE
Abstract-Résumé: In research already conducted by our team on what contributes to the quality of patient care, we found that patients are able to provide quality of care ratings that are similar to those given by providers, and more reliably as well. With our growing understanding that the health care system needs to consider the patient's view point when deciding what is and is not good care, we want to study the patient experience with care and their ability to rate the quality of care.  Our plan is to follow stroke and acute myocardial infarction patients and their care providers from the hospital to rehabilitation to recovery.  We will use questionnaires, focus groups and interviews to collect information on the patient experience as well as ratings of care.  Using the information we collect, we will work with patients and providers to identify ways to improve care for heart attack and stroke patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Eph receptors in the regulation of Death Receptor-induced apoptosis in T-ALL
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS OF LEUKAEMIA; APOPTOSIS; DEATH RECEPTORS; EPH RECEPTORS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; T CELL LEUKAEMIA
Abstract-Résumé: Treatment of leukaemias often requires bone marrow transplantation and the subsequent anti-leukaemia immunotherapeutic response is crucial for cancer elimination. While cancer cells are frequently killed by the anti-leukaemia response, its efficiency is low in paediatric T cell leukaemia (T-ALL). This may be due to the ability of T-ALL cells to survive signals initiated by the Death Receptor (DR), Fas.   Killing T-ALL cells by activating the other DRs, DR4 and DR5, is also inefficient, which hinders their utilization. This is unfortunate, as DR4 and DR5 kill specifically cancer cells, and represent attractive therapeutic targets. It is important to identify molecules, protecting T-ALL from DRs, as their suppression may enhance the anti-T-ALL response, and support involvement of DR4 and DR5 in T-ALL treatment.  Eph receptors are cell-surface proteins that can transfer signals inside the cell. Our recently published work shows that two Eph receptors, EphB3 and EphB6, are expressed on T-ALL cells. Our work also shows that Eph receptors transmit signals inside leukaemic T cells and support their survival by blocking DR-induced molecular modifications. This strongly suggests Eph receptors may actively support T-ALL ability to escape the anti-leukaemia immune response and to survive activation of DR4 and DR5. We plan to identify the specific Eph receptor that supports survival of T-ALL cells and to investigate the mechanism of its action, as this protein is likely to represent a new efficient target for leukaemia therapy. We also plan to examine if this protein has the ability to rescue cancerous T cells from the anti-leukaemia immune response and from DR5 or DR4 activation in the animal model. Our work should reveal new mechanisms of T-ALL resistance and may trigger the development of novel T-ALL therapies, inhibiting specific Eph receptors to increase the efficiency of anti-leukaemia immunotherapeutic approaches and to involve DR5, and DR4 in T-ALL treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: A South to South collaborative project to understand and address the HIV vulnerability of male sex workers in Nairobi, Kenya
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL AND BEHAVIOURAL ASSESSMENT; COMBATTING HOMOPHOBIA; COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; ETHNOGRAPHY; HEALTH SERVICES BARRIERS; HIV PREVENTION; MALE SEX WORK; MIXED METHODS; SOUTH TO SOUTH COLLABORATIONS; STIGMA AND DISCRIMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: During the early years of the HIV epidemic, a denial by many African governments in acknowledging the existence of HIV/AIDS resulted in incomplete surveillance, leading to an inaccurate understanding of the magnitude of the epidemic as well as those at risk.  Furthermore, by the mid-1980s, AIDS in Central, Eastern and Southern Africa was characterized as a heterosexual epidemic with homosexual transmission considered as being absent or occurring at a very low level.  Today, HIV prevention and intervention efforts in many parts of Africa continue to primarily center on heterosexual transmission dynamics and grossly fail to encompass the needs of men who have sex with men (MSM). The silence around the homosexual transmission of HIV has been abetted by ongoing human rights violations, homophobic government pronouncements and policies, stigma and violence. Reports of high HIV prevalence and incidence among MSM in Africa have gone virtually unaddressed, until recent calls to action. Previous research conducted by our team shows that a subset of MSM in Nairobi, those who practise sex work, are highly vulnerable to HIV infection. Between 2009 and 2012, 510 male sex workers (MSWs) attended a Nairobi-based clinic. The baseline HIV prevalence was 40.4% and the annual HIV incidence among uninfected participants was 11.8%. Reliable evidence that can explain why this group is highly vulnerable to HIV infection is urgently needed to develop an effective intervention. The proposed study has the following overarching aims: (1) to produce a reliable base of evidence that can explain the individual, social and political factors that shape the HIV-vulnerability of male sex workers in Nairobi and (2) to set up a community-based intervention that can address these various levels of vulnerability. This project will contribute to a dynamic collaboration, sponsored by the Gates Foundation, between HIV scientists, health workers, policy makers and community leaders in Kenya, India and Cana

Abstract-Résumé: Each of the medications that are currently used to stop the progression of HIV infection causes numerous side effects that carry a strong social, psychological, emotional, and physical burden. Yet, very little research has been conducted to explore the experience of side effects in the context of HIV and situate this experience outside the biomedical framework. In light of the recent expansion of antiretroviral treatment coverage, the use of antiretroviral treatment as prevention, and the introduction of antiretroviral treatment as pre-exposure prophylaxis, we believe that more explorative and descriptive research on this particular topic is warranted. The proposed project draws on Deleuze and Guattari's concept of assemblage and will follow the methodological principles of grounded theory.

Keywords-MotsClés: 1980S; ETHNIC COMMUNITIES; HAITIAN; HISTORY; HIV/AIDS
Abstract-Résumé: This is an historical study of HIV in Montreal's Haitian community during the 1980s.  Through interviews (doctors, community workers, nurses and religious leaders), as well as archival research, we will document the impact of this virus in this community.    Epidemiological data from Montreal indicates that the majority of HIV/AIDS cases were found among Haitians in the initial years of the epidemic. Despite this data, there is no large-scale study which documents this history.  The proposed project fills this gap in the history of infectious disease in Canada.    In addition to an historical documentation of how HIV/AIDS affected Haitians in Montreal, as well as their response, this research will underline the important role of history itself as a central element of social scientific understandings of disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CO-MORBIDITIES; DISABILITY; EPISODIC NATURE OF THE DISABLEMENT; GENDER SPECIFIC DIFFERENCES; HIV; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: As HIV evolves into a chronic illness people are living longer with HIV and experiencing disability related to the virus and side effects of medication. The episodic nature of the disability associated with aging with HIV is not well understood. In this longitudinal qualitative study we will conduct interviews of older men and women living with HIV on four occasions over a 20 month period to understand the age related changes in functioning, disability and health that occur over time. The findings will assist in the development of gender and age specific social and health services to minimize disablement and promote health and well- being in older adults living with HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modeling the public health impact, affordability, and cost-effectiveness of HIV self-testing in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: COST-EFFECTIVENESS; HIV/AIDS; MODELING; PUBLIC HEALTH IMPACT; SELF-TESTING
Abstract-Résumé: The number of people living with HIV/AIDS in Canada increased steadily during 2009-2012, creating an economic burden to society as a whole. An efficient way of controlling the HIV epidemic is to bring people into care early on and to prevent further transmission, which is only possible if people are aware of their HIV status. Unfortunately, about 25% of Canadians living with HIV are unaware of their status. Although HIV testing is available in Canada through health facilities, many avoid it because of privacy concerns, long waiting time, stigma and discrimination. These barriers can be partially circumvented with self-test kits, which allow people to test themselves at home, with counselling and linkage to care arranged by phone.   An over-the-counter HIV self-test, designed to be used at home, has been available since 2012 in the United States, stirring the debate over the approval of a similar test in Canada. However, the potential public health impact of introducing self-tests in the Canadian context remains unknown. In this proposal, we will investigate the impact that HIV self-tests will have on detecting new cases in individuals that are unaware of their status, and the cost associated with adding self-testing as a complement to facility-based testing in Canada. A human research study to answer this question would take many years. Hence, we propose to build a mathematical model that will combine epidemiological and economic data to project the likely public health impact and the cost-effectiveness of offering a comprehensive self-testing strategy in Canada. This work will help inform and guide policymakers at federal, provincial and territorial levels regarding the introduction of HIV self-tests in Canada. The question is novel, the timing is right, and the study findings will be of significance for Canada and similar settings worldwide.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of separase and cohesin in Ty1 transposition
Keywords-MotsClés: BUDDING YEAST; CHROMOSOME SEGREGATION; COHESIN; GENOME STABILITY; HIV1/AIDS; INTEGRASE; RETROTRANSPOSON; RETROVIRUS; SEPARASE; VIRAL DNA TARGETING
Abstract-Résumé: Retroviruses such as human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1), which is the cause of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), infect cells by integrating their viral DNA into the host genome.  A protein called HIV-1 "integrase" is required for insertion of HIV-1 viral DNA into the genome, a process that also requires host proteins. We are using the model system budding yeast to study which host proteins are required for targeting retroviral DNA into the genome.  Ty1 retrotransposons, which integrate into the yeast genome, are similar in structure and lifestyle to retroviruses.  We have made the exciting discover that Ty1-integrase, which is conserved with HIV-1 integrase, interacts with a protein called separase.  Separase is well known for its conserved role in mediating separation of chromosomes during mitosis by cleaving cohesin, which we have found also interacts with Ty1-integrase.  In this proposal, we will determine how separase and cohesin target Ty1-integrase to the yeast genome.  Understanding the basic mechanisms of viral integration will help design antiviral integrase inhibitors which is important for clinical applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of Maternal Disease on Maternal and Fetal Drug Exposure
Keywords-MotsClés: ABC TRANSPORTERS; ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; DRUG TRANSPORT; FETAL DRUG EXPOSURE; HIV INFECTION; INFLAMMATION; MALARIA; PHARMACOKINETICS; PLACENTA; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: The use of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) in HIV-infected pregnant women is necessary for preventing disease progression in the mother and transmission of HIV to her fetus.  Although pregnant women account for a large portion of patients on these drugs, there is a lack of knowledge which presents risks in that too high a dose may cause maternal or fetal toxicities and too low a dose can lead to treatment failure and risk of fetal HIV infection. Several drug transporters found in the placenta limit fetal exposure to drugs and other noxious chemicals by actively pumping compounds out of the fetal compartment. Over the past 5 years our laboratory has shown that viral and bacterial infections can cause changes in drug transporter levels in the placenta and other tissues. The implications of these changes on maternal drug exposure, safety, and  effectiveness are enormous, yet, in spite of this, very little regarding this phenomenon is currently known. Furthermore, virtually nothing is known about the impact of disease on fetal drug exposure. Indeed, co-existing infections are common in HIV-infected pregnant populations worldwide, thus investigating their impact on maternal and fetal exposure to HAART is warranted. Studies within our laboratory over the next 5 years will address: (1) the regulation of placental and maternal drug transporters in HIV and other co-infections and (2) the resultant impact of disease and co-infections on maternal and fetal exposure to HAART therapy. This information will enable us to predict potential drug-disease interactions and will assist in developing drug and dosage guidelines to improve therapy for HIV positive women during pregnancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Virus-cell interactions in the regulation of HIV translation
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAR1; HIV; HIV INFECTION; HIV TRANSLATION; INNATE IMMUNITY; LYMPHOCYTES; MONOCYTES; PACT; PKR; TRBP
Abstract-Résumé: Normally, when a virus enters a cell, it triggers a cell-virus battle. If the cell wins, the virus is eliminated and there is no disease. If the virus wins, it will hijack the cellular functions for its own benefits, it will modify the normal cell function and this will result in a disease. In the case of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), most of the time, the cell does not react well enough to counteract the viral progression. We study why the cells are not able to win the battle against HIV. Indeed, we have identified that the cells do have a reaction at the beginning of the infection by producing some factors against the virus.  However, these factors are rapidly inactivated in contact with the virus. In this study, we want to elucidate the intimate mechanisms that lead to the inactivation of some antiviral cell factors. A better understanding of this inactivation following HIV infection will lead to the identification of key components that are responsible for the failure of the cells to clear HIV infection. It will provide clues to increase the natural reaction of the cell to eliminate the virus.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cytomegalovirus Immune Memory Inflation and Immunosenescence in Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: AGE-RELATED MORBIDITY; CYTOMEGALOVIRUS; HIV INFECTION; IMMUNE SUPPRESSION; IMMUNOSENESCENCE; MEMORY INFLATION; TREC ASSAY
Abstract-Résumé: With effective antiretroviral therapy preventing the progression of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection to the acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) HIV-infected individuals are living longer but continue to suffer more morbidity and mortality than the general population. Various factors may contribute to elevated morbidity and mortality including long term effects of HIV infection itself, long term exposure to antiretroviral drugs and co-infection with other pathogens. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a common virus infecting more than 80% of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-infected individuals.  Infection with CMV is generally a clinical problem only in newborns and people with weakened immune systems. In the old elderly (people > 80 years), the immune response against CMV grows to unusually high levels, which changes how the immune system looks and acts. These changes produce an "Immune Risk Profile" (IRP), which is associated with mortality, frailty, physical signs of immune system aging, diabetes, mental decline and other age-related morbidities. In HIV-infected individuals, the immune response against CMV grows to levels associated with these age-related morbidities at much younger ages.  In this and other ways, HIV-infected individuals appear to undergo accelerated aging, which makes them susceptible to age-related co-morbidities earlier in life. We and others have shown that the size of the immune response against CMV in HIV-infected individuals affects immune system recovery. The aim of this research is to address potential causes of the unusually large expansion of the CMV immune response in HIV infection.  Different treatments, some already available and others under development would be indicated by the results.

TitreApplicationTitle: Contribution of Dynein light chain-1 for efficient HIV-1 reverse transcription and the underlying molecular mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: DYNEIN LIGHT CHAIN-1; HIV-1 ENVELOPE GLYCOPROTEIN; HIV-1 INTEGRASE; HIV-1 REPLICATION; HIV-1 REVERSE TRANSCRIPTION; HOST/VIRUS INTERACTION; MACROPHAGES; P21-ACTIVATED KINASES 1; RESTING T CELLS; REVERSE TRANSCRIPTION COMPLEX
Abstract-Résumé: The human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) pandemic is a major health problem worldwide. During virus infection, the HIV-1 virus must convert its own RNA into double stranded DNA (a process called reverse transcription) before HIV-1 can replicate in the cell. The HIV-1 has its own protein, called reverse transciptase, for the DNA synthesis, but it also has to use the cell's machinery for effective reverse transcription to occur. However, the cell's proteins that are used by HIV-1 to help the virus perform reverse transcription are not known. Recently, we identified a cellular protein, Dynein light chain-1 (DYNLL1), which works together with another viral protein, integrase, to allow efficient reverse transcription. We also found that an HIV-1 envelope protein (gp120) stimulated the reverse transcriptase process. We think that gp120 acts through a signaling pathway that includes Pak1, which regulates the DYNLL1 protein. In this proposal, we will continue to study how HIV-1 uses cell proteins to help with its own replication. We also want to study how gp120 stimulates HIV-1 reverse transcription. The results of this study will help us to discover the new mechanism/s underlying HIV-1 reverse transcription and may provide information to develop novel strategies to control HIV-1 infection through blocking reverse transcription.  This study is relevant to the CIHR HIV/AIDS Research Initiative research priority area: HIV Pathogenesis, and Prevention, Technologies and Interventions. Finding new interactions between HIV-1 and host signaling pathways that favor HIV-1 reverse transcription will help us to better understand how HIV works. Also, results of this project may reveal new ways to control HIV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lentivirus infection of brain: impact of therapy on HIV/AIDS
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; HIV/AIDS; INFLAMMATION; LENTIVIRUS; MICROGLIA
Abstract-Résumé: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infects the brain and sets up a reservoir of virus there, early in the course of the disease. HIV-1 infection of the brain causes breakdown of neurons, resulting in a syndrome called HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND). This syndrome currently affects ~20% of persons with HIV/AIDS who receive highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). HAND is defined by memory loss, difficulty in making decisions, and slowed mental and physical abilities. HAND is a major clinical problem, leaving patients with impaired ability to work and/or to care for themselves as well as a reduced chance of surviving HIV/AIDS. The effects of HAART on HIV-1 in blood are well understood, but we know much less about its impact on the brain as a viral reservoir and on HAND. To eliminate virus throughout the body, we must understand HAARTs effects on production of virus in the brain. We will investigate the effects of HAART on HIV-1 infection of brain cells, as well as how HIV-1 causes HAND. In our experiments, we will grow human brain cells in the lab, infect them with HIV-1, and measure HIV-1 production. We will also measure associated inflammation of cells and death of neurons. In similar experiments, we will measure the individual effects of current antiretroviral drugs on HIV-1 production, inflammation and death of neurons. Additionally, we will measure viral production in brain compartments during infection by the closely related feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV). In the FIV model, we will also test the effects of current antiretroviral drugs on brain cell injury and death. From these data, we will determine the effects of antiretroviral drugs on the HIV-1 reservoir within the brain and their effects on degeneration of neurons. These data will offer a rational route to optimize HAART, to potentially clear HIV-1 from the brain, and to prevent or treat HAND.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hepatitis C virus infection in pregnancy: pathogenesis and mother-to-child transmission.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODY-DEPENDANT CELLULAR CYTOTOXICITY; ANTIBODY-MEDIATED NEUTRALIZATION; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS TYPE 1; IMMUNE RESPONSES; LIVER DISEASE; MOTHER-TO-CHILD TRANSMISSION; PREGNANCY; T CELLS; TRANSMISSION BOTTLENECK
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C is a disease of the liver caused by a virus called « hepatitis C virus », or « HCV ». The health of women with hepatitis C generally improves when they are pregnant, but worsens after childbirth. Why this is happening is unknown but might have to do with how their body responds to the HCV virus, what we call the « maternal immune response ». In addition, women who are infected with HCV can transmit the infection to their infant during pregnancy and at the time of childbirth. However, it is not known whether infection takes place early or late in pregnancy, and it is not clear which route the virus travels to infect the unborn child. It is common to be infected with both HCV and human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1), the virus that causes AIDS, because both viruses can be transmitted the same way. In pregnant women who are infected with both HCV and HIV-1, transmission of HCV to the infant is 4 times more common. Again, the precise reason for this is unknown. In an attempt to respond to these various questions, we will study the relationship between the HCV, HIV-1, and the maternal immune response in a group of pregnant women who are infected with HCV or infected with both HCV and HIV-1. Results from these experiments will enable us to perfect the procedures presently used to prevent the transmission of viral infections from mother to child.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroplasticity and mental illness
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN; GENETICS; MENTAL ILLNESS; NEUROPLASTICITY; PREVENTION; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Over the past decade, scientists have been exploring the implications of brain plasticity: the relatively new knowledge that our brain's neural pathways change to compensate for illness or trauma, or to respond to changes in the environment. The idea of brain plasticity has captured the public's imagination with popular books such as The Brain that Changes Itself as well as electronic "brain training" programs that promise enhanced mental skills and protection against cognitive declines with age.   Brain plasticity also holds potential in the prevention or treatment of mental illness or addictions. Scientists are unraveling how the complex interplay between a person's biological factors combine with life experiences such as trauma to lead to changes in the brain and the development of mental illness. In recent years, the pace of research into brain function has greatly accelerated, due to new technologies and techniques such as next-generation genetic sequencing equipment, non-invasive brain stimulation and advanced brain imaging technologies. Advances will continue, given global investments into brain research. In spring 2013 alone, the European Commission announced 150 million for 20 brain projects, while U.S. President Obama launched a US $100 million initiative to map the brain. At the same time, there is much greater interest and openness among the public and media on mental illness than even a decade ago.   Therefore, a cafe on brain plasticity applied to mental health would be timely and would support CIHR's objectives. Audience members would hear about advances on a topic of current public interest. The cafe would demonstrate that CIHR is committed to supporting Canadian scientists who are at the vanguard of this research. Finally, it would show how growing knowledge of neuroplasticity is being translated into clinical treatment approaches, with tangible benefits for people with mental illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Intersection of Resident-Centered Care and Best Practices for Nutrition Care in Long-term Care
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS
Abstract-Résumé: The objective of this presentation is to describe the intersection of resident-centered or person-centered care in long-term care (LTC) with nutrition care best practices in order to understand where nutrition policy initiatives could enhance quality of care for LTC residents, especially those with dementia. Resident-centered philosophy of care was contrasted with current best practices in nutrition care with particular attention to points of convergence and dissonance. Formally recommended best practices and adopted standards of care for LTC nutrition were collected, examined, and compared with resident-centered care directives.  Health care aides provide the majority of direct resident care within LTC, with relatively little training in nutrition care. Policies and standardized care procedures help to eliminate 'guesswork' in nutrition care provision by aides, but the philosophical bent of resident-centered care does not easily accommodate highly structured nutrition care protocols. Tension exists between the tenets of a healthcare system in providing quality care and the intention that LTC is, first and foremost, the resident's home. This disconnect is highly visible with regard to nutrition care.  Examination of the intersection of resident-centered care and best practice guidelines for nutrition care can help identify potential policy solutions to enhance resident care and quality of life within LTC. Policies that increase staff understanding of nutrition care goals, empowerment, and engagement in the nutrition-care decision-making process may be more successful at meeting both aims than structured or rigid nutrition care policies and protocols.

TitreApplicationTitle: Can you feel the heat? A psychophysiological examination of the arousal patterns of sexuallly functional and dysfunctional men
Keywords-MotsClés: AROUSAL PATTERNS; ASSESSMENT AND DIAGNOSIS; ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION; ICS TRAVEL AWARDS; SEXUAL DESIRE DISORDER; SEXUAL DYSFUNCTION; THERMOGRAPHIC IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Subjective (SA) and genital arousal (GA) levels are highly correlated in sexually functional men; few studies, however, have examined this relationship in sexually dysfunctional men. Research has also yet to identify whether men with desire versus arousal disorders can be differentiated based on their psychophysiological patterns of arousal.  The goal of this study was to compare patterns of SA and GA in a community sample of men meeting DSM-IV-TR criteria for hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD), erectile dysfunction (ED), both HSDD and ED, and healthy controls. Sixty-two men (16 controls, 9 HSDD, 23 ED, 14 combined), aged 20-48, completed a sexual diagnostic interview, and watched two film clips (neutral and erotic), while genital temperature was recorded with a thermal imaging camera, and SA was measured both continuously and discretely. Results revealed strong, positive relationships between SA and GA for all groups during the erotic film; weaker relationships, however, were found for those with HSDD and HSDD/ ED. Results also indicated an increase in genital temperature for controls and HSDD men during the erotic film; there was no significant change in genital temperature for those with ED and with HSDD/ ED. Overall, HSDD/ ED men showed significantly lower average genital temperature during the erotic film, and less change in temperature during the neutral film than controls. All groups reported increases in SA during the erotic film, except for those with HSDD/ ED for whom SA did not significantly change. Finally, those with HSDD showed greater change in SA during the neutral film than other groups. Results converge with previous findings on SA-GA concordance in healthy men, and reveal unique patterns of response for those with sexual difficulties, with those in the HSDD/ ED group showing greatest impairment. Implications for conceptualization, diagnosis and treatment of these disorders will be discussed, and comparisons with women will be made.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural racism and its impact on Indigenous Health - a comparative study of Canada, Finland and Norway
Keywords-MotsClés: HAUDENOSAUNEE; INDIGENOUS HEALTH; INDIGENOUS RESEARCH METHODS; RESEARCH ETHICS; SAMI
Abstract-Résumé: Structural racism is defined as the macro-level systems, social forces, institutions, ideologies, and processes that interact with one another to generate and reinforce inequities among racial and ethnic groups.  There are many studies to document health inequalities among Indigenous peoples worldwide.  How do experiences of oppression in the past have an impact on the present day health and wellbeing of Indigenous peoples?  Studies suggest that present day social forces driving racial inequalities in health are conceptualized as being the result of historical legacies of social oppression, with racism as the link between race and health.  Furthermore, studies of disparities should more seriously consider the multiple dimensions of racism as fundamental causes of health disparities, particularly structural racism.  By investigating forms of structural racism from an Indigenous perspective we can build on the discourse about oppression and its link to the present health inequalities experienced by Indigenous peoples.  The data from a previous Canadian and Finnish comparative study was analyzed further for this project, which was mostly qualitative data in addition to simple descriptive statistics and the Norway quantitative data comes from the SAMINOR data set, a population based study of health and living conditions in areas with both Sami and Norwegian inhabitants in Norway. Discussed in this presentation are the background, methodology and theoretical framework for the dissertation and the first two articles produced and plan for further articles. An emphasis of this discussion will be on the use of both Indigenous and Western methods in the project and research ethics practices in different countries when working with Indigenous peoples.

TitreApplicationTitle: Thinking about Responsibility, Environment, and Northern Community Health: How different conceptions of responsibility can matter for the health of our communities and our environment
Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENT; HEALTH; IDEALS; INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES; NORTHERN COMMUNITIES; RESPONSIBILITY; VALUES
Abstract-Résumé: There are many different cultural values and ideals about how best to divide up responsibility for our own health and for the health of the environment that we live in so that we can all be as healthy as possible.  Different people have different views about how much of this responsibility should be taken on by governments and other organized institutions versus how much of this responsibility should be shouldered by individuals.  In this Cafe, we will discuss research that has been done on answering the question: How do different cultural ideals about the responsibilities that organized groups (such as institutions and governments) have versus the responsibilities that individuals have, affect how healthy people end up being and how healthy the environment that supports them ends up being?   This question is important because it affects things like how much money governments should spend supporting our health and whether there are more cost-effective ways to promote health instead.  Knowing the answer to this question helps us to figure out how best to shape the health and environmental policy of groups like governments.   We will focus our discussion specifically on how these policies and commitments affects the health and health-environments of Northern communities.  We are also going to discuss research that has been done on answering the question: How do different approaches and attitudes to dividing up responsibility for health between health care workers (such as physicians) and patients, actually end up affecting health outcomes?  As we will see, the approach to dividing up responsibility has a particularly big effect when it comes to the health of those people who have been in the past been more disempowered in the doctor-patient relationship.  Thus, answering this question can help us figure out how to further improve the health of members of Indigenous communities, women, and children.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Canadian HIV Cure Enterprise (CanCURE)
Keywords-MotsClés: CD4+ T LYMPHOCYTES AND MYELOID CELLS; HIV CURE; HIV ERADICATION; HIV LATENCY; HIV PERSISTENCE; HUMAN  TRIALS; HUMANIZED BLT MICE MODEL; IMMUNE-BASED THERAPIES; NON HUMAN PRIMATE MODEL; ONCOLYTIC VIRUSES
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the success of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in decreasing mortality for HIV-infected patients, ART has not cured HIV/AIDS. The failure to eradicate HIV infection during ART stems from the virus' ability to persist in the body, in multiple cell types and tissues and, in quantities below the levels detected by standard tests. Without lifetime therapy, the virus quickly rebounds resulting in accelerated morbidity and mortality. The most commonly studied form of persistence is in CD4 cells that are "resting" and harboring virus out of view of drugs or from the immune system. However, evidence indicates that other long-lived cells, known as myeloid cells, contribute to HIV persistence. Cells that allow virus persistence are called virus reservoirs (VRs) and represent a significant barrier preventing an HIV Cure.  While much is known about HIV persistence, many puzzles remain about the source of persistent HIV, the mechanisms underlying its establishment and maintenance, and the ways to eradicate VRs. The Canadian HIV Cure Enterprise (CanCURE), a collaboration of leading Canadian HIV researchers proposes an integrated and innovative research program across a number of platforms (human, animal, in vitro model) to: 1) Identify and exploit insufficiently characterized properties of myeloid cells, especially macrophages, that act as VRs and contribute to HIV persistence; 2) Conduct detailed mechanistic studies aimed at understanding how these VRs are established and maintained; 3) Identify new drug candidates that capitalize on these discoveries to reverse persistence and evaluate novel therapeutic strategies that enhance immune recognition and/or elimination of VRs; and, 4) Test whether novel immune-based therapies influence persistence in ART-treated patients in clinical trials. These studies are all aimed at finding new effective approaches to curing HIV infection in humans by eliminating persistent HIV infection from VRs in ART-treated patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: H. Chertkow Expression of Interest for CCNA
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN DISEASE; COGNITION; DEMENTIA; DIAGNOSIS; PREVENTION; QUALITY OF LIFE; THERAPY; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The neurodegenerative brain diseases (NDD)- Alzheimers Disease (AD) and other dementias in particular - will be the diseases of the 21st century due to aging of our population. The decision to establish a Canadian Consortium for Neurodegeneration and Aging (CCNA) represents a timely response to this urgent health problem. Our Expression of Interest (EOI) to establish the CCNA includes 37 principal applicants (9 are junior researchers), and 285 other members of the Canadian dementia research community grouped into 20 research teams and supported by seven new national platforms. Virtually every highly published dementia researcher in Canada is part of this submission. The 37 Principal Applicants include 4 from B.C., 5 from Alberta, 1 from Saskatchewan, 13 from Ontario, 11 from Quebec, and 3 from Nova Scotia. Our mission can be summarized as follows: to create teams that will do transformative research, advancing our understanding of the biology, natural history, clinical presentation and management of AD and other NDD. We will create a novel cohesive clinical research infrastructure in Canada. We will catalyse development of new molecules and therapies, which can be tested in appropriate patient groups we will establish within the CCNA, to lead to new treatments and approaches to prevent the disease through delaying its onset. Such efforts will be complemented by Teams seeking to advance care of affected individuals and their families through better training of caregivers, use of new technologies at home, and assessing specific functional challenges such as driving. The approach of this consortium will also focus on the unique needs of rural and indigenous communities. Our Teams will be national, rather than local or regional, and will promote the active engagement of junior researchers, building the next generation of dementia researchers. We will also establish a committee to address the ethical, legal and social issues pertaining to research on dementia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interactions between dietary protein intake and polymorphisms in the insulin growth factor family: Effects on obesity development in the Québec Newborn Twin Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH COHORT; CHILDREN; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTION; GENETICS; GROWTH FACTOR; IGF; NUTRITION; OBESITY; SOCIAL INEQUAILITES
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity development during childhood, when children are most vulnerable to environmental and parental influences, has a dramatic impact on subsequent risk of obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and cancer in adulthood. The proposed research project will use pre-existing data from the Quebec Newborn Twin Study (QNTS), a longitudinal birth cohort of twins (n=300 pairs) born from 1995-1998 and their parents. Randomized controlled trials and observational studies show that dietary protein intake in excess of metabolic needs early in life is associated with both obesity and increased production and activity of the insulin-like growth factor (IGF) axis (comprising insulin, IGF1 and IGF2, their receptors and binding proteins). Further, variations in the IGF genes have been associated with differences in birth weight, growth, adiposity, body mass index (BMI) and early onset  puberty, in both human and animal models. Considering this evidence, the proposed project will answer this specific research question: Does high protein intake during the first years of life potentiate the effect of polymorphisms in the IGF family on the development of obesity and precocious puberty during the critical growth period of birth to adolescence? We will  examine parental influences (genetic and obesity status) because 1) insulin and IGF2 are known to be under specific genetic transmission patterns and 2) parental obesity is an independent predictor of offspring obesity. The phenotypes of interest are growth trajectories from birth to adolescence, as well as early pubertal and obesity development during the transition from preadolescence to adolescence. The unique strengths of this project are the prospective data collection from birth to adolescence, the deep sequencing of genes in the IGF pathway and the ability to reduce variance by controlling for genetic and environmental background of each twin pair, both monozygotic and dizygotic, reared together.

Abstract-Résumé: The Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs (AMC) research team is working toward the establishment of the First Nations Epicentre of Excellence to improve the quality of life for all First Nation citizens of Manitoba and to promote their physical, emotional, mental and spiritual wellbeing through the creation of a First Nations Health Data Centre  for health - for health related research, surveillance, and training.  The AMC have always recognized that health information, knowledge and research is critical when it comes to accessing funding, influencing government policy or assessing the effectiveness of policies, services, programs, or public health interventions that effect Manitoba First Nations (MFNs). In pursuing governance of health information and research we recognize the need to build the infrastructure of a statistical institute to collect, analyze, translate and disseminate the information as absolutely necessary if we are to make any improvements in our state of health. The AMC research team has worked towards this vision through the following journey:   1.In 1996 AMC received mandate through Chiefs in Assembly to carry out the Regional Health Survey (RHS), the only national survey across Canada that is First Nations designed, developed and delivered on-reserve. The AMC Research team delivered 3 successful waves of the RHS (1997-98, 2002-03 and 2008-10); RHS data sets are currently housed within the AMC Research Centre; and MFNs Statistical Institute Concept Paper 2005.  2.The AMC Health Information Research Governance Committee (HIRGC) provides governance and guidance over the RHS and regional research projects that involve Manitoba First Nations to ensure research is based on a. Free prior and informed consent, both collective and individual b. First Nations principles of Ownership, Control, Access and Possession (OCAP), as it relates to data and information and; c. First Nations ethical principles (whether Anishinaabe, Ininew, Dakota, Dene or Oji Cree.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tourette's Syndrome: Facts and Fiction

Abstract-Résumé: Tourette's Syndrome (TS) can affect up to one in 100 individuals of all ethnicities, genders, and backgrounds, with a prevalence ranging from 0.4 percent to 3.8 percent in children. However, popular portrayals of Tourette's Syndrome (TS) and tic disorders are often exaggerated or otherwise misrepresentative. In the proposed Cafe Scientifique, experts on Tourette's Syndrome and tic disorders will share knowledge about the development, symptoms, and treatment of TS. This event, hosted by Dr. O'Connor and Dr. Lavoie, both CIHR-funded experts on tics and Tourette's, will constitute a unique opportunity for experts to collaborate with the general public to promote awareness of TS and debunk myths about the disorder. In addition to Drs. O'Connor and Lavoie, a participant from our research and treatment centre will be invited to attend the event and to provide a first-hand account of living with Tourette's Syndrome. His or her participation will contribute to the informal and intimate nature of the Cafe Scientifique and will serve to provoke and facilitate discussion between experts and Cafe participants. Cafe attendees will learn to distinguish the facts about TS from the fiction, increase their awareness of the disorder in their environments, and learn about available resources for individuals in Quebec living with TS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Striving Towards Excellence: Addressing Gender Diversity & Bias in Nursing Education and Clinical Practice
Keywords-MotsClés: CAFE SCIENTIFIC; GENDER DIVERSITY; NURSING EDUCATION; NURSING PRACTICE; NURSING RECRUITMENT; PUBLIC DISCUSSION
Abstract-Résumé: Diversity is often discussed in nursing. Administrators now recognize, that the nursing profession must be reflective of a variety of ethnic, racial, cultural, and religious backgrounds in an effort to provide care to a wide, and fast growing diverse patient population. Just as racial and ethnic diversity is essential for nursing's future, so is gender diversity. Nursing however, has seldom addressed gender diversity and as such, the numbers of men and, individuals who self identify with other gender identities such as transgendered, remains low in the nursing workforce. Additionally, nursing educators and the nursing profession as a whole, must be cognizant of heterosexism, which implies that heterosexuality is the accepted, societal norm and, its associated implications in nursing practice and education. Just as improving cultural and racial diversity requires action, achieving gender diversity also requires a proactive approach, addressing both the internal organization and the external recruitment and retention of men and other gender diverse individuals in the nursing workforce.   As nursing seeks to be more representative of the general population it serves, nursing faculties, schools and colleges must strive to recruit and retain a diverse cohort of students, and make all efforts to address gender diversity in education and nursing practice.   The proposed Cafe Scientifique will address the issue of gender diversity in nursing practice and discuss ways to help promote diversity in nursing recruitment and retention, education and clinical practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Minding the Gap - the Good, the Bad and the Ugly - Therapeutic Implications of Gap Junction Channels
Keywords-MotsClés: CHANNELS; COMMUNICATION; DISEASE; GAP JUNCTIONS; HEALTH; OUTREACH; PANNEXINS
Abstract-Résumé: While the public generally appreciates the need for health research as it relates to understanding and treating human disease, we will present this in context of the need for, and understanding of, the basic science that underpins disease and treatment, specifically as this relates to human mutations in genes making specific membrane channel proteins. These proteins, called connexins, form unique channels (i.e., gap junction channels) that are the only cellular structures that permit a direct exchange of small biological molecules between the cells in contact. These "intercellular channels" permit the passage of ions and metabolites among a common population of cells. By controlling this exchange, they can be viewed as key players in maintaining normal functions of the body, in particular organs and tissue, a process referred to as homeostasis. They also play a critical role in other basic physiological processes such as development, tissue differentiation and maintenance of tissue functions.  The link between connexins and human disease has been reinforced as the identification of the number of connexin genes has extended to 21, and mutations in 9 of these genes are linked to various diseases.  These include developmental disorders, cataracts, skin disease, cardiovascular disease, stroke, epilepsy and cancer. We will also the value of model systems designed to explore the mechanisms of these mutations and possible therapeutic insights. In addition, participation of graduate students will demonstrate how basic research is essential to the training of our future scientists. Some of their research will be available at the Cafe in the form of lay-friendly poster presentations.  Furthermore, the participation of  "special guests" with specific diseases due to connexin mutations will personalize the message.

TitreApplicationTitle: Employing HIV Peer Research Associates: Are We Providing Enough Support?
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY BASED RESEARCH; GIPA/MIPA; HIV/AIDS; PEER RESEARCH ASSISTANT
Abstract-Résumé: Employing people living with HIV as peer research associates is gaining popularity today as Community Based Organizations and researchers attempt to integrate the greater involvement of people with HIV more meaningfully into new research projects. The HIV community is responding by promoting the development of industry standards for employing workers with HIV to adequately provide support based on the unique needs of this group of workers. Often unskilled in the conventional sense of their job descriptions, peers bring accessibility to the community, rich relationship opportunities and subject relevance, and personal history to their work. Specific supports are required to address the emotional, physical, financial, and personal intensity impact this employment has on these workers. By openly discussing and including the input of peer workers to establish industry standards for support provision that can be adapted to various forms of peer employment, we will offer a valuable resource for researchers, Community organizations, Health Authorities, and others who seek to employ people living with HIV on research projects. This Cafe Scientifique will be organized to discuss industry support standards for peer research associates living with HIV. Researchers, community organizations, Health Authorities and peer workers themselves will be invited to discuss types of supports currently available for people living with HIV working as research associates. The Cafe organizing team will present existing examples of support services and ask participants to comment on their effectiveness, and for their ideas on how to address gaps in current support services.

Keywords-MotsClés: APPROCHES PSYCHOSOCIALES; DIABETE; FACTEURS DE RISQUES; GLYCEMIE; GERONTOLOGIE; INSULINE; MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER; MALADIES INCURABLES; MALADIES METABOLIQUES CHRONIQUES; SANTE COMMUNAUTAIRE
Abstract-Résumé: Projet 1 La maladie d'Alzheimer est une forme de demence qui engendre la perte progressive et irreversible des fonctions mentales et de la memoire. Elle est frequente chez les personnes agees et represente environ 65 % des cas de demence. Les causes exactes de la maladie d'Alzheimer ne sont pas elucidees de facon claire a ce jour. cependant, des facteurs genetiques et environnementaux comme certaines anomalies genetiques, des facteurs de risque cardio-vasculaires (hypertension, l'hypercholesterolemie, l'obesite, le diabete)ou encore l'intoxication a certains metaux lourds, contribuant a son apparition et a son developpement, sont connus. De nombreuses recherches a travers  le monde tentent de creer des outils permettant de diagnostiquer la maladie a un stade plus precoce. Mieux connaitre la maladie d'Alzheimer permettait de la prevenir ou de la controler ? Telle est le sujet qui sera debattu au cours de ce cafe pour sensibiliser le grand public et de repondre aux questions qu'il se pose sur la maladie d'Alzheimer.  Projet 2 Le diabete est une maladie chronique qui se manifeste lorsque le corps est incapable de produire suffisamment de l'insuline ou de l'utiliser correctement pour controler le taux de sucres dans le sang. Lorsque le taux de sucre dans le sang atteint ou depasse 2 g/L, le diabete est avere. C'est une maladie grave dont les complications sont difficiles a gerer et les consequences peuvent conduire a un deces premature, a l'invalidite ou a d'autres maladies, qui touche de plus en plus de personnes dans le monde entier. Toutefois, les personnes atteintes du diabete peuvent prendre des mesures pour controler et reduire les risques de complications. Les experts qui animeront ce cafe scientifique decriront les differents types de diabete, exposeront ses complications et ses consequences, et insisteront  sur les mesures de prevention et de controle du diabete.

TitreApplicationTitle: La chirurgie de l'obésité est-elle un traitement miracle du diabète de type 2 ?
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETE DE TYPE 2; OBESITE
Abstract-Résumé: Nous assistons a une epidemie fulgurante d'obesite et de diabete de type 2 dans nos contrees socioeconomiques developpees et partout dans le monde en raison des habitudes de vie (sedentarite) et une alimentation riche en graisses. L'obesite est etroitement liee au diabete de type 2  et precede bien souvent le diagnostic de ce diabete. Par ailleurs, La chirurgie bariatrique demeure le traitement efficace de l'obesite. Dans notre  lutte contre le diabete de type 2, est-il alors possible d'envisager une place a la chirurgie de l'obesite (dite bariatrique)  dans le traitement du diabete de type2; existe-t-il des liens entre le traitement de l'obesite et du diabete. Cette question importante fait l'objet de travaux de recherche effectues par les chercheurs de l'Universite de Sherbrooke et de l'Universite Laval dans le cadre du programme de leur chaire de recherche respectivement sur le diabete et l'obesite. Reunis a titre d'invites experts du diabete et de l'obesite sur le  plateau du cafe scientifique propose, ils causeront et informeront le grand public des grandes avancees de recherche accomplies sur la question tant a Sherbrooke qu'a Quebec.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Science of Sex(uality)
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETICS; HEALTH; MEDIA; PUBERTY; SEX; SEXUALITY
Abstract-Résumé: During the exhibit The Science of Sex(uality) THEMUSEUM would like to present two Cafe Scientifique forums to examine the health topics in the area of sex and sexuality.   The information presented in the forums are helpful to he public, as there are many misconceptions about sex and sexuality that can be cleared up and sharing information and ideas in a relaxed environment is the easiest way to disseminate correct information and share thoughts.   Sharing information about sex and sexuality can help prevent sexually transmitted infections and diseases, prevent unwanted pregnancies, help young people deal with a multitude of issues relating to sexuality and growing up, and help people of all ages navigate through a subject that is often taboo. With a great deal of grossly incorrect information available, THEMUSEUM wishes to work with CIHR researchers to make new and truthful information available to the public based on current research.

TitreApplicationTitle: How do sex differences influence your brain's response to cancer therapies?
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL DEFICITS; BRAIN; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; GENE EXPRESSION; RADIATION THERAPY; SEX DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Radiation is an important diagnostic and treatment modality in the fight against cancer.  However, this type of therapy can have many detrimental side effects.  Among those, radiation therapy (RT) can cause significant neurological and cognitive impairments under for patients.  Specific, RT-related impairments include deficits in attention, concentration, memory and executive and visuospatial functions.  One discovery from recent research is that the level of impairment experience by a patient receiving RT therapy may be related to sex.  In addition, it is now well accepted that the effects of RT are seen in tissues and organs that are not directly treated with radiation.  These are known as bystander effects.  Unfortunately, the mechanisms underlying these impairments and remote effects are not well understood.  The panel of the current proposal, Drs. Olga Kovalchuk and Bryan Kolb, have led the way in the study of sex differences in the effect of radiation on the brain and untreated tissues following RT of the brain.  In more recent studies, this team will analyze the underlying mechanisms of the sex dependent cognitive impairments and resulting behavioural changes.

Abstract-Résumé: Cafe Scientifique at Simon Fraser University (SFU) engages the public with a series of five informal discussions each year connecting research to health. The series enjoys great support from the community and the University for its alignment with SFU's strategic vision of three interconnected themes: Engaging Students, Engaging Research, and Engaging Communities. The Faculty of Science at SFU will host this year's events in Vancouver and Surrey, British Columbia. Each of this year's proposed Cafes will tackle an important health-related topic that is of significant interest to the community, and will feature members from SFU's Departments of Biomedical Physiology and Kinesiology, Biological Sciences, and Molecular Biology and Biochemistry. The first Cafe will discuss how the powerhouse of cells plays a role in health and disease. The second Cafe will discuss how bacteria cause disease. The third Cafe will focus on how to manage the burden of chronic disease. The fourth Cafe will delve into the science of stem cells for treating disease. The final Cafe will discuss ways to entice older adults to start and continue daily physical activity to improve health. Through these discussions we will engage with the community-at-large, and demonstrate how research can impact their lives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Café scientifique sur la médecine personnalisée
Keywords-MotsClés: CAFE SCIENTIFIQUE; MEDECINE PERSONNALISEE
Abstract-Résumé: Avec les progres de la recherche genomique, la medecine personnalisee risque de transformer radicalement l'approche en matiere de soins de sante. Comment? En permettant aux medecins et autres intervenants de proposer aux patients des interventions  medicales «sur mesure»  en fonction de leur profil genetique, qu'il s'agisse du diagnostic, du choix d'un traitement adequat ou de prevenir des maladies. Ce domaine fait d'ailleurs l'objet d'importants investissements en recherche. En partenariat avec Genome canada et les IRSC, le gouvernement canadien a notamment annonce en mars dernier l'octroi de 150 millions de dollars pour 17 nouveaux projets de recherche en medecine personnalisee, dont huit au Quebec seulement. Cette nouvelle approche medicale pose toutefois plusieurs enjeux scientifiques, mais aussi ethiques, juridiques, economiques et sociaux dont nous aimerions debattre. A titre d'exemples : quelles sont les maladies principalement ciblees par cette approche? Quelles sont les dernieres avancees?  Quelles sont les limites et la validite des biomarqueurs utilises (compagnon diagnostic)? Comment gerer l'enorme masse de donnees genomiques necessaire a la medecine personnalisee? Comment garantir la confidentialite des informations recueillies? Faut-il craindre les exclusions basees sur le profil genetique? Cette approche va-t-elle permettre de reduire les couts associes a la prescription de traitement inefficaces ou va-t-elle necessiter un investissement massif dans notre systeme de sante?

TitreApplicationTitle: Café scientifique «Intégration des aînés dans la communauté: défis et nouvelles interventions»
Keywords-MotsClés: PARTICIPATION SOCIALE DES AINES
Abstract-Résumé: Les personnes agees de 65 ans et plus representent une proportion importante de la population. On estime que d'ici 25 ans, cette proportion va augmenter et meme doubler dans plusieurs pays et que pres de la moitie des personnes agee auront des incapacites. Definie par l'implication optimale de la personne dans les activites qui lui procurent des interactions avec les autres dans la communaute, la participation sociale est un enjeu majeur de notre societe, un determinant cle d'un vieillissement reussi et en sante.  Afin de permettre aux personnes agees de vivre le plus longtemps possible a domicile, il est important d'organiser un cafe scientifique dont l'objectif est de sensibiliser le grand public aux defis et aux nouvelles interventions de participation sociale. Par la tenue de cet evenement, les organisateurs veulent creer un espace convivial et susciter une discussion entre le grand public, les acteurs communautaires et la recherche sur les defis et les nouvelles interventions de participation sociale. Ainsi, il sera possible de favoriser la sante et la qualite de vie des aines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genomics and Personalized Medicine: Challenges and Promises for Health Care
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHICS; GENETICS; HEALTH; SEQUENCING; TECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of this Cafe Scientifique is to generate a discussion about the personal, social, ethical, and legal issues pertaining to genomics, genetic testing, and personalized medicine in healthcare. We will engage the general public in an interactive conversation with a panel of scientific, medical, and legal experts about how genetic information can be used to guide medical treatment. We will discuss both the benefits and the risks of personal genome sequencing and genetic testing, exploring the personal and emotional consequences of genetic testing (including the 'burden of knowing'), discrimination, and potential privacy and legal issues, such as gene/genome patenting. Some of the questions we hope to cover include the following: What is genome sequencing? Would you (the general public) want to sequence your genome or offer your genetic information for research? Why or why not? What does giving 'consent' for genome sequencing really mean? What are researchers doing with this genetic information? What responsibilities do researchers that utilize this information have to the donors? Are there hidden risks of donating your DNA for research or genetic testing? Would you or your relatives want to know if you were at risk for a serious disease (even if the test was not definitive and/or no cure was available)? How is personalized medicine changing the practice of medicine and helping to improve healthcare? Is genetic information distinct from other personal health information (e.g. family history)? How could employers or insurance companies use your genetic information to discriminate against you? How can the government help to protect an individual's genetic information? Why do biotechnology companies want to patent genes? Should genes or genomes be allowed to be patented? What is the future of personalized medicine?

TitreApplicationTitle: Earl W. Davie Symposium
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; GENETICS; HEMOSTASIS-THROMBOSIS; INFECTION; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNITY
Abstract-Résumé: The so-called Waterfall pathway for blood clotting was described in the 1960s by Dr. Earl W. Davie. This major breakthrough set the stage for this annual symposium in his honour, and which is fortunately able to be held in his presence. Dr. Davie's groundbreaking discovery of how blood clots form and the role that blood plays in controlling this, has impacted on a wide range of disciplines, particularly on how these pathways contribute to hemophilia, deep vein thrombosis, heart attacks, strokes, arthritis, cancer, wound healing and infectious diseases. All medical disciplines have derived benefit from his discoveries.  This 1-day symposium is dedicated to expanding our knowledge of the role of this and related blood-based pathways in health and disease. Leading international and local scientists and clinicians will highlight the blood-borne pathways that link the clotting system with those involved in infection and inflammation. We will also be honoured this year by a presentation by Nobel Laureate Dr. Edmond Fischer. The topic is highly relevant to many medical disciplines, including in particular, Infection and Immunity. The symposium will be highly educational and informative, and will lead to important and meaningful collaborations.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Cafe Scientifique Proposal:  "How to keep your brain healthy as you get older"
Keywords-MotsClés: CIHR CAFE SCIENTIFIQUE PROPOSAL; HOW TO KEEP YOUR BRAIN HEALTHY AS YOU GET OLDER
Abstract-Résumé: The issue of healthy aging, particularly healthy brain aging, is an important one to Canadians. Media outlets often headline the latest scientific breakthroughs in this area, and mass-market advertisements to promote programs and products that claim to protect our brains from age-related deterioration and decline. But beyond these mass media messages, maintaining vascular health indeed has important implication on brain health, as it is associated with risk for negative health outcomes such as dementia, stroke  and Alzheimer's disease. Vascular disease may manifest in subclinical, or 'silent' strokes, characterized by progressive cognitive decline. In fact, central to the recently released Canadian Best Practice Recommendations for Stroke Care related to Stroke Prevention and Cognition were recommendations regarding the prevention of first stroke or transient ischemic attacks and maintenance of vascular health through the "promotion of healthy lifestyles to minimize vascular risk, education to the general public, stroke survivors and their families, aggressive risk factor management and timely access to specialized stroke prevention services"(Coutts et al., 2012; Eskes et al., 2012). This proposal aligns with these best practices to offer a Cafe Scientfique entitled: "How to keep your brain healthy as you get older". This Cafe will focus on the description of the issue of keeping the brain healthy as we age, and will include discussion of the scope of this health issue, impact on Canadians, current state of evidence, and strategies for prevention and management of these issues.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cancer: What's physical activity got to do with it?
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CANCER PREVENTION; CANCER SURVIVORSHIP; EXERCISE; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; SEDENTARY BEHAVIOR
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is one of the most distressing and debilitating diseases of our time and it is likely that there are now over 1 million cancer survivors in Canada. Evidence now strongly suggests that physical activity plays a critical role across the cancer continuum; from prevention, through to post treatment and post diagnosis, and well into survivorship. We are proposing to conduct a Cafe Scientifique (Cancer: What's physical activity got to do with it?) that brings together 3 CIHR funded researchers (all current) from across Canada as well as one local community cancer advocate from the Canadian Cancer Society. The primary objective of this Cafe is to engage residents of Medicine Hat and Southeastern Alberta with local, provincial, and national leaders in physical activity and cancer research. Our Cafe is unique in that we are proposing to hold the Cafe in the medium-sized city of Medicine Hat, Alberta. Medicine Hat is a vibrant city in Southeastern Alberta, but unfortunately has some of the lowest physical activity prevalence rates in the province. We believe a Cafe of this nature, in this city and region (which is largely rural), will foster discussion and engagement amongst the residents. We plan to hold the Cafe in May, 2014.

TitreApplicationTitle: Food insecurity is compounded by increased mercury and lead exposure among Inuit in the Canadian Arctic
Keywords-MotsClés: ECOSYSTEM APPROACH TO HUMAN HEALTH; FOOD SECURITY; INTERNATIONAL POLAR YEAR INUIT HEALTH SURVEY; INUIT; LEAD; MERCURY; NUTRITION
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Food insecurity is high in the Canadian Arctic, and related to poor nutrient status among adult Inuit. Food safety issues such as exposure to the environmental contaminants mercury (Hg) and lead (Pb) is another concern but the relation between food security and contaminant exposure is unknown.  Objective: To study the relationship between exposure to Hg and Pb and food security status among Canadian Inuit adults.  Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 2 595 Inuit adults from 36 communities from Inuvialuit Settlement Region, Nunavut and Nunatsiavut. Data on household composition, traditional food harvesting and consumption, socio-economic indicators was collected. Food security was assessed using the 18-item USDA questionnaire. Blood Hg (B-Hg) and Pb (B-Pb) levels were measured. ANOVA and multiple regressions were used to explore the relations between exposures and food security.  Results: B-Hg and B-Pb were higher in participants living in food insecure households and answering positively to the question "In the last 12 months, were there times when the food for you and your family just did not last, and there was no money to buy more?". When controlling for age, sex, smoking, drinking, country food preference and the presence of an active hunter, there was a positive association between B-Hg and B-Pb and increasing household food insecurity.   Discussion: As food insecurity, poor nutrient status and exposure to contaminants are public health concerns in the Canadian Inuit, there is a need to understand the interdependent dynamics behind these issues in order to promote food security and safety.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inuit Food Sharing Practices as a Means of Reducing the Negative Effects of Social, Economic and Environmental Change in Rigolet, Nunatsiavut, Labrador
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS
Abstract-Résumé: Traditional wild foods are fundamental to Inuit health and food security, and Inuit communities are experiencing new challenges to accessing these foods due to climate change and complex social and economic changes. Focusing on the community of Rigolet, Nunatsiavut, Labrador, this presentation will explore the viability of Inuit food sharing networks as a means of addressing food security issues. The objectives of this research project are, (1) to document and characterize common sources of food within Rigolet, (2) to track the movement of food within the community and between households, (3) to identify factors that facilitate or detract from the movement of food, and (4) to determine whether sharing networks function differently in times of stress. This research that will be presented is part of two on-going projects; the Inuit Health Adaptation to Climate Change project and the Inuit Traditional Knowledge for Adapting to the Health Effects of Climate Change project projects, which are currently being conducted in Rigolet in partnership with the Rigolet Inuit Community Government. The project is being conducted within a participatory research framework that seeks to ensure that the research methods and results are in cohesion with the experience and knowledge of Rigolet as a community. The participatory methods include semi-structured interviews, card sorts, and eight weeks of house visits with partner households to maintain a detailed inventory of foods within these households.

Abstract-Résumé: The purpose of our Cafe Scientifique is to further engage and exchange with the Yarmouth/Tri-County public through conversation with our team of national researchers, local stakeholders, and community leaders on the subject of bereavement and care following the death of a loved one. Abstract-Résumé: Five Cafe Scientifiques are planned in 2013-2014 to be organized and hosted by the Office of Vice-President (Research & International). Each panel has a minimum of two CIHR-funded researchers. Community organizations are represented on the panels wherever possible. Cafes are promoted to target audiences  as well as the broader public, university and healthcare communities in Winnipeg. The Battle Against the Flu Virus - Our research experts will share perspective and advances on their fight against the flu, from diagnosis to prevention and development of a better flu vaccine. Practical Solutions for Developmental Disabilities - Moving research knowledge from the researcher to those who need that information can make a real difference in the lives of those who have developmental disabilities.
