Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) and a Need for a 21st Century Human Rights Response - We explore, through the lens of research, clinical care and advocacy, the story behind why we need to address this disability, medically and socially, in a way that protects the rights of women, men, children, families and communities affected by FASD, a lifelong disability.

TitreApplicationTitle: Spirituality and Healing in Healthcare: How Does the Integration of Spirituality Influence Health Outcomes or Relieve Suffering?
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT; CULTURE; DIVERSITY; HEALING; HEALTHCARE; RELIGION; SPIRITUALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Traditionally spirituality or religious perspectives have been given little attention among healthcare professionals, unless the perspectives were seen to pose a threat to the implementation of a recommended course of treatment.  Spiritual care is generally not seen as a primary responsibility of healthcare practitioners, and is normally referred to hospital chaplains, who were incorporated into hospital care almost 40 years ago, although this service has been under threat in recent years (Stirk, 2004).    However, an increasing diversity of spirituality and religion of healthcare consumers and their families is prompting attention within the healthcare system.  Notably, results of the 2011 National Household Survey report that 76.1% of Canada's population identified as having a religious affiliation.  Of these, 67.3% identified as having an affiliation with a Christian religion, 7.2% reported religious affiliations with Muslim (3.2%), Hindu (1.5%), Sikh (1.4%) and Buddhist (1.1%) faith systems.  This was up from 4.9% a decade earlier, as recorded in the 2001 Census.  The remaining 1.6% of respondents identified themselves as Jewish (1.0 %) and 'other' religious affiliation (0.6%) (Statistics Canada, 2013).  Thus, the value of holistic healthcare, which gives consideration to the spiritual, social, psychological, as well as the biological aspects of health and wellbeing, has become an important emerging healthcare policy and practice issue.   The objective of the proposed Cafe is to stimulate cross-cultural discussion and awareness amongst the general public, including various stakeholders in healthcare (recipients of healthcare and caregivers, healthcare professionals, educators and students, as well as policy makers), about the role spirituality and spiritual care may play in the health and welfare of healthcare consumers.

TitreApplicationTitle: What Makes for Quality of Life When You Have an Advanced Life-Limiting Illness?
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC ILLNESS; END-OF-LIFE; FAMILY CAREGIVING; PALLIATIVE CARE; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: What can health care do for you if we cannot cure your illness? The primary cause of sickness and death in Canada is chronic disease. As we age, the likelihood of living with at least one chronic illness rises steeply. Canadians are living longer and many are living sicker. A recent report from the Canadian Institute for Health Information highlighted gaps in healthcare for people living with chronic illness and pointed out that Canadians living with chronic diseases may not be receiving all the care they need. Women tend to be disadvantaged along with rural residents and those with low income. When we cannot cure your illness, the focus must turn to maximizing comfort, supporting quality of life and engaging with families where most of illness care occurs.  In other words, the focus becomes living well. Our research indicates that we can support quality of life and that different strategies may be needed for persons with illness as compared to family caregivers, for women as compared to men, and for rural residents as compared to urban residents. However, our research also raises fundamental questions about how to think about quality of life when there is progressive advanced illness that is accompanied by loss and, inevitably, death. Our findings raise important areas for discussion - how can we support quality of life for all involved family members regardless of gender, place of residence, or whether they are providers or recipients of care? How can we support quality of life throughout progressive illness?

TitreApplicationTitle: "I always feel like they will judge me:" Why is talking about sex so hard? African newcomer youths' voices and youth sexual health
Keywords-MotsClés: AFRICAN NEWCOMER YOUTH; GENDER; HIV AND STIS; INTERRACIAL INTIMACIES; MIGRATION; RACE; RACISM; SEXUAL SILENCE; STIGMA; YOUTH SEXUAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: With a remarkable presence of newcomer youth between the ages of 16 and 25 years of age from African countries immigrating to Winnipeg in the past few years, a need for research and action towards addressing sexual health has become evident. The need to understand the role of migration, gender, race, culture, and coming of age in a new sociocultural environment in relation to vulnerability for HIV and STIs has fueled community-based research in the prairie city. These Cafe Scientifiques are oriented towards two main groups, the local African newcomer youth at large and the adults from African newcomer communities as well as the general public, in order to discuss research findings and to engage in conversations about the issues facing the youth. In particular, anthropologist researchers, peer researchers, and local service providers and knowledge users will present their points of view on topics related to sexual health as a human right, about sexuality as a taboo topic within African communities, and about the stigma experienced by African youth in their navigation of new sexual cultural norms. The launching of a website created by youth participants of a CIHR project will be used as a means to spark discussion. The voices of the youth will be encouraged by providing a Junior Cafe for them exclusively while at the same time the panelists will seek to engage the wider general public and adults from newcomer communities in a youth-focused presentation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Demystifying what it means to be at 'High Risk' for Breast Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BRCA1; BRCA2; BREAST CANCER; BREAST DENSITY; HIGH RISK; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Breast Cancer Foundation - Ontario Region will host a Cafe Scientifique to demystify what it means to be at high risk for breast cancer.   Breast cancer affects more women than any other type of cancer. The Canadian Cancer Society (CCS) estimated that 22,700 women would be diagnosed with breast cancer, and 5,100 would die in Canada in 2012. Breast cancer tends to present earlier and be more aggressive in women at high risk. The definition of high risk encompasses several different criteria, including diagnosis of a mutated BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene, a first-degree relative of a mutation carrier, a greater than 25% lifetime risk of breast cancer (determined by validated risk assessment tools), or radiation to the chest prior to the age of 30. Although only 2% of the Canadian adult female population are at high risk for developing breast cancer, the issue of risk is relevant to everyone, and the more informed everyone is, the less confusion there will be about risk factors, risk reduction options, and screening. For women at high risk for breast cancer, there are options for reducing risk, including modifying diet, exercise, and alcohol intake, as well as more drastic, and permanent, preventive measures, such as prophylactic mastectomy or oophorectomy (removal of the ovaries).   For this Cafe Scientifique, we have assembled several leading experts in the field, three of whom hold CIHR funding for their research, and will engage a woman at high risk, to unpack and examine these complex issues in easy to understand language that is reflective of the realities of everyday life. Our Cafe Scientifique will create a space for critical reflection about what is currently known about the factors that place women at high risk for breast cancer, and what can be done about them, as well as where current CIHR-funded research is heading, and where future research should be directed to drive us towards a future without breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modelling the transmission-dynamics of anogenital and oral HPV infections, and impact on related cancers.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANAL CANCER; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS INFECTIONS; MATHEMATICAL MODELLING; OROPHARYNGEAL CANCER; SEXUAL BEHAVIOR; SMOKING; VACCINATION POLICIES
Abstract-Résumé: From 1992 to 2007, the incidence of oropharyngeal cancer (OC) in Canada increased by 20%. This trend contrasts with the decrease in oral cavity cancer, most likely due to the decline in smoking. An even higher increase (40%)  was observed in anal cancer (AC)   incidence. Accumulating evidence supports the hypothesis that increasing oral and anal infection by human papillomavirus (HPV) is the cause of these additional cancers. This new reality is of concern for many developed countries: authors project that by 2020, HPV-related OC will have surpassed cervical cancers in numbers. However, by not taking in account the evolution of sexual behavior, extrapolating current trends based on past OC and AC incidence amounts to speculation. Yet, health policies such as the inclusion of boys in current girls-only HPV vaccination programs will need to rely on a  solid understanding of how OC and AC incidence will evolve in order to accurately analyze the benefits versus costs. It is why an investigation of potential causes of this trend is important. Following this global objective, this project aims more specifically to understand how changes in sexual behavior through the past decades can explain a higher incidence of oral-anal HPV. Additional objectives include a better understanding of the role of each site   (anal/oral/genital) and sexual act on overall transmission and assessing the impact of various vaccination strategies. We will approach this problem by using mathematical modelling. The idea of modelling sexually transmitted diseases is tried  and has been successfully used already for genital HPV but has never been applied to multi-site HPV. We will use data on sexual behaviour, smoking, and on oral-anal HPV prevalence to fit models.  In the pursuit of said objectives we will gain a better comprehension of HPV multi-sites transmission and the evolution of its spread which will allow us to determine optimal vaccination strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: When a pregnancy leads to a tumor: Gestational Trophoblastic Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: ABNORMAL PREGNANCIES; INFERTILITY; MISCARRIAGE; MOLAR PREGNANCIES; PLACENTA; STILLBIRTH; TUMOUR; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Pregnancy and the enlargement of one's family often lead to happiness and celebration. Unfortunately, not all pregnancies result in the term-birth of a healthy baby. Embryo loss occurs in half the pregnancies. Even scarier, 1/600 pregnancy results in a rare type of tumor that can potentially put the future mother's life at risk. Among the treatments for these tumors, one of them is as drastic as removing the woman's uterus. We propose to hold a Cafe Scientifique to discuss this group of tumors called: Gestational Trophoblastic Diseases (GTDs). We will begin by explaining what these tumors are and how they appear during or following a pregnancy. We will then go on to discuss subsequent pregnancies, the increasing risks of miscarriages related to GTDs and the possibility of infertility. As GTDs are rare and little information is accessible, our aim is to inform our audience members, answer their questions and hear their concerns on this subject.

TitreApplicationTitle: Is it Criminal to have HIV?  Barriers to Knowing your Status.
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV CRIMINALIZATION; HIV STIGMA; HIV TESTING; HIV/AIDS; POINT OF CARE TESTING
Abstract-Résumé: Rates of HIV infection continue to rise in Canada and in Newfoundland and Labrador (NL); however rates of HIV testing have declined in this province.  Up to 26% of those infected with HIV do not know their status, therefore barriers to HIV testing must be identified, discussed and overcome.  It is recommended that HIV testing should become a routine part of medical care, but concerns about confidentiality, fear of stigma and discrimination, and accessible HIV testing have all been identified as barriers to getting tested.   The risk of being criminally charged if someone has HIV and does not disclose their HIV status to sexual partners before having sex is another barrier to 'knowing your status'. This criminalization, or 'law and order' approach, serves to stigmatize people living with HIV and undermines proven HIV prevention strategies and programs. Point of care testing or 'rapid HIV tests' may help overcome some of the barriers by providing more testing opportunities for those with less access to medical care or for those with privacy concerns, while also reducing the anxiety associated with waiting for HIV test results. Presently, point of care testing for HIV is not available in NL as it is in other provinces. Education about the use, advantages and disadvantages of point of care testing is needed.    This Cafe Scientifique event will provide an opportunity for the public to engage in dialogue with a panel of experts and renowned scientists about barriers to HIV testing, and point of care testing as a potential solution. Issues related to criminalization of HIV, along with the associated problems of stigma and discrimination, will also be discussed. This session will be of interest to the general public, including those at risk of and living with HIV.  This free event is being hosted by Memorial University, the AIDS Committee of Newfoundland and Labrador, and Eastern Health, with support from the CIHR Cafe Scientifique program.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pediatric HIV infection: exploring determinants of a functional cure.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; FUNCTIONAL CURE; HIV-AIDS; IMMUNOLOGY; INFLAMMATION; MOTHER-TO-CHILD TRANSMISSION; PATHOGENESIS; PEDIATRICS; VIRAL RESERVOIR; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: HIV is the virus that causes AIDS. Infection with HIV can be treated using medications called « antiretroviral » drugs. However, HIV infection cannot be cured even with these medications, in part because the virus is able to hide and remain hidden in various parts of the body. This means that patients infected with HIV have to take antiretroviral medications continuously for the rest of their lives to remain healthy. These drugs can also be used to prevent pregnant women from transmitting the virus to their babies. Recently, researchers in the United States reported that a young child who contracted HIV from her mother and was treated soon after birth with a potent drug combination apparently became free of the virus later on. This report suggests that in some cases, children who acquired HIV infection from their mother around the time of birth could be « cured » of the infection if intensive drug treatment is prescribed immediately after birth. Five potentially similar cases have since been identified in Toronto and Ottawa. The objective of this proposal is to examine whether the amount of HIV that remains hidden in the patient despite effective treatment is lower in HIV-infected children who are treated early on with antiretroviral medications, as compared to children in whom treatment is introduced at a later age. We will also do blood tests to measure signs of inflammation and to assess how children who start treatment earlier as compared to later respond to HIV infection in general. Results from these studies will help us determine if early intensive treatment with antiretroviral medications is capable of reducing the amount of HIV hidden in the body or, in some cases, leads to a cure from HIV infection in children who contract HIV by mother-to-child transmission.

TitreApplicationTitle: Does A Community Based Program to Improve Health for People who are Obese Work?
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY; INTERNVETIONS; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity rates in New Brunswick are the highest in Canada. What can be done to reduce the obesity levels in New Brunswick?  No "magic bullet" exists.  In this public presentation, a panel of experts will examine one tool in the toolkit of the obesity reduction instruments. A research team based in Fredericton, NB received CIHR grants for the Healthy Eating, Active Living for Tomorrow's Health (HEALTH) study. The team developed an intervention based on moderate physical activity, nutritional education and goal setting, over a 12 month period, for two rural and two urban groups of people with obesity. The good news is that the active six month intervention was successful and participants' health outcomes improved considerably. The not so good news is that after the six months of self-management many of the participants' health outcomes reverted back to base-line. The bad news is that the intervention had a high drop-out rate. From the study we learned that it is difficult for many people living with obesity to make lifestyle change, but it is not impossible and is worth doing. In this Scientific Cafe we would like to have an honest discussion about the challenges and rewards of trying to make lifestyle changes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Breaking the ice - What is the status of breastfeeding in Labrador communities?
Keywords-MotsClés: BREASTFEEDING; HEALTH BENEFITS; INFANT FEEDING; NUTRITION
Abstract-Résumé: The Baby-Friendly Council of Newfoundland and Labrador (Baby-Friendly NL) Breastfeeding Research Working Group is an experienced medical, nursing, and research team from the Faculty of Medicine/School of Pharmacy at Memorial University, the NL Provincial Perinatal Program, the NL Centre for Health Information, and the Baby-Friendly Council of NL. We are working on a large three-part study looking at why women breastfeed (BF) their babies. The aim is to increase BF rates in NL, since we fall far below the Canadian average. Breastfeeding is known to be "best for baby" because it has both short-term benefits (protects infants and young children against diarrhea, respiratory tract infections, ear infections, meningitis, and urinary tract infections) and long-term benefits (protects against chronic illnesses, such as obesity and Type I and Type II diabetes). Breastfeeding is also known to have extended long-term effects by reducing healthcare costs. This is significant locally since NL reports some of the highest rates of all 3 chronic conditions, yet the lowest rates of initiation and duration rates of BF nationally and internationally. Programs supporting a "baby-friendly" atmosphere in hospitals and throughout community programs can improve BF rates. More importantly, interventions to support expectant and new mothers in the area of infant feeding are key to improving the health of both mother and child. This application for a Cafe Scientifique to be held in Happy Valley-Goose Bay, NL is submitted as a follow-up to ones in St. John's, NL (eastern region) in 2010; Corner Brook, NL (western region) in 2012; and Gander, NL (central region) in 2013 on this very important topic. Funding for a fourth Cafe will allow the expansion of this dialogue into the remaining region of Labrador/northern Newfoundland. The audience of interest is expectant/new mothers and fathers, their support persons, healthcare practitioners, and all interested members of the general public.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epilepsy:  The challenges and the future of understanding
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUGS; EPILEPSY; HEALTH CARE; POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is a physical condition characterized by sudden, brief changes in functioning of the brain works.  It is a symptom of a neurological disorder - a disorder that affects the brain and shows itself in the form of seizures.  In 50 - 60% of cases, the cause of epilepsy is unknown  .  Approximately 0.6% of the Canadian population has epilepsy. This includes those who take anticonvulsant drugs or who had a seizure within the past 5 years.  Due to the stigma surrounding epilepsy and the prejudice with which society has historically treated people with epilepsy, many persons with the disorder are reluctant to admit it or to seek treatment. Thus the prevalence of epilepsy is likely much higher.  Each day in Canada, an average of 42 people learn that they have epilepsy.  Each year an average of 15,500 people learn they have epilepsy; 44% are diagnosed before the age of 5, 55% before the age of 10, 75-85% before age 18 and 1% of children will have recurrent seizures before age 14.  Hence, approximately 60% of new patients are young children and senior citizens.  In approximately 50% of cases of childhood epilepsy, seizures disappear completely.  This Cafe Scientifique was devised in order to provide a synopsis of the future drugs that are in development, the success of invasive techniques in an attempt to cease seizures, and the current policy challenges in epilepsy treatment and recognition.  It is envisioned that enlightened discussion will occur between members of the public and the speakers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lots about Clots for Grandmothers, Mothers and Daughters
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH PROMOTION; HORMONE REPLACEMENT THERAPY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; ORAL CONTRACEPTION; PREGNANCY; SEX DIFFERENCES; THROMBOSIS; WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a serious cardiovascular condition that includes deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) refers to blood clots forming most commonly in the deep veins of the legs that can break off and travel to the heart, ultimately lodging in the arteries of the lungs, a condition known as pulmonary embolism (PE), causing death and disability. Women have a heightened risk of developing blood clots during unique periods in their lives when hormone exposure is increased. These life stages include adolescence and early adulthood with use of birth control medications, pregnancy, and the postmenopausal period during which hormone replacement therapy may be used. Birth control pills increase a woman's risk of VTE by 2 to 8 times. During pregnancy and the first few months after the baby is born, the risk of VTE is increased 5-fold. Finally, hormone replacement therapy increases a woman's risk of VTE by 2 to 4 times. McGill University's Jewish General Hospital leads a nationally-recognized, comprehensive, multidisciplinary Centre of Excellence in Thrombosis and Anticoagulation Care (CETAC) that is comprised of out-patient and in-patient care, training of medical and nursing students, residents and fellows, and numerous grant-funded basic science and clinical research initiatives in VTE. Clinician-researchers of CETAC will organize and host a Cafe Scientifique titled "Lots about Clots for Grandmothers, Mothers and Daughters", whose objectives are to educate women and the general public about the symptoms of VTE, situations that increase the risk of VTE during a woman's lifecycle and ways to prevent VTE from occurring. Moreover, we will highlight differences between men and women regarding risk of VTE and its complications and describe our Program's ongoing research efforts to better understand these differences. Our Cafe will inform women as well as men about VTE, an important public health concern.

TitreApplicationTitle: Les cafés scientifiques de l'Artère-Bioéthique
Keywords-MotsClés: APPLICATION DES CONNAISSANCES; BIOETHIQUE; DIFFUSION DE LA RECHERCHE; INTERDISCIPLINARITE; INTERSECTORIALITE; PARTAGE DES CONNAISSANCES; PARTICIPATION DU PUBLIC; SCIENCE ET SANTE; VALORISATION DE LA RECHERCHE; ETHIQUE DELIBERATIVE
Abstract-Résumé: La mission premiere des cafes scientifiques de l'Artere-Bioethique est de rassembler de facon ponctuelle (bimestrielle) des chercheurs, des professionnels, des etudiants et des neophytes du milieu des sciences et de la sante dans une atmosphere conviviale et propice a l'echange interdisciplinaire, avec pour objectif de briser l'isolement entre les departements et les facultes universitaires interesses au domaines des sciences et de la sante. Ces rencontres se veulent egalement un pont entre le milieu academique et le milieu communautaire, permettant d'une part a l'expert de se confronter aux defis de la vulgarisation scientifique et d'autre part, au citoyen interesse d'exprimer et d'enrichir ses reflexions sur les enjeux  contemporains en bioethique. Ainsi, l'equipe de l'Artere-Bioethique propose chaque annee une serie de cinq cafes gratuits et ouverts a tous, portant sur des themes d'actualite (ex. le suicide assiste, la fertilisation in vitro et le don de gametes, la medicalisation de la psychiatrie et la sortie recente du Manuel diagnostique et statistique des troubles mentaux - DSM-V). Les cafes scientifiques de l'Artere-Bioethique se tiennent a tous les deux mois - de septembre a mai - au Cafe l'Artere (cooperative de solidarite equipee d'une salle de diffusion/projection et situe en plein coeur de l'ile de Montreal) en debut de soiree (18h-20h). Les cafes commencent par une courte presentation de la question du jour (ex. presentation de la problematique et du vocabulaire associe, etude de cas, support visuel) par un expert-chercheur subventionne par les Instituts de recherche en sante du Canada (IRSC) [30 min]. Ensuite, les enjeux ethiques associes a la problematique sont souleves par un paneliste versee en ethique et par un representant de la collectivite [20 min]. Puis, un moderateur anime une discussion approfondie entre l'audience et les panelistes [1 hre] pour favoriser l'echange et contribuer a creer un carrefour entre la bioethique et la societe.

TitreApplicationTitle: Research Findings on Driving and the Elderly: Canadian Driving Research Initiative for Vehicular Safety in the Elderly (Candrive)
Keywords-MotsClés: CANDRIVE; DRIVING; OLDER ADULTS
Abstract-Résumé: Driving is the primary mode of transportation for many older people and allows them to maintain their independence and mobility. Aging has been associated with declines in cognitive capacity, vision and physical abilities that may impair one's ability to drive safely. However, we know that older adults should not have their driving licenses revoked simply on the basis of age or an age-related medical diagnosis; many are still safe to drive. To ensure the well-being of older adults while at the same time maintaining public safety, we need to find fair and equitable means to ensure that no one is deprived of the driving privilege unjustly. Canadian Driving Research Initiative for Vehicular Safety in the Elderly (Candrive), funded by CIHR, was developed to do just that. It is a national longitudinal study involving seven sites and over 900 older drivers to generate knowledge for use by transportation policy makers, clinicians and the general public to improve the safety and quality-of-life of older drivers in Canada. Our proposed Cafe would provide us with the opportunity to share some of our findings, lessons learned, and future directions with those with an interest in this area.

TitreApplicationTitle: How do we manage chronic disease as we age?
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BEHAVIOURAL CHANGE; CARDIOVASCULAR; CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that 1 in 3 Canadians will likely suffer from a cardiac event in their lifetime and, by 2031, close to one quarter of Canadians will be over the age of 65 years. As the population ages, we will see an increase in the rate of cardiovascular diseases (CVD) that will affect quality of life. There is a high incidence of other chronic health problems (e.g. diabetes, obesity, depression) among elderly people with CVD; therefore, it is important to understand the complex patient (i.e. patients experiencing multiple conditions at one time) and to provide resources accordingly. The majority of cardiovascular rehabilitation programs in Canada are structured to provide tools, practical tips, and strategic support specific to elderly people who have suffered a cardiac event in order to help them better manage their disease and improve the quality of their lives.  Some examples are: tailored exercise programs, nutritional counselling, stress reduction, and education to increase their understanding of the disease itself. The main objective of the Cafe will be to provide the public with practical advice and tips on how to manage chronic disease and improve quality of life as we age.

TitreApplicationTitle: Putting your heart into it: The science of vascular aging
Keywords-MotsClés: CAFE SCIENTIFIQUE; CANADIAN LONGITUDINAL STUDY ON AGING; CARDIO/CEREBROVASCULAR; GERIATRICS; INTERDISCIPLINARY; POPULATION-BASED RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Canada is experiencing an unprecedented change in the make-up of its population, with seniors accounting for nearly 15 per cent of all Canadians.  By 2036, nearly one in four Canadians will be age 65 or older. With rapid demographic change underway, there is a critical need for high-quality evidence to inform clinical, health and social policy decision-making that is directed towards improving the health and well-being of Canada's seniors.  A strategic initiative of the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging has brought together a team of 160 researchers and collaborators from across the country to answer the most pressing questions on aging. The goal is to develop a research platform that will enable state-of-the-art, interdisciplinary, population-based research and evidenced-based decision-making that will lead to better health and quality of life for Canadians.   The CLSA collects information on the changing biological, medical, psychological, social, lifestyle and economic aspects of people's lives as they age. One area of particular focus is cardio/cerebrovascular domain, including stroke, hypertension, heart attack and angina. Through this Cafe Scientifique, leading health research experts will explore what the evidence says about how to maintain health and protect against age-related changes to the heart and blood vessels. This lively discussion will focus on the impacts of vascular aging and how scientific research is shedding new light on the prevention and management of related chronic diseases.

This Science Cafe will focus on the role of nutrition on kidney function in optimizing overall health and to promote a better understanding of kidney disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Physical Activity in Health Aging
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BARRIERS; COMMUNITY PROGRAMS; EXERCISE; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: As the body ages, there is typically an increased risk of disease, disability, and poor health. However, many of the health problems we associate with old age can be reduced through regular exercise.  Physical activity (i.e., playing sports, walking, gardening, lifting weights) is an important part of healthy aging as it helps people live independent, productive lives.  However, physical activity levels typically decrease with age, which has important consequences for both personal and public health. The goal of this CIHR Cafe Scientifique is to engage with members of the public around the topic of physical activity in later life.  Specific topics that will be covered include the biological and psychological benefits of physical activity with respect to age and emerging areas of aging and activity research.  A special emphasis will be placed on exploring barriers and facilitators of an active lifestyle.  Through an open discussion with activity and aging researchers and members of the public, we hope to start people thinking and talking about the role of physical activity in healthy aging. Based on the discussion content, we will also generate a document of physical activity concerns and recommendations from the view of the public through which organizations can use to improve physical activity programs and policies.

TitreApplicationTitle: "You see, when they designed the programs they didn't think people were going to live that long anyway": Rethinking service provision for people living with long-term HIV
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CHRONIC ILLNESS; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; EPISODIC ILLNESS; HIV
Abstract-Résumé: With the widespread use of anti-retroviral therapy in developed countries people are living longer with HIV. Although HIV is often referred to as a chronic disease, what it means to live with HIV as a long-term chronic illness is poorly understood in both HIV-related research and service provision. AIDS Service Organizations (ASOs) and those living long-term with HIV have identified a number of challenges to the provision of care and support services as people continue to live longer with the disease. This Cafe Scientifique event will centre on the findings from a CIHR-funded study examining the priorities and challenges of people living long-term with HIV and the organizations that support them.  This knowledge translation event provides an opportunity for a dynamic and interactive dissemination of recent research findings, bringing together stakeholders to discuss what we - as individuals, organizations and communities - need to do differently to respect and respond to the realities of living long-term with HIV. Dr. Winston Husbands will present the study findings, highlighting potential shifts for service provision appropriate to HIV as a long-term chronic and episodic illness. Three additional presenters (Dr. Kelly O'Brien, Dr. Ann Stewart, and Kenneth King) will speak to issues related to living long-term with HIV from their perspectives as a researcher, clinician, and a community member.  The venue for this Cafe will be the 519 Church St. Community Centre, an LGBTQ space and downtown location. The Cafe will address topic pertinent to people living with and affected by HIV, ASOs, clinicians, and researchers interested in issues related to living long-term with HIV. Because the Cafe content speakers to issues related to aging and chronic illness, this Cafe will target intersectoral participation from individuals and organizations working in mental health, employment services, aging and long-term care, rehabilitation, other chronic illnesses, and government.

TitreApplicationTitle: An AIDS-free generation: What will it take?
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO SERVICES; HIV/AIDS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; STIGMA AND DISCRIMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: With biomedical advances in highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) and increasing investment in HIV vaccine research, there is great hope and anticipation that we are on the brink of "solving" AIDS. Yet the "end of AIDS" cannot be achieved without effective population health interventions working to ensure HIV/AIDS treatment and preventive services are accessible and appropriate to those who need them most. Two Cafe Scientifique events in Victoria, British Columbia, will unpack the question of "An AIDS-free generation: What will it take?" by sharing evidence on the status of HI:AIDS prevention and eradication. The Cafes aim to: (a) provide an opportunity for members of the public to engage with health researchers and contribute their views on HIV/AIDS treatment and prevention; and b) increase public awareness and discussion about the needs of those infected and affected by HIV and the factors that influence access to health care and other services, including stigma, discrimination, and socioeconomic status. A panel of researchers specializing in HIV/AIDS from the University of Victoria and three community members working in HIV/AIDS prevention and treatment will discuss some of the social and structural factors that have challenged HIV/AIDS prevention and eradication efforts and present evidence from innovative and promising initiatives that are working to overcome them.

TitreApplicationTitle: Borders, Babies and Body Parts: The Ethical Dilemmas of Medical Tourism
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHICS; MEDICAL TOURISM; ORGAN TRADE; REPRODUCTION; REPRODUCTIVE TOURISM; SURROGACY
Abstract-Résumé: Medical tourism (international medical travel initiated by individuals seeking care in other countries for any number of reasons) is an ethically problematic phenomenon. As this global business continues to expand, its effects challenge global health equity, particularly in low- and middle-income countries trying to attract wealthier, fee-paying patients. The growth in private facilities catering to such patients may 'crowd out' access to essential health care for poorer citizens in these countries. Two other types of medical tourism pose particular concerns: reproductive tourism and organ transplant tourism (often referred to as the organ trade). In the proposed Cafe Scientifique, three experts will discuss the ethical issues which arise from these three forms of medical tourism: the growth in globalize private medical markets for those able to pay, the surge in reproductive medical travel and the persisting organ trade. The objectives are to address what we know about medical tourism, what we don't know but should know, and why we, as Canadians, should be concerned ethically about the phenomenon.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sharing Experiences, Changing Lives: The Canadian Index of Wellbeing
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH; POPULATION HEALTH; WELL-BEING
Abstract-Résumé: Until recently, the success of Canadians has been gauged by Gross Domestic Product alone, presuming economic growth = health and hence better quality of life and well-being. New developments in the measurement of wellbeing - led by Canadians for Canadians - has changed this landscape.  The Canadian Index of Wellbeing (located at the University of Waterloo) delivers a broader depth of understanding that, when partnered with GDP, gives citizens and decision-makers the full package of information they need to plan for a healthy, sustainable future.    The objective of this Cafe Scientifique is for expert health researchers to share how the wellbeing of Canadians is tracked and measured using the CIW to ensure better health and quality of life, with Canadians from all sectors of society. Audience members will have the opportunity to contribute their views on current research and future directions. The Cafe Scientifique will be open to members of the general public who have an interest in health and well-being and the importance of the links between economic and other aspects of population health. This topic is of tremendous interest among general publics - influenced by substantial recent media coverage around a range of indices related to: happiness, wellbeing, health, quality of life, and the relationships between them.  An audience member email distribution list will be developed as a result of the Cafe. The list will form the basis of a communication strategy between the researchers and audience members, including a report of the Cafe, and notifications of similar upcoming community-based events and participatory research opportunities. This strategy will encourage audience member and health researcher engagement and communication, and knowledge sharing opportunities into the future.  The vision is to establish an engaged citizenry that will help us measure, monitor and enhance the long-term health and well-being of the Canadian population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transsexual people: The visible and invisible persona
Keywords-MotsClés: CROSS-SEX HORMONAL TREATMENT; RISK OF HIV TRANSMISSION; SEX REASSIGNMENT; TRANSGENDER
Abstract-Résumé: Gender identity represents the sense one has of being male or female. A significant incongruence between gender identity and physical appearance is known as gender identity disorder leading often to depression and social outcast. Manifestations of gender identity issues range from simply living as a member of the opposite sex to partial or maximal physical adaptation through hormonal and surgical treatment. Social rejection, discrimination and violence exacerbate the risk of sexual transmitted infection including HIV in these transsexual persons. The number of persons seeking help for gender identity disorder in Canada has recently increased based in part on the change of legislation, cultural values, hormonal therapy and surgical techniques. Persons undergoing sex reassignment can be reassured that serious short-term complications of cross-sex hormonal treatment appear to be uncommon. However, long-term effects on risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and cancer are not well known.  We will address a historical perspective on transsexual positive actions and on the criss-crossing forms of marginalization that include sexual stigma, transphobia, HIV-related issues in the context of community and social norms in Quebec . We will provide a frame-work to promote health equity and optimal medical management for these persons.

TitreApplicationTitle: Managing the Seams: Transitions in Health Care for Older Adults
Keywords-MotsClés: CARE TRANSITIONS; COMPLEX NEEDS; HEALTH CARE SYSTEM; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION AND EXCHANGE; OLDER ADULTS; SYSTEM NAVIGATION
Abstract-Résumé: Older adults with complex health problems, such as those with hip fracture, frequently require care from multiple health professionals across a variety of settings. Increasingly, it is recognized that care quality and patient safety may be most at risk during the transition between health care settings. Despite the frequency and importance of transitions, transitional care has received little attention in research, health policy and clinical practice. The InfoRehab Transitions project focused on the transitional care experiences of older hip fracture patients, and involved interviews with patients, their family members, and health care providers at each transition in care. The aims of our Cafe Scientifique are: to provide an opportunity to share what was learned through our research project regarding what is currently working well to connect parts of the health care system for older patients, what areas need improvement, and what patients, family members and health care providers can do to make transitions go as smoothly as possible; encourage residents of Kitchener-Waterloo (KW) region (including patients, health care providers, community stakeholders, and the general public) to engage with researchers, and contribute their views on the research findings, implications, and future directions; promote knowledge sharing, the free flow of information and transparency between the research community and residents of KW region through presentations and interactive discussions in a comfortable and dynamic environment; continue to foster collaborative relationships with our partners and acknowledge their contributions to the InfoRehab Transitions research program; and generate interest in future research initiatives. At the conclusion of the cafe, it is hoped that each participant will better understand the challenges faced by complex older adults undergoing care transitions and will take away knowledge and skills to better navigate the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Of Mice and Men: Making Sense of Health Science in the Media
Keywords-MotsClés: EVIDENCE; EVIDENCE-BASED; HEALTH; HEALTHCARE; MEDIA; NEWS; REPORTING
Abstract-Résumé: Canadians are becoming increasingly interested in staying, or becoming, healthy and learning about the latest health trends and developments. The news media has been quick to cater to this interest by producing many reports on health and medical issues. Every day new health research studies are covered in the media worldwide. One day you may read coffee is bad for your health; the next day you'll hear the same cup of java reduces your risk of disease. How does one sort through the complex and often conflicting world of scientific research to make sound health decisions? The media has incredible influence over public perception: nearly nine out of 10 Canadians make decisions affecting their health as a direct result of media reports on health and health research. However, due to the complexity of health science, and poor reporting practices, these reports often contain skewed facts or conflicting data. The Canadian Cochrane Centre (CCC) supports media sharing health information, but lobbies for responsible reporting based on the totality of evidence. While many health writers take care to ensure their writing is informed by the best available evidence, this is not always the case. But, just as journalists should use many types of information and sources to produce stories, the public should seek to verify what they see and read in the media. This Cafe Scientifique is an opportunity to educate the public to interpret health and medical media reports with caution while using critical appraisal skills to distinguish responsible reporting from sensationalized and misinformed journalism. The CCC will discuss examples of health news stories to identify problematic reporting practices while presenting trusted information sources the public can use to validate media reports, including The Cochrane Library. This event will provide a discussion forum where researchers and the public alike can exchange ideas about health reporting in an open environment.

Abstract-Résumé: Concerns about the impact of the environment on children's health are high. People worry about the health effects of pollution. Many diseases such as asthma, autism and cancer are said to be linked with pollution. Some of these concerns, however, may not be correct and could lead to myths. Thus, it is important for people to discuss their concerns together. It is helpful, as well, to check with the experts. Child Health and the Environment is quite a new topic in Canada. People need to know about research that has been done.  We will hold a Cafe Scientifique in Edmonton. In this event, the public and the experts will talk about pollution and its effects on children's health. People will learn where children may be exposed to pollution. They will learn which are most harmful exposures. There will be conversations on how to protect children from the sources of pollution. We will encourage a friendly exchange of questions, answer and concerns.  The cafe will invite the public, parents, students, and health workers. We will attract interest using flyers, posters, emails and internet. Through all these, we hope to set up a group with an interest on children's environmental health. We expect this group will stay in touch after the cafe.

TitreApplicationTitle: Housing First:  Lessons learned from the Toronto site of 'At Home/Chez Soi'

Abstract-Résumé: 'At Home/Chez Soi' is national research project, funded by the Mental Health Commission of Canada (MHCC), which explores how the Housing First model can address the unique needs of the growing number of homeless people with mental illness across Canada. CRICH was selected as the research partner for the Toronto site of 'At Home/Chez Soi' project and staff met with participants for over 2 years to assess the impact of the Housing First approach in a variety of outcomes related to housing, health status, functioning, quality of life, and service use, in addition to the economic costs associated with service use.  This Cafe would provide a forum for the public to learn about the Housing First model, including how Housing First can be used to address the ongoing problem of homelessness in Toronto, in addition to a discussion of some of the lessons learned from the past 4-years of the 'At Home/Chez Soi' study with CIHR-funded researchers, service providers, policy-makers, and people with lived experiences of homelessness and mental illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multiple Sclerosis: To B or not to B?
Keywords-MotsClés: B LYMPHOCYTES; CLINICAL TRIALS; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: MS is an illness affecting the brain and the spinal cord (central nervous system, CNS) of 55,000 to 65,000 Canadians. In MS, the CNS is attacked by immune cells that are inappropriately activated and subsequently migrate from the blood into the CNS. A number of clinical trials now demonstrate that removing B lymphocytes, a sub-type of immune cells, prevents formation of MS plaques and decreases symptoms. These therapies cannot be used for long-term treatment, due to potential complications. Our team of leading clinical-neurologists (Drs. Prat, Bar-Or) and basic-scientist (Dr. Gommerman) will focus on these B lymphocytes and their roles in MS with the goal of understanding how B cells are involved in MS in order to develop safer more effective therapies. In pursuing these goals, we wish to engage with patient populations as well as their families, friends and care-givers in a two-way conversation, communicating our research goals whilst gathering information from these stake-holders on what excites them about the future of research on B cells and MS. We will hold a Cafe Scientifique in order to bring together these stake-holders for an informal lecture on the state of the art with respect to MS therapies (in particular B cell directed therapies) and our research objectives. This will be followed by a Question and Answer period facilitated by Dr. Andreas Laupacis (Knowledge Translation expert) who will serve as a moderator. The ultimate goal will be to educate the public on our research goals, encourage fresh thinking about MS therapies and approaches to MS research, and learn from our stake-holders about the issues that matter to them.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Neuroscience of Stress
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; BRAIN; NEUROSCIENCE; PTSD; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: This is a proposal from Brain Awareness Montreal (BAM) to collaborate with CIHR for a Cafe Scientifique on "stress and the brain" as part of the 2014 BAM Cafe Scientifique series. Through this series, BAM seeks to increase public awareness of brain research and incite interest in neuroscience. Our Cafes Scienfiques have always centred on interactive discussions between a panel of expert scientists and the general public.  While moderate acute stress may actually be good for us, exposure to extreme or chronic stress can cause and/or worsen mental disorders such as posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression, as well physical illnesses, particularly cardiovascular disease. In Canada, work time lost to stress has been estimated to cost Canadian businesses about $12 billion annually. The World Health Organization predicts that by 2020, stress will be the second leading cause of death. Sadly, stigma surrounding stress-related disorders, particularly those that are psychological or neurological in origin, hinder recovery by causing those affected to withdraw from society and avoid seeking treatment when they need it most. As such, increased public awareness of the effects of stress, via events like our Cafe Scientifique, is key. We hope that such opportunities for knowledge sharing will ultimately help reduce stigma toward patients suffering from stress-related disorders and their families. We further hope that the conversation will be beneficial not only to those individuals suffering from stress-related pathology, but also to the general public, because we all deal with stress on a daily basis.  For the Cafe Scientifique, our panel of selected speakers will discuss various facets of stress, including the latest advances in research on the neuroscience of stress, its short- and long-term effects, current therapeutic interventions, and practical tips for stress reduction. Finally, some light entertainment will be provided to uphold the spirit of the cafe.

Abstract-Résumé: In recent years, public health has urged people to try active commuting when getting to and from work, school, or while doing short errands.  Active commuting can be anything other than motorized transport and includes riding a bike, walking, or running to name a few.  Active commuting can increase a person's overall level of physical activity, which in turn can improve their health.  However, there are risk with active commuting, especially if you need to share a roadway with fast moving cars, such as when you're bicycling.  To reduce this risk, many people have suggested universal mandatory helmet laws should be imposed.  This would mean that everyone, no matter their age would have to wear a helmet.  This Cafe Scientific aims to look at issues surrounding safe and sustainable bicycle safety including pros and cons of imposing mandatory helmet laws.

TitreApplicationTitle: Coconut Oil Cures and Dentures Cause Dementia: why is the science of dementia so hard to understand?
Keywords-MotsClés: CAFE SCIENTIFIQUE; DEMENTIA; EVIDENCE BASED; OUTREACH; PUBLIC
Abstract-Résumé: By 2030 about 750,000 Canadians are expected to have dementia. In Nova Scotia that number will be disproportionately higher (over 28,000 people or 2.5% of the population) reflecting its older than average age structure. It is no wonder that dementia is second only to cancer as a health concern for older Canadians. In Canada, as of 2009, 77% of the population were online at home, and many now use this tool to address their fears and concerns. The explosion of  information online and in traditional media means that those with an interest in dementia must do a lot of sifting through evidence based and other information - which often sit side by side.  Accessing quality research in a format easily understood is a challenge for the public, with inaccurate representations of research and scientific verbiage or  jargon at times being used to encourage interest in a treatment or intervention. Among the general public in Canada, scientific literacy (knowledge of scientific concepts sufficient to impact a person's ability to function in a  modern, industrial society) is estimated to be below 20% . Low levels of health literacy (the degree to which individuals can obtain, process and use basic health information to make decisions)  are also a problem for many Canadians, particularly as they age. Recognizing  high-quality evidence, knowing how to look for this, and understanding  its fundamental importance to quality dementia care and treatment is often asking much of the general public - so how can we help them? The purpose of this Cafe Scientifique is to open a discussion about how the public can better understand and interpret the science (and pseudo science) of dementia as it appears in the media and online world  - what is  the difference between evidence-based information and anecdotal claims, and why is this important?

TitreApplicationTitle: Lower your risk of getting colorectal cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; COLORECTAL CANCER; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH SERVICES; SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: In the past, First Nations have enjoyed lower rates of cancer incidence and mortality compared to non-Aboriginal populations. However, for some cancers including colorectal cancer, incidence is now as high among First Nations men as among non-First Nations men. The cancer picture in First Nations has changed owing to increased life expectancy, a growing population, and multiple modifiable risk behaviors, e.g. poor diet, tobacco smoking, low uptake of cancer screening. Moreover, because First Nations people are diagnosed at a later stage of their disease compared to non-First Nations people, survival tends to be worse. Preliminary work with health care practitioners in Kahnawake (an educational session held in March 2013) revealed a lack of awareness that screening occurs in healthy people. In the proposed Cafe we will address how routine screening may lower people's risk for developing colorectal cancer, possible ways to improve accessibility to CRC screening, and touch upon the modifiable risk factors that are pertinent to the First Nations community. Findings from our research on a telehealth method of delivering CRC screening will be discussed as will findings from our work on patient indicators of quality in colonoscopy.

TitreApplicationTitle: SickKids Café Scientifique: 2013 Program
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA; C. DIFFICILE; CAFE SCIENTIFIQUE; CHILD HEALTH; DIARRHOEAL DISEASE; GLOBAL CHILD HEALTH; HUMAN DEVELOPMENT; NUTRITION; PROBIOTICS; VITAMIN SUPPLEMENTS & FORTIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: SickKids plans to host a series of two Cafe Scientifiques in the 2013/14 season.   Gut instinct - are probiotics the miracle 'bug' that will treat what ails us? We've all seen the advertisements claiming that a tasty yogurt teeming with probiotics is just the ticket for making us feel better, healthier and more energized. But what are probiotics and how do they really contribute to our health? Our panel will provide an overview of what probiotics are, how they have been proven to be effective in treating disease, what the future holds for probiotics and finally how individuals might take advantage of the therapeutic power of probiotics in their daily lives.   It's a Small World After All - Global Child Health leads to a Better World At SickKids our vision is Healthier Children. A Better World. Not only do our research activities benefit the health outcomes of children here in Toronto, but also around the world. Our Global Child Health program champions child-focused issues of global importance and works with program partners (including governments and UN agencies) to advocate for, and assist with, the transfer of knowledge leading to the implementation of interventions of proven value to children everywhere. Our panelists will discuss the health and nutritional challenges facing the world's children and the share how their efforts are addressing some these problems head on.

TitreApplicationTitle: Healthy Spryfield/Pictou County: What role does food play?
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY; FOOD POLICY; FOOD SECURITY; HEALTH; HEALTH DISPARITIES; NOVA SCOTIA; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; SOCIAL POLICY; SYSTEMS CHANGE
Abstract-Résumé: This Cafe Scientifique addresses a need to connect citizens in Nova Scotia with key information about food security issues and be a catalyst for discussion about the connections between health and well-being, food, and strategies for building food security.  Through the Cafe environment, community members, leading researchers, community health and food advocates, and health practitioners will engage in meaningful conversations that draw on leading research presented by the panellists to create links between food security issues, peoples' daily lives, health and well-being, and the opportunities for positive change at the regional and national levels.

TitreApplicationTitle: Infection: What is it? How to find it. How to beat it!
Keywords-MotsClés: CITIZEN ENGAGEMENT; INFECTION; KNOWLEDGE DISSEMINATION; SEPSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Infection is a problem that touches us all. Whether missing school or work due to the common cold, or suffering from more serious forms of infection such as sepsis, we all know someone whose life has been impacted by infection.  In recognition of the human and economic burden of infection, juxtaposed against a surprising lack of public awareness, September 13th was recently declared World Sepsis Day http://www.world-sepsis-day.org. To complement other activities our group will conduct in relation to World Sepsis Day this year, we will hold a Cafe Scientifique in October 2013 on the topic of infection.  The target audience of interest for our cafe is children and their caregivers, and we have therefore selected the East Hamilton Boys and Girls Club as the venue for our event. As suggested by the title, three issues relevant to the topic of infection will be discussed at the Cafe: 1. What is infection?  2. How to find infection when it exists, and 3. How to beat infection!  Our health research expert speakers, who are conducting CIHR-funded investigations into sepsis, will address these three issues, providing a stimulus for subsequent discussions. A fun and interactive hand hygiene exercise will also be provided to further engage the children in attendance and reinforce learning.  We will promote our free and accessible Cafe Scientifique to the public using a variety of tools and strategies including poster advertisement, website advertisement, and through use of social media platforms such as Twitter. We will also incorporate the use of Twitter and Twitterfall into Cafe discussions, which will serve to broadly disseminate the content of our Cafe to members of the public.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cafe Scientifique 2014: "In Other Words": The Art&Science of Urban Well-Being in Toronto
Keywords-MotsClés: ART; CAFE SCIENTIFIQUES; DATA VISUALIZATION; ECOLOGICAL DATA; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; URBAN HEALTH; YOUTH ENGAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Youth are potentially very important but neglected participants in public conversations about urban health.  This Cafe Scientifique is intended to address this gap. Young health researchers based at the Centre for Research on Inner City Health and young artists from NIA Centre for the Arts are using creative methods to communicate complex research evidence to youth audiences, through graphic design and videography. The result is an art installation aimed to promote youth awareness, engagement, and dialogue about social determinants of health in Toronto`s neighbourhoods and the factors that can lead to change. We propose to launch this art installation as a Cafe Scientifique in a youth-friendly venue that provides both gallery space and theatre-style seating for a 2 hour panel presentation and audience discussion.  Our objectives are: to create a conversation with youth about the social determinants of health inequality in Toronto and community actions to respond to inequality; to raise awareness about career options in science and the arts that can contribute to social change; and to promote public awareness of the role of CIHR. This event is expected to gain widespread media attention in Toronto. CIHR will be credited in all media announcements.

TitreApplicationTitle: Increasing age and declining mobility: What do we need to know?
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; DEPRESSION; FEAR OF FALLING; MOBILITY; SEX-GENDER DIFFERENCES; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF DISABILITY; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: Mobility defined as the ability to walk safely and independently in one's natural environment, is critical for one's independence in daily activities, for continuing social interactions and for maintaining overall quality of life. Therefore, preserving mobility and delaying mobility disability in late life is vital for active and healthy ageing. Paradoxically, mobility declines with increasing age even when not accompanied by overtly catastrophic co-morbid conditions.  In older persons, disability usually occurs first in mobility followed by a downward spiral of progressive disablement2 becomes. However, it is generally accepted that detecting mobility deficits during an early or preclinical stage is likely an important opportunity for implementing preventative measures. From pioneering research to recent papers on characteristics of non-disabled people with poor lower extremity function, it appears that mobility disability prevention must happen at the community, as well as the individual level. Although, in older persons the intricate pathway to the initiation of the disablement process, which is disability in mobility, is not clearly understood unless preceded by a catastrophic event (e.g. stroke), some possible predisposing risk factors have been explored. The proposed `Increasing age and declining mobility: What do we need to know?` scientific cafe will provide an opportunity for an interactive dialogue with older persons living in the Kingston and surrounding areas about the possible risk factors of mobility disability.

TitreApplicationTitle: Myths About Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL PHONES; FAMILIAL GENETICS; HEREDITARY RISK; MYTHS; SECOND-HAND SMOKING
Abstract-Résumé: When it comes to difficult, complex topics like cancer, myths abound. Cancer researchers frequently field questions and public inquires on cancer and many such myths surrounding cancer.   This Cafe Scientifique series aims to directly address some of the more common cancer myths around familial genetics and the risk of inheriting cancer, second hand smoking as a cause of cancer, and cell phone usage and risk of brain cancer. By providing public opportunities for dialogue and learning around topics of importance in cancer, this proposal aims to debunk the common myths about cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: How well do you smell?  Or other ways to diagnose movement disorders early.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; COGNITION; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; OLFACTION; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: By the time that patients are diagnosed with Parkinson's disease, many of the cells in the brain have already been irreparably damaged. There is a need to identify those individuals who are destined to develop Parkinson's disease and treat optimally and early and before appreciable deterioration has occurred in the brain.  In the next 30 years, the number of people in Canada diagnosed with Parkinson's disease will double. Finding ways to identify and intervene will be crucial in order to avoid the collapse of our already overburdened health care system.  This Cafe will focus on cutting edge research on Parkinson's disease undertaken by Nova Scotia investigators.  This Cafe is meant to be interactive between the audience and the speakers. Our objectives are to :  1.increase awareness of the prevalence and risk factors associated with the development of PD;   2. share and discuss recent scientific information regarding the potential biomarkers for preclinical diagnosis of PD and other neurodegenerative disorders; and  3. critically examine current options for early and effective treatment of PD and other neurodegenerative disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Medications and Memory: Friend or Foe? Risks and Benefits of Medications for Older Adults with Dementia
Keywords-MotsClés: BPSD; COGNITIVE ENHANCERS; DEMENTIA; MEDICATION BENEFITS; MEDICATION RISKS; MEMORY; OLDER ADULTS; PANEL DISCUSSION; PUBLIC AWARENESS
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 500,000 Canadians suffer from dementia and this expected to increase to over a million by 2035.  The role of medications in the treatment of dementia is controversial and confusing for physicians and for the public. Cognitive enhancing medications are prescribed to 50% of people with dementia but many questions remain about their effectiveness and optimal use. The role of medications to treat the behavioural and psychiatric symptoms of dementia is also controversial as Health Canada has issued warnings about the use of antipsychotic medication for this condition. In addition, many medications used for treatment of common health conditions can worsen memory and cognition and increase symptoms of dementia. This Cafe Scientifique will apply the most up-to-date research and the clinical experience of the presenters to help participants to minimize the risks of medications and to ensure the most appropriate use of medications to treat symptoms of dementia. The Cafe will be relevant for persons with dementia, their caregivers and for health providers.

TitreApplicationTitle: You have my undivided attention: The ADHD lounge
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT ADHD; ATTENTION DEFICIT HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER; CAFE SCIENTIFIQUE; CHILD ADHD; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; PUBLIC AUDIENCE
Abstract-Résumé: We would like to collaborate with the CIHR in hosting a Cafe Scientifique on ADHD across the lifespan. Through the Cafe Scientifique, we seek to incite the interest of people of all ages and socioeconomic and cultural backgrounds, with the main goal of increasing public awareness of clinical and neurobiological research in the field of ADHD. The driving force behind the proposed Cafe Scienfique is the initiative to set the platform for interactive discussions between a panel of expert scientists/clinicians and the general public. We have selected ADHD as one of the most pertinent topics for a Cafe Scientifique, as it affect 8-12% of children and 5% of adults. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurological disorder which causes difficulties in controlling ideas and focus (inattention), gestures (physical restlessness) and behavior (impulsivity). Importantly, studies have shown that a significant portion of children with ADHD will continue to experience difficulties throughout adulthood. Classic signs in adulthood ADHD include difficulty focusing, organizing, planning and following-through on plans. Fortunately, the misconception that ADHD is a childhood disorder is starting to change, and awareness of, and education about, ADHD continues to improve. As part of this educational effort, we propose to organize a Cafe Scientifique that will focus on some key aspects of child and adult ADHD that are of popular interest to the general public. For the Cafe Scientifique, our panel of selected speakers will discuss various facets of ADHD including the latest advances in the field, their own work, along with the feasibility of current therapeutic interventions. Finally, some light entertainment will be provided to uphold the spirit of the cafe.

Keywords-MotsClés: CAFE SCIENTIFIQUE - PUBLIC FORUM
Abstract-Résumé: :  We constantly hear about disease and illness in our own cities and abroad.  Consequently, it is not surprising that patients sometimes question the quality of care they receive.  When a patient goes to the hospital or visits their doctor, they expect to receive the best care possible.  The best health care is only possible when delivering the latest innovations in health research.   This Cafe Scientifique will give people the opportunity to learn about some of the ways Lawson researchers are advancing health care at their local hospitals. Our approach at Lawson is to start with a clinical problem, take the problem back to the lab to find a solution, and then test this solution at the bedside.  Attendees will learn about how our researchers do this and bring new and innovative approaches to health problems.

Abstract-Résumé: With the intent of hosting an educational and informal discussion on how gender informs work and health, recognizing that governments, regulatory agencies and workers' organizations play key roles in fostering healthy work environments, this Cafe will better inform the general public, workers/employees, employers, human resource professionals and unions, as well as those with an interest in or working in workplace health.  The audience (present, in person, and present virtually) members will be encouraged to ask questions related to gender, work and health in order to stimulate discussion on how these three concepts interface to foster healthy work environments.   The proposed Cafe will be held at and by McMaster University (Hamilton, ON).  Panelists include two McMaster Faculty who are IGH Chairs in Gender, Work and Health (Allison Williams and Joy MacDermid), together with senior scholar, Dr. Janet Fast, from the University of Alberta, and a representative from the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety (CCOHS), the partner organization affiliated with the IGH CIHR Chairs in Gender, Work and Health Program.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tools in the Prevention of Sudden Cardiac Death: Designer Drugs, Genomics and Fancy Devices
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GENOMICS; RISK FACTORS; SUDDEN CARDIAC DEATH
Abstract-Résumé: Technology in medicine is advancing rapidly. This is as true in diseases of the heart as it is in other areas. Heart and blood vessel disease remain the leading cause of death in Canada and at least half of all deaths occur suddenly. This is usually due to an irregular heart beat leading to cardiac arrest that is not compatible with life unless intervened upon quickly. Sudden cardiac death (SCD) affects many individuals without warning and even in those we identify at high risk of this happening we aren't able to effectively help.  We are excited by a wide range of new technology that has greatly increased the chance of living with life-threatening heart disease, or identifying those at risk. Within the Libin Cardiovascular Institute at the University of Calgary, heart rhythm scientists are involved in these exciting discoveries. The theme of this Cafe Scientifique is new technology to identify and treat subjects at risk SCD.  We will explore basic fundamental science that is exploring designer drugs to treat life-threatening heart rhythm irregularities. The human genetic code allows us to identify defects in cellular proteins that control the movement of ions in and out of cells. Abnormalities in these systems can lead to premature death. Other scientists study the genetic code in animal models and patients. Finally, these discoveries are translated to humans at risk with the use of novel monitoring equipment or cardiac defibrillators. Clinical trials originating from the University of Calgary are aiming to redefine how we treat these individuals.  Our target audience will be subjects interested in technology and medicine who may have been touched by Sudden Cardiac Death in their friends or family. We will reach out to the general community through our established communication pathways within the Libin Cardiovascular Institute.

TitreApplicationTitle: How to Enhance Older Drivers' Safety?
Keywords-MotsClés: DISCUSSION WITH MEMBERS OF THE PUBLIC; OLDER DRIVERS' SAFETY
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Association of Occupational Therapists (CAOT) is pleased to apply for the opportunity to organize and host two CIHR Cafes Scientifiques on "How to Enhance Older Drivers' Safety". Older drivers need to be part of the discussion between researchers, stakeholders and practitioners in order to design and offer services which enhance safe driving practices, contribute to healthy living, wellbeing, injury prevention, reduced mortality and enhanced public safety. The issue of medical risk, age and driving has attracted major media attention over the past few months and will most certainly interest a large and diverse audience. The two Cafes would be held in Ottawa,  privileged location as it is home to several major national seniors and health care professional agencies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innovations in Nursing Homes-Are They Making a Difference?
Keywords-MotsClés: CARE DELIVERY; NURSING HOMES; SYSTEM IMPROVEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Nursing homes across Canada are grappling with the care needs of an aging population with older buildings, staff challenges and fiscal constraints. At the same, nursing homes want to support resident-centered care.  To address these challenges, nursing homes in Nova Scotia are undergoing significant change.  The design of new facilities being built is based on smaller, home-like settings and there are changes in staff practices and changes in how residents receive physician-medical attention.  The Cafe will offer an opportunity to learn about these changes and in what ways they are contributing to resident-centered care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Should your tax dollars pay for IVF?
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSISTED HUMAN REPRODUCTION; BIOETHICS; IN-VITRO FERTILIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: There are plenty of stories of infertile couples spending enormous amounts of time, money, physical and emotional energy trying to conceive a baby through In-Vitro Fertilization (IVF). Currently only two provinces publicly fund IVF. Ontario funds IVF for infertility due to blocked fallopian tubes and has done so since 1993 (following the report of the Royal Commission on New Reproductive Technologies). More recently, since August 2010, Quebec funds IVF for all residents irrespective of the reason for accessing the technology. Canadian organizations such as the Infertility Awareness Association of Canada and Generations of Hope are currently lobbying provincial governments across Canada to follow Quebec's lead and urging individuals to show their support. These organizations claim that publicly funded IVF will result in fewer multiple births (as has been the case in Quebec) and will result in long-term savings to the health care system. (As yet there are no published figures to support this claim.)  A Cafe on public funding of IVF is timely given that the Quebec government is now undertaking the first review of its funding practice. This review includes a public consultation and thus not surprisingly we are witnessing a resurgence of public debate and discussion about funding priorities. We anticipate that by the time we hold the Cafe, Quebec's review will be available. This Cafe will examine ethical, social and financial implications of publicly funded IVF. Questions to be discussed at the Cafe include: Is there evidence to support the claim that publicly funded IVF would result in fewer multiple births, resulting in savings to the healthcare system in the long-term? What is the best means to bring about good medical practice in IVF? Would taxpayer dollars be better spent on more essential health care services?

TitreApplicationTitle: Substance Abuse Prevention in First Nations Communities
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; COMMUNITY BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; COMMUNITY CAPACITY DEVELOPMENT; INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, Indigenous communities face health inequities which are related to long standing social, political and economic disparities between Indigenous communities and the general public. Addiction and substance abuse are of particular concern to Indigenous communities, as Elders and community members recognize increasing rates of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) among children born in their communities.   In response to substance abuse and increased rates of FASD, the Alexis Nakota Sioux Nation invited the University of Alberta to partner in a collaborative effort to establish a school-based substance abuse prevention program. After successfully adapting, implementing and evaluating three years of a Life Skills Training program, the Maskwacis First Nations became aware of the project and initiated a partnership with the U of A to establish a similar program in their communities.  We will host two Cafe Scientifiques; one in Alexis Nakota Sioux Nation and one in the Maskwacis First Nations,both near Edmonton, Alberta. In these two Cafe Scientifiques, we will discuss addiction and substance abuse in First Nations through a panel which include two CIHR funded researchers (Dr. Lola Baydala and Dr. Cheryl Currie), and key community members (Ms. Natasha Rabbit, Ms. Sherry Letendre and community Elders).
