TitreApplicationTitle: Analyze This: What You Should Know About Psychotherapy
Keywords-MotsClés: KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MENTAL HEALTH; PSYCHOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Most Canadians with mental disorders have not received mental health care within the previous year, and even those who do receive care may not receive the most effective interventions. A large body of research has consistently demonstrated positive outcomes of psychotherapy for a wide variety of mental disorders. Psychotherapy is more effective than antidepressant medications in the longer term. However, the rates of psychotherapy use have diminished slightly over the past 10 years. There are many barriers to the public's use of and access to psychotherapy, including: lack of knowledge of psychotherapy's effectiveness, misconceptions about psychotherapy, stigma associated with seeking a psychological intervention, and limited access and availability for some. The objectives of this Cafe are to provide members of the public with: up-to-date knowledge of the research on psychotherapy and factors that contribute to its efficacy; evidence-based information on what to expect from and how to make the best use of psychotherapy; a forum to exchange information about barriers to accessing psychotherapy, including stigma, economic factors, and availability; and stimulating discussions about psychotherapy among members of the general public and psychotherapy research experts. Two of three panelists are psychotherapy researchers who will present the evidence base on whether, when, how, and why psychotherapy works. The third panelist will share her personal experience in advocating for greater access to psychotherapy for those suffering from an eating disorder. By attending the Cafe, members of the public will be able to develop informed opinions about psychotherapy and its use in the treatment of mental disorders. This Cafe Scientifique will also address common misconceptions about psychotherapy, and generate discussions and knowledge exchange about overcoming barriers to accessing and using psychotherapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rapid Testing Approaches: Bringing HIV Services to Populations Vulnerable to HIV
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO CARE; GENDER AND HEALTH; HEALTH EQUITY; IMMIGRANT HEALTH; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; RAPID TESTING; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: In 2011 the Public Health Agency of Canada estimated that 25% of people living with HIV in Canada were unaware of their infection.  Many of these undiagnosed are from populations vulnerable to HIV: people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, people from HIV concentrated epidemic countries (prevalence >1%), youth, pregnant women, sex-workers, low income and socially disadvantaged people, Aboriginal people and other minorities. Our recent Cochrane Systematic review based showed rapid testing approaches were associated with increased uptake and receipt of HIV testing and retesting in persons vulnerable to HIV.  These findings have implications for communities vulnerable to HIV as a way to aid in combating and controlling the spread of HIV.  The proposed Cafe Scientifique will engage migrant communities of people from the HIV concentrated epidemic regions of South Asia, East Africa, and Latin America.  Researchers and community leaders will collaborate to create an nonthreatening atmosphere to conduct informal health discussions about HIV infection and rapid testing.

Abstract-Résumé: L'objectif des Cafes scientifiques de l'IRCM est de sensibiliser le grand public a l'importance de la recherche sur l'amelioration de la qualite de vie da la population. Le public cible est le grand public et les personnes concernees par la FK, particulierement les personnes atteintes et les membres de leurs familles, sans exclure les professionnels de la sante. Le cafe sera aussi offert en diffusion simultanee sur le Web. Les personnes en ligne auront acces au clavardage et pourront poser leurs questions aux conferenciers. TitreApplicationTitle: We Are Family - The importance of parents, peers and partners in pain relief
Keywords-MotsClés: FAMILY; NEWBORNS; PAIN; PAIN MANAGEMENT; PAIN RELIEF; SOCIAL CONTEXT; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: As of 2011 15% of Nova Scotians aged 12 and over report they usually have pain or discomfort that is moderate to severe and/or prevents usual daily activities. Chronic pain affects every aspect of a person's life including their ability to work, their emotional, mental and physical health as well as their relationships with family, friends and society. Pain affects everyone across the lifespan. This can start in children where even the healthiest of newborns undergo almost a dozen needle injections in their first year of life with almost another dozen before they reach adulthood. Additionally 20% of children experience recurring or persistent pain, and extends into older adults who experience prevalence of pain as high as 80% among individuals in long term care facilities and 65% for those living in the community.   However, there is poor management of pain in our society due to under-recognition of the problem, lack of education regarding pain assessment and treatment in graduating health care professionals and inadequate funding for research regarding pain. Moreover, awareness of the important contribution of family and friends in pain relief has been underscored and the incorporation of social support networks has been underutilized in the management of acute and chronic pain across the life span. Thus, this is an important topic for individuals and families, local communities and the province as greater understanding of family participation in pain relief is needed. TitreApplicationTitle: Les 10 premières minutes de vie
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLAITEMENT; CONTACT PEAU A PEAU; NAISSANCE; PREMIER CRI; SATISFACTION; TOLERANCE A LA DOULEUR
Abstract-Résumé: Les premiers instants de vie constituent une periode riche en evenements physiologiques et comportementaux. Pour le foetus, la transition de la vie intra-uterine foetale a la vie aerienne est un phenomene complexe. A la naissance, trois mecanismes vont conditionner l'adaptation du nouveau-ne : la programmation comportementale, l'afflux de substances neuroendocrines et l'activation de la sensorialite. Cette periode de passage a ete decrite comme une periode stressante pouvant meme etre douloureuse pour le nouveau-ne. Pour la mere, la fin de l'accouchement est une periode de fatigue, de stress, d'emotion et d'impregnation hormonale. Pour la plupart des mammiferes, le contact etroit entre la mere et l'enfant a la naissance apparait comme naturel, alors que pendant des annees les pratiques hospitalieres les ont separes. Le contact peau a peau a beaucoup ete etudie avec la methode "kangourou" utilisee avec les nouveau-nes prematures. On s'apercoit aujourd'hui que les bienfaits d'un tel contact privilegie ne s'appliquent pas seulement aux naissances prematurees et semble favoriser le deroulement de l'allaitement et la diminution du stress de la mere et de l'enfant. Son instauration peut par contre parfois se heurter a certains obstacles, comme les contraintes d'une salle d'operation dans le cas des cesariennes. Cette rencontre presentera les avantages du contact peau a peau a la naissance, les obstacles a son instauration et les moyens de les surmonter.

Les chercheurs et cliniciens en ophtalmologie et science de la vision s'efforcent a trouver des solutions. Parmis elles, l'entrainement visuel est une strategie de readaptation accessible et prometteuse. Couplee a l'administration de stimulatants cognitifs, elle pourrait etre encore plus performante. Alternativement la greffe de cellules souches au niveau de la retine est une technologie prometteuse pour restaurer la vision. Le cafe propose une discussion passionnante sur ces themes actuels.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inflamm-aging: What do we know about the effect of inflammation on HIV treatment and disease as we age, and how does this affect our search for a Cure?
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; HIV; IMMUNOLOGY; INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: HIV infection causes substantial inflammation. Inflammation is a natural biological defense reaction to attacks on the body by a virus, bacteria or even a physical injury. But long term inflammation can cause harm, even after a person starts on effective antiretroviral therapy. Inflammation may affect brain function, accelerated aging, premature frailty, transmission of HIV and the possibility of an eventual HIV cure. This Cafe will discuss CIHR-funded research related to "inflamm-aging". Dr. Rupert Kaul and Dr. Mario Ostrowski, together with community scholars and research collaborators Dr. Ron Rosenes and Mr. Robert Reinhard, will discuss the findings and community implications of their CIHR-funded research from 3 projects: 1. CIHR team grant in HIV vaccine discovery: novel mechanisms and strategies of protection; 2. Defining the clinical and immune causes of disproportionately high HIV levels in semen; and 3. CIHR emerging HIV team grant: the role of common co-infections in HIV susceptibility, immunopathogenesis and secondary transmission. We will focus on the following areas that are of wide interest to the HIV/AIDS community: how HIV damage in the gut causes inflammation, why standard cART along is very slow to reverse this damage, and whether complementary therapies might help; how HIV causes "exhaustion" of many important immune cells, and how this process might be reversed to improve health outcomes. The venue will be the Vic Public House, and the event is timed to coincide with the 2013 OHTN Conference, which draws HIV/AIDS community members, service providers and researchers to Toronto from across Ontario. The main goal is to stimulate discussion between the broad HIV/AIDS community and CIHR-supported research experts. With the information technology assistance of the OHTN, we will webcast the Cafe, allowing knowledge users from AIDS Service Organizations and geographically disparate individuals to hear what is said and to join the discussion.

Abstract-Résumé: This Cafe Scientifique brings together experts in ethics that disagree about who should decide when to withdraw life-sustaining care, in order to explore the meaning of ethics "expertise" and the contribution of bioethics research to public life. The difficult question about who should decide when to withdraw care has come to the forefront of societal attention in the recent Rasouli case in Ontario, which has been widely covered in the media and is expected to be heard by the Supreme Court this year. Experts have variously held that patients (or their families) should decide when to withdraw care, according to their own values; that physicians should decide, according to medical criteria; or that society should decide, according to national health spending priorities. Disagreement among experts on this important issue illustrates the unique nature of ethical expertise and helps the public to think critically about the role of ethics in public policy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Strategies for the Treatment and Prevention of Pressure Ulcer

Abstract-Résumé: Pressure ulcer is common. It can affect people with impaired mobility and sensation in a wide range of settings. In Canada, it affects over 25% of patients in acute care. The numbers are even higher in non-acute settings. The cost is staggering. It is estimated at $3.5B in Canada each year. One of the major reasons for such drastic healthcare burden is that pressure ulcers, especially those originating deep over the bone are difficult to detect. To change that will not only require better treatment. Better methods of prevention will be critical as well. The latter can be achieved through increased awareness, vigilance and aided by new technology. At this meeting, we will bring out those salient points for discussion and to establish a consensus on the rationale of future direction. Such dialogue is greatly needed. To make a meaningful difference in the fight against pressure ulcer will require collaboration between many parties include healthcare providers, patients, support groups and the public.

Abstract-Résumé: Stem cells have been hailed as the Holy Grail of modern medicine. Are they really? There is no doubt that stem cells can do remarkable things, but is there a limit to what they can achieve? Can we make body parts bigger, stronger and last longer thanks to regenerative medicine (RM) - RM harnesses the power of stem cells, biomaterials and molecules to repair, regenerate or replace diseased cells, tissues and organs - and should this be a goal? In this Cafe Scientifique, experts will discuss regulatory and ethical issues around creating super athletes, super soldiers and super heroes through stem cell- and biomaterials-based medical enhancements to our bodies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Proposition de recherche  Julie Robert, Coordonnatrice en communications, recherche Affaires publiques et Planification stratégique, Centre universitaire de santé McGill Café scientifique : «  Douleur chronique : mal invisible et énigmatique »
Keywords-MotsClés: «  DOULEUR CHRONIQUE : MAL INVISIBLE ET ENIGMATIQUE »
Abstract-Résumé: Encore en 2013, la douleur chronique reste une maladie mysterieuse tres repandue avec des couts importants pour la societe et le systeme de soins de sante. Ce mal « invisible » a non seulement des sequelles physiques mais egalement psychologiques sur des millions de personnes a travers le monde. Aujourd'hui la douleur chronique est consideree comme etant plus commune que les maladies cardiaques.  Meme si la science progresse dans le domaine du diagnostic et des strategies therapeutiques, cette maladie multifactorielle reste enigmatique. Les mecanismes  derriere ce mal sont loin d'etre elucides et il n'y a pas encore de cure.  Les experts internationaux predisent une explosion des cas de personnes souffrant de douleur chronique au cours des 25 prochaines annees, en raison du vieillissement de la population. Il est donc urgent d'impliquer les omnipraticiens dans le diagnostic et la prise en charge des maladies chroniques. C'etait d'ailleurs une des points cles des Nouvelles lignes directrices Canadiennes pour le traitement de la fibromyalgie mises a jour en 2012.   Jusqu'a 30% de la population canadienne souffrent quotidiennement de douleur chronique moderee a severe. Plus de 60% des personnes qui prennent des medicaments antidouleur prescrits par leurs medecins estiment qu'elles ne sont pas soulagees par les traitements actuels et eprouvent des difficultes a participer a des activites sociales ou familiales.   Une meilleure connaissance des mecanismes a l'origine de ces douleurs encore incurables est donc essentielle pour pallier la souffrance de ces personnes en attente de traitements efficaces. De plus, sachant que l'approche therapeutique traditionnelle n'est pas assez efficace pour la plupart des personnes atteintes de douleur chronique, les efforts doivent etre mis sur l'amelioration du mode de vie a divers niveaux (sommeil, humeur, alimentation, exercice) afin d'assurer le controle de la maladie.

Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLICATIONS; DEVELOPPEMENT DE MEDICAMENTS ANTIVIRAUX; GRIPPE; INFLUENZA; RESISTANCE
Abstract-Résumé: La saison grippale represente a chaque annee une periode de questionnement sur les aspects de vaccination, d'impacts sur les populations, sur l'economie et sur les traitements disponibles qui est soulevee par les medias. Ceci emmene un interet de la part du public, mais souvent aussi certaines inquietudes. Nous proposons un Cafe Scientifique pour repondre a certaines de ces questions. Les epidemies de grippe entrainent de nombreux arrets de travail et hospitalisations et peuvent meme provoquer jusqu'a 8000 deces chaque annee au Canada. Selon le ministere canadien des finances, une pandemie de grippe au Canada pourrait entrainer une perte de 14 milliards de dollars et une baisse de son PIB de 1,2%. L'impact de la grippe se traduit aussi par un taux d'absenteisme important dans nos ecoles. La pandemie au virus H1N1 a donne lieu a la mise en place de mesures inedites au Canada tandis que l'emergence frequente de nouvelles souches de virus (telle H7N9 en Chine recemment) a relance l'inquietude sur la propagation d'un virus hautement transmissible et sur le developpement de nouvelles resistances aux traitements.   Ce cafe scientifique a pour but d'expliquer au grand public l'impact de l'influenza sur la vie quotidienne des gens et les termes frequemment utilises tels que pandemie et resistance. Les panelistes presenteront de facon vulgarisee ce qu'est une pandemie, ce que signifie reellement l'emergence d'une nouvelle souche grippale et les defis rencontres lors du developpement de nouvelles therapies et par l'augmentation de resistance aux traitements.  Sous-objectifs : 1.Informer les participants sur l'influenza et les complications qui y sont associees. 2.Expliquer l'emergence de nouvelles souches grippales et de resistance aux traitements 3.Expliquer l'apport des sciences sur l'amelioration des soins et la percee importante effectuee a Sherbrooke sur le traitement de la grippe en soulignant l'importance du financement de la recherche.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sharing the gift of life: organ donation and transplantation in Canada.
Keywords-MotsClés: HEART TRANSPLANT; ORGAN DONATION; PUBLIC ENGAGEMENT; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: 4500 Canadians are currently on transplant waiting lists across the country. As wait-lists continue to grow in Canada, patients suffer prolonged illness and many die before a suitable donor is found. In 2010, 16% of kidney and/or kidney-pancreas, 19% of lung, 22% of liver and 24% of heart transplant candidates died on a Canadian wait-list without receiving a transplant. The growing imbalance between supply and demand for organs means that Canadians needing a transplant face a 30-40% lifetime probability of never receiving one. The Canadian National Transplant Research Program (CNTRP) and the University of Ottawa Heart Institute (UOHI) are partnering to present the CIHR Cafe Scientifique on Organ Donation and Transplantation.  The purpose of this event is to encourage members of the general public to truly engage in the topic of organ donation and transplantation and contribute their own views on potential solutions and future directions.

Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD DEVELOPMENT; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTIONS; MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES; MENTAL ILLNESS; PARENTS--PSYCHOSOCIAL FACTORS; PSYCHIATRY; PSYCHOSOCIAL; RISK; STRESSFUL LIFE EVENTS; SUPPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Mental health problems seem to run in families, putting certain children and youth at high risk. Over the years, researchers have debated whether this is primarily the result of nature (e.g. genetics) or nurture (e.g. parenting or other elements of the developmental context). This Cafe explains how genes and environment interact to co-produce greater risk or greater protections against mental health problems at the early stages of childhood development. It also explains ways in which we can strategize for building up mental health capacity in our children and young people, now and for the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Getting Ahead of Autism: Innovative Assistance for Persons with Autism
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; HEALTH CARE RESEARCH; PUBLIC AWARENESS; SUPPORT SERVICES
Abstract-Résumé: Health Canada recently reported that 1 in every 150 children has autism (Health Canada Website). According to many researchers the incidence is even higher, and the Federal and Provincial governments have made autism a higher priority. Medical scholarship on autism has established that certain risk factors like prematurity in a pregnancy can lead to a child developing autism. These findings have sparked great interest in health forums across Canada, the US, and the world as numbers of children diagnosed with autism continue to rise. Important questions are being raised by many. How do parents treat and care for their children after a diagnosis? How do educators and communities respond to the needs of persons of any age with autism in order to best serve them in their ongoing development? How can I better understand what it feels like to have autism?   These and many other questions will be answered though our Cafe event. The objective of the Cafe will be to showcase the latest research on autism, make the public aware of resources and support networks available, and promote recent advances of care for those diagnosed with autism. The Cafe will feature expert speakers and researchers on the topic of proper care for individuals with autism, encouraging Canadians from all sectors of society to engage CIHR health researchers and contribute their views on current research. By first addressing how autism may develop and its root causes, the Cafe will engage its audience on how best to respond to individuals with autism in homes, care centers, and in the community. Additionally, our speakers will suggest research and findings that promote innovative treatments with autistic children and mature autistic adults. Not only will this Cafe  shed light on the causes of autism, but it will improve public understanding of the health and well-being of persons with autism and how best to deliver quality care to Canadians who need it most.

TitreApplicationTitle: NK cell receptor-mediated direct fungal recognition and cytotoxicity that is defective in HIV-infected patients but restored using IL-12

Abstract-Résumé: ICS Travel Awards  Persons living with AIDS are at risk of developing devastating fungal infections. The most deadly fungus, Cryptococcus neoformans causes pneumonia and meningitis and kills over 600,000 persons with AIDS per year. We have been working to bypass the immune defect in AIDS patients to combat this dreaded infection. It has been known for many years that a class of white blood cells called natural killer (NK) cells can bind and directly kill fungi. However, the NK cell receptor that is used to recognize the fungus had not been discovered. Moreover, it was not known whether the NK cell receptor might be defective in AIDS patients and explain part of the problem. In the work to be presented at this meeting, we will describe how we screened over 2600 different antibodies to discover the receptor. We also found that expression of the receptor is defective in AIDS patients, but can be restored with a molecule (interleukin 12) that boosts immunity. Once the expression of the receptor was restored, the NK cells from AIDS patients killed Cryptococcus normally.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impaired neurogenesis in the aging forebrain: defining the kinetics and underlying mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS
Abstract-Résumé: In the adult mammalian brain, stem-cells are still present in different regions and can give rise to new neurons, this phenomenon is called neurogenesis. One of the regions is the subventricular zone of the lateral ventricles. This neurogenesis plays a role in the olfaction and in brain repair mechanisms after an injury. However this neurogenesis decreases during aging. The major issue in the aging field is that the mechanisms underlying this decline in neurogenesis are still unclear. During my PhD, the main objective is to determine the different mechanisms that are responsible for the decrease in neurogenesis. In conclusion by identifying the different mechanisms altering the stem-cells functioning, we would ultimately be able to find therapeutic approches to restore their activity during aging and potentially, in neurodegenerative diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health care throughout the life course: Aging with physical impairments
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE HEALTH  CARE; DISABILITY; HEALTH; HEALTH CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Life expectancy for people with physical impairments is increasing and people are now expected to reach old age even after living with impairments for many decades. Many people who are aging with physical impairments often experience additional chronic conditions. These chronic conditions or complications from their impairment can lead to increased health care use and unmet health care needs. The unmet health care needs can be due to several factors, including: lack of physician knowledge about their impairments, additional health problems, worsening health, and lack of a holistic, multidisciplinary approach to health care. As a result many people who are aging with long-term physical impairments have learned to adapt and manage their own health. My research uses a life course perspective to understand the way 18 people with permanent impairments have learned to self-manage their health and health care experiences. Data were gathered through in-depth, semi-structured interviews.  Many of the participants wished they could have access to publically funded physiotherapy, massage therapy, and chiropractic services. These services are needed throughout their life because they often have complex needs resulting from additional chronic conditions or health problems as they age. Access to alternative health care was especially important for the participants who have work-related impairments. These types of services might improve the quality of life for people with work-related impairments as they age and may help them to continue working.  I will conclude with offering suggestions for improvements in the health care system, health policies, and in Workers Compensation Boards that will better meet the needs of people aging with physical impairments. My research will also provide helpful tips for people who are aging with physical impairments as they age and navigate the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: YB-1 regulates stress granule assembly and protects cells from stress
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS
Abstract-Résumé: Stress granules (SGs) are large, cytoplasmic, protein-RNA complexes that play major roles in modulation of gene expression and cellular homeostasis. SG formation protects cells under unfavourable conditions. Cells that are incapable of forming SGs are more vulnerable to stresses than cells that are capable of forming SGs. Many proteins that are associated with SGs play a critical role in the formation of SGs, and the absence of one or more of these proteins make the cells less efficient in SG assembly and more sensitive to stress. The transcription and translation regulation factor YB-1 is recruited to SGs, but its exact function in SG formation is not clear.  We demonstrate that siRNA-mediated downregulation of YB-1 led to a significant reduction in the efficiency of SG assembly in two sarcoma cell lines, U2OS and Rh-30. We also found that si-YB-1 cells with an inefficient stress granule formation were more sensitive to stress induced by arsenite or H2O2 compared to si-control cells. YB-1 influences SG assembly via two distinct mechanisms. First, it acts as a scaffold protein to recruit mRNA and other associated RNA-binding proteins into SGs. Second, YB-1 regulates the translation of important SG proteins G3BP1 and TIA-1, controlling their availability during SG assembly. Taken together, YB-1 is critical in SG formation and cell survival.

TitreApplicationTitle: Environmental Exposures, Helicobacter pylori Infection and Gastritis in Canadian Arctic Communities
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH; GASTRITIS; HELICOBACTER PYLORI
Abstract-Résumé: Helicobacter pylori (H.pylori) are bacteria that infect the lining of the stomach. H.pylori is found all over the world, but some populations are more affected by the infection and related disease than others. Initial infection typically occurs during childhood and can persist life-long in the absence of treatment. Chronic infection is associated with inflammation of the stomach lining and rarely serious stomach disease, including peptic ulcers and stomach cancer. This research examines the role of the environment in transmission of H.pylori and development of related disease in Canadian Arctic communities, where 58-70% of tested residents have the infection.  Residents if Aklavik, NT and Tuktoyaktuk, NT took part in a community-based research project on H.pylori infection in 2007 and 2011, respectively. Participants were tested for the infection and data on demographics, medical history and frequency of exposure to environmental sources were collected through structured interviews. Stomach biopsies were obtained in 2008 in Aklavik and examined through a microscope for signs of inflammation, graded as none, mild, moderate or severe. The frequencies of the infection and severe inflammation were compared between people who were and were not exposed to environmental sources using statistical models.   Results indicate that the infection does not occur more frequently in individuals exposed to environmental sources that could potentially be contaminated with the bacteria, relative to participants who were not exposed to these sources. This includes environmental exposures such as untreated water, sewage, cats and dogs. Preliminary analysis of the effect of exposure to mice indicates that prevalence of H.pylori infection is higher in individuals who reported having mice in their home, relative to those who are not exposed to mice. This analysis also provided evidence of a possible link between untreated water consumption and prevalence of severe gastritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preliminary Results Examining the Inter-generational Effects of the Indian Residential School Experience Using Grounded Theory.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL WOMEN; GENDER-BASED ANALYSIS; HEALING; ICS TRAVEL AWARDS; INDIAN RESIDENTIAL SCHOOLS; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: ICS Travel Awards:   Past research into Canada's history of the Indian residential school (IRS) assimilation policy (1879-1998) revealed that Aboriginal children were often traumatized.  Many were diagnosed with Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and this trauma was found to be passed onto later generations.  Research findings showed that medical professionals often viewed survivors' response to trauma from a clinical lens only and rarely considered how culture and the Indigenous holistic understanding of health would view it differently.  As a result, professionals overlook the varied experiences and the possibility that while trauma existed, many survivors were able to reframe their experiences to not only strengthen themselves but next generations as well (Denham 2008).  My doctoral research aims to find the broader spectrum of experiences and outcomes of the IRS experience by determining: a) What is the main concern of female IRS survivors and their daughters as it relates to the IRS experience? and b) How do they continually work to resolve this concern?  I start with the assumption that variation exists in how individuals responded to the IRS experience and in the outcome and transmission of these experiences to next generations.  Instead of using structured interviews that ask leading questions (e.g. about either psychiatric outcomes or resilience), I listen to female participants' own stories and words and then ask them more detailed questions based on their experiences.  The goal of this research is to develop a theory that comes from the experiences of IRS female survivors and their daughters that accounts for the variation in responses and outcomes.  Understanding this process by means of a theoretical framework will foster the development of culture-based tools to address family disruption and promote life opportunities. Coming from a gendered perspective, preliminary findings of this research study will be presented.

TitreApplicationTitle: Food security from the perspective of Nunavimmiut
Keywords-MotsClés: BOURSES DE VOYAGE D'ACI
Abstract-Résumé: Bourses de voyage d'ACI   Few qualitative studies on the experience and understanding of food security have been conduct with Inuit in Canada. This limit the ability to develop interventions and measurement that fully take into account the socio-cultural and economic context of Inuit communities. In this exploratory research, individual qualitative interviews with nineteen Inuit women from different generations, occupations and socio-economic status of one community in Nunavik (Quebec) led to a better understanding of food sufficiency, food insecurity experience, as well as coping strategies and community resources to maintain a satisfactory food situation. Additionally, a workshop with elders explored different sensations of food as they are described in Inuktitut. This workshop allow for a deepening of the cultural concepts surrounding the experience of eating and food security. Community participation was ensured by consulting key individuals in the community from cultural, health and wellness sectors throughout the research process. In short, the results suggest that the notion of what constitutes "sufficient food" is built from individual experiences and socio-cultural context, and tends to vary across generations. Many of the participants interviewed experienced food shortage in the recent past. However, resources within extended family and community tend to alleviate the situation when it was transitory.  Food sharing networks are an important feature of food security in the community studied. Participants identified possible food security solutions at the community and regional level. Finally, results and overall research process led to some reflections on the measurement of food security as well as methodological considerations for future research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inhibition pharmacologique du système chimiokinergique CCL2/CCR2 réduit les comportements douloureux associés au cancer osseux
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTAGONISTES; CANCER DU SEIN METASTATIQUE; CHIMIOKINES; DOULEUR CANCEREUSE OSSEUSE; PLASTICITE NEURONALE; REMODELAGE OSSEUX; REACTIVITE GLIALE; RECEPTEURS COUPLES AUX PROTEINES G
Abstract-Résumé: Malgre les avancees majeures en therapie contre le cancer, la prise en charge de la douleur chez les patients atteints de metastases osseuses demeure un defi clinique. En effet, plus de 50% des patients souffrant de douleurs osseuses ne sont pas soulages par les analgesiques disponibles. Il a recemment ete demontre que la chimiokine CCL2 et son recepteur CCR2 jouent un role majeur dans les etapes conduisant au developpement des douleurs chroniques d'origine inflammatoire et neuropathique. De facon parallele, il a ete montre que l'axe CCL2/CCR2 promouvoit le developpement et la proliferation des metastases du cancer du sein au niveau de l'os et qu'il est central dans le processus de remodelage osseux. Base sur la dualite fonctionnelle des chimiokines, nous proposons donc d'investiguer la pertinence de cibler le systeme CCL2/CCR2 afin de diminuer les douleurs induites par le cancer osseux. Nos recherchent reposent sur un modele de metastases osseuses du cancer du sein chez le rat. Ce modele mime le developpement metastatique et les douleurs osseuses associees tel que repertorie en clinique. L'action sur le couple CCL2/CCR2 pourrait reduire la plasticite neuronale qui s'opere dans le developpement des douleurs chroniques. De plus, nous etudieront egalement l'efficacite de nos composes sur l'inhibition de la croissance tumorale et de la degradation de l'os induite par le cancer. Ainsi, en agissant de facon concertee sur les mecanismes de transmission de la douleur, la croissance tumorale et le remodelage osseux, le couple CCL2/CCR2 represente une cible prometteuse dans le traitement de la douleur causee par les metastases osseuses.

Abstract-Résumé: The relationship between First Nations and the federal government is deeply rooted in the past with a series of shared events with often different meanings. This review examines the relationships between First Nations and the federal government in terms of the delivery of health services; an area of Canadian public policy that has also experienced a fairly high level of change over the last century.  Delivery of health services to First Nations has evolved from direct services by federal employees, mostly nurses, to increased delivery of health services by First Nations. This evolution in service delivery is based on the 1979 Indian Health Policy, the 1989 Transfer Policy and more recently from partnerships endeavours such as the BC Tripartite Framework Agreement on First Nations Health Governance. Across the country, First Nations are looking at options for establishing and/or strengthening partnerships with federal and provincial governments as well as health authorities.  Literature on concepts of collaboration sometimes refer to unequal relationships, but limited attention seems to have been given to the concept of working together in situations where there is a special relationship with the Crown. How can we, First Nations and governments, work together and succeed in improving access and quality of health services, and ultimately health outcomes?  What would be the key ingredients for success?  This review begins to examine a few options including trust, commitment, collaborative capacity and a changing role for public service managers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Monotherapy with Glucagon-like peptide-2 exhibits site specific trophic effects on small bowel mucosa, but not colon mucosa or enteric submucosal neurons, in the fasted state
Keywords-MotsClés: ENTERIC NERVOUS SYSTEM; GLUCAGON-LIKE PEPTIDE-2; ICS TRAVEL AWARDS; INTESTINAL ADAPTATION; RATS; SHORT BOWEL SYNDROME; WHOLE MOUNTS
Abstract-Résumé: ICS Travel Awards Purpose: Short bowel syndrome (SBS) and intestinal failure often occur after major resection of the small bowel in infants. It has an incidence of 24.5 per 100,000 live births and mortality rate of 2 per 100,000 per year in Canada. Infants with SBS are unable to absorb the nutrients necessary to grow and survive through regular feeding and are dependent on intravenous nutrition, leading to complications of infection, liver failure and death. This study examines the effect of hormonal therapy with Glucagon-like Peptide 2 (GLP2) on small bowel adaptation to determine if it can improve efficiency and absorptive capacity. We hypothesize that GLP2 is stimulatory for both the intestinal lining and nerves in fasted rats maintained with intravenous nutrition. Methods: Rats with normal length of bowel were maintained with intravenous nutrition with or without GLP2 for 7 days. Small bowel and colon were inspected to determine effect on the bowel lining and on the density and types of intestinal nerves for possible adaptive changes. Results: GLP2 treatment significantly increased small bowel length, weight, circumference, and bowel lining thickness. No differences were found in the colon lining or in nerve density.  There was a weak trend towards a change in the types of nerves found in the colon with GLP2. Conclusion:  GLP2 improves the growth of the small bowel lining consistent with adaptive changes while fasting. GLP2 did not affect the colon lining or nerve density. There was, however, a weak trend towards a change in the types of nerves found in the colon with GLP2. Further studies will be performed to determine if this nerve effect amplifies with surgically induced short bowel syndrome as it does for the bowel lining. If GLP2 is found to stimulate growth of the absorptive lining and nerves, we may help to cure short bowel syndrome and save lives by improving the nutrition, health and growth of these babies after translational studies are performed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Why do you care? Exploring the experience of health care providers working with persons with dementia in primary care memory clinics
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS
Abstract-Résumé: Objectives: Providing care for persons with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) is challenging, given the stressors and uncertainties experienced by persons with dementia and their families, the complexities of assessment and management, and the limited efficacy of available treatments.  While some research has looked at the experience of families who care for persons with ADRD, little is known about the experience of primary health care providers. We explored the experiences of health care providers working with persons with dementia.   Method: Using a phenomenological approach, semi-structured interviews were completed with interprofessional team members in two primary care-based memory clinics in Southern Ontario. Health care providers were asked about their experiences working with persons with dementia in a team context.  Interviews were analyzed using Colaizzi's (1978) method of analysis of phenomenological data.   Results: Health care providers discussed their motivations for working with persons with dementia, how they came to be part of a memory clinic team, what they valued and found rewarding in their work, and the challenges and frustrations they experienced. Working as part of a team could be challenging but was also a major source of encouragement.   Conclusions: Although primary care is playing an increasingly important role in dementia care, future research should examine experiences of health care providers in other settings. A deeper understanding of health care providers' experiences working with persons with dementia yields insights into how these workers and teams can be better prepared and supported to provide care to persons with dementia and their families.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Claudin Family of Tight Junction Proteins Is Essential for Neural Tube Closure
Keywords-MotsClés: CHICK EMBRYOGENESIS; CLAUDINS; CLOSTRIDIUM PERFRINGENS ENTEROTOXIN; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; ICS TRAVEL AWARD; NEURAL TUBE CLOSURE; TIGHT JUNCTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Neural tube defects (NTDs) are a group of congenital malformation affecting the brain and spinal cord that occur when the neural tube fails to close during embryonic development.  Although perinatal folic acid supplementation has reduced the risk of neural tube defects by 60-70%, they still remain the second most common birth defect with an incidence of 1 per 1000 live births.  While both genetic and environmental factors are known to cause NTDs, how these factors mechanistically interfere with the normal events of neural tube closure remains poorly understood.  The chick embryo is a suitable model in which to study neural tube closure because the tissue movements that lead to neural tube closure are identical to those that occur in the human embryo.  I have shown that removal of multiple members of the claudin family of tight junction proteins from the chick embryo leads to open NTDs at the level of the brain, spinal cord and, in many cases, along the entire length of the embryo.  This pleiotropic phenotype is similar to what is observed in humans, even when the disorder is caused by a single gene.  I am using the chick embryo to investigate which of the morphogenetic events required for neural tube closure are regulated by claudins.  I am also sequencing claudin genes in a human cohort with NTDs to identify mutations in claudin genes.  This study will provide a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying normal neurulation and the interplay between genetic mutations and environmental events that lead to NTDs.

TitreApplicationTitle: The orphan nuclear receptor liver receptor homolog-1 (Lrh-1, NR5A2) regulates transcriptional reprogramming during decidualization in a human endometrial cell line.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL LINE; DECIDUALIZATION; IMPLANTATION; MISSCARRIAGE; UTERUS
Abstract-Résumé: During human menstrual cycle a dramatic transcriptional reprogramming of endometrial stromal cells occurs, leading to a receptive state of the endometrium in a process known as decidualization.Multiple transcriptional regulators have been identified that are essential for decidualization of stromal cells.  Lrh-1 is an orphan nuclear receptor and a transcriptional regulator known to be involved in many reproductive events.  Our studies showed that Lrh-1 is expressed in the mouse uterus and is essential for proper decidualization of the endometrial stroma.  We have further demonstrated its occurrence in human endometrium during both the secretory and proliferative phases of the menstrual cycle.  Our goal is to define the Lrh-1 transcriptional network regulating reprogramming of stromal cells into decidual cells by characterizing the gene expression pattern during decidual fibroblast differentiation. To address this hypothesis, we employed an in vitro model using a human endometrial stromal cell line (hESC).  Our experiments demonstrated that the hESC cell line can undergo decidualization in vitro when treated with the progestin medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) and cAMP. The expression of Lrh-1 increases multiple fold during decidualization in vitro, parallel with increased expression of the  markers for decidualization, prolactin (PRL)and insulin like growth factor binding protein-1 (IGFBP1) gene activation.  To assess the effect of an Lrh-1 overexpression, we created a model by transfecting the cells with a construct constitutively expressing Lrh-1, resulting in 5 fold increases in abundance of transcripts for the decidualization marker genes PRL and IGFBP and a precrocious development of the decidual reaction.  Moreover, ChIP-seq  analysis demonstrated that PRL has a distal Lrh-1 binding site at -170kb from the PRL transcription start site.These results indicate that Lrh-1 regulates distinct sets of target genes during decidualization of the human stroma.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effects of a 6 week resistance training program in juvenile idiopathic arthritis: pilot study
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCELEROMETER; CHILDHOOD HEALTH ASSESSMENT QUESTIONNAIRE; DYNAMOMETER; INFLAMMATION; JUVENILE ARTHRITIS; MUSCULAR FITNESS; PAIN; REAL TIME DATA CAPTURE; RESISTANCE (STRENGTH) TRAINING; ULTRASOUND
Abstract-Résumé: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common rheumatic disease in children, affecting 1 in 1000 children each year. Not only do children with JIA experience joint swelling, but also chronic pain, decreased muscular fitness and decreased function. In healthy and clinical populations strength training demonstrates a decrease pain perception and increase muscular fitness and function; however a paucity of research using strength training in JIA exists. This pilot study aimed to understand the effects of a 6 week, 3 times a week, home-based strength training program in children with JIA. The primary outcome was a comprehensive measure of pain reported on a tablet application (before exercise, after exercise and end of each day). Secondary outcomes included inflammation, muscle strength, muscle thickness and functional ability. Seven participants (14.4 years) completed a total of 12.4 ± 3.8 out of a possible 18 exercise sessions. Significant pain changes did not exist throughout the exercise program (p>0.05). Pain before exercise was significantly correlated to perceived exercise difficulty (p<0.05). Muscle thickness at the leg increased from before to after the 6 weeks (p<0.05). No other significant differences existed (p>0.05). The results of this pilot study suggest pain is extremely variable between individuals, showing a need for a larger study examining the effects of strength training on pain in JIA. As well, this suggests that pain is a barrier to physical activity as it can increase the perceived difficulty of exercise. Strength training is also able to improve muscular fitness. Although initial results are promising, further research is required to attain definitive results on pain, inflammation, muscle strength and function. If strength training is feasible and beneficial in this population, the Canadian Healthcare System would benefit economically by decreasing the need for pain medication, physiotherapists, and occupational therapists.

Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE; CAP-DEPENDENT TRANSLATION; DROSOPHILA NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION; EIF4E-BINDING PROTEIN (4E-BP); HOMEOSTATIC PLASTICITY; SYMPATHETIC GANGLION; SYNAPTIC STRENGTH; TARGET OF RAPAMYCIN (MTOR)
Abstract-Résumé: Synaptic connections are continuously modified, a feature of synapses that is required for higher brain functions such as learning and memory. While synaptic structure and function continuously change, many signaling mechanisms work in concert to stabilize synaptic function to reach a balance or homeostasis. Amounting evidence suggests that malfunction of these homeostatic mechanisms may underlie neuropathology and neurodegeneration. Revealing the molecular mechanisms at play is central to understanding nervous system function, both in health and in pathological states. Taking advantage of Drosophila genetics, we have uncovered that the target of rapamycin (TOR) critically regulates synaptic homeostasis at the Drosophila larval neuromuscular junction. TOR acts by enhancing cap-dependent translation by phosphorylating two down-stream bona fide targets: 4E-BP (the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E -binding protein), and S6K (the p70 ribosomal S6 kinase). Phosphorylated 4E-BPs no longer inhibit cap-dependent translation initiation. According to our model, loss of 4E-BP function should enhance synaptic function. We therefore asked whether loss of 4E-BP function alone is sufficient to enhance synaptic transmission. To test this idea, we have conducted our studies in 2 ways. In one, we characterized synaptic function at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction of 4E-BP loss of function mutants. In the second, we tested whether Cap-dependent translation mechanisms play a similar at neuronal-neuronal synapses in mammals as it does in Drosophila. For the latter experiments, we are examining synaptic strength at synapses in sympathetic ganglia of 4E-BP1/BP2 double mutant mice. Our results at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction indicate that 4E-BP acts as a constitutive negative regulator of synaptic strength. Interestingly, our results from synapses in the 4E-BP1/BP2 double mutant mice suggest that that 4E-BP's function is conserved from flies to mice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Androgens Act in a Sex Dependent Manner to Increase Adult Neurogenesis in the Dentate Gyrus.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGENS; HIPPOCAMPUS; NEUROGENESIS; SEX DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Adult neurogenesis involves the proliferation, differentiation, migration, and survival of neurons in the rodent dentate gyrus. Gonadal steroids have been shown to independently modulate these aspects of adult hippocampal neurogenesis. We previously reported that androgens, acting through the androgen receptor, increased the survival of neurons in the dentate gyrus of adult male rats.  However, neither castration nor androgen replacement affected the proliferation of neurons suggesting androgens effects on neurogenesis were specifically related to cell survival. These previous studies, though, only examined the effects of androgens on neurogenesis in males. Thus, in the current study, we explored the effect of systemic injections of the androgen, dihydrotestosterone, on adult hippocampal neurogenesis in ovariectomized female rats. We replicated our previous finding in male rats as dihydrotestosterone increased the number of BrdU positive cells following 30 days of treatment. Additionally, castration and DHT treatment did not affect the number of Ki67 expressing neurons, suggesting androgens affect survival and not proliferation. Surprisingly, though, systemic DHT treatment did not increase the number of BrdU positive cells and did not affect the number of ki67 expressing cells in the dentate gyrus of females. Together, these data suggest androgens act in a sex dependent manner to increase adult hippocampal neurogenesis. Additionally, given the lack of an effect of DHT in females suggests the sex difference in response to androgens in adulthood may be organized during a perinatal critical period. The sex dependent effects of androgens on adult hippocampal neurogenesis may have implications for the treatment of neurological disorders that show sex-dependent changes and affect the hippocampus.

TitreApplicationTitle: Autophagy as a Biomarker and Resistance Mechanism to Clinical Imatinib Mesylate Treatment in CML Stem/Progenitor Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CELL METABOLISM; CHRONIC MYELOID LEUKEMIA (CML); CLINICAL RESPONSE; COMBINATION THERAPY; DRUG RESISTANCE; GENE SIGNATURE; IMATINIB MESYLATE/GLEEVEC; NOVEL PREDICTIVE BIOMARKER; STEM/PROGENITOR CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a white blood cell cancer that is treated with the chemotherapeutic agent Gleevec (imatinib mesylate, IM). However, only some patients respond to the treatment well while others do not, making cancer care ineffective and therefore warrants further research.  Several studies are performed to understand why some patients respond better to Gleevec than others. One focus of the research is directed to the changed metabolic needs of cancer cells. Cancer cells have a high energy demand and use a recycling process called autophagy to survive starvation during chemotherapy resulting in cancer relapse.  Autophagy is a process in which cells digest their organelles to reuse nutrients and thus energy. It occurs at low levels in healthy cells but is misused by cancer cells for more energy to fuel rapid growth. Here, we studied how autophagy is deregulated in CML cells compared to healthy individuals and if it could be a useful marker in predicting if a patient will likely respond to Gleevec therapy or not.  We identified that key autophagy proteins are higher in CML than normal, such as ATG4, ATG5 and Beclin-1. Further, we found that there are differences in ATG4 and ATG5 levels between patients that respond to Gleevec vs. patients that do not respond. Interestingly, these characteristics are detectable in patients before any therapy and might thus be useful in the future for the prediction of patient's chemotherapy responses. Moreover, we showed that inhibiting autophagy (by decreasing ATG4 protein) makes CML cells sensitive to Gleevec and thus improves how effective the therapy is. These exciting results suggest that a combination of autophagy inhibition and Gleevec treatment might be a valid approach to improve cancer care for patients in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of cell migration and integrin recycling by the endosomal adaptor GGA3
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CANCER; CELL ADHESION; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL MIGRATION AND INVASION; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; ENDOCYTOSIS AND INTRACELLULAR TRAFFICKING; LIVE CELL IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Normal functioning of the human body and tissue formation requires a tight control of cues and signals sent from one cell to another. A plethora of signals are interpreted by cell surface molecules called receptors and based on these signals, cells respond in a variety of ways. Sometimes they promote growth or induce death but they can also promote a cell to move through the body. This process occurs normally during embryonic development but also occurs in cancer in an uncontrolled manner when a cell from a tumour metastasizes and colonizes another part of the body. Typically, the process of metastasis is what ultimately leads to death in cancer patients. The molecules that the cell uses to adhere to its surroundings are called integrins and are used when a cell migrates. When they are activated by signals, they are taken up within the cell and either destroyed or transported to a surface of cell where it is needed. I propose that by elucidating the mechanisms that control this decision between integrin destruction or recycling, we can understand how the cell controls movement and ultimately use this for therapeutic benefit. I plan to investigate the molecules that control integrin transport inside the cell using state of the art microscopic techniques, as well as established biochemical methods. This fundamental understanding is crucial for our interpretation of clinical trials that are currently ongoing which use drugs that target integrins. The study that I propose will be used to explain possible clinical outcomes and will ultimately aid in the rational improvement and refinement of therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mobilizing Aboriginal Women's Right to Healthy Food in Winnipeg

Abstract-Résumé: "ICS Travel Awards" According to Article 25 of the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights, food is a human right. Yet, the inability of people to achieve this right in Canada represents a profound injustice. Food insecurity can be defined as the inability to adequately access nutritional food in a socially acceptable and dignified manner (Davis & Tarasuk, 1994, Canadian Dietetic Association, 1991). Among Canadians, food insecurity is experienced by a disproportionate number of Aboriginal people relative to other population groups. The purpose of my research will be to characterize the geography of food insecurity from the perspectives of low-income Aboriginal women living in Winnipeg. In a one-year project, I employed a mixed-method feminist participatory research approach to uncover geographic barriers (physical and social) that low-income single Aboriginal mothers encounter in their efforts to secure nutritional food for their families. Recent research has shown that food insecurity has both physical and mental health implications. For example, my undergraduate thesis research found that women's dignity is undermined in multiple ways during food acquisition and provisioning activities. To better understand the contextual dynamics of food dignity, I have worked closely with the women of Ka Ni Kanicihk, a community-based non-profit organization in Winnipeg dedicated to providing Aboriginal focused programs and services.  Our research has documented how an inadequate transportation system, experiences of racism during grocery shopping journeys, and challenges in securing affordable healthy foods represent three forms of injustice faced by these women. Moreover, our participatory approach has helped us to document how young mothers have developed creative strategies to navigate unjust urban and governmental systems andbecome motivated to share their stories and survival strategies with others.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stimulating Intrinsic Repair for DMD (SIRD)
Keywords-MotsClés: DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; HUMANIZED MICE; MDX MICE; PRECLINICAL STUDIES; REGENERATIVE MYOGENESIS; SATELLITE CELLS; WNT7A
Abstract-Résumé: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is a rare and devastating genetic disease of childhood manifested by progressive debilitating skeletal muscle weakness and wasting, and ultimately death. The Rudnicki group recently identified a role for Wnt7a/Fzd7 signaling in stimulating the regeneration of muscle by acting at two levels. Wnt7a acts on satellite stem cells to drive their symmetric expansion, and also acts on myofibers to stimulate hypertrophy. Delivery of Wnt7a significantly ameliorated dystrophic changes in the mdx mouse model of DMD. The research team represents an outstanding multidisciplinary group of investigators, who are uniquely positioned to conduct the proposed basic and preclinical studies. The overall goal of the project is to assess the utility of Wnt7a and its variants as protein therapeutics for the stimulation of intrinsic regeneration for the treatment of DMD. We propose to characterize the Wnt7a/Fzd7 signaling pathway at the molecular level and identify downstream target genes to elucidate mode of action. We will characterize the long-term effects of intramuscular injection of Wnt7a protein on muscle intergrity and strength in dystrophin-deficient mdx mice. We will globally express Wnt7a in skeletal muscle using a MLC1-Wnt7a transgene. We will investigate the basis for the suppression of the inflammatory response by Wnt7a. Finally, we will assess the activity of Wnt7a on human satellite cells and myofibers in mice carrying humanized DMD muscle. These experiments will advance our knowledge of Wnt7a signaling in muscle and illuminate the therapeutic potential of Wnt7a as a protein biologic to stimulate intrinsic repair in a muscle-wasting disease like DMD. Furthermore, the information generated by the proposed studies will inform the preclinical development of Wnt7a towards undertaking a first Phase I clinical trial.

Abstract-Résumé: Food Allergy is an increasing problem in Canada which engenders a major burden on families, schools and the health care system. In order to address potential therapies for food allergy, more must be learned about the basic differences between individuals who do not have food allergy and those that do. In trying to develop treatments that can lead to Food Tolerance rather than Food Allergy, we have built a strong multi-university, multi-disciplinary team. Our team will investigate the differences in genetic profiles for food allergic and food tolerant individuals to help predict future food allergy patents within families. We will address environmental contaminants that may activate the immune system and thus increase the risk of food allergies. We will also test novel treatment strategies based on strong fundamental science from group members. This study, which will be known as GET-FACTS (Genetics, Environment and Therapies: Food Allergy Clinical Tolerance Studies) will put Canada at the forefront of western countries in the search for novel methods to help stem the food allergy epidemic.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dysregulation of RNA in the pathogenesis of ALS
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; MICRORNA; NEUROFILAMENTS; PATHOGENESIS; PRECLINICAL MODELS; RNA
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS, Lou Gehrig's disease) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of certain neurons that relay messages from the brain to skeletal muscles. The result is gradual loss of the ability to move, to swallow, to speak and eventually to breathe. ALS is classified as a rare disorder, but the devastation of this disease impacts well beyond the patient to families and the community. Studies in both familial and sporadic forms of  ALS are pointing to abnormalities of RNA processing being a key common mechanism of pathogenesis. The cell produces multiple forms of RNAl. Messenger RNA (mRNA) is the template of DNA used to make proteins. RNA-binding proteins, several of which are mutated in ALS, complex with mRNAs to transport them out of the nucleus to make proteins where they are needed. Whether that protein gets made also depends on the stability of the mRNA template, which is regulated by microRNAs (miRNA). Members of our team are identifying changes in expression of these miRNAs in ALS neurons with significant impact on production of neurofilament proteins and their assembly into filaments (neurofilaments) that support the cellular architecture and several important processes of cellular homeostasis and response to stress. Our consortium will determine how dysregulation of miRNAs contribute to multiple forms of ALS and model these changes in tissue culture and animal models to use for preclinical therapeutic investigation. Although the mechanisms involved in dysfunction and loss of neurons in ALS are complex, we expect our work will show that neurofilament regulation is important and can be used as a representative measure of outcome for developing and testing therapies.

Abstract-Résumé: Glial cells play a central role in brain water and ion homeostasis and the maintenance of low extracellular potassium during neuron cell activity. These functions are impaired in a rare type of leukodystrophy called MLC (megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts). Mutations in MLC1, the first gene defective in MLC, impair the cell surface expression of the MLC1 and reduce the activity of volume-regulated chloride channels (VRAC). We have established a subset of biochemical and functional interactions among the VRAC, the ClC-2 chloride channel, GlialCAM (the second gene defective in MLC) and MLC1, which likely represent components involved in the regulation of glial cell water homeostasis and chloride fluxes. Using state-of-the-art biochemical and cellular assays, as well as novel knockout mouse and zebrafish models, we will decipher the relationships between the VRAC and ClC-2 chloride channels and the MLC-defective proteins MLC1 and GlialCAM. In addition, we will identify the components of the cellular quality control mechanisms that prematurely degrade MLC1 mutants either at the ER or cell surface. We plan to perform novel genetic and chemical screens in order to identify pharmacological chaperones that restore the MLC1 mutant cell surface expression/function and could be used as therapies for MLC. This project will be instrumental to gain insights into the pathophysiology of MLC disease and other brain defects in fluid homeostasis, hopefully providing the first therapeutic solutions for MLC patients.

Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM; CYP24A1; FGF23; HYPERCALCEMIA; HYPERCALCIURIA; NAPI-II; NEPHROCALCINOSIS; NEPHROLITHIASIS; PHOSPHATE; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: Idiopathic infantile hypercalcemia (IIH) is a rare genetic condition characterized by hypercalcemia and nephrocalcinosis with unknown long-term implications and limited therapies. The cause was unknown until recently when a team including Jones/Schlingmann on this grant proposal showed that the main underlying defect in a cohort of German families involved mutations of the vitamin D inactivating enzyme, CYP24A1. (Schlingmann et al New Engl J Med, 2011). We hypothesize that mutations in CYP24A1 lead to aberrant control of vitamin D hormone levels in blood and tissues and impaired mineral ion homeostasis, leading to soft-tissue calcification as a result of long-term hypercalcemia. This proposal will attempt to create a broad consortium of clinicians and scientists from Europe and Canada studying CYP24A1 and other genes causing hypercalcemia in order:- 1) To provide better methods for diagnosis, monitoring and long-term surveillance of IIH and related hypercalcemic conditions 2) To use mouse models to recreate and investigate IIH and provide new approaches for the treatment of IIH and related hypercalcemic conditions. Our studies will incorporate genetic testing, employ a unique CYP24A1 enzyme assay to recreate the patient defect in the test-tube and the latest and most sensitive LC-MS/MS technology to detect enzyme products in the blood of IIH patients. This will be augmented by novel CYP24A1 knock-out and knock-in animal models; and SLC-34 knockout animal models to mimic human hypercalcemic conditions in the mouse and then study their long-term biological consequences.

Abstract-Résumé: Atrial fibrillation is an irregular beating of the heart and is one of the most common causes of stroke in Canada.  Fortunately, medical research,  has produced several treatments, including blood thinners and blood pressure lowering drugs, which can reduce the risk of stroke by over 75%. However; there are challenges which prevent Canadians from benefiting from this research. The CSPIN network seeks to link world-class atrial fibrillation a stroke researchers from across Canada so that they may share not only their ideas and expertise, but so that they may conduct collaborative research in an efficient way.  The network will develop at least 7 research studies; including: 1) A study using new technology to identify people with silent atrial fibrillation, so that they may get the appropriate treatment; 2) A study to ensure that patients who visit their family doctor or a pharmacy with atrial fibrillation get the treatment that they need; 3) Two studies to see if blood thinners can prevent stroke in patients with pacemakers and in patients who have had a heart procedure to treat atrial fibrillation, 4) A study to see if patients having open-heart surgery have fewer strokes if the surgeon removes a small piece of redundant tissue, 5) A study to determine if blood thinners can prevent a repeat stroke and 6) A study to determine if blood thinners can prevent memory loss and dementia among younger patients with atrial fibrillation. This network will involve over a thirty world-class physician researcher from Halifax to Victoria and will also involve nurses, public health individuals and pharmacists. The network will work with governments and other groups to develop economical, sustainable programs, so that Canadians can benefit directly from the results of this work. The network will also invest significant resources to help attract and train the next generation of Canadian stroke researchers; making Canada a leader in this field for years to come.

Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Respiratory Research Network (CRRN), in close partnership with the Canadian Lung Association (CLA) and other partners, will improve patient care and outcomes through creation of an enduring national network of investigators and research platforms to enable innovative, collaborative, respiratory health research that influences decision making and ensures high quality training and career development of a new generation of investigators.  The goals of the network are to bring together researchers across disciplines and research themes/pillars to work together in a coordinated fashion in order to improve understanding of the origins and progression of chronic airway diseases in Canada.   Our network is composed of more than 50 investigators located at research institutes, academic medical centres, government, public health agencies, and universities across Canada.  Our proposed research plan will span all four pillars of health research and will include strong research training and knowledge translation components. The over-arching plan for CRRN is the development of a network approach and research platforms to establish an enhanced understanding of the biology, patho-physiology, prevalence, health outcomes and costs, as well as potential health service and policy solutions related to the origin and progression of airway disease.   Our goal is to understand the full burden of chronic airway diseases in Canada (both diagnosed and undiagnosed) and to generate new knowledge that will inform public policy and lead to interventions to reduce the burden of asthma and COPD.  As the network matures the platforms that we establish to study airway disease will be adopted to study other respiratory diseases as well.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the impact of maternal and infant nutrition on infant/child health.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; BIRTH COHORT; CARDIO-METABOLIC; DIETARY PATTERNS; EPIGENETICS; ETHNICITY; GENE-DIET INTERACTIONS; MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH; MICROBIOME; NUTRITION
Abstract-Résumé: A mother's nutritional choices while pregnant may have a great influence on her baby's development, both in the womb, and during infancy. There is evidence that what a mother eats during pregnancy may interact with her genes to affect her child's susceptibility to poor health outcomes including childhood obesity, pre-diabetes, allergy, and asthma, which share common causes. It is also known that what an infant eats can change his or her intestinal bacteria, which may influence the development of these poor outcomes. To clarify these relationships, we will bring together four birth cohorts which have enrolled mothers and their children from across Canada, across income levels, and from diverse ethnic groups (i.e. South Asian, Aboriginal).  We will study the interplay among 4 factors: gene expression, maternal and infant nutrition, and the infant gut bacteria; and the role they play in childhood health.    Our findings will provide a solid evidence base to inform Dietary Guidelines in pregnancy, the development of randomized clinical trials to provide additional high quality evidence, and will be relevant to diverse and high-risk populations of Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translational approach to establish the cardiometabolic health effects and mechanisms of action of fish nutrients: from animal models to obese insulin-resistant subjects
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; FISH NUTRIENTS; HUMAN SUBJECTS; INSULIN RESISTANCE; METABOLOMICS; NUTRIGENOMICS; OBESITY; TYPE 2 DIABETES; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: Few Canadians meet the weekly recommendations of fish consumption and thus intakes of not only n-3 PUFA but also of fish proteins and vitamin D are low in the general population and even lower in obese subjects. Moreover, many Canadians, especially obese subjects, have low (<50 nmol/L) or suboptimal (<75 nmol/L) serum concentrations of vitamin D. Low intake of those fish nutrients increase the risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D) and cardiovascular disease (CVD). The overall goal of this programmatic grant application is to investigate the effects and the mechanisms of action of fish peptides and vitamin D, along with fish omega3 fatty acids on cardiometabolic risk factors in animal models of obesity-linked T2D and CVD and in human obese subjects. We plan to use nutrigenomic and metabolomic approaches to study the individual responses to fish peptides and vitamin D interventions and to discover new gene/metabolite networks underlying these effects, and potentially novel biomarkers to predict the risk of T2D and CVD in obese subjects.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development, implementation, and evaluation of a breastfeeding curriculum for pediatric residency programs
Keywords-MotsClés: BABY-FRIENDLY INITIATIVE; BREASTFEEDING; MEDICAL EDUCATION; MEETING; PEDIATRIC RESIDENTS; PHYSICIANS; PLANNING GRANT; POSTGRADUATE EDUCATION
Abstract-Résumé: Breast milk is the ideal food for babies, as it protects newborns against infections and other conditions.  It also protects mothers against some types of cancers.  By making children and mothers healthier, breastfeeding reduces the costs to society by decreasing rates of hospitalizations, especially in young infants.    Exclusive breastfeeding (feeding no other foods or liquids than breast milk) is recommended for the first 6 months after birth.  In Canada, breastfeeding rates are high right after birth, but they drop quickly over the next few months.  Only 14% of mothers exclusively breastfeed their child at 6 months.    We know that doctors' recommendations have a direct impact on how long women will breastfeed, and that helping mothers with breastfeeding problems is part of physicians' responsibility.  Unfortunately, residents (doctors-in-training) in Canada do not learn how to help mothers breastfeed during their training period.  We also know from our previous recent study that the beliefs, confidence, attitudes and knowledge of Canadian primary care doctors (family doctors and pediatricians) are suboptimal when it comes to breastfeeding.  This is true also in many other parts of the world.  Given the health, social and economic advantages that breastfeeding provides to babies, mothers and society in general, improving breastfeeding duration is an important public health initiative.  There is therefore a great need to develop a solid learning program for pediatric residents, so as to give them the skills they need to help mothers breastfeed.  We therefore propose to bring together a group of breastfeeding researchers, breastfeeding experts, medical education experts, residents and mothers to develop a program that we will ultimately put in place in residency programs across the country.  This has the potential to increase breastfeeding rates significantly and make our children healthier.   The meeting is planned for April 17th and 18th 2014, in Ottawa.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advancing provincial/territorial public health capacity for health equity
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH SYSTEMS; KNOWLEDGE DISSEMINATION; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; POPULATION HEALTH; PROVINCIES/TERRITORIES; PUBLIC HEALTH ORGANIZATIONS; PUBLIC HEALTH PRACTICE; PUBLIC HEALTH SYSTEMS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The health status of individuals, and of the Canadian population as a whole, is the result of many factors. Health is affected by genetics, personal behaviour, medical treatment, and - most of all - the environment in which people live and work. As a result of social policies that affect factors influencing health, such as income and employment, people burdened by lower education, poorer food quality, inadequate housing and other disadvantages live less healthy and shorter lives.  In Canada, provinces and territories are responsible for the management and delivery of health services, including public health, the part of the health system that promotes health and prevents disease. Public health has leadership to ensure health of whole communities. Because of this, provincial and territorial public health decision-makers have central roles to help the  Government of Canada achieve a pledge it made in 2012 to reduce the gap between the least and most healthy.   The proposed event, to be held May 29-30, 2014, will help provincial and territorial public health decision makers take a more pivotal role in improving policies and practices, and indirectly impact the activities of local and regional health authorities. The planned event will bring together public health leaders with researchers who specialize in learning about ways that public health systems can help narrow the gap in health status, and improve the overall health of the Canadian population.   The meeting will be made up of three segments: 1) education about research findings that will help provincial and territorial public health decision-makers better set priorities, use policy levers and assign resources; 2) sharing among public health leaders about promising and proven mechanisms being tested in different provinces and territories; and 3) identifying knowledge gaps and planning next steps to continue networking and support for policy, program and practice improvements to advance health equity.
