TitreApplicationTitle: Dissemination of the Policy Readiness Tool: Increasing Capacity for Healthy Public Policy Development Locally, Provincially and Nationally
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE PREVENTION; DIFFUSION OF INNOVATIONS; DISSEMINATION; HEALTHY PUBLIC POLICY; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; MUNICIPALITIES; PAN-CANADIAN; POLICY READINESS; PRACTITIONER TOOL
Abstract-Résumé: The purpose of this dissemination activity is to share a practitioner tool that can be used to help develop healthy public policy at the local level. Specifically, the tool will be shared with practitioners, community organizations, municipalities, the general public, policy developers and advocates across Canada. The Policy Readiness Tool (PRT, www.policyreadinesstool.com) is a short tool that helps users to a) assess a municipality's readiness for policy change, and then b) target their actions using evidence-based strategies and resources. While the PRT is currently available online in a PDF format, a recent evaluation has indicated that users are interested in more. We propose to: create an online version of the PRT to assess readiness for policy change; update the resources provided; create an online community for PRT-users to share their experiences, educate users about the PRT, and facilitate discussions about its use; and evaluate how well this all works. This dissemination activity will ensure that the PRT is used in practice. It will increase user's knowledge about policy development and implementation. This is very important because healthy public policy is a key strategy for reducing chronic disease and improving health. In addition, while individuals, organizations, and communities may see the potential of implementing policy, they may lack the training, experience or resources to do so. The sharing of this user-friendly, evidence-based tool across Canada will help practitioners and lay users to do this.

Abstract-Résumé: This research project investigates the safety of ondansetron, a drug that is used to treat severe nausea and vomiting.  The work is in response to a safety question raised by Health Canada and the Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network regarding the effect this drug may have on the heart. More specifically, this study focuses on children and pregnant women, two groups of patients who may be particularly susceptible to developing adverse reactions from this medication.  We will ask children from British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec and pregnant women from British Columbia and Ontario, who receive ondansetron, to participate in this study. In participating patients, we will monitor their heart while they receive the drug and collect information about previous conditions and other medications the patients receive to see if use of ondansetron in certain circumstances increases the risk of heart problems.   We believe that a person's genetic make up may also help us understand which patients are most likely to suffer an adverse effect from ondansetron. Thus, we will collect a DNA sample from all study participants and conduct genetic analyses to determine if certain genetic factors put patients at increased risk of heart problems from ondansetron.  Results of this study will help doctors decide how to best use ondansetron so it is safe for children and pregnant women who require treatment of severe nausea and vomiting.

TitreApplicationTitle: Resynchronization/defibrillation for Ambulatory Heart Failure Trial in patients with Permanent AF (RAFT-PermAF)
Keywords-MotsClés: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; CARDIAC RESYNCHRONIZATION THERAPY; DEFIBRILLATOR; HEART FAILURE; MORBIDITY; MORTALITY; MULTICENTRE; OPTIMAL MEDICAL THERAPY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Atrial fibrillation (AF) and heart failure (HF) are two common heart conditions that are encountered with an increase in death and suffering. When both these two conditions occur in a patient, the patient's prognosis is poor with a reduced quality of life. These patients are frequently admitted to the hospital and have increased risk of death.In these HF patients who are in AF all of the time, who would otherwise be a suitable candidate for an implantable defibrillator to prevent sudden cardiac death, whether adding pacing of both ventricles will reduce death and suffering.  Other studies have shown that adding pacing to both ventricles is of benefit in HF patients with mild to moderate symptoms and have a regular heart rhythm. We now want to explore if this therapy will benefit those patients with a permanent irregular heart rhythm (AF). We will also be assessing the cost effectiveness of this treatment strategy and the life quality for these patients. This study may have a dramatic impact on the way we manage these patients with atrial fibrillation and heart failure and may improve the outlook and well being of these patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Highly active anti-retroviral therapy use during pregnancy and the risk of mother-to-child transmission, congenital malformation, and neonatal death
Keywords-MotsClés: HAART USE; MAJOR CONGENITAL MALFORMATIONS; MOTHER TO CHILD TRANSMISSION; NEONATAL DEATH; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: Present data suggest that pregnant HIV women should be treated during gestation to prevent MCTC and neonatal death. However, there is no consensus as to whether treatment should be initiated in the first trimester (when organogenesis occurs) or later (when theoretically vulnerability for drug-induced congenital malformation would be lower). With this study, we aim to answer the following research questions: 1) is the risk of maternal to child transmission (MTCT) of HIV altered when highly-active antiretroviral treatment (HAART) is started during the first trimester of pregnancy and continued thereafter compared to when HAART is started later in pregnancy (2nd or 3rd trimester) among HIV positive pregnant women, 2) is fetal exposure to HAART during the first trimester of pregnancy associated with an increased risk of major congenital malformations (MCM), compared to the risk of MCM in the general population, taking into account HIV status, and 3) is exposure to HAART during pregnancy associated with a significantly decreased risk of neonatal death when compared to the general population of pregnant women, taking into account HIV status. Case-control analyses will be conducted within three pre-established pregnancy cohorts (Quebec, Saskatchewan and US Medicaid pregnancy cohorts) taking advantage of already established cohorts with population-based administrative health data, representing approximately 400,000 (Quebec), 230,000 (Saskatchewan), and 7,104,231 (US) pregnancies (HIV and non-HIV pregnancies). All analyses will be performed within each cohort separately (with common protocols). Pooled estimates will be calculated using meta-analyses methodology. All HAART will be considered including darunavir. This will be one of the few studies worldwide and the first study in Canada looking at MTCT, MCM and neonatal death associated with HAART use during pregnancy, which will have great public health implication.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pregnancy Complications Identify Women at Risk for Developing Cardiovascular Disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CLINICAL GUIDELINE DEVELOPMENT; COLLABORATIVE RESEARCH PROJECTS; INTERVENTION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PREGNANCY; PREGNANCY COMPLICATIONS; PREGNANCY RELATED CARDIOVASCULAR RISK FACTORS; PREVENTION; WORKSHOP
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Heart Health Strategy and Action Plan, states that women including younger women, are at increased risk of heart disease. It identifies improving heart health awareness and prevention of heart disease among women as a national priority. Pregnancy is a time when women see a doctor on a regular basis. Therefore, for most Canadian women, checking for heart disease risk factors at the time of pregnancy and treating them after delivery should be done to prevent future health problems. Furthermore, the development of common pregnancy complications is perhaps the earliest marker for a woman's risk of future heart disease. Unfortunately, pregnancy complications are not recognized by most women and their doctors as risk factors for future health problems. Early detection and treatment of risk factors can prevent most heart disease which is important considering that heart disease costs Canadian's more than 22 billion dollars a year. The GOAL of this workshop is to bring together Canadian and international experts to develop research questions and strategies to better inform the patients and their health care providers about the link between pregnancy complications and future heart disease. The outcome of this will be an improvement in women's long-term health and will ensure that women receive effective and equal care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strengthening the link between transport policy and public health through awareness raising and cross-disciplinary collaboration
Keywords-MotsClés: AIR POLLUTION EXPOSURE; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PUBLIC HEALTH; TRANSPORT POLICY; TRANSPORTATION INFRASTRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: The impact of transportation on public health is a topic that has recently gained significant attention. Around the world, government agencies, community organizations, and citizens themselves have begun to understand that transportation infrastructures and services as well as personal mobility choices are linked with the health and well-being of urban populations. Despite transportation's undeniable social benefits, it is also associated with a range of health impacts notably related to air pollution and physical activity.  We propose knowledge dissemination along three dimensions: A scientific workshop which aims at bringing together transportation modellers, air quality modellers, population exposure experts and epidemiologists in order to promote a discussion of truly integrative research,  A workshop with policy-makers at the three levels of government with transportation planning and public health responsibility in order to discuss ways of transcending individual portfolios to achieve more integrated policy decisions,  Scientific cafes to be held among citizens at large in selected Canadian cities.

TitreApplicationTitle: The SOX Trial: Disseminating the unexpected results of a large, CIHR-funded North American RCT of elastic compression stockings to prevent the post-thrombotic syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: DEEP VENOUS THROMBOSIS; ELASTIC COMPRESSION STOCKINGS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; OUTCOMES RESEARCH; PLACEBO CONTROL; POST-THROMBOTIC SYNDROME; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: We are requesting funds to enable us to disseminate the important and unexpected results of the SOX Trial (active vs. placebo elastic compression stockings (ECS) worn for 2 years to prevent the post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS) after deep vein thrombosis (DVT)), a CIHR-funded randomized controlled trial that was recently completed and analysed.  The SOX Trial's results will lead to substantial change in clinical practice and thus require rapid, targeted dissemination. In contrast to two previous methodologically less rigorous studies, the SOX Trial, the first multicenter, placebo-controlled trial of ECS to prevent PTS, showed that ECS are not effective. The implications of our findings are that 1) clinicians should not routinely prescribe ECS to their patients with DVT, 2) the next version of the American College of Chest Physicians' guidelines as well as all other evidence-based guidelines addressing management of thrombosis should be modified to reflect the SOX Trial's results, and 3) research efforts must be refocused to evaluate new interventions to prevent PTS, a frequent, potentially debilitating but underappreciated complication of venous thrombosis. Our dissemination activities will include 4 webinars given by SOX Trial investigators via Thrombosis Canada (an organization dedicated to education and research in prevention and treatment of thrombotic disease that includes physician and non-physician healthcare professionals from across Canada) and via SSVQ (Societe des sciences vasculaires du Quebec), a non-profit, Quebec-wide scientific organization whose mission is to create an interdisciplinary forum to optimize and disseminate vascular disease knowledge to health professionals and patients. These events will ensure the wide diffusion of our trial's results to front-line practitioners who care for patients with venous thrombosis, and will help to increase awareness about PTS. We will also develop a PTS Clinical Guide in collaboration with Thrombosis Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving DECIsion-making about goals of care for hospitalized, elDerly patiEnts: A multicentre, interventional study.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CARE; ADVANCE CARE PLANNING; AGING; COMMUNICATION AND DECISION MAKING; END OF LIFE CARE; GOALS OF CARE DISCUSSIONS; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: There is a real problem with modern healthcare at the end of life. Most elderly patients with advanced, life-limiting illnesses prefer to receive treatments aimed at improving quality of life and symptoms in their final days. Yet, the use of invasive and expensive technologies at the end of life continues to increase. Mounting evidence suggests that the unwanted use of technology at the end of life has negative effects, including poorer quality of life for patients in those last days and high levels of anxiety and depression amongst bereaved family members. Moreover, as the use of life sustaining technologies increases, the cost of care at the end of life increases dramatically placing enormous strain on finite health care resources.  Our prior research has identified that improving communication and decision-making at the end of life is a high priority for these patients and their families. The objective of our next study, the DECIDE II Study (Improving DECIsion-making about goals of care for hospitalized elDerly patiEnts), is to evaluate the effect of an innovative decision support intervention on outcomes that are meaningful and relevant to seriously ill, elderly, hospitalized patients, their family members, and the health system. We need to hold a face-to-face meeting of the research team, with healthcare decision-makers, patient and family representatives, and other stakeholders to receive their input into the development of the study intervention, methods, and outcomes so that we maximize the potential for our study to address concerns that are of greatest importance to these stakeholders. Thus, the purpose of this proposal is to seek funding to support this protocol development and stakeholder engagement meeting. By improving communication and decision-making at the end of life, we have the opportunity to dramatically improve patients and families experiences as they journey through their final days and prevent unwanted aggressive medical care at the EOL.

TitreApplicationTitle: Meeting of Canadian Researchers on Elder Care
Keywords-MotsClés: ELDER CARE; HEALTH HUMAN RESOURCES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LONG-TERM CARE; QUALITY OF CARE; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: Canadians are living longer than ever before. Estimates are that in thirty years, the number of Canadian 65 years or older will be more than double what it is today. With advanced age comes the increased chance of physical and mental ailments that require significant care from family and community members or in institutional care. With our many successes in keeping seniors healthier and in the community longer, people who are admitted to care facilities have more complex needs and are much more vulnerable.  There are several highly regarded Canadian groups of researchers working to improve the quality of care and the quality of life of seniors, as well as the quality of life of those who care for them. We propose a meeting to bring together these research groups to develop a national network of researchers that will share ideas and work towards common goals in a coordinated effort. These goals will be discussed at the proposed meeting and the outcome will be a grant application for the CIHR Partnerships for Health System Improvement (PHSI) funding opportunity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing a Canadian Model of Innovation in Nursing Systems:  Better Work - Better Care
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTION RESEARCH; HEALTH CARE QUALITY; HIGH ENGAGEMENT WORK PRACTICES; INDUSTRIAL ENGINEERING; MUSCULOSKELETAL DISORDERS; NURSING SYSTEMS; ORGANIZATIONAL DEVELOPMENT; PROCESS IMPROVEMENT; SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Can nurses really do a good job of looking after patients if they are themselves working in pain or under stress?  Poor working environments compromise nurses' ability to provide good patient care and leads to turnover from their employer and profession at the time when there is expected to be a shortage of 60,000 nurses in Canada by 2022.  Recently there have been attempts to use engineering methods from manufacturing to improve health care delivery.  While these methods have improved efficiency, they have also led to worsening working conditions for nurses - with more heavy lifting and less time to attend to each patient.  This is contributing to the nursing shortage and compromising the quality of care in hospitals.  The problem is that these improvement efforts have neglected the critical "Human Factor" in professional work. We propose to develop an approach to improving nursing work in ways that improve the speed and quality of patient care delivery.  Our multidisciplinary team includes engineers, human factors specialists, psychologists, work sociologists, and nurses.  We will develop a new model for improving nursing work that engages the caregivers directly in improving the way they care for patients.  We will draw on traditional engineering approaches - but combine them with Human Factors approaches in ways that improve, not degrade, the job of the nurses.  We will give nurses the tools to innovate in their own workplaces to improve their situation at work and improve the way they deliver care.  This planning grant will fund a two-day workshop necessary for this diverse research team to develop a practical "Canadian" model of innovation. It will also set the stage for field trials to evaluate and further refine this much-needed comprehensive improvement approach that is nurse-centered and patient focused.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fonctionnement familial chez des familles vivant avec le VIH : des savoirs partagés
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNICATION MERE-ENFANT; FONCTIONNEMENT FAMILIAL; METHODOLOGIE QUALITATIVE ET QUANTITATIVE; TRANSMISSION VERTICALE; VIH/SIDA; EDUCATION A LA SEXUALITE
Abstract-Résumé: Une etude conduite par notre equipe et financee par les IRSC (no de reference: 209155) aborde la question du fonctionnement des familles vivant avec le VIH. Elle tend a decrire les patrons de la qualite de vie (QdVF) des familles quebecoises dont la mere vit avec le VIH et a identifier les caracteristiques qui agissent comme facteurs de vulnerabilite et de resilience, tout en contrastant les temoignages sur le fonctionnement familial a partir de la perspective de plusieurs membres.   Les analyses en cours permettent de cerner trois types d'enjeux affectant particulierement les femmes vivant avec le VIH et leurs enfants : 1) les barrieres aux soins percues par les meres vivant avec le VIH et la satisfaction quant aux services recus; 2) les roles et les responsabilites des enfants affectes par le VIH au sein de la famille; 3) la communication entourant la sexualite dans ces familles.  En continuite avec cette reflexion soutenue par les IRSC, la presente demande propose, a travers  des activites de dissemination, de produire une douzaine de feuillets d'information (fact sheets) correspondant a ces trois types d'enjeux. La conception des feuillets d'information suivra les etapes de realisation suivantes : 1) mise sur pied d'un comite consultatif constitue de partenaires cliniques et communautaires; 2) echange avec des acteurs cles dans le cadre des journees de formation Outillons-nous offertes par la COCQ-SIDA; 3) mise en ligne sur le web des feuillets pour consultation et telechargement; 4) planification d'un lancement dans le cadre de la Journee mondiale de lutte contre le sida le 1 decembre 2014. Ces strategies de dissemination visent a potentialiser la diffusion des resultats de recherche et les rendre plus accessibles aux professionnels de la sante, decideurs politiques, aux intervenants d'organismes communautaires, ainsi qu'aux personnes vivant avec le VIH. Elles auront des retombees sur les services sociaux et de sante offerts aux familles vivant avec le VIH.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effets et répercussions des activités d'évaluation des technologies et modes d'interventions en santé et services sociaux au niveau local: l'expérience québécoise
Keywords-MotsClés: APPLICATION INTEGREE DES CONNAISSANCES; PROJET COLLABORATIF; REUNION DE PLANIFICATION; UNITE LOCALE D'EVALUATION DES TECHNOLOGIES; EVALUATION DES EFFETS ET REPERCUSSIONS; EVALUATION DES TECHNOLOGIES EN SANTE; EVALUATION DES TECHNOLOGIES ET DES MODES D'INTERVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Assurer des soins de sante de qualite et securitaires pour tous dans un contexte de rarete des ressources est un defi majeur auquel doivent repondre les systemes de sante. L'evaluation des technologies et des modes d'intervention en sante et services sociaux (ETMISSS) est un domaine multidisciplinaire qui produit une information de haute qualite sur l'efficacite clinique, le rapport cout-efficacite, les repercussions sociales,  ethiques et sur les patients des technologies et interventions dans les domaines de la sante et des services sociaux. Ce domaine d'evaluation a ete developpe pour soutenir les gestionnaires et les cliniciens dans leurs prises de decisions concernant les technologies et l'organisation des services et des pratiques cliniques. Au Quebec, un grand nombre de ces decisions etant  prises a l'echelle locale (agences regionales de sante et de services sociaux, centres de sante et de services sociaux, hopitaux et instituts universitaires), un nombre croissant d'unites locales d'ETMISSS ont ete mises en place au cours des dernieres annees. Cependant, il y a tres peu de donnees concernant l'impact de ces unites et de leurs activites. Les decideurs et les differents acteurs interesses par l'ETMISSS s'interrogent donc sur la meilleure facon d'evaluer les effets et repercussions de ces unites locales. Le but de cette reunion de planification est de developper un projet de recherche qui permettra d'evaluer les effets et repercussions des activites d'ETMISSS au niveau local sur les decisions concernant les soins et services de sante, en tenant compte des perspectives de tous les utilisateurs (gestionnaires, professionnels de la sante, personnel en ETMISSS et patients). Tout en developpant une etroite collaboration, les participants a cette reunion etabliront les bases d'un projet de recherche qui sera presente dans le cadre du  programme de « Partenariats pour l'amelioration du systeme de sante » des IRSC.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exporting an effective and feasible multidisciplinary vulvodynia program to the community
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY TREATMENT; GENITAL PAIN; MULTIDISCIPLINARY CARE; PROVOKED VESTIBULODYNIA; SATELLITE CLINIC; VULVODYNIA
Abstract-Résumé: The study of women's health issues is increasingly receiving the sophisticated scientific attention that has been lacking in past decades. New discoveries in the identification, diagnosis, and treatment of various women's health topics has led to improvements in the life span and quality of life of Canadian women. Within the domain of women's genital pain and sexual medicine, however, barriers exist in women locating providers with adequate knowledge and training in this area, resulting often in years of suffering without an accurate diagnosis. Vancouver Hospital in the UBC Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology is home to North America's first Multidisciplinary Vulvodynia Program; a specialized clinic that offers gynecologic, psychological, and pelvic floor physiotherapy integrated treatment for women with genital pain. Our program has been found to be feasible, effective, and well accepted by patients. Here we aim to develop a training program that would allow us to export our program to one satellite site in BC: the Department of Gynaecology at the University of Victoria. If our methods are found to be feasible and effective, we have a longer term plan to develop satellite sites across the province of BC, and possibly across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Contraception & Abortion in BC: Experience guiding Research guiding Care
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATION; FAMILY PLANNING; HEALTH HUMAN RESOURCES; HEALTH SERVICES DELIVERY; INTERDISCIPLINARY; INTERPROFESSIONAL; KNOWLEDGE DISSEMINATION; PATIENT ORIENTED RESEARCH; QUALITY OF CARE
Abstract-Résumé: WHY: This meeting follows our CIHR funded research planning meeting of April 2011, convening again a broad range of provincial collaborators for dissemination of the findings from the BC Abortion Provider Survey (BCAPS) developed at that meeting. We seek to communicate and discuss effective strategies for health system improvements based on the challenges, gaps and opportunities found.   WHO: Partnering with the BC Ministry of Health, Options for Sexual Health BC (a not for profit organization), and representatives from hospital, academic, and clinician groups, we plan to bring together the province's key family planning knowledge users, experienced senior health services administrators and patient representatives further cementing the working health systems research collaborations with our BC Contraception & Abortion Research Team. Specifically addressing a lack of current rural family planning professionals, our partner the Rural Coordination Center will provide salary stipends and travel funding to encourage rural physician participation.   WHAT: A one-day meeting The open morning session will invite a broad range of BC sexual and reproductive health professionals to hear top speakers convey the latest evidence on family planning, from an international and national perspective, and a presentation of the findings of the BCAPS project. This will be followed by an interactive audience-panel discussion. The invited afternoon session will engage interdisciplinary working groups consisting of key knowledge users, patient groups and health system leaders looking at specific issues and challenges identified by the research of our group, as well as highlighting models of excellence from some rural communities.  Facilitated groups will explore health system improvement options to ensure women of BC have equitable access to high quality family planning services. TitreApplicationTitle: Continuing Medical Education to Provide Health Care Professionals with Evidence-Based Tools to Treat Behavioral and Medical Pediatric Sleep Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: DISGNOSIS; EVIDENCE-BASED INTERVENTION; HEALTH CARE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; MENTAL HEALTH; RECOGNITION; SLEEP DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Clinical studies show that poor sleep is implicated in the development and persistence of prevalent childhood mental disorders including depression, anxiety, and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder. In the general population, pediatric sleep disorders affect 30% of otherwise healthy children. In this population, sleep disorders cause behavioral problems,inattention, poor academic performance, and emotional dysregulation. Hence, effective treatment of such disorders is critical if the mental well-being of youth is to be effectively improved. Although highly effective evidence-based behavioral interventions that significantly improve functioning and mental well-being in those with pediatric sleep disorders are available, most healthcare providers have not been trained in pediatric sleep medicine. As a result, such providers cannot adequately help children and adolescents with significant sleep disorders. It is therefore essential to close the current gap between known effective evidence-based interventional treatment of pediatric sleep disorders and existing practice within child healthcare settings. Thus, the objective of the proposed activity is to provide pediatric sleep education and training to healthcare professionals who treat children and youths, and to facilitate the integration of effective evidence-based interventions to treat pediatric sleep disorders into practice. To achieve this goal, we propose to conduct a practical training workshop, and post-workshop follow-up, with the aim of assisting participants to incorporate evidence-based strategies into their pediatric practice. We are particularly well-prepared to undertake the proposed work; the team has the depth and breadth of expertise and experience needed to achieve the desired goal. Our work will have an important positive impact because we expect to provide healthcare providers with non-pharmacological means allowing them to promote the mental health of Canadian youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing an Immigrant Health Atlas to Improve Primary Healthcare

Abstract-Résumé: Our research program proposes to enhance provincial health data analysis capacity and integrate Telehealth datasets, and in turn, enable researchers, programmers and policymakers to successfully measure and address barriers to primary healthcare faced by vulnerable immigrants. The Canadian Collaboration for Immigrant and Refugee Health (CCIRH) is a national collaboration of over 150 researchers, primary care practitioners, immigrant community champions, and program and policy planners dedicated to improving the health of immigrants and refugees.  We plan on building a unique dataset using existing resources and health records to create an "Atlas of Immigrant Health" that will link data from Ontario, British Columbia and Quebec and will help inform the next generation of technological interventions such as Telehealthcare.  This meeting proposes to bring together data analysts and provincial champions in the Telehealthcare industry to identify data capabilities and research priorities to improve the uptake and usefulness of their service by immigrant and refugee clients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Respiratory health care delivery improvement in airway diseases; asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and alpha1 antitrypsin deficiency.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHA1 ANTITRYPSIN DEFICIENCY; ASTHMA; CHRONIC BRONCHITIS; CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; EMPHYSEMA; PATIENT EDUCATION; QUALITY IMPROVEMENT; SELF-MANAGEMENT; SMOKING CESSATION; TOBACCO CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: The management of common respiratory diseases such as asthma and COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease including emphysema and chronic bronchitis) is often poor. Professor Chapman's research has shown that typical Canadian patients with asthma have poor control of their disease and suffer from preventable disability. Similarly, COPD is often undiagnosed or is diagnosed late in its clinical course. COPD is expected to be the third most common cause of death in Canada and around the world in the very near future. Not only is the personal toll of these diseases severe but their cost to the health care system is substantial. Our failure to manage these diseases better is not for lack of medical and scientific knowledge; research has identified many diagnostic and treatment strategies of value. Unfortunately, such strategies are often neglected in day-to-day clinical practice. Professor Chapman's GSK-CIHR Research Chair in Respiratory Healthcare Delivery will support a program of research to improve the care of these common diseases. A broad program of initiatives will be undertaken over the next five years to improve physician decision-making, particularly with respect to asthma diagnosis and monitoring. As well, the support services of non-physician health care providers will be improved by the wide dissemination of certification programs in asthma education, COPD education and smoking cessation education.  Professor Chapman will pilot several initiatives aimed at improving the self-management of patients with COPD so as to reduce their reliance upon walk-in clinics, emergency departments and hospitals. Finally, following work that establishes the value of specific treatment for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (a genetic form of emphysema), Professor Chapman will work with international colleagues to improve the delivery of this valuable augmentation therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sex Workers and the Impacts of Criminalizing HIV-Nondisclosure before Sex: A Qualitative Study
Keywords-MotsClés: CRIMINALIZATION OF HIV; GROUNDED THEORY; HEALTH SEEKING BEHAVIOUR; HIV/AIDS; HIV/STI RESOURCES; HIV/STI TESTING; HIV/STI TESTING/COUNSELLING; SEX WORK; VULNERABLE/AT-RISK POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, failure to disclose one's positive HIV-status before sexual activity constitutes a crime under certain circumstances. While the Canadian Supreme Court's decisions in October, 2012, offer some clarity on the conditions/practices that might prevent persons living with HIV from criminal prosecution (i.e., low viral load an use of condom), there remains no failsafe way to prove these criteria were met. Research is urgently needed on the extent to which current HIV-disclosure legislation may be undermining the protective health and health-seeking behaviours (e.g., HIV/STI testing and treatment) of sex workers, an historically vulnerable population for HIV-infection. Therefore, the fundamental aim of this study is to understand how HIV-disclosure legislation is impacting the health of sex workers and use this information to respond to their needs through informed policy, education for sex worker' health service providers, and accessible health/legal risk information for sex workers. Specifically, this study aims to determine: (1) The extent to which the recent court rulings have shaped sex workers' willingness to seek HIV-testing; (2) The implications for relationships of trust between sex workers and their support/service providers when discussing potentially criminal sexual practices; (3) How sex workers characterize the potential risk factors and legal implications of an HIV+ status when using a condom and/or with viral load below detectable levels; and (4) The extent to which sex workers are concerned that knowing and/or disclosing their HIV-status may result in violence, stigma, and/or future criminal charges. The proposed study will use a theoretical sampling strategy to recruit HIV+/-, male/female sex workers (n=16) for semi-structured, in-depth interviews, with a focus on persons with additional vulnerabilities such as Aboriginals, gay/bisexual men, and those with substance dependencies.

TitreApplicationTitle: HIV Needs Assessment for African Caribbean and Black People residing in Middlesex-London, Ontario

Abstract-Résumé: African, Caribbean and Black people constitute a highly vulnerable population to HIV/AIDS in Canada. This study aims at informing practice with regards to the needs of this population. It will consist of a needs assessment for the services of Regional HIV/AIDS Connection (RHAC). The main aim of my research is to evaluate the diverse needs of these communities with regards to HIV/AIDS and the extent to which the services offered by the RHAC address them.  I intend to use data previously collected through a survey designed by the Black, African and Caribbean Canadian Health (BLACCH) Study, a mixed-methods community-based research project aiming at assessing the Social Determinants of Health and improving health care access among this population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring Experiences with HIV/AIDS, Addiction Services and Research among Urban Aboriginal People Who Use Drugs in British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; ADDICTION SERVICES; COMMUNITY-BASED; HEALTH; HIV PREVENTION AND TREATMENT; ILLICIT DRUG USE; QUALITATIVE; RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: The HIV/AIDS epidemic continues to be significantly impacted by illicit drug use. In Vancouver, recent studies have shown that Aboriginal people who use drugs (APWUD) experience higher rates of HIV infection and poorer HIV treatment outcomes. APWUD are less likely to access HIV-focused prevention and treatment programs and addiction treatment services. In comparison to other British Columbians living with HIV/AIDS, individuals of Aboriginal ancestry are also more likely to die of HIV-related causes without ever having received antiretroviral therapy. Although these gaps have been well documented, the individual successes, strengths and barriers, related to HIV and addiction service access among APWUD have not been thoroughly investigated. In addition, though APWUD experience elevated HIV infection rates, they report lower rates of HIV-related risk behaviours. It appears therefore, that current research methods are failing APWUD, and there is a need for new community-based research (CBR) approaches and action focused on HIV/AIDS and specific to APWUD.  The Western Aboriginal Harm Reduction Society (WAHRS), created in 2002, is a grassroots organization run by APWUD. WAHRS seeks to celebrate their inherent strengths as indigenous peoples, recover a holistic traditional philosophy, create sound communities, develop networks and coalitions, and improve the quality of life for people who are Aboriginal and use illicit drugs. WAHRS has a longstanding partnership with the British Columbia Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS (BC CfE). Together, through this proposal, we aim to explore the strengths and barriers to HIV and addictions services for APWUD and uncover means to develop culturally safe and relevant community-based responses to HIV and illicit drug use.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the Experiences of First Nations, Métis and Inuit Youth with HIV/AIDS Prevention Programs in Labrador.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL YOUTH; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; HIV/AIDS; LABRADOR; PRE- AND POST-QUESTIONNAIRE; PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: National HIV/AIDS data indicates that Aboriginal youth are largely over-represented, addressing a need for research that is accepted and effective for this unique population. Despite these alarming signs, there is a lack of policy, programs and research that provides information as to what strategies are relevant to the experience of young Aboriginal peoples. The legacy of colonialism, structural racism, profound marginalization and the multigenerational effects of residential schools that characterize the shared history of Aboriginal peoples explain increased HIV vulnerability, thus declaring an urgent need for youth attracting, culturally appropriate, and community specific strategies. Research must be understood in the context of risk environments where many Aboriginal youth experience poverty, low education levels, lack of employment opportunities, sexual and physical violence, and street involvement, leading to a reduced ability to protect themselves from HIV risks. Stemming from this evidence and a need indicated by a community organization, the Labrador Friendship Centre (LFC), a research team was created to understand the impact of HIV prevention programs on Aboriginal youth in Labrador. Proposed data collection strategies involve delivery of a pre and post questionnaire to high school students, following a dynamic sexual health presentation, in eight communities in central and southern Labrador. This research aims to provide recommendations on specific groups within the youth population that may be in need of further support and/or programming that meets their unique needs. The LFC and other collaborating communities will be able to use the project's evaluative findings to refine HIV/AIDS programming for youth in the years to come. The incorporation of arts-based and community-engaging activities may be effective in starting community dialogue, increasing knowledge on HIV/AIDS, and improving young peoples' confidence to practice safe sexual activity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Women, HIV and Aging: The intersecting marginalized social identities, access to services and their impact on the quality of life.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO SERVICES; HIV/AIDS; HOUSING; MARGINALIZED  SOCIAL IDENTITIES; QUALITY OF LIFE; WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: There is a growing number of women aging with HIV. In general, women in Canada experience more adverse social determinants of health than men. The adverse social affects are compounded by the HIV positive status and socially constructed gender role/expectations. In addition, lack of age appropriate services compounds the negative impact on their health.   As the number of women with HIV/AIDS increases, under-representation of their experiences and dearth of literature on their marginalized social identities limit their access to services and make them more vulnerable to adverse social effects, poor health outcomes, and quality of life. It is imperative to take a proactive approach and explore the experiences and intersections of issues that this growing population experiences. The proposed study will generate knowledge to bridge the gap in information and create strategies to address the barriers to health care and support services.   This community-based research study is grounded in GIPA/MIPA principles. Peer Research Assistants will conduct in-depth interviews to explore experiences of 50+ women living with HIV. The findings of this pilot study will be used to develop a more comprehensive Ontario based research study. Collaborations developed through this study will strengthen partnership to develop more comprehensive action plan and strategies to address the barriers identified.

TitreApplicationTitle: Community-Based Affirmative Coping Skills Training to Reduce HIV/AIDS Risk for Sexual Minority Youth: An Open Pilot Feasibility Study
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; COPING; GROUP INTERVENTIONS; INTERVENTION RESEARCH; SEXUAL MINORITY YOUTH; SEXUAL RISK BEHAVIORS
Abstract-Résumé: Sexual minority youth (SMY), young people who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, or queer and other non-majority identities are vulnerable to HIV infection because of factors such as risky sexual behaviors and depression. The proposed study will test a group intervention, affirmative coping skills training (AFFIRM), that has been developed through community partnerships. Specifically this project will develop a community led advisory team of youth, agency staff and researchers to examine the preliminary effectiveness of AFFIRM to reduce risk behaviors and depression while increasing coping and better health of SMY. This project will also engage youth and community members in planning and developing solutions to support youth health together in a strengths-based model that could be expanded on a national level.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards a community-based research agenda on the experiences and HIV risk environment of men in the sex industry: The CHAPS Project
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; MEN; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; MEN'S HEALTH; SERIAL CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDIES; SEX BUYERS; SEX WORK; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: HIV incidence and prevalence in Canada continues to rise, with nearly half of existing and new infections occurring among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM).  Commercial sex sexual networks can play a key role in the risk for HIV and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), due to heightened exposure and high-risk sexual activities within networks, and social and structural vulnerabilities of individuals involved in sex work. There is little known in the Canadian context about how gender and sexual orientation can influence HIV risk to male sex workers (MSWs) and sex buyers. Male sex workers who have sex with men may experience additional and unique forms of stigma and marginalization, including homophobia and transphobia. To date, research on sex work in Canada and globally has focused on female sex workers. This critical gap in existing knowledge MSWs (transgender inclusive) and sex buyers, has resulted in only a partial understanding of the lives and realities of men involved in the sex industry. We therefore propose to initiate the Community Health Assessment of Men Purchase and Sell Sex (CHAPS) Project, a community-based partnership between the Gender and Sexual Health Initiative (GSHI) and the HUSTLE Program of the Health Initiative for Men (HIM). The purpose of this catalyst grant is to develop the GSHI-HIM CBR partnership, conduct exploratory ethnographic mapping and pilot qualitative interviews to examine themes such as initiation into sex work/buying, sexual services provided/purchased, negotiation of condom use, gender and sexuality, and drug/alcohol use or abuse. In addition, community consultations as well as participatory analysis and knowledge translation activities will ensure that the voices of the men themselves are integrated into this qualitative work as well as the future research agenda. This research will be guided by the expertise and experience of HIM's peer-driven HUSTLE outreach program for male and trans sex workers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of genetic polymorphisms in drug metabolizing cytochrome P450 enzymes expressed in the brain for affective disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: NEUROTRANSMITTERS; PSYCHIATRY
Abstract-Résumé: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes are an important class of drug metabolising enzymes, proteins that help eliminating external substances such as drugs or toxins that have been ingested or absorbed by the organism as well substances that are produced by the organism itself (endo¬genous substrates). Several findings suggest that two CYP enzymes, CYP2C19 and CYP2D6 have endogenous substrates, are in the brain, and may play directly a role in the genesis and course of affective illness, but as yet we do not know precisely what the substrates are; they may also alter the metabolism of drugs used in psychiatry. The genes coding these two CYP enzymes occur in the population with variants that show extreme effects on their activity. For example, as a result of their genetic makeup, some individuals have no functioning CYP2D6 protein in their organism, while others have so much CYP2D6 that its function is enhanced 10-15 times. Studies in man show differences in the vulnerability for affective disorders among carriers of these CYP variants, and in brain activity obtained with modern neuroimaging methods. Furthermore, these CYPs are capable to metabolise drugs directly in the brain, thus changing the way in which they act in individual carriers of genetic variants. Hence, this genetic variation is not only a clue to the role of these CYPs in the brain, but may also have practical consequences for the treatment of mental disorders. This project brings together groups that work with laboratory animals that carry genetic variants of these two CYPs and groups that use neuroimaging methods to assay the effect of genetic variants naturally occurring in the population on brain function. These groups will work together to see if changes in the animals are also visible in neuroimaging data collected in the population. Using these different approaches together will help answering the question of the role of these CYPs in normal brain function and in affective disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: VGLUT3 and vulnerability to addiction
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE; BEHAVIOR; BIOCHEMISTRY; BRAIN; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GLUTAMATE; NEUROTRANSMISSION; REWARD AND ADDICTION; VGLUT3
Abstract-Résumé: Addiction leads to substantial human suffering as well as to tremendous economical costs for our society. A secret to the understanding of this pathology lies in unraveling the function of a specific brain region named nucleus accumbens (NAc). The NAc regulates several behavioral outputs that are affected in addiction: motor control, learning of habits, reward-related learning. To communicate with each other, brain cells, neurons, use a combination of electrical and secreted chemical signals, called neurotransmitters. Amongst these brain neurotransmitters, dopamine, acetylcholine, GABA and glutamate are key players in the NAc. Dysfunction of communication in the NAc underlies the development of drug dependence. For instance, dopamine transmission in the NAc is critical for reward prediction as well as addiction to drugs such as cocaine, morphine, nicotine amphetamine and alcohol. Acetylcholine-secreting neurons (known as TANs) also regulate many of the pathological alterations in addiction. We have recently made the astonishing discovery that acetylcholine-secreting neurons can release the neurotransmitter glutamate in addition to acetylcholine. This finding suggests that these neurons can communicate with other cells in the NAc using two different chemical codes. Hence, by using these two separate "languages" TANs can provide distinct forms of information to other neurons in the NAc. We have recently uncovered evidence that it is glutamate release, and not acetylcholine release, by these "bilingual" neurons that is critical in mediating drug-induced effect. Furthermore, we have identified individuals suffering from severe addictions, who carry mutations in the machinery allowing glutamate release from TANs. The ultimate goal of our current proposal is to decipher how TANs, by sending two chemical codes, regulate the NAc diseased states. Understanding this "neuronal bilingualism" will lead to the refinement of medications for the treatment of NAc-related diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of TAO2 in brain connectivity and Autism Spectrum Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDERS; BEHAVIOR; BRAIN DEVELOPMENT; DENDRITIC SPINES; GENETICS; NEURAL CONNECTIVITY; SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) are neurodevelopmental disorders in which individuals have disrupted social communication and repetitive stereotyped behaviors, which lead to life-long difficulties. Approximately 1 percent of individuals in Asia, North America and in Europe have an ASD, which demonstrates the need to better understand these disorders, and find effective treatments to improve quality of life. In this regard, one of the key discoveries in recent years is that a person's genetic blueprint plays a very important role in risk for ASDs. This means there are genetic risk factors for ASD, and by understanding how these genes cause abnormal brain development, we will better understand the origins of ASDs to develop better treatments. In the current grant, using an integrated approach, we propose to study the TAO2 gene, which is either missing or duplicated in individuals with ASD. Our group is already collaborating with the Autism Sequencing Consortium to discover new mutations in TAO2 that may cause ASD, which will help in the future development of more accurate genetic diagnoses of ASDs. We will complement this genetic approach with cellular and molecular studies to better understand the normal function of TAO2 in the development of brain connections and autism-related behaviors in mouse models. Additionally, we will determine how mutations in TAO2, found in ASD individuals, may contribute to abnormal brain connectivity. We aim at studying the exciting possibility that another ASD-linked gene named FMR1 may control the function of TAO2. We believe this will lead to the identification of a new autism genetic pathway that ultimately would allow discovering drugs that through TAO2 modulation would ameliorate deficits observed in patients with ASD. Ultimately, we believe our studies will be very important not only to understand how TAO2 regulates brain function but also how it may be causative of ASDs via the novel FMRP-TAO2 genetic path.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: GÉNOMIQUE, PROTÉOMIQUE ET BIOINFORMATIQUE; SANTÉ MENTALE
TitreApplicationTitle: Discovering genetic risk variants for neuropsychiatric disorders and their consequences using dogs, humans and mice
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ATTENTION DEFICIT AND HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER; CHILD NEUROPSYCHIATRIC DISORDER; GENETICS; OBSESSIVE COMPULSIVE DISORDER
Abstract-Résumé: Children with psychiatric disorders such as obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) suffer from highy disabling symptoms that interfere with their ability to function in day-to-day life. We know that not only can these disorders persist into adulthood but they can also put the child at risk for later development of other problems including depression and substance use disorders. OCD and ADHD run in families, strongly suggesting that genes are involved in the development of these conditions. We also know that these disorders affect specific brain circuits. Despite our progress in learning about these conditions, we still do not really understand what genes are involved in ADHD and OCD and how variation in these genes can lead to dysfunction in brain circuits. One exciting but as yet under-explored avenue of research in these disorders is based on the study of animals that exihibit compulsive, impulsive or hyperactive traits similar to what is seen in OCD and ADHD. Both dogs and mice exhibit these traits and can provide different kinds of clues. Dogs, particularly purebred dogs are particularly helpful because their genomes tend to be more similar (each breed is effectively like a large family) which makes mapping of genes easier than in humans who are genetically more different from one another. Mice, on the other hand are particularly useful because it is possible to test the influence of genetic variants on their brains in a very precise manner in a laboratory setting. Our group, the Comparative Behavioural Genomics Consortium (CBGC) will take the highly innovative approach of studying OCD- and ADHD-related traits across humans, dogs and mice. By doing so, we hope to gain novel insights about how genetic variants lead to childhood psychiatric disorders and ultimately to identify new avenues for early identification and treatment of these devastating conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: The International Orthopaedic Multicenter Study in Fracture Care (INORMUS)
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATION; GLOBAL BURDEN; LOW AND MIDDLE INCOME COUNTRIES; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: Injury is a serious cause of mortality and morbidity.  Through a combination of injury prevention and development of trauma care systems, rates of traumatic injury are declining in the Western world.  In contrast, the rates of traumatic injury are increasing in industrializing nations.  The World Health Organization estimates that trauma will be the third largest killer in the developing world by 2030.  For every death, several thousand people experience temporary or permanent disability as a result of trauma.  Many of these debilitating injuries are orthopaedic fractures.  In order to begin to address global disparities associated with traumatic injury and to improve the health care of fracture patients worldwide, international collaborations are needed to understand the incidence, injury patterns, and outcomes associated with orthopaedic fractures. The International Orthopaedic Multicenter Study in Fracture Care (INORMUS) will be a landmark observational cohort study of 50,000 patients sustaining fractures and presenting to orthopaedic fracture units across hospitals in Asia, South America and Africa. This study aims to quantify the outcomes of fracture care in industrializing countries, identify potentially modifiable patient and treatment factors associated with mortality, and contribute to the multinational effort to understand the global impact of orthopaedic trauma. We recently completed a pilot evaluation of over 5,000 acute fracture patients treated in India.  Our pilot study's success was largely due to the regular communication and meetings between investigators in India and the Canadian Methods Centre. As we plan for the global INORMUS study, a critical first step will include a face-to-face meeting of our international research team to consolidate our global relationships, prioritize research activities, develop strategies for further funding opportunities, and reinforce the group's vision-to reduce the burden of injury in industrializing nations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Containing Suicide Contagion Among Inuit Youth Aged 12-19 in Nunavut
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTION PLANS; DEFINE MEASURABLE OUTCOMES; GENDER AND CULTURE; INUIT IN NUNAVUT; JOINT RESEARCH ISSUES AND INTERVENTIONS; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; NETWORKING; SUICIDE CONTAGION; WRITTEN REPORT FOR DISSEMINATION; YOUTH AGED 12-19
Abstract-Résumé: Suicide is a major health issue in Nunavut.  Suicide deaths (1961-2009) have increased, and the suicide rate (1981-2007) for both genders is much higher than the Canadian average, particularly for males age 15-24 (Suicide Prevention Strategy Working Group, 2010).  Thus, the chances of exposure to others' suicide and suicide contagion are significant.  Suicide contagion is seen in a clustering of suicide deaths following direct or indirect exposure to a suicide death (Gould, 2001).  Research indicates that adolescents are particularly susceptible to it (Colucci & Martin, 2007), particularly when the suicide decedent is of the same ethnicity (Stack, 2000).  Recent findings show that exposure to a schoolmate's suicide predicted suicide ideation and suicide attempts in young people aged 12-17, and that the effects lingered 2 years after for those aged 12-15 (Swanson & Colman, 2013).  Given the Nunavut suicide statistics, the importance of containing suicide contagion among Inuit youth, cannot be under-estimated.  Suicide prevention efforts in Nunavut are undertaken by communities, organizations, and the government. The present project involves a gathering of knowledge users, community partners, and health researchers from Nunavut and Ontario to network, exchange knowledge, and consolidate a partnership for the purpose of identifying gaps in the area of suicide contagion among school-aged Nunavut youth aged 12-19, and developing research priorities and prevention strategies to contain suicide contagion.   The three primary outcomes from this meeting are (i) identification and prioritization of joint research interests and prevention strategies with outcome measures, (ii) action plans to develop further the research interests and prevention strategies and identify potential funding sources where necessary, and (iii) a written report in English and Inuktitut versions for dissemination.

TitreApplicationTitle: Moving Health Research Forward with a Coordinated International Bioinformatics Training Effort
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVANCING HEALTH RESEARCH; HEALTH INFORMATICS; INTERNATIONAL COORDINATION; SKILL DEVELOPMENT; SUSTAINABLE TRAINING PROGRAMS; TRAINING AND EDUCATION; TRANSLATION OF BIOINFORMATICS SKILLS
Abstract-Résumé: The genomic era has brought exciting advances and opportunities to the health and life sciences research fields. Many new tantalizing discoveries in fields like cancer, HIV, diabetes, IBD and autism wait buried in the -omic data for skilled researchers to decipher their meaning. Bioinformatics has thus become a necessary skill for all health and life science researchers. Faced with the challenges imposed by this steady introduction of new high-throughput technologies, increasingly larger and more complex data sets, and an explosion of new informatic tools and databases, researchers worldwide are seeking bioinformatics training and knowledge translation opportunities to advance their health research activities. Without these skills, research progress is haltingly slow because of a lack of trained professionals capable of working with -omic era data. In an effort "to share not duplicate effort, to share not duplicate cost, and to work together in a mutually respectful way towards common training solutions and a sustainable future", international bioinformatics training organizations have come together to form the Global Organization for Bioinformatics Learning, Education and Training (GOBLET). With a common training goal in mind, bioinformatic leaders from these various international societies, networks and organizations have joined together under GOBLET to coordinate worldwide bioinformatics training activities. The critical next step for GOBLET to achieve a coordinated international effort in bioinformatics training activities that will advance health and life science research is to establish priorities and an action plan for GOBLET. This CIHR proposal brings together leaders from 21 bioinformatics organizations, under Canada's lead, for a 2.5-day face-to-face action planning meeting to develop a set of action items, a draft internationally coordinated funding application and a publication that will advance health research on the international stage.

Abstract-Résumé: This request is for funding to bring together and build a new international team with an interest in patient education and the dissemination of arthritis best practices in primary care. This purpose of this project is to produce a summary of CPGs on RA, revised tools based on evidence in the literature, and input from the team including our user groups at the organization level (The Arthritis Society, Arthritis and Osteoporosis Victoria, and the patient level (Patient Partners in Arthritis & Canadian Arthritis Patient Alliance) The team will also develop an outline of the key content areas needed for the various methods of delivery for the PGrip program, including key messages, revised existing PGrip tools, and new tools needed for faculty, providers, and patients which are appropriate for an online learning environment. This will help to ensure the relevance and acceptability of the PGrip program to these user groups. Furthermore, another objective of this project will be to produce a research proposal for a RCT for submission for funding to the Operating Grant competition in the winter 2014. The team will help develop the protocol for this project including the research questions, objectives, methodology, evaluation, and dissemination strategies. This will ensure that the methods of delivery for the PGrip program are developed in a way that is acceptable to the user groups, that recruitment strategy will work, and that the program is feasible and sustainable. An international collaboration will aid in the implementation of the RCT, generalization of results, and in the recruitment of a potential larger sample size in order to reach the ideal statistical power.

Abstract-Résumé: The aim of the planning  grant, 'Shifting sands and rising tides: toward an understanding of the sexual health and related health care risks and needs of migratory workers,' is to build a research action plan that will address the health risks that migratory workers may face. By reviewing published an unpublished literature, holding regular telephone calls, hosting conversation cafes, and holding a two-day planning meeting, and a results sharing webinar, we plan to involve research team members, interested community members and government officials in every aspect of this work. At the end of our planning, we will have developed a list of priority projects which will include policy suggestions and at least one application for funding to a larger CIHR competition (Partnerships for Health System Improvement, Operating Grant). We expect to develop a plan to address identified gaps in knowledge, barriers to accessing health care services (e.g., testing, treatment), and risk taking behaviours that put migratory workers more at risk for getting HIV/AIDS and other sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections (STBBIs). We will share this information widely through our local, regional, and national partners.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vascular Network
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CARDIOVASCULAR; CLINICAL INTERVENTIONS; COHORTS; HEALTH SYSTEMS; HYPERTENSION; POLICY CHANGE; PREVENTION; RISK FACTORS; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Many of the most devastating diseases can be directly linked to a common cause: damage to the vascular system often caused by common risk factors. The vascular system includes not only the main arteries feeding the heart and brain, eyes, kidneys and all other organs of the body, but also the small vessels, which regulate vascular resistance and the distribution of blood flow to the tissues and the life-sustaining exchange of nutrients and gases throughout the body.   The Vascular Network will leverage its broad base of participants, partners and end-users to catalyze an integrated, multi-disciplinary approach to vascular conditions. The Network will focus on three priority areas in order to achieve its vision: integrated research; capacity generation; and knowledge translation.  Network research will focus on 2 themes. The goal of Theme 1 is to bridge the gap between the research evidence and clinical practice as it relates to the prevention and detection of vascular conditions and to ensure individuals receive the best possible patient-oriented care.The goal of Theme 2 is to bring about, within the next decade, simple diagnostic tools that would indicate an accelerated risk or an early warning for small vessel disease, eventually leading to chronic impairment in function of a major end-organ such as the brain, heart, lung or kidney. To foster the career development of trainees, the Network and its contributing partners will make a significant investment in Network scholars, graduate students, trainees and young investigators. The knowledge translation efforts of the Network will focus on three key activities: knowledge translation of Network research; knowledge translation impacting health policies; and developing platforms to enable knowledge translation and exchange within the vascular community.

TitreApplicationTitle: A community consultation with Aboriginal peoples in Alberta to develop culturally appropriate access indicators in urgent care
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES; ACCESS INDICATORS; ACCESS TO HEALTH CARE SERVICES; COLLABORATIVE PARTNERSHIP; CULTURALLY APPROPRIATE CARE; URGENT CARE
Abstract-Résumé: This proposed planning grant will plan the last stages of the Access Research Initiative to delineate culturally sensitive access indicators. Our research to date includes two data sets from an Aboriginal health intervention, three exploratory projects that investigated Aboriginal peoples' experiences of access to health care services in urban and inner city settings, and two dissemination projects implementing a participatory process with the community validating the access findings. Following an Aboriginal Knowledge Circle consensus method and community-based participatory research we will engage community members and knowledge users in the formulation of the process to be used to develop access indicators. The program methods are innovative to generate knowledge relevant to Aboriginal people. The development of access indicators are a required step to informing appropriate policy for Aboriginal peoples for best practices in urgent care. The research objectives of this planning grant are: 1. To engage Aboriginal people, knowledge users and researchers as a steering committee in the process to plan a community consultation; 2. To hold one and a half day community consultation to formulate the research process for the development, refinement and validation of access indicators; 3. To develop a research proposal for the CIHR Knowledge to Action call based on the findings from the Community Consultation; and 4. To publish one community report and one academic paper outlining the outcomes of this planning grant in an open access peer-reviewed journal. The anticipated outcomes include strengthening and broadening collaborative partnerships with key knowledge users and Aboriginal communities in Alberta, the establishment of the Aboriginal Knowledge Circle, and the submission of the Knowledge to Action grant. This proposed planning grant addresses a priority need to accelerate the resolution of a critical problem for Aboriginal peoples' access to urgent care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ethical problems in pediatric medicine: Developing interdisciplinary knowledge and action
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD HEALTH; ETHICS; INTERDISCIPLINARY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PEDIATRIC SERVICES; PEDIATRICS; PRIORITY-SETTING
Abstract-Résumé: Children are recognized as a vulnerable population, given their limited capacities to assert their own interests. This vulnerability is borne out in clinical practice and research. Children are commonly "innovation orphans" (adapted from the term "research orphans"), as research and practice developments are predominantly centered on adult interests, which are then adapted to children without adequate research grounding. One area where this is especially problematic is pediatric ethics. Inadequate attention has been devoted to major ethical problems that arise from advances in pediatric medicine and how practices should be adapted to address these problems. This project engages urgently-needed dialogues between researchers and stakeholders to identify knowledge and action development priorities and plan strategies to address ethical problems in pediatric health services. This project is especially innovative because it will enable the building of a rich team of interdisciplinary researchers and "inter-perspective" stakeholders to develop an integrated plan for future research and practice development, through participatory priority-setting and planning meetings. Expected outcomes include: (1) building a team of expert interdisciplinary researchers and inter-perspective stakeholders; (2) identifying priorities for the development of pediatric ethics knowledge and action; and (3) developing plans to address these priorities, including the preparation of an operating grant proposal. This project will immediately advance our understanding of ethical problems in pediatric medicine and result in a prompt translation of project outcomes, launch empirical research and needed development of practice standards for children in Canada and internationally. We will develop a robust new field of interdisciplinary inquiry: Interdisciplinary Studies of Pediatric Ethics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Psoriatic arthritis BioDAM Planning Meeting
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; BIOMARKERS; PROGNOSIS; PSORIASIS
Abstract-Résumé: Psoriasis is a common skin disease affecting 3% of our population. Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) is a specific arthritis that affects 30% of patients with psoriasis that often leads to progressive joint damage, disability and poor quality of life. Early aggressive treatment can limit joint damage, disability and improve quality of life. However, identifying patients with PsA who are at high risk for severe joint damage is difficult. Identifying markers in the blood that predict joint damage will help in targeting aggressive treatment to those deemed to be at high risk of joint damage, while limiting exposure to expensive and potentially toxic therapy to those at low risk. We therefore plan to conduct a large international multicentre study led by Canadian researchers to identify markers for joint damage in patients with early PsA. Researchers with expertise in all aspects of the study have been identified and have expressed interest in participating in this proposed study. The purpose of this planning meeting is to further develop the scientific concepts behind the proposal, discuss overall study design as well as study specifics including methods of data collection and analysis, intellectual property, commercialization, ethical and legal issues as well as plans for knowledge transfer to the scientific and lay community. Results of the proposed study will help us develop blood tests that may identify patients with early psoriatic arthritis at high risk of severe joint damage. Simple blood tests developed through this program may help in appropriate management of patients with psoriatic arthritis, and thus ultimately prevent disability and improve quality of life in thousands of Canadians suffering from psoriasis and PsA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mental Health and Criminal Justice: Advancing a National Research Agenda
Keywords-MotsClés: CRIMINAL JUSTICE; CRIMINALITY; FORENSIC MENTAL HEALTH; LEGISLATION; MENTAL HEALTH; POLICIES; SERVICES; VIOLENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Recent high-profile cases have amplified debate and controversy about the Canadian criminal law regarding persons who commit crime but who are not held responsible because of their mental disorder. In response, the Canadian government has proposed amendments to the law regarding victims' rights and the treatment of persons who are considered to be high risk. Critics have lamented the absence of research evidence to support the Bill. The exact same situation arose last year with another Bill pertaining to Criminal Justice issues. These current examples point to the need to develop a stakeholder infrastructure and research agenda that can be sustained over time as changes in legislation and health services are implemented. This all the more timely as the Senate tabled an Act to establish the Canadian Commission on Mental Health and Justice explicitly stating the need to promote evidence informed policy making. The proposed planning activities will bring together important legal, forensic mental health, general mental health to identify critical questions, research priorities, and an agenda for multi-systemic research agenda in mental health and criminal justice, identify potential sources of datasets, resources, and build a national working alliance to develop new team and research proposals. The resulting framework will also enable future research examining the impact of new laws and policies on the handling of mentally disordered accused.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards Improving Treatment Adherence and Outcomes of Patients with Gout
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; GOUT; MEDICATION ADHERENCE; PATIENT OUTCOMES
Abstract-Résumé: Gout is a very painful type of arthritis that occurs when too much uric acid builds up in the body leading to hard, crystal-like deposits in the joints. It affects over 1 million Canadians and this burden is expected to increase with the aging of the population. Unlike other forms of arthritis, gout is a "curable' disease and effective medications that lower uric acid levels are available. However, because patients do not adhere to their treatment, they continue to do poorly, suffering from repeat gout attacks and disability. While much is known about the widespread problem of poor medication adherence in gout, there is very limited research on interventions to address this problem. Because of the complexity and extent of the problem, research requires innovative models of care to deliver the intervention, collaborative teams involving members across different health care disciplines, such as rheumatology, primary care, and pharmacy, and engagement with patients, clinicians, and decision makers. The objective of this planning grant is to build team and research capacity as well as a methodological framework to guide future research that aims to improve treatment adherence, and ultimately patient outcomes in gout.

TitreApplicationTitle: Seniors, risk and successful aging: Towards a broader understanding for rehabilitation
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTONOMY; CRITICAL INTERPRETIVE SYNTHESIS; INTERDISCIPLINARY RESEARCH; REHABILITATION; RISK; SENIORS; SUCCESSFUL AGING
Abstract-Résumé: Rehabilitation specialists work with seniors to restore, maintain or enhance function. The goal is to ensure that the growing population of Canadian seniors continue to live enjoyable, healthy and active lives. The prevention and management of physical risk has become a key focus of this work. While this is important, when potential physical risks are over-emphasized, seniors may become fearful, isolated, inactive and depressed. Health providers may not see their senior patients as people who have successfully dealt with difficult and risky situations in the past, and have knowledge and skills important to dealing with current problems. As well, a focus on seniors' health issues as the cause of risk limits identification of environmental and social interventions that might help reduce risk for large numbers of people. There are two main objectives to our work. The first is to examine how risk is currently considered in rehabilitation with seniors through a close examination of the literature in this area, with specific attention paid to rehabilitation for stroke and low vision. The second is to consider how a broader understanding of risk can be used to optimize rehabilitation with seniors through learning from seniors themselves and researchers in gerontology, psychology, public health, sociology, women's health, critical disability theory, ethics and law. To do this, we are holding a two-day meeting between seniors, clinicians, researchers, administrators and policy makers to reflect on current understandings of risk and rehabilitation with seniors, and generate new ways of understanding and addressing risk. Together we will help us develop alternate ways of looking at risk in later life, and for addressing risk within rehabilitation assessment and interventions.  In the last part of our meeting, we will develop research plans to get these new ideas into seniors' care and to evaluate how these enhanced understandings of risk can improve care for Canadian seniors.
