TitreApplicationTitle: The road ahead for older Canadians: Utilizing the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging to create a research network and agenda on environment and healthy aging
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADIAN LONGITUDINAL STUDY ON AGING; ENVIRONMENT; GERONTOLOGY; MOBILITY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; TRANSPORTATION
Abstract-Résumé: The neighbourhood and community environments in which people live, work and play can contribute to aging in both positive and negative ways. However we have insufficient knowledge about which environmental characteristics are important to health and well-being. Longitudinal studies, those in which the same group of study subjects are observed multiple times over the study's duration, can improve our understanding of these relationships. The extensive, individual-level data from 50,000 people that will be collected in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) provides an ideal platform for studies of the impact of the neighbourhood environment on health. Furthermore, there are other detailed Canadian data-sets on the neighbourhood environment which can be combined with the CLSA data for new research. It is timely to build a new research network to carry out a research agenda on aging and the environment. Our Workshop will bring together International experts in the built and social environments with experts in aging research, policy and services, and will serve as a springboard for building this network and research agenda, and for developing research grants for several Canadian cities. The Workshop will yield new partnerships and concrete plans for new research and learning that can ultimately re-shape policy, practice and community design to encourage and support healthy aging, including active participation of older adults in all aspects of community life. The Workshop will be integrated with a CLSA Public Forum on healthy aging and the environment. The integration of these events conforms to CIHR's Citizen Engagement Framework, creating an opportunity for Workshop organizers and participants to have a conversation with the public and other stakeholders about their perceptions of neighbourhood impacts on health and aging. Information thus gathered will be useful for framing subsequent Workshop discussions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Re-thinking ASOs? Responding to the End of AIDS Exceptionalism through East-West Collaboration
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS EXCEPTIONALISM; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; HIV/AIDS POLICY; HIV/AIDS SERVICE ORGANIZATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Recent and planned shifts in HIV/AIDS policies and funding programs collectively signal the end of "AIDS exceptionalism." In the past, federal HIV/AIDS-targeted funding was "protected"; however, today, shifts away from this are prompting a national rethinking of the role of community-based AIDS service organizations(ASOs), including their scope, mandate, and founding values. As a result, ASOs from coast to coast are under pressure to develop integrated models of service delivery, which may include - in addition to HIV - hepatitis B & C, other sexually transmitted and blood borne infections (STBBIs), mental health and tuberculosis. How will this change affect the next generation of HIV/AIDS-related interventions, services, and programs? How can we ensure that ASOs will continue to meet client's complex needs? This project will harness the momentum of processes underway in both the Atlantic Region and in British Columbia to collectively identify a research agenda that will identify the most effective ways to deliver community-based programs in the post-AIDS exceptionalism era. We will host two simultaneous one-day planning meetings - one in the Atlantic region (covering Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador) and one in BC - where participants will develop community-based research directions that will help ASOs determine whether integrated models for delivering HIV/AIDS services will continue to meet the complex and exceptional needs of people with HIV, and if so, how these services might be best designed. This project will strengthen the response to HIV/AIDS in Canada  by building inter-provincial and national research partnerships and collaborations, promoting evidence-based programming, and informing policy directions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Partnering to promote health care equity for ethnic minority older adults
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO HEALTH AND SOCIAL SERVICES; ETHNIC MINORITY OLDER ADULTS; HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SERVICES DELIVERY; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE
Abstract-Résumé: Recent immigrant older adults and some visible minorities who have aged here-together known as ethnic minority older adults (EMOA)-both experience health inequities in Canada. These are primarily related to difficulties with the complex process of accessing suitable care. However, Canadian research on the topic is extremely fragmented and hard to find, and knowledge users (KUs) who design policy and programs do not have the evidence they need to help them to address access barriers experienced by EMOA. Effort is needed to consolidate existing evidence and design research that fills knowledge gaps with respect to access so as to generate a decision-making tool that can guide KUs in their decisions across different health and social care contexts. Our team of 13 multidisciplinary academics and multisectoral KUs is uniquely positioned to meet this challenge.  First, however, it is essential that we convene to ensure that we share a common understanding of 'access' and the requirements of CIHR's 'Partnership for Health System Improvement' (CIHR) competition that we will target to complete this work. With the proposed planning grant, students hired by each pair of academics and knowledge users in six sites from British Columbia to Newfoundland will review the EMOA literature on topics of interest to the KU on their team. Each will produce topical reports identifying the different dimensions of access that are evident in those studies. These will inform a presentation that the KUs will make about their interests and understanding of access at a 1.5 day face-to-face meeting of team members in Vancouver in June 2014. They will also be consolidated into a single report that will form the basis of discussion at the Vancouver meeting and a peer-reviewed publication. The meeting will provide an opportunity to consolidate our understanding of access and its relationship to our KUs interests and to identify our strategy for applying for funding in Fall 2014.

Abstract-Résumé: Discussing medical mistakes with children and families is a hard task. Medical mistakes in children's hospitals is a common occurrence, and yet we know nothing about children's views on medical mistakes. This study hopes to look at current research and policies from across Canada to get a better understanding of what we know and what we still need to know. We will share this information with doctors, professionals working in patient safety, children and families and ask them for their thoughts. After we gather all this information, we will come up with a plan for future research in this important area of study.

TitreApplicationTitle: Développement d'une recherche participative basé sur la communauté sur le thème de la paternité en milieu autochtone.
Keywords-MotsClés: AUGMENTATION DU POUVOIR D'AGIR; AUTOCHTONE; PATERNITE; RECHERCHE PARTICIPATIVE BASE SUR LA COMMUNAUTE
Abstract-Résumé: Recemment, l'etat de sante des Autochtones a ete qualifie de 'crise de sante publique'. Parmi tous les groupes ethniques du Canada, les hommes autochtones accusent les taux les plus eleves de maladie mentale, de dependances et de suicide. Depossedes de leurs roles de pourvoyeurs, de protecteurs et de peres, les hommes autochtones sont a toute fin pratique oublies. Les enfants autochtones, quant a eux, sont surrepresentes a travers les services de protection du Canada. Malgre les risques accrus de mortalite, de morbidite et de problemes psychosociaux encourues par les enfants autochtones, l'information portant sur la paternite en milieu autochtone est presqu'inexistante. Les peres representent une ressource precieuse, mais non-exploitee pour soutenir la sante physique et mentale de leur progeniture. Devant les taux alarmants de morbidite et de placement sous la LPJ des enfants autochtones et le manque flagrant d'information sur la paternite en milieu autochtone, il est primordial d'augmenter les connaissances sur l'engagement paternel afin de soutenir les hommes et d'ameliorer les indicateurs de sante des enfants. Ainsi, ce projet de planification vise a developper une recherche participative base sur la communaute portant sur le theme de la paternite autochtone avec les partenaires du milieu. Les objectifs specifiques sont de 1-documenter les besoins en information exprimes par les intervenants, qui pourraient favoriser la mise en place d'actions efficaces de soutien a l'engagement paternel; 2-donner la parole a des peres autochtones de facon a documenter leurs besoins; 3-mettre en lien les intervenants du milieu autochtone avec ceux du Regroupement pour la Valorisation de la Paternite (RVP) afin que la thematique des peres autochtones y soit consideree et integree; et 4-synthetiser de facon preliminaire la litterature et recenser les programmes visant a soutenir l'engagement paternel en milieu autochtone.

Abstract-Résumé: Research evidence is an important input to support health system policymaking. However, health system policymakers and those who support them often do not have dedicated resources and capacity to find and use relevant research evidence in a timely manner. The purpose of this initiative is to convene a half-day meeting with provincial and territorial policymakers to foster partnerships between the project team and the meeting attendees, and to facilitate deliberations that will contribute to the development of a rapid response service based at the McMaster Health Forum that will provide timely access to research evidence for policymakers on health system issues. The meeting will be informed by a pre-circulated report describing existing rapid responses services around the world, describe the key features of a proposed model, and identify key implementation considerations. The event will take place before April 2014 at the McMaster Health Forum (Hamilton, Ontario).

Abstract-Résumé: Researchers from the University of Manitoba/UNBC have a long standing relationship with the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs (AMC), aiming to build health research and health service delivery capacity within the AMC and Manitoba First Nations communities. This proposal seeks funding for a delegation from the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs to participate in a series of meetings to be held in Wellington, New Zealand in December 2013. These meetings will lead to (1) an AMC EpiCentre-Whakaraue partnership; (2) an International Indigenous Health Services Research Alliance that will include university-based and Indigenous organizations-based researchers: this initiative is unprecedented world-wide; (3) discussions between AMC and Maori health researchers to develop an Indigenous understanding of primary healthcare centred on Indigenous epistemologies, healing and medicine: these discussion stand to set the foundation for an international program of research that will possibly lead to more effective and responsive primary healthcare services for Indigenous peoples.

TitreApplicationTitle: Counselling the Relational Unit in Addiction Treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION AND MENTAL HEALTH; CONCERNED SIGNIFICANT OTHERS; HEALTH SYSTEMS IMPROVEMENT; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; PARTNERSHIPS; PLANNING; RESEARCH COLLABORATION; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: In addiction services, treatment of problem gambling and substance disorder focuses predominantly on the addicted individual (AI). However, a growing body of evidence now demonstrates that relationship problems, between AIs and their concerned significant others (CSO), can exacerbate addictive behaviour and impede recovery. Therefore the resolution of relationship problems is critical. Despite this now recognized need, progress has been slow in developing treatment models and services that work with CSO and AI as an interactive unit.  One innovative model, Congruence Couple Therapy (CCT) offers a holistic approach to identify and alleviate relationship problems between problem gamblers and their CSO through conjoint counselling. In a recent pilot randomized controlled trial, the model has shown to significantly reduce problem gambling symptoms, mental health distress, and improve couple communication and relationship. However, translating research pertaining to new interventions in clinical practice and system change requires an intentional process. Therefore, we propose a 2-day workshop that will bring together Alberta health system knowledge users (decision-makers, counsellors and patients) and university researchers to  exchange knowledge relevant to the above described gap in service.  Our objectives are to:  1. Share research that supports the importance of couple and family counselling in addiction and mental health. 2. Define gaps, priorities and opportunities in services for couple and family counselling.  3. Share research demonstrating the effectiveness of CCT. 4. Consider the potential of CCT for enhancing services in addiction and mental health. 5. Form partnerships between researchers and stakeholders to address the need for research and development pertaining to services and treatments that include CSOs. 6. Obtain commitments and define responsibilities in the development of a PHSI application and other projects.

TitreApplicationTitle: A global health research collaboration on engagement in HIV care: UBC, AMREF and AKU
Keywords-MotsClés: ENGAGEMENT IN CARE; GLOBAL HEALTH; HIV/AIDS; INTERNATIONAL COLLABORATION; RESEARCH PARTNERSHIPS; RETENTION IN CARE; SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA
Abstract-Résumé: HIV has transformed from an acute, fatal disease to a chronic disease requiring long-term medical management. To optimize patient health outcomes and the success of HIV care and treatment programs, it is critical that patients remain engaged in HIV care; however, in both North America and sub-Saharan Africa, a large proportion of patients are insufficiently engaged in care. This planning proposal brings together three organizations with HIV/AIDS research and care expertise, the University of British Columbia (UBC), the African Medical and Research Foundation (AMREF), and Aga Khan University, East Africa, to collaborate on global health research focussed on patient engagement in HIV care. The benefits of international collaboration are increasingly apparent and include enhancing the research process, boosting individual skills and abilities, and strengthening research institutions. Researchers from these organizations, together with citizen representatives, research trainees, and government stakeholders, will meet in Nairobi, Kenya for a two day forum in March 2014. The objectives of the forum are to: (1) identify HIV engagement in care research priorities that are common to AMREF, AKU, and UBC; (2) provide a forum to discuss relevant upcoming funding opportunities; (3) develop plans to move research ideas generated during the meeting into a research grant application. (4) promote the development of new international partnerships between investigators from UBC, AMREF and AKU; and (5) further solidify an existing collaboration between AMREF and UBC. Through carefully planned sessions and networking opportunities, the forum has been specifically designed to fulfil our aim of fostering new international partnerships to ultimately improve patient engagement in HIV care, both in Canada and abroad.

TitreApplicationTitle: Application of a Next-Generation Healthy Living Guide: Optimizing Successful Aging through Integrated Knowledge Translation
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY PATTERNS; COMMUNITY PARTICIPATION; HEALTH PROMOTION; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LIFE COURSE TRANSITIONS; SUCCESSFUL AGING
Abstract-Résumé: Current healthy living guides focus on exercise, nutrition and avoiding risky behaviours such as tobacco use. Occupational therapists have developed an evidence-based framework that considers activity patterns that contribute to health and wellness. This framework, entitled Do-Live-Well, represents the foundation for a next generation healthy living guide, offering ways to consider the range of activities and behaviours that contribute to health and well-being and can form the basis of a broad population health promotion strategy. This framework can be adopted by people to consider their behaviours in the context of everyday life, in particular during times of transition in work, health, and living situation. It is consistent with evidence on factors that contribute to successful aging, but application of the framework in the context of healthy aging needs further examination. This project will explore how the framework can be employed at times of life course transition, specifically, at times of retirement, onset of disability, and moving to long term care. This grant will bring together older adults, experts in aging, policy makers from public health and other relevant arenas, to initiate and further plan an integrated knowledge translation project that will focus on how best to apply the Do-Live-Well framework in the context of healthy and successful aging. The project will involve two stakeholder meetings. The first, by webinar, will entail review of the Do-Live-Well framework, and consideration of its application in the context of healthy and successful aging. The second meeting, in person, will focus on development of a research plan, using an Appreciative Inquiry approach. The project will result in a research proposal in which all stakeholders have collaborated on the development of the research question(s) and methodology, identification of appropriate outcome measures, and formulation of plans for analyses and end of grant knowledge translation.

TitreApplicationTitle: L'éducation et la santé : regard sur les parcours éducationnels des jeunes autochtones (18-24 ans) et les répercussions sur leur santé globale et celle de leur communauté.
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOCHTONES; DEVELOPPEMENT; SAINES HABITUDES DE VIE; SANTE GLOBALE; EDUCATION POSTSECONDAIRE
Abstract-Résumé: Cette subvention de planification vise le developpement d'un projet de recherche d'envergure qui permettra de mieux comprendre le lien qui existe entre l'education des Autochtones, leur developpement harmonieux et leur sante. En effet, grace a cette subvention nous voulons mettre sur pieds un partenariat ralliant le centre de formation de la main d'uvre Huron-Wendat (CDFM) et deux universites (UQTR et UQO) afin de developper un projet de recherche-action qui contribuera a mieux comprendre les liens qui existent entre l'education et la sante globale chez les Autochtones. Plus precisement, le projet de recherche qui resultera de cette planification repondra aux questions suivantes:  Quelles strategies sont employees pour soutenir la reussite des etudiants autochtones? Comment le cheminement scolaire et la reussite contribuent-ils a la sante et au bien-etre des jeunes autochtones? Quelles sont les enjeux associes a la reintegration de la communaute par les diplomes de ces centres? Comment, a long terme, ces diplomes influencent-ils leur communaute, agissent a titre de modeles et inspirent les plus jeunes en matiere d'education et de saines habitudes de vie? Ces questions sont extremement pertinentes pour le developpement des connaissances et sont precisement celles que l'on espere exploiter dans le projet de recherche d'envergure que nous voulons construire grace a la presente subvention.

Abstract-Résumé: Very little information exists describing the best methods to support obesity prevention strategies. Resilience is a psychological factor that helps explain why some youth thrive despite living in or surviving adverse experiences. We think that resilience play an important role in obesity prevention programs, especially within Aboriginal communities.  The proposed workshop will bring experts in the fields of resilience and obesity to develop a strategy to study the importance of resilience in the successful adoption of behaviours in obesity prevention programs tailored to Aboriginal youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Consolider le partenariat communauté-université pour offrir aux hommes ayant des relations sexuelles avec d'autres hommes du Burkina Faso un programme de prévention du VIH adapté culturellement.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTATION CULTURELLE; BURKINA FASO; HRSH VIVANT AVEC LE VIH; PARTENARIAT INTERNATIONAL; PROGRAMME; PREVENTION TRANSMISSION VIH/ITS; REDUCTION DES RISQUES SEXUELS; SANTE SEXUELLE HRSH; EROTISME
Abstract-Résumé: La presente demande a comme but de creer une alliance communaute-universite durable dans la lutte au VIH aupres des hommes ayant des relations sexuelles avec d'autres hommes (HRSH) au Burkina Faso. C'est par des rencontres de travail entourant la validation culturelle d'un programme de prevention du VIH developpe au Quebec (projet Phenix) qui sera adapte aux realites des HRSH de REV+ (association communautaire de Bobo Dioulasso, Burkina Faso), que les contours de ce partenariat se definiront. Les activites de planification visant l'adaptation culturelle repose sur un comite tripartite impliquant la Chaire de recherche du Canada en education a la sante (CReCES, Universite du Quebec a Montreal) et les organismes communautaires Maison Plein Cur (MPC) (Montreal) et REVS+ (Bobo Dioulasso). L'equipe burkinabee fera aussi appel a des HRSH qui frequentent son organisme pour participer a titre de collaborateurs a la validation du programme Phenix adaptee. Des partenariats existent deja entre REV+ et la MPC et entre la MPC et la CReCES. Par ce projet,  la CReCES, REV+ et MPC veulent concretiser leur partenariat. L'adaptation culturelle de Phenix sera faite selon les etapes proposees par Tortolero et al. (2005) ainsi qu'en fonction des strategies decrites par Kreuter et al. (2003) pour augmenter la pertinence culturelle d'une intervention de sante. Differentes phases d'echanges et discussions entre les partenaires par conference telephonique ou en presentielle sont prevues. A la fin de ce processus, REV+ aura un programme de prevention du VIH et des ITS adapte aux besoins des HRSH qu'il rejoint; une demande de fonds pour soutenir l'implantation et l'evaluation du programme sera prete a soumettre; le partenariat communaute-universite aura ete consolide; un renforcement des capacites aura ete experimente entre les partenaires en ce qui concerne l'adaptation culturelle d'une intervention et d'eventuels impacts sur la sante sexuelle des HRSH rejoints sont anticipes.

Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC WOUNDS; EXCESSIVE SCARRING; IMPAIRED WOUND HEALING; INFLAMMATORY SKIN DISEASES; PERIODONTAL DISEASE; PSORAISIS; SKIN; SKIN DISEASES; SKIN REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Normal skin function is essential to maintaining good health and quality of life. Approximately half of the population in Canada suffers from a skin disorder, disease or trauma. Many of these conditions reduce quality of life for patients and their families while some others are life-threatening. For example, the aging world population is creating new medical challenges since the normal healing process is disrupted in the elderly who often suffer from diabetes or blood circulation problems. Excessive scarring that occurs following severe burns or traumatic wounds, is an equally serious clinical problem with limited treatment options. Also common skin diseases such as psoriasis have no satisfactory treatments. The ultimate goal of the current application is to increase the capacity to perform research on skin diseases and conditions in Canada, leading to novel and effective therapies for treatment. To achieve this goal we have initiated the creation of a multidisciplinary team, Skin Repair, Regeneration and Restoration Research Group (SR4G), representing a consortium of new and established investigators in basic and clinical research disciplines.  One of the major components will be to foster participation of patient alliance groups and patient advocacy groups.  Our specific objective is to hold a symposium with the participation of all the stake holders to identify priority research areas, to develop partnerships and consolidate teams to apply for major research funding opportunities at the provincial, national and international levels.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mental Health Recovery in Canada: Developing and Sustaining a Pan Canadian Community of Practice
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY OF PRACTICE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MENTAL HEALTH; MENTAL HEALTH POLICY; MENTAL HEALTH PRACTICE; PARTICIPATORY; RECOVERY
Abstract-Résumé: The overall aim of this grant is to bring together knowledge users, decision makers, and researchers from across Canada to develop Pan Canadian research on the implementation of recovery throughout the system of mental health services. Mental health recovery is defined as "a way of living a satisfying, hopeful, and contributing life" despite limitations caused by mental illness. Traditional mental health services foster dependency, discouragement, and even stigmatization. Recovery-oriented mental health services are different from those of traditional "treatment and cure" health services, where the focus is on symptom relief and relapse prevention. In recovery-oriented services, the person's quality of life is central. Recovery-oriented services should promote hope, self-mastery, a meaningful life, and belonging in the community. Recovery is the central focus of Canada's first Mental Health Strategy, Changing Directions,Changing Lives. In response to the critical need for system transformation the Mental Health Commission of Canada initiated a Pan Canadian Community of Practice on mental health recovery. The specific objectives of this grant are: (1) to collaborate with the Pan Canadian Community of Practice on Recovery to develop a CIHR Partnership for Health System Improvement grant; (2) to strengthen emerging partnerships and to foster new collaborations among recovery stakeholders across Canada (3)publish an article on the work of the Pan Canadian Community of Practice on mental health recovery.  The specific activities planned are: a 2-day in person meeting in Toronto with members of the Community of Practice to be held in April 2014. At this meeting we will discuss and finalize a research proposal for the CIHR Partnership for Health System Improvement Grant competition. Leading up to this 2 day meeting we will organize a series of 5 conference calls/webinars We will also publish an article on the work of the Pan Canadian Community of Practice.

Abstract-Résumé: This collaborative project with the South Asian Cochrane Network and Centre is aimed to support the development of a planned active Cochrane Branch in Nepal, and to collaboratively identify a focus of activities for this branch, such as migrant health. The Cochrane Collaboration has emerged as a world leading organization in systematic reviews. In 2006 the World Health Assembly promoted systematic reviews, in both developed and developing countries, as a reliable basis to inform healthcare decision making.  This will project gather selected multisectoral partners from variety of backgrounds (e.g. health researchers, and/or knowledge users) in Kathmandu, Nepal to expand and strengthen networking and partnerships for Cochrane Collaboration.   We plan to identify priority themes for Cochrane activities in Nepal that will build critical appraisal and research synthesis skills for the use of evidence in clinical practice.  In the long term, this project will bring the international reputation and expertise of the Cochrane Collaboration to develop an ongoing, collaborative health research partnership between Canada, Nepal, and South Asia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Enhancing health outcomes and well-being of people with balance and mobility limitations by expanding the implementation of community-based exercise programs: A knowledge mobilization workshop
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS; ADULTS; BALANCE AND MOBILITY LIMITATIONS; BARRIERS AND FACILITATORS; COMMUNITIY-BASED EXERCISE PROGRAMS; CONSENSUS; HEALTH PROMOTION; IMPLEMENTATION STRATEGIES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; SCALING UP
Abstract-Résumé: People with balance and mobility limitations from chronic disease face multiple barriers to accessing safe and affordable exercise programs in the community to maintain their health. We developed a research-informed group exercise program that involves the practice of functional everyday tasks, like standing up from a chair, and doing stairs, for people with stroke, acquired brain injury, and multiple sclerosis. We showed that this program, called Together in Movement and Exercise (TIME), was safe and feasible to deliver in recreation centres by fitness instructors who were trained by physical therapists. Although multiple recreation providers became interested in offering the TIME program, they report a number of challenges such as difficulty recruiting, increased cost due to a high instructor to participant ratio, lack of buy-in from staff, and repeat registrations leading to wait lists. We propose to hold a one-day meeting in Toronto, Ontario in May 2014 to identify challenges and strategies to address the challenges to implementing, expanding and sustaining the provision of community-based exercise programs for people with balance and mobility limitations. We will invite a range of stakeholders to the meeting including physical therapists, fitness instructors, recreation providers, advocates, researchers, educators, health policy experts, stroke network representatives, trainees, and people with balance and mobility limitations and their caregivers. Through the prioritized challenges and action plans that we develop, we hope to inform education, research and health policy. Moreover, we will form a network of stakeholders to support the delivery of the TIME program through knowledge exchange, research and mentoring. By increasing access to safe and affordable exercise, we hope that Canadians living with balance and mobility limitations will become more physically active and enjoy the same health benefits as able-bodied individuals.

Abstract-Résumé: The planning grant will support collective community input for a project to explore First Nation [FN] people cardiovascular health and health care services in Manitoba [MB]. Dialogues with FN and non-FN individual community members began 18 months ago, which has demonstrated support for developing a research study. At this point, a collective meeting that brings together community individuals will strengthen supportive networks and synergize community input. One meeting will gather representatives from the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs [AMC], MB Cardiac Sciences Program, other community individuals linked with cardiovascular or FN health, and the research team. We will discuss our collective and diverse visions concerning cardiovascular health among FN people; provide critical feedback on the proposed project, and generate ideas for knowledge translation processes. At the second meeting, the research team will discuss the feedback from the first meeting and how best to integrate into the development of a CIHR grant application. The final meeting, organized with AMC, will open our dialogue with MB FN Health Technician network regarding the proposed project.  Meetings will be held in Winnipeg late fall 2013 to early 2014. Objectives:  1) To facilitate active and meaningful collaborations among MB FN health leaders, Cardiac Sciences Program leaders, Aboriginal and Northern Health Office, and our research team.    2) To further develop our proposed project through integrating community input that includes voiced priorities and relevance among different sectors.  3) To nurture collaborative relationships essential for the success and reach of the research study, and meaningful knowledge translation strategies.  We anticipate hearing many ideas concerning FN cardiovascular health. We intend to share all research questions so to inspire additional future studies. Our ultimate long-term goal is to open new ways of seeing, knowing, and engaging heart health among FN people.

Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S HEALTH; CHILD HEALTH; RESPIRATORY HEALTH; SUPPORT INTERVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal children are vulnerable to lung problems, including asthma, linked to negative impacts on psychosocial health, quality of life, and health care costs. Although support deficits, loneliness and isolation are major concerns for these vulnerable Aboriginal children and their families, relevant innovative support interventions (e.g. using social networking techniques) are not widely accessible. The objectives of this planning grant are to consult with knowledge users and researchers regarding implications of previous research for future support intervention studies, build pertinent multi-sectoral partnerships engaging stakeholders from public, program, policy and practice domains and diverse disciplines, and seek consensus regarding priority support interventions for grant applications. The anticipated outcomes include: 1) discussion document summarizing insights from previous research on support intervention preferences of Aboriginal children and parents affected by respiratory health problems; 2) final report on research priorities identified in planning meeting focused on accessible and innovative support interventions to be designed and tested for Aboriginal children and families; and 3) fact sheet, presentations, refereed article(s) and draft grant proposal outline including relevant partnerships. Key national groups for Aboriginal people's health (Aboriginal Nurses Association of Canada, National Collaborating Centre  for Aboriginal Health, Alberta Network Environments for Aboriginal Health Research), respiratory health (Asthma Society of Canada, Canadian Network for Respiratory Care), and child health (Canadian Institute of Child Health), have confirmed their support. Thirty three Aboriginal leaders, parents, policy influencers, program planners, practitioners and researchers representing multiple sites, sectors, and disciplines will participate in this planning meeting.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing an Interdisciplinary Team to Understand HIV/STI Prevention Priorities among Key Populations of Youth in Two Regions of Peru
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV/STI PREVENTION; SEXUAL HEALTH PROMOTION; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; YOUTH IN PERU
Abstract-Résumé: With the failure of the latest vaccine trial, HVTN-505, announced in April 2013, HIV prevention efforts remain essential (Lancet, 2013).  Social and structural factors contributing to HIV/STI transmission include stigma regarding sexual violence, HIV infection and sexual orientation. While HIV prevention and overall sexual health programs targeting youth in Peru have been implemented , key populations of youth (sex workers, male youth and transgender) continue to be overrepresented in new cases of HIV and STI in Peru.  In this CIHR Planning grant we aim to develop an interdisciplinary, international research team to understand HIV/STI prevention priorities among youth in two culturally and geographically diverse cities in Peru, Lima, the capital city, and Ayacucho, in the Andean region. Team members represent social science and clinical researchers from Canada,  Peru and USA. We plan: 1) to conduct a review of existing research, legislation, policies and practices on HIV/STI prevention in Peru; 2) to conduct in April 2014 knowledge users (youth) and stakeholders consultations (health care providers, community organizers) in both locations and, 3 ) to conduct  in June 2014 two community forums with community partners, stakeholders, health researchers and knowledge users from Ayacucho and Lima. The goal of the consultations and community forums would be to share HIV/STI and sexual health priorities across these two cities and to plan a viable, cultural, age and gender appropriate HIV prevention and health promotion research project with youth in these two diverse regions. The lessons learned of developing the planned international, interdisciplinary team will serve to the following knowledge translation (KT) goals:  a) to inform a CIHR Community-based HIV Research Catalyst Grant; and b) to inform peer reviewed and non-peer reviewed publications/ presentations regarding HIV/STI prevention research priorities among youth in Peru.

Abstract-Résumé: Our previous research demonstrates that the work of staff in long term care (LTC) could at times be better organized and that communication in some areas could be improved. We have identified some strategies that might help to improve this. The goal of the planning grant is to hold an event with people from LTC organizations, government and Alberta Health Services. During the event we will discuss the strategies to see which one(s) should be implemented and how. We will also conduct a review of the literature to find out if and how others have implemented these strategies. The information will be used to develop a research proposal to implement selected strategies and measure the outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Building the Bridge(s) - The Diaspora Declaration: Development of a Global HIV/AIDS Framework and Agenda
Keywords-MotsClés: AFRICAN AND BLACK DIASPORA; GLOBAL HIV/AIDS FRAMEWORK; HIV AND ETHNICITY; HIV PREVENTION; HIV SUPPORT AND CARE; HIV-ENDEMIC COUNTRIES
Abstract-Résumé: African and Black (ABD) populations bear a disproportionate burden of HIV infection and experience disturbing disparities in access to care and support, in comparison to other populations within countries across North America, Western Europe and Oceana. In 2009, 67% of people living with HIV globally were in Africa, but when you include the numbers of people living with HIV in regions with significant new/historic ABD populations, over 80% of the people living with HIV self-identify or are described as Black.  Due to intersecting vulnerabilities including discrimination based on ethnicity, HIV and migrant statuses, ABD populations face challenges in developing and utilizing effective communication and advocacy platforms to address these inequalities. In response to this critical gap, this project will develop a Diaspora Declaration as a platform to galvanize policy, advocacy, research and service delivery recommendations to address HIV/AIDS epidemics amongst ABD populations. This Canadian-led effort will foster strategic national/international collaborations that support the engagment of ABD people living with HIV/AIDS, community networks, researchers, public health advocates, and other stakeholders to achieve the following aims: 1. To undertake a national consultation, utilizing key informant interviews and an extensive literature review, to inform the development of a Diaspora Declaration grounded in the current ABD context; 2. To create a web page with social media capabilities, to build a database of supporters for the draft Diaspora Declaration for sustained mobilization activities; 3. To launch the Diaspora Declaration at the 20th International AIDS Conference in Melbourne, Australia in July 2014; 4. To disseminate the final version of the Diaspora Declaration globally aiming to secure a target of 10,000 individuals/organizations that endorse the platform.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Scleroderma Patient-centered Intervention Network (SPIN) Feasibility Trial Planning Meeting
Keywords-MotsClés: FEASIBILITY TRIALS; PATIENT-CENTERED CARE; RARE DISEASE; SCLERODERMA
Abstract-Résumé: Improving patient-centered care is prioritized in Canadian health care, but interventions designed to reduce disability and improve health-related quality of life are typically not available for rare diseases. The Scleroderma Patient-centered Intervention Network (SPIN) received a 5-year CIHR New Emerging Team (NET) Grant in Rare Diseases. SPIN is a collaboration of patient organizations, clinicians, and investigators from Canada, the USA, and Europe organized to develop and test interventions that can feasibly be made available to the relatively small and dispersed number of people suffering from the rare disease scleroderma. Scleroderma is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by thickening of the skin and fibrosis of internal organs, resulting in significant disability from limitations to physical mobility, pain, fatigue, depressive symptoms, and body image distress due to disfigurement. At the 1st Annual SPIN Scientific Meeting, SPIN investigators and patient partners developed administrative and investigative infrastructures to support the objectives of the newly formed team. SPIN is comprised of a Steering Committee, a patient Advisory Board, 4 project teams dedicated to the development and testing of specific psychosocial and rehabilitative interventions, and SPIN Cores to support project teams (e.g., Information Technology, Measurement). At the 2nd Annual SPIN Scientific Meeting, the 4 project teams worked to incorporate advances in overall design (e.g., technology, measures) into individual intervention plans and developed an overall framework for each. The CIHR NET grant does not include funds to support a full annual meeting of all investigators and patient partners. Thus, this proposal, if funded, will support the 3rd Annual SPIN Scientific Meeting, where SPIN project teams and SPIN Cores will provide progress reports, finalize individual interventions in terms of content and delivery, and outline a plan to test the feasibility of each.

TitreApplicationTitle: Establishing the Chair's Advisory Council (CAC) for the Inaugural Heart and Stroke Foundation(HSF)/Northern Ontario School of Medicine (NOSM) Aboriginal and Rural Health Research Chair
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; CARDIOVASCULAR RISK REDUCTION; COMMUNITY COLLABORATIVE RESEARCH; GUIDELINES IMPLEMENTATION; RURAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease and stroke and cancer are the number one killers world-wide. Rates of cardiovascular diseases in Northern and Aboriginal communities exceed those of the rest of the country putting them at a greater risk of heart disease and stroke, compared to the general population. Cancer rates among First Peoples are increasing faster in comparison to overall Canadian cancer rates. NOSM has developed and delivers a distinctive model of distributed, community engaged, and socially accountable, medical education. The HSF Chair in Aboriginal and Rural Health at NOSM is responsible for developing scientific advancement in the field of chronic disease management of cardiovascular disease, diabetes and cancer in Aboriginal and rural communities. The Chair will lead activities promoting knowledge transfer and exchange through initiatives such as provincial, national and international meetings and forums, promotion of clinical practice guidelines, linking quality improvement efforts to evidence based best practice and other KT strategies. The Chair will integrate with other Aboriginal and Rural Research Units across Canada to establish virtual collaborative research networks, understand the community's priorities and support efforts to establish mentorship and networking. The Chair shall provide leadership and promote a shared vision across a large geographic area with diverse populations. The Chair's Advisory Council (CAC) is critical in assisting the Chair to maximize research, training and knowledge translation outcomes, provide advice and recommendations for political, legal, organizational, technical, cost management, cultural and personnel issues, planning, implementation and evaluation and to represent the stakeholders. In keeping with NOSM's distributed learning model, the CAC will hold regular meetings using video conferencing.  The purpose of this planning grant is to organize, establish and evaluate the inaugural meeting of the CAC.

TitreApplicationTitle: Addressing the Burden of Cardiometabolic Disease in Aboriginal Peoples Through Culturally Appropriate Interaction Design
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; APPS; CULTURALLY APPROPRIATE; EXERCISE; INTERACTION DESIGN; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; SMART PHONE
Abstract-Résumé: Modern technology and Western activities that promote inactivity are thought to place Aboriginal peoples at an increased risk for cardiometabolic disease. There is a clear need for best practice guidelines for the prevention and treatment of cardiometabolic disease. However, most guidelines have been developed without considering the unique needs of Aboriginal peoples. Moreover, there is an acknowledged translation gap between the research evidence and the application of this knowledge in the real-world setting (particularly within Aboriginal communities). In our collaborations with Aboriginal peoples, we are aware of the lack of culturally appropriate resources for Aboriginal youth and adults. Aboriginal community leaders often complain of inadequate continuing education and/or culturally appropriate resources to deal with the primary and secondary prevention of chronic disease (and obesity). We have recently created a series of recommendations for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiometabolic disease. We have recently sought to improve the translation of this information by creating novel interaction designs (i.e., the specific shaping of digital media for people's usage) through innovative web- and phone-based applications. However, we recognize that our messaging may be of limited value to Aboriginal peoples without a clear understanding of the needs of Aboriginal communities. Addressing this knowledge translation gap is essential for effectively meeting the needs of Aboriginal peoples. Accordingly, this planning meeting will bring together world-leading experts in the primary and secondary prevention of cardiometabolic disease, application designers, and Aboriginal leaders. It is our intention to use this planning grant as the catalyst for the development of new resources and collaborative grants that facilitate the translation of knowledge related to the primary and secondary prevention of cardiometabolic disease in Aboriginal peoples.

TitreApplicationTitle: Laying the Groundwork for the Development of Model Ethics Curricula and Teaching Tools in Public Health
Keywords-MotsClés: CURRICULA; EDUCATION; PEDAGOGY; PROFESSIONAL ETHICS; PUBLIC HEALTH ETHICS; TRAINING TOOLS
Abstract-Résumé: Health professionals must uphold high standards of ethics in order to garner trust and support from the public for health initiatives; in addition, this is an essential component of professional practice (e.g., professional codes of ethics). To master ethical decision-making, professionals must learn through experience as well as formal training and instruction by specialists from diverse backgrounds of expertise. This project will foster the development of ethics instruction for public health professionals and researchers, a group for which formal ethics training in Canada is nascent and in high demand. We will survey Canadian schools of public health to map the state of ethics curricula and training resources. The survey findings will be written up into a stimulus paper, to be then used at a day long workshop that will bring together educators in public health ethics from across Canada. This networking event will enable ethics educators to comment on the survey data and share their experiences and thoughts about what is currently and what should be included in public health ethics education. These recommendations will serve as the starting point for structuring a model ethics training curricula (e.g., content, form, innovative teaching approaches) for Canadian public health programmes, which will be disseminated to public health organisations and university programme directors. Through an online discussion platform (including a wiki, forum, and resources), we will provide this newly established network of ethics educators with opportunities to continue to share educational materials, and more importantly, set the foundation for a long-term collaborative environment for improving and innovating in public health ethics education.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translating research into a videogame to disseminate knowledge about cannabis, psychosis, and early intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: CANNABIS USE; FIRST EPISODE PSYCHOSIS; QUALITATIVE STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: In order for society to benefit from the latest scientific research on a preventable risk factor, it is generally accepted that individuals who could benefit the most should be made aware. However, when the relevant research pertains to youth, researchers will need to use more innovative methods than scientific reports to get their attention. Although it may not be necessary or sufficient, recent research suggests that marijuana use three times a week for three months or longer during the teenage years is a significant risk factor for the development of psychosis among vulnerable youth. We propose to raise awareness of this little known risk factor.  This project translates and disseminates this research knowledge about marijuana use, psychosis, and early intervention by using a youth friendly medium - an animated video game/app. As a communication strategy, interactive gaming technology has the potential to be more appealing and accessible to youth than mainstream educational activities. The game will be designed by game developers, who will work collaboratively with the co-applicants to better appreciate the research findings and to integrate the knowledge into the game. The inspiration will come from stories that emerge out of two qualitative studies containing descriptions of real life and first-time experiences with marijuana use, psychosis, and the healthcare system. The game will then be disseminated at a forum for youth and youth leaders in order to foster an action plan to market the game online to youth, particularly those who are weekly marijuana users. The game/app will have the potential to disseminate this research knowledge, possibly increasing awareness of this modifiable risk factor for psychosis and reducing the risk of psychosis among vulnerable youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards a practical solution for prescription drug misuse
Keywords-MotsClés: KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PAIN EDUCATION; PAIN MANAGEMENT; PRESCRIPTION DRUGS
Abstract-Résumé: Misuse of prescription medications has been identified as a significant problem. At the same time, opioids are a simple and effective treatment for many pain problems. The recent announcement of the Canadian Centre on Substance Abuse (CCSA) strategy on misuse of prescription drugs, "First Do No Harm: Responding to Canada's Prescription Drug Crisis", identified a number of areas in which greatly improved communication needs to occur. First Do No Harm was developed by a broad based group including pain physicians, addiction specialists, public health, law enforcement officials, representatives of the community and Aboriginal Peoples.  As the next step towards addressing these issues, we will bring together a group of champions to discuss concrete solutions to the problems which we face; the competing need to identify patients with clinical needs and separate them from individuals trying to deceive the caregivers, and treatment of addiction as a medical problem while minimizing the social harms. The proposed activity is a meeting which will take place in May, 2014.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nourishing Communities: HIV/AIDS Food Security Study Dissemination in BC
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; FOOD SECURITY; HIV/AIDS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The CIHR-funded Food Security Study was the first community-based research initiative in Canada to examine food security and health outcomes among people living with HIV in three provinces - British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec. The "Nourishing Communities: HIV/AIDS Food Security Study Dissemination in BC" project will mobilize the findings from the BC arm of the study and bring the project full circle. Within the study, of the total 328 participants recruited in BC 236 (72%) reported being food insecure - a level approximately seven times greater than in the general Canadian population. These findings point to the need to move research to action. Because the policy and service contexts are so different within each of the three provinces involved in the study, the dissemination strategies of Nourishing Communities will focus on knowledge translation activities in BC, while sharing the products and learnings with the teams in Ontario and Quebec. Nourishing Communities will implement a strategic approach to bring findings back to communities that participated in the study, including people living with HIV/AIDS, policy makers and community-based organizations, as well as disseminating to academic audiences. This will be achieved through the creation of dissemination products (such as postcards and fact sheets), regionally specific presentations, and articles and presentations for academic audiences. Additionally, we will host a half-day Community Dialogue, where participants will develop a BC Action Plan on HIV/AIDS Food Security. Nourishing Communities will build capacity among team members to mobilize evidence, and will build momentum in the HIV/AIDS community and beyond to address a critical issue for the health and well-being of people living with HIV/AIDS in our province.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bone and Oncology New Updates meeting 2014 (BONUS 9 Symposium)
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE METASTASES AND ONCOLOGY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MULTI-DISCIPLINARY SYMPOSIUM; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Bone remains the most of the common place that cancers spread to. Bone metastases are incurable, difficult to treat, and are often associated with pain, reduced quality of life and skeletal events such as fractures. The care of these patients is complex, involving many clinical disciplines including; nursing, palliative care, physiotherapy, orthopaedic surgeons, medical and radiation oncologists, and palliative care to name a few. Trans-disciplinary information is required if we are to ultimately deliver optimal and consistent care for Canadian patients. In order to facilitate cross-disciplinary information exchange and initiate new collaborations, we have hosted the annual BONUS (Bone and Oncology New Updates) meeting for the past 8 years. This proposal is requesting funds to support the next conference which will again consist of keynote lectures from National and International speakers covering a range of bone issues pertinent to oncology health care professionals and the research community. The BONUS 9 Symposium will be April 24-25, 2014 in Ottawa, Ontario. The topics will cover normal skeletal function, as well as the effects of cancer and cancer therapies on normal and metastatic bone. As in previous years we will divide the meeting sessions into CIHR research priority themes. Each session will contain a mixture of basic, clinical and translational research work, and will be pertinent to all tumour types that commonly spread to bone. Through a series of presentations and interactive sessions (including a new dedicated session on knowledge translation) we will exchange unpublished new research findings and generate multi-disciplinary collaborations thus initiating exciting Canadian research endeavours that will shape future basic and clinical research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Toward Equity in Cancer Screening:  Multicultural Tools and Strategies for Improving Breast and Cervical Screening Among Canadian Newcomers
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST; CANCER; CANCER SCREENING; CERVICAL; COMMUNITY-BASED; CULTURAL SENSITIVITY; HEALTH PROMOTION; PEER LEADERS
Abstract-Résumé: By detecting breast and cervical cancer early, mammograms and Pap tests save the lives of many Canadian women. However, immigrant and refugee women often lack information about cancer screening or cannot access crucial screening services which contributes to low rates of screening in these communities. The CARES program (Cancer Awareness: Ready for Education and Screening) was developed to promote collaboration between community agencies and hospitals with the goal of reaching out to these vulnerable under or never screened women. CARES works with peer leaders from diverse cultural backgrounds to raise awareness about breast and cervical cancer. They provide information sessions in the communities where newcomer women live, work, worship or access community services. Feedback from participants and peer leaders have led to improvements in these multi-lingual educational tools.  Research and evaluation of the CARES program will provide knowledge about how the tools and program could be adopted in other settings.  The goal of the proposed activity is to share these valuable resources and findings to benefit as many under or never screened women as possible. The grant will make CARES educational materials available online in a variety of languages along with a step by step toolkit for adapting and using them in community settings. CARES team leaders, representatives from community agencies in Ontario serving South Asian and Chinese immigrant populations, and representatives from organizations in the cancer field will meet to discuss research findings from the CARES project as well as the educational resources and toolkit. Meeting participants will work together to plan ways to best use CARES research findings and resources in their communities and engage, inform, and support screening in under-served women. This meeting will spark collaboration and provide the tools needed to effectively reach under/never-screened women across Ontario and nation wide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Raising Awareness for Rett Syndrome: Connecting Scientists, Clinicians, and Parents
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM-SPECTRUM DISORDER; BETTER TREATMENT OPTIONS; BRAIN AND BEHAVIOR; GASTROINTESTINAL IMPAIRMENTS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; ORTHOPEDIC INTERVENTIONS; RETT SYNDROME; SEIZURES; SOCIAL WELFARE AND CONDITION MANAGEMENT; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder affecting primarily females that arises from mutations of the MECP2 gene. Rett syndrome occurs with a frequency of about one in every 10,000 female births, making it one of the top genetic causes of severe mental impairment in girls worldwide. Rett syndrome has only been recognized as a specific condition since about 1983, and to this day it remains under-recognized, and is often confused with the completely unrelated condition of Tourette syndrome. Girls with Rett syndrome do not display "ticks", but rather suffer from co-morbidities such as epilepsy, Parkinson-like dystonia, brittle bones, breathing apnea, severe gastrointestinal reflux, curvature of the spine, and they often display bouts of anxiety and depression. It is difficult to care for, or clinically manage, a Rett syndrome patient also, as Rett syndrome girls are not able to speak and have minimal if any meaningful communicative use of their hands. There is hope for Rett syndrome patients, however, as recent scientific studies in mouse models of Rett syndrome strongly suggest that the condition can be corrected - but more research in this direction is needed. One of the goals of the conference we propose is to bring together the leading Canadian researchers in this field to foster collaborations to address these needed issues. In addition, though, ongoing clinical trials and new rehabilitative treatment options are now showing promise for better treating and managing girls with this condition.  And recent technological advances in eye-gaze based computer systems offers the possibility of opening communication with these girls for the first time. But, surprisingly few parents and caregivers, general practitioners, or policy makers know much about these advances. Thus, a second goal of our meeting is to provide information to members from these groups so it can be distributed to others within their  geographical and professional areas.

TitreApplicationTitle: Third Canadian Symposium on Hepatitis C Virus
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO CARE; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEPATITIS C; IMMUNOLOGY; PUBLIC HEALTH; SOCIAL SCIENCES; VIRAL HEPATITIS; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) affects at least 240,000 people in Canada and causes more years of life lost than any infectious disease in the country. The CIHR and the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) have identified liver disease due to HCV as a major public health problem. Understanding how to provide better care for HCV-infected individuals requires integration between researchers and policy makers across the four CIHR pillars (Biomedical, Clinical, Health services and Social, Cultural, Environmental, and Population Health). On February 23, 2012, the National Canadian Research Training Program in Hepatitis C (NCRTP-HepC) organized the 1st Canadian Symposium on Hepatitis C Virus (CSHCV), leveraging funds from CIHR and industrial sponsors. On March 4, 2013 the NCRTP-HepC organized the 2nd CSHCV, with the support of CIHR and non-CIHR donations. Both symposia were highly successful, attracting leading international faculty with excellent attendance leading to dialogue and knowledge translation between attendees across the four CIHR pillars. The goal of this CIHR Meetings, Planning and Dissemination Grant request is to seek support for a Third CSHCV, to be held on February 7, 2014, again organized by the NCRTP-HepC. The theme of this year's symposium will be "Expanding Care for HCV-infected Individuals". In August 2011, new therapies were approved by Health Canada that have led to higher rates of HCV eradication amongst treated individuals. By 2015/2016, more effective and less toxic therapies will be available that will lead to even higher success rates and shortened courses of therapy. However, treatment uptake is poor in Canada. The limitations to treatment uptake are numerous including financial, geographical, cultural and social barriers. With CIHR support, we aim to address these challenges and intend that the CSHCV will continue as an annual forum for exchange among researchers, policy makers and community members involved in HCV spanning the four CIHR pillars.

TitreApplicationTitle: 31st Annual Meeting of the Canadian Biomaterials Society
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIALS; BIOSENSORS; CARDIOVASCULAR MATERIALS; DENTAL MATERIALS; DRUG DELIVERY; IMPLANTS; ORTHOPAEDIC MATERIALS; SURFACE MODIFICATION; TISSUE ENGINEERING; TISSUE REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Biomaterials, defined as bulk materials or surfaces that interact in some way with the body, are an ever-present part of the health care system. The Canadian Biomaterials Society (CBS) is a student-focused, not-for-profit organization dedicated to enhancing biomaterials science and technology development and training in Canadian universities, industry, and government. The 31st Annual Meeting of the Society, to be held on the campus of Dalhousie University from June 4 to 7, 2014, will provide a forum for sharing the latest discoveries in biomaterials research, device development and novel clinical applications. There will be a special emphasis on networking, with opportunities for both formal and informal interactions amongst trainees, professors, clinicians and industrial partners from across Canada. The scientific program will highlight notable international experts spanning the broad biomaterials spectrum, with much of the program focused on tissue repair and regeneration required as a result of injuries and aging-related or chronic diseases, including osteoarthritis, osteoporosis and cancer; notably, these are strategic research priorities of the Institute of Musculoskeletal Health and Arthritis (IMHA). In typical CBS tradition, this meeting will emphasize student participation through oral and poster presentations, and co-chairing of sessions. Following the precedent set at our last meeting, we will again be seeking Continuing Medical Education (CME) accreditation of this event to further promote knowledge exchange amongst clinicians and scientists, with the goal of realizing greater translation of innovations from the laboratory bench to bedside. The long-term benefits, then, are improved personal health together with more effective (and efficient) health care solutions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implementing a new software-based quantitative photographic posture assessment tool in the clinic: translating knowledge into practice
Keywords-MotsClés: POSTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Teens who have spinal deformities are at greater risk of back pain in adulthood. Moreover, poor posture has been associated with pain. Our team has developed and easy-to-use software program for posture analysis from digital photos. The goal of this project is to implement this new tool into routine clinical practice. We will train physiotherapists in different orthopaedic centres using this tool. After a training period, physiotherapists will comment on the practical usefulness of this photographic posture assessment method.  By being able to assess posture easily and objectively, physiotherapists will be able to better serve their patients by providing rational treatments. They will also be able to monitor posture, which up to now required sophisticated assessments that are not accessible to most clinicians.  By implementing a simple, easy-to-use, quantitative postural evaluation tool (with integrated software), we believe that we will help clinicians accurately assess and monitor their patients.  In terms of the patients themselves, they will be able to see changes in their posture based on these measurements. This may increase adherence to treatments such as exercises or wearing of braces.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ethics Program Evaluation in Canada: Synthesizing Research Evidence and Expert Practice to Improve Ethics Quality in Healthcare
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHICS PROGRAM EVALUATION; ETHICS TRAINING; EXPERT CONSENSUS; PERFORMANCE EVALUATION; QUALITY IMPROVEMENT; SCOPING REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Ethics is increasingly recognized as a key component of high quality patient care. Hospitals and other healthcare organizations are investing resources in ethics programs to address a myriad of ethical issues arising in clinical and organizational decision-making. Accreditation bodies are emphasizing ethics mechanisms in their evaluation of hospital practices.  Among practicing healthcare ethicists, there is growing interest in evaluating ethics program effectiveness and in developing professional practice standards to ensure the quality of ethics programs and services. Over the last decade, a number of research and practice-based initiatives have been launched in Canada and elsewhere. However, a robust knowledge synthesis has yet to be conducted. As a result, there is continued uncertainty about how ethics programs should be evaluated or how practice standards should be met. Hence, the overall project goal is to bridge this gap by synthesizing knowledge about ethics program evaluation to improve ethics quality in health institutions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Addressing and Redressing Issues of Respiratory Health and Housing Among First Nations People: Program & Policy Options
Keywords-MotsClés: FIRST NATIONS; HOUSING; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; POLICY INTERVENTIONS; PROGRAM INTERVENTIONS; RESPIRATORY HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Living conditions in many First Nations communities are characterized by personal, social and physical environments that are associated with adverse respiratory outcomes. While some issues may be amenable to address at the community level, other issues require redress at the policy level. This one-day symposium will highlight knowledge about the linkages between adult and child respiratory health outcomes and housing environments in First Nations communities, focusing on program and policy intervention possibilities. Beginning with brief presentations from First Nations community-based respiratory health research to establish a knowledge base, invited speakers that follow will highlight their experiences with housing & respiratory health interventions and opportunities at the program and policy levels. Attendees will include multiple stakeholders (e.g. First Nations community members, FINIH, INAC, FSIN, & NITHA). The objective is to learn about interventions currently taking place in Canadian First Nation communities, and stimulate discussion on successes, strengths, challenges, and opportunities. The results of the Symposium will be summarized in a major Canadian journal such as the Canadian Journal of Public Health, as well as in a summary report posted in an open-access electronic format.  An edited version of  videotaped presentations will be posted on the web. The symposium will promote knowledge exchange among Canadian First Nations communities and stakeholders of housing and respiratory health issues and possibilities for program and policy interventions.

Keywords-MotsClés: CONTINUING EDUCATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; MENTORSHIP; RESEARCH REPORTING
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Association for HIV Research (CAHR) is the professional organization for HIV and AIDS research in Canada or by Canadians. CAHR includes all researchers and all disciplines of the scientific approaches to HIV and AIDS, for the purpose of its better prevention and treatment and ultimately for its eradication and cure. The annual CAHR Conference is the premier gathering in Canada for those working in the field of HIV, as well as policy makers, persons living with HIV and other individuals committed to ending the pandemic. The 2014 Conference programme will present new scientific knowledge and offer many opportunities for structured dialogue on the major issues facing the global response to HIV. A variety of session types, from abstract driven presentations to symposia, bridging and plenary sessions, will meet the needs of various participants. Other related activities, including ancillary meetings, the new investigator workshop and exhibitions, will contribute to an exceptional opportunity for professional development and networking. In an effort to support and facilitate knowledge translation and dissemination of the outcomes and discussions held at CAHR Conference 2014, CAHR will be working with the Canadian Journal of Infectious Diseases and Medical Microbiology to produce a Journal Supplement. Publishing a Conference Proceedings Supplement in this journal is a very effective means of disseminating scientific findings and materials to relevant target stakeholders. The final product will be distributed with the subsequent issue of the Canadian Journal of Infectious Diseases & Medical Microbiology to CAHR members, Conference attendees, and other key HIV/AIDS stakeholders. In addition, the supplement will be highlighted in all promotional material for the Canadian Journal of Infectious Diseases and Medical Microbiology, and will be posted on websites for both the Journal and CAHR.

TitreApplicationTitle: National Youth Dialogue on Canada's Role in Global Health and Development
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADIAN HEALTH POLICY; CIVIC PARTICIPATION; DELIBERATIVE DIALOGUE; DISSEMINATION; EVIDENCE BRIEF; EVIDENCE-INFORMED POLICYMAKING; GLOBAL HEALTH; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; YOUTH DIALOGUE; YOUTH LEADERSHIP
Abstract-Résumé: Health is now truly global, with serious implications for trade, security, well-being and development. Canada would benefit from considering the available research evidence on the risks and opportunities that changes in global health pose to Canadians and people everywhere. Over the past few years, the McMaster Health Forum has conducted a number of research activities on Canada's role in global health. We have undertaken extensive literature reviews, interviewed key informants, produced evidence briefs, and convened a stakeholder dialogue that included policymakers, civil society leaders, researchers and health planners. While these activities helped Canadian leaders to identify global health risks and opportunities to address them, a crucial voice was absent from these discussions. Youth leaders - who represent the future of Canadian society - are often not engaged as potential users of research evidence. Youth leaders represent thousands of other young people as the presidents of student governments, health professional student associations and research networks. These students can help ensure that research informs policy directions for Canada. We propose hosting a national youth dialogue to foster the uptake, application and dissemination of research evidence on Canada's role in global health and development among 25 of the country's top youth leaders. Students will discuss the problem, policy options and implementation considerations. The dialogue captures an important voice that Canadian officials have not yet heard and supports youth-driven outputs (e.g., a Youth Charter, letters to Ministers, op-eds, social media advocacy campaigns). It also develops a new community platform for youth to contribute to future health discussions with research evidence rooted at the core. A national youth dialogue represents an important first step toward cultivating a culture of evidence-informed decision-making and knowledge translation among Canada's future health leaders.

TitreApplicationTitle: From Bench to Bedside - Translation & Sharing of MS Research
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIERS TO KNOWLEDGE IMPLEMENTATION; DISSEMINATION OF NEW MS RESEARCH; ENHANCING TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH EFFORTS; FROM BENCH TO BEDSIDE; HEALTHY AGING AND LIFESTYLE IN MS; INFLAMMATION AND IMMUNE RESPONSE IN MS; KNOWLEDGE UPTAKE AND EXCHANGE; NEUROPLASTICITY IN MS
Abstract-Résumé: In a world where information is available at our fingertips, people are much more aware of what is happening in the world of MS research. There is a heightened demand from the MS community and beyond to learn more about the work of researchers, the research process and how it is being applied.   Through the delivery of research based education seminars in the fall of 2014, the MS Society in partnership with CIHR will open up lines of communication between researchers, people living with MS, healthcare professionals and students in communities across Atlantic Canada.  Dr. Michelle Ploughman and Dr. Alain Simard will disseminate new findings from their studies around healthy aging and inflammation in MS, while also speaking on the research process. The seminars will allow researchers to connect with their communities directly and address questions attendees may have.   Ploughman will speak to the modifiable components in our environment and how these variables relate to healthy aging with MS. Her presentation will increase peoples appreciation of how research can be applied to inform health related decisions and will stimulate discussion.  Simard will provide attendees with a deeper understanding of biomedical research by speaking to the steps involved in bringing research from concept to clinic to patient use.  For people living with MS, the seminars will provide a deeper understanding of MS and the process behind research. For students and researchers, the seminars will be a catalyst for potential new relationships and collaborations, as well as an opportunity to hear directly from patients, those at the center of their work. For healthcare professionals, the seminars provide an opportunity to learn about components of research that may improve treatment plans and overall knowledge in disease progression and management.

TitreApplicationTitle: Partnering to promote healthy living through leisure participation for children and youth with physical disabilities: Child Health Initiatives Limiting Disability through leisure - CHILD Leisure-Net
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD PHYSICAL DISABILITY; HEALTH PROMOTION; LEISURE; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Participation in leisure activities has undisputed physical and mental health benefits. Children and youth with physical disabilities such as cerebral palsy, arthritis or developmental coordination disorder are less engaged in leisure activities when compared to peers, and activities tend to be more passive and home-based. Many barriers to participation, such as accessibility, family and peer support and availability of adapted programs are potentially modifiable. Moreover, families are not adequately informed of existing resources and programs supported by policies in local communities. We and others have conducted recent studies on leisure participation in children and youth with physical challenges and factors that influence engagement. We propose to organize two workshops in Quebec and Ontario, to translate these research findings to key stakeholders. Participants will include families, individuals with physical disabilities, health care providers, researchers, grassroots organizations and policymakers. As part of this dissemination event, stakeholders will interact with the aim of collectively formulating ideas to overcome barriers to participation. In addition to the workshop event, a short YouTube video on the challenges and successes of engagement in leisure activities for children with physical limitations will be made, as a dissemination strategy to the public at large. We will create an App for families to locate resources and programs that support participation. Finally, this activity will provide the impetus to create a network (CHILD Leisure-Net) to partner the various stakeholders to enhance knowledge sharing, participatory research and development of new programs and policies that promote leisure participation. A diverse and committed team of stakeholders has been assembled with the goal of enhancing active, healthy lifestyles to promote the well-being of children and youth with chronic, lifelong musculoskeletal and other physical disabilities.

The meeting on February 20-21, 2014, Vancouver, BC, entitled, 'Health Beyond Bars: Towards Healthy Prisons in Canada', aims to foster national uptake of preventive health research findings within prison settings in Canada. A CCPHE Knowledge Translation (KT) committee will plan the meeting: each committee member represents a key stakeholder organization with health interest and influence within Canadian correctional organizations. Following the February 2014 meeting, the CCPHE KT committee will continue to plan for uptake of the preventive health research findings within Canadian correctional settings, as guided by the recommendations that will be generated during the meeting's discussions.
