Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; CRIMINOLOGY; DEMOGRAPHY; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginals are over-represented in the Canadian prison system. This study used demographic and incarceration data to estimate the number of years that Aboriginals and non-Aboriginals spend in federal prisons across Canada and in provincial institutions in British Columbia. The results suggest that there are substantial differences in the amount of life years lost to incarceration; Aboriginals lose more life years to prison than non-Aboriginals. The purpose of this dissemination grant is to host a working conference to: 1) Gather community agencies who work with Aboriginal communities to facilitate networking and dialogue; 2) Disseminate study findings to community agencies; 3)Solicit feedback on the findings of the study from community agencies; 4) Facilitate the development of strategies to address health consequences of Aboriginal over-incarceration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Addressing Primary Health Care Service Gaps for Late Preterm Infants and their Families
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED INTERVENTIONS; HEALTH CARE SERVICE GAPS; INTEGRATED HEALTH CARE SYSTEMS; LATE PRETERM INFANTS; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE
Abstract-Résumé: The preterm birth rate is rising globally, with Canada experiencing a 25% increase over the past decade. Late preterm infants (born 4 to 6 weeks early) constitute approximately 75% of these early births and are the fastest growing group of preterms. Late preterm infants have higher rates of hospital readmission, more developmental problems, and their mothers are at greater risk for stress, anxiety and depression, in comparison to their term counterparts. Current provincially-based public and community health care services have not been tailored to address the unique needs of these infants and their parents. Thus, the goal of the two-day Planning Grant meeting is to inform the team's goal to develop, test and implement an intervention tailored to address health care service gaps, reduce rehospitalization and improve outcomes for late preterm infants and their families. The meeting will enable researchers and stakeholders to establish partnerships, outline gaps in primary health care services, and identify opportunities for integrating an intervention into existing programs to address gaps. Specifically, the meeting objectives are to: (a) discuss the direct health care, support, and knowledge needs of late preterm infants and their families from hospital to home through to the first year of life; (b) reach consensus on the priority issues and needs of these infants and parents; (c) identify the mismatch between needs versus community programs offered; (d) examine research interventions that target at-risk infants and their parents; (e) reach consensus on elements to comprise an intervention for late preterm infants and parents; and, (f) identify the best processes for implementing the intervention. A pre-meeting environmental scan of existing community health programs will also inform the dialogue. Meeting invitees will include practitioners, decision-makers, policy-makers, parents, and national experts in maternal-infant care, and interventions for premature infants.

Abstract-Résumé: Integrating Care for Individuals with FASD Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) is the leading cause of developmental disabilities in Canada.  FASD is caused by prenatal exposure to alcohol and results in a spectrum of lifelong neurobehavioural disabilities including cognitive delays or learning difficulties, emotional problems and secondary disabilities such as depression, substance abuse, legal problems and withdrawal from school.  FASD affects an estimated 1 in 100 births although higher rates are reported in some communities.  The effects and disabilities caused by FASD require services and treatment from multi-sectoral providers and agencies in the context of developing a better system-wide response to FASD.    In April 2014, we will conduct a workshop in Winnipeg that will bring together health system and provincial leaders from multiple stakeholder groups that typically work to address children and families affected by FASD.  Examples include leaders and policy decision-makers from the following: Pediatric/Primary care and FASD clinicians, Community Care, First Nations health, Education, Social Services, Justice, Public Health, Provincial and Local government and Police.  The workshop will identify and generate consensus on research and policy needs that will help improve our abilities to respond to FASD and also to better integrate care among the different providers/agencies for individuals affected with FASD.

Abstract-Résumé: The Inclusive Early Childhood Services Systems planning meeting objective is to identify the effects of early childhood service integration on children with disabilities. The province of Ontario is undergoing significant systems level change in early childhood social policy with the intent of improving access and integration of kindergarten, child care, and early intervention and other social services, but it is unclear how these policy changes will affect developmental, health and education experiences and outcomes for children with disabilities. Disablement is often the result of an interaction between individual characteristics (such as genetic and environmental factors), social experiences (such as poverty and racialization), and community social capital (such as health services, child care, and culturally relevant supports). We will bring together partners to examine this experience in the public policy context of Ontario.  The Inclusive Early Childhood Services Systems research partners include municipal community leaders who have the capacity to bring together public health, child care, family support, early intervention and aboriginal early childhood policy planners, along with research experts in qualitative and quantitative methodologies. A two-day planning meeting and follow up teleconference meetings will allow the research team and invited participants to: 1) Collaboratively develop the research questions; 2) Identify of existing data and appropriate methodologies to answer the research questions; and 3) Establish parameters for ongoing collaboration and team development for the purpose of conducting a longitudinal study of experiences of families accessing specialized services.

TitreApplicationTitle: Children's Health Research Integration Stimulus Project(CHRISP):Community Based Research Collaborations in Northeastern Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; CHILD AND YOUTH HEALTH; COLLABORATION; COMMUNITY-UNIVERSITY; FRANCOPHONE; INTERDISCIPLINARY; KNOWLEDGE DISSEMINATION; MENTAL HEALTH; NORTHEASTERN ONTARIO
Abstract-Résumé: The 'Children's Health Research Integration Stimulus Project' (CHRISP) is the first major research initiative of the newly established 'Evaluating Children's Health Outcomes' (ECHO) Research Centre at Laurentian University in Sudbury, Ontario. In the year that ECHO has existed, we have identified a research direction that is community-based, and we have strong interest and support from community partners to pursue collaborative research. CHRISP supports the implementation of a structure and process that will connect researchers with community partners and service providers, leading to a large-scale research study in our region.     Preliminary consultation with over 30 community organizations lead ECHO researchers to determine that the concept of resilience could encompass most, if not all, of the organizations' identified research priorities. Accordingly, CHRISP's focus is on improving resilience in children, their families, and their communities. Resilience includes physical and mental health, and the impacts of ecosystem change on children's health. Key vulnerable groups that have been identified include Francophone and Aboriginal children, children with mental health issues, and children with disabilities.     CHRISP is a creative monthly meeting process comprised of 6 half-day working sessions alternating with 6 shorter lunch-in-action sessions. During the working sessions invited world-class researchers will help to stimulate and shape research proposals. The lunch-in-action sessions will be held at various community partners to maintain momentum in the development of research projects. There are tremendous opportunities to enhance children's health in northeastern Ontario through research, especially within a municipality the size of Sudbury where organizations are in close proximity. By bringing ECHO researchers and community partners together, we are poised to make a difference in children's health research within our region.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder: an institutional ethnography examining communication pathways between multidisciplinary support systems and diagnosed youth.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES' HEALTH; CHILD AND YOUTH HEALTH; COMMUNITY-BASED; FETAL ALCOHOL SPECTRUM DISORDER; GENDER & HEALTH; HEALTH SERVICES & POLICY; HUMAN DEVELOPMENT; INSTITUTIONAL ETHNOGRAPHY; INTERDISCIPLINARY; MENTAL HEALTH & ADDICTIONS; STRENGTHS-BASED
Abstract-Résumé: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is caused by prenatal exposure to alcohol. It commonly results in permanent impairments to cognitive, social, behavioural and emotional functioning. Although the exact number of people living with FASD in Canada is not known, people with FASD are over-represented in the child welfare and correctional systems. There is also an unusually high percentage of children and youth diagnosed with FASD in several Canadian Aboriginal communities.   This research seeks to understand the everyday lives of families and youth affected by FASD in two communities in Newfoundland and Labrador. The goal is to understand how institutions (such as health, education, child welfare, community programs, justice) impact the daily lives of youth living with FASD. Specifically, this project uses qualitative methods to examine the relationships between youth with FASD diagnoses, their families and communities, and government systems including education, health care, child welfare, and corrections. This study will identify gaps in care and promote best practices for the prevention of mental health and addictions problems among youth with FASD.   The research study that is briefly outlined above is the basis for the knowledge dissemination and mobilization plans detailed in this application.  Dissemination Activities This study is designed to include knowledge sharing activities at each stages of the project, including during research development, design, data collection, and analysis. The community information and dissemination strategies have been co-designed with community partners.  I am requesting support for the dissemination of the final research results. The knowledge dissemination activities include: 1) round table discussions and community meetings; 2) individual meetings with community stakeholders, policy and decision-makers; and 3) lay summaries, three-page and ten-page reports, and presentations.

Abstract-Résumé: The Obesity Research Boot Camp is a unique training activity designed for students and new professionals entering the obesity research and practice field. The objective of the Obesity Research Boot Camp is to increase multi-disciplinary understanding of obesity among future researchers and practitioners and to create a sense of community among professionals interested in obesity.  The curriculum covers all aspects of obesity ranging from epidemiology and public health to cell biology, energy, regulation, clinical management. The Annual Obesity Research Boot Camp consists of eight days of intensive teaching and networking and is offered to 24 Canadian and international trainees and new professionals. Over the last eight year, a total of 192 students have successfully graduated from the annual Obesity Research Boot Camp. Results from a recent social networking analysis of Boot Camp graduates show that the program is effective in stimulating collaborations between participants. In addition, the program also helps trainees advance their career and contributes to their continuing engagement obesity field.  The 2014 Annual Obesity Research Boot Camp will be held in Kananaskis, Alberta.

TitreApplicationTitle: Disséminer pour mobiliser. Des enjeux de la prévention du VIH et de l'accès aux services chez les hommes ayant des relations sexuelles avec d'autres hommes, à l'ACTION
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCES AUX SERVICES; APPLICATION DES CONNAISSANCES; DISSEMINATION; ENGAGEMENT DES CITOYENS; HOMMES AYANT DES RELATIONS SEXUELLES AVEC D'AUTRES HOMMES; INTEGRATION ET COORDINATION DES SERVICES; INEGALITES SOCIALES DE SANTE; MOBILISATION COMMUNAUTAIRE; PREVENTION COMBINEE; PREVENTION DU VIH/SIDA
Abstract-Résumé: La presente demande propose des activites qui contribueront a la dissemination, a l'echange et a la mise en pratique de donnees permettant de faire le point sur les enjeux actuels de la prevention aupres des hommes ayant des relations sexuelles avec d'autres hommes (HRSH) dans la communaute gaie montrealaise et d'evaluer la capacite communautaire a mettre en place des interventions combinees. Le projet comporte quatre objectifs : 1) disseminer les resultats engendres par deux volets de recherche realises en 2012 sur les enjeux de la prevention aupres des HRSH et les defis lies a l'acces aux services preventifs de tous ordres; 2) mobiliser les HRSH de divers milieux pour recueillir leurs interpretations de ces resultats a la lumiere de leurs propres experiences et besoins et pour recueillir leurs propositions pour l'action en matiere de prevention combinee du VIH/sida a Montreal; 3) organiser un forum communautaire dont l'objectif sera l'etablissement de priorites d'action en matiere de prevention combinee du VIH/sida chez les HRSH a Montreal; 4) rediger et diffuser des Actes ou figurent les constats souleves et les plans d'action elabores lors du forum communautaire. Les activites proposees visent d'abord les utilisateurs de connaissances tant communautaires que du reseau de la sante, les citoyens, puis les chercheurs impliques en prevention. Elles leur permettront de clarifier leurs positions et d'orienter leur travail vers un objectif commun et partage. Dans l'ensemble, ce projet favorisera l'acces aux services de prevention chez les HRSH, contribuant ainsi a la reduction des inegalites sociales de sante, et il facilitera l'integration et la coordination de ces services de maniere a favoriser la mise en place d'interventions combinees, jugees plus efficaces pour reduire la transmission du VIH a l'echelle individuelle et communautaire.

TitreApplicationTitle: Addressing oral health inequalities among children of newcomers: lessons learned from community-based research
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIERS TO PREVENTIVE ORAL HEALTH; IMMIGRANTS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NEWCOMER FAMILIES; ORAL HEALTH AWARENESS; ORAL HEALTH EDUCATION; PEDIATRIC ORAL HEALTH; REFUGEES
Abstract-Résumé: The oral health status of young children from recent immigrant or refugee families is very poor compared to the rest of the Canadian population. There are many barriers encountered when trying to access newcomer families to provide oral health care to their young children, such as language and cultural issues. Two community-based organizations, comprised of members from the many linguistic and cultural groups within the Edmonton region, have been successful in helping newcomer families access health care services and navigate the government systems. Over the past 6 years, we have worked closely with these organizations to access the newcomers and learn about the oral health needs of these children (birth to 6 yrs). We have also identified barriers to the uptake of existing oral health services specific for these families. These two organizations have invited us to share our research findings to their workers. The proposed event will increase the workers awareness of extensive oral health care needs of the young children. As well, we will provide clear direction as to how workers can facilitate a family's access to regional oral health services and programs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing a Website to Inform Canadian Patients about Ethical Issues in Medical Tourism
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHICS; MEDICAL TOURISM; ONLINE DISSEMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Medical Tourism is a practice where patients, including many Canadians, travel to another country and pay out-of-pocket for medical care. Many ethical concerns have been raised about medical tourism. Medical tourists may have difficulty determining the quality of care abroad and are challenged in accessing follow up care for their procedures once home. They may burden their home health systems if they require emergency or follow-up care. Moreover, many of the countries serving as destinations for medical tourists may have trouble taking care of the health care needs of their own citizens, a problem which medical tourism may make worse. Based on these and other ethical concerns (and funded by a CIHR Catalyst: Ethics grant), we developed a 1-page information sheet for Canadians considering engaging in medical tourism that informs them about a range of ethical issues related to medical tourism. While developing it, we received feedback from medical tourism stakeholders that a website linked to the information sheet would be extremely helpful for potential medical tourists. These stakeholders noted that a website would allow for more information than is provided in the sheet's current form, could be updated as new information on the ethical issues related to medical tourism becomes available, and would be more visible to patients looking into medical tourism online. Through this Dissemination Grant we will: 1) Design a website that will complement our existing information sheet on the ethical issues related to medical tourism; 2) Continuously update this website so potential medical tourists can make well-informed decisions about their health; and 3) Enhance our team's role in engaging with potential medical tourists in order to raise awareness of the potential impacts of this practice. These goals will allow us work with diverse medical tourism stakeholders in disseminating important information about the ethical issues raised by medical tourism.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Activités de dissémination - Annonce de priorités : éthique
TitreApplicationTitle: Cool, calm and collected: CAHR/UWW Data collection skill development workshop
Keywords-MotsClés: DATA COLLECTION; ETHICS; HIV; METHODS; RIGOUR; WORKSHOP
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Association for HIV Research (CAHR) is the professional organization for HIV and AIDS research in Canada or by Canadians. CAHR includes all researchers and all disciplines of the scientific approaches to HIV and AIDS to improve prevention and treatment and ultimately for its eradication and cure. A key element of CAHR's mission is to promote education and the development of new researchers.  Universities Without Walls (UWW), the educational and training arm of the CIHR Centre for REACH in HIV/AIDS, provides a national interdisciplinary learning and mentorship program, connecting academics, community members and policy makers to explore HIV research together. Together, CAHR and UWW will be hosting the first ever HIV/AIDS Data Collection Skills Development Workshop at the CAHR 2013 Conference in St. John's, Newfoundland. While students may learn about data collection methods in their university studies (e.g. informed consent, recruitment, design, instrument and question construction and rigour), few get the opportunity to explore challenges related to methods and develop the skills necessary to respond effectively and collect data with skill and confidence. UWW evaluations indicate that new HIV researchers need opportunities for workshops to build on skills learned in the classroom by simulating complex data collection scenarios. The workshop has the further objective of integrating discussion of research ethics with research methods to promote critical thinking about the impact of the research process on participants and research outcomes. This workshop will provide a unique opportunity to address a number of key gaps in graduate training with a focus on the realities of conducting HIV research with vulnerable populations. Accordingly, this new workshop will aim to provide new researchers with the opportunity to develop data collection tools and practice the skills necessary to implement ethical data collection in the field.

Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; SIGNALLING PATHWAYS
Abstract-Résumé: This Conference is aimed at enhancing the diffusion of scientific information amongst Canadian scientists, health care workers and stakeholders interested in signal transduction pathways and their involvement in human diseases, in particular cancer. It will be held at the Banff Conference Centre and will include speakers working on various aspects of cell signalling and cancer, both basic and translational, from across Canada. In addition, a tenth of the speakers will be from the United States. An attendance of 150-200 scientists is expected, including principal investigators, postdoctoral fellows and graduate students. It is expected that this Conference will both highlight and enhance the quality of research on signal transduction and cancer in Canada.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Cell-Matrix Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic mutations in extracellular microfibrillar systems lead to a wide spectrum of connective tissue disorders with severe cardiovascular, skeletal and ocular symptoms. The goal of this project is to identify components, mechanisms and cell dynamics of microfibril biology in health and disease by a multi-disciplinary approach using biochemical, cell biological and mouse models. I expect that information obtained from this work will increase knowledge of microfibrillar function and will directly contribute to the design of diagnostic, therapeutic and preventative strategies for the associated disorders. This will benefit affected individuals and the society in Canada and worldwide.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: EXERCISE RECOMMENDATIONS IN HEALTHY AGING
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: The aging of the population is associated with an increased prevalence of chronic diseases (such as type 2 diabetes) and disability. Unfortunately, both conditions lead to dramatic losses of physical function and increased human and financial burden.  Learning from exercise physiology principles, we will develop specific exercise programs, efficient at preventing these health problems in individuals who have been identified at risk. Using my expertise in conducting large exercise trials, this Canada Research Chair will thus seek to improve older adults health by proposing exercise recommendations aimed at preventing type 2 diabetes and physical disability in high risk older adults.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Oncogenesis and Metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Macrophages teach benign cancer cells how spread and become metastatic and therefore lethal. Macrophages must chew their way from the blood through the tissue material that surrounds the tumor in order to reach the cancer cells in the tumor. Macrophages use the cell surface protein, S100A10, to remove tissue barriers and arrive at sites of inflammation. We will use the PyMT mouse model of breast cancer to determine if macrophages require S100A10 to a reach the breast tumor site and promote tumor and metastatic growth.  Knowledge of how S100A10 affects tumor metastasis will provide promising targets for clinical intervention.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Human Vision and Eye Movement
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: This program explores how the human brain processes visual input and generates eye movements. In particular it focuses on the recognition of objects like faces and words. It uses functional MRI to reveal the network of brain regions involved, and adaptation techniques to show how these objects are represented in the brain. Such information is applied to study neurological patients, and to the design of rehabilitative strategies to improve perceptual function. Eye movements are used to study cognitive influences on behaviour, and how these might be disrupted in patients, such as those with schizophrenia.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: One in 5 Canadians over the age of 40 suffer from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD kills more than 10,000 Canadians each year and is the number one reason why adult Canadians become hospitalized. Nearly $4 billion dollars are spent each year in Canada for COPD care, which will grow to $10 billions/yr by 2030 unless new solutions can be found. The major reason for the high cost of COPD care in Canada is hospitalizations owing to "lung attacks". We want to prevent these lung attacks by developing a simple blood test that can be used in a doctor's office to predict which COPD patients will have a "lung attack" in the next few months and which patients will not. We also want to develop a simple blood test to diagnose lung attacks in their earliest stages (before the onset of a full blown attack). These blood tests will help doctors to treat and prevent full blown lung attacks from taking place, so patients can be treated at home and thus reduce the number of patients having to seek emergency care at hospitals.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Diabetes and Pancreatic Beta-cell Function
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes mellitus is characterized by insufficient production of the hormone insulin, resulting in elevated blood glucose levels. Dr. Poitouts research program has two main objectives: 1- To define the role and mechanisms of action of the receptor GPR40, a novel drug target for the treatment of diabetes; 2- To understand the signaling and molecular mechanisms by which chronically elevated fatty acids alter the function of the pancreatic beta-cells that secrete insulin. The long-term goal of this program is to improve the prevention and treatment of diabetes, which affect 8% of the Canadian population.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Nucleosome Assembly and Genome Integrity
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, NA
Abstract-Résumé: DNA Packaging Proteins and DNA Repair Cells are constantly exposed to chemicals that cause extremely harmful DNA breaks. Fortunately, cells contain a number of dedicated proteins that repair DNA. In order to gain access to DNA and repair the damage, cells first need to modify proteins that tightly package DNA. We showed that vitamin B3 blocks fungal-specific enzymes that modify DNA packaging proteins, leading to catastrophic DNA damage in fungal pathogens. We investigate whether vitamin B3 will prove valuable to fight human infections. This is important because systemic infections associated with high mortality rates frequently occur following cancer chemotherapy.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Neurosciences
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: I study spinal cord development, disease and treatment using a simple vertebrate model.  We pioneered the use of zebrafish for these studies by generating models of neural progenitor differentiation and of neurodegeneration genetics.  We also collaborate on nematode worm and mouse models.  We will characterize the roles we discovered for the neurotransmitters glycine and GABA in regulating neural progenitor differentiation during development, during regeneration following injury and during degeneration in peripheral neuropathy.  We will also explore genetic and synaptic networks that may be common to neurodegenerative diseases and will develop models to be used for screening compounds as novel therapeutics.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Neurobiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: The Canada Research Chair in Molecular Neurobiology is focused on understanding why many drugs that target receptor proteins called G protein-coupled receptors become less effective for the treatment of disease and how these receptors that respond to these drugs can be targeted to treat both neuropsychiatric and degenerative diseases such as anxiety and depression, Huntingtons disease and Alzheimers disease.  Dr. Ferguson is developing novel reagents to investigate alterations in receptor activity both in single live cells and animal models of disease.  Dr. Fergusons research will be important for the development of strategies and therapies to treat neurological diseases.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Predictive Genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and its complications represent a major health burden in Canada. The development of reliable detection tools for early identification of patients at risk for T2D complications is critical. We propose to progressively replace outcome markers that are included in current risk index scores by validated outcome predictors, in the form of DNA-based markers of susceptibility. Diabetes and pre-diabetes affect over 9 million Canadians and 366 million worldwide. There is substantial evidence that if diabetes predisposition or complications are detected in time, they can be prevented or delayed through lifestyle changes or medication.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza and other respiratory viruses are a leading cause of medical consultations and hospitalizations in Canada. However, there are limited therapeutic options for these viruses and current influenza vaccines have suboptimal efficacy. In the next seven years, Dr Guy Boivin's research group will study the evolution of these respiratory viruses over time and the emergence of resistance to current antivirals. In addition, his team will continue the development of innovative therapeutic strategies based on combination of antivirals and anti-inflammatory molecules. Finally, he will pursue the development of more protective vaccines by using potent adjuvants and new routes of administration (intra-nasal and intra-dermal).

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Translational Visual Science
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Diseases such as glaucoma, macular degeneration, multiple sclerosis, and stroke can cause irreversible blindness because they cause death of neurons, a cell type that does not replace itself in humans. The goal of Dr. Levin's research is to develop novel treatments that protect or preserve neurons from various kinds of injury, based on study of the mechanisms by which the injury causes neuronal death. The eventual goal is to translate these treatments into therapies that could be used to preserve vision in patients with progressive or unremitting disease of the visual system.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Allergy & Immune Tolerance
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Larchés research program is focused on developing curative treatments for chronic inflammatory diseases, which significantly burden Canadians health and the health care system.  To date he has developed four allergy vaccines (cat; ragweed; house dust mite; grass pollen) that are currently in clinical trials). He will continue to develop three other allergy vaccines (tree pollens; mould) and evaluate whether a peptide vaccine can address the pressing problem of severe peanut allergy, over the tenure of his next CRC. Dr. Larché will continue this work by translating his technology into non-allergic chronic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and transplant rejection.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Human Stem Cell Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Bhatias research focuses on achieving appropriate differentiation of human stem cells to endpoint cell types that can be used for either cell transplantation in patients or cells in large quantities in vitro for drug discovery and disease modeling. As understanding human stem cells requires a fundamental elucidation of self-renewal pathways, Dr. Bhatias research directly impacts cancer biology, specifically cancer stem cells. Dr. Bhatia has created novel tools and methodologies to generate and manipulate human stem cells towards improved differentiation, but also compared cancer stem cells to normal counterparts towards developing novel and robust quantitative assays to identify selective drugs.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Matrix Dynamics
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Diseases of connective tissues (e.g. periodontal diseases, arthritis) are high prevalence health care problems. Connective tissues are distributed throughout the body and play key roles in supporting, attaching and stabilizing tissues and organs. The proposed research program examines the fundamental mechanisms that regulate connective tissue remodeling. The applicant's research program will build upon his existing strengths and greatly improve understanding of the cell signalling systems that regulate connective tissue remodeling. This knowledge will provide new opportunities for therapies that prevent untimely and inappropriate matrix remodeling as is seen in fibrotic diseases of periodontium, kidney, heart and joints.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Proteomics, Bioinformatics and Functional Genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: Research in Dr. Boone's laboratory makes use of the powerful experimental accessibility of a model organism, the budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, to understand the cell growth and division of normal and diseased states. Dr. Boone's research program will develop and apply novel functional and chemical genomic approaches to establish a comprehensive functional wiring diagram of a cell. This research is highly relevant to the genetic bases of complex diseases and the discovery of drug targets and it will provide an unprecedented genome-scale view of gene function and the first global genetic network of a cell.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: RNA transport
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: The instructions for life are encoded in DNA and are stored within a specialized compartment of the cell called the nucleus. The sharing of this information is essential for life and is accomplished by copying DNA into a secondary molecule called RNA, which is transported out of the nucleus to be shared with the rest of the cell. It is well established that changes in RNA transport are associated with disease and viral infection. My work aims to understand the mechanism of RNA transport and provide a foundation for improved understanding, diagnosis, and treatment of human disease.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Viral Pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Viral infections of the lungs are the leading reason for hospital admissions of children in Canada. Whereas Respiratory Syncytial virus and influenza are much more common virus infections, there is a virus called Coxsackie that causes severe heart infection in infants that goes on to cause heart failure, the only treatment for which is heart transplantation. There is no effective antiviral strategy to treat infections by any of these viruses, and so by understanding these viruses we are discovering common traits between virus infections such that we can develop broad-spectrum antiviral drugs to treat infection by any virus.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: T helper cell function during infection
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Infections ranging from viruses to parasites elicit vigorous antibody responses critical for host protection. In fact, vaccine efficacy is defined by the generation of robust pathogen-specific antibodies. These effective humoral immune responses depend on helper T cells that directly interact with B cells to induce antibody production. Using novel approaches to investigate how T and B cells communicate across diverse settings of infection, the overall goal of my research program is to identify the fundamental mechanisms that lead to protective humoral immunity and use this information to improve current vaccine and therapeutic approaches for clinical application.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Cancer Stem Cell Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this research program is to investigate the unique properties of human cancer stem cells and to develop therapies that target them. Similar to normal stem cells, cancer stem cells are rare cells that are the only cells capable of initiating and sustaining the disease, producing all the subsequent cancer cells in a patient. There is evidence that these cells influence patient outcome through, for example, resistance to therapy and by causing relapse.  By increasing our understanding of these cells we will improve patient survival through improved prognostic indicators and the development of novel treatments.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Cytoskeletal Dynamics and Cell Division
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: For a fertilized egg to become a person, or for tissues like the skin and digestive tract to be replenished due to wear and tear, cells must multiply. We are working to understand how one cell physically splits into two copies of itself. Knowing how cells normally multiply is key to treating cancer cells that grow abnormally, so our work will inform the development of anti-cancer drugs that target the tumor and not other tissues.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Hematopoiesis and Lymphocyte Development
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Our blood is produced from bone marrow stem cells in the process of hematopoiesis. This process requires precise regulation of gene expression and DNA repair, and its disruptions result in many life-threatening disorders. Chromatin modifying proteins control DNA packaging, gene expression, DNA repair, and thus stem cell differentiation in development and hematopoiesis. In recent work we demonstrated that chromatin modifying factor MYSM1 is required for blood cell production. Our work aims to provide a comprehensive characterization of the functions of MYSM1 and other members of its protein family in stem cells, hematopoiesis, and immunity, enhancing our fundamental knowledge of these systems, and in the long-term contributing to better treatment of hematological disorders.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolomics for Functional Enzyme Discovery
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Renewable energy sources
Abstract-Résumé: There are two tremendous gaps in our understanding of cell metabolism. First, there are many chemical reactions that are known to occur as cells break down nutrients, yet we do not know the genes that enable these reactions. Second, current metabolomics technology has discovered hundreds of chemicals in cells that are not predicted by the current knowledge of metabolism. This proposal will identify the missing enzymes, characterize these new compounds, and discover the role of these new pathways. New enzyme pathways will provide new drug targets for blocking the growth of cancer cells.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Medicinal Chemistry
Keywords-MotsClés: Pharmaceutical products, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: We aim to develop a novel class of anti-cancer drug that target critical mediators of human cancer progression. Persistently activated STAT5 protein is prevalent in leukemia, promoting resistance to cell death and contributing directly to drug resistance. We plan to inhibit STAT5 through the development of novel therapeutics that block its cancer-promoting role in leukemia. Our particular molecular designs and approach represent an entirely novel route to inhibit a critical tumor-promoting protein, thereby generating a more useful class of anti-cancer drug.Our objective is to develop the first drug-like STAT5 inhibitor and validate its application in treating blood cancers.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolism in Human Stem Cells and Cancer Development
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The rise in obesity over the past decade and its link to diabetes and cancer has increased interest in fat tissue biology. Therefore, the nominees research focuses on the role of fat in a disease setting, by studying fat development from stem cells obtained from healthy, diabetic patients, obese patients or patients suffering from cancers. The fat cells produced from sick versus healthy patients will be examined to gain a better understanding of the role of fat development in these devastating diseases; and will also provide an opportunity to identify new drug treatment approaches and cell source for soft-tissue reconstruction.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Computational Cancer Genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding the properties of tumour cells relies on analyzing their genomes for mutations. Reecent advances in DNA sequencing have enabled addressing three fundamental questions in cancer:  i) What mutations are present in different types of cancers?  ii) Which mutations alter the phenotype of cancer cells? iii) What mutations, or combinations of mutations, lead to selective advantages for tumours?    Motivated by these questions, I will develop and apply novel computational solutions to optimally analyze and interpret cancer genomes, improving scientific understanding and therapeutic options for breast, ovarian and lymphoid cancer patients.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Brain lipid metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: Nutrition and food hygiene, Health
Abstract-Résumé: My program examines how fatty acids enter and are handled within the brain.  We are finding that fatty acids are consumed in cell-to-cell communication within the brain.  By knowing how fatty acids enter the brain, we can use radiolabelled fatty acids to image cell-to-cell communication within the brain.  Furthermore, by understanding how fatty acids are consumed in the brain, we can make dietary strategies to increase or decrease their utilization in the brain.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Virology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: In the past decade, viral pathogens have posed a major threat to the Canadian public health infrastructure. Dr. Lees laboratory is interested in understanding the molecular mechanisms at play in the tug-of-war between viruses and host. Specifically, how viruses enter cells and, once they enter, how they are antagonized by innate immune molecules. Immunological recognition and restriction of viral pathogens is fundamental for fighting infectious disease. Dr. Lee adopts an innovative and interdisciplinary approach that merges cutting-edge structural, biochemical, biophysical, immunological and virological techniques to discover new targets and models for the design and development of novel therapeutics.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Patient Reported Outcomes Assessment
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: People with advancing chronic and life-limiting illness present significant challenges to healthcare delivery. These people have complex and multifaceted healthcare needs that seriously affect their quality of life. Routine and comprehensive quality of life assessments can help to make their concerns visible to healthcare professionals so that they can be effectively monitored and addressed. An innovative way to assess patients quality of life concerns and healthcare needs is through the use of patient-reported outcomes. This research aims to establish and evaluate the routine implementation of patient-reported outcomes assessment tools in healthcare delivery for people with advancing chronic life-limiting illness.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Biology and Epigenetics
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: Every living organism is composed of thousands of biological macromolecules capable of forming intricate networks and controlling a plethora of cellular processes.  One of the best approaches to visualize and understand such complex interactions is X-Ray crystallography. This technique allows the resolution, at the atomic level, of the most important and fundamental biological molecules including, but not limited to, DNA, RNA and proteins.  More tangibly, being able to visualize these biological macromolecules has become a powerful asset in the elucidation of molecular determinants triggering cancers and the development of new therapeutic molecules.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Children's Mental Health and Violence Prevention
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding bullying and its link to mental health functioning is incredibly important, considering that approximately 630,000 of Canadian school-aged children (10%) are humiliated and oppressed on a daily basis by their peers. These children suffer from a plethora of issues including concurrent and later maladjustment in academic, externalizing, and internalizing areas. The primary objective of my research program is to examine the etiology, developmental course, and consequences of peer victimization and aggression, focusing on understanding the mechanisms associated with bullying. I am especially interested in researching the neurobiology of peer victimization and understanding why many anti-bullying programs do not work.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Posttranslational Protein Modifications and Metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Vitamin K is an essential micronutrient that is needed for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, including coagulation factors and proteins implicated in mineralized tissue functions. Recent findings suggest that partial vitamin K deficiency may also be linked to the development of obesity, insulin resistance and diabetes. We are interested in uncovering this new function of vitamin K in energy metabolism. Our approach includes the use of genetically modified mouse models in which components of the vitamin K cycle are inactivated in different organs. We are also aiming at identifying new vitamin K dependent proteins implicated in obesity and diabetes.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Bioengineering in Orthopaedics
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed research program is centered on the analysis and modulation of the biological mechanisms of hip implant failures, as well as bone tissue engineering. The ultimate objectives of this research are to improve implant longevity and therefore decrease the morbidity and costs associated with revision surgeries, as well as to offer new treatment options for patients suffering from bone loss. Research is being conducted to better understand the biological mechanisms leading to periprosthetic osteolysis, a major cause of implant failure, and develop therapeutic approaches to control this biological phenomenon. New bone tissue engineering therapies promoting bone substitute mineralization and vascularization, currently a critical challenge in bone tissue engineering, are also being developed. This research is unique and will lead to the development of innovative approaches to prolong implant longevity and improve bone regeneration.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Human Stem Cell Lineage Commitment
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) can differentiate into all adult cell types, including tissues lineages, such as lung, that could have value in therapeutic treatments or as material for drug discovery. However, such applications is hindered by a lack of understanding about the mechanisms that modulate both the initial steps of hPSC lineage commitment and the later specification of lung tissue. Dr Draper studies the genetic pathways and epigenetic processes that regulate how and when hPSCs cells make fate choices that lead to the production of functional lung tissues, yielding insights that will benefit patient care.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Health Promotion and Chronic Disease Management
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed research program aims to examine distance-based health promotion strategies in which to improve health outcomes. These initiatives are designed to improve physical activity behavior and reduce sedentary behavior. Researchers have advocated for the need to develop and assess the efficacy of interventions that employ distance medicine-based approaches (e.g., home-based approaches). Our previous research indicates that among cancer survivors, these approaches are effective at facilitating health behavior change, and are well received. This research program addresses an issue of relevance and importance to the growing numbers of cancer survivors and individuals with chronic disease living in Alberta.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Knowledge Translation in Children's Health
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Canada has the capacity to become a world leader in child health research, however commitment and strategic investment in knowledge translation research is critical. Canada is among the most prosperous nations in the world, yet Canadian childrens health outcomes are surprisingly poor. In part, this is due to a failure to apply the best available research evidence in clinical practice, otherwise known as knowledge translation (KT). Surprisingly, the failure to use the best available research  - even for common acute child health conditions- is pervasive and can result in unnecessary medical treatments, increased suffering and increased health care costs. My research program focuses on improving child health outcomes by developing and evaluating strategies that improve knowledge translation.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Disability Prevention and Rehabilitation
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: Most of us suffer from musculoskeletal pain at least once in our lifetime.  For many, the effect of this pain is benign and short-lived.  However, 1 in 10 Canadians experience disability because of musculoskeletal pain every year. Why people become disabled and others not is a question that  has puzzled researchers for years.   The proposed research program in Disability Prevention and Rehabilitation will investigate the multi-causal nature of musculoskeletal disability and develop methods to prevent and rehabilitate this condition.  This novel research will target the individual and environmental causes of disability and engage knowledge users in the implementation of solutions.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolism and Obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Gregory Steinberg, CRC, researches how obesity causes diverse obesity-related diseases, and how nutrition and exercise maintains good health.  Obesity has complex etiology, yet with it affecting one in four Canadians, strategies for preventing and treating obesity and its related disorders are urgently needed. Dr. Steinbergs research into how fat metabolism maintains health and longevity, and its connection with inflammation and commonly used therapeutics, aims to develop obesity and related diseases medicines. Specifically, he studies how genetically modified mice respond to exercise or consume high calorie foods, using whole-body imaging and advanced physiological testing, including protein chemistry and molecular biology.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Critical Care Rehabilitation and Knowledge Translation
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Khos research focuses on effective and creative methods of physiotherapy to help patients stay as strong as possible while they are in the intensive care unit (ICU).  Patients in the ICU are the sickest in the hospital, and need life-saving technology such as breathing machines. If patients survive their critical illness, 1 in 4 have severe weakness impairing their quality of life for up to 5 years after ICU discharge.  As our population ages and the demand for breathing machines increases, Dr. Khos rehabilitation research will help improve function and quality of life in ICU survivors.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Swallowing Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Swallowing disorders (dysphagia) are common in adult patients. There is evidence that dysphagia itself can place patients at greater risk for pneumonia, malnutrition and dehydration. These medical complications slow recovery. Dysphagia can cause choking when food or liquid enters the lungs. Initially, patients fear that their choking will cause them to suffocate and die. Over time, patients are embarrassed by their choking and thus feel forced to dine alone thereby creating feelings of isolation, despair and depression. This research will determine whether early detection of dysphagia with screening will reduce these medical complications and thus improve the patients recovery.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional and Evolutionary Genomics of the Immune System
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the recent advent of vaccines and antibiotics, there are still nearly 15 million deaths every year attributable to the effects of infectious diseases. Although a significant proportion of inter-individual variation in susceptibility to particular microbes can be attributed to environmental factors, a substantial portion is thought to be due to host genetic factors. We propose to use a unique combination of genomic and statistical approaches to identify genes and regulatory pathways that contribute to inter-individual variability in susceptibility to infections. Our work may lead to the implementation of novel preventive strategies against infectious diseases and other immune-related disorders.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Determinants of Healthy Communities
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Social medicine
Abstract-Résumé: Cape Breton and Atlantic Canada experience greater health disparities and decreased access to health-sustaining resources when compared to the Canadian average. Supporting and strengthening the health and well-being of individuals and communities, and enhancing and expanding the determinants of healthy communities in this region, are important health research priorities. This Canada Research Chair in Determinants of Healthy Communities will create a Centre for Community-Engaged Health Research dedicated to researching, supporting, and enhancing the determinants of healthy communities through community-engaged methods and approaches, capacity building and training, a focus on health equity, and a dedication to knowledge dissemination and mobilization.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic Diversity
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Antibodies are fundamental components of the immune system. Humans and other animals produce a vast repertoire of antibodies; sufficiently large to recognize and neutralize virtually any pathogen or toxin. This entails changes (mutations) of the antibody genes that happen in the B lymphocytes during the immune response. We focus on identifying and determining the function and regulation of the proteins that are part of the mechanisms mutating the antibody genes. The efficiency of these mechanisms determines the efficiency of the response and thereby, our health. Defects in these mechanisms cause immunodeficiency. Conversely, malfunctions lead to autoimmune diseases and cancer.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Perinatal Community Health
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Dennis's multidisciplinary program of research has remained highly focused on improving maternal outcomes that impact child development. Her research, which has examined the identification, prevention, and treatment of postpartum depression, is now extending to the examination of the mechanisms through which the risk of maternal, paternal, and dual parental depression translate into child development outcomes. Further, she is evaluating innovative interventions to improve breastfeeding exclusivity rates. Dr. Dennis's research will lead to the development of effective interventions that will significantly impact Canadian families by improving the overall health of new parents while also preventing poor outcomes among children.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in NKT cell Immunobiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) cells play protective or deleterious functions in many diseases, such as cancer, autoimmunity or inflammation. These evolutionary-conserved lymphocytes act at the crossroad between innate and adaptive immunity. They are functionally versatile and can tune the quality and magnitude of immune responses. Although iNKT cells constitute promising targets for future vaccination and immune therapies, we need to better understand their biology to safely target them in the clinic. Our lab works toward deciphering the fundamental mechanisms controlling iNKT cell activation and functional plasticity, and deciphering the functions these cells play during infection and inflammatory bowel disease

NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention de fonctionnement - Appel transnational conjoint sur les maladies rares
DomainesScientifiquesFR: VISION; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Retinitis Pigmentosa diagnosis and therapy: retinal remodeling and optogenetic reactivation of degenerated retina
Keywords-MotsClés: BLINDNESS; OPTOGENETIC; PHOTORECEPTOR; PLASTICITY; RETINA; RETINITIS PIGMENTOSA; THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a hereditary rare disease of the retina leading to incurable blindness. When most photoreceptors degenerate and lose their ability to respond to light, a substantial quantity of dormant cone photoreceptors can persist. The RP retinal tissue therefore contains these dormant cones and two additional neuronal layers. Reactivation of this residual tissue with retinal prostheses can restore some vision in blind patients. We recently showed that optogenetic reactivation of cone photoreceptors with a photosensitive ionic pump could provide an alternative strategy for a greater visual acuity. However, after the photoreceptor degeneration, the retinal tissue continues to undergo a cellular and molecular remodeling, which needs to be considered to optimize future clinical trials. Our first aim is to characterize this tissue plasticity at the functional and anatomical level using optogenetically reactivated tissue. The second aim is to define whether this retinal remodeling can be stopped when the tissue is optogenetically reactivated. Finally, to improve RP diagnosis, we will develop a mathematical analysis of electroretinogram, the clinical electrophysiological measurement of retinal activity, to uncover nearly extinguished signals. Using optogenetically-modified animals, we will also further assess the cellular significance of electroretinogram measurements. OPTOREMODE will therefore pave the way to clinical trials for optogenetic reactivation of the retina in RP patients and improve their diagnosis.

Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 500 000 Canadians are living with Alzheimer's disease (AD). These individuals may have difficulty remembering their loved ones, managing their finances, or performing everyday activities such as getting dressed and making breakfast. Currently, there is no cure for Alzheimer's disease because it is not possible to repair the brain tissues that are progressively damaged in this disorder. As a result, the newest research focuses on ways to identify this devastating illness early on so that degeneration can be prevented and symptoms can be avoided. Non-invasive neuroimaging techniques, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have made it possible to see changes in brain structures that occur early on in the disease process, and there is some preliminary evidence that the earliest changes take place in the brain's connections. This project will use the largest database available to examine both tissue damage and functional changes in the brain's connections. By comparing MRIs from groups of healthy people to those who eventually develop Alzheimer's disease, it will be possible to determine whether these measures can be used as early indicators. The results will have the potential to improve early identification of Alzheimer's disease, so that preventative measures can be applied to spare Canadians from experiencing the ruinous effects of this degenerative disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Manifold learning of longitudinal measures in Alzheimer's disease from the ADNI database
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; CLASSIFICATION; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MANIFOLD LEARNING; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; PREDICTION MODELS; SHAPE ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: It is expected that treatment decisions for Alzheimer's disease (AD) will greatly benefit from diagnostic and prognostic tools that identify individuals likely to progress to dementia sooner. Towards this end, biomarkers of AD based on brain imaging and other types of data have the potential to offer relatively high power to detect longitudinal changes in subjects scanned repeatedly over time. As part of the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), a number of studies analyzed differences in structural changes in MRI, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or imaging data to classify healthy controls from patients with AD or with mild cognitive impairment (MCI); but few have attempted to combine these biomarkers even though they tend to provide complementary information for the diagnosis of AD and MCI. In order to discover compact and meaningful representations of complex multimodal and temporal data, manifold learning has demonstrated the ability to capture the essence of data in a way that fundamentally outperformed linear methodologies. The overall objective of the research proposal is to develop a new manifold learning framework for longitudinal measures used in the context of the neuroimaging datasets. Specifically, the proposed research project will develop an unsupervised framework which can offer a low-dimensional embedding of a neuroimaging data stemming from multiple sources and apply the method on the ADNI dataset to detect early predictors of AD and assess the progression of health controls, as well from MCI to AD. This research project will contribute state-of-the-art tools to learn developmental trajectories of subcortical structures and propose predictive models for the progression of pathologies. The envisioned framework will offer a tremendous advantage in its adaptability to different datasets by transforming complex structures into simplified representations and have a major impact in the discovery of early predictors for neurological disorders.

Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a degenerative brain disorder causing dementia. Treatments to slow or reverse AD are unrealized as are the means for early definitive disease diagnosis. The brain relies on glucose metabolism for many functions and, with radioactive glucose injections and appropriate scanning, changes in brain glucose uptake patterns can signal abnormalities in brain cell function associated with AD. However, detecting abnormal glucose uptake patterns at early stages of AD, prior to development of major brain cell loss and cognitive symptoms, has been difficult. In our imaging studies of an AD mouse model we have observed early, abnormal glucose utilization patterns when we compare glucose metabolism between different regions of the same brain. Traditionally, comparisons are made to only one region, called the cerebellum. Using our new method, the patterns of metabolism in an AD mouse model in the early stages of AD development differ from age-matched normal mice in brain regions responsible for memory and behavior. In this study, we will determine whether these same measurements can be applied for the early diagnosis of AD in humans. To test our novel approach, we will use the extensive clinical and neuroimaging database of the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). It is anticipated that differences in relative glucose metabolism patterns also exists in people with early memory changes that later develop AD. The results may provide an early diagnostic test for AD. Early detection of AD with a brain scan will greatly enhance our ability to diagnose AD at a time when treatments can be most effective.

Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is one of the most common forms of dementia related to ageing. AD currently affects more than 450,000 Canadians, and this number is expected to double in the next two decades (Alzheimer's Foundation for Caregiving in Canada; Statistics Canada). Early recognition of the symptoms that may develop into AD, such as memory loss and mild cognitive impairment, provide an opportunity to slow their progression with the application of emerging therapeutic interventions. These novel medical treatments have been shown to work best when administered at the earliest stages of the disease. Thus, development of more effective therapeutics targeting these early signs should benefit from early identification of the precursor stages of AD.   The pathogenesis of AD affects brain tissue microstructure. These events in turn affect cerebral activity (electrophysiology) and energy metabolism (chemistry). Neuroimaging studies have shown the existence of characteristic anatomical and functional connectivity patterns in subjects with AD or mild cognitive impairment. Measuring the brain's structural and functional integrity may allow us to predict symptom progression, identify subjects at risk for AD, and offer earlier therapeutic intervention.

Abstract-Résumé: With the population aging, the number of people in Canada with Alzheimer disease is expected to increase by 250% in the next 25 years.  The Alzheimer's disease neuroimaging initiative (ADNI) has provided a wealth of information on the progression of this disease and how various indicators of disease change over time.  One of the most important questions when evaluating people with memory complaints is whether they will some day go on to have Alzheimer's disease.  We will use specific measurements of brain damage developed in our laboratory along with other indicators of disease measured in the ADNI study participants to determine if we can predict who and when they will suffer from dementia. A method to predict who will get Alzheimer's disease before they have symptoms will improve treatment planning and help in finding a cure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interactions between Pbp1/ATXN2 and repetitive DNA in cellular lifespan control
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ATAXIA; ATAXIN 2; CALORIE RESTRICTION; CHROMATIN; LONG INTERGENIC NON-CODING RNA (LINCRNA); RESVERATROL; RIBOSOMAL RNA GENES (RDNA); RNA-DNA HYBRIDS; SIRTUINS
Abstract-Résumé: Why do we age, how does it promote disease, and can we control aging? Our bodies are built from millions of living entities called cells. Each cell has a copy of our DNA, which is arranged in thousands of units called genes. The cell often needs multiple copies of particular genes to survive. In fact, more than half of human DNA is repetitive. However, repeats create problems. Every time a cell divides, it makes a second copy of its DNA. Major errors can occur as cells copy DNA repeats. For example, repeated genes can get mixed up uncontrollably between the two DNA copies being prepared for cell division. This leads to the gain/loss of DNA creating so many errors that cells eventually fail to copy DNA and divide. But cells have processes that protect repetitive DNA. We previously found that cells stabilize repetitive DNA by anchoring it to internal cellular structures, much like people literally standing on each others' shoulders in a human tower benefit from holding on to a nearby post. In addition, longevity proteins called sirtuins stabilize repeated DNA by compacting it into tight structures. This would be analogous to people sitting on each others' shoulders in the human tower. This research group has new data indicating that a protein present in yeast and humans stabilizes DNA repeats via a new process similar to that of a police officer ensuring that observers of the human tower do not try to sabotage it. This research will reveal how this protein achieves its policing role to protect repeated DNA and maintain yeast/human cellular lifespan. Mutations in this protein are linked to the neurological diseases ataxia and also ALS.  These diseases disrupt the brain, body movement control, and eventually life. This research will test contributions of DNA repeat instability to disease and point to therapeutic avenues. All in all, this project may allow us to counteract cellular aging and prevent/cure its related diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Connecting the Cell-Type Specific Chromosome Architecture to Gene Regulation, Development and Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCERS; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; CHROMOSOME ARCHITECTURE; DEVELOPMENTAL SYNDROMES; EMBRYONIC STEM CELL; EPIGENETIC; GENE REGULATION; GENOMIC; PLURIPOTENCY; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Like computers, our cells depend on operating systems to drive normal functions. The gene expression programs are the source code our cells rely on to play their biological functions. Corrupted programs can trigger disease. Embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are under scrutiny for their potential in regenerative medicine and represent a great model system to study rules controlling the gene expression program. Factors regulating gene expression programs are often mutated in human diseases and ESCs are a unique model-system to study these transcription-related disease mechanisms. Cellular operating systems require a web of connections to deliver an accurate gene expression program. Each individual gene can be access following a precise number of commands that need to be executed in an orderly fashion. From the last 30 years of research, multiple regulators emerged to control the cell-type specific gene expression program including transcription factors, chromatin regulators and other co-factors. These factors influence the immediate environment surrounding a gene. Using ESCs, we recently discovered a secondary architecture across the genome established by SMC complexes, a protein family conserved through evolution. SMC complexes connect the regulation of the gene expression program with the chromosome architecture opening a new folder of possibilities to regulate genes.   Subunits of SMC complexes are often mutated in cancer and developmental syndrome including the Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS). CdLS is an autosomal dominant syndrome affecting 1 per 10,000 live births and typically characterized by a wide array of developmental defects. Defining how the cellular operating system is regulated is crucial to get one step closer to understanding defective gene expression programs in diseases such as CdLS. Furthermore, this research could open new treatment avenues for other diseases caused by transcription-related events.
