TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the Physical and Functional Interactome of Mitochondria in Yeast
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFINITY PURIFICATION; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MITOCHONDRIAL BIOLOGY; MITOCHONDRIAL GENETIC INTERACTIONS; MITOCHONDRIAL PROTEIN COMPLEX; NETWORK BIOLOGY; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEOMICS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: Mitochondria generate the majority of a cell's energy supply and are required for a large number of diverse cellular functions, including ion homeostasis, respiration, and cell death. Mitochondrial biochemical processes are highly integrated both within and outside the mitochondria (i.e. extramitochondrial pathways). Due to their importance in basic cellular processes, defects in mitochondrial function cause or contribute to a diverse set of human diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders and cancer. Yet, despite their known importance, the role of mitochondrial dysfunction in human diseases is often difficult to pinpoint due to incomplete information about mitochondrial proteins, interactions, and pathways. This proposal seeks to address this deficit by creating detailed mitochondrial physical (protein-protein) and functional (gene-gene, or genetic) interaction maps. Large-scale proteomic and genetic screening procedures, optimized by the proposed research, will be used to comprehensively identify the physical interactions, multiprotein complexes, and pathway relationships among mitochondrial genes in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Physical interaction data will be combined with complementary information on epistatic relationships among these same genes to guide identification of functional pathways and essential mitochondrial complexes. This integrative approach will uncover novel functional mechanisms in mitochondrial biology, facilitating discovery of new therapeutic targets for the treatment of mitochondrial diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Genetic Determinants of Human Sleep and Circadian Rhythms
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIGRAPHY; CEREBRAL CORTEX; CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS; POLYMORPHISM; SLEEP; STATISTICAL GENETICS; STROKE; TRANSCRIPTOME
Abstract-Résumé: Sleep and circadian rhythms (24h biological rhythms regulated by an internal biological clock) have a huge impact on human performance, and affect many common diseases.  However, despite their importance to human biology and performance, our knowledge of the genes important for human sleep and circadian rhythms is incomplete. The overall goal of this study is to identify genes associated with sleep and circadian behavior, to explore the mechanisms whereby they act, and to apply these findings to the prediction of sleep and circadian rhythms in the real world.  To do this, we will take advantage of the observation that sleep and circadian behavior varies between individuals and some of these differences appear to be inherited.  We will use actigraphs - wristwatch-like accelerometers - to non-intrusively measure sleep and circadian behavior in several preexisting large groups of volunteers in Ontario and elsewhere.  Using already-available genetic data form these same individuals, we will examine for natural gene variants associated with variation in sleep and circadian behavior, and examine the effects of these variants on gene expression.   Finally, we will apply our findings to the prediction of sleep and circadian behavior in a community-based population, and to the prediction of stroke timing in individuals who have suffered a stroke.     This study has the potential to identify new genes regulating human sleep and circadian behavior, thereby deepening our understanding of human sleep and circadian rhythms.  In so doing, it may eventually lead to new treatments and management strategies for shift-work, jet lag, and sleep disruption that have enormous social and medical consequences for millions of Canadians, and may facilitate genetically-guided personalization of school, work, travel and other schedules to optimize human performance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the mutations driving non Hodgkin lymphomas and developing plasma-based assays for tumour detection and monitoring
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; DRUG TARGETS; GENOMICS; NON HODGKIN LYMPHOMA; SEQUENCING; SOMATIC MUTATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Lymphomas are a diverse and complex collection of cancers that all arise from cells of our immune system. Some lymphomas are indolent, meaning they grow slowly and result in few symptoms, whereas others are aggressive and can lead to death in a short amount of time. It is well known that specific changes to the DNA in these cells ("mutations") contribute to the formation of these cancers. By understanding the way a cell changes to become a cancer, we can begin to determine how these cells might be efficiently destroyed and thus work towards more effective therapies. Follicular lymphoma (FL) and mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) are two lymphomas that are rarely cured. There is limited knowledge of the mutations that produce these illnesses. This study will use new approaches that can rapidly read ("sequence") the DNA to better understand how FL and MCL cancers arise. We will use similar techniques to compare the genetics of these two diseases to other lymphoma types. This information should allow us to learn how to better diagnose the different lymphoma types and thus better identify the most appropriate treatment for each patient. It has recently been observed that patients with cancer have a detectable signature in their blood from the tumour cells. This study will implement methods for detecting this signature in lymphoma patients, which may allow us to indirectly observe changes to the tumour. We will test whether these assays yield information about tumour growth and whether or not a cancer is responding to therapy. Such tests may ultimately provide clinicians with early indication of disease resistance or relapse, thus providing valuable time needed to alter treatments as necessary.

TitreApplicationTitle: Expanding the number of treatable intellectual disabilities through an integrated "-omics" approach
Keywords-MotsClés: DISCOVERY; GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY; INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; METABOLOMICS; WHOLE EXOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Intellectual disability (ID) affects 2-3% of children and adults, or 140-210 million people worldwide. Defined strictly as low IQ, ID can have devastating lifelong effects on all aspects of life. The health cost of ID equals that of stroke, heart disease and cancer combined. The burden on families is incalculable. In most cases of ID, we do not know the cause (the majority is genetic), and so cannot provide effective treatment. ID can be an unchangeable fate for a child.  Via our "Treatable Intellectual Disability Endeavour in British Columbia" (TIDE-BC) research, we found 81 published ID conditions that could be treated for underlying cause. These "inborn errors of metabolism" usually affect important enzymes and are treated using special diets, medications or stem cell transplants. In TIDE-BC, by careful screening, we identified treatable causes of ID in 5% of patients so far. In some cases, treatment has completely changed the child's life.   Here, our team of doctors and scientists will use a comprehensive and individual approach to discovering more treatable genetic causes of ID. We have studied 8 families so far, and found one new treatable cause and five probable causes. Next ,we expand our approach in a total of 50 families, and the results will be directly implemented it into clinical practice via TIDE-BC. Ultimately, our aim is to be able to quickly diagnose the cause of ID in our patients, so we can provide correct treatments to each child to prevent brain damage and optimize health outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of Gene-Gene Interactions within an Early Risk Pathway for Alzheimer's Disease on Established and Novel MRI-based Phenotypes
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER; GENETICS; IMAGING-GENETICS; MRI; PHENOTYPE
Abstract-Résumé: A considerable proportion of the risk for Alzheimer's disease is due to genetic factors. However, aside from one well-known gene, Apoliprotein E (APOE), little has been uncovered regarding how other genetic factors might cause risk for Alzheimer's disease. In parallel, it is important to identify risk for Alzheimer's disease before clinically observable onset of memory problems and behavioural disturbances. To do that we need to study the relationship between variation in Alzheimer's risk genes and neuroimaging measures, since the brain signature of these risk genes can be measured prior to disease onset. The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) has now completed neuroimaging, genetics, and other biological measures on many hundreds of healthy people, people with Alzheimer's disease, and people in pre-Alzheimer's states known as early and late mild cognitive impairment. This database provides us with an opportunity to explore the effects of previously unexplored genetic interactions on several brain imaging measures. We will not only do this on established brain imaging measures of risk, but also on newer measures that our team has developed that target a part of the brain known as the medial temporal lobe, where the genes we are interested in have known effects on brain structure. If we can show that genes interact to impact brain structure in a way that is over and above that of any one gene alone, we can better predict who will develop Alzheimer's disease. Also, we can develop new treatments targeted toward those specific genetic risk pathways.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying new physiological biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease from functional and perfusion MRI
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; ARTERIAL SPIN LABELING PERFUSION; CARDIAC PULSATILITY; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; RESTING STATE FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; SMALL VESSEL DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common type of dementia and is the result of accumulating beta-amyloid plaques and tau protein tangles, regional loss of brain tissue and a myriad of cognitive symptoms. Diagnostic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be used to quantify the brain tissue lost due to AD, but this structural information provides only one perspective on the disease. Functional and perfusion MRI approaches can also be used to understand the effects of AD, by providing physiological information that pertains to the blood vessels, an important consideration given that cerebrovascular dysfunction is common in AD. In this proposal we will capitalize on the AD Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and attempt to establish the value of functional and perfusion dataset, for their ability to provide biomarker information of cerebrovascular dysfunction in the progression of AD. The objectives of this proposal are to: 1) use resting state fMRI to isolate cardiac pulsatility effects in white matter as a global measure of cerebrovascular dysfunction and 2) use arterial spin labeling perfusion images to establish an optimized analysis approach that yields the sensitivity to detect the progression from mild cognitive impairment to AD. A secondary objective will be to investigate the role of a genetic marker known to be implicated in AD pathology, the APOE e4 allele, in exacerbating cerebrovascular dysfunction. To carry out this research we propose to implement our unique analysis approaches on over one hundred resting-state fMRI and over three hundred arterial spin labeling datasets currently available in ADNI. This research will advance AD research by developing novel non-invasive imaging biomarkers. A positive outcome this proposal could lead to rapid implementation of these imaging-based tools into the neurodegenerative research currently being conducted at the research institutes represented by the applicants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing the Relationship of White Matter Hyperintensities to Neuropsychiatric Symptoms in Patients with Alzheimer's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ADNI; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; IMAGING; VASCULAR DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Cerebral white matter damage, seen on MRI, are assumed to be ischemic lesions and are very common in aging patients as well as patients with Alzheimer's disease. Neuropsychiatric symptoms are common in all types of dementia. The most common neuropsychiatric symptoms encountered in dementia are delusions, hallucinations, agitation, depression, anxiety, apathy, and irritability. These symptoms are a major source of patients' distress, caregiver burden, and a primary contributor to institutionalization. Moreover, while psychotropic drugs may alleviate certain neuropsychiatric symptoms, some have severe effects including a 2-3 times increased risk of a cerebrovascular event, including a stroke. There is increasing awareness that changes in white matter can be associated with neurobehavioral changes including some of the neuropsychiatric symptoms listed above. In AD, the relationship between neuropsychiatric symptoms and the extent and location of white matter damage is unknown. Since vascular disease is treatable, a reduction in vascular-related neuropsychiatric symptoms may prevent (or delay) institutionalization thus saving costs to the health care system while improving quality of life for the patient and family.

Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) continues to adversely impact patients and their families.  One of the main challenges is in early detection of the disease when AD may not present itself much differently from the normal ageing process. Being able to correctly detect AD at a very early stage is very important in the treatment of the disease. A step forward would be to better understand how Alzheimer's disease progresses and develop detection methods that can be used to improve the accuracy of early detection. To do this we will use an international database which contains clinical and imaging data from thousands of patients. We will study two main topics:  First, we will ask which factors are different in normal ageing from the early signs of AD. Second, we will aim to better understand how these factors change as the disease progresses across its different stages. To achieve this, we will use new mathematical techniques we have successfully applied in other disease areas.  Our findings can help change how we think about AD and how doctors treat AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroimaging correlates of delusions in Alzheimer's Disease and related dementias
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; DELUSIONS; IMAGING; PSYCHOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a brain illness that is becoming more common as the population ages.  In about half of patients, false beliefs, referred to as delusions, may develop.  These symptoms are often associated with negative outcomes, such as increased aggression, more rapid functional decline, and premature placement in a long term care facility.  In spite of being common, it is unclear why these symptoms arise and what part of the brain is involved.  Based on preliminary data from analysis of the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database, a large North American database that holds clinical and imaging data on patients with AD, we were able to conclude that reduced grey matter in the right frontal lobe of the brain may be associated with the development of delusions.  However, it remains unclear as to whether these findings also occur in other types of dementia (such as Parkinson's dementia and vascular dementia), or in patients with more severe dementia, and how these findings relate to brain tissue changes at autopsy.  This study proposes to examine structural brain changes in a sample of Alzheimer and related dementia patients with and without delusions matched for age, education, type of dementia, and disease severity using the National Alzheimer's Co-ordinating Centre (NACC) database. The NACC database, compared to ADNI, includes patients with other types of dementia diagnoses, a broader range of disease severity, and neuropathology. We hope the findings from this study will validate our previous findings and ultimately be used to develop effective treatments for AD patients with delusions by identifying a target in the brain for treatment.

Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BIOMARKER; EARLY DIAGNOSIS; FUNCTIONAL CONNECTIVITY NETWORK; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; MULTIVARIATE ANALYSIS; NEUROIMAGING; RESTING-STATE
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) will reach epidemic proportions in the next 25 years. Early diagnosis of AD would dramatically increase the effectiveness of treatment. At an early stage, AD patients display memory loss, but this is not sufficient to differentiate healthy aging from early signs of AD. Likewise brain atrophy, a common measure of AD, is not sufficient for diagnosis at an early stage. This is likely due to the activity in healthy brain regions that compensate for dysfunction and gradual degeneration of the affected regions. By using imaging technology to identify these adaptations, in conjunction with the cognitive and atrophy measures, we plan to develop an effective biomarker for AD.   Neuroimaging methods non-invasively measure brain activity. From these measures we can quantify relationships between different brain areas and measures changes in brain density. The project will rely on a public database that follows AD patients over time, and will take into account compensatory changes in activity between brain regions, changes in structure as the brain atrophies and cognitive measures such as memory loss. By combining these measures and methods we will develop a new diagnostic tool to differentiate patients with mild cognitive impairment who will progress to a dementia of the Alzheimer's type from those who remain stable.   We expect the methods developed in this project to improve the effectiveness of early diagnosis of AD. In addition we anticipate this method will provide us a basis to better understand the dynamics of the illness.

Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; ANGIOTENSIN CONVERTING ENZYME (ACE) INHIBITORS; ANGIOTENSIN RECEPTIVE BLOCKERS (ARB); ATROPHY AND HIPPOCAMPAL VOLUME LOSS; BETA AMYLOID; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; HYPERTENSION; MULTIMODAL IMAGING; RISK MODELLING; SMALL VESSEL DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) affects more than 35 million people worldwide. Approximately 750,000 Canadians have cognitive impairment or AD, a number expected to double within a generation. High blood pressure is an important risk factor for the development of AD and 62% of Canadians at the age of AD onset have high blood pressure. High blood pressure is believed to cause damage in the brain's white matter, appearing as hyperintense lesions (bright spots), increased ventricle size, and brain tissue loss on brain imaging (e.g., MRI). A potential factor in the development of AD is that this damage leads to the build-up of a protein called Beta-amyloid (Abeta), which is found in the brain of patients with AD. Medications called angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) and angiotensin receptive blockers (ARBs) are the most commonly prescribed treatments for high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease prevention. However, these medications have very different effects on how the brain processes and eliminates the Abeta protein from the blood vessels, which might have an important impact on brain structure and cognitive ability. The proposed study will determine whether 1) the risk of increased damage and build up of amyloid in the brain seen on different types of brain imaging differs in elderly adults taking ACEI medication for high blood pressure compared to those taking ARB medication and 2) the risk of decline in cognitive ability differs in people taking these different medications. Our research team will use information from the ADNI database to identify adults treated with these different medications and test for differences in brain damage and cognitive abilities between individuals in each medication group. This study could have an important impact on which medications are prescribed for high blood pressure in elderly adults at risk for AD and may also provide new information about what processes in the brain are involved in the development of AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of Nanotopographies on Osteoblast Adhesion, Migration and Fibronectin Fibrillogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS
Abstract-Résumé: The success of orthopaedic and dental implant materials depends on proper balance of bone formation and resorption around the implant. Osteoblasts, which form bone, adhere and sense their environment via focal adhesions. Changes to the substratum topography, is a desirable way to influence cell behaviour, as it persists for the lifespan of the implant. By understanding the response of osteoblasts to different topographies, implant design can be improved.  The aim of this study was to assess the influence of nanotopographies on osteoblast adhesion, migration and fibrillogenesis. Rat calvarial osteoblasts were seated on glass slides, with nanotopographies etched into the surface (lines, dots). Immunocytochemistry was used to assess adhesion site anchoring proteins vinculin, tensin and extracellular matrix (ECM) molecule fibronectin. Time-lapse video (TLV) was used to analyze cell migration on the surfaces. Focal contacts formed at the peaks of topographies in cells on dot surfaces, while cells on grooved surfaces formed focal contacts parallel to the long axis of the topography. Cells on smooth surfaces formed large adhesion plaques with random orientation. Fibrillar adhesions showed similar, but less pronounced patterning as focal contacts. TLV showed cells on line surfaces migrated in the direction of the topography while cells on other surfaces migrated randomly. No significant difference was seen in migration velocity or distance travelled between surfaces, but cells on lines and dot surfaces tend to travel faster and farther than on smooth surfaces. After 24 and 72 hours, cells on grooved surfaces developed fibronectin fibrils aligned with the topography, while fibronectin on dot and smooth surfaces had a random orientation. Substratum nanotopography has the potential to manipulate osteoblast adhesion, migration and ECM secretion. Understanding how nanotopographies affect osteoblast physiology allows the design of novel implants that facilitate osseointegration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gendered Experiences, Health Considerations, and Biological Markers of Asexuality
Keywords-MotsClés: ASEXUALITY; BIOLOGICAL MARKERS; CLINICAL ASSESSMENT; GENDER; MENTAL HEALTH; PHYSICAL HEALTH; SEX; SEXUAL DYSFUNCTION; SEXUAL ORIENTATION; VAGINAL PHOTOPLETHYSMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Asexuality is loosely defined as a lack of sexual attraction, and estimates suggest that 1% of the population may be asexual. Despite asexual's assertion that this is a sexual orientation, critics suggest that asexuality is better classified as a sexual dysfunction. The implications of the outcome of this debate are significant given the current push towards pharmaceutical treatments for sexual dysfunction. Health care providers may prematurely seek biomedical cures for asexuals who seek treatment, perhaps due to a distressed partner and potential interpersonal strain resulting from differing levels of desire. Research suggests that asexuals do not experience distress, and among asexuals, there are advocacy efforts towards destigmatizing asexuality and legitimizing it as a sexual orientation. Asexuality research has focused on the characterization of asexual individuals. Very little is known about the gendered experience and biological features of asexuality, impact on a person's quality of life, and implications for the health provider working with asexuals. This study aims to advance research on asexuality by investigating the gender, physical, and mental health correlates of asexuality using a combination of questionnaires, clinical interviews and psychophysiological sexual arousal testing to compare asexual, homosexual, bisexual and heterosexual individuals. We hope that this research will lead to educating and reducing stigma surrounding asexuality, and will further determine how asexuality differs from sexual dysfunction, and in fact may represent a sexual orientation. By furthering our understanding of the distinctions between sexual dysfunction and asexuality, this research will lead to improved diagnostic sensitivity in the future, and improve health care of asexual individuals. In addition to contributing to the very small literature on asexuality, the findings will shed light on potential medical implications with interest to the wider community.

TitreApplicationTitle: Kikiskisin Ná: Do you remember? Utilizing Indigenous methodologies to understand experiences of mixed blood Indigenous peoples in identity re-membering
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS
Abstract-Résumé: The overall goal of this research was to create a space for individuals to express the impacts of systems, relationships and the ways in which people come to understand their overall wellbeing and connection to ancestors through stories in personal identity development.  This project expressed a Muskego Inninuwuk methodology as a foundation to explore experiences of individuals who possess both Indigenous and non-Indigenous ancestry in the development of their identities. The use of natural conversations facilitated sitting with and listening to Cree Elders and engaging with the stories of mixed-blood Cree individuals about the stories of their identities.   Identity is the way that we answer the question who am I? It is a search for a place to belong, to connect to those around us in a way that can provide safety and meaning in how we understand who we are. Individual's search for belonging, membership and ultimately connection is a natural human desire linked to wellbeing and health. My research explored personal stories and those stories of our ancestors, to reconnect us with our essential and authentic selves.   Elders shared with me stories of disconnection and intergenerational experiences that caused diversion from the natural progression of Cree identity development as impacts of colonization. From this they also shared their stories of re-connection and healing. Common experiences expressed by mixed-blood Cree participants highlighted the impact of colonization on their understanding and expression of themselves as individuals and as members of larger community, the complexity that underlies their experiences of identity, and how their understanding of wellbeing is connected to healing. Stories shared processes of healing, decolonization and resurgence of Indigenous ways of knowing, being, and doing in reclamation of self.

TitreApplicationTitle: Supporting Community-based Organizations to Reduce Risk: HIV/AIDS specific Primary Healthcare services in select OECD member countries
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED ORGANIZATIONS; HIV/AIDS; INDIGENOUS PEOPLES; OECD; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Community-based organisations (CBOs) play a critical role in the delivery of primary healthcare (PHC) services for those affected by HIV/AIDS. This presentation will explore the role of CBOs, with a focus on Indigenous oriented CBOS, in the provision of HIV/AIDS specific PHC services in selected OECD countries, (i.e. Norway, Sweden, New Zealand, Australia, and Canada) and to provide recommendations. Drawing from a review of literature, we compared the role of CBOs in addressing HIV/AIDS through PHC service delivery in five countries with HIV prevalence rates of or lower than 0.2%, similar population dynamics, rural and remote regions, Indigenous populations, and similar healthcare systems including CBOs. We compared the nation-states' commitment to CBOs in terms of: (1) meeting the needs of Most At Risk Populations (MARPs); (2) CBOs engagement in developing policy; and, (3) funding sources, programs and allocation of funding specific to CBOs.  CBOs play a significant role in the delivery of HIV/AIDS-specific PHC services in all selected countries. While similarities do exist, we found that Canada, Australia, and to a lesser extent, New Zealand, could greatly benefit from the lessons learned in Norway and Sweden, where the coordination of CBOs by the nation/state health system, as well as the development of clear mandates are key to the provision of timely PHC services for those at risk of developing and those living with HIV/AIDS. Internationally, many countries with similar demographic characteristics and health systems could greatly benefit from strengthening CBOs through clearer mandates and dependable access to funding.

Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injury is devastating due to the physical, societal, and economical harms incurred on individuals as well as on our society. Although the spinal cord contains all the circuitry necessary to locomotion, in the absence of commands from the brain, people with spinal cord injuries are unable to walk. Motor recovery can be partially achieved by strategies or therapies intended to regenerate axons from the brain to the spinal cord. Some of these approaches have reported such promising results in animal models that clinical trials are currently underway. However a major obstacle to achieving this goal is the lack of identification and characterization of appropriate targets at the brain and spinal cord levels, as well as the lack of knowledge of the mechanisms of plasticity of these targets. The current program aims to investigate the pathways between the brain and the spinal cord that are important to initiation and modulation of locomotion. This will enable us to identify and characterize the nervous circuits that need to be repaired in order to improve functional recovery following spinal cord injury or neurotrauma affecting the gait.

Abstract-Résumé: ICS Travel Awards In 2000, midwifery was regulated in the Canadian province of Manitoba. Since the inception of the midwifery program, little research has been done to analyze the utilization of regulated midwifery services. Currently, many women are denied access to midwifery care due to the shortage of midwives in Manitoba. A lack of successful educational programs has contributed to the shortage of midwives. The purpose of this study is (1) To describe the utilization of midwifery health care services in Manitoba from 2000/2001 to 2009/2010 and; (2) To explore factors influencing the utilization of regulated midwifery services in Manitoba.  This research will provide valuable information to policy makers regarding what barriers have impacted the utilization of midwifery services in Manitoba. In spite of scientific evidence that supports the midwifery model of care, there remains an inherent struggle to justify and sustain the profession globally. The findings will have implications for maternal/child health professionals to work at improving collaborative efforts to facilitate access to midwifery services for women.

TitreApplicationTitle: A grounded theory of the process of transition for adolescents toward the self-management of their hearing health care
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT; CHILDREN; HEALTHCARE; HEARING LOSS; SELF-MANAGEMENT; TRANSITION
Abstract-Résumé: With the development of universal newborn hearing screening programs many support groups and programs have been developed to support families with infants and young children identified with hearing loss. However, resources and support are often decreased or eliminated as children get older. There is a significant body of literature that examines transitioning adolescents toward the self-management of their healthcare needs associated with chronic diseases. However, limited research exists in this area of audiology for adolescents and there are few resources to assist audiologists and parents through this stage. This study used a constructivist grounded theory approach to examine the process of transition for children and adolescents toward the self-management of their hearing healthcare; the identification of barriers and facilitators to a successful transition and the role of parents, audiologists, and teachers of the deaf and hard of hearing throughout this process. Participants included children and adolescents, 10-18 years of age with hearing loss. In-depth interviews were conducted with the children and children were asked to complete a take-home journal. Interviews were also conducted with individuals who provide significant support for these children including parents, audiologists, and teachers of the deaf and hard of hearing. Data analysis followed a constant comparative method to develop a theory to explain the process of transition for these children. Findings from this study will contribute to the advancement of knowledge in the areas of audiologic management and counselling for children and adolescents with hearing loss.

TitreApplicationTitle: Involvement of leptin in the obesogenic effects of early-life exposure to low-doses of the endocrine disruptor bisphenol-A (BPA)
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL NEUROSCIENCE; DIABETES; ENDOCRINE DISRUPTION; NEUROENDOCRINOLOGY; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity, and its associated metabolic dysfunctions such as type-II diabetes and the metabolic syndrome are a growing epidemic in Canada.   Bisphenol-A (BPA) is a component of polycarbonate plastic, and is commonly found in food and drink containers.  Owing to its chemical structure, BPA has been characterized as an endocrine disrupting compound - a chemical capable of mimicking naturally occurring hormones.  Since BPA can leach out from containers into the food or liquid they hold, human exposure is of serious concern.  Indeed, BPA can be detected in over 90% of Canadians.  Because the hormonal environment during development sets the stage for long-lasting, if not permanent effects, knowing the effects of exposure to BPA early in life is of particular interest.    Our lab has previously shown that early-life exposure to BPA leads to obesity and metabolic alterations reminiscent of the metabolic syndrome.  In this study, we sought to explore how BPA, acting in the capacity of a hormone, affects the development of brain circuitry involved in regulating the processes of feeding and metabolism.  We find a number of alterations in hypothalamic circuitry that could account for the obesogenic effects of BPA.  Moreover, in our most recent study we have further elucidated the genesis of this effect by demonstrating that the early postnatal leptin surge - a phenomenon critical for successful development of brain metabolic circuitry - is stunted and delayed in  BPA exposed mice.  This provides a mechanistic basis for our observations.

TitreApplicationTitle: p66ShcA is a Molecular Driver of Breast Cancer Plasticity by Promoting an Epithelial to Mesenchymal Transition
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CLAUDIN-LOW; DIFFERENTIATION; EPITHELIAL TO MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION (EMT); ERBB2-DRIVEN BREAST CANCER; MET SIGNALING; PLASTICITY; RECEPTOR TYROSINE KINASE SIGNALING; SHCA
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic and clinical studies demonstrate that the Src homology and collagen A (ShcA) adaptor protein is indispensable during breast cancer progression; however the role of the longest isoform (p66ShcA) remains poorly understood. We discovered that p66ShcA is specifically expressed in human basal breast cancer cell lines. Intriguingly, injection of ErbB2-driven breast cancer cells stably overexpressing p66 into the mammary fat pad gave rise to tumors with mesenchymal features relative to vector controls. The epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) endows epithelial cells with mesenchymal characteristics and promotes an invasive phenotype. Indeed, further characterization revealed p66ShcA tumors underwent an EMT distinguished by reduced expression of luminal markers: E-cadherin, claudins 3/4/7, and cytokeratins 8/18 co-incident with increased expression of mesenchymal markers vimentin and smooth muscle actin (SMA). This corresponded with elevated cytokeratin 14 positivity in p66 tumors. Moreover, mRNA expression of EMT-inducing transcription factors: Slug, Twist 1/2 and Zeb 1/2 were significantly elevated in p66ShcA tumors. Corroborating our data, endogenous p66ShcA is upregulated in a novel Met-driven transgenic mouse model of basal breast cancer (MMTV-Met-p53+/-) that undergo an EMT. Notably, we identified activated Met signaling in ErbB2-driven p66ShcA tumors. We hypothesize p66ShcA may elevate Met signaling in order to promote an EMT. Finally, we show that increasing p66ShcA mRNA levels stratify primary breast tumors with elevated EMT markers, independently of breast cancer subtype. Our data provide compelling evidence suggesting that p66ShcA promotes the dedifferentiation of breast tumors by catalyzing an EMT.

TitreApplicationTitle: Unraveling the role of the MAPK pathway in alternative splicing regulation through CDK12 phosphorylation
Keywords-MotsClés: CLONAGE; MAP KINASES; PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEINES RECOMBINANTES; PROTEOMIQUE; RT-PCR A HAUT-DEBIT; VOIES DE SIGNALISATION; EPISSAGE ALTERNATIF
Abstract-Résumé: Alternative splicing is a process by which the human cell uses distinct gene blocks to generate several proteins from a single primary sequence. Consequently, the cell can produce a vast array of proteins from a more efficient genome size. As similar protein isoforms often have different or even opposite functions, the flexibility granted by this process is also crucial in fast adaptation to stress and external cues. It is thought that more than 95% of all expressed genes are subjected to splicing. Misregulation of alternative splicing therefore often leads to diseases, namely up to 50% of all known genetic diseases but also cancer. Indeed, malignant cells often take advantage of the flexibility yielded by alternative splicing to proliferate, invade surrouding tissues and escape death. Although the field of splicing research is expanding quickly, how this process is regulated by the cell is still poorly understood.  ERK1/2 is central protein kinase involved in the control of cell growth and division. It is activated downstream of one of the most often mutated oncogene in cancer, leading to anarchic cel growth and tumor invasion. Many functions of ERK1/2 have been thoroughly studied, but several novel partners continue to arise indicating an even larger role. Interestingly, our lab has identified several potential regulators of alternative splicing as direct targets of ERK1/2. In the present study, we describe the mechanism by which ERK1/2 phosphorylates one of these, the CDK12 protein kinase.  This research subscribes in a cancer-related perspective, as we also evaluate how overactivation of ERK1/2 driven by upstream oncogene mutation affect alternative splicing in favor of tumor progression. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms of this process can also shed light on new pharmacological targets and deliver a unique take from a signaling standpoint.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inhibition of FOXM1 reduces Enzalutamide resistant prostate cancer cell viability
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER STEM CELLS; ENZALUTAMIDE; ICS TRAVEL AWARDS; NOVEL TARGET; PROSTATE CANCER; RESISTANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer (PCa) initially responses to androgen ablation or castration, but progression to incurable castrate-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) often occurs within three years. Androgen receptor pathway inhibitor Enzalutamide (ENZ) has produced promising survival gains of patients with CRPC. However, resistance to this novel therapy also rapidly occurs and novel treatment strategies are needed.  We have recently developed a unique ENZ and castrate-resistant LNCaP xenograft model. To identify key regulators and active pathways in ENZ resistant cells, genome-wide gene expression analysis was performed and analyzed using systems biological approaches. We identified that forkhead box M1 (FOXM1) is one of the key upstream regulators activated in ENZ resistant PCa cells. FOXM1 is overexpressed in several cancers and it is an important regulator of cancer characteristics such as cell cycle, proliferation, invasion, metastases and cancer stem cells. Interestingly, our in silico gene expression analysis indicated that induced FOXM1 target gene signature significantly reduces disease free survival in prostate cancer patients. Moreover, FOXM1 signature was highly expressed in high Gleason score samples in silico. Furthermore, FOXM1 staining correlated with high Gleason score in our tissue microarray data.   Using systems biological approaches, we further found out that the antibiotic ionophore and oxidative stress inducer Monensin that was previously identified as a cancer-specific PCa and a potential cancer stem cell inhibitor, reduces FOXM1 pathway activity in ENZ resistant cells. The in vitro validation results indicated that Monensin reduced cell viability, FOXM1 transcriptional activity as well as FOXM1 protein, gene and its target gene expressions in ENZ resistant PCa cells.   Taken together, the results suggest that inhibition of FOXM1 by Monensin is a potent novel mean to target ENZ resistant prostate cancer.

Abstract-Résumé: Fetal growth restriction (FGR) with infants small for their gestational age at birth, is a major contributor to perinatal illness and death, and for risk of later adverse health outcomes with heart disease, diabetes and neurodevelopment disability. The studies proposed seek to determine the extent to which maternal undernourishment as a causative factor for FGR, also disrupts placental development leading to lowered oxygen in the fetus and thereby increased "oxidative stressors" as potential mediators of injury. The experimental design will use a well studied model of maternal nutrient restriction in pregnant guinea pigs shown to result in placental structural abnormalities and FGR, along with comparative study from human pregnancies with data obtained from a large tertiary care centre patient population. If maternal under nourishment is found to result in lowered oxygen and "oxidative stressors" in relation to the degree of FGR, then treatment strategies aimed at decreasing these stressors can be tested.

TitreApplicationTitle: Complications in Cardiac Hemodynamics and Glucose Metabolism As a Result of Low Birth-Weight and Western Diet Determined by Perfusion CT and PET.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR; COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; GUINEA PIG; IN UTERO; INSULIN RESISTANCE; PERFUSION; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; WESTERN DIET
Abstract-Résumé: The increasing incidence of cardiovascular disease is a major burden on our healthcare system. A critical precursor is the development of insulin resistance (IR) where insulin's ability to stimulate the usage of glucose is impaired. Recent evidence suggests that IR can be a result of suboptimal pregnancy conditions, particularly in situations resulting in babies born of low birth-weight (LBW). Confounding this problem is the readily available western diet (WD, high-fat/high-sugar) in our society. Studies now show the pivotal role a WD plays in the development of IR in liver and heart which subsequently leads to diabetes and heart disease. Additionally cardiac IR is associated with reduced heart size, and impairment of cardiac function. Thus the study of LBW and WD effects on the development of IR in the heart is an important area of research with significant implications. However, despite numerous studies outlining the independent effects of LBW or WD on adult health, the interactions between LBW and WD remain unknown.  We postulate that the combination of LBW and WD will exacerbate the development of heart IR. Our objective was to utilize non-invasive imaging techniques to identify physiological changes in the heart associated with IR development. Using a well established model in the guinea pig, we investigated the physiological changes of LBW and WD. Combining with the latest technology in computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography (PET), we were able to non-invasively characterize changes blood flow and glucose metabolism in the left ventricle. We demonstrated that guinea pigs born of LBW and fed a WD have a reduced heart blood flow in addition to reduced glucose metabolism. These changes are indicative of an alteration in insulin sensitivity and improper cardiac function. Therefore this leads us to conclude that the combined LBW and WD insults may lead to the exacerbation of the IR deficits, resulting to its expression in early adulthood.

Abstract-Résumé: Early childhood development, or ECD, programs are ideally positioned to address the serious health inequities that are experienced by many Aboriginal children. Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINE BEAD ARRAYS; CYTOKINES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; IMMUNITY; PRENATAL MATERNAL STRESS; PRENATAL PROGRAMMING; T HELPER CELLS; WHOLE BLOOD CULTURES
Abstract-Résumé: Psychological stress is capable of altering the body's immune system, but, it is unknown if experiencing psychological stress during pregnancy affects the development of the fetal immune system and what are the long term consequences of such exposure. Project Ice Storm has been following a group of children born from mothers exposed to psychological stress caused the 1998 Ice Storm in Quebec for more than 15 years. We have shown that stress during pregnancy can produce changes in the child's body and psychological functioning. We are currently investigating how stress during pregnancy changes the development of the baby's immune system, and establish what type of changes are produced. When the participants were thirteen years old, we took samples of their blood to analyzed two important indicators of immunity: the proportion of the main types of immune cells, and cytokines, the molecules through which immune cells communicate with each other.  We observed that higher levels of stress in the pregnant mother are related to a small but noticeable reduction of the proportion of T helper cells, which control the type of reaction that the immune system produces facing an infection. T helper cells control other immune cells through the production of cytokines. We also found that higher levels of stress in the pregnant mother induce higher levels of two different groups of cytokines. One group increases inflammation, and the other is normally related with immune responses against parasites, but also associated with allergies and asthma when these cytokines are excessive. The results obtained from our research provide a link between stress in the pregnant mother and health in her child long after birth. This information has an enormous potential for the guidance and implementation of preventive and interventional strategies that could reduce the frequency of diseases associated with the immune system, in this particular case, allergies.

Abstract-Résumé: ICS Travel Award Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are the leading cause of lost-time claims in Ontario, and are a significant burden to society costing employers an estimated $1 billion between 2003 and 2007(1). Ergonomists work to identify workplace risks for MSDs so as to improve worker health and safety. Fast and proactive estimates of MSD risks can be achieved using avatars in virtual reality workstation simulations. When performing these simulations, an assumption is often made that all workers move in an optimal way using the safest posture possible. Despite this over-generalization, this technology has led to significant health-related benefits to workers(2). Research is now needed to account for the fact that there are often multiple ways to perform a given task. Behavioural scientists predict that movements are chosen based on perceived comfort rather than optimal injury-prevention criteria. The present study examined movement patterns during simple reaching tasks in order to better understand the role that comfort plays in how people choose to move, rather than how they ought to move. Twelve participants were asked to pick up a waist-height key-like disk and insert it into a shoulder-height target while their hand orientation was tracked using a motion capture system. Task comfort was manipulated by altering the position of the disk and the target location between trials. Posture differences were compared across 24 different conditions. The study findings help inform when, why, and how movement choices put people at a greater risk of MSDs. TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Youth Network for Innovation in Mental Health
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS PORTALS; EVIDENCE-BASED; HIGH-VOLUME LOW-INTENSITY; IMPLEMENTATION SCIENCE; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE AND TRANSFER; MENTAL HEALTH LITERACY; PARTICIPANT DRIVEN; PRIMARY CARE CAPACITY; SCHOOL MENTAL HEALTH; YOUTH MENTAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Although mental illness is one of the largest burdens of disease in young people (WHO, 2001), the majority of Canadian youth who need mental health care do not receive it when they need it and where they need it.  The goal of the Canadian Youth Network for Innovation in Mental Health (CAYNIM) is to improve the way in which youth and families are able to access mental health care. By creating links between schools and primary health care, increasing the mental health literacy (i.e., knowledge and understanding of mental health) of youth and the people in their daily lives (e.g., families, educators, youth service workers), and enhancing the mental health competency of primary care practitioners (e.g., doctors, nurses, etc.), youth in need will be identified earlier and receive more timely and effective care.  The mental health training, and identification and care of youth with mental illness will be informed by "Best-In-Class Interventions" (BICI's), which are bundles of feasible interventions that research finds effective or promising, and that families/youth find acceptable. BICI's can then be implemented and evaluated by trained providers in schools and primary health care settings at designated implementation sites nationwide that are reflective of Canada's diverse landscape. These bundles help ensure that youth in remote/disadvantaged locations will have access to the same effective treatments as youth in urban/well-serviced areas.   Transformative change is not an easy process. Creating entirely new structures is expensive, difficult and likely to be met with considerable resistance. A major benefit to CAYNIM's approach is that it changes how existing systems (e.g., schools and primary health care) relate to one another, rather than creating new stand-alone programs that would have difficulty succeeding in a 5-year time frame. The pathways to care proposed by CAYNIM are effective, feasible, cost-effective, and most importantly, driven by youth and families.

Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH SERVICES; MENTAL HEALTH; SCHOOLS; SCREENING; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: The majority of serious mental illnesses and addictions begin during adolescence. It is clear that the effectiveness of early intervention is limited by the barriers that youth face in accessing mental health/addiction services and by the often ineffective delivery of services. This has led to a crisis of access for youth who require levels of mental health service that are developmentally sensitive and youth-friendly. The irony is that the population most "at risk" for serious mental disorder is the least well served by our mental health services. Our overall strategy is to develop a network that leads to transformational systems change in youth mental health and addiction services for youth aged 11 to 25. We believe change can be achieved if we have a network that engages all relevant stakeholders, especially youth and families. We are proposing an easily accessible, continuous, comprehensive, youth/family centred, coordinated, compassionate and culturally sensitive evidence-based mental health care model. A school-based targeted prevention program will be provided to students with early signs of mental health/addiction problems identified through screening or self-referral. It will be linked to an "Integrated Collaborative Care Team" that consists of aggressive out-reach services to places where youth in need find themselves. Each youth will have a case navigator and receive peer support, and based on a comprehensive, standardized assessment, will receive either a low intensity intervention for youth with mild to moderate problems or a high intensity intervention for youth with more severe problems. It is our ethical and professional responsibility to implement and evaluate models of care that are evidence based and responsive to youth and their families. We are confident that the models that we are proposing will transform the mental health system for youth in Canada and will reduce the burden of suffering associated with mental health disorders in this country.

Despite this being known, the outcomes of mental disorders have remained unacceptable. Only 20-25% of Canadian youth who need help for mental health issues actually get it. TitreApplicationTitle: Safety of antiepileptic drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIEPILEPTIC DRUGS; COMPARATIVE SAFETY; NEURODEVELOPMENTAL OUTCOMES; TERATOGENICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is a condition in which the individual experiences recurrent seizures.  It is the most common chronic neurological condition, affecting 0.6 to 1% of the population. Antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) can prevent seizures and avoid their consequences.  Given that approximately 1/3 of people receiving AEDs are of reproductive age and almost half of pregnancies are unplanned, the fetus may be exposed to AEDs in the first trimester of pregnancy, which is the critical stage of fetal organ differentiation and development. Many AEDs can cross the placenta and therefore pose risks to the fetus including major congenital malformations, minor anomalies, fetal growth restriction, early cognitive and developmental delays, and infant mortality amongst others. This review will provide information to Health Canada, women and their health care providers about these risks and will facilitate evidence-informed decision making.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparative safety and effectiveness of antiretroviral therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; HIV INFECTION; PREGNANCY; TERATOGENICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Data from the World Health Organisation estimated that there are 1.5 million HIV+ pregnant women worldwide and approximately 57% of them are receiving effective antiretroviral (ARV) therapy. Infants, that are born of HIV+ women who are not adequately treated, are at risk of HIV infection.  In particular, these infants are at risk for HIV transmission during pregnancy, the intrapartum period or potentially through breastfeeding. HIV infection in the neonate is associated with substantial mortality and morbidity.  ARV therapy can reduce maternal-to-child transmission (MTCT) in pregnancy and after delivery.  It can also reduce mortality and morbidity in HIV-infected individuals. Concerns have been raised about the impact of ARV therapy on the fetus and infant.  For example, exposure to maternal ARV therapy may be associated with preterm birth, anemia and low birth weight.  And, some studies have suggested a potential increased risk of congenital abnormalities with ARV therapy. We will complete a systematic review and network meta-analysis of the comparative safety and effectiveness of ARV therapy in exposed infants. This study will inform efforts of policy makers, clinicians and patients who are considering therapy.

Abstract-Résumé: Our goal is to advance an international research agenda that will address research priorities in HIV and rehabilitation by sustaining and expanding partnerships among researchers, clinicians, and community organizations in Canada, United Kingdom (UK) and Ireland. We will plan and implement a 3 day meeting in London, UK October 6-8, 2014. In the first part of this meeting we will facilitate knowledge transfer and exchange (KTE) and enhance partnerships in HIV and rehabilitation research and clinical practice, among people living with HIV, researchers, clinicians, and representatives of community organizations in Canada, UK and Ireland. In the second part of the meeting we will plan two collaborative international research proposals that will address research priorities identified at the recent CIHR-funded International Forum on HIV and Rehabilitation Research. This meeting will be integral to enhancing a productive international collaborative research team of researchers, clinicians and people living with HIV called the Canada-UK-Ireland HIV and Rehabilitation Research Collaborative. We will conduct this meeting in partnership with the Canadian Working Group on HIV and Rehabilitation, British Rehabilitation in HIV Association (RHIVA) and align it with the British HIV Association (BHIVA) Conference to broaden opportunities for KTE and partnership building among the international HIV community. Outcomes from this meeting will include a detailed report, video library of speaker sessions that will be broadly disseminated on knowledge user websites, and the development of two grant applications submitted to funding opportunities in Canada, Ireland and UK. Overall, this meeting will promote knowledge creation, transfer and exchange on HIV rehabilitation in a meaningful way to relevant stakeholders and establish partnerships that will implement an international, coordinated and sustainable response to address new and emerging research priorities in HIV and rehabilitation.

TitreApplicationTitle: SNRI, bupropion and mirtazapine use during pregnancy and the risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIDEPRESSANTS; BUPROPION; CARDIAC MALFORMATIONS; MIRTAZAPINE; PERSISTENT PULMONARY HYPERTENSION OF THE NEWBORN.; PREGNANCY; SNRI
Abstract-Résumé: Studies from the US and Scandinavia have shown that SSRI use during pregnancy, specifically after the 20th week of gestation, was associated with an increased risk of PPHN, a severe condition leading to disability and mortality. As of now however, limited data are available on the risk of PPHN associated with other types of antidepressants such as SNRI (venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine), bupropion, and mirtazapine. Given that PPHN is a rare condition (0.5% prevalence), large population-based cohorts are needed to quantify its association with gestational use of antidepressants. The same holds for the risk of cardiac malformations (a risk factor for PPHN) associated with SNRI, mirtazapine and bupropion. Hence, the objectives of this proposed study are to quantify the association between SNRI, bupropion, and mirtazapine use during pregnancy and the risk of PPHN, and major cardiac malformations (CM). This study will be performed in 2 provinces (Quebec, Saskatchewan) and in the US. All three provinces/state have access to cohorts of pregnant women built with the linkage of administrative databases. Study methodology will be the same in each participating provinces/state and statistical analyses will be performed within each province/state separately. Province-specific results will be combined using meta-analysis methods with the province being the unit of analysis. This will be one of the few studies worldwide and the first study in Canada looking at the important risks of PPHN and CM associated with SNRI, bupropion and mirtazapine use during pregnancy, which will have great public health implication.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimizing Chronic Hepatitis C Treatment Using Pharmacogenomic Biomarkers
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVE SURVEILLANCE; ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS; HEPATITIS C THERAPY; PHARMACOGENOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a global health problem. After 20 or more years of chronic HCV infection, many patients develop liver problems and some will require a liver transplant or die. In Canada it is estimated that more than 250,000 suffer from chronic HCV infection.  This research project investigates the effectiveness and safety of drugs used to treat chronic HCV infections in Canada. The work is in response to questions raised by the Canadian Agency for Drug and Technologies in Health (CADTH) and the Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network (DSEN) regarding the use of genetic markers to optimize therapy for individuals with HCV. Currently four drugs are available in Canada to treat HCV infections, each with varying risk/benefit profiles and costs.  Canadians from British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario who receive therapy for HCV will take part in this study. In participating patients, we will collect information about their HCV therapy, how they have responded, and any adverse effects related to the drugs they take.  Because we know that a person's genetics helps us understand who is more likely to respond to each HCV drug regimen and potentially who is more likely to suffer an adverse drug reaction, we will collect a saliva sample from all patients and conduct genetic analyses.  Based on our results we will develop a prediction tool to help doctors decide on the best HCV drug therapy regimen for each patient. This will also help the Canadian health system most effectively manage the costs of treating patients with HCV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing an interprofessional care (IPC) assessment tool for healthcare teams: A one-day planning forum
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSESSMENT; CLIENT/PATIENT CARE; CONCEPT MAPPING; CONSENSUS BUILDING; EVALUATION; HEALTHCARE TEAMS; INTERPROFESSIONAL CARE
Abstract-Résumé: There is a growing interest in interprofessional care (IPC) as a way to provide and deliver better healthcare. However, it is difficult to evaluate whether this mode of healthcare delivery is better because current tools that are used to measure IPC are limited. Through discussions with key leaders in the area of IPC, it was determined that there are three gaps in the evaluation literature: 1) There does not appear to be any evaluation tool with which healthcare teams may assess and evaluate themselves as an IPC team (as opposed to individual perceptions of certain healthcare professionals); 2) The client/patient perspective does not appear to be included in the development of IPC healthcare team evaluations. If clients/patients are to be included as genuine members of the IPC team, they need to be included in the development of an IPC evaluation tool and; 3) The client/patient does not appear to be considered as a participant in an IPC healthcare team evaluation. A deeper understanding of client/patient healthcare preferences is required to improve quality and services. The purpose of this planning proposal is to host a one-day forum to bring together the IPC community across Canada to form working groups. These working groups will be charged with creating demonstration projects that support the development of an IPC assessment tool for healthcare teams that include clients/patients as part of the healthcare team. There will be a series of pre-forum and forum activities to facilitate this process. Using a concept mapping approach, a primary outcome of this process is to further the development of key demonstration projects within 12 months of the forum.

TitreApplicationTitle: SWAT: Smart Wheelchairs for Assessment and Training of Older Adults
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING AND MOBILITY; CONSENSUS WORKSHOP; DATA; PLANNING; POWERED WHEELCHAIR ASSESSMENT; POWERED WHEELCHAIR TRAINING; SENSORS; SMART WHEELCHAIRS
Abstract-Résumé: Older adults often need powered wheelchairs to help maintain their independence and mobility. Clinicians are responsible for assessing and training users for powered wheelchair use, and typically make decisions regarding powered wheelchair provision using existing assessment tools. These tools, however, offer little to no decision-support, and do not help inform clinicians' decisions regarding the ability of a user to improve his/her driving performance with additional training and/or modifications to the wheelchair itself.  Many researchers have developed smart wheelchairs that provide navigation assistance to drivers who are unable to operate powered wheelchairs safely. These smart wheelchairs are capable of collecting and generating large amounts of historic and real-time data regarding the drivers' needs, abilities, and preferences. Limited research has been conducted to investigate how these data can be used by clinicians during the assessment and training process.  The SWAT initiative will bring together engineers, computer scientists, occupational therapy researchers and clinicians all over the world to explore how smart wheelchairs and the data they collect/generate can be used by clinicians in powered wheelchair assessment and training of older adults. The aim of this planning grant will be to create a research proposal that will examine the application of smart wheelchair data, design of protocols for collecting and sharing this data with clinicians in a meaningful, impactful, and clinically valid manner, and development of new clinical decision-support tools and processes. The outcomes of this grant can potentially revolutionize current assessment and training processes by using existing technology to offer more decision-support to clinicians, and, in turn, possibly provide new opportunities for independent mobility to the aging population.

TitreApplicationTitle: The British Columbia Centre for Addiction Clinical Trials

Abstract-Résumé: Despite the enormous burden of disease attributable to harmful drug and alcohol use, there remain major challenges in implementing evidence-based prevention and treatment modalities for substance use disorders. In particular, while remarkable advances have been made in basic science, clinical and behavioral research in the area of addiction, many evidence-based tools remain greatly under-utilized.  In this context, urgent action is required to develop and incorporate evidence-based treatment strategies to address the health and social harms of substance misuse in Canada. Vancouver, British Columbia is perfectly positioned to be a site in the Canadian Research Initiative in Substance Misuse as the city has a long-standing epidemic of illicit drug use for which many substance misuse programs have been implemented. Building on this environment, we seek to fulfill the following objectives:  1)To develop The British Columbia Centre for Addiction Clinical Trials (BCCACT) involving the development of a collaborative team of substance misuse researchers, service providers, the affected community and collaborating organizations; 2)Through this new initiative, to consult with local and regional health authorities to identify needs, gaps and opportunities for further developing health research on substance misuse treatments and interventions; 3)Through this new initiative, to identify pertinent research questions, emerging issues and priorities in substance misuse treatment and prevention in British Columbia and nationally;   4)Through our proposed structure, to develop plans for knowledge translation and dissemination of evidence-based research findings to knowledge users locally, nationally and internationally.  Our team includes an expert network of knowledge users, service providers and substance misuse research scientists, which perfectly positions us to facilitate collaborative research and implementation of evidence-based approaches to substance misuse.

TitreApplicationTitle: High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin - A Canadian Viewpoint from CIHR funded studies
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME; CANADIAN WORKSHOP; DIAGNOSTIC TESTS; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; GUIDELINES; HIGH-SENSITIVITY CARDIAC TROPONIN; LABORATORIES; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; MYOCARDIAL INJURY; SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: In 2000 the cardiology community changed the way doctors' diagnosis a heart attack.  A laboratory test, cardiac troponin (cTn) test, became an important tool for doctors to make this diagnosis.  Over the next 12 years, many studies (including our CIHR-funded studies) provided the evidence on when to measure cTn in the emergency room and what levels should be used to determine if a patient has had a heart attack.  The importance of our work is apparent in that 4 of our studies were referenced by the latest international guideline for heart attacks [Third Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction(MI)] published in 2012.    However, as we and others were accumulating the evidence on how to use current cTn tests, the diagnostic companies were at the same time changing and improving these tests by making them more precise and able to measure smaller concentrations of the protein.  This resulted in a new generation of tests, called "high-sensitivity cardiac troponin" (hs-cTn).  As these are new tests, information, data and evidence is required on how to interpret them. Also, this information should be provided to doctors and laboratory professionals so that the hs-cTn tests are used appropriately to guide care.  The 2012 MI guideline does not provide any help here as there was limited evidence at the time of writing.  This was confirmed by the recently released Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health report (2013)  that cited the need for "...further research exploring different clinical algorithms to optimize patient and health system outcomes associated with high-sensitivity cardiac troponin testing."  Within the last year several studies have been funded by CIHR and the results will soon be available.  Our workshop will bring together CIHR-funded and International researchers to discuss their research findings with a goal to produce a document on hs-cTn testing that is current, evidence-based, and relevant to Canadian healthcare providers and patients.

Abstract-Résumé: Each year in Canada, about 1,300 children and adolescents are diagnosed with cancer. During their course of illness, adolescents with cancer will experience physical (pain, nausea, fatigue, hair loss, weight loss, changes in body image) and emotional (stress, anxiety, depression) symptoms related to the disease, invasive procedures, and or chemotherapy and radiation. These symptoms are highly distressing, are often poorly managed, and restrict physical and social interactions. These symptoms can negatively impact quality of life and can challenge many aspects of normal adolescent development. Many adolescents with cancer also do not realize the serious health problems associate with cancer treatments or the need for follow-up care after completion of their cancer treatment. Therefore, it is important to develop programs to make it easier for youth with cancer to cope with and manage their disease. This pilot study will test the feasibility, impact on patient health outcomes and cost-effectiveness of an Internet-based program that will provide knowledge, disease management and transition skills, and social support to ultimate improve the quality of life of youth with cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: After the Asylum: The Legacies of Community Mental Health
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY MENTAL HEALTH; DEINSTITUTIONALIZATION; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; MENTAL HEALTH; PUBLIC HISTORY; STIGMA
Abstract-Résumé: Psychiatric deinstitutionalization began in the 1950s and continues into the present day. Deinstitutionalization has had profound and widespread effects across many sectors of Canadian society, including the economy, the workforce, public health, public policy, education and human rights. But what do we know of the history of this critical evolution in mental health provision? In 2007 a pan Canadian team of researchers came together to study the history of psychiatric deinstitutionalization and the relocation of mental health care from residential facilities into community settings. The diverse research findings and multi-media research products of the Open Doors / Closed Ranks: Locating mental health after the asylum project demonstrate that academic and community partnerships which explore past practices and models offer contemporary policy makers and mental health practitioners a valuable set of tools for future decision-making. The project team is planning a public outreach dissemination, engagement and planning event, Through Open Doors: Legacies of Community Mental Health, for Fall 2014 in Vancouver, BC. Our event will bring a broad set of key stakeholders (mental health practitioners, policy actors, mental health care users, caregivers and educators) together for three days of concentrated, multi-media events and discussions about the ongoing legacy of deinstitutionalization. The events are designed to foster better mental health policy and practices and to function as a means of combating institutionalized stigma to create inclusive mental health communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health Literacy, HIV Risk, and Men Who Have Sex with Men: Building a program of research through national and international collaborations
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATION; HEALTH LITERACY; HIV RISK; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; RESEARCH; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: Effectively applying HIV prevention strategies "in the heat of the sexual moment" requires accessing, understanding, and using health information about HIV risk. These skills--called "health literacy" skills--can be challenging to apply as complex new information about HIV prevention strategies emerges (e.g. reduced risk of transmission from HIV treatments) and due to the plethora of information available via digital media (e.g. Facebook, Twitter, websites and mobile apps). This is particularly important for gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (MSM) given the high rates of HIV infection in this population. Clinicians and health agencies interacting with MSM also have a tough time navigating this new landscape, and there are different social, cultural and legal perspectives on HIV risk. Research in this area is only beginning, and there is a pressing need for effective interventions to improve health literacy for MSM.  We aim to bring together Canadian and international researchers, knowledge users, and policy-makers in health literacy, risk communication, HIV prevention and gay men's health to meet over two days in Vancouver in 2014. Our goal is to build an interdisciplinary team to collaboratively develop a national and international program of research and identify projects to better understand the relationship between health literacy and HIV prevention for MSM (at the individual, provider and society levels). By integrating this meeting within the BC Gay Men's Health Summit, we aim to discuss, share information, and learn from a wide range of community members, service providers, policy-makers and researchers in this area to identify the most important research questions to fill critical knowledge gaps, which will lead to effective health literacy interventions. By increasing the health literacy skills of MSM and their providers we can improve the understanding and appropriate use of effective HIV prevention strategies to reduce HIV among MSM.

TitreApplicationTitle: Treating Drug Addiction with Animal Assisted Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL ASSISTED THERAPY; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; DRUG ABUSE; EVIDENCE BASE DEVELOPMENT; HEALTH AND WELLNESS; HEALTH INTERVENTION; INDIGENOUS TRADITIONAL CULTURE; PROGRAMMING AND POLICY IMPROVEMENT; TREATMENT; UNIQUE HEALTH INTERVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Drug addiction is a serious health concern in Canada. Building on our growing community-based research team's history of collaborative work, the aim of this project is to better understand how Animal Assisted Therapy (AAT) can assist Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal youth and adults in their treatment for drug addiction. Many individuals who abuse drugs have traumatic life experiences and use drugs to help cope with the experiences. Research has shown that AAT can assist individuals in dealing with trauma and other mental health concerns, but not a lot has been done in the addictions field.  Based on our team's extensive practice and research-based experiences with AAT, addictions and trauma, our aim is to develop a unique research project addressing all three fields together. Applying a One Health framework, which acknowledges the interdependent relationship between humans, animals and the environment to achieve optimal health, we will undertake a literature review, visit sites, review data and host a meeting to gain a better understanding of how dogs and horses assist in adult and youth residential facilities to achieve client wellness. We will focus on three key elements of AAT as a treatment intervention for drug abuse: the client's interaction with the program, the human handler, and the animal. The expertise of our diverse team members well-positions us to undertake this project while adhering to specific ethical standards for working with animals, humans and specifically Aboriginal people.   The results of the project will allow our community-based team to incorporate best practices into drug dependency intervention programs. Organizing our team to gain a comprehensive and collective understanding of AAT, trauma and drug abuse treatment will provide the necessary foundation to develop a stage II CRISM Team Grant to establish integrated Nodes of research to cooperatively develop, validate, refine and deliver new treatment options with others.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining a Comprehensive Approach to Measuring Pain in Neonates and Infants: A Consensus Conference
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSESSMENT; BEHAVIOURAL INDICATORS; BIOMARKERS; CORTICAL INDICATORS; INFANTS; MEASUREMENT; NEONATES; PAIN; PHYSIOLOGIC INDICATORS
Abstract-Résumé: Across all ages, pain is a subjective phenomenon. Accurate assessment is essential to adequate pain management in infants. As infants are not able to self-report pain, clarifying how they perceive painful stimuli is challenging. Despite the development of multiple infant behavioural observation pain assessment measures and the increasing study of biomarkers and cortical indicators of pain, (a) there is a significant disconnect between behavioural pain measures, biomarkers and cortical indicators and (b) basic and clinical researchers communication is sparse. To address these issues, we are seeking funds for a 2-day consensus conference that will bring together leading clinical and basic science research experts in infant pain and measurement to a) discuss basic science and clinical measurement issues; b) determine the best measures, indicators and approaches to assess pain; and c) generate key research questions to guide the integration of current and novel infant pain measures and indicators. The anticipated outcomes from our proposed consensus conference are: 1) A comprehensive evidence informed and consensus-based list of validated infant pain assessment measures, biomarkers and cortical pain indicators. 2)  Identification of key research questions to evaluate pain and integrate various types of indicators using current/existing and novel methods. 3) New alliances between basic science and clinical researchers.
