TitreApplicationTitle: Teens Taking Charge:  managing my Transplant on Line:  A pilot feasability and outcome study
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; COMPLIANCE; COST SAVINGS; EDUCATION; KIDNEY TRANSPLANT; PILOT STUDY; SELF MANAGMENT; TRANSITION
Abstract-Résumé: Transplantation is not a cure for teenagers with organ failure but a chronic disease that requires ongoing monitoring and carefully following of medical treatments. We have built an interactive website that gives teenagers tips and tools to help them handle taking their medicine, make good choices about the foods they eat, and live a healthy lifestyle. The website includes six general modules for teens that have had any organ transplant (Introduction, lifestyle, stress, transition, medications and diet), and five specifically about kidney transplants. (Assessment, listed and waiting, what happens at the time of transplant, preparing for discharge and complications and self-monitoring).   It also includes a discussion board so teens can talk to other teens and many video clips of teens talking about how transplant has affected their life. Research findings show that there are a lot of teenagers with transplants find it difficult to regularly take their medications and stick to their diets.  Some also have difficulty fitting back in at school and living a healthy life.  This can influence how long the transplanted organ will work and will affect the teenager's quality of life.  In the first study we did, teenagers told us that they would like to be told everything possible about their disease and treatment and for it to be presented in a way that is flexible and available to them at home.  This website has been designed to meet these identified needs.   The goal of this pilot study is to find out if an interactive website about having a kidney transplant will help teenagers take better care of themselves.  We also want to find out if using the website will help teenagers move more easily into adult care and be more responsible and independent in their care and if it will save money. This study will also help us figure out how many teenagers should be included in a larger future study with the goal of impacting all teenagers with an organ transplant across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Caring for Kids New to Canada: A webinar series to improve health care for immigrant and refugee children, youth and families
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN AND YOUTH; IMMIGRANT AND REFUGEE HEALTH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NEWCOMER HEALTH; PAEDIATRICS; WEBINAR
Abstract-Résumé: Caring for Kids New to Canada is an integrated knowledge exchange project that seeks to improve health care for immigrant and refugee children. Led by the Canadian Paediatric Society, the core product is an open access, bilingual web resource for health care providers, the first phase of which was launched in June 2013 at www.kidsnewtocanada.ca and www.enfantsneocanadiens.ca. The CPS seeks to expand the reach and impact of this unique resource by developing a webinar series aimed at health professionals, community organizations and others who care for immigrant and refugee children and youth. The webinars will feature leading Canadian experts in newcomer paediatric health addressing topics that are identified by knowledge users as important to providing effective care. This medium allows for interaction between users and content developers, is inexpensive and convenient for participants, and can be accessed in both live and recorded formats, thus further extending its reach. The webinars will also encourage users to access the website for more information on a range of topics that have the potential to improve care.

TitreApplicationTitle: The PainSquad+ Real-time Pain Management System for Adolescents with Cancer: A Feasibility, Quality and Cost Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; CANCER; COST; E-HEALTH; FEASIBILITY; PRELIMINARY EFFECTIVENESS; QUALITY; SMARTPHONE
Abstract-Résumé: Pain is a common, distressing and costly symptom experienced by adolescents with cancer and often occurs outside of the hospital environment. Adolescents with cancer are in a unique developmental stage that may mean pain characteristics (for instance pain severity), the impact of pain, and pain treatment outcomes are different in adolescents compared to children and adults. This means that unique strategies are needed to solve the adolescent cancer pain problem. In response, our group has developed and begun testing the PainSquad+ pain management smartphone app. This app will provide adolescents with pain management support the moment they are in pain, including when they are not in the hospital. To create PainSquad+ we are using multiple study phases. To date, we have reviewed current pediatric cancer pain research, held a meeting with experts in cancer, pain and smartphones to decide on the needed PainSquad+ features, developed a clinical map detailing how PainSquad+ will help adolescents in pain and developed a prototype app. The current project will include a pilot study, using a rigorous scientific design (randomized controlled trial), to: (a) test the feasibility of conducting a large-scale PainSquad+ experiment and (b) begin examining how effective PainSquad+ is at helping adolescents manage pain and decreasing healthcare system costs. We anticipate that once developed and tested for effectiveness, PainSquad+ will improve pain treatment and ultimately quality of life in adolescents with cancer.

Abstract-Résumé: Substance misuse causes major health and social harms in Canada, and Ontario specifically. However, key evidence-based prevention and treatment interventions for illicit and/or prescription drug misuse are lacking. This proposal assembles a team of diversely skilled and experienced Ontario-based investigators from socio-behavioral, clinical and basic sciences, together with a group of key knowledge users from related intervention service provider, policy, public health and family/consumer domains in Ontario, towards the development and implementation of innovative and cost-effective (prevention and treatment) interventions for substance misuse. The team will be led by four Co-PIs - bringing exceptional and world-leading skills and expertise in intervention research for substance misuse focusing on different drugs, settings and populations - together with the diversely qualified Knowledge User group. The team is supported by and has access to first-class (institutional and community-based) research environments and support structures, including CAMH, Canada's largest addiction and mental health research hospital. The team furthermore brings outstanding KT potential, as well as national and international connections for pan-Canadian and international collaborations under the CRISM initiative.

TitreApplicationTitle: Self-management and clinical decision support of multiple chronic conditions through the use of mobile health telemonitoring
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; CLINICAL DECISION-MAKING TOOL; HEART FAILURE; MOBILE TELEMONITORING; MULTIPLE CO-MORBIDITIES; PATIENT SELF-MANAGEMENT; QUALITY OF LIFE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: The number of people with multiple chronic conditions (MCCs) is growing and is threatening the sustainability of our healthcare system, especially due to the high cost of frequent hospitalizations.  These patients face many challenges in trying to self-manage their conditions, including complex decision-making and contradictory clinical management advice. However, through better patient self-care and clinical management, significant reductions in healthcare spending and improved health outcomes could be achieved. Although telemonitoring systems that allow patients to monitor their physiological state (e.g. weight, blood pressure) and receive both automated and real-time feed back from doctors are useful, these systems tend to be inconvenient and costly to implement in existing clinical settings. We believe that delivering telemonitoring through a mobile phone will enable patients with MCCs to readily track their health, receive automated feedback based relevant to their unique situation, and improve communication with their health care team, in a more cost effective and intuitive way. In order to test the effectiveness of the intervention, we propose a 6-month randomized controlled trial of 135 patients.  Given that the study will include only patients with MCCs, the participants will be required to be diagnosed with at least 2 of the following: heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and chronic kidney disease. Patients will be assigned to either (1) the control group receiving usual care, or (2) the group using the mobile system with usual care. We hypothesize that our mobile intervention for the management of MCCs will be a cost-effective and scalable tool that will improve health outcomes and quality of care, while empowering and reassuring patients and their family.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANALGESICS; HYPERALGESIA; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; MISUSE; OLIGOANALGESIA; OPIOIDS; PAIN; PREVENTION; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Pain that persists for months is categorized as chronic. Chronic pain is reported by 20% of the Canadian population and has major societal and economical impacts.  Misuse of strong pain medication (opioid narcotics such as morphine, oxycodone) is sometimes necessary.  Risk of opioid misuse (taking the medication for reasons other than pain relief) is estimated at 5% in chronic pain patients.  Medication abuses, overuse, misuse that could drive to addiction are harmful to an individual's health and their families. In the Canada, it was estimated that health and societal costs are over 60 billion dollars per year (medical, work lost, juridical). In the first phase of the Canadian Initiative in Substance Misuse, we propose a Workshop on Opioid Misuse with knowledge users (patient advocacy groups, clinicians, research, Canadian Pain Societies and health organizations) to identify what information is made available, find the best strategies to implement or refine available tools to detect risk of pain medication misuse, and how to manage it in doctor's clinics.  Strategic knowledge transfer strategies (e.g., web, media and professional journal, telemedicine and decision makers meetings) are to be planned.

TitreApplicationTitle: Can e-therapies reduce waiting lists in secondary mental health care? A randomised controlled trial
Keywords-MotsClés: DEPRESSION; E-THERAPY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is common and disabling but access to specialist treatment is often delayed with waiting lists of up to a year not uncommon. Also treatment is frequently limited to drug therapies because of long waiting lists to see psychological therapists face to face despite recommendations by NICE and others about the importance of non-drug therapies.   One way to address this problem is to use computerized e-therapies which deliver structured cognitive behavioral treatment via a computer where the therapy can be accessed in a location and at a time that is convenient for patients and where there is no waiting list. There is evidence that computerized therapies are as effective as face to face therapies for mild to moderate depression. What has not been done is to assess the effectiveness of these therapies in more severe disorders and assess where they fit into existing pathways of care. Furthermore there is evidence that using a human "coach" to assist people through the program using text, email or phone results in better outcomes.   The aim of this proposal is to answer the question "In patients with depression attending out-patient mental health services does adding a computerized therapy to their treatment where they are coached by an e-therapy case manager, result in better outcomes that are more cost effective than usual treatment alone plus written information about self-help resources?"

Abstract-Résumé: Prescription monitoring programs (PMPs) are an important strategy to combat prescription drug abuse; however, there is a need to evaluate the outcomes of these programs. This year the National Advisory Council on Prescription Drug Misuse developed a strategy entitled First Do No Harm: Responding to Canada's Prescription Drug Crisis, which recommended the establishment of "an ongoing formal program of research on the effectiveness of PMPs, core components, and impact including unintended consequences". This proposal is aimed at directly fulfilling this recommendation. In this application, the intervention to be evaluated is prescription monitoring to prevent and reduce the non-medical use of pharmaceutical drugs. The service providers and knowledge users include those designing and administering prescription monitoring programs. The goal of this project is to build teams of academic researchers and PMP service providers across Canada to establish an ongoing formal program of research to 1) evaluate the effectiveness of PMPs, 2) determine the core components of PMPs that contribute to effectiveness, and 3) identify the unintended consequences of PMPs.

Abstract-Résumé: Substance misuse remains a significant global public health problem which carries a heavy burden for abusers and their families alike. This disorder is associated with suffering and severe health problems in patients, distress among family members, as well as tremendous costs to society. Unfortunately, prevention strategies still need to be effectively implemented and only a minority of addicted individuals receives adequate treatment. Moreover, conventional treatment strategies are often insufficient in treating addiction and no medication is yet available for a number of substances such as stimulants and cannabis. It is now widely accepted that research that could address these needs should involve not only scientists, but also clinicians, policy-makers and affected individuals. While individuals interact with each other at various levels (clinical, administrative), this is rarely as part of a cohesive interdisciplinary group. Substance users are for the most part absent of the knowledge generation and transfer processes. It is the premise of this proposal that a research network involving researchers from different horizons along with advocacy groups, service providers and policy-makers would lay down strong foundations on which effective interventions could be developed, tested and implemented in clinical settings. We propose herein to engage in a series of activities designed to facilitate the formation and development of an inter-institutions, inter-disciplinary, cross-jurisdictional research team, towards the establishment of a pan Canadian research network in addiction. This goal will be achieved by a thorough assessment of needs, workshops, teleconferences and meetings. This network is designed to stimulate new collaborations between partners with varying expertise; it could be crucial for both patients and the society by helping to develop new interventions, which could eventually allow interrupting the destructive cycle of substance misuse.

TitreApplicationTitle: A population based surveillance system for detection of high risk CKD
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; DISEASE SURVEILLANCE; ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORDS; RISK PREDICTION
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major public health problem. The end stage of CKD can lead to kidney failure, which requires treatment with dialysis. Patients with CKD who require dialysis suffer from increased risks of infections, heart disease and have a poor quality of life. Early identification of patients at high risk of progression to kidney failure can lead to better treatments and may reduce the rates of dialysis. In order to identify high risk patients with CKD, we are proposing a surveillance system using the eCHART laboratory database in Manitoba. Our system will include all patients who have a blood or urine test in Manitoba, beginning 2010, and will identify patients with CKD. We will then examine the province for variations in quality of care, and use our risk prediction models to identify patients who are at high risk for kidney failure. Together, these initiatives will improve outcomes for patients with kidney disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; EXERCISE; HEALTH SERVICE DELIVERY; INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE; PULMONARY REHABILITATION; SMARTPHONE; TELEHEALTH; TELEREHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Pulmonary rehabilitation is a recommended exercise and education treatment for individuals with chronic lung disease, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It improves physical fitness and quality of life, and reduces shortness of breath.  Despite these benefits, only 2% of Canadians with COPD have access to a pulmonary rehabilitation program in their community.  Smartphone technology may provide a solution. We propose a study to develop and evaluate a smartphone system for pulmonary rehabilitation that will enable patients to exercise in their own community. Patients will use the same monitoring tools as the hospital-based programs but will be able to exercise in their own community when it is convenient for them. This project has the potential to increase the access to this important health care service for patients with COPD and other chronic lung diseases.

Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL INTERVENTION; CLINICAL CARE PATHWAY; COLLABORATOIVE NETWORK; HEALTH POLICY & ECONOMICS; HEALTH SERVICES; PERSONLAIZED TREATMENT; PHARMACOLOGICAL INTERVENTION; POLY-DRUG USE; STEPPED CARE; SUBSTANCE MISUSE
Abstract-Résumé: We plan to link academic research, service delivery, advocacy, and community engagement partners in the area of substance misuse within Alberta.  Our aim is to develop a functional research-practice-advocacy network in substance misuse to capitalize on existing services and research capacity so that we can identify high priority practical research directions of importance to to service providers and policy makers.  Our proposed integrated team that will link to other addiction research collaborators within Canada to develop the capacity for Canadian partners to run multi-centre trials related to behavioural and pharmacological treatment interventions for substance misuse. This team will also be able to conduct important systematic research designed to promote the innovative use evidence-based interventions in Alberta-based addiction services. The long-term objectives of the proposed collaborative research initiative are:  1. To reduce the health, social, and economic costs of substance misuse to Canadians by establishing a regional centre of excellence for substance misuse research, education, and knowledge exchange with respect to services and population health; 2. In partnership with treatment providers, policy makers, and funders, increase Canada's capacity to produce rigorous research on the development, maintenance, and resolution of substance misuse;  3. To increase uptake of evidence-based prevention and treatment for substance misuse among Canadian stakeholders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health Systems Guidance Appraisal Tool - Better Guidance For Better Health Systems
Keywords-MotsClés: GUIDELINES/GUIDANCE; HEALTH MEASUREMENTS; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HEALTH SYSTEM; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LOCAL; NATIONAL & GLOBAL HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Health systems guidance (HSG) are systematically developed statements produced at global and national levels to assist in decisions about solving a health system challenge, to assist with the implementation of these solutions, and to direct the monitoring and evaluation of the solution's implementation efforts. For example, what is the best way to provide a vaccination program for citizens of low- and middle-income countries? The World Health Organization and national and provincial agencies have called for methods to help develop this type of guidance so that they are of high quality and based on the best available research evidence. Currently, nothing like this exists to help HSG developers. Our objective is to design and test a tool aimed at directing the development, reporting, and appraisal of HSG. To do this, we have brought together an international team of researchers and collaborators with experience and expertise in HSG . For this study we have looked for ideas and items related to HSG appraisal that have been published in scientific journals and other sources. We found that there is a need to develop a high quality tool for evaluating HSG.  We are applying for this funding opportunity to support us organize a one day workshop event that we schedule to occur alongside an international conference in Cape Town South Africa in September 2014. This conference, the Health Systems Global International Symposium will unite global experts health systems/policy expert. We will be organizing this one day satellite workshop session during which we will be discussing our research findings and brainstorming with these experts in order to obtain valuable feedback, constructive critiques, suggestions and to garner additional support for the tool. This will provide a platform where these stakeholders can further contribute to the development and refinement of the tool. This will also enhance the trustworthiness of our study.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intersectoral Collaboration for Promoting Health Equity: Beyond the Usual Suspects
Keywords-MotsClés: BRITISH COLUMBIA; BUSINESS COMMUNITY; DELIBERATIVE DIALOGUE; HEALTH INEQUITIES; INTERSECTORAL COLLABORATION; PUBLIC HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH ASSOCIATION OF BC; SHARED PROSPERITY
Abstract-Résumé: In British Columbia (BC), people who live in richer areas have better health and live 10 years longer on average than those in poorer areas, particularly aboriginal communities. These differences are caused by social and economic conditions, particularly poverty. BC has the highest rate of poverty in Canada, so reducing poverty is an important strategy to reduce unfair differences in health between groups. Although public health has not traditionally collaborated with business because of significant differences in approaches, values, and objectives, the two groups are beginning to identify shared objectives, such as reducing unfair social differences, and promoting prosperity for all. Recently, leadership by socially responsible business organizations in the province is opening opportunities for creating public health-private sector partnerships to achieve common goals. The Public Health Association of BC (PHABC) holds an annual conference to address important public health issues. For the 2014 conference, we are proposing to hold a dialogue between the public health and business communities to promote learning on both sides about the goals and aims of each group by engaging in a respectful conversation about our shared goals and our major areas of difference. The business community believes that any new spending must come from economic growth and does not support fiscal policies such as changes to the tax structure. In contrast, PHABC does not agree to economic growth at the expense of disadvantaged populations and supports progressive taxation policies. To reconcile these differences and find a way to move forward on a common agenda for shared prosperity and improved equity in health, we need to understand each other better and learn more about the basis for each group's position. Through a public event, in which well known speakers from both sides of the discussion will present, we will provide an opportunity for public engagement in the dialogue.

Since 2008, CCIC has sponsored an annual meeting to provide a forum that highlights work from internationally recognized speakers, together with work from Canadians and trainees. TitreApplicationTitle: Risk in birthing choices: is it worth the labour?
Keywords-MotsClés: CAESAREAN SECTION RATES IN BC AND CANADA; CONSUMER HEALTH MOVEMENTS; HEALTH POLICY; HISTORY OF; MATERNAL AND FETAL HEALTH; MEDICAL DECISION-MAKING CONTEXTS; RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN BIRTHING PRACTITIONERS AND WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: Health practitioners are located at the nexus of diverse perspectives on fear and risk and have to navigate challenging terrain in meeting the need of mothers, children and the health care system. Exploring this diversity in risk calculation presents an opportunity to develop a robust and conscious set of strategies for health carers to respond practically to pregnancy and birthing needs but in a way that might reduce the high incidence and associated implications of caesarean section rates in Canada. We propose to gather together a research team composed of birthing women, practitioner, stakeholder and academic members of relevant expert and women's knowledge communities that will work together to create a community-based research program with the objective of gaining a fuller understanding of the complexities of the decision-making contexts in which decisions are made to surgically intervene in a birth. This project will prioritize the voices of women themselves in recognition that women are active managers of their own health, place this decision-making context within a historical and comparative frame, identify relevant wise practices from Canadian new immigrant, vulnerable women, and Indigenous communities concerning alternative experiences, and help foster the development of pilot intervention programs aimed at reducing caesarean ratse in British Columbia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Telling Stories About Storytelling: Critical engagements with narrative and new media for health in northern British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: CREATIVE EXPRESSION AND HEALTH; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; ENVIRONMENTS AND HEALTH; FIRST NATIONS HEALTH; HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH PROMOTION; KNOWLEDGE TO ACTION; NEW MEDIA; RURAL AND REMOTE HEALTH; STORYTELLING AND NARRATIVE
Abstract-Résumé: Culturally safe practices for the promotion of health and well-being, and illness prevention, are especially important in northern British Columbia, where rural, remote and First Nations communities experience a disproportionate burden of ill-health compared to the rest of the province. Based on past experience of community-based and First Nations oriented work, our research team has identified storytelling as an increasingly important means to understand and respond to the health issues faced in northern BC communities. Our proposal seeks to bring communities, storytellers, researchers and health professionals together to explore the role of narrative and new media approaches to storytelling and the use of these approaches to inform culturally safe research, education and health promotion tools well-suited to respond to the particular health challenges of northern and First Nations communities in BC. The foundation for this project is a strong team of established researchers and a history of successful research collaborations with communities and health authorities in northern BC (including the newly established First Nations Health Authority and the Northern Health Authority). Building from this base, the proposed project aims to: 1) examine the potential for narrative, story and digital storytelling to contribute to addressing health priorities for communities and health authorities in northern BC; 2) identify avenues for partnership and collaborative action for using these approaches; and 3) design a preliminary research strategy that will provide the foundation for future research in this field. We consider this project a timely opportunity to strengthen understanding of the cultural relevance and potential use and impact of using narrative, storytelling, and place-based strategies to address health disparities in northern and First Nations communities, and to use this understanding to enhance health promotion and health equity in northern BC.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of self-care medication reconciliation app for patients with chronic kidney disease
Keywords-MotsClés: MEDICATION RECONCILIATION; MOBILE HEALTH TECHNOLOGY; SELF-CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Patients who have complicated conditions such as chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at high risk for problems related to their medications. Often these problems occur because doctors and patients do not communicate the right type of medication information to each other. This causes many prescribing errors and can lead to patient harm, emergency visits, or hospitalizations. To address this communication problem, hospitals now use a process called "medication reconciliation" to confirm the medications patients are taking when they enter and leave the hospital. However, the way that medication reconciliation is currently being done, patients are not actively engaged or given tools to effectively communicate the medications they are taking, changes that have been made, and what they are having trouble with. Directly engaging patients in this process might help solve this problem, and mobile technologies on smartphones may be a solution. Our study team has developed a mobile application (app) called My KidneyCare, which has a specific medication component to help patients communicate their medication information to all their doctors. This app can feed medication information from the clinic's medical record to the patient's smartphone, and any changes made to the medication list can be entered by the patient and sent back to the central server to notify their doctors. We plan to study this app to test if it will decrease errors related to medications. We believe that if patients use this app to report their medications to their doctors, fewer errors will occur, which should eventually lead to reduced patient harm and healthcare use.

TitreApplicationTitle: Replacing ambulatory clinic follow-up with remote home monitoring using smartphones in breast reconstruction patients: Is it cost-effective?
Keywords-MotsClés: AMBULATORY SURGICAL PROCEDURES; BREAST RECONSTRUCTION; COST-EFFECTIVENESS; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; TELEMEDICINE
Abstract-Résumé: With the rising health care costs, the Ontario government sees technology as a way to constrain growth in health care costs and eliminate barriers due to distance. Women's College Hospital (WCH) in Toronto offers breast reconstruction following mastectomy for breast cancer. Patients often travel significant distances to have this specialized surgery. At WCH, we use the QoC Health Inc mobile application to monitor breast reconstruction patients' home recovery. This technology eliminates one or more in-person clinic visits. This project speaks to the Ontario government's action plan by providing patients with timely contact to their surgeon from the comfort of their home. This technology has the potential to address wait times by freeing up specialty surgeon clinic time so that they may engage in new consultations and attend to patients in the emergency department. The first step to widespread implementation involves demonstrating cost-effectiveness. This study compares the costs of telemedicine follow-up care using the QoC Health Inc mobile application to conventional in-person follow-up care. We will consider all societal borne costs, and a narrower health system perspective that may be of key interest to health administrators and policy decision makers. Demonstrating cost-effectiveness will support local program expansion from already engaged administration and broader interest will be gained through conferences and publication that appeal to knowledge users and policy decision makers. This technology is generalizable to a wide variety of ambulatory surgeries, and therefore has the ability to impact a larger and growing population. We believe this work is in keeping with the Canadian Institute of Health Research's mandate to fund integrated solutions to support the continuum of personal and population-based care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Games and Telerehabilitation for Balance impairments and gaze dysfunction: Testing model in clients with Peripheral Vestibular Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: BALANCE IMPAIRMENTS; GAME-BASED-THERAPY; GAZE DEFICITS; PERIPHERAL VESTIBULAR DISORDERS; TELAMONATORING; TELAREHABILITATION; WALKING STABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: People with chronic disabilities struggle with compliance to long-term treatment plans. Accessibility to rehabilitation is difficult for a large percentage of people due to difficulty with transportation or living in rural areas. There is a need for innovative treatments to address these issues. Our research goal is to develop therapeutic eHealth applications that will lead to better long-term health outcomes and cost-effective delivery systems for individuals with neurological disorders and the aging population. We have produced an innovative Telerehabilitation platform (TRP) that combines computer game-based exercises and electronic monitoring tools. Computer games have received considerable interest from researchers and clinicians as a model for learning a range of complex tasks and facilitating the transfer of skills to daily life activities. These emerging Telerehabilitation technologies have potential to improve clinical outcomes by making therapies and exercise more engaging, motivating and effective as well as increasing accessibility to treatment regardless of where they live. The research objective of the present study is to test the therapeutic effectiveness of the TRP delivered in the home compared to usual care delivered in an outpatient physical therapy clinic. For this purpose we will test the intervention in individuals with peripheral vestibular disorders with balance and gaze impairments causing blurred vision and dizziness. We believe motivation to perform tedious home programs can be improved with engaging, fun and interactive computer gaming as part of the rehabilitation process. Additionally we believe the TRP is a cost-effective way to deliver rehabilitation as it will streamline rehabilitation services by leveraging therapist time spent with clients and allow clients to practice at times that are more convenient for them. We expect this will produce significant and cost-effective outcomes in populations with chronic disabilities.

TitreApplicationTitle: RESPECT: a tool to improve patient care quality and safety & facilitate team learning
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ARREST; EARLY IDENTIFICATION; ELECTRONIC HEALTH TECHNOLOGY; PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: This application is to evaluate an intervention to improve the ability of community hospital teams to recognize, treat and learn from patients in their care.  The idea is simple: and in two parts. The first part is to help provide better care immediately. Sick children are identified by a score based on their Heart Rate and other 'vital signs'. Next these children are carefully discussed using a new tool to structure team discussions create a shared 'mental model' and prepare in case things do not improve. The second part comes later, as an education session. The idea is to learn from the care that was provided to these sicker children. Education sessions loosely based on the situation - as it happened in the community hospital. These sessions will be conducted by pediatric experts from academic centers. We think this learning will make the team stronger and better able to treat the next sick patient.     We think that the two parts of the 4RESPECT intervention will help the team perform better so that children will be stabilized better before transfer, and get better more quickly. If this system works well it may even prevent the need to transfer children.   In this project we will study the effect of the 4RESPECT intervention on patient outcomes, how doctors, nurses and others find it, and how much time it takes to run - with the costs associated. The study team has partnered with a software company and the team at Thunder Bay Regional Health Sciences Center.  The intervention has great potential to increase the safety and quality of pediatric care in community hospitals.

TitreApplicationTitle: The use of text messaging to improve the hospital-community transition and prevent readmission in patients with cardiovascular disease (Txt2Prevent)
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; HEALTHCARE COSTS; HOSPITAL READMISSIONS; MYOCARDIACL INFARCTION; TELEHEALTH; TEXT MESSAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death and hospitalizations in Canada. At some point, patients with heart disease will likely end up admitted to a hospital. This can often be a confusing time for patients. After discharge, patients are at a high risk of being readmitted to hospital due to the challenges faced in transition from hospital to home care. Patients who have support in how to care for themselves at home have a lower risk of problems and being readmitted to hospital. In this study, we propose to develop and test a program that sends text messages to patients within the first 60-days after hospital discharge. The text messages will be sent at regular intervals and will prompt the patient on follow-up care, medication use and healthy lifestyle behaviours.   Patients will be recruited during their hospitalization for either heart attack, angina or heart surgery and randomly assigned to either the text message program (Txt2Prevent) or usual care. After 60 days, we will compare the rate of hospitalizations and death between the two groups. We will also assess patient self-management, medication use, quality of life and satisfaction with the program, as well as costs to the health care and patient. We anticipate that the Txt2Prevent program will result in less hospitalizations at a low cost.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team - The Treatment of Comorbid Substance Dependence and Mental Illness
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY AND MOOD DISORDERS; CLINICAL TRIALS; COMMUNITY PARTNERSHIPS; COMORBIDITY; DUAL DIAGNOSIS; FAMILY INTERVENTIONS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PRIMARY CARE; SUBSTANCE DEPENDENCE; TREATMENT OUTCOME
Abstract-Résumé: Dependence on opiates, alcohol and other drugs of abuse are major health problems in Canada. The costs associated with substance dependence are extensive; exacting an enormous toll in terms of health care costs, mental illness, poor quality of life, unemployment and crime. Concomitant risks include the transmission of the human immunodeficiency (HIV), hepatitis B and C viruses, and tuberculosis, as well as a high incidence of death due to overdoses.  Previous studies conducted by the applicants have shown that substance dependent patients with concurrent mental disorders have poorer outcomes in treatment; they are less likely to complete detoxification and outpatient care, they experience higher levels of relapse, and they suffer from higher levels of polysubstance abuse, undiagnosed/ untreated chronic pain syndromes, as well as untreated mood and anxiety and personality disorders. The current proposal seeks to develop a Team dedicated to the development of efficacious "integrated" interventions for concurrent disorders, appropriate for multiple practice environments. The current Team is comprised of patients, researchers, clinicians and service providers at the Addictions Unit and Allan Memorial Institute of the McGill University Health Centre, as well as community partners in local front-line health clinics (Centre de Sante et de Services Sociaux (CSSS)). The Team has extensive research and treatment experience, as well as the necessary infrastructure, facilities and trained personnel to conduct randomized controlled trials of new medications, family and CBT-oriented psychotherapy trials, qualitative research, knowledge syntheses as well as knowledge translation, training and dissemination activities.

Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; BRITISH COLUMBIA; CLINICAL RESEARCH; COLLABORATION; COMORBIDITY; HOMELESSNESS; KNOWLEDGE USERS; ORGANIZATION; SUBSTANCE USE DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: The Canada Research Initiative for Substance Misuse network aims to reduce a documented gap in clinical and practice based treatment research. It targets a population characterized by illicit substance use and non-medical use of medications, that is often marginalized and out of touch with the health care system. British Columbia has been faced with a high burden of severe drug related problems for decades and has a history of innovative approaches to address these substance use disorders. Key stakeholders in BC are motivated to join the applicants in a concerted team effort to establish a research network, which provide an opportunity to improve the current situation. The lineup of internationally known and connected interdisciplinary researchers provides expertise in different forms of interventions studies and translating evidence-based knowledge into practice. The effort to develop a CRISM Node in BC thus constitutes a timely opportunity to coordinate and focus academic researchers in the field, and team up with knowledge users and health authorities. A number of ongoing studies provide a fertile ground for future collaborations. The initial funding will be employed to link the different groups and develop a structure which makes sure all necessary components for practice based studies are readily available, increase the teams' motivation to engage and commit to change, and identify priorities in studying new and adapted interventions and implementing available evidence. The specifics of a formalized organizational structure need to be determined among all stakeholders. Thus, we plan to engage treatment providers and researchers into an iterative process to communicate and exchange ideas and information. This process will be supported by a survey assessing characteristics and needs of individuals entering different treatment settings.

TitreApplicationTitle: Girls, Women, Prescription Drug Use, Trauma and Chronic Pain
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC PAIN; GIRLS AND WOMEN; PERSCRIPTION DRUG USE; TRAUMA; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Prescription medication misuse, and particularly use of opioid pain relievers among women is increasing and a continuum of prevention, brief intervention and treatment responses are needed in response. Bringing together a team of researchers, service delivery agencies and advocates from BC and Ontario we will identify research and practice needs, and opportunities to address prescription drug use issues among three vulnerable groups: Aboriginal women, pregnant women, and women with a history of trauma. An environmental scan, a scoping review of non-drug interventions for chronic pain, and web-based and in-person consultations with a variety of researchers, providers and community partners will be conducted to identify priority issues and inform the development of research questions related to girls and womens prescription medication misuse and the range of needed prevention and treatment responses. This project will: strengthen research and practice links; contribute to the development of gender-sensitive and trauma-informed approaches to reduce prescription drug misuse and risks; and enhance understanding among service providers about key sex- and gender- related factors associated with prescription drug misuse.

Abstract-Résumé: Every year, millions of people die from Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, the causative agent of Tuberculosis (TB), which is a treatable infectious disease. It is estimated that one-third of the worlds population is infected with TB, including one third of the 34 million people infected with HIV. The majority of individuals control TB infection in a hidden or latent state, however in 5-10% of people TB reactivates to cause disease. Co-infection with HIV drastically increases the chances of TB reactivation and has contributed greatly to the high number of deaths due to HIV both within Canada and worldwide. Progression of TB disease from latency to reactivation and clinical symptoms is a continuous process of bacterial replication and counterbalancing immune responses that are not well understood.   We propose to study the immune responses to tuberculosis from latency, to TB reactivation, and following TB treatment in HIV/TB co-infected individuals in Nairobi, Kenya focusing on HIV high-risk female sex workers who are part of a well-established cohort supported by the University of Nairobi and the University of Manitoba. As TB is endemic in Kenya, this population is at very high risk of developing HIV/TB co-infection and this study represent an opportunity to better identify new diagnostics capable of identifying TB latency, TB activation, and TB cure in the context of HIV infection. We also propose to define immune responses specific to HIV over the spectrum of TB disease. This will provide important information on the effect that different stages of TB disease have on immune response to HIV and how this information may inform HIV and TB treatment options in populations where an HIV vaccine may eventually be used.  Together, these studies will better inform our understanding of TB latency, reactivation, and disease as well as determine the effect of TB on HIV immunity and potential vaccine responses in the millions of HIV/TB co-infected people.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intestinal microbiota, immune activation and vaccine responsiveness of the HIV-exposed infant
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA SEQUENCING; FEEDING PRACTICE; HIV-EXPOSED; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNE ACTIVATION; INFANT; INNATE AND ADAPTIVE IMMMUNITY; INTESTINAL MICROBIOME; VACCINE RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: The human intestine is colonized with microbes (bacteria) during birth and through dietary exposure. Collectively, the bacterial cells (microbiota) help with the uptake of dietary nutrients, develop and maintain immune functions and defend against invading pathogens (germs). The composition of the intestinal bacteria differs between individuals and is highly variable in the first year of life. Of interest, factors in breast milk are known to support protective microbiota and premature weaning is known to change the infant's intestinal microbiome. Alterations in the commensal bacterial composition of the intestine may explain why babies born to HIV+ women who are exclusively breastfed are less likely to get infected with the virus than babies who receive both breast milk and non-sterile food supplements. Disturbances in intestinal bacteria may also explain the reduced efficacy of some childhood vaccinations in developing countries. Under the proposed research, we will apply advanced analytic tools to determine the genetic microbial composition of the intestine of infants currently enrolled in a large African cohort of 600 HIV+ and 100 HIV-negative mother-infant pairs, that is designed to explore the effect of different feeding practices on immune system activation and vaccine responsiveness among breastfed versus mixed fed infants. The bacterial composition and diversity of the intestine will be associated with different feeding practices, vaccine responses, infant immune activation and disease susceptibility. Additionally, microbes in the saliva will be associated with the intestinal microbiome and the immune factors. Overall, this study will aim to identify characteristics of the infant intestinal microbiome that are essential for optimal immune system development, in order to prevent breast milk HIV transmission and optimize infant vaccination strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining mucosal determinants of HIV risk in the CAPRISA 004 trial using high throughput proteomic approaches
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV/AIDS; INNATE IMMUNITY; MICROBICIDE; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the development of several partially effective HIV prevention tools, HIV-1 continues to infect 2 million individuals per year. As these new infections disproportionally affect women the development of better female-controlled prevention options remains a global public health priority.  A recent clinical trial (CAPRISA-004) demonstrated that protection by microbicides is possible, offering 39% protection for women.  However this is below the threshold to make it a viable prevention option on a large scale.  Improving this efficacy represents a major hurdle, as we still do not know why some individuals are infected more easily than others.  To date, studies have been narrow and/or underpowered and unable to fully explain the biological basis of HIV susceptibility.    The women who became infected in this large clinical trial represent the best model to understand risk factors of HIV acquisition and may provide invaluable clues on the biological processes that lead to increased risk of infection. Our initial research of CAPRISA-004 participants shows that mucosal factors in the genital tract may be contributing to HIV infection risk.  However this picture is incomplete as mucosa contains many thousands of factors, many involved with immunity and inflammation. We have developed advanced proteomic-based methods and mathematical modeling techniques to study mucosal immune systems which can provide an unbiased global snapshot of the immune state of the mucosal environment.  This 'systems biology' approach will help us to better understand the biological drivers of these responses and potentially which factors are predictors of HIV acquisition.   Determining what factors made these women susceptible to HIV may give us new insight into risk factors for HIV and help lay the knowledge foundation for the development of the next generation of microbicides and/or vaccines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of a new "intracellular immunization" strategy restricting HIV-1 infection and inducing host immune response
Keywords-MotsClés: APOBEC3G; GENE THERAPY; HIV MUCOSAL INFECTION; HIV PREVENTION; HOST ANTIVIRAL PROTEIN; HUMANIZED MOUSE MODEL; IMMUNE RESPONSE; INTRACELLULAR IMMUNIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: APOBEC3G (A3G), a deoxycytidine deaminase, is a powerful host antiviral factor that is able to restrict HIV infection by causing virus hypermutations.  Moreover, A3G was also shown to act as an inducer of the adaptive immune response. However, during a wild type HIV infection, the antiviral and immunological actions of A3G are counteracted by HIV Vif protein since it induces A3G degradation and blocks A3G virus incorporation. Hence, how to reactivate the antiviral effect of A3G during HIV infection is of considerable interest, as it will provides a basis to develop a novel therapeutic strategy to block HIV infection.   Our research group has studied the mechanism of anti-HIV action of A3G and found that by fusing A3G to a HIV-targeting polypeptide (R88), the R88-A3G could change pathway to target into virus and regain anti-HIV activity even in the presence of HIV Vif. Our study clearly showed that when R88-A3G was introduced into human primary PBMCs and macrophages, a significant inhibition of HIV infection was observed. Furthermore, our recent data has demonstrated that R88-A3G was able to target HIV latently infected cells and block the infection and dissemination of different HIV, including drug resistant viruses. All of these data provide the proof of concept for a new anti-HIV strategy based on a natural antiviral molecule. In the proposed study, we will continue our effort to investigate whether introducing R88-A3G into humanized mice is able to restrict HIV infection and meanwhile to spontaneously induce an effective immune response against subsequent HIV challenge. We believe that the fully characterization of this system will lead to develop this approach as new prevention and therapeutic strategy against HIV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel p75 Receptor Antagonist for Therapy of HIV-Related Sensory Neuropathy
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL; DORSAL ROOT GANGLION SENSORY NEURONS; HIV; IN VIVO DRUG TREATMENT; MECHANICAL ALLODYNIA; NERVE CONDUCTION; NEUROPATHIC PAIN; P75 RECEPTOR ANTAGONIST; SKIN INNERVATION
Abstract-Résumé: Worldwide, millions of patients infected with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) suffer from sensory nerve pain (HIV-SN) and numbness in their hands and their feet. The success of anti-retroviral medication means HIV patients are no longer dying from the disease. Instead they are living with chronic exposure to this 'nonreplicating' HIV virus which can lead to secondary effects such as HIV-SN. There is no treatment for HIV-SN as pain medications are ineffective; therefore a novel treatment is desperately needed.   We will test the ability of the novel p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75ntr) antagonist LM11A-31 (LM) for treating HIV-SN and loss of skin innervation at the site of HIV-SN.  We will test the overarching HYPOTHESIS that: LM successfully treats HIV-SN. The overarching hypothesis is based on our published observations showing that:  1. Chronic expression of HIV viral protein R (Vpr) in our HIV-mouse model leads to chronic pain and loss of nerve innervation at the footpad, as seen in HIV patients.  2. Vpr exposure in cultured rodent and human sensory neurons inhibits axonal growth and this is prevented by blocking p75ntr.  3. The drug LM blocks the p75ntr in multiple animal models and has been shown to be safe and effective. LM is currently undergoing Phase 1 clinical trials which means it will likely be approved for human use by the time our proposal is complete (personal communication from our collaborator, and engineer of this drug, Dr. Frank Longo).  In summary, our proposal will test the ability of LM to treat HIV-SN and prevent the loss of epidermal nerves in the footpad of our HIV mouse model. This would provide the basis for a Phase 2 Clinical trial to treat HIV-SN patients with LM in hopes to cure to this debilitating condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: A pilot randomized trial of a polypill to prevent cardiovascular disease and cancer among people living with HIV
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA; SUPPLY CHAIN MANAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with HIV infection are at a heightened risk for cardiovascular disease and cancers. In settings with low human and health resources, simplified methods of delivery of care are needed to provide primary care. We propose to undertake a pilot randomized trial of a polypill, containing blood pressure drugs, a statin, and aspirin, among an aging (>50 years) HIV+ population in Rwanda. Our pilot study will examine the our ability to enroll patients; the success of our data collection proceses; determine an appropriate period of follow-up; ascertain the optimal drug ingredients; and obtain initial data to inform a sample size calculation for a future trial. Our study aims to recruit 400 participants and follow them for a 1- year period. We will measure surrogate outcomes including lipid status, blood pressure, thrombotic factor as well as major clinical events.

TitreApplicationTitle: Detection of HIV-1 ASP and characterization of its modulation of viral replication through induced autophagy
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTISENSE PROTEIN; ANTISENSE TRANSCRIPTION; AUTOPHAGY; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; ELISA DETECTION; HIV-1; LEUKAPHERESIS; MAGNETIC BEAD-BASED CELL SORTING; MONOCYTES AND MACROPHAGES; MULTIMERISATION
Abstract-Résumé: Previous studies have suggested the existence of a new Human Immunodeficiency Virus type 1 (HIV-1) gene termed Antisense Protein (ASP).  The proposed encoded protein has been difficult to detect in infected cells, and this has been a major source of concern and have contributed to the important controversy surrounding the existence of ASP. Our lab has succeeded in detecting the ASP protein by different approaches and we are confident that the ASP gene produces a protein with an important role in HIV-1 replication. In this proposal, we are interested in detecting the ASP protein in several cell types important for HIV-1 replication and in obtaining data on its possible function in cells infected by HIV-1.  Through these studies, we will use some of our newly developed tools to further detect the ASP protein in cells from infected individuals. These experiments will be conducted in various cellular contexts such as mammalian cell lines and primary cells (dendritic cells, macrophages and CD4+ T lymphocytes) isolated from blood samples.  The presence of the protein in infected patients will also be demonstrated by detection of specific antibodies. A series of experiments will also be designed to address the potential function played by the ASP protein. Hence, from our recent data showing the capacity of this protein to agglomerate in large complex, we will search for a possible link between the presence of the ASP protein and a cellular phenomenon termed autophagy recently shown to be important for the life cycle of the virus in macrophages.  As a final objective of the current proposal, we will thus look at the impact of ASP on HIV-1 replication through its capacity to induce autophagy. Confirming the existence of a controversial viral protein in HIV-1 represents an important step in reaching a better understanding of HIV-1 replication and pathogenesis. The ASP protein might further become a new interesting target for anti-retroviral therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular characterization of HERC5, a novel multifunctional antiviral protein.
Keywords-MotsClés: E3 LIGASE; HERC5; HIV/AIDS; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTERFERON; NUCLEAR EXPORT; POSITIVE EVOLUTIONARY SELECTION; RESTRICTION FACTORS; SUPER-RESOLUTION MICROSCOPY; VIRUS ASSEMBLY
Abstract-Résumé: Interferons are proteins produced by our cells in response to pathogens, particularly viruses. Interferons act by triggering the production of hundreds of proteins that generate a harsh environment for viruses. Restriction factors comprise a small number of interferon-induced proteins that on their own serve as powerful blockades to virus replication. Recent work by our group has contributed to the growing body of evidence suggesting that a recently discovered antiviral protein called HERC5 exhibits several hallmarks of a restriction factor. HERC5 shows strong signatures of rapid evolution, is induced by interferon and virus infection, and has antiviral activity as it major biological function. This study proposes to further characterize the molecular mechanisms underlying HERC5 activity and how viruses evade its activity. Our goal is to better understand the role HERC5 plays in innate immunity. Our research will aid in the development of improved animal models for virus infection, identify novel targets for antiviral therapies, and further facilitate the use of viral vectors for clinical gene delivery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of Blys/BAFF as a new therapeutic target for limiting immune activation and viral reservoirs during HIV/SIV infection
Keywords-MotsClés: BLYS/BAFF; DENDRITIC CELLS; HIV/SIV DISEASE PROGRESSION; LYMPHOCYTES B AND T; VIRAL RESERVOIRS
Abstract-Résumé: Although the vast majority of HIV-infected individuals can now achieve and maintain viral suppression with modern antiretroviral therapy (ART), their life expectancy remains limited and they continue to be at much higher risk for diseases commonly associated with aging. B lymphocyte dysregulations are often observed during HIV infection, and not fully restored by ART, contributing to abnormal levels of immune activation and inflammation that may drive these clinical events, sustaining a global impairment of the humoral immune compartment and favouring the development of autoimmune manifestations and malignancies, as well as promoting HIV reservoirs. Dendritic cells (DCs) are involved in the outcome of B-cell development, differentiation and survival, mainly through production of growth factors such as B lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS/BAFF). We have recently demonstrated that BLyS over-expressing DCs are increased in the blood of HIV-infected progressors, as soon as in the acute phase of infection and persisting despite successful therapy, being concomitant with B-cell dysregulations. The present proposal aims to further determine the impact and the mechanisms by which BLyS/BAFF affect immune activation and viral reservoirs expansion during HIV/SIV infection. We believe that these studies will provide strong evidence to support novel therapeutic approaches viewed to control BLyS levels as an adjunct treatment to ART to reduce both HIV target cells and systemic immune activation that are the hallmarks of HIV disease progression.  .

Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIV/AIDS; RWANDA; TREATMENT AS PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Treatment as prevention with antiretroviral therapy (ART) can reduce the infectiousness of a person living with HIV. Although this has been demonstrated in clinical trials and small observational studies, the real-world effects of treatment as prevention remain a critical knowledge gap. Additional prevention strategies, such as voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) and prevention of mother to child transmission (PMTCT), are prevention strategies that may affect population level HIV epidemiology. In collaboration with the National University of Rwanda School of Public Health (NURSPH), the Rwanda Ministry of Health (MoH), the Rwanda Biomedical Centre/Institute of HIV Disease Prevention and Control (RBC/IHDPC), the goals of this research project are to use data from the Rwandan national surveillance system on HIV epidemiology  (TRACnet) to evaluate whether treatment as prevention has had a protective effect at a national level and whether the addition of VMMC and PMTCT provides an additive protective effect.

Keywords-MotsClés: HIV/AIDS; MOBILE TECHNOLOGY; PMTCT; TREAMENT ADHERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Among the most important elements of HIV care is the prevention of mother to child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV; however, adherence remains an important barrier. Cell phone text messaging and directly observed (supervised) treatment have been used to improve adherence to antiretroviral therapy among HIV+ patients in  Sub-Saharan Africa. There is now considerable enthusiasm about using these methods can be an affordable way to improve both adherence and retention to care among women during and following pregnancy.  We intend to conduct a factorial randomized controlled trial of two-way text messages and supervised treatment to promote adherence to PMTCT drugs as well as clinic attendance among expectant mothers in Rwanda.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phylogenetic-based prevention interventions to curb the Montreal Men- Having-Sex with Men (MSM) epidemic
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV TRANSMISSION; MOLECULAR EPIDEMIOLOGY; PHYLOGENETICS; PRIMARY HIV INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: The HIV-1/AIDS has evolved into an increasingly complex global pandemic spreading unevenly among men having sex with men (MSM), intravenous drug users, and heterosexual groups, each influenced by a complex array of biological, behavioral and cultural factors. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is the key to the control of epidemics. Recent successes of Treatment-as-Prevention (TasP) initiatives have led to a utopian vision for HIV eradication, advocating universal HIV testing, treatment after diagnosis and pre-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk groups. Innumerable operational, behavioral, ethical, and fiscal issues question the feasibility and acceptability of TasP for population rather than individual benefit.        Evolving trends in MSM epidemics raise sobering concerns that early stage infection, often undiagnosed, will impact on the size and duration of transmission outbreaks. Our highly cited studies have used population-based phylogenetic surveillance to show that primary (0-6 months) and recent (6-18 months) stages of infection are fueling the Montreal MSM epidemic, contradicting classical epidemiological models that predict major roles of acute (0-40 days) and chronic (2-40 years). Large viral networks are the fastest-growing MSM sub-epidemic growing from 25% (9 PHI/cluster) of infections in 2007 to an alarming 54% (16 PHI/cluster) of infections in 2012. There is a public health urgency to address the MSM epidemic and optimize control programs (targeted testing, early treatment, and risk-reduction interventions) to interrupt PHI-related transmission cascades.Past funding led to the SPOT rapid testing site providing detailed demographic, testing habits, partnerships and risk behavior information needed to define risk correlates of PHI clustering and evolutionary trends where 9% of viruses are super-spreaders contributing to 54% of new infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prioritizing Community Engagement and Involvement in Understanding HIV Risk among People Who Use Drugs in Ottawa: The PROUD Study
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; DRUG USE; HIV/AIDS; OTTAWA
Abstract-Résumé: Grounded in a community-based participatory research framework, the proposed study aims to better understand the HIV risk environment and prevalence of HIV among people who use drugs in Ottawa, Ontario and surrounding communities. The PROUD Study will rely on peers' expertise stemming from their lived experience to guide all aspects of this CBPR project. The study will enroll 1200 drug users (defined as anyone who has injected or smoked drugs other than marijuana in the last 12 months) into an open cohort study. Participants will complete a one-time questionnaire administered by a trained peer or medical student, who will then administer a point of care HIV test. Recruitment, interviews and testing will occur in either the fixed research site or various community settings across Ottawa and its surrounding areas, to ensure that hidden populations who do not access services are reached. Prospective follow up will occur through linkages to health care records available through ICES. Recruitment into PROUD began in March 2013 and to date, over 400 participants have been enrolled.  There will be three waves of recruitment to enroll 600 participants from the downtown area of Ottawa; 300 from other known areas within Ottawa where drug users reside; and 300 from surrounding communities in Ontario. It is expected that the findings of this study will result in a greater understanding of the HIV risk environment among illicit drug users and the development of community-based models that enhance HIV testing and treatment referral, while building community capacity and fostering ownership of the study among the community of people who use drugs in Ottawa. Furthermore, it is expected that the CBPR methods developed in this study will contribute to new knowledge of successful approaches to CBPR which take into account the meaningful engagement and self-determination of people most affected by HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analyse des conditions d'acceptabilité et d'intégration de l'autotest en contexte communautaire et supervisé
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCEPTABILITE; AUTOTEST; DEPISTAGE DU VIH; DEPISTAGE ORAL; HOMMES AYANT DES RELATIONS SEXUELLES AVEC D'AUTRES HOMMES; INTERVENTION COMMUNAUTAIRE; INTEGRATION AUX SERVICES; PREVENTION; SUPERVISION ET ACCOMPAGNEMENT INDIVIDUALISE; VIH/SIDA
Abstract-Résumé: En utilisant l'infrastructure de SPOT, site communautaire offrant le depistage rapide, gratuit et anonyme du VIH a des hommes ayant des relations sexuelles avec d'autres hommes (HRSH), l'objectif principal du projet est d'evaluer les effets de l'offre de depistage avec l'autotest oral sous supervision (ATS) sur la proportion d'HRSH qui auront recours au depistage, notamment a l'autotest a la maison (ATM), dans la periode de 18 mois suivant l'intervention. Les objectifs secondaires sont d'identifier les recours a l'ATM sur une periode de 18 mois et de decrire, par l'entremise d'entretiens qualitatifs a la fin de la periode de suivi, l'experience des HRSH qui ont eu recours a l'ATM. La recherche proposee est un essai randomise ouvert. Les participants (N =1334) seront repartis aleatoirement entre deux conditions: l'ATS ou le test INSTI (test rapide sanguin). Lors de la rencontre initiale (J0) ou ils recevront le depistage ATS ou INSTI, ils participeront a un entretien dirige explorant les raisons du depistage, leur perception de l'ATM et leurs pratiques a risque. Ce meme questionnaire sera complete en ligne 18 mois plus tard. Apres J0, ils seront suivis pendant une periode de 18 mois, au cours de laquelle ils auront acces au depistage de leur choix: l'ATM ou le test INSTI administre a SPOT. On estime que 50% reviendront pour un depistage dans le groupe ATS, comparativement a 37,5% dans le groupe INSTI. Une plus forte proportion du groupe ATS choisira l'ATM (85%) versus 70% dans le groupe INSTI. Parmi les HRSH ayant essaye l'ATM, 35 seront invites a participer a un entretien visant a mieux comprendre leur experience. Cette etude fournira des donnees sur l'acceptabilite et l'integration de l'autotest dans un contexte communautaire et supervise et sur l'eventuel potentiel de cette strategie pour augmenter le nombre d'HRSH qui connaissent leur statut serologique.

TitreApplicationTitle: Brain degeneration and regeneration in preclinical models of Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; DRUG DELIVERY; GENE THERAPY; MRI-GUIDED FOCUSED ULTRASOUND; NEUROTROPHINS
Abstract-Résumé: With aging, the risk to develop Alzheimer's disease increases. Alzheimer's disease is characterized by deficits in brain functions, which seriously impact daily living. Brain cells are deteriorating and their capacity to survive and communicate with other parts of the brain becomes compromised, leading to deficits in critical functions such as learning and memory.  Our research aims to promote general cell health by providing therapeutics that support cell survival and help in maintaining cellular integrity and plasticity, thereby assuring adequate cell-to-cell communication. We propose a novel treatment which uses ultrasound to deliver therapeutics to the brain. The area of the brain where treatment is required is identified using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).  Non-invasive imaging and delivery of therapeutics to the brain using ultrasound is currently being tested in pre-clinical models of Alzheimer's disease. Ultrasound technology is being developed for human applications, and it has the potential to improve the quality of life for people living with Alzheimer's disease in the future.

Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this project is to understand why some obese individuals lose weight easily whereas others have a great deal of difficulty losing weight, even when diet adherent.  Over the last few years our group has discovered that there are important genetic and metabolic factors that govern weight loss success. This large study will further our understanding of this question and hopefully lead to effective and tailored  therapies for obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Telephone-Based Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Bariatric Surgery Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: BARIATRIC SURGERY; COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY; EATING DISORDERS; OBESITY; QUALITY OF LIFE; TELEPHONE-BASED THERAPY; WEIGHT LOSS
Abstract-Résumé: Bariatric (weight loss) surgery is the most effective treatment for extreme obesity, but surgery does not treat underlying psychological and behavioural issues.  Currently, psychotherapy ("talk therapy") for eating problems is not routinely offered with surgery, and many people start to regain weight one year later.   Objective: This study will examine if adding a convenient and accessible psychotherapy by phone one year after surgery will lead to increased weight loss two years after surgery.  Primary Hypothesis:  Relative to the Control group (who will get routine care), the group of individuals who get psychotherapy will have lower weights 2 years after surgery.  Secondary Hypotheses:  Relative to the Control group, the psychotherapy group will report significantly less maladaptive eating behaviours and significantly greater quality of life.  Method: 330 participants recruited from the Toronto Western Hospital Bariatric Surgery Program will be randomly assigned to 1 of 2 groups:  1) Control (Usual Standard of Care) or 2) Tele-CBT (a 7-session telephone-based cognitive behavioural therapy [a type of "talk therapy"] intervention focused on developing coping skills to improve maladaptive thoughts, emotions, and eating behaviours, specifically designed for bariatric surgery patients, delivered 1 year post-surgery).  They will have their weight measured and will complete measures of eating behaviour and quality of life prior to the intervention, and again at several time points extending to 2 years post-surgery.   Implications: If Tele-CBT is found to improve bariatric surgery outcomes, it could become the standard of care in Canadian bariatric surgery programs and beyond, and be routinely offered to patients who cannot feasibly attend CBT sessions due to physical or practical barriers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Autocrine motility factor and the Gp78 ubiquitin ligase: Role in cancer progression
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOCRINE MOTILITY FACTOR; AUTOPHAGY; BREAST TUMOR PROGRESSION AND METASTASIS; CALCIUM HOMEOSTASIS; ER STRESS AND CELL DEATH; ER-MITOCHONDRIA INTERACTION; GP78 UBIQUITIN LIGASE; HER2; P38 MAP KINASE; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Autocrine motility factor (AMF) and its receptor, Gp78, promote tumor cell motility and metastasis and are closely associated with malignancy in various cancers. Curiously, Gp78 is found both at the cell surface where it internalizes AMF from outside the cell and inside the cell, within the endoplasmic reticulum, where it targets proteins for degradation. Gp78 is localized to regions of the endoplasmic reticulum that interact closely with mitochondria. We have shown that Gp78 degrades mitochondrial proteins and controls the movement and destruction of mitochondria.  Both these cellular organelles play important roles in cell death and we hypothesize that AMF and Gp78 act at these sites to promote tumor cell survival and thereby tumor progression and malignancy.  We will now study how AMF regulates Gp78 function in breast cancer. Recent data has shown that AMF cleaves the cell surface receptor HER2, rendering tumor cells resistant to treatment with the clinical therapeutic agent trastuzumab (Herceptin) that is currently used in the clinic to treat breast cancer patients with HER2 positive tumors. Intriguingly, Gp78-positive breast cancers are HER2-negative and the relationship between AMF regulation of tumor cell survival through Gp78 and its ability to cleave HER2 remains unknown.   We have generated a transgenic mouse that expresses Gp78 in mammary tissue and found that Gp78 overexpression increases mammary cell proliferation. We will now generate a mouse overexpressing AMF in mammary tissue and also study mice that lack Gp78. These studies will allow us to determine the relationship between AMF interaction with Gp78 and HERs and breast cancer progression. We will also actively develop new therapeutics that might both inhibit AMF regulation of Gp78 and its ability to cleave HER2, potentially developing novel therapeutics that may enhance the efficacy of trastuzumab for the treatment of breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeted Polymeric Nanotechnology for Multi-Modality Treatment of HER2 Positive Breast Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: AUGER ELECTRON RADIOTHERAPY; BLOCK COPOLYMER MICELLES; BREAST CANCER; DOCETAXEL; DRUG DELIVERY; HER-2; IMAGING; NANOTECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer (BC) is a heterogeneous disease that can be divided into different subtypes based on evaluation of specific markers on BC cells. Human epidermal receptor 2 (HER2) is one of the markers that is commonly evaluated for subtype identification. HER2 positive (HER2+) BC is associated with a significantly worse prognosis than HER2- BC and increased risk of recurrence and death. Approximately 15-30% of BC cases are reported to be HER2+. The introduction of the HER2 targeted therapy, trastuzumab, administerd in combination with effective chemotherapies such as docetaxel has transformed treatment for patients with HER2+ disease resulting in significant improvements in overall outcomes. However, once patients develop metastatic BC there are not curative options and the disease will eventually progress in all patients. Indeed, it is the development of trastuzumab resistance that remains a significant therapeutic challenge. The proposed research directly addresses this clinical challenge through the development of powerful new nanotechnology which has been engineered to deliver Indium-111 as radiotherapy and docetaxel as chemotherapy to trastuzumab resistant, HER2+ BC cells. This research builds on recent clinical data that show that targeting of a cytotoxic agent to HER2+, trastuzumab resistant tumours can overcome resistance. In our proposed treatment strategy, we use pharmaceutically safe materials to deliver the cytotoxic agents, Indium-111 and docetaxel, for the selective killing of HER2+ BC cells, as a synergistic and potent combination therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Computational multimodal radiologic profiling as a prognostic biomarker for individualized prostate cancer therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; COMPARATIVE GENOME HYBRIDIZATION; DATA MINING; IMAGE-BASED DIAGNOSIS; MACHINE LEARNING; MULTIMODAL IMAGE REGISTRATION; MULTIPARAMETRIC IMAGING; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; PROSTATE CANCER; QUANTITATIVE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer is a complex phenomenon on the molecular level. Our central research question is whether these complexities can be captured using imaging technologies. My proposal aims at developing methodologies for image-based prognostic evaluation of the prostate gland that are multiparametric, multimodal, and are linked to molecular and pathologic biomarkers of the disease, with the intention of the imaging eventually replacing or complementing these biomarkers. We propose the extraction and analysis of quantitative features from multiparametric MRI (T2, perfusion and diffusion) and registered multiparametric ultrasound (B-mode, Doppler, raw ultrasound RF signals, and elastography) along with texture parameters that quantify the statistical distribution and higher order relationships of the pixel intensities in all MRI and ultrasound modalities. This will create a large set of parameters that characterize a region of interest or lesion in the prostate tissue. These imaging features will form the radiologic profile of the tissue. After surgery, we will acquire the molecular profile with genomic and proteomic technics. Using this data, we will work towards the following goals: Imaging and registration - To build the technology and acquire data for registration of multiparametric ultrasound and multiparametric MRI and to create a comprehensive radiologic profile of prostate tissue. Fusion of imaging and molecular signature - To study the associations between the radiologic profile and molecular profile of prostate cancer in order to find feature subsets in the radiologic profile that can be used as surrogates for the molecular profile. Classification for diagnosis and prognosis - To develop a machine learning framework based on supervised learning in which the molecular profile and the radiologic profile inform one another to improve the prognostic value. This work could elevate "imaging markers" to reliable and valid prognostic biomarkers.
