TitreApplicationTitle: Pharmacomodulation de produits cytotoxiques d'origine naturelle par glycosylation
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITE ANTICANCEREUSE; CYTOTOXICITE; GLYCOSYLATION; HEMISYNTHESE; IDENTIFICATION STRUCTURALE; MECANISME D'ACTION; PRODUITS NATURELS; RELATIONS STRUCTURE-ACTIVITE; SYNTHESE ORGANIQUE; SELECTIVITE
Abstract-Résumé: En 2012, plus de 186 000 nouveaux cas de cancer ont ete diagnostiques et pres de 75 700 deces ont ete causes par cette maladie au Canada. Environ la moitie de ces nouveaux cas sont attribuables aux cancers colorectaux, du poumon, de la prostate et du sein. Pres de 40 % des deces sont attribuables aux cancers du poumon et du colon. Ces chiffres demontrent bien qu'il est important de developper de nouveaux agents chimiotherapeutiques pour mieux traiter le cancer du poumon et le cancer colorectal. La recherche de nouveaux composes bioactifs pouvant etre utiles dans la prevention ou le traitement du cancer represente un grand defi a l'echelle mondiale. Plusieurs agents anticancereux actuellement sur le marche sont des produits d'origine naturelle (paclitaxel, vinblastine, vincristine, etc.). En fait, il a ete estime que plus de 73 % des anticancereux developpes depuis 1940 etaient de source naturelle. Malgre la contribution importante des ressources naturelles dans la decouverte de nouveaux medicaments, moins de 10 % des especes vegetales ont ete etudiees pour leurs activites biologiques et au niveau chimique. A la lumiere de ces chiffres, il semble opportun d'etudier les ressources vegetales afin d'identifier des nouveaux produits utiles dans le traitement du cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting Strategies for the Anterolateral Territory: a prospective randomized clinical trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; COMPOSITE GRAFT; CORONARY ARTERY BYPASS GRAFTING; DOPPLER VELOCIMETRY; ISCHEMIC HEART DISEASE; LEFT INTERNAL MAMMARY ARTERY; LONG-TERM FOLLOW-UP; MULTI-SLICE COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL; SAPHENOUS VEIN GRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiac bypass grafting (CABG) surgery is an efficient way to provide blood to the vessels supplying the heart when these vessels are diseased, thus relieving chest pain and improving patient survival. The best CABG conduit, or graft, is an artery found behind the breastbone (LIMA) which is usually connected to an anterior heart vessel (LAD) supplying a large territory of the heart. We conceived an original technique to expand the reach of the LIMA to all the anterolateral territory using a short venous graft taken from the leg. Preliminary published data with this novel CABG technique are very promising with several added benefits: the blood flow in the LIMA is increased which may lead to better long-term patency (i.e. fewer occluded grafts); the delicate LIMA-to-LAD connection is easier to perform; and shorter venous grafts are required which is particularly useful when they are too short to reach their usual site of connection for blood inflow (aorta). We propose the clinical trial AMI-PONT to assess whether the results in term of graft patency with this novel CABG strategy are not inferior, or not worse, than a conventional CABG strategy combining separated LIMA-to-LAD graft and vein graft for other target vessels of the anterolateral territory. Two hundred CABG patients will be distributed at random in two groups and will undergo either the novel or the conventional CABG strategy. Patients will be followed for ten years, and will undergo at one year a noninvasive scan using X-rays to safely, quickly and precisely evaluate graft patency. We have strong reasons to believe that the novel CABG strategy provides non-inferior graft patency for the other anterolateral targets without untoward effects. This study could have a profound impact on the cardiac surgery field.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of Myocardial changes during BReast Adenocarcinoma therapy to detect Cardiotoxicity Earlier with MRI- The EMBRACE-MRI Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CARDAIC MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; CARDIAC TOXICITY; CARDIAC TROPONIN; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; HEART FAILURE; MYOCARDIAL EDEMA; MYOCARDIAL STRAIN; VENTRICULAR DYSFUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most common cancer amongst Canadian women. 15-20% of breast cancers have high levels of a protein called HER2, which is associated with worsening survival. Treatment of these patients with anthracyclines followed by trastuzumab (which targets HER2) improves survival. Unfortunately, these drugs together can cause heart muscle injury resulting in heart dysfunction or failure in up to 42% of patients over the long term. Once heart failure (HF) occurs, about 60% of patients will not live past 2 years. Studies have suggested that patients with heart injury caused by anthracyclines are the ones who are more likely to develop HF with subsequent addition of trastuzumab. Therefore, tests to detect heart injury after anthracyclines may allow doctors to start heart protective medications with the hope of preventing HF. Animal and small patient studies have shown that an increase in the water levels of the heart muscle (edema) may be an early sign of heart injury from anthracyclines. Cardiac MRI is a unique technique that has been shown to detect edema as a marker of heart injury in various diseases. Our study will test the theory that, in women receiving therapy for breast cancer, heart edema detected by MRI at the end of anthracyclines will identify patients who will later develop heart dysfunction or HF during trastuzumab. MRI studies with novel techniques will be done pre-therapy, after anthracyclines, and at end of trastuzumab.  We will determine if patients with edema after anthracyclines are more likely to develop heart dysfunction or HF later. Ultimately, we hope to use cardiac MRI to identify high risk patients and study various heart protective medications to prevent HF. This will improve the personal health of cancer patients by allowing them to live free of heart disease after their cancer therapy. At a population level, this will allow doctors to provide care that can be uniquely designed for each patient based on their individual heart risk.

TitreApplicationTitle: Arterial-venous specification during adult neovascularization
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ARTERIAL-VENOUS SPECIFICATION; INTRAVITAL EPIFLUORESCENCE VIDEOMICROSCOPE; NEOVASCULARIZATION; PERIVASCULAR CELLS; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; SKIN FOLD WINDOW CHAMBER; TRANSGENIC MICE; VASCULAR BIOLOGY; VESSEL REMODELING
Abstract-Résumé: The blood vessels that form our vascular system (arteries, veins and capillaries) provide the blood supply that sustains the different organs in the body. As these vessels have different roles, they display specific characteristics that allow them to perform their different functions. In cardiovascular diseases (such as heart attack), organs suffer from a lack of blood supply and stop functioning properly. Thus, developing new therapies to generate new vessels and increase blood flow is critical to restore organ function. Despite modest success reported in therapies to generate new blood vessels, positive effects were not maintained long term, suggesting that not only we need to generate more vessels but they must be the right vessel type. The formation of different blood vessel types such as arteries and veins is essential to create functional vessels. However, the mechanisms involved in the creation of the specific vessel types in adults are unknown. We will study how the different vessels are formed in health and disease. Our hypothesis is that cells called perivascular cells (located on the outside of the vessels), that have been shown to mediate vessel maturation, are controlling vessel type assignment. We will study this by using genetically modified mice to identify different vessel types and by inducing or blocking perivascular cell binding to vessels. Our goal is to understand the molecular and cellular factors controlling the formation of blood vessel types in health and disease (diabetes). This study will provide important information on how to control vessel type formation and may help improve therapies for lack of blood supply. We will also contribute to the training of high qualified personnel, increasing the availability of a highly skilled work force. Since cardiovascular disease is one of the leading causes of death in Canada, costing over $20 billion every year, we expect these studies to have a major impact in the health of the Canadian population

TitreApplicationTitle: EmPhAsIS: Empowering Pharmacists in Asthma management through Interactive SMS
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENCE; ASTHMA; E-HEALTH; ECONOMIC EVALUATION; INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY; PHARMACIST; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; TREATMENT PERSISTENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is a chronic disease affecting 8-12% of Canadians. While there are effective and inexpensive treatments for asthma, adherence to such treatments is disappointingly low. As a result asthma remains uncontrolled in a significant proportion of patients, causing avoidable medical costs, productivity loss, and reduced quality of life.  Community pharmacists are at a strategic position in the chain of health care delivery. They have the knowledge and skills acquired through years of training and are often the last health professional patients encounter in their interaction with the health care system. It is, unfortunately, a recognized fact that pharmacists' expertise and training is under-utilized in Canada, in a role hitherto focused on dispensing. One reason for this can be the traditional focus on unilateral delivery of care from the physician to patient. According to Health Canada, a quality health care system in the 21st century will be based on "continuous healing relationships", characterized by continuous communication and information flow, facilitated by information technology, among all the links in the chain of health care delivery. Community pharmacists in such a system can be seen as active members of a multidisciplinary health care team.  In this research we propose and evaluate an intervention for monitoring and improving individual's adherence to asthma medications through mobile text messaging. Community pharmacists in this framework will play a central role providing care and linking patients and physicians. Our study is the first intervention that uses accessible information technologies to promote the role of community pharmacists in the management of asthma. Pharmacists in Canada are increasingly advocating for, and obtaining the rights to, expand their scope of practice, and our proposed intervention can benefit from this impetus to improve the quality of asthma care in our communities

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring frailty and its role in the assessment of high risk medications and risk for poor health outcomes in vulnerable populations.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE HEALTH DATA; COHORT STUDY; CONSENSUS PANEL REVEW; CONTINUING CARE; FRAILTY; HEALTH OUTCOMES; QUALITY INDICATORS; RESIDENT ASSESSMENT INSTRUMENT DATA; SENIORS; SUB-OPTIMAL MEDICATION USE
Abstract-Résumé: We have created an interdisciplinary team of researchers, clinicians and policy makers to identify key medication concerns for seniors receiving home care (HC) and long term care (LTC) services across Canada. The continuing care sector typically serves the very old and highly vulnerable members of our society. Unfortunately, because their health needs are so complex and variable, it is the very old and highly vulnerable that are often excluded from research into new drug therapies. As a result, we often do not know how to safely and effectively use drugs in older individuals receiving continuing care services. A better understanding of how to detect vulnerability (or frailty) among older HC and LTC clients might help health professionals to identify those most likely to experience a poor outcome following the use of a high risk medication. This information could be used by care providers to identify different therapies and/or new ways to care for such vulnerable persons that would lead to improved health outcomes and quality of life. The strength of our proposal lies in our rich data sources. Continuing care settings in Canada are increasingly adopting the Resident Assessment Instrument (RAI) to measure and monitor the overall health and functional status of their clients. Members of our team have completed work with items available from RAI and other health databases to explore new measures for identifying older adults with heightened vulnerability (frailty) potentially placing them at risk for adverse drug-related outcomes. Building on this earlier work, we propose to (i) conduct an expert panel review of quality indicators for appropriate drug use relevant to HC and LTC; (ii) utilize linked RAI and administrative health databases for HC and LTC settings in Ontario and Saskatchewan to assess how well our revised medication quality indicators and frailty measures are able to predict those most at risk for sub-optimal medication use and poor outcomes.

Keywords-MotsClés: EFFECTIVENESS; EXERCISE; FAMILY MEDICINE; LIFESTYLE INTERVENTION; METABOLIC SYNDROME; NUTRITION; PRIMARY CARE; RANDOMIZED CONTROL TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) refers to a group of factors (high cholesterol, sugars, and blood pressure, and being overweight) that increase the risk for heart disease, stroke, diabetes and their complications. In Canada, 20% of adults have metabolic syndrome. People with MetS have been shown to have double the annual health care costs and higher frequency of services than those without MetS. The high rate of MetS, along with an aging population translates into enormous financial burden for health systems, patients and families. Progression of MetS to diabetes and heart disease can be significantly reduced by change in diet and exercise. Unfortunately, applying the research related to lifestyle interventions has been low amongst family doctors. This is due to various challenges such as lack of time, resources, and training amongst family doctors. Canadian Health Advanced by Nutrition and Graded Exercise (CHANGE) developed a program that builds upon previous diet and exercise research. This program can be delivered by a team of health professionals (dietitian, kinesiologist and family physician) within a primary care setting. The CHANGE intervention overcomes the challenges found in primary care by providing a program that patients can easily access when visiting their family doctor. A pilot study has shown the CHANGE program can be implemented within primary care settings with positive results. It is now important to evaluate the effectiveness of this intervention in reversing MetS within a variety of settings. If the CHANGE intervention can be shown effective in reversing MetS in diverse settings, widespread implementation could save millions of dollars for Canadians and the health care system relating to medications and procedures for these expensive medical conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and Validation of a Non-invasive assay to Diagnose Rejection in Renal Transplant Recipients
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLOGRAFT REJECTION; CYTOKINES; IMMUNE MONITORING; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTERLEUKIN-6; PERIPHERAL BLOOD CELLS; REJECTION DIAGNOSIS; RENAL TRANSPLANTATION; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH; TRANSPLANT OUTCOMES
Abstract-Résumé: In the last two decades, thanks to the development of new immunosuppressive medication, the rejection rate of transplanted kidneys in the first year following transplant have decreased substantially. Unfortunately, this success has not translated into a significant increase in the long-term graft survival. This is now the most challenging task in transplantation: to prevent premature graft loss. We know that rejection is the main mechanism leading to premature graft failure. The problem lies in the fact that it is often diagnosed late, because we need to perform a biopsy to confirm the diagnosis. This is a complex and sometimes risky procedure, such that it cannot be used repeatedly to monitor the transplanted kidney. There is no doubt that a simple test, for instance based on a peripheral blood puncture or urine sample, would be an ideal tool.  Our main objective is to develop such a test and to make it applicable in the clinical setting. Our preliminary studies have shown that in kidney recipients with rejection, two different markers, IL-6 measured in the blood, and CXCL10 measured in the urine, can distinguish rejectors from non rejectors. These samples were procured by a simple routine test and are therefore simple techniques that seems promising to identify patients in rejection. We now want to know if, by measuring these markers, we can predict which patients will develop a rejection episode, before irreversible damage occurs within the graft.  Our hope is that this new knowledge will help us to diagnose rejection earlier and hence maximize treatment, in order to improve the life expectancy of the transplanted kidneys and their recipients.

Keywords-MotsClés: BEST PRACTICES; CHRONIC DISEASE; HEALTH CARE DELIVERY; INFLAMMATORY ARTHRITIS; MODEL OF CARE; STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT; STANDARDIZED CARE
Abstract-Résumé: With Canada's aging population, increased obesity and increased sedentary life, the burden of chronic diseases has been a growing concern. Although the provincial health care systems have attempted to respond to the changing health care needs, the management of chronic conditions has been criticized for being inadequate and often failing to meet the needs of the patients. Arthritis is a prime example of a prevalent chronic condition with barriers to accessing quality care. Today, it is reported that 1 in 6 Canadians aged 15 and older are reported to have arthritis. By 2040, it is predicted that 1 in 4 Canadians will suffer from arthritis. The total economic burden of the two most prevalent forms of arthritis - rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and osteoarthritis - alone is predicted to grow from $33.2B in 2010 to over $68B in 2040. The Arthritis Alliance of Canada (AAC) represents over 35 organizations across Canada. It provides a central focus for member organizations to work together on national arthritis-related initiatives. Using the highly successful process used to develop and implement the knee and hip replacement surgery models of care in Alberta and Ontario, AAC is leading the pan-Canadian standardized model of care (MoC) initiative for inflammatory arthritis (IA), the most common forms of which are RA, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, reactive arthritis, gout, and lupus. IA leads to inflammation and progressive damage of the joints causing pain and severe disability. The aim of the national IA MoC is to ensure that best practices and procedures are used by the IA health care team across Canada. With content experts, key leaders and champions across Canada on board, the development of the pan-Canadian standardized IA model of care is well underway. AAC looks to the CIHR Dissemination Events programs to fund the dissemination of the standardized IA MoC across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Closing the knowledge translation and exchange circle: translating evidence from a peer-led summit for heterosexual men with HIV into action.
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; HEALTH SERVICES; HIV/AIDS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION AND DISSEMINATION; KTE
Abstract-Résumé: Held in September 2012, the Research, Policy and Advocacy Agenda Setting Summit for Heterosexual Men with HIV was a peer-led meeting of heterosexual men with HIV from across Ontario which identified the research, policy and advocacy priorities of this community. The planning and execution of the summit were notable for the high degree of  involvement by a community advisory board (CAB) of heterosexual men with HIV. The overall purpose of this proposal is to bring together heterosexual men living with HIV, community-based researchers, frontline workers and policy makers involved in the funding and delivery of services for people with HIV to promote the dissemination and uptake of the knowledge generated during the summit. We plan to implement a highly structured, community led knowledge translation and exchange approach to: 1) report the findings back to the community of heterosexual men living with HIV; 2) identify key messages from the summit for translation and dissemination to stakeholders involved in the planning of services for persons with HIV; and 3) host the Heterosexual Men With HIV Knowledge Translation and Exchange Forum, an event that will bring together members of the community of heterosexual men with HIV, policy makers, community-based researchers and frontline workers from community agencies to discuss the policy and practice implications of the findings generated from the Research, Policy and Advocacy Agenda Setting Summit for Heterosexual Men with HIV. In addition, we will develop an online community of interest for sharing all documents and information generated from the dissemination events. The CAB have been involved in all facets of the planning of dissemination events and will lead all activities at the proposed events, including delivery of presentations, moderating all discussions, and preparation of fact sheets, reports and presentations for policy makers and knowledge users.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gaining informatics skills to support translational cancer research: Canadian Bioinformatics Workshop on Cancer Genomics 2014
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO INFORMATICS TRAINING; COMPUTATIONAL SKILLS TO ADVANCE CANCER RESEARCH; DISSEMINATION OF INFORMATICS SKILLS; FASTER TRANSLATION OF CANCER RESEARCH OUTCOMES; INFORMATICS FOR CANCER GENOMICS; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCE ANALYSIS FOR VARIANT DETECTION; PATHWAY ANALYSIS AND FUNCTIONAL RELEVANCE OF VARIANTS; RNA SEQUENCE ANALYSIS FOR FUSION GENE DETECTION
Abstract-Résumé: As for other aspects of human and health research, bioinformatics skills play a fundamental role in cancer research today, particularly given the complex biology of the cancer genome and the introduction of many high-throughput technologies into cancer research projects. Cancer researchers are increasingly seeking computational skills to aid analysis, comprehension and translation of their research. However, acquiring this level of advanced bioinformatics skills specific to the uniqueness of the cancer genome is challenging because adequate training programs do not exist. The Canadian Bioinformatics Workshops (CBW) proposal herein seeks to disseminate its leading edge bioinformatics knowledge and skills to cancer researchers through a cancer-specific workshop. The CBW is seeking $25,000 in support from the CIHR to host a Bioinformatics for Cancer Genomics (BiCG) workshop in 2014 and specifically, to sponsor trainee attendance at the workshop. The flagship BiCG workshop is a 5-day intensive, hands-on workshop designed to guide researchers through the key bioinformatics concepts and tools required to analyze cancer genomic data sets. Participants will gain experience in genomic data visualization tools, which are applied throughout the development of the skills required to analyze cancer -omic data for gene expression, genome rearrangement, somatic mutations and copy number variation. Strategies for pathway analysis and functional evaluation on the resultant cancer variant list and integration of clinical data will also be provided. By providing a comprehensive program in cancer-specific bioinformatics tools, the BiCG workshop has shown to enhance the informatic skill set of the cancer research community in Canada, thereby enabling translational cancer research and personalized cancer therapy discoveries.

TitreApplicationTitle: SPIRIT: Improving quality and efficiency of clinical trial protocols
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHICS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; RANDOMIZED TRIAL PROTOCOLS; RESEARCH TRANSPARENCY
Abstract-Résumé: The protocol of a clinical trial plays a central role in the design, conduct, and external review of the study. However, half of trial protocols submitted to research ethics boards are incomplete. Incomplete protocols can hinder transparency; lead to time wasted on protocol revisions; delay ethics approval; promote inconsistent trial conduct; and in the worst case, produce invalid data.  To address these concerns, the Canadian-led SPIRIT Initiative (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) produced evidence-based guidance for developing trial protocols. Published in Annals of Internal Medicine, BMJ, and Lancet, SPIRIT aims to provide high-quality standards for trial protocols, while helping to streamline the process from protocol development to ethics approval. High-quality protocols can promote transparency, do a better job of protecting trial participants, and help the trial meet its objectives.  Targeted dissemination activities and implementation tools will be critical to raise awareness and increase use of SPIRIT by trial investigators (core users) and ethics boards (core facilitators). We propose to create and disseminate two implementation tools for SPIRIT: an online educational module offered to 65,000 users monthly through the Collaborative Institutional Training Initiative (CITI); and a web-based protocol development software for investigators and research ethics boards. Our deliverables will consist of an interactive educational module available on the SPIRIT and CITI websites; the launch of a user-friendly protocol software tool; and support from research ethics boards through references to SPIRIT in their policies, and agreement to collaborate on integrating our software tool into ethics submission platforms. Success will be measured quantitatively by the numbers of registered users and endorsements. We will also evaluate the effectiveness of our implementation tools through an online user survey administered via CITI.

Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; HEALTH PROMOTION; ONLINE INFOGRAPHIC; PREVENTION; RISK FACTORS; STATISTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Over half of all cancers can potentially be prevented using the knowledge we have now. But successfully conveying the information to the public and creating behaviour change remains a challenge. Using the Internet as a means for health promotion is growing in popularity. We will leverage existing cancer information to develop an online tool to educate Canadians. The proposed online interactive infographic will be based on annual cancer statistics and prevention information developed by the Canadian Cancer Society. The infographic will allow users to learn about the burden of cancer in Canada and about ways to reduce their risk. The infographic will be available on the Society's website at cancer.ca and be actively promoted by the Society and its cancer system partners.

Abstract-Résumé: The Vancouver Housing First Speakers Bureau is a peer-driven initiative formed in April 2011 by participants from the Vancouver At Home project (Oct2009-Mar2013). Vancouver At Home is part of the Mental Health Commission of Canada's national research demonstration project exploring a Housing First approach to mental health and homelessness. The Speakers Bureau provides a platform for people with histories of homelessness and mental illness to engage with the community, open the dialogue on issues related to mental health and homelessness, and discuss the impact of Housing First in their lives - an emerging service model that serves to transition the most vulnerable homeless individuals into permanent housing. This proposal aims to extend the reach of the Bureau by connecting Speakers Bureau members to researchers, and provide new opportunities to co-present their 'insider' knowledge alongside the dissemination of study results to diverse audiences in policy, academic and non-academic settings. Involving peers in knowledge dissemination activities will advance mutual learning, promote more informed and balanced policy discussions, and share power in decision-making with people who have historically been excluded from conversations about the development of policies and programming that directly impacts their lives.

Abstract-Résumé: Our previous work has demonstrated how research combined with an integrated approach to KTE can lead to action, fueling improvements in policy and programs for communities. By disseminating our results widely and purposefully to professionals working in the school system, urban planning and health promotion, and to those working in local government in addition to community members and laypeople, we expect to stimulate discussion and increase awareness of food environments' role in the health of children and families. Our proposed activities consist of holding a 2.5 day conference opening with a free public lecture, followed by a conference and then a more focused strategic planning day; a half-day workshop bringing together school and municipal leaders to discuss school food environments; preparation of a fact sheet series and a plain language report.

TitreApplicationTitle: ACKTIONS: Accelerating Community-Led Knowledge to Action Systems
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE PREVENTION; COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT; HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTHY LIVING; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; KNOWLEDGE TO ACTION
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed dissemination event "ACKTIONS: Accelerating Community-Led Knowledge to Action Systems" is designed to bring together key stakeholders/knowledge users in research, policy and practice in Saskatchewan(SK), Manitoba(MB) and Ontario(ON) to share and learn from four First Nation communities who have been developing and implementing knowledge to action systems to reduce chronic disease.  The four communities represent experiences from a  remote northern First Nation (Northlands Denesuline First Nation), an Independent First Nation(Sagkeeng First Nation), a progressive First Nation (Ochapowace), and NorWest Co-op Community Health Centre (an Urban Health Center providing services to First Nation and new immigrants/refugees). As part of the two day face-to-face meeting in Winnipeg, MB the four communities will share resources, tools and tangible examples of how they have built and expanded their capacity to use and develop knowledge (collating existing reports and traditional/community knowledge, and/or gathering new data) to plan, implement and monitor/evaluate their health promotion/chronic disease prevention activities to improve health within their communities. The event will create the opportunity for communities and knowledge users to support each other through the sharing of stories, reflection on their activities and collective development of possible solutions including partnerships, new initiatives, research, or further opportunities for funding and in-kind contributions.  It is also anticipated that the event will further stakeholders knowledge and understanding of community-led knowledge to action systems enabling them to take action to accelerate effective, evidence-based and coordinated planning, delivery and continuous improvement of their healthy living and chronic disease prevention initiatives.

TitreApplicationTitle: XVIth International Congress of Virology (ICV2014)
Keywords-MotsClés: VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The International Congress of Virology (ICV) is the premier international meeting in the field of virology. The conference covers all aspects of virus infection, from entry into the cell through replication and assembly, to uncovering the molecular basis of pathogenesis, to prevention and therapy. The 2014 meeting will be held in Montreal, Quebec from July 28 to August 1, 2014 and feature plenary sessions, concurrent workshops, and poster sessions. Plenary speakers will present cutting-edge findings about the dynamic interactions of viruses with the cells and organisms they infect as well as host counter-measures to combat infection. Workshop conveners, chosen for their expertise in the topics covered in each session, will lead lively and open discussions following each presentation. Workshop presentations, chosen from the abstracts submitted for the poster sessions, will highlight exciting new developments in virus research. The poster sessions are an important and prominent aspect of the ICV, providing yet another opportunity for participants to present and discuss their research. Meeting participants will include well-known established investigators who have made seminal contributions to the field, young investigators launching independent research careers, postdoctoral fellows and graduate students, and investigators from industry, drawn from a diverse, international community. The ICV will be held in conjunction with the International Congresses of Bacteriology and Applied Microbiology and Mycology and offer a unique opportunity for interactions across the broad discipline of microbiology. Daily bridging sessions, including a symposium of Nobel laureates, will bring together attendees of all three meetings. The impact of this meeting will come in promoting the free exchange of new findings and ideas in virology and fostering new scientific collaborations among investigators throughout the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Signalisation Québec 2014
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGIE DU CANCER; IDENTIFICATION DE CIBLES THERAPEUTIQUES EN ONCOLOGIE; SIGNALISATION INTRACELLULAIRE
Abstract-Résumé: Au cours des annees, la recherche biomedicale a permis d'ameliorer considerablement les traitements pour lutter contre le cancer. Neanmoins, cette maladie est maintenant la plus meurtriere au Canada. Il est donc primordial d'identifier des cibles therapeutiques alternatives pour contrer cette pathologie devastatrice. Pour y arriver, les chercheurs oeuvrant dans la discipline de la signalisation cellulaire s'afferent a decouvrir les dereglements au sein des cellules cancereuses qui stimulent l'apparition et favorisent la progression de la maladie. Ceci represente la pierre d'assise pour l'elaboration de medicaments qui permettront de retablir l'equilibre cellulaire et de freiner la progression du cancer. Le colloque Signalisation Quebec 2014 regroupera environ 150 experts en signalisation cellulaire et oncologie provenant de 6 universites (Laval, McGill, Montreal, Sherbrooke, UQTR, Toronto) et affilies a 17 centres de recherche reconnus. Les objectifs de cette rencontre sont de disseminer les percees scientifiques des chercheurs en oncologie et de potentialiser les retombees des travaux de recherche par le biais d'echanges d'idees et d'expertises favorisant l'etablissement de collaborations interinstitutionnelles synergiques. De plus, le colloque Signalisation Quebec 2014 contribuera a la formation de la releve scientifique en permettant aux etudiants et stagiaires d'acquerir de nouvelles connaissances et de presenter leurs travaux en oncologie. Donc, cet evenement aura des retombees importantes a court et a long terme sur l'evolution des traitements pour combattre le cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using oral traditions to support oral health: Sharing what we have learned about Kungatsiajuk (the healthy smiles) of Southern Labrador Inuit youth
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; CHILDREN AND YOUTH; HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTH SERVICE DELIVERY; ORAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal children in Canada face shocking rates of tooth decay. Poor oral health influences a wide spectrum of chronic health conditions, including diabetes, obesity, and heart disease. To date, examples of community-based Aboriginal oral health research is exceedingly rare. After four years of collaboration, in 2011 our Kungatsiajuk Research Team (which is comprised of representatives from the south Labrador Inuit communities of NunatuKavut, academic researchers and dental professionals) was successful in securing a three-year CIHR Open Operating Grant. This project has identified the oral health status of NunatuKavut youth and listened to youth and their care-givers discuss oral health priorities for their communities using a community-based approach. The objectives outlined for this dissemination plan have been formulated based on the three top themes that have emerged from our story-telling sessions with youth and their care-givers. These objectives include: 1) Getting at the root causes of oral health disparities for Inuit youth through an exploration of power differentials between dentist and patient. 2) Making oral health knowledge more palatable for Inuit youth and their caregivers. 3) Providing recommendations to brush up existing oral health promotion and oral health resource and service delivery policies so that they are more aligned with the needs and realities of Inuit youth. Using the stories of Inuit youth as a catalyst for discussion, this dissemination plan will: 1. Offer a short-film contest for Inuit youth as a means for youth to convey what they would like health professionals to know about their communities. 2. Through an Aboriginal Youth Oral Health Forum create opportunity for dialogue about, and identify future research and policy directions regarding, oral health promotion and oral health resource and service delivery issues within Aboriginal communities.

Abstract-Résumé: The second Canadian Symposium on Telomeres and Genomic Integrity will be held on May 28-31, 2014 near Quebec City. The on-site organizer for this symposium is Dr. Jean-Yves Masson from Laval University. The Symposium is an evolution of previous Canadian Symposiums on Telomeres and Telomerase, a bi-annual meeting that was running since 1997 and that has expanded to attract and bring together a wider audience with interests in telomere maintenance and genomic integrity. Both fields converge on critical pathways in the onset and progression of cancer and aging and the added benefit from the enlarged topic is invaluable. This year, we have two internationally renowned keynote speakers: Dr. Peter Baumann (Stowers Institute, Kansas City MO) and Dr. Andre Nussenzweig (National Cancer Institute, USA), both mentors and role models for young investigators. Peter Baumann's research focuses on telomere maintenance, DNA repair and chromosome stability using both fission yeast and mammalian cells as model systems. Andre Nussenzweig aims to uncover the cellular mechanisms that detect DNA damage and repair DNA in order to maintain genome integrity. The organizers are excited at the opportunities and interactions that this meeting will bring for the fundamental, clinical and translational research aspects of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: 23rd Annual Canadian Conference on HIV/AIDS Research
Keywords-MotsClés: CAREER PREPARATION; CONTINUING EDUCATION; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; MENTORING; NETWORKING; NEW RESEARCHERS; RESPONSIVE PROGRAMMING
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Association for HIV Research (CAHR) is the professional organization for HIV and AIDS research in Canada or by Canadians. CAHR includes all researchers and all disciplines of the scientific approaches to HIV and AIDS, for the purpose of its better prevention and treatment and ultimately for its eradication and cure. The annual CAHR Conference - taking place May 1-4, 2014 in St. John's, NL -  is the premier gathering in Canada for those working in the field of HIV, as well as policy makers, persons living with HIV and other individuals committed to ending the pandemic. It provides a platform for assessment of where we are, evaluation of recent scientific developments and lessons learned, and supports participants in charting a course forward. Canadian researchers remain at the forefront of HIV research, focusing on all aspects of the disease, from exploring the basic underpinnings of the disease, understanding the intersection of aging and complications of HIV/AIDS, improving care and treatment, to developing interventions to reduce the risks and rates of complications. The 2014 Conference programme will present new scientific knowledge and offer many opportunities for structured dialogue on the major issues facing the global response to HIV. A variety of session types, from abstract-driven presentations to symposia, bridging and plenary sessions, will meet the needs of various participants. Other related activities, including ancillary meetings, the new investigator workshop and exhibitions, will contribute to an exceptional opportunity for professional development and networking. CAHR 2014 will be a tremendous opportunity for researchers and community members from coast to coast to share the latest scientific advances in the field, learn from experiences, and develop new ways to treat and prevent HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neutrophil 2014
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNITY; INFECTION; INFLAMMATION; NEUTROPHILS
Abstract-Résumé: Our immune system protects us from invading microbes. It does this mainly by mobilizing our white blood cells, among which the most prevalent type are called neutrophils. The latter are usually the first cells to infiltrate a site of infection or injury, where they accumulate in large numbers. In addition to their well known role in ingesting and destroying microbes, neutrophils also influence the recruitment into injured tissues of other white blood cell populations, and to influence their functions. More recently, it has become evident that neutrophils can also participate in, and modulate, the immune response. Finally, several important discoveries involving neutrophils in various diseases have cast this white blood cell firmly into the limelight in the field of immunology.     Up to 2012, the international neutrophil community had never held a meeting entirely devoted to this important cell population. Thus came the Neutrophil in Immunity meeting into existence. It was a resounding success, with 260 scientists from 31 countries. At the close of the meeting, the participants strongly insisted that there be another such meeting in 2014, as not all aspects of the rapidly expanding field of neutrophil biology could be addressed. For this reason, and in light of exciting advances made in the field since 2012, we were compelled to organize the follow-up symposium that will bring together basic and clinical scientists working in the field of neutrophil biology, as well as students, post-docs, and industry researchers. The Neutrophil 2014 meeting (www.theneutrophil.com) will be held in Montreal, Canada, from May 31 to June 3, 2014. Although neutrophil-centric meetings are still in their infancy, they have already sown the seeds of a series of such events. in this regard, a 2016 meeting is also in the early stages of planning, this time at a European venue. The 2014 meeting thus represents a truly pivotal event for the neutrophil research community.

TitreApplicationTitle: The 4th International Scientific Workshop on Antiretroviral Treatment as Prevention of HIV Infection (TasP)
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV/AIDS; INTERNATIONAL WORKSHOP
Abstract-Résumé: Investigators from the BC Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS are requesting CIHR funding for the 4th International Scientific Workshop on HIV Antiretroviral Treatment as Prevention (TasP) to be held on April 21-24, 2014 in Vancouver, BC. There is widespread recognition of the enormous potential of antiretroviral treatment to both save lives and prevent new HIV and TB infections, but the challenge of expanding TasP globally remains. The TasP Workshops are the only gatherings dedicated exclusively to this issue and provide unparalleled opportunities for researchers, affected communities, and policy-makers to speak openly and candidly about pressing international research and policy issues related to TasP science and implementation. These efforts ensure that researchers are addressing the most pressing needs and that TasP-related research findings are appropriately communicated to facilitate optimal implementation and impact. The 2014 Workshop will accomplish multiple objectives, which include: reviewing the state of TasP research; facilitating coordination and harmonization among TasP related initiatives; and fostering collaboration between TasP-related research and policy initiatives. Given positive evaluation feedback from previous TasP Workshops, the 2014 Workshop will follow the same basic structure of a four-day single-track meeting with five plenary sessions, five oral abstract sessions, and five poster sessions. All formal presentations will be webcast, and a final report will be prepared. The 2014 Workshop aims to significantly impact the future of TasP-related research and policy-making globally by providing a unique and dedicated collaborative environment for sharing successes and challenges in researching and implementing TasP in a range of settings. The outcomes of this Workshop will also inform international responses to HIV/AIDS including WHO and UNAIDS initiatives to ensure improved access to HIV treatment and HIV care globally.

TitreApplicationTitle: CONSORT-C: Pediatric clinical trials reporting guideline extension
Keywords-MotsClés: KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; RANDOMIZED TRIAL PROTOCOLS; RESEARCH TRANSPARENCY; SCIENTIFIC REPORTING
Abstract-Résumé: Our knowledge about children's bodies and behaviours continues to grow. We are still learning how growth from childhood to adulthood affects treatments, interpretation of health outcomes, and how the health care system differs as a function of age and development. Research to support the effectiveness and safety of medications in young children can only be generated if high-quality randomized controlled trials are conducted and reported appropriately. For ethical reasons, children should only be involved in trials that will generate reliable results. To improve health care in children, well-reported high-quality clinical trials are required to guide health care decisions.  The CONSORT-C (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials - Children) extension of the existing CONSORT statement for trials in adults aims to improve the quality of information reported from trials conducted in children. These reporting standards provide evidence-based recommendations about the core content that should be included, or reported upon, in scientific publications. Development of these standards involves (a) the systematic assessment of published guidelines, and (b) the consideration of expert, consumer, and knowledge user input. Both will be used to create a checklist and detailed explanation document to guide researchers in reporting of pediatric trials. Ideally, CONSORT-C will be endorsed and employed by healthcare and related organizations. The use of CONSORT-C by journals, trial registries, and ethics boards will result in clear and transparent reporting of all pediatric trials.  The potential impact of this work is large. Clear and complete reporting of clinical trials serves the interests of all stakeholders, including children and their families. Such reporting also uncovers gaps, oversights and errors in research if they exist. CONSORT-C will provide clarity and structure for published reports, and improve the translation of knowledge from the literature to bedside care.

TitreApplicationTitle: 5th American Conference on Human Vibration, June 10-13, 2014
Keywords-MotsClés: HAND-ARM VIBRATION EXPOSURE; MACHINE AND TOOL VIBRATION CONTROL; PHYSIOLOGICAL AND BIODYNAMIC RESPONSES; VIBRATION HEALTH EFFECTS AND INJURIES; WHOLE-BODY VIBRATION; WORKPLACE VIBRATION CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Exposure to workplace vibration and shock has been associated with decreases in health, comfort, and occupational and social functioning. The consequences of exposure are being studied in terms of physiological responses, neurological responses, musculoskeletal stresses, motion perception, health effects, interference with activities, and combinations of these effects. The 5th American Conference on Human Vibration (June 10-13, 2014) will provide a distinctive opportunity for knowledge transfer and dissemination in multi-disciplinary subjects relevant to vibration related injuries and health effects, including both basic and applied science through epidemiology, physiology, engineering, pathology, health and safety, prevention and ergonomics.  Co-hosted by the Universities of Guelph, Laurentian, and Western in 2014, since its inception in 2006, the conference has been held every two years but has always been hosted in the United States (2006: Morgantown West Virginia; 2008: Chicago Illinois; 2010: Iowa City, Iowa; 2012: Hartford, Connecticut). Support from CIHR will help to ensure that an exceptional conference and dissemination event is put together.  International experts in vibration will share advances in epidemiology, methodologies for quantifying and assessing occupational vibration exposures, monitoring health of exposed populations, experimental and analytical studies characterizing the biodynamic, physiological and psychological responses of the body exposed to occupational vibration and standards and proposed legislation intended to protect workers from occupational vibration exposure and mechanical shock. The conference will include both oral and poster presentations. Two leading experts will be invited to give keynote addresses (on whole-body vibration exposure and hand-arm vibration exposure).  A panel is also being planned to bring clinicians, exercise physiologists,and health and safety professionals together for the first time to discuss vibration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Northern Uganda Leadership Forum: Acknowledging the Impact of HIV and Trauma in Post Conflict Northern Uganda
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFLICT/POST CONFLICT; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIV/AIDS; UGANDA
Abstract-Résumé: The war in Northern Uganda has resulted in countless deaths, child abductions, widespread violations of human rights, destruction of the social and economic fabric of society and the displacement of the majority of the population. There are reasons to be concerned that the aftermath of war provides fertile ground for the spread of HIV. Unfortunately, information about HIV in the North are limited compared to those available for the rest of the country. The purpose of our grant is to estimate the spread of HIV, to determine risk factors for HIV, to assess war-related trauma and sexually transmitted infections as risk factors for HIV transmission, and to identify individual, socio-cultural and structural factors that oppose access and utilization of HIV prevention and care services. We have achieved several critical milestones: getting ethics approvals in both countries, hiring a local research team, conducting mapping and census of all districts, and achieving our enrollment target of 2400 people. The first round of study involving all 2400 participants has been completed and round 2 has recently been initiated. Unfortunately with regards to HIV infection, the prevalence rates we found are much higher than those recently published in the 2011 Ugandan AIDS Indicator Survey (UAIS), particularly among women. It is critical now that these important analyses are communicated back to Northern Ugandan political leadership, community and young people. We are proposing a series of three knowledge dissemination events to be conducted in July, August and October of 2013.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aussi disponible en français: Dissemination of the Best Practice Recommendations for Canadian Harm Reduction Programs to Francophone Stakeholders
Keywords-MotsClés: BEST PRACTICE RECOMMENDATIONS; COMMUNITY BASED; EQUITY OF ACCESS; EVIDENCE BASED; FRANCOPHONE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER
Abstract-Résumé: Across Canada, many harm reduction programs such as needle and syringe distribution programs provide services by and for francophones. With this project, our goal is to ensure that francophone service providers, policy makers, and service users are aware of, have access to, and can use the most up-to-date scientific evidence and recommendations about harm reduction programs that provide service to people who use drugs and are at risk for HIV, hepatitis C (HCV), and other harms. To achieve these goals, we will translate into French the 2013 'Best Practice Recommendations for Canadian Harm Reduction Programs that Provide Service to People Who Use Drugs and are at Risk for HIV, HCV, and Other Harms: Part 1' developed and released by the Working Group on Best Practice for Harm Reduction Programs in Canada. The Working Group includes members from across Canada who are service providers, policy makers, service users, and academic researchers. The translated document will be disseminated via the Canadian AIDS Treatment Information Exchange (CATIE) website that currently hosts the English version of this document which was downloaded more than 1700 times between July 2013 and September 2013. Once uploaded to the CATIE website, we will host two webinars to provide options for attendance. Members of the team will present the Best Practice Recommendations at Canadian conferences that target service providers. We will also prepare two French plain-language articles that highlight key recommendations for Point de mire sur la prevention (aka Prevention in Focus, see www.catie.ca/fr/pdm). This dissemination strategy mirrors the successful English strategy. By engaging in French-focused dissemination activities, we aim to ensure equity of access to evidence-based practice recommendations and through this enhance the quality, consistency, and effectiveness of HIV, HCV, and other harm prevention services for people who use drugs across all regions of Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing System-Level Arthritis Performance Measures For AAC Framework
Keywords-MotsClés: INFLAMMATORY ARTHRITIS; PERFORMANCE MEASURES; QUALITY INDICATORS
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory arthritis (IA) is a term used to describe a group of diseases that cause pain and swelling of the joints. The most common form of IA is rheumatoid arthritis (RA) which affects nearly 1% of the Canadians from all ages causing debilitating chronic pain and disability if left untreated. Research has shown that early detection and treatment of IA (including RA) is crucial for effective care and improved outcomes. Unfortunately, about 30% of Canadians with RA may not be receiving appropriate care - they are not cared for by a rheumatologist and are not receiving effective therapies. To address this issue, we propose to bring together experts in IA care with health policy decision makers/planners and patients to develop a set of system-level measures which can be used to identify where quality healthcare is lacking and propose changes to improve care. For example, if measures indicate that there is insufficient access to specialist care in a particular area, then strategies could be developed to improve access such as funding additional specialist clinics. These measures will be used to ensure quality healthcare is available for all people living with IA. Once complete, the results of this work can also be used to improve the care of other chronic arthritic conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Disentangling the role of biological and behavioural drivers of early HIV risk in female sex workers in India, Kenya, and Ukraine
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL AND BEHAVIOURAL FACTORS; FEMALE SEX WORKERS; HIV; INDIA; KENYA; SUSCEPTIBILITY; UKRAINE
Abstract-Résumé: Female sex workers (FSWs) are at high risk of becoming infected with HIV and of passing the virus onto their clients. But not all FSWs are at equal risk of HIV infection and commercial sex differs in how much it contributes to HIV epidemics across countries. Although differences in sexual behaviours and practices among FSWs partially account for variable HIV risk, this explanation ignores differences in human biology (making some people more likely than others to become infected when exposed) and differences in the biology of the HIV virus (making some viruses more infectious than others). It is likely that biology and behaviour act simultaneously on FSWs' HIV risk and HIV transmission at the population level. However, to date, no one has unravelled these biological and behavioural factors to explain why some FSWs experience a greater (and earlier) risk of HIV infection and why some HIV epidemics are driven by commercial sex work while others less so. Our research team received CIHR funding for a behavioural survey (with HIV testing) of FSWs in India, Kenya and Ukraine to estimate their HIV risk before entry into and during their early years in sex work. This baseline survey offers an unprecedented opportunity in three different countries to jointly study the biological and behavioural factors at play, and to start dissecting their complex interactions and how they influence an individual FSW's HIV risk and a country's HIV epidemic.  Thus, we are applying for a planning grant to support a workshop for current and new team members to discuss in person and come up with a clear and feasible research agenda to tackle this complex question. Workshop participants will also brainstorm creative ways to leverage the existing infrastructures of the FSW survey and expand its biological research. This workshop will be important for developing a solid and well-defined plan for moving this innovative research agenda forward.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strengthening organizational capacity for public health equity action: Developing a research agenda
Keywords-MotsClés: CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK; HEALTH EQUITY; ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY; PUBLIC HEALTH; RESEARCH AGENDA
Abstract-Résumé: The World Health Organization, WHO, has identified the high priority of research that explores how health systems can contribute to actions that eliminate differences in health between more and less advantaged populations, called health inequities, within a generation. This is a goal which the WHO views as an ethical imperative and a matter of social justice. In Canada, persistent health inequities challenge health system sustainability and have a negative impact on the economy.      Public health, the part of the health system that promotes health and prevents disease, is ideally situated to play a leadership role in promoting health equity. However, there is evidence that current capacity of public health in Canada to address health inequities is highly variable.  A concerted effort to strengthen this capacity is an essential next step to realizing the WHO's challenge to improve the health of all Canadians, but especially those most vulnerable.    Our research team has developed a Conceptual Framework of Organizational Capacity for Public Health Equity Action, or OCPHEA, in consultation with key Canadian public health decision-makers. The framework was identified by these individuals as being novel and having direct application to current public health priorities they face. Further research to determine the feasibility and best practices to apply the Framework is necessary as a next step for OCPHEA.     The purpose of the proposed meeting, to be held May 5th to 6th, 2014, is to provide an opportunity for key Canadian public health knowledge users, academic researchers, and additional health equity and organizational capacity experts to come together for a collaborative discussion about their goals for strengthening OCPHEA and how the Framework could be used to achieve those goals, and to identify potential research projects that could test the application of the Framework in the context of real world public health practice in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Planning Grant for Traumatic Brain Injury Research
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH SYSTEMS IMPROVEMENT; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: The burden of traumatic brain injury (TBI) in Canada is significant. Death from TBI accounts for 20% of all trauma fatalities. In 2003 to 2004, there were 16,811 admissions for TBI with 1,368 deaths. Death can occur immediately at the scene, within a few hours, or later due to complications. Complications can be reduced by providing timely access to coordinated trauma care. Equally as devastating are the long-term cognitive, emotional and behavioral problems that plague survivors of TBI.  The purpose of this grant is to bring together researchers, decision makers and knowledge users throughout BC to identify the facilitators and barriers to timely and appropriate care of TBI patients. Early identification, transfer and management of these patients in centers with established TBI protocols and neurocritical care expertise decreases mortality and improves long term outcomes. However, given the large geographic distribution of BC, residents and health care professionals are confronted with significant obstacles in accessing care for TBI patients. Furthermore, these barriers may fall disproportionately on patients with lower socioeconomic status, which itself may be associated with worse outcomes in TBI.  After videoconferencing with the project team, the principal applicant will travel to all health authorities in BC to engage with site knowledge users, decision makers and a patient and/or family of a patient with TBI. Once site visits are completed, a final videoconference will be held to review and consolidate the information gathered and to develop a clear research question for an upcoming CIHR PHSI application.  Through this planning grant we will better understand the current challenges in providing access to care and barriers to efficiently delivering care.  We will then be able to develop important research questions with the goal of reducing mortality and improving functional outcomes in patients with TBI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advancing mental health and HIV research, policy, and programming through intersectionality
Keywords-MotsClés: EQUITY; HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTH SERVICES; HIV/AIDS; INTERSECTIONALITY; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; MENTAL HEALTH; PROGRAMMING
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal aims to bring together an interdisciplinary, cross-sectoral team of researchers and partners from the Public Health Agency of Canada to explore how population-based approaches to mental health and HIV services/supports can be advanced through use of an intersectionality framework. The purpose of these proposed activities is to set priorities for a program of research and develop a strategic research plan in order to submit an application to the CIHR Partnership for Health System Improvement. Intersectionality is an innovative and effective framework for addressing health inequities in policy as it uniquely encompasses and addresses the multi-factoral and multi-level complexities of health disparities. Considering this, an intersectionality approach would offer a significant contribution to the complex and interrelated fields of mental health and HIV policy research. The fields of mental health and HIV continue to face barriers regarding how to address the complex needs of diverse and vulnerable populations. Specifically, the proposed planning activities will include: (1) an environmental scan; (2) multiple iterative video-conference team meetings to set the priorities and develop an initial research plan; (3) a full-day in-person team workshop during the International Intersectionality Conference to incorporate feedback from the conference and further develop the research plan. Exploring the wide-ranging, intersecting factors that cause health inequalities in HIV and mental health is as an essential step towards the evolution of population health research. Ultimately, the proposed planning activities will address common challenges in the fields of HIV and mental health, open the door for collaborative work, consolidate country-specific efforts, and fundamentally improve empirical and explanatory knowledge to strengthen health sector responses to mental health and HIV policy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strategic Planning to Support First Nations Communities Participating in the FORGE AHEAD Program
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; ACCESS TO HEALTH CARE; DIABETES MELLITUS TYPE 2; HEALTH CARE SERVICES; PARTICIPATORY ACTION RESEARCH; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; STRATEGIC PLANNING; TEAM-BUILDING
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed planning activities, including a face-to-face meeting,  will enhance existing partnerships as well as foster the development of new partnerships by bringing together members of a national steering committee that includes First Nations (FN) community representatives, academic investigators and policy decision makers from across Canada. The activities aim to increase the committee's understanding of FN communities' research priorities, knowledge, values and cultures and will be focused on obtaining feedback and enabling shared-decision making related to the development of grant applications for funding that will support the participation of FN communities in the FORGE AHEAD program. The FORGE AHEAD program aims to facilitate the development of innovative models of care and community-driven activities to improve the prevention and management of diabetes within Indigenous communities. Respecting the Ownership, Control, Access and Possession principles and CIHR Guidelines for Health Research Involving Aboriginal People, the input of FN representatives will be critical to ensure that efforts are aligned and relevant to the needs of FN communities. Working together collaboratively with other members of the steering committee, FN representatives will be involved in teleconferences and other communication strategies during the Spring and Summer of 2014 to finalize the face-to-face meeting agenda, identify potential funding opportunities, and inform the overall planning process. During the face-to-face meeting in the Fall of 2014, in Toronto, Ontario, all partners will review preliminary activities and findings of the FORGE AHEAD program and funding opportunities in detail to develop a strategic plan for the procurement of additional funds to support FN partners in participating in the FORGE AHEAD program and to explore the possibility of extending recruitment to include additional FN communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Supporting Family Caregivers of Seniors: Improving Care and Caregiver Outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: SUPPORT FOR FAMILY CAREGIVERS
Abstract-Résumé: Family caregivers are important to the care of seniors. They provide care and basic services. They help keep seniors at home as long as possible. Their free services equal $25 Billion! However, family caregiving comes at a cost. Caregivers may need to stop working outside of the home. They may have problems with money and childcare. They are often older women who have their own health problems. Unpaid caregivers may be under a lot of stress. Sadly, this can lead to depression and other health concerns.  Researchers have tried to help family caregivers deal with stress. They have offered coaching and counseling. They have created support groups and training. They have even used the telephone and internet to offer help. These supports have been useful. Yet, many cannot access these supports. This is not enough. Much more needs to be done. Much more needs to be understood.  We will hold a 2-day conference on caregiver support. We will bring caregivers, health care providers and researchers together. On day 1, we will listen to experts talk about what is known about caregiving. We will hear what seniors, caregivers and healthcare providers have to say about caregiving. We will also talk about ways to support caregivers. On day 2, we will plan 3 research projects to help caregivers. We will come up with 3 research plans. Grants will be prepared to ask for funding for the research.  Broad partnerships will be formed in the 3 research projects. Researchers from the World Health Organization (WHO) and University of Calgary will lead a study on caregiver support through the internet. This study will be for adaptation in WHO countries. Researchers from the Palliative Institute (Edmonton) and McGill University will lead a study on support for caregivers in palliative care. Researchers from Covenant Health, Alberta Health Services, University of Alberta and Alzheimer will lead a study on caregiver support for seniors with complex needs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-term Cardio-Respiratory Outcomes of Extremely Pre-term Infants: A Workshop to Guide Development of a Current Canadian Study
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC FUNCTION; CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; EXERCISE; HEART FAILURE; LUNG HEALTH; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PREMATURITY; PULMONARY FUNCTION; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION; PULMONARY IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Our goal is to understand the lung and heart health of babies that were born too early (extremely premature infants). This is important because 10% of children are born prematurely and more of these little babies  are surviving every day. These infants can have many problems with their health.  Some may not be obvious when the babies are little but these health concerns can become major issues as the baby becomes a young child and an adult.    There are promising therapies that may be able to improve the future long term health of premature infants.  But, it is impossible to know if they are helping if we do not have a good understanding of what happens to these babies over time, in the first place.  Earlier long term studies of premature infants were done in a time when babies were not as small (or premature) and the medical care they received was different.    We are proposing to start with a two day meeting of experts from across Canada.  This meeting will bring together health care professionals who come from different specialties (neonatology, respirology, exercise physiology and cardiology).  We will first discuss the best way to look after former premature infants over time, after they leave hospital and then we will create a framework for a large national study of former premature infants in Canada today.  By doing this, we will be able to know what the specific heart, lung and exercise problems are that former premature babies face as they grow up, and also the best ways to manage these problems.  In the end we hope to improve the long-term health of premature babies and maximize their chances of living long and productive lives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Building a Team for Multi-Jurisdictional Research to Improve Patient Flow
Keywords-MotsClés: MIXED METHODS; PATIENT FLOW
Abstract-Résumé: Every Canadian health region grapples with the issue of patient flow:  how to ensure that patients move smoothly through the system to receive the care they need, when and where they need it.  While emergency department overcrowding is the most obvious symptom of stagnant flow, flow is known to be a system problem that all parts of the healthcare system must work together to improve.  Yet little is known about what flow-improvement strategies - especially system-level strategies - are really effective.  This Planning Grant process will bring together researchers and decision-makers - including the CEOs of four regional health authorities spanning four Western provinces, the President of Accreditation Canada, and others - to plan research that will meet healthcare leaders' need for guidance on this important and complex issue.  We are planning (a) a meeting in each region and at Accreditation Canada to present the findings of recent Winnipeg-based flow research and consult with local decision-makers about their priority questions and needs (April-May 2014); (b) an "environmental scan" of key structures and services in each region, to understand the differences among regions and avoid comparing apples with oranges; and (c) a full-day planning meeting (June 2014) to share information and develop a proposal for a full-scale research proposal (to be submitted to the Partnerships for Health System Improvement competition in the Fall of 2014).  Findings of the planned research will help health regions across Western Canada provide patients with more timely access to care.

TitreApplicationTitle: 1st International Symposium on Stress-Associated RNA Granules in Human Disease and Viral Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CACHEXIA; CANCER; MICRORNAS; NEUROSCIENCE; ONCOGENES; P-BODIES; STRESS GRANULES; SYMPOSIUM; VIRUSES
Abstract-Résumé: The field of RNA granule biology and how it impacts human disease is developing at a rapid pace. RNA granules are structures that manage the efficiency of gene expression in cells. When cells sense different kinds of stress (e.g. environmental stress or the stress of viral infection), RNA granules help to pause and reprogram cellular gene expression, so the cell can survive the stressful event. Thus, RNA granules play important roles in maintaining a healthy cell. It is becoming increasingly appreciated that defects in RNA granule formation and function are a feature of many human diseases. Because of this, we are initiating an international symposium to bring together leaders in the field of RNA granule biology as it relates to human disease. The symposium will take place on the campus of Dalhousie University in downtown Halifax, Nova Scotia, from June 9th to June 11th 2014 and will involve a minimum of 60 participants as well as pharmaceutical companies. This is the first symposium of its kind, and the goal of the organizing committee is to generate new knowledge in this emerging area of research and foster new collaborations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing a Research Agenda on Resident-to-Resident Elder Abuse
Keywords-MotsClés: DEMENTIA; GERONTOLOGY; HEALTH; INTERDISCIPLINARY; KNOWLEDGE MOBILIZATION; LONG-TERM CARE; RESIDENT-TO-RESIDENT ELDER ABUSE; SAFETY
Abstract-Résumé: Resident-to-resident elder abuse (RREA) is an under-researched issue that negatively affects the health and well-being of residents in long-term care homes. This one-day meeting will function as a planning event for key Canadian and international studies in the area of RREA, and also as a knowledge exchange event, as participants explore the implications of RREA for their research and practice initiatives.  The event will bring together leading experts in the study of RREA with delegates from research, practice and the community to exchange and mobilize knowledge in this area.  The outcomes from this meeting will result in formal partnerships between researchers and stakeholders on priorities and methodologies to develop grant proposals to address this serious issue. The proposed meeting is important because it will be the first dedicated effort towards addressing RREA in long-term care homes in Canada. Key outcomes of the meeting include a raised awareness and better understanding of the challenges of RREA; forging new research and practice partnerships and agendas; and the identification of priority actions and next steps in the detection, management and prevention of RREA.

TitreApplicationTitle: A planning study with former National Longitudinal Survey of Children and Youth (NLSCY) participants
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD HUNGER; LONG-TERM FOLLOW-UP STUDY; NATIONAL LONGITUDINAL SURVEY OF CHILDREN AND YOUTH; PARTICIPATORY PLANNING; SEVERE FOOD INSECURITY
Abstract-Résumé: Between 1994 and 2008/2009, the National Longitudinal Survey of Children and Youth (NLSCY) identified and followed a group of 768 children and youth, within the full sample of 15056 participants, who reported the experience of hunger. In previous analyses of this survey, we found that childhood hunger experience has long-term negative health and mental health effects.  The NLSCY has come to an end and these children have now entered adulthood. We aim to engage 25 former NLSCY participants in a planning process leading to a long-term follow-up study of those who reported child or youth hunger. The objectives of the planning process are to identify: 1) the key research questions that former NLSCY participants believe would be important to have answered about how the hunger experience in childhood affects physical and mental health, and socioadaptive functioning; 2) means by which information should be collected from former participants (such as interviews, blood-draw); and 3) strategies to engage former NLSCY participants in the proposed study. Over the course of six months, the planning process will involve teleconferences with sub-groups leading to a deliberative dialogue process conducted over two days with a small number of former participants to hear from experts and to prioritize research questions, suggest data collection methodologies, and provide guidance on how the study should be executed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Setting the research agenda for addressing weight-related issues in children with physical disabilities: a consensus building workshop.
Keywords-MotsClés: CONSENSUS; DISABILITY; NUTRITION; OBESITY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood obesity is a major health problem, with 25-30% of Canadian children now overweight or obese. Children with disabilities are 2-3 times more likely to be overweight and obese than their nondisabled peers. They are also often less physically active with poorer diets. This is alarming because obesity has negative consequences for all children, but in children with disabilities, it can cause serious additional problems, such as pressure sores, pain and severe muscle loss. This makes it harder for a child to be active which puts them at greater risk of obesity, which in turn reduces independence and increases the burden on caregivers and healthcare services. Despite this, children with disabilities have mostly been excluded from health promotion programs and research. To address this inequality, we will hold a 2-day workshop in Toronto with the goal of promoting collaborations between Canadian researchers and clinicians around childhood obesity and disability. Workshop attendees (researchers, clinicians and families) will discuss existing research and hear personal experiences from families and youth. Gaps in current knowledge will be identified by attendees, and through consensus discussions, the group will select 4-5 of these gaps as priorities. Within each area, specific research questions will be formulated using a structured framework, to be pursued post-workshop. Outcomes of the workshop include a published document summarizing the discussions; a research network with a website where members can indicate their expertise and interests with a view to collaboration; one special issue of a journal dedicated to the topic of childhood obesity and disability; and a workshop at the 2015 Canadian Obesity Summit to showcase the new research network's activities. At least one grant application will be submitted based on the topics identified at the workshop, with the expectation of long-term collaboration between the attendees and others in the research community.
