TitreApplicationTitle: Evidence for Pathways out of Childhood Adversity: Expert Meeting on Orphans and Vulnerable Children in Uganda
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD PROTECTIONS; HIV/AIDS; UGANDA
Abstract-Résumé: In low-resource settings, the burden of HIV/AIDS has led to millions of children below the age of 18 who have lost one or both parents to HIV, and are at increased risk of having or becoming infected with the virus. The syndemics of poverty and HIV in Uganda have contributed to 2.6 million orphans, 1.1 million of whom are orphaned to HIV/AIDS. This planning grant will fund an expert meeting to bring together leading researchers and care providers from the fields of child protections and HIV/AIDS. A two-day learning forum will be held in Uganda to: 1) provide overviews of each partner organization, share key achievements and challenges related to HIV and orphans and vulnerable children action-research; and 2) discuss specific upcoming funding applications, review potential research designs and prepare a timeline and roles for submitting a successful proposal. With millions of orphans and vulnerable children in need of support and protection, there is an urgent need to develop and design studies to evaluate and provide evidence to identify and support pathways out of childhood adversity.

Keywords-MotsClés: CONSULTATIONS; CRITICAL INTERPRETIVE SYNTHESIS; ETHICS; HIV; HIV CLINICIANS; HIV SERVICE PROVIDERS; TREATMENT-AS-PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: This planning grant will bring HIV care providers, community members, and researchers from across Canada into dialogue concerning the sociocultural and ethical impact of new HIV treatment and prevention approaches. Recently, treatment and prevention have merged to become what is being called treatment-as-prevention. Called "TasP" for short, this approach promotes increasing individual HIV testing, and early initiation of HIV drug treatment, to reduce the spread of HIV at the population level. This planning grant will comprise a critical interpretive synthesis (CIS) of TasP literature, a series of consultations with HIV stakeholders in key areas of the country, and the development of a pan-Canadian research project based on the CIS and consultations. The goal of this project is to develop a larger program of research that will examine the sociocultural and ethical dimensions of how HIV stakeholders interpret TasP and integrate it into clinical and personal health practices for people living with HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translating Knowledge to Organizational Change: Exploring the Role of Video Ethnography to Promote Clinical Learning and Health System Improvement
Keywords-MotsClés: CARE COORDINATION; CARE FOR OLDER PEOPLE; COMMUNICATION; EVALUATING IMPROVEMENT INTERVENTIONS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; ORGANIZATIONS; PROFESSIONAL CULTURE; VIDEO-ETHNOGRAPHY; VIDEO-REFLEXIVITY; WORK-BASED LEARNING
Abstract-Résumé: Health consumers worldwide are receiving increasingly sub-standard care and are suffering harm because of poor communication and information-sharing among health professionals. This three-day meeting of international and Canadian experts will think about and decide how video-playback can be used to understand and improve health care communication and information sharing. Those present will be consumers, policy makers, health professionals and researchers. Problems in communication and information-sharing need serious thought and debate before doing studies. Most attempts to solve this problem have not worked. This is because there are serious but hidden problems in what people believe about health and how health services are arranged, which make it difficult to share information properly. For example, health organizations are arranged based on particular knowledge and separate parts of the human body. This requires an extra special effort, not supported naturally by the way health services are arranged, to ensure smooth information-flow. The problems are so big that many researchers and policy-makers ignore them and only work on small parts of the problem.  Videos can improve health services in local units despite these problems. Its images and sounds are so strong that people feel emotionally driven to make changes to their roles and local workplaces. In local workplaces, positive relationships can overcome the problems stated above. Since these problems happen across whole health systems, the goal of the meeting of experts is to see if the powerful ability of video recordings to push for change in health services can do the same at a larger level where policy and financial decisions are made. The meeting will provide a detailed five-year research plan for studies, and papers and talks from the studies and the meeting itself, and practical projects to improve the way clinicians work together and share information.

TitreApplicationTitle: Establishing Methodological Quality Criteria for Scoping Studies: Advancing the Field of Knowledge Synthesis within the Context of Aging, Chronic Disease and Rehabilitation
Keywords-MotsClés: KNOWLEDGE SYNTHESIS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; METHODOLOGICAL QUALITY; REHABILITATION; SCOPING STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: Scoping studies are an important and popular method of knowledge synthesis in health research. However, lack of methodological criteria to evaluate the quality of scoping studies severely limits the potential of this research methodology.  Our goal is to advance the development of methodological quality criteria for conducting and reporting scoping studies in order to enhance knowledge synthesis and translation of aging and rehabilitation research. As part of a Canada-United Kingdom (UK) partnership, we will plan and implement a two-day meeting involving researchers, clinicians, policy makers, students, and people living with chronic disease on October 30-31st, 2014. The first half of the meeting will facilitate knowledge transfer and exchange (KTE) on scoping studies, and establish a clear definition of scoping study as a research methodology. Stakeholders will share their scoping study experiences in order to identify methods for overcoming identified challenges and outline a rigorous approach to scoping study conduct. The second half of the meeting will be dedicated to establishing consensus surrounding the methodological steps of scoping studies that will lay the foundation for future quality criteria, and formalizing plans for an international Canada-UK Scoping Study Research Collaborative. The scoping study steps determined at this meeting will be broadly translated within health research and clinical disciplines. The Collaborative will pursue the future development, pilot testing and validation of these criteria in order to advance the quality of knowledge synthesis and KTE for older adults with chronic diseases in Canada and the UK. This community-academic partnership involves integrated KTE and capacity building among researchers, clinicians and knowledge users. It will advance the field of scoping studies and strengthen the potential of scoping methodology to enhance practice and policy in the field of aging, rehabilitation and chronic disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Guideline development for improved study design and conduct in pediatric clinical trials: SPIRIT-C
Keywords-MotsClés: KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; RANDOMIZED TRIAL PROTOCOLS; RESEARCH TRANSPARENCY
Abstract-Résumé: "Lack of research, poor research, and poorly reported research are violations of children's human rights," declared Richard Horton, editor-in-chief, The Lancet. Research that focuses on children's health has the potential to benefit families, communities, and populations. Unfortunately, child health research is not always standardized or conducted in the best and safest ways possible. Errors in study design and implementation can make research findings less meaningful or in some cases, unusable. Clinical studies, or trials, must provide reliable information in order to improve the care we provide to children. A well-written research proposal, or protocol, allows for a better review of scientific, ethical, and safety issues before a trial begins, and enhanced findings upon completion. Currently, there are no standards for the development of clinical research protocols in child health research.   The Canadian-led SPIRIT initiative (Standard Protocol Items for Randomized Trials) has created standard guidelines that outline important items that should be addressed in study protocols. The goal of these guidelines is to improve the quality of clinical studies and our understanding of the study results. However, trials involving young children require additional standards. SPIRIT-C (Children) will be an extension of the SPIRIT checklist focusing on children, or pediatric population. This study will (a) seek agreement on the minimum items required in a children's trial protocol, (b) develop a plan to put together recommendations for evidence-based use of the checklist by researchers, and (c) plan a knowledge translation strategy in order to share the SPIRIT-C guidelines and promote buy-in and use by researchers. By standardizing how researchers conduct trials in children, the SPIRIT-C guidelines may improve the safety, use and impact of clinical research.

Keywords-MotsClés: BALANCE; CONSENSUS; EXPERT PANEL; FALL PREVENTION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; POSTURAL CONTROL; STANDARDIZED OUTCOME MEASURES
Abstract-Résumé: The ability to maintain balance is important in daily life and in avoiding falls and injuries. Measuring balance is important for finding balance problems and treatment planning. However there are so many ways of measuring balance (more than 60 different tests) that it is difficult to know which tests to use. The goal of this project is to bring balance and falls experts together to decide on and recommend a few tests that should always be used to measure balance. This will give a common point of comparison and will help researchers, healthcare providers and government the best treatments to improve balance and prevent falls.

TitreApplicationTitle: Supporting the Mental Health of Refugee Adolescents and Parents
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT HEALTH; CHILD HEALTH; MENTAL HEALTH; PARENT HEALTH; REFUGEE HEALTH; SUPPORTIVE INTERVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Refugee adolescents and parents are vulnerable to mental health problems including depression, postpartum depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Support deficits, loneliness, and isolation are major concerns. However, gaps in culturally relevant and supportive health services persist. Moreover, culturally appropriate, accessible (eg.technology enabled) support interventions have not been designed and tested for refugee adolescents and parents in Canada. This planning grant focuses on: 1) identifying  priorities for relevant support intervention research and knowledge translation (KT) in consultation with researchers and knowledge users from program,practice and policy domains; 2)building partnerships engaging multiple health- related disciplines, sites, and sectors, 3) developing  plans for pertinent  intervention research and KT proposals. Representatives of key national and provincial groups influencing health services (eg. Alberta Health ),mental health (eg.Canadian Mental Health Association),child and adolescent health (eg.Canadian Institute for Child Health), public health services (eg.Public Health Agency of Canada, Alberta), and access to services for refugees (eg.Citizenship and Immigration Canada) will participate in this planning project. Thirty-four participants including 17 researchers and 17 knowledge users (eg. decision makers,  practitioners, policy influencers,program planners) are interested and will be invited to this planning meeting. Presenters reflect research and KT expertise in  international,national and provincial perspectives on mental health, child/ adolescent health, parent health,refugee health, and implications for health- relevant supports and services. Anticipated outcomes include 1) a summary report 2)research and KT priorities, 3) fact sheet, 4) presentations,5) papers/articles, 6) partnerships and 7) a preliminary proposal ( eg.Partnerships for Health System Improvement)

TitreApplicationTitle: Establishing a Pediatric Obsessive Compulsive Disorder Research Network
Keywords-MotsClés: DECISION MAKERS; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NETWORK; OBSESSIVE COMPULSIVE DISORDER; STAKEHOLDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is a common, serious and under-recognized illness affecting nearly one Canadian child in every two classrooms. These children repeatedly experience unwanted thoughts and perform behaviours that cause significant distress, time loss and functional impairment. OCD is identified as a leading international cause of non-fatal illness burden. In youth, ongoing OCD disrupts crucial aspects of development to the same degree as adolescent psychoses. However, access to proper diagnosis and treatment within the health care system are often delayed for several years, which decreases chances of improvement.  We propose to create the first formal Canadian national network dedicated to research on Pediatric OCD. Our central aim is to bring together researchers, affected patients and families, their care providers, and health system decision-makers. Over the course of three main planning activities at provincial, national and international levels this network of researchers and knowledge users will set priorities and develop a research plan to improve understanding and care of Pediatric OCD in Canada. The network will then actively seek funding to support this research and knowledge translation plan from CIHR and other relevant funders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dynamic regulation of NMDA receptor function in the adult hippocampus
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; CORTICOSTERONE; DEPRESSIVE DISORDER; EXTRASYNAPTIC RECEPTORS; HOMEOSTASIS; PATCH-CLAMP RECORDING; PHOSPHORYLATION; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING; STRESS; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Depression affects as many people in Canada as cancer. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), despite their slow acting pharmacological profile and limited efficacy in close to 40% of depressed patients, remain the first line treatment for depression. New anti-depression treatments are, therefore, urgently needed. A recent ground breaking discovery in the field of depression is the antidepressant effect of blocking N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs), a glutamate receptor for brain cell communication. NMDAR antagonists have unprecedentedly fast-acting antidepressant effects that appear hours after administration. Perhaps most importantly, they ameliorate depressive symptoms in patients who are resistant to SSRIs. What remains poorly understood, however, are mechanisms underlying the antidepressant action of NMDAR antagonists. In this proposal, we hypothesize that the antidepressant effect of NMDAR antagonists is related to alterations of this receptor in the hippocampus, a brain region that displays shrinkage in depressed patients. Particularly, hippocampal NMDAR changes produced by a stressful life event, a risk factor associated with the onset of depression, are responsible for the formation of depressive symptoms. To test this hypothesis, we will examine the impact of stress on NMDAR function in the hippocampus. In addition, we will examine the contribution of NMDAR changes to the formation of depression-related symptoms in a mouse model of chronic stress. Our findings will reveal if stress-related changes of hippocampal NMDARs are related to the therapeutic effect of NMDAR antagonists. Given the strong association between depressive episodes and stressful life events, changes in hippocampal NMDARs could be a stress-induced molecular mechanism underlying depression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gender Differences in Youth Suicide - Implications for Suicide Prevention

Abstract-Résumé: Suicide is the second leading cause of death in youth, with the bulk of these deaths occurring in males. We seek to better understand why to inform prevention efforts. We propose three studies among Ontario youth (aged 10 to 25 years) to provide new knowledge on: 1) gender differences in health service access 2) gender differences in health service quality and 3) gender differences in suicide means. Ontario's size, universal medical insurance and secure linkable, longitudinal administrative data make these studies possible. We will involve policy and decision-makers, clinicians, family and youth. The knowledge gained will help develop and evaluate prevention efforts (and standards) for suicidal youth. Also, we will develop and solidify the methods needed to monitor the uptake of prevention efforts. We see this project as important first step towards ultimately preventing youth suicide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of a novel clinical marker of endometriosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE; DIAGNOSTIC MARKERS; ENDOMETRIOSIS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; ESTROGENS; FERTILITY; MENSTRUAL CYCLE; PELVIC PAIN; REPRODUCTION; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Endometriosis is a chronic, painful, progressive, inflammatory disease that has a profoundly deleterious effect upon women's role performance, social functioning, emotional well-being, relationships with medical practitioners, vitality, and employment. The annual costs associated with surgically confirmed endometriosis in Canada alone are approximately 1.8 billion dollars. Moreover, the health care costs associated with endometriosis are similar to or greater than other chronic diseases such as Crohn's disease, diabetes, asthma, migraines, and rheumatoid arthritis. Sadly, women with endometriosis experience significant delays of up to 12 years before a definitive diagnosis is achieved. The gold standard for diagnosis remains laparoscopic visualization of endometriotic implants followed by histopathological confirmation of disease. Although risks to patients from laparoscopy are rare, they are significant and women with endometriosis can expect to undergo multiple diagnostic and operative laparoscopies over the course of their disease. Thus, there is an urgent need to identify novel non- or semi-invasive clinical markers of endometriosis. Our preliminary data suggest that the plasma concentrations of BDNF are significantly higher in women with endometriosis compared to healthy controls. Therefore, we hypothesize that this protein is a potentially valuable candidate clinical marker of endometriosis. Consequently, we propose a pre-clinical discovery phase project to better characterize the concentrations of BDNF in the blood as a potentially useful semi-invasive diagnostic test for endometriosis. We further postulate that blood concentrations of BDNF could be used to monitor disease progression and patient response to treatments. We also plan to determine the mechanism(s) underlying the expression of this protein as we think this could also be a potential therapeutic target that we will explore in future applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of sex differences in radiation responses: an in-depth analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA HYDROXYMETHYLATION; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; GENE EXPRESSION; HORMONES; RADIATION THERAPY; RADIATION-INDUCED CANCER; SEX DIFFERENCES; SMALL RNA
Abstract-Résumé: The key report on the Biological Effects of Ionizing Radiation (BEIR VII) published in 2006 by the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) of the USA has shown that women may be at a significantly greater risk of suffering and dying from IR-induced cancer than men who get the same dose of radiation. Yet,  mechanistic data on sex differences in radiation effects are scarce.  The DNA content of each cell in a given higher organism is identical: our liver and brain cells contain the same DNA, but they are very different in their shapes and functions. This is due to the existence of different patterns in reading and translation of genes for the type of cells in question, referred to as 'gene expression'. This is the domain of the emerging science of epigenetics (literally, 'beyond genetics'). Remarkable features of epigenetic changes include simple chemical modifications of the 'C' base in DNA by attachment or removal of methyl (-CH3) groups. Highly methylated regions of DNA are turned off or silenced - a kind of cellular dimmer switch. Most amazing and contrary to popular opinion that DNA sequences determine everything, epigenetic changes can extend beyond cell division to reproduction. Although epigenetic changes are inheritable, they are reversible. A lot still has to be learned about the role of epigenetic changes in living cells and organisms and their interactions with the environment. In my laboratory, we have found that males and females respond to radiation differently due to distinct epigenetic changes in DNA methylation. These changes may lead to different levels of radiation toxicity. Currently, we would like to further our understanding of molecular and cellular changes induced by radiation in males and females. In the long term, understanding the molecular basis of bystander and adaptive effects in males and females may contribute to the development of sex-specific diagnostic and treatment regiments and sex-specific radiation protection guidelines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transmasculine Individuals' Experiences with Pregnancy, Birthing, and Feeding Their Newborns: A Qualitative Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH; BREASTFEEDING; CHESTFEEDING; GENDER; MALE CHEST-CONTOURING SURGERY; PREGNANCY; QUALITATIVE DESCRIPTIVE METHODOLOGY; SEX; TRANSGENDER; TRANSMASCULINE PREGNANCY BIRTH BREAS
Abstract-Résumé: Transmasculine individuals are labelled as female at birth, but they identify and transition to the masculine side of the gender spectrum later in life. The transition could range from wearing masculine clothing to having medical therapies or surgical procedures. Many transmasculine individuals take testosterone to develop a deeper voice, a male distribution of body fat and muscle mass, and male patterns of hair growth. Some individuals opt for sex reassignment surgeries which might include chest contouring surgery, hysterectomy, and/or phalloplasty. Transmasculine individuals who have not had a hysterectomy are in a unique position, given their gender and biological attributes, to make choices about pregnancy, birthing, and breast/chestfeeding. These men are a minority in maternity care and are often misunderstood by health care providers. The purpose of this study is to interview transmasculine individuals who have given birth and to bring forth their narratives. The interviews will be analyzed for patterns and themes to provide a comprehensive description of their experiences with pregnancy, birthing, and infant feeding. This analysis will: 1) serve as a foundation for further research, 2) be useful for transmen who are considering a pregnancy, and 3) assist in creating resources for health care professionals (e.g., lactation consultants, midwives, nurses, and physicians) to provide appropriate care and support for their transmasculine patients and clients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sex differences in stress, neuroendocrine and serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) 5-HT1A receptor responses.
Keywords-MotsClés: GLUCOCORTICOID STEROID HORMONES; HYBRIDIZATION- AND IMMUNO-HISTOCHEMISTRY; MICROSCOPY; NEUROANATOMY; NEUROENDOCRINOLOGY; SEROTONERGIC DRUGS; SEROTONIN RECEPTOR PHARMACOLOGY; SEX DIFFERENCES; SEX STEROID HORMONES; TRACT TRACING AND STEREOTAXIC SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is a hormonal system that regulates glucocorticoid steroid hormone secretion that is essential for maintaining physiological balance in the face of real or perceived threats on the body. Glucocorticoid hypersecretion, however, has been implicated in the development of mood disorders.  The incidence of depressive disorders is higher in women compared to men, yet the mechanism responsible for this disparity is unknown. Stressful experiences and alterations in the serotoninergic (5-HT) neurotransmitter system have been implicated as factors contributing to depression. The majority of studies on 5-HT and stress interactions, however, have been conducted in male subjects only. Thus, most of what we think we understand about stress and depression may not be the same between males and females. To study this possibility we use anatomical techniques and assess neuroendocrine and behavioral responses using a rodent model. Previous studies indicate that the 5-HT 1A receptor is tied to the stimulatory effects of serotonin on the HPA axis, and plays an important role in the mechanism of action of antidepressant drugs. Our recent findings suggest brain-specific, sex differences in serotonergic regulation of the HPA axis. Males, but not females, adapt to repeated stress exposure by showing decreased glucocorticoid responses. We also have new evidence to show that male and females differentially rely on the 5-HT 1A receptor to regulate glucocorticoid secretion. We hypothesize that normal adaptation to stress occurs as a consequence of changes in 5-HT 1A receptor function, and that this mechanism may help us understand the substrate underlying individual and gender-based differences in susceptibility to stress-related disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Walk of Life - The Health Benefits of Everyday Activity
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR CHANGE; BUILT ENVIRONMENT; CHRONIC DISEASE; MIDDLE AGE; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; RETIREMENT; SEDENTARY BEHAVIOUR; SELF-MANAGEMENT; SOCIAL ENVIRONMENT; WALKING
Abstract-Résumé: Physical activity is an important part of a healthy lifestyle; however, meeting physical activity guidelines is a frequent challenge for many people, and especially older adults. More recent evidence recognizes that even people who are physically active enough to meet recommended guidelines can spend most of their day sitting- and this can lead to an increased risk for disease and death. Uptake and adherence to an active lifestyle is important for health, yet the challenge exists to create a supportive environment for adults to remain active and engaged in their daily life. Physical activity has many benefits including optimizing physical function, encouraging socialization and improving overall quality of life. Therefore this randomized controlled trial will test a new approach to help middle-aged women add more physical activity into their daily lives. The Everyday Activity Supports You (EASY) Program encourages physical activity in the community by providing self-management tools and strategies. Participants in the EASY Study intervention group will receive a self-management program to reduce sitting time and increase physical activity through: group education sessions;  individualized prescription with an exercise professional; and an activity monitor. The program is 18 months in duration including a 4 week ramp-up phase, a 5 month activation phase and a 12 month maintenance phase to determine if participants maintain their physical activity patterns. Given the many benefits of physical activity, and the soaring costs associated with an inactive lifestyle, the high number of aging Canadians would benefit from this novel approach of encouraging active living, with improved benefits for the wider community.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of mRNA processing bodies in genome stability
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA DAMAGE; DNA REPLICATION; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENOME INSTABILITY; HIGH CONTENT SCREENING; MRNA DECAY; TRANSLATION; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Before a cell can grow and divide it must duplicate its DNA. Mistakes during the copying of the DNA can lead to the kinds of changes that are frequently seen in cancerous cells. These changes are important for cancer development, progression, and treatment, but there is little information about how they arise. Understanding how they arise could lead to improvements in cancer detection and treatment. We will study how proteins that turn genes off prevent mistakes during the copying of the DNA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dietary microRNAs
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL (MICE); BIOINFORMATICS; DIET; FOOD SOURCES; GENE REGULATION; HUMAN HEALTH; MICRORNA; NUTRITION
Abstract-Résumé: MicroRNAs are small endogenous non-coding RNA species that play a crucial role in finely tuning gene expression, which is required to maintain homeostasis and to remain healthy. Expressed in the vast majority of eukaryotes, such as humans, animals and plants, microRNAs may regulate ~60% of the genes in human, suggesting that microRNA (de)regulation of gene expression may play a significant role in human health and diseases.      Our health status and fitness is largely determined by the composition of our diet, an observation that came from studies of the human health benefits of certain foods and diets, especially the mediterranean diet (MedDiet). However, in most cases, the molecular mechanisms underlying these beneficial effects remain largely unknown.      As omnivorous, our diet is extremely diverse and derive essentially from living plants and animal species, processed or not, that contain, in addition to the commonly known nutrients (eg, proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, vitamins, minerals, etc.), genetic material, such as DNA and RNA. These observations prompted us to hypothesize that microRNAs contained in the food that we ingest may be absorbed by the digestive system, distributed to the organs and cells of our body and influence our health status and fitness through the regulation of specific genes. The existence of exogenous (dietary) microRNAs is supported by recent studies reporting (i) the stability of plant microRNAs in cooked foods, (ii) the detection of microRNAs in gastric juice, and (iii) the presence of rice microRNAs in the blood and tissues of mice fed with rice.      Expected to bring novel insights and perspectives to the relationship between nutrition and human health, this proposal may eventually allow us to plan and envision the development of preventive health interventions and medical therapeutic approaches based on the prescription of food containing beneficial microRNAs or the administration of specific microRNAs through the diet.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targets of the human papillomavirus E7 oncoprotein and their role in oropharyngeal cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: E7; EPIGENETICS; HEAD AND NECK CANCER; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS; INNATE IMMUNITY; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; VIRAL ONCOGENE
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that viruses are responsible for about 15% of human cancers. In this respect, viruses are a risk factor for cancer second only to tobacco. Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is thought to account for about two-thirds of these cancers. This includes nearly all cervical cancers and an increasingly large number of cancers or the oropharynx. Infection with HPV forces quiescent cells to enter the cell division cycle, causing warts. This abnormal cell proliferation may initiate progression to the cancer phenotype in combination with virally induced chromosomal instability, evasion of the host immune response and suppression of programmed cell death. E6 and E7 are the two key viral proteins that are required for these activities. They function by interacting with various cellular regulators to reprogram cell growth. Our studies focus on learning more about the mechanism by which this occurs, with the aim of using this information to improve treatment of these virally induced cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Redox regulation of the innate antiviral response in airway epithelial cells: regulation and function of DUOX2.
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE REGULATION; INFLAMMATORY RESPONSE; NADPH OXIDASE; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; RESPIRATORY VIRUS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Infection by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in young children and ederly is associated with acute severe respiratory tract illness, such as broncholitis or pneumonia, which cause substantial morbidity and mortality. Despite intensive research, the development of efficient vaccine or treatment failed. The search for novel RSV treatment remains a priority. More information is needed to understand how the first line of defense, known as innate immune response, is orchestrated. Indeed, although the inflammatory process is a normal response essential to fight against foreign invaders, an exaggerated response correlates with the severity of the virus-associated disease. Our research endeavor is aimed at characterizing the molecular mechanisms involved in the regulation of this response. Our work specifically focuses on the role of reactive oxygen derivatives, which are produced by the conversion of oxygen by specific enzymes present in the airway epithelium. These derivatives are well known to contribute to tissue damage, but our work and the work from other groups worldwide have shown that these reactive compounds are also critical for the defense against invading viruses. Antioxidants are at the forefront of therapeutic development. We believe that our research is essential to design novel therapeutic agents that are urgently needed to fight respiratory diseases associated with virus infections, such as bronchiolitis and pneumonia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Skin cell therapy for the long term treatment of alopecia areata
Keywords-MotsClés: AA TREATMENT; ALOPECIA AREATA (AA); DERMAL FIBROBLASTS; SKIN DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Alopecia areata (AA), defined as a non-scarring autoimmune hair loss disease, has a serious impact on the quality of life for AA patients worldwide. It is well established that infiltrated immune cells, known as CD4+ and CD8+ lymphocytes, target the hair follicles of AA patients. Various therapeutic regimens are currently used for the treatment of AA; however, none of them can prevent or cure the disease. Our preliminary results generated from an AA mouse model revealed that none of the  mice received skin cells producing an immunosuppressive factor known as IDO developed AA while 80% of control animals developed extensive AA within 8-16 weeks after transplantation of AA affected skin.  Here we hypothesize that IDO expressing skin cell therapy can prevent the progression of AA by suppressing the CD4+ and CD8+ cells attacking hair follicles.  To address this hypothesis, we will test  4 different objectives through which 1) The potential role of skin cell therapy not only in prevention but  also in progression of AA in those patients who already suffer from this disease will be evaluated, 2) The  factors that affect the capacity of IDO producing  fibroblast therapy in reversing the autoimmune AA disease will be tested and finally 3) The last 2 objectives will reveal the mechanism by which this cell therapy  improves or even cures this disease.  In conclusion, we strongly believe that, if it is proven to be true, our novel cell therapy approach would overcome the AA autoimmunity and prevent the progression of AA. Potentially this may be a long lasting, possibly permanent treatment for patients who suffer from this devastating skin disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of BRIL in the pathogenesis of osteogenesis imperfecta type V.
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE PHYSIOLOGY/PATHOLOGY; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CULTURE; MICRO COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; OSTEOGENESIS IMPERFECTA; PCR; TRANSGENIC/KNOCKIN MOUSE MODELS; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: Brittle bone disease, or osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), is a heritable connective tissue disorder that is mainly characterized by bone fragility and often short stature.  In the large majority of patients, OI is caused by mutations in the two genes that encode collagen, the primary building block of bones.  Clinically, such patients are classified into OI types I to IV.  Other rare types of OI (VI to XI) are caused by mutations in at least 6 other genes, all directly involved in the proper assembly of collagen fibers.  OI type V (OI-V), is a bone fragility disorder resembling OI caused by collagen mutations with regard to many skeletal characteristics, such as fracture incidence, long-bone deformities, vertebral compression fractures and abnormal spine curvature.  OI-V, however, has unique clinical and radiographic features not seen in other types of OI.  They include uncontrolled bone masses growing on shafts of long bones like tibia and femurs, and fusion of the forearm bones.  All patients identified with OI-V have a single mutation in the BRIL (Bone-Restricted Ifitm-Like) gene.  The mutation causes the production of an abnormally long BRIL protein, which is believed to cause unwanted negative effects on the skeleton. However, it is still totally unknown how the mutant BRIL protein causes such variable and marked defects in the affected patients.  The present project is aimed at elucidating some of these questions.  More precisely, we propose to fully characterize animal (mouse) models we have generated and which should mimic symptoms observed in patients with OI-V.  These will represent unique and valuable tools to study the mechanisms by which the mutant BRIL is detrimental to the skeleton.  Biochemical and structural data gathered recently about BRIL and further exploited in the current study should be amenable to devise effective pharmacological treatments for OI-V, and be tested pre-clinically in the current mouse models.

Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMINERALIZATION; COLLAGEN; CRYO-TEM; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; HYDROXYAPATITE; IN VITRO MINERALIZATION MODEL; NON-COLLAGENOUS PROTEINS; PERIODONTAL DISEASE; PERIODONTIUM; PROTEIN-MINERAL INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Periodontal disease is the most common infection in Canadian adults, and incidence is expected to increase as the population ages.  In this disease, the attachment of teeth to the jawbone is destroyed by bacterial infection.  Despite the high prevalence and significant economic burden of periodontal infections, there are major obstacles to effective and long-lasting treatment.  In particular, reattachment of the ligament that connects to tooth root to the jawbone is still not possible.  Here we propose to study the mechanism by which the ligament attaches to the root of the tooth in healthy teeth in order to design more effective strategies for achieving re-attachment in treatment of periodontitis.  This will be achieved by the application of advanced electron microscopy techniques to study native tissues, along with the development of novel laboratory model systems to probe the molecular factors controlling tooth attachment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immunosuppressive function of S100A8 in arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; CYTOKINES; IMMUNOSUPPRESSION; IN VIVO MODEL; S100 PROTEINS; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Calprotectin is an association of S100A8 and S100A9, two proteins expressed by white blood cells. Recent data indicate that S100A9 stimulates inflammation, while S100A8 is rapidly oxidised at the inflammatory site and reduces the inflammatory response. We recently demonstrated that S100A9 plays an important role in rheumatoid arthritis inflammatory response. In contrast, preliminary experiments suggest that S100A8 protects from arthritis in a mouse model. We hypothesize that S100A8 expressed during inflammation suppress the immune response against the joints. We will induce arthritis in mice deficient in S100A8 to determine the role of S100A8 in arthritis. We will also examine the effect of S100A8 on immune cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Coordination of myofibril assembly through the giant scaffold protein obscurin
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFINITY PURIFICATION; CONFOCAL IMAGING; DROSOPHILA; GIANT SCAFFOLD PROTEIN OBSCURIN; M-LINE; MUSCLE; MYOFIBRIL ASSEMBLY; MYOPATHY; SARCOMERE FUNCTION; YEAST TWO-HYBRID SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Muscle cells typically contain dozens of myofibrils, each consisting of many sarcomeres, the smallest functional contractile unit of muscle. Sarcomeres are highly organized protein complexes that consist of myosin-containing thick filaments anchored in the middle of the sarcomere, called M-line, and actin-containing thin filaments anchored at the borders of the sarcomere, called Z-line. Thin and thick filaments together with additional proteins enable muscle contraction. The initial step of muscle or myofibril assembly is the formation of a regular array of sarcomeres. We have previously shown that the giant scaffold protein obscurin plays a crucial role in myofibril assembly, especially required for the proper anchoring of thick filaments at the M-line. Here we plan to identify and characterize proteins interacting with obscurin to understand the mechanism of obscurin function within and outside of the M-line. We will also study the architecture of myofibrils by a novel super-resolution microscopy technique. This will give us a better understanding of how muscles obtain the ability to contract, and how contractility gets impaired in muscle disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Patient-centred interprofessional shared care model for low back pain management
Keywords-MotsClés: CLUSTER RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; LOW BACK PAIN; PATIENT-CENTRED CARE
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that 50-80% of the adult population will experience low back pain (LBP) in their lifetime. Although generally acknowledged as having a favourable outcome, growing evidence suggests that LBP is a chronic remitting and relapsing condition for many. It is this group that incurs the largest costs in terms of healthcare utilization and loss of productivity within the LBP population. In Canada, medical expenditures for LBP are estimated between $6 and $12 billion annually. Canadian patients with LBP who seek care are faced with a choice of healthcare and provider options, with little or no collaboration between providers, often leading to fragmented patient care. Treatment results for patients with non-specific LBP in general, when managed as a single group, are suboptimal. Current research suggests that a more specific approach to the management of LBP could lead to tailored treatments and improved outcomes.   The Ontario Ministry of Health and Long Term Care has recently approved a pilot study to explore the effect of a shared care model using standardized assessment of LBP patients by allied health professionals (physiotherapists and chiropractors). This model requires a formal evaluation to inform relevant stakeholders whether the model should be abandoned, revised, or implemented across Ontario. We propose to initiate two randomized controlled trials to establish if this patient-centred inter-professional shared care model for LBP is effective. One trial will recruit patients attending to primary care providers and the second trial will recruit patients referred to spine surgeons in Ontario. The primary outcome will be functional recovery; we will also capture quality of life, return to work, and complete cost-effectiveness analyses. If the use of inter-professional shared care is effective in improving LBP-related outcomes, our research proposal will provide essential evidence to support a fundamental change in the management of LBP in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Canadian Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome (CHILDNEPH) Project
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; KIDNEY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LONGITUDINAL REGISTRY; MULTI-LEVEL MODELING; NEPHROTIC SYNDROME; PRACTICE VARIATION; QUALITATIVE METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood nephrotic syndrome is a common childhood kidney disease. Children with nephrotic syndrome leak protein from blood into urine. Many of those affected can have a relapsing course of disease.  Steroids are the treatment of choice for nephrotic syndrome and repeated treatment courses of steroid can lead to significant toxicity. In our previous work, we found wide variability in treatments used for childhood nephrotic syndrome in Canada, in particular the dose and duration of steroids prescribed. We also compared current management practices for nephrotic syndrome with recently published Clinical Practice Guideline that summarizes the best evidence for effective treatments of nephrotic syndrome.  We found several gaps between what is published in the Guideline and what is done in practice.  The extent of variation in steroid treatment protocols, factors driving this variation and impact of variation on patient outcomes are unknown.  Therefore, there is a need to identify and understand factors influencing variability in treatment and to determine whether variability in treatment affects patient outcomes.  Our work plan is as follows. First, we will study factors influencing total steroid exposure during the first presentation of nephrotic syndrome and subsequent relapses.   Second, we will interview physicians and nurses who care for patients with nephrotic syndrome to understand reasons behind their choices in dosing and duration of steroid therapy. We will also determine the effect of the amount of steroids used to treat first presentation of nephrotic syndrome on the risk of getting a subsequent relapse.  In summary, this study will help us understand the factors that influence treatment variability and will help us develop strategies to implement a standardized protocol to treat childhood nephrotic syndrome in the future.  We will also use the results of this study to design clinical trials to study effectiveness of treatments for nephrotic syndrome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Amino Acid Metabolism in Pregnancy
Keywords-MotsClés: AMINO ACID METABOLISM; DIETARY PROTEIN; INDICATOR AMINO ACID OXIDATION; NUTRITIONAL REQUIREMENTS; PREGNANCY; STABLE ISOTOPES
Abstract-Résumé: Protein is a key component of the diet which allows growth and maintenance of health. All body proteins are made up of 20 amino acids. Among these 20 amino acids there are 9 amino acids, which our body cannot make, and therefore must come from food sources, and are called essential amino acids. The rest of the 11 amino acids can be made in our body if there is enough calories and protein in our food. But under some conditions, such as infants, people with disease, pregnant women, many of these 11 amino acids cannot be made in the body, and must come from food as well, and are then called conditionally essential amino acids. Until recently, studying pregnant women and their protein (amino acid) needs has been difficult, because previous methods require invasive techniques and week-long test diets which could harm the actively growing fetus. We have recently started to use a very minimally invasive state-of-the-art method, using stable isotopes and collection of breath samples in women during early pregnancy (11-20 weeks) and during late pregnancy (31-40 weeks). Stable isotopes are completely safe, and these methods are rapid and quick and require only one day of the test diets. We are in now in a position to study the different conditionally essential amino acid needs during different stages of pregnancy which will help in making diet recommendations to make sure both mother and baby are actively growing, and have a healthy, successful pregnancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Language ability and structural brain development in preschool children: predictors of reading readiness
Keywords-MotsClés: LANGUAGE; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEURODEVELOPMENT; READING
Abstract-Résumé: Problems with reading are common in children, and can lead to lifelong difficulties learning and in adult life (i.e., career). Early identification of reading problems allows for early treatments, which are more effective than later interventions. Currently, reading problems are not diagnosed until after children begin school. Brain abnormalities are associated with reading problems in school-aged children, and these abnormalities might exist before reading begins. However, very few studies have examined brain development in young children, and it is not known how brain structure and language are related during early childhood.  We hypothesize that brain areas involved in reading are more mature in young children (age 2-6 years) with better language abilities compared to children with poor language abilities. We also think that faster brain development will predict better reading readiness when children start school (age 5-6 years). To test this, we will measure language ability and brain structure (using magnetic resonance imaging) in children aged 2-6 years. We will follow these children over 3 years and measure their reading readiness at age 5-6 years. Understanding relationships between language, reading readiness, and brain maturation in young children will help identify early abnormalities that lead to reading problems, and will identify times when treatments may be most effective. Our ultimate goal is to improve outcomes for children with reading disabilities.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of proposed change in federal health funding policy on health programs operating in Yukon First Nations communities
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; COMMUNITY HEALTH; DISEASE PREVENTION; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH PROGRAMS; MATERNAL-CHILD HEALTH; NUTRITION; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; POPULATION HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The federal government currently funds and operates health programs in northern Canadian Aboriginal communities through a variety of intersectoral partnerships and funding arrangements. A recent report by Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada recommended expansion of grant-based funding in communities deemed "desirable" on the basis of compliance and accountability. Differences in community size, remoteness and capacity mean that not all First Nations communities are able to access competitive program funds. The resulting landscape of health program implementation is one where existing inequities in health are further exacerbated by unequal implementation of federal health program funding and services. The proposed research is a community-centered evaluation of the capacity of Yukon First Nations to access and implement federal health programs, with the goal of developing capacity and thereby improving health outcomes for Yukon residents. Using a conceptual model which locates the local health system within larger national program frameworks, the study methodology evaluates existing health programs, maps program delivery, identifies key actors and roles in access and implementation of programs, examines the impact of social organization, power and political culture on programs, and incorporates two robust knowledge translation phases that ground the research in participatory process. With a strong research team and territorial partnerships, the proposed research examines the implementation and intersection of existing programs under the current funding model, processes that are not yet well understood, with the goal of improving the capacity of communities to access health program funds in an increasingly competitive federal funding environment. The research has wider implications for other indigenous communities who contract with government and non-governmental service providers to access population health interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of periodontal inflammation by the platelet cytoskeleton
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOSKELETON; FILAMIN A; PERIODONTITIS; PLATELETS
Abstract-Résumé: Proper function of the immune system is essential for protection against infectious disease and maintaining human health. During the onset of infection, white blood cells and platelets release signaling molecules known as cytokines, which orchestrate a protective inflammatory response. When cytokine release is de-regulated, excessive inflammation results that causes cell and tissue death and loss of function. This is seen in periodontitis (gum disease), which is characterized by gingival (gum) inflammation and destruction of tooth-supporting connective tissues and bone. The purpose of this grant application is to study the mechanisms and identify the proteins responsible for maintaining the health of periodontal tissues. In addition to regulating blood coagulation (clotting), platelets are emerging as pivotal components of the host inflammatory response. We will study in human and mouse platelets, how infection causes cytokine release. The current project will focus on two major questions. First, we will identify the molecular signals that operate during periodontal infection and learn how these signals affect platelet function. We will also test the hypothesis that a group of proteins known as filamins mediate the release of cytokines from platelets. In this context, an improved understanding of platelet function could have important implications for rational treatment of inflammatory diseases, including periodontitis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Finding the complex patient in patient-centred care: an institutional ethnography of chronic pain management in family medicine
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNOGRAPHY; MULTIDISCIPINARY CARE; PAIN MANAGEMENT; PRIMARY CARE; QUALITATIVE METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: For people who suffer from chronic orthopedic (OA) pain, the family doctor often plays a key role in their education, care and access to other specialists such as orthopaedic surgeons or physiotherapists.  Therefore, effective communication and teamwork among these various care providers is very important. The proposed study will study the coordination of these different standpoints using interviews and observations. Interviews will be conducted first with primary care physicians who are involved in the care of patients with chronic OA pain. Interviews will also be done with those who work directly or indirectly with these primary care doctors, including the specialist physicians, nurses, physiotherapists, provincial agency representatives, patients and their family members. The results from this study will be shared with a wide range  of people who are involved in delivering care to OA patients in order to improve care delivery across the province. This approach has the potential to help us better understand how to improve clinical practice, with the ultimate goal of improving the health of patients and their families suffering from chronic OA pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the role of immune cells' bioenergetics in the pathophysiology of inflammatory arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; AUTOIMMUNITY; CYTOKINE; ENERGY METABOLISM; INFLAMMATION; RHEUMATIC DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: More than one million Canadians are affected with inflammatory types of arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus. Among all causes of disability, arthritis ranks first among women and second among men, costing the Canadian economy more than $30 billions annually. Current therapies are expensive and do not completely eliminate the inflammation or provide a cure, often requiring the usage of multiple treatments concurrently. The underlying causes of inflammatory arthritis are not completely understood, but it is well established that the progressive joint destruction that occurs during disease progression results from inappropriate activation of cells of the immune system. Immune cells require energy for housekeeping functions as well as for specific immune functions, and alterations in bioenergetics are often associated with diseases such as diabetes and cancer. Energy metabolism of immune cells is increased in patients with rheumatic diseases, suggesting that the assessment of their bioenergetics could be suitable for monitoring disease activity. This present research study will aim to characterize the bioenergetics and intracellular signaling events occurring in the different immune cell types involved in the pathophysiology of inflammatory arthritis and determine whether therapies can modulate the energy metabolism of these cells. This research will inform us about the diseases and their treatments, leading to new biomarkers and perhaps pave the way for new treatments of inflammatory disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dry mouth, oral health and in vivo "plaque transplantation": Exploring novel avenues of therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: CARIOLOGY; HEAD/NECK RADIOTHERAPY; HUMAN IMMUNO-DEFICIENCY VIRUS; HYPOHIDROTIC ECTODERMAL DYSPLASIA; HYPOSALIVATION; ORAL MICROBIOLOGY; ORAL MICROBIOME; SALIVARY PROTEOME; SJOGREN'S SYNDROME; STREPTOCOCCUS MUTANS
Abstract-Résumé: Dry mouth that occurs from the reduction in saliva (known as hyposalivation), can negatively affect the quality of life. Individuals affected by hyposalivation have problems eating, swallowing, tasting, and speaking. They also experience an increased incidence of dental cavities and suffer from fungal infections, as well as mucositis. To date, little is known how the lack of saliva affects global bacterial profiles (i.e. microbiome) present in dental and tongue plaque, as well as how the types and amounts of salivary proteins are altered under these conditions. In this study, we will examine the bacterial communities and salivary protein profiles using oral plaque and saliva from four hyposalivating patient cohorts affected by 1) Sjogren's Syndrome, 2) head/neck radiotherapy, 3) Hypohidrotic Ectodermal Dysplasia, and 4) Human immunodeficiency virus/ acquired immuno-deficiency syndrome, relative to that in healthy individuals with normal salivary flow. Using subject plaque samples, we will isolate and characterize clinical strains of the cariogenic pathogen, Streptococcus mutans, using molecular and microbiological methods. By cataloging their virulence properties, our long-term aim is to predict predisposition to caries by searching for the presence and abundance of particular strains in caries-prone populations. Furthermore, using whole plaque or health-associated indicator species, we will use a hyposalivating rat model to test whether recurrent introduction of these potentially "good" bacteria can undermine the cariogenic effects of pathogenic bacterial communities in these animals. We expect that in vivo "plaque transplantation" of health-associated species or whole plaque from healthy donors will reduce caries incidence in these animals. Taken together, we expect results from our work will help develop more personalized and effective treatment strategies to improve oral health and the quality of life in individuals affected by dry mouth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of Antisense Therapy for Muscular Dystrophies
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTISENSE THERAPY; EXON SKIPPING; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Muscular dystrophies are devastating and incurable inherited diseases. They are genetic disorders that weaken the muscles. There is currently no effective treatment except palliative therapy for any form of muscular dystrophy. Our research focuses on identifying molecular therapies for muscular dystrophies, especially in the promising field of antisense therapy. Antisense therapy is an approach to fighting diseases using DNA-like molecules. Our exon skipping therapy employs a cocktail of synthetic DNA-like molecules as "DNA Band-Aids" to target the mutated parts of the gene, and produce functional proteins. We will identify antisense drugs to rescue several forms of muscular dystrophies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Effect of Nocturnal Wear of Dentures on Sleep and Oral Health-Related Quality of Life: A Randomized Cross-Over Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLETE DENTURE; ORAL HEALTH; QUALITY OF LIFE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED  TRIAL; SLEEP
Abstract-Résumé: Tooth loss and sleep problems are common conditions in elders. Tooth loss can influence sleep quality by changing the shape of the lower face and upper airway. While some studies suggest that sleeping without dentures can worsen sleep quality in toothless elders, others suggest the opposite. Consequently, there are currently no evidence-based practice guidelines regarding whether dentures should be used at night, and dentists and doctors do not know how to properly advise their patients on these issues.  To address this knowledge gap, over the past 5 years we have carried out research examining the quality of sleep of a group of edentulous elders. In addition, we conducted a pilot study to examine the link between night-time denture wear and sleep. Our results indicate that edentulous elders who wore their dentures at night had high levels of daytime sleepiness. Furthermore, use of dentures at night seemed to increase the risk of apneic events in those elders who had mild sleep disturbance. While intriguing, these results require confirmation in larger samples. In line with our previous research, the aim of the proposed study is to produce reliable evidence that clinical practice guidelines could be based on and which could be used by dentists and doctors who treat toothless elders. We will enroll 56 toothless elders who will be randomly assigned to wear and not wear their dentures at night for two periods of 15 days. Sleep studies will be conducted at the homes of participants. The participants will also be asked to respond to questions on sleep quality and oral health-related quality of life. Ultimately, the results of this study will help improve the health and quality of life of millions of elders in Canada and around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Municipalités amies des aînés en Montérégie, Québec, Canada : consolider l'action sur les déterminants sociaux de la santé et le vieillissement actif des aînés.
Keywords-MotsClés: AINES; CONCERTATION INTERSECTORIELLE; DETERMINANTS SOCIAUX DE LA SANTE; DEVELOPPEMENT DES COMMUNAUTES; ENVIRONNEMENT SOCIAL ET BATI; MONTEREGIE; MUNICIPALITE AMIE DES AINES; PARTICIPATION ET INCLUSION SOCIALE; QUEBE
Abstract-Résumé: Municipalites amies des aines (MADA) est un programme international porte par l'OMS. Au Quebec, ce programme est soutenu et finance par le Secretariat aux aines et a ete implante dans 700 municipalites entre 2008 et debut 2013. Une evaluation de projets pilotes a montre que le mode de concertation n'etait pas optimal, les actions en decoulant ayant des resultats inegaux sur les saines habitudes de vie, sur l'habitation abordable et peu d'effets sur la participation des aines isoles et demunis.  Notre projet de recherche-action participative concerne 5 MADA contrastes (contextes differents, milieux ruraux et urbains) dans la region de la Monteregie, au sud de Montreal, region qui connaitra un vieillissement accelere dans les vingt prochaines annees. Dans une MADA, les balises de l'action s'appuient sur le vieillissement actif, un processus consistant a optimiser les possibilites de bonne sante, de participation et de securite afin d'accroitre la qualite de vie pendant la vieillesse. Les actions concernent plusieurs spheres pouvant avoir un impact direct sur la sante des populations ainees (ex : habitat, inclusion sociale, services de sante). MADA est fondee sur la construction de liens sociaux, le dynamisme des communautes et leur mobilisation, au cur du developpement des communautes; qui constitue une strategie privilegiee d'intervention pour l'equite en sante dans le domaine de la sante publique. Dans une perspective d'equite en sante, la recherche participative presentee vise a comprendre l'action sur les determinants sociaux de la sante (mecanismes), sur les caracteristiques du milieu (contexte) et sur les changements attendus (retombees), ce qui permettra d'elaborer un modele d'action et des outils de transfert de connaissance. En apportant notamment des precisions sur la facon dont les differents mecanismes se conjuguent, le projet contribuera a faire connaitre les retombees sur les aines et le role des differents acteurs mis en jeu dans des demarches MADA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of a Play-Based Preschool Recreation Program: Exploring the Impact of Community Investment on Play-Based Learning on Health and Health Equity
Keywords-MotsClés: EVALUATION; FREE PLAY; HEALTH; HEALTH EQUITY; MIXED METHODS; MUNICIPAL POLICY; NATURAL EXPERIMENT; PRESCHOOL CHILDREN; PROGRAM DELIVERY; RECREATION SPACES
Abstract-Résumé: In the preschool years, play builds a strong foundation for lifelong learning and healthy development.  It contributes to the conceptual foundations of literacy, mathematics and scientific thinking, as well as building social competence and confidence, emotional resilience and self-control, and physical strength and coordination.  The social and physical environments of early childhood have changed profoundly in the last 50 years, as a result of urbanization, changing family demographics and technology.  Play spaces and play experiences are increasingly structured, organized and institutionalized.  Strathcona County Recreation, Parks and Culture (RPC) has recognized the importance of encouraging free play amongst children and has invested $350,000 into the development of LovetoPlay: a unique, leading edge, and innovative play-based preschool space and program.  LovetoPlay aims to enhance preschool children's developmental experiences by focusing on open-ended, play-based learning in a purposively designed environment. It will begin in January 2014. This presents a time-sensitive opportunity to evaluate the impact of this investment.  We will evaluate LovetoPlay by looking at how play is fostered in the environment, while exploring parental, instructors' and children's perspectives, in comparison to 2 preschool spaces of similar size and also operated by RPC.  Part 1 will involve before and after interviews with parents and instructors at each preschool site.  Part 2 will assess the physical features in each of the preschool spaces.  In Part 3 the nature of children's play behaviours will be observed multiple times in each space.  Part 4 will involve working directly with the children to have them share their stories, take pictures, and map and tour adults around the preschool spaces.  This research will contribute to our understanding of the design and program features that facilitate play and promote health in institutionalized program settings for young children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Housing in the Canadian Arctic: Assessing the impacts of rehousing for Inuit health
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH; EQUITY; HOUSING; INUIT; MENTAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: A large proportion of Inuit households live in inadequate housing conditions. In 2006, 39 and 49 percent of the population in, respectively, Nunavut and Nunavik reported living in overcrowded houses, vs. 3 percent of non-Aboriginal Canadians. These poor housing conditions are compromising population health and communities' capacity for social and economic development. Studies have shown that rehousing may improve health directly or indirectly through psychosocial pathways. To date few studies have assessed the health impacts of rehousing in Aboriginal communities, and none among the Inuit. Set in Nunavik and Nunavut, this interdisciplinary project aims to examine whether rehousing - by reducing exposure to overcrowding and improving housing quality - is associated with better health directly, and indirectly through psychosocial pathways. This intervention focusses only on the social housing sector. In the Canadian Arctic, 60 percent of the population in Nunavut and over 90 percent in Nunavik live in social housing. Single-person and family households will be recruited to the study; within households, all adults aged 18 years and older will be invited to participate. Data will be collected 4-6 weeks prior and 15-16 months after rehousing. Questionnaires will assess: housing conditions; mental and physical health, and stress; psychosocial factors, and socioeconomic information. Objective health measurement (blood pressure) will also be taken. This project will provide novel evidence pertaining to health and psychosocial impacts of rehousing, in relation to changes in overcrowding and housing quality. This type of project has been identified as required to build effective evidence-based cases justifying greater investments in affordable housing in the Arctic. Evidence will be integrated in the formulation of housing strategies currently underway in Nunavik and Nunavut. This project has been developed in collaboration with regional housing and health organizations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Évaluation des interventions mises en oeuvre dans le cadre de la norme Entreprises en santé: implantation, impact économique pour l'employeur et impacts sur la santé physique et mentale des salariés.
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPPEMENT D'INTERVENTION; EFFETS SUR LA SANTE; IMPLANTATION D'INTERVENTION; INTERVENTION DE PREVENTION; SANTE ET SECURITE AU TRAVAIL; EVALUATION ECONOMIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: Le projet porte sur l'evaluation des interventions liees a la norme "Prevention, promotion et pratiques organisationnelles favorables a la sante en milieu de travail" (BNQ 9700-800/2008), visant a ameliorer la sante physique et mentale des travailleurs. Les interventions prevues a cette norme portent sur quatre spheres: l'environnement de travail, les pratiques de gestion, l'equilibre travail/vie personnelle et les habitudes de vie. Les objectifs de ce projet sont 1) Analyser la coherence entre les besoins identifies par le diagnostic realise en entreprise et les interventions decrites dans le plan d'action de l'entreprise; 2) Analyser le contexte et evaluer le processus d'implantation des interventions, les obstacles et les facteurs facilitants; 3) Mesurer la variation de la prevalence des facteurs de risque vises par la norme et des indicateurs de sante avant et apres l'intervention; 4) Mener une analyse economique des couts de l'implantation des interventions reliees a la norme du point de vue de l'employeur; 5) Analyser la variation des couts du point de vue de l'employeur avant et apres l'implantation des interventions, en termes d'absence pour maladie, de presenteisme, de primes d'assurance-sante. Dix entreprises seront selectionnees pour participer a l'evaluation (2600 salaries). Le devis de recherche propose est quasi- experimental avant-apres. Il est base sur une methodologie mixte incluant des methodes quantitatives et qualitatives. Des donnees preliminaires ont deja ete collectees (mesure pre-intervention) et seront mises a disposition pour le present projet. Les interventions sont en cours d'implantation. Ce projet vise a collecter les donnees post-intervention indispensables a l'evaluation. Il permettrait une amelioration de la norme, l'instauration d'un mecanisme d'evaluation, et un transfert de connaissances vers les entreprises, via le partenariat avec le Bureau de Normalisation du Quebec et le Groupe Entreprises en Sante.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implementation and Impact Evaluation of a Safe Active School Travel Planning Program
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVE TRANSPORTATION; MENTAL HEALTH; MIXED METHODS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; POPULATION HEALTH; SCHOOL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Over 90% of Canadian youth do not accumulate the recommended minimum amount of daily physical activity (PA) and low levels of PA among youth have detrimental effects on physical and mental health. Promoting PA is an important public health strategy, and while active transportation to/from school (ATS) could be an important way to increase PA, currently only one in four children walks to school, compared to more than one half just a generation ago. School Travel Planning (STP) is a comprehensive process that promotes young students and their families to use ATS instead of inactive modes of commuting by eliminating the barriers for children to safely walk or cycle to school. Past research on STP comes from large urban and suburban areas, and while it shows promise for improving PA levels, there is lack of evidence of its effect in smaller rural and northern communities. The objective of our research is to assess the implementation and impact of a STP intervention in participating elementary schools in the North Bay Parry Sound District on ATS and PA in children in a small-medium sized population center in a northern context. Our secondary objective is to assess the impact of the STP intervention on mental health indicators of children engaging in ATS. We will use a variety of methods, including observations, interviews, surveys, and objective measures of PA (i.e. accelerometers and global positioning systems) to: (1) explore facilitators and barriers to ATS among students; (2) evaluate the impact of the STP intervention; (3) measure and track changes in PA and active travel behaviours; and (4) evaluate the influence of ATS on mental health indicators among students (junior kindergarten to grade 8). This natural experiment represents a valuable opportunity for increasing daily PA levels and improving health outcomes in children at a population level through ATS while yielding important findings on the ATS behaviours in small to medium population settings.

Abstract-Résumé: Changes in Aboriginal law have transformed both the legal standing and the community expectations of Indigenous people on health care matters. Until recently, Aboriginal people accepted health care as it was provided, viewing it as a government program rather than a legal right. Recent Canadian court decisions and the United Nations Declaration of the Rights of Indigenous Peoples have changed the legal /policy environment. Focusing specifically on the health care rights of Aboriginal people, the CRC program will produce policy-relevant research designed to meet Aboriginal needs and to promote greater understanding of the connections between law and Aboriginal health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Population and statistical genetics
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Thanks to rapid technological progress, we are now able to study thousands of genomes, with unprecedented potential to identify disease genes, understand biological mechanisms, and learn about human evolution. However, modeling diverse human groups is challenging, and as a result most minority populations are underrepresented in medical studies. This project aims at building better mathematical and computational genetic models for diverse populations. These models will help us understand the history of these populations, and the genetic basis of diseases and traits in all populations. Most importantly, it will facilitate a more representative inclusion of minority populations into medical research.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Disease Genomics and Epigenomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes and obesity are complex diseases caused by multiple genetic and environmental factors. In past years the genes have been systematically identified. The proposed research includes systematic mapping of environmental influences on gene function by next-generation sequencing technologies with capacity of assessment of millions of sites in our genome susceptible for environmental modulation. Using these tools we will compare environmental marks in the genome including adipose and blood tissues in twins and in French-Canadian population. This work represents a pioneering effort to understand how to best use new technologies to assess environmental influence important in modulating inherited risks for disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Clinical trials with targeted cancer therapeutics demonstrate that the benefit of these agents is frequently limited to small groups of patients. Moreover this benefit is often limited due to the rapid development of resistance. Thus, understanding molecular mechanisms of drug resistance will enable the rational development of treatment strategies to overcome such challenge.My research uses unbiased functional genomic tools to study cancer-relevant pathways and to guide cancer therapy. I aim to identify novel genes and networks that modulate response to cancer drugs, and to uncover genetic dependencies between the major signaling pathways in cancer that can be exploited therapeutically.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Positron Emission Tomography
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: High definition pictures of the inside of living, functioning human brains will be produced at a quality which has never been seen before. These detailed pictures of brain chemistry give insights into human brain function and help reveal what is happening when things go wrong. The scanners which provide these pictures depend largely on the software used, and this work will devise a suite of intelligent techniques which will bring out improved performance from each brain scanner, ensuring reliability of the pictures. Brain images can then be easily shared between medical centres, accelerating our understanding of brain diseases like Alzheimers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic Epidemiology of Common Complex Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Daley's research is focused on genetic susceptibility to common complex diseases with a focus on cardiopulmonary disease such as asthma. Asthma is a chronic disease of the lungs and airways and affects approximately 300 million people worldwide. There is an urgent need to study and develop novel interventions as the incidence of asthma is increasing worldwide.  Furthermore, there is accumulating evidence that, during the period of early life, the initiation of allergic disease may result from genetic and environmental modification of the immune system. Dr. Daleys research is focused on the genetic, environmental and molecular mechanisms underlying common complex diseases, results from her work  will make significant contributions to advancing the future of personalized medicine.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Biomaterials and structured interfaces
Keywords-MotsClés: Pharmaceutical products, Health
Abstract-Résumé: The main objective of the research program is to design innovative biomaterials for the treatment of joint articular diseases and central nervous diseases. We are planning to develop biomaterials whose structure and function are directly inspired by natural proteins present in humans that fail to perform adequately during the progression of the diseases. Using this strategy we aim to develop new treatments for diseases that have currently no available cures such as osteoarthritis or multiple sclerosis.
