TitreApplicationTitle: Heart Failure
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a common and devasting condition with high morbidity and mortality. Although there have been significant advances in the therapy of heart failure in recent decades, such as the introduction of drugs that block certain pathways (beta-blockers and angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors), there is still a major unmet need for better therapies for many patients with heart failure. However, disappointment related to late-stage clinical failures of a number of new agents has reduced the drive for further drug development in this field. We will embark on a complete set of experimental approaches in order to enhance our understanding of the underlying disease mechanisms and targets, and highlight key issues that need to be addressed to improve the chances of success for novel therapies directed against these targets. We aim to develop potential new drugs which can be used to reduce the morbidity (suffering) and mortality (death) inflicted by heart disease.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Pulmonary immunology, inflammation and host defense
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: The pulmonary system often mediates the first line of defense against intruders and yet lung-specific immunity, inflammation and host defense are not well characterized.  A major research impediment has been the inability to directly observe the lung responding to a real infection or inflammatory stimulus in a live, breathing animal.  Recently, Dr. Yipp has established pulmonary immune system imaging in live animals.  This innovative technology provides the foundation to directly address fundamental questions about lung immunity and inflammation.  Performing lung imaging will provide a platform to understand lung immunity and to develop novel respiratory specific therapeutics.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Healthcare Operations Management
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Hospital structure and organization of medical care
Abstract-Résumé: Canadians are generally proud of their healthcare system with universal access to health  services. However, universal access coupled with unlimited need for health services brings a gap between demand and the limited supply of health services. This gap manifests itself through the wait times patients experience when accessing health services. In recent years, there have been recommendations around tackling the underlying causes of long ED wait times. The proposed Research Chair will pursue two ambitious objectives: 1) Development, empirical validation, and analysis of a dynamic prioritization mechanism to manage ED wait times; and 2) Design, empirical validation, and analysis of an ED-informed discharge planning guideline.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Molecular Neurobiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: In degenerative diseases such as Alzheimers and Parkinsons disease, neurons die and are irretrievably lost. It is now certain that neuronal death represents the end event of an extended disease process.  Progressive degeneration of axons and dendrites can start years before neurons die and long before disease symptoms appear. Therefore, identifying the cellular and molecular processes that drive the destruction of axons and dendrites is a priority because it may yield therapeutic interventions that will halt or slow in neurodegenerative diseases. Our goal is to identify cellular events that can be targeted to combat acute and chronic neurological disease.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Genetics of the Nervous System
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Dr Rouleau dedicates his career to research and care of patients with neurological disorders; while doing so he trains young scientists. He has contributed to the identification of over 20 disease-causing genes and pioneered de novo studies in complex disorders. High-throughput sequencing now empowers human genetics and his team is expert at analyzing datasets to identify genetic variations across poorly understood neurological disorders (e.g. amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, schizophrenia). Whenever novel variations are deemed important, he also conducts functional studies (using cellular and model organisms). Dr Rouleau aims to be a dynamic researcher at local, national and international levels.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Translational Cancer Immunology
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Bramsons research is focused on developing methods to direct cancer patients immune systems to attack their tumors.  To this end, Dr. Bramson and his team have created methods to re-educate immune cells in a petri dish and train the immune cells to destroy tumors.  Since the cancer patients immune system is often rendered poorly functional due to repeated courses of chemotherapy and radiation treatment, the methods developed by the Bramson lab also enhance the function of the immune cells and increase their potency as tumor killers.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Microbial Chemical Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: Multidrug resistant bacteria continue to be a health-care burden in both hospital and community settings.  Remarkably, in the past fifty years, only a few new chemical classes of antibiotics have reached the clinic.  Existing antibiotics are directed at a small number of targets, principally cell wall, DNA and protein biosynthesis.  Indeed, multidrug resistance among bacterial pathogens is thought to be due in large part to a limited repertoire of antibacterial chemical matter.  Recognizing the need for new therapies, the Brown research group is searching for novel chinks in the armor of bacteria for the design of truly novel antibacterial drugs.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Mitochondrial Dynamics and Translational Medicine
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a lung vascular disease in which excessive cell growth (proliferation) and insufficient cell removal (apoptosis) block blood vessels. Lung cancer shares this proliferation/apoptosis imbalance. Structural changes in mitochondria, notably fragmentation, contribute to the proliferation/apoptosis imbalance. This shared disorder in mitochondrial dynamics reflects increased mitochondrial fission and impaired mitochondrial fusion. Fission and cell division are coordinated to equitably distribute mitochondria to daughter cells. Blocking fission (or enhancing fusion) slows proliferation, induces apoptosis and regresses disease. We will define the molecular basis for disordered mitochondrial dynamics in PAH and cancer and exploit this to devise new treatments.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: CRC in Musculoskeletal Research
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis causes tremendous individual suffering and enormous costs to society. The mechanisms underlying this disorder are not well understood, resulting in a lack of treatments. Work by us and others provides strong evidence for a close link between skeletal development and osteoarthritis. We will continue our studies on the connection between skeletal development and osteoarthritis using both animal models and human samples. We have generated a wealth of knowledge and established key methods to make substantial progress on these studies. This will ultimately result in improved management of osteoarthritis and relieve the burden on both individuals and society.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Cell Signaling, Learning and Memory
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The emergence of intelligence, the ability to remember, analyze data and make rational decisions, was a milestone in evolution.  Intelligence occurs in organisms that possess highly developed nervous systems, but molecular mechanisms of intelligence evolved in simple microbes. In the past ten years we have developed experimental strategies and conceptual tools to understand the molecular mechanisms that underlie memory. The Chair in Cell Signaling, Learning and Memory aims to study the molecular organizing principles of memory. Similar mechanisms likely exist in higher organisms, including normal processes such as the embryonic development and memory imprinting, to neurodegenerative diseases and cancers.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Pharmacogenomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: A current challenge of medicine is to bring advances in genomics into the clinic to better tailor treatments to individual patients. The Pharmacogenomics program identifies genomic changes that affect adverse effects and treatment efficacy, and aims to more effectively identify patients who will respond particularly well to specific drug therapies and also to identify those who may experience greater side effects. We also develops genome-based and metabolomic biomarkers to better understand cancer biology, identify individuals at risk of cancer recurrence and novel drug targets. This translational and multidisciplinary research will thus lead to a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanism associated with drug response and cancer progression and contribute to the development of new therapeutic approaches based on individual patient and disease profiles. Findings will contribute to the basis for providing personalised cancer therapy, and it has clearly the potential to improve drug treatments for Canadians.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Intracerebral Hemorrhagic Stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: An intracerebral hemorrhagic stroke (ICH) is a bleed into the brain with devastating consequences including high mortality and significant disability in survivors. My research uses rat models of ICH to better understand mechanisms of brain damage and the factors that influence survival and behavioral recovery. Using this approach I also develop and test neuroprotective and rehabilitation treatments. The use of mild hypothermia is one example of a promising treatment that will be studied to reduce stroke damage and brain swelling. It is expected that this pre-clinical research will lead to more effective treatments for ICH survivors.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Molecular Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Our research is directed towards understanding how the genetic information encoded in our DNA is utilized and maintained within cells. We use methods that allow us to image the DNA in 3D detail as it is acted on by proteins that control the action of genes and repair damage to the DNA. Our work has led to an understanding of how the breast cancer associated protein, BRCA1, works to protect our DNA from damage, and how specific mutations in this protein impact its function and lead to breast cancer.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Transplantation Surgery and Regenerative Medicine
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: A critical organ shortage means that Canadians requiring an organ transplant face a 30-40% lifetime risk of never receiving one. Dr. Shapiro is leading a major Canadian initiative to explore oxygenated life-support systems that could dramatically improve organ availability and quality. In cellular transplantation for diabetes, Dr. Shapiro led the Edmonton Protocolislet transplant team. He now plans to use patients own stem cells asregenerative medicine to repair islets at the time of diagnosis, and in parallel, carry out first-in-human trials with embryonic stem cells.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Patient-Centered Health Interventions: Design and Evaluation
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: The implementation of patient-centered health interventions (PCHI) involves a collaborative process in which health professionals and patients discuss alternative treatments; select the treatment that is consistent with patients preferences; and tailor treatment to fit patients needs. Evaluating the effectiveness of patient-centered health interventions requires new research methods that account for this collaborative process. The research plan examines the utility of different methods for: allocating patients to treatment, assessing and quantifying of implementing tailored interventions, assessing the contribution of therapeutic alliance, measuring improvement in outcomes, and developing best practice guides. The goal is to produce evidence that is useful in guiding clinical practice.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Preventive Medicine and Population Health
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Since 1991 and culminating with my first term as a CRC in Preventive Medicine and Population Health, I have led the creation of and research on two global changes in health sciences education.  First, medical education and clinical systems are now acknowledging and acting on my research showing that medical student and physician health affect patients preventive practices and health, with major consequent commitments to improve physician health from the American, Canadian, Colombian and Norwegian Medical Associations.  And second, as health sciences education has become more electronic, I am globally leading research on the population health effects of that transformation.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Embryonic Stem Cell Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Embryonic stem cells have the potential to develop into a variety of cell types and therefore offer a powerful new source of cells and tissues for use in cell replacement therapy or organ repair. Dr. Kellers research program aims to characterize how embryonic stem cells develop into different cell types in order to gain new insights into early mammalian development. These studies will lay the foundation for use of stem cell-based therapies to repair, replace or regenerate aging, injured and diseased organs.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Health Services Research
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Tus research program in the area of cardiovascular outcomes focuses on measuring and improving access to quality cardiac and stroke care in Canada.  He has developed quality indicator measuring tools, linked population-based databases and created report cards that measure health systems performance and cardiovascular health across different dimensions, ethnic groups and geographical loci.  This enables health care providers to measure the quality of care and identify opportunities for improvement.  This ongoing research aims to evaluate new technologies and methods for the prevention and treatment of heart disease and assist policymakers to improve Canadas health care system and patient outcomes.

Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Immunization Research Network (CIRN) represents over 150 investigators from more than 40 Canadian institutions, comprising leading experts in vaccine-related evaluative research from a wide array of disciplines. CIRN facilitates collaborative research among vaccine researchers and stakeholders, provides a training environment, and provides two-way knowledge exchange among researchers and decision makers by improving established knowledge exchange and policy development mechanisms. The network develops and test methodologies in vaccine safety, effectiveness, and adverse events; examines vaccine hesitancy and strategies to address it; evaluates current programs for vaccine coverage and effectiveness, and creates and supports a rapid response research capacity. CIRN comprises 3 cross-disciplinary Research Streams: Program Decision Support, Vaccine Evaluation, and Program Evaluation; each includes investigators spanning CIHR's 4 pillars. CIRN is supported by 6 research infrastructures: the Clinical Trials Network of 8 sites capable of rapid trials as well as long-term studies; the Serious Outcomes Surveillance Network of 43 adult hospital sites provides CIRN with surveillance and vaccine effectiveness capability across the full age spectrum; the National Ambulatory Network, with a cohort of 20,000 health care workers, seniors, and children measures adverse events following immunization; the Special Immunization Clinics Network designed to provide standardized clinical assessment of adverse events following immunization; the Provincial Collaborative Network provides a collaborative platform in which to undertake evaluative programmatic applied public health research; and the Reference Laboratory Network of 5 sites maintains a CIRN biobank and will provide a coordinating role for matching laboratory capabilities in participating academic and public health laboratories with CIRN project needs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metformin: A radio- and chemo- sensitizer in prostate cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CASTRATE RESISTANT PROSTATE CANCER; DOCETAXEL; HYPERINSULINEMIA; INSULIN/IGF SIGNALING; IONIZING RADIATION; METFORMIN; OBESITY; PROSTATE CANCER; PROSTATE CANCER STEM CELLS; XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Cancer Society estimates that 26,500 men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer (PCa) the disease this year, with 4,000 men succumbing to the disease. The incidence of PCa varies dramatically, with higher levels in developed countries. This is partly attributed to 'Westernized lifestyle' comprising of high energy diets with lack of physical activity, resulting in obesity. Increasing levels of obesity have been echoed by substantial increase in non-insulin dependent diabetes (NIDDM).   Intrinsic radioresistance minimize insult of ionizing radiation and upregulates pro-survival pathways. We will determine if reduction in hyperinsulinemia can prevent radiation-mediated pro-survival IGF1 signalling, whereby metformin is acting as a radiosensitizer? Secondly, since hyperinsulinemia effect tumor progression, treatments which ameliorate insulin resistance may prevent progression to the hormone refractory state. A major problem that cancer patients face is the increased toxicity with chemotherapy using docetaxel. Hence, combining metformin with lower doses of docetaxel would be of high clinical relevance.   After hormone blockage cancer stem cells is capable of regenerating the tumour population resulting in relapse. Hence it is important to eliminate frequently replicating tumor cells as well as abolish the slow dividing stem-like cells that are responsible for tumors regeneration. Consequently, successful elimination of CSCs may be an effective therapeutic strategy to be adopted in order to achieve complete remission from this disease.  We hypothesize that metformin can sensitize cells and markedly improved the response of PCa cells to conventional radiotherapy and chemotherapeutic drugs by eradicating tumor cells as well as cancer stem cells (CSC) in the tumors. Our overall findings will support the fact that metformin may possess anti-cancer stem cell effects, which may contribute to its anticancer and chemosensitizing effect against prostate cancer.

Abstract-Résumé: The RASP project aims to assess the process and outcomes of three suicide prevention and wellness promotion initiatives in the Arctic. This proposal is a collaboration between Alaska and two Canadian Arctic communities in order to identify and investigate promising interventions in those fields. Researchers and community members will study the ASIST training in the Inuvialuit Settlement Region, the Community Liaison Wellness Worker program in Nunavik, and the Teck John Baker Youth Leaders (TJBYL) Program in Alaska. A mixed method approach will be used. Results will generate a full report with detailed recommendations on how to improve the interventions and scale them up to other Arctic regions in the globe.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strengthening Community-Based Stroke Care: A Mixed-Methods Study to Evaluate a Mobile Health Solution
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT; COMMUNITY CARE; COSTS; EVIDENCE-INFORMED CARE; HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTH-RELATED QUALITY OF LIFE; INTERPROFESSIONAL CARE; KNOWLEDGE TO ACTION; MOBILE HEALTH TECHNOLOGIES; STROKE REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Most stroke survivors live with other chronic health conditions that can negatively affect their recovery and overall health and well-being. Although stroke care has improved, there are still many challenges to the delivery of community-based stroke care. These challenges include:  poor coordination of care across health care providers and settings; limited communication among health care providers; limited use of evidence-based treatment guidelines; difficulties navigating community services and supports; and limited client and family caregiver involvement in making healthcare decisions. We developed a new mobile health (mHealth) application, Communicating Better Stroke Care (CBSC), to address these challenges to improve the overall quality of stroke care at home. This study will expand this work to: 1) explore the feasibility and acceptability of this mobile tool,  2) determine its impact and usability for home care providers, stroke survivors, and their family caregivers, and 3) determine its impact on the costs of use of health services. The mHealth application will be used and evaluated by home care managers, home care providers, stroke survivors and their family caregivers involved in a multi-centre trial in Ontario and Alberta. We will use questionnaires and interviews to evaluate the app. The overall goal of this new mobile technology is to improve the quality of stroke care in the home care setting through: 1) more comprehensive assessment of client and family needs, 2) increased used of best practices for stroke care, 3) better coordination of community services, 4) real-time availability of useful information to enhance coordination of care and transitions across health care settings, and 5) empowerment of clients and family caregivers to be active partners in their own care. We will work with clients, family caregivers, and health system decision-makers to determine how the mHealth app can be adapted and used more broadly.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adjuvant Endocrine Therapy in Breast Cancer: A Novel E-health Approach in Optimizing Treatment Adherence in Seniors
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENCE; ANTI-ESTROGEN THERAPY; BREAST CANCER; CANCER CARE TRAJECTORIES; E-HEALTH; GERIATRIC ONCOLOGY; GUIDELINE COMPLIANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Anti-estrogen therapy is an effective breast cancer treatment, decreasing the risk of recurrence and death by 40%. To benefit from it, patients must take a daily pill for five years. Studies show that a third of patients have difficulty completing five years of therapy, because of side effects, other health issues or lack of support. This means that many women face the unnecessary risk of avoidable breast cancer recurrence.  Doctors and nurses are often not aware that their patients are having challenges completing five years of treatment. After all, patients self-administer the anti-estrogen pills, with minimal contact with the care team. This is particularly true for seniors with breast cancer. Over 40% of new breast cancers occur in women >65 years old. These patients are at higher risk of discontinuing anti-estrogen therapy, even if they benefit the most from it. Older women can encounter other health issues during the five years of treatment that will negatively affect the completion of their anti-cancer therapy (ER visits, hospitalizations, new drugs, etc). They are also more prone to abandon treatment before completion. Seniors with breast cancer thus represent a high risk population.  We propose an electronic breast cancer care optimization tool targeting specifically the needs of older women with breast cancer. Every transaction within the health care system (doctor, pharmacist, hospital) generates an administrative claim. These are stored in data repositories and are a rich source of health service use information. The e-health tool we propose will access these records and continuously process data, providing the most accurate snap shot of treatments at any given time. By providing this type of real-time information specific to each patient in the form of alerts, our e-health tool will allow cancer care teams to optimize breast cancer survival, by targeting efforts on patients having recently discontinued treatment or at risk for discontinuing therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting Emergency Delirium with an Interactive Computer Tablet(PreDICT)
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTER ASSISTER; DECISION SUPPORT TECHNIQUES; DELIRIUM; DIAGNOSIS; EMERGENCY MEDICINE
Abstract-Résumé: Delirium is a common, serious complication of medical care that robs its victims of the ability to think clearly and make sense of their environment. Delirium appears suddenly, can cause hallucinations and fearful, agitated behaviour, and unfortunately can result in a prolonged or even permanent decline in the ability to think clearly. Older adults in the Emergency Department (ED) are at high risk of developing delirium. Currently, ED staff have difficulty detecting delirium, in part because patients with delirium will have fluctuations in their level of confusion over time, and may at times seem normal.  The purpose of this study is to test an interactive computer program that checks patients' ability to think clearly. The computer program uses a tablet format familiar to many older Canadians. Ultimately, this new technology promises to allow hospital staff to predict which patients are becoming delirious, and to then take actions to prevent delirium.

TitreApplicationTitle: Promoting Health of Older Adults through CHANGE technology
Keywords-MotsClés: EXERCISE; FAMILY MEDICINE; LIFESTYLE INTERVENTION; METABOLIC SYNDROME; NUTRITION; PRIMARY CARE; TECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) refers to a group of factors (high cholesterol, sugars, and blood pressure, and being overweight) that increase the risk for heart disease, stroke, diabetes and their complications. In Canada, 40% of older adults have metabolic syndrome. People with MetS have been shown to have double the annual health care costs and higher frequency of services than those without MetS. The high rate of MetS, along with an aging population translates into enormous financial burden for health systems, patients and families.  Progression of MetS to diabetes and heart disease can be significantly reduced by change in diet and exercise. Unfortunately, applying the research related to lifestyle interventions has been low amongst family doctors. This is due to various challenges such as lack of time, resources, and training amongst family doctors. Canadian Health Advanced by Nutrition and Graded Exercise (CHANGE) developed a program that builds upon previous diet and exercise research. This program can be delivered by a team of health professionals (dietitian, kinesiologist and family physician) within a primary care setting. The CHANGE intervention overcomes the challenges found in primary care by providing a program that seniors can easily access when visiting their family doctor. A demonstration project has shown the CHANGE program can be implemented within primary care settings with positive results. One important challenge for the generalizability of the CHANGE intervention is access to dietitians and kinesiologists in rural or remote locations. Using e- Health technology solutions can overcome these barriers to access. To maximize the uptake of the CHANGE concept, it is essential that we evaluate whether these technologies can be cost effective methods of increase access to effective lifestyle interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: A mixed-method study to explore, assess, and explain the translation of a complex set of evidence-based rules into practice through electronic medical record based decision support: How can STOPP effectively be deployed in primary care?
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT; ELECTRONIC MEDICAL RECORDS; RATIONAL PRESCRIBING; STOPP CRITERIA
Abstract-Résumé: Adverse drug events are a leading cause of preventable harm to patients. The impact is higher in seniors who are often on more medications. Several rule sets have been developed to help reduce inappropriate prescribing. STOPP is one evidence-based rule set to aid prescribers in avoiding medications that can cause harm in patients 65+. Computer-based clinical decision support (CDS) can be an effective way to help apply evidence, such as STOPP, at the point of care. Helping prescribers avoid potentially inappropriate prescribing is one way to avoid adverse events, improve quality, and reduce costs.   This mixed methods study seeks to assess and understand the impact of using an advanced CDS tool to present the STOPP criteria to support prescribers at the point of decision-making. We ask the overarching question:  How can clinical decision support tools effectively translate a complex set of evidence-based rules into primary care clinical practice?  The work is divided into 3 phases.   PHASE 0: Focuses on designing an electronic CDS tool to reduce potentially inappropriate prescribing. We employ a user centred method to design a CDS tool based on the STOPP rules to help primary care prescribers. This is already funded and underway.  PHASE 1: Through funding from this catalyst grant, we will build on Phase 0 with a randomized control trial. We will measure change in potentially inappropriate prescribing (as defined by STOPP criteria) by primary care prescribers (e.g. family doctors) who are using the CDS tool from Phase 0, as compared to those who are not. We will leverage the UBC primary care research network to efficiently measure prescribing changes related to the STOPP criteria.   PHASE 2: As part of this grant, we will then complete a qualitative follow up with participants to aid in understanding how primary care prescribers perceived the CDS. This will help explain Phase 1 findings and provide additional information to enhance future decision support tools.

TitreApplicationTitle: Men, High Risk Work and Workplace Health and Safety Practices
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH PROMOTION; HIGH RISK OCCUPATIONS; INJURY PREVENTION; MASCULINITIES; MEN'S HEALTH AND AGING; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; QUANTITATIVE RESEARCH; SEX AND GENDER ANALYSIS; WORKPLACE CULTURE; WORKPLACE HEALTH AND SAFETY
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, 97% of the victims of all workplace fatalities between 1993 and 2005 were males. Men who work in high risk industries such as construction, mining, fish harvesting, forestry and who work with electricity may experience the greatest risk of workplace injuries (both physical and psychological). Men's behaviour at the workplace may be influenced by cultural expectations to be tough and fearless in the face of risk and danger, as well as economic incentives to complete work quickly, which can lead to less of a focus on occupational health and safety.   Despite the human, health and economic costs associated with men's occupational injuries, there is currently very little understanding of the best methods and strategies for improving health and safety practices at workplaces which employ men in high risk work. To develop best practice strategies, our cross Canada team of researchers, health and safety partners and organizations will study high risk occupations such as construction, forestry, fish harvesting and electrical work. This will include: 1) reviewing accident reports to understand what risks are most significant to men; 2) examining workplace health and safety policies and practices in high risk work environments and 3) interviewing workers, employers, unions and health and safety personnel to understand how each group learns about, understands and manages workplace risks. We will use what we learn from our studies to develop practical health and safety tools and educational programs to enhance men's health and safety at the workplace.

Abstract-Résumé: There is substantial public investment in sport based, in part, on the premise that sport participation can lead to positive health and developmental outcomes. However, there is a 'darker' side of sport participation. One area of concern is the association between alcohol use and sport participation among young males. Unfortunately, we lack fundamental observational and analytic studies in a Canadian context. The objectives of the proposed research are: (1) To build a network of scholars and stakeholders in the areas of sport and addiction (the Youth SPort and Alcohol Network or YOUTH-SPAN). (2) To develop a research program to examine the scope of, and relevant factors that influence, the use of alcohol among young male sport participants in Canada. This is important research because it is necessary to understand the potentially modifiable risk factors in order to design effective interventions in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Masculine identities, health and social violence on Prince Edward Island (PEI)
Keywords-MotsClés: BOYS' HEALTH; COMMUNITY CAPACITY BUILDING; COMMUNITY-UNIVERSITY PARTNERSHIP; CONFLICT RESOLUTION; FEMINIST LENS; GENDER SENSITIVITY; HEALTHY MASCULINITY; INTERDISCIPLINARY ACTION RESEARCH; MALE ROLE MODELS; RESEARCHER DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Preliminary research with boys age 10 to 12 revealed that the negotiation of a masculine identity is a source of stress and confusion for PEI boys, particularly those whose developing identities do not match prevailing masculine stereotypes. This may place them at risk of various stress related health problems. Efforts to fit into prevailing stereotypes, some of which are socially toxic, may result in unhealthy risk taking, antisocial and violent behavior patterns and poor scholastic performance.  This may in turn result in personal injury, chronic disease or dysfunctional relationships that can feed into family and community violence. In this research project we will document the prevailing norms defining masculinity in rural and urban, Aboriginal and non native communities of Prince Edward Island.  The potential impacts of various brands of masculinity on individual, family and community well being will be examined in light of cultural and socio-economic conditions on the Island. Participatory Action Research will be performed in collaboration with boys, their family members, mentors and youth workers.  Research, and community engagement to identify and develop interventions that can encourage healthy masculinity, will be facilitated by Women's Network PEI and the Native Council of PEI who have strong track records in providing youth and family programming.

TitreApplicationTitle: Promoting Fathers' Mental Health
Keywords-MotsClés: FATHERHOOD; GENDER; HEALTH SERVICES; MENTAL HEALTH; MIXED STUDIES; VULNERABLE MEN; WELL-BEING
Abstract-Résumé: The mental health of men and women is a high-priority public health issue not only in Canada but in all Western societies. Paternal depression is known to interfere with parenting quality and to increase the risk of children developing mental, behavioural, and social problems and evidence is accumulating that these negative effects begin in the early infant environment. Aside from these observations, research on paternal mental health during the period extending from pregnancy to early childhood is still in the preliminary stages since research to date has primarily focused on maternal depression. As such, data on mental health disorders among Canadian fathers and on risk factors that might predict such problems as depression and anxiety are almost non-existent. The FAME Team aims to promote the well-being of men expecting and raising young children as well as to improve health and social services for vulnerable fathers at risk for mental illness. To achieve these goals, the team members will build  models explaining the mental health and services utilization of Canadian fathers. They will propose and test innovative interventions for promotion, prevention and screening related to the mental health of fathers of young children. Healthy fathers contribute to the development of their children and the well-being of families.

TitreApplicationTitle: La santé des jeunes hommes présentant des facteurs de vulnérabilité : mieux comprendre et intervenir.
Keywords-MotsClés: HOMME; HOMMES AUTOCHTONES; HOMMES ET IMMIGRATION; MASCULINITES; PATERNITE; PAUVRETE; PROMOTION DE LA SANTE; SANTE; VULNERABILITE; EGALITE DE GENRE
Abstract-Résumé: Les hommes se retrouvent en surnombre pour 14 des 15 principales causes de deces au Canada (Robertson, Galdas, McCreary, Oliffe et Tremblay, 2009). C'est bien connu, ils utilisent moins les services preventifs et ils attendent plus tardivement pour demander de l'aide ou faire appel au medecin (Dulac, 2001; Lefebvre, 2004). A plusieurs egards, les jeunes hommes sont consideres comme un groupe particulierement a risque, notamment sur le plan des accidents de la route, au travail et dans le sport. De maniere generale, ils prennent plus de risques et adoptent moins de comportements de sante que leurs aines (Lefebvre, 2004; Tremblay, Cloutier, Antil, Bergeron et Lapointe-Goupil, 2005). Peu de recherches se sont interessees au rapport que les jeunes hommes etablissent avec leur sante. Ainsi, ce projet vise a suivre plus etroitement une cohorte de jeunes hommes entrant dans l'age adulte, afin de generer des connaissances nouvelles sur le plan de la sante et du bien-etre des hommes. Plus particulierement, l'etude proposee s'interesse a des sous-groupes de jeunes hommes presentant des facteurs de vulnerabilite specifiques: peu scolarises vivant en contexte de pauvrete, issus de l'immigration et les Autochtones.

Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-ORIENTED PRIMARY CARE; E-HEALTH; HEALTH COMMUNICATION; HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTHY BEHAVIORS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MAPPING INTERVENTIONS; MEN'S HEALTH; MIXED METHOD-DATA LINKAGE-PROSPECTIVE COHORT; PARTICIPATIVE-ACTION-RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: In New Brunswick (NB), men have lower life expectancy, higher rates of heart disease, and are four times more likely to commit suicide than women (Government of New Brunswick (GNB), Service New Brunswick, 2011). Furthermore, men in NB have the second highest incidence of cancers in the country (Hayward & Colman, 2003). Many men are estranged from primary care services and take few positive healthy practices to protect and maintain their health (Oliffe et al., 2010). The recent primary care reform offers a window of opportunity to influence change and include men-centered approaches to address relevant health issues with inclusive and integrated approaches to care. Our dynamic and responsive research team fosters collaboration among practice leaders, researchers, and decision makers to develop, implement and evaluate innovative approaches to the delivery of men-centered health care services and interventions. These approaches will be cost-effective and the measurable outcomes will advance the well-being of men living in NB and their families. These approaches will also promote continuous collaboration between men, primary care, and public health to leverage resources and tailor gender sensitive interventions and services.

Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR CHANGE; BONE HEALTH; CARE GAPS; FRACTURES; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; QUALITY OF LIFE; TEAM
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis is a significant musculoskeletal health condition that often remains silent until a fracture occurs. Importantly, osteoporosis is a substantial health concern for men, despite the common notion that it is a "women's disease". Although post-menopausal women have a higher risk of a low trauma hip fracture (the most serious of all low trauma fractures), men have a higher rate of death, risk for poor outcomes and institutionalization after hip fracture. Therefore, we aim to contribute to best practice on bone health in boys and men by characterizing the trajectory of fracture risk in boys, and reducing the risk of low trauma fracture in middle-aged and older men through behavioural and lifestyle interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing and Testing a Multidimensional Theory of Suicide among Middle-Aged and Older Men
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY SAMPLE; ESCAPE THEORY FO SUICIDE; GENDER; LIFE TRANSITIONS; MASCULINITY; MIDDLE-AGED AND OLDER MEN; MULTIDIMENSIONAL THEORY OF SUICIDE; PSYCHIATRIC INPATIENT; SUICIDE; VETERANS
Abstract-Résumé: More Canadians died by suicide in 2011 (N = 3,728) than by motor vehicle accidents, homicide, and HIV combined (N = 3,181). Older men have among the highest suicide rates in Canada and globally, due in part to their use of highly deadly means of suicide and a reluctance to seek help. Men's suicide rates increase at retirement age and rates escalate throughout old age; retirement and other life transitions thus may be a critical period for effective intervention.   A multidimensional model of suicide risk among men is needed to understand the reasons for the increased risk of suicide as men age.  These models must consider masculine gender roles and their impact on mental health, personality, emotional experiencing and expression, and life transitions. This theory needs to be tested with the aim of making mental health treatment more acceptable and accessible to men and ultimately preventing suicide. Our theory-building research will encompass diverse samples for example:  community residing men experiencing transitions in their employment status; men dealing with declining physical and/or mental health as a result of newly diagnosed illness or worsening of existing medical conditions; and men recently diagnosed and admitted with mental disorder. The diverse samples will include men representing different sociocultural backgrounds, ethnicities, and life-styles. Across the diverse samples, we will adopt measures of our central concepts that will be uniformly tested in all samples. These concepts include: masculine gender roles, emotional processing, self-identity, autonomy, self-control, narcissism, shame, perfectionism and the role of life transitions as precipitating factors.  Also across studies, our primary outcomes will be suicide ideation and suicide behaviour. The Research Team will focus on synthesizing the research results into a multidimensional theory of suicidality in middle-aged and older men that can influence interventions and suicide prevention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Promoting Physical and Mental Health in Men Facing Fertility Issues
Keywords-MotsClés: MALE INFERTILITY; MOBILE HEALTH; ONCOFERTILITY; PSYCHOSOCIAL INTERVENTIONS; YOUNG ADULT CANCER PATIENTS
Abstract-Résumé: The present proposal aims to address issues of health promotion in two groups of men facing infertility concerns: 1) men undergoing assessment and treatment for infertility; 2) young adult cancer survivors whose diagnosis and treatment may have adversely affected their fertility. These are men who are at high risk for both physical and emotional problems, and whose specific needs are seldom addressed in research. Since men are less likely than women to seek treatment for physical or emotional issues, there is an urgent need to develop new ways to promote health and wellness in these men. Mobile health, the practice of medicine and public health on mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets, may be a promising way to do so. In order to develop a mobile health intervention, we will review existing educational resources on the Internet and from medical clinics, to see if they meet quality standards. We will survey men in our target groups about their knowledge of health risks associated with infertility and ask them about their information and support needs based on their experiences with the health care system in the assessment and treatment of infertility and fertility preservation. We will also ask health professionals about the types of educational and support resources that are available, and what is needed. This information will help us to develop a mobile health (mHealth) application (app) to provide easily accessible information, support, and tools to promote a healthy lifestyle in men facing fertility concerns. We will evaluate the effects of this type of intervention on quality of life, patient empowerment, and patient satisfaction.

TitreApplicationTitle: HealtheSteps: Engaging Boys and Men in a Healthier Lifestyle
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESSIBILITY; CHRONIC DISEASE PREVENTION; COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT; FAMILY PRACTICE; HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTH TECHNOLOGY; LIFESTYLE INTERVENTION; POINT OF CARE; RURAL AND REMOTE
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic disease (CD) is a growing epidemic in Canada. Canadian boys and men, especially those living in rural and remote regions, are at risk for a number of lifestyle-related CDs including type 2 diabetes (T2D), high blood pressure (BP), cardiovascular disease (CVD) and stroke. CDs share many risk factors including overweight, physical inactivity, and unhealthy diet. Poor health outcomes suggest that Canadian boys and men continue to fall short in adopting healthy lifestyles that could prevent CD. Currently, a gap in scientific research exists about health promotion strategies that are effective for males; and the barriers and enablers to their participation in CD prevention and  management (CDPM) programs. We have assembled a pan-Canadian and international team with a commitment to excellence who will build on our existing work in this area. The HealtheSteps community-based program of research and knowledge translation offers lifestyle prescriptions (exercise, healthy eating), coaching, and technology supports to help Canadians become more physically active, eat better, and improve their overall health. Our research shows that those at risk for T2D and CVD who take part in our program increase their step counts, lose weight, lower their BP and cholesterol, and improve their overall sense of well-being. Our multidisciplinary team of academic, clinical, health technology and industry, First Nations and Metis, and community health programmer partners will adapt the HealtheSteps program to meet the needs of rural and remote-dwelling Canadian boys and men based on consultations with representatives of these vulnerable populations; improve health literacy, behaviours and outcomes; and study other social ecological factors that influence health at the interpersonal, organizational, community and policy levels. We aim to improve knowledge about the participation of boys and men in CDPM programs that will lead to novel, sustainable strategies and evidence-informed policy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Why do boys get hurt more? Masculinity and Risk Taking in the Outdoors
Keywords-MotsClés: FATHERS; INJURY PREVENTION; OUTDOOR PLAY; RISKY PLAY
Abstract-Résumé: Why do boys get hurt more? Masculinity and Risk Taking in the Outdoors addresses the high injury rate among boys and young men. Not only do injury death rates increase as children become youth, peaking at 66 injury deaths per 100,000 among young men, but rates among these young men are 3.3 times higher than for young women. Extensive research indicates the importance of outdoor risky play for the prevention of injuries and promotion of a healthy lifestyle. This program of research will focus on the apparent paradox that keeping boys safe as they get older means letting them take risks while they are younger. The outdoor environment readily lends itself to healthy risk opportunities and healthy lifestyles through active play.  The goal of our overall research program is to investigate why boys are injured more than girls, and to develop injury prevention strategies that include healthy outdoor risky play promotion. Our teams program objectives are 1.To reframe parents perceptions of risk and injury prevention to promote outdoor risky play. 2.To better understand the contributions of individual and contextual factors as determinants of outdoor risky play through geographically and socially mapping access to play spaces. 3.To reframe population level perceptions of risk and injury prevention through social marketing to promote outdoor risky play. This Team unites researchers and knowledge users from disparate fields to develop innovative approaches for addressing the leading cause of death to Canadian boys, injuries. There is an urgent need for new approaches to injury prevention for boys. Canadian society needs a significant contribution to look beyond current norms about risk taking and redefine injury prevention to allow for healthy child development while reducing serious injuries.

TitreApplicationTitle: Father's lasting influence: Molecular foundations of transgenerational transmission of the paternal environment
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD HEALTH; DDT; DNA METHYLATION; ENDOCRINE DISRUPTORS; FOLATE; HISTONE; INUIT; ORGANOCHLORINE; PATERNAL HEALTH; SPERM
Abstract-Résumé: We know that maternal exposures can affect child health, but recent disturbing findings suggest that the effects of environmental exposures can be transmitted by fathers, causing adverse birth outcomes and chronic disease in their children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. A possible mechanism for paternal transmission of environmental information is via his sperm epigenome. The epigenome is a group of tags on DNA that tell it what to do. We will use state-of-the-art approaches and build on existing research investment with international collaborators to examine the father's role in transmitting the effects of his exposures to his future generations. There are international rules restricting organochlorines (such as PCBs and some pesticides, including DDT), because they stay in the environment and do not break down. However, DDT is still allowed in many parts of the world where malaria is a danger, such as South Africa. Due to natural weather currents, organochlorines accumulate in the Arctic, where they have never been used. Hence, Inuit populations have a high body burden of environmental contaminants, which may contribute to the major health disparity between them and non-Aboriginal Canadians. We will examine the sperm epigenome of Inuit and South African men and assess abnormalities due to organochlorine exposure. Using a rat model, we will try to fix the damage caused by contaminants using folate, a common vitamin that is prescribed to pregnant women to prevent birth defects. We hypothesize that folate will prevent and repair damage the damage to father's sperm epigenome and protect his future generations. We will collaborate with teams in Europe and South Africa to test our ideas. Our team includes people from Health Canada, the Institut national de sante publique du Quebec and the Nunavik Nutrition and Health Committee, who will ensure that our research will be communicated to Canadians to improve the health of men, boys and their future generations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Shape the Path: Targeting the health and mobility of older men through key community partnerships
Keywords-MotsClés: BUILT AND SOCIAL ENVIRONMENT; COMMUNITY-BASED; HOME CARE; INTERVENTIONS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION AND EXCHANGE; MOBILITY; OLDER MEN; RESIDENTIAL CARE; STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The World Health Organization tells us that "mobility...is the best guarantee of retaining independence and being able to cope." We broadly refer to mobility, as the physical capacity of individuals to move themselves. Mobility is key to one's health and it is embedded into the activities we perform every day. Limited mobility is a significant risk factor for further physical disability, brain health impairments, and is associated with an increased risk of early death. Therefore, maintaining mobility is fundamental to healthy aging and to retaining one's independence for as long as possible. This is particularly true for men who are at high risk for diseases often born of inactivity (i.e., cardiovascular disease, diabetes).  "Shape the Path: Targeting the health and mobility of older men through key community partnerships" is a program of research that aims to answer three questions related to men's mobility:  What supports or stands in the way of men's mobility in three distinct settings (community, home, residential care)? What factors influence men's mobility and health across these settings? What factors influence government and municipal decision makers to implement best practices related to men's mobility and health? Our research team from across disciplines and community partners from across sectors are committed to use novel approaches to answer these questions. We will also call upon our vast network of partners to move our research findings into action to make a difference to the health of men in Canada and beyond.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of paternal age on the health of gametes: risk of potential adverse outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ARTIFICIAL REPRODUCTIVE TECHNOLOGIES; CHROMATIN; EPIGENETICS; INFERTILITY; SPERM; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Over the past 20 years, there is a clear trend for men to start having children at an increasingly older age. It is well-recognized that there is an association between maternal age and decreased fertility, higher incidence of abnormalities and diseases in their children; however, we are only beginning to grasp the impact of paternal age on fertility and progeny outcome. The objective of this Team Grant application is to examine how the trajectory of aging presents health challenges faced not only for older men but also for their children. Men older than 40 yrs take a longer time to make their partner pregnant and have a higher rate of infertility; partners of these men have a higher incidence of miscarriage. Paternal age is also linked to a higher risk for progeny to develop complex multi-gene diseases, such as autism, schizophrenia, and bipolar disease. Since sperm continue to be produced in men constantly throughout adult life at a rate of about 1000 sperm every heartbeat, decreased sperm cell function is likely to be associated with decreased sperm quality and not number. The central hypothesis underlying this program is that the trajectory of aging alters the quality of the sperm being delivered to the oocyte and that there is a direct relationship between infertility, paternal age, chromatin quality, epigenetic marks, and progeny outcome.  The proposed studies represent a unique approach. There has been little attention to the quality of men's sperm as men move along their aging trajectory. The consequences of increased paternal age are only beginning to be demonstrated in studies from other countries. Our team has gathered the essential complementary expertise to make significant advances in this field. Our results will not only have positive consequences for men as they appreciate the link between aging and sperm chromatin quality but will also serve to decrease the health burden on future generations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Global exchanges, local interventions: meeting the HIV prevention and health care needs of men who have sex with men (MSM) in Canada, Kenya and China
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; GLOBAL HEALTH; HIV CARE AND TREATMENT; HIV INTERVENTIONS; HIV PREVENTION; MIXED METHODS; MSM; PROGRAM SCIENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Over the last six years, the global epidemiology of HIV infection continues to be clear with respect to men who have sex with men (MSM)-we are in the midst of seeing the expansion of HIV epidemics in these subpopulations. We propose to establish a community-based intervention research (CBIR) team and program to A) generate new knowledge around the barriers that inhibit MSM from accessing HIV-related health services; and B) to foster new opportunities for co-learning, by creating a dynamic global interchange of intervention knowledge as our team proceeds through intervention design, service delivery, surveillance, and refinement in Canada, Kenya, and China. This program will break new ground by expanding upon a program science approach-an emerging paradigm in global public health that embeds research processes throughout the life cycle of HIV interventions to ensure a more effective response, at every stage, as informed by sound scientific evidence. More specifically, the CBIR team has the following aims: 1) to build a community-centered and accessible global evidence base that describes and analyses the individual, environmental and structural barriers that inhibit MSM from accessing and/or navigating between HIV prevention, care and treatment in Winnipeg, Chengdu and Nairobi; 2) to assemble, refine and strengthen local responses to HIV/STI epidemics among vulnerable communities of MSM in these three cities, drawing upon the evidence and analysis built in objective 1; and 3) to fostering more egalitarian relationships between scientists, clinicians and knowledge users, by incorporating community-based principles throughout the program-so as to democratize the flow, interpretation, and ownership of the specialized knowledge produced through this intervention research program. This CBIR program will be framed as much by community wisdom and experiential knowledge as by public health rationalities and priorities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reducing HIV Vulnerabilities and Promoting Resilience Among Self-Identified Heterosexual African, Caribbean and Black Men in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: AFRICAN; CAPACITY BUILDING; CARIBBEAN AND BLACK; COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT AND MOBILIZATION; GENDER RELATIONS; HETEROSEXUALITY; HIV VULNERABILITIES; MASCULINITIES; RESILIENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Research evidence shows that heterosexual African, Caribbean and Black (ACB) men experience social inequality that increases their vulnerabilities to HIV. At the same time, ACB men have been left adrift by programs, services and research that have struggled to keep pace with the changing epidemiology of HIV. The goal of the proposed research program is to reduce HIV vulnerabilities and promote resilience through active engagement of self-identified heterosexual ACB men in community HIV responses, programs, research, and policy. We will engage and mobilize self-identified heterosexual ACB men who are: aged 16 and over; residing in the Greater Toronto Area, London, Ottawa, and Windsor and HIV-positive or have never been diagnosed with HIV. We will also engage service providers and other relevant stakeholders to work closely with heterosexual ACB men. The research program objectives include: a) mobilizing self-identified heterosexual ACB men to address conditions that contribute to HIV related health disparities; b) examining social and behavioural vulnerabilities to HIV among self-identified heterosexual ACB men; c) identifying individual and structural factors that promote resilience and reduce HIV risks among self-identified heterosexual ACB men; d) building individual, community, and organizational capacity and leadership to address HIV disparities among self-identified heterosexual ACB men and communities through research, programming, and policy; and e) generating new knowledge and supporting its translation into intervention, practice, and policy in Ontario and Canada. We will use multiple methods of recruitment and a combination of methods for data collection and KTE. Our research program will address the programming and policy gaps affecting heterosexual ACB men in Ontario, reduce HIV-related and other social stigma, enhance HIV prevention messaging in ACB communities, and strengthen ACB men's involvement in community responses to HIV in ACB communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Men's Silent Diseases: Prevention and Management of Cardio-Metabolic Diseases among Men
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIO-METABOLIC HEALTH; HEALTH SERVICES; LIFESTYLE; MEN; PRIMARY PREVENTION; RISK FACTORS; SECONDARY PREVENTION; TRAJECTORY
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed CIHR Team is an interdisciplinary research group that will investigate the complex interactions between traditional and novel bio-psychosocial, behavioral and environmental cardio-metabolic risk factors related to the developmental trajectory of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases in men.  Our objectives are to: 1) identify specific bio-psychosocial, behavioural and environmental factors influencing cardio-metabolic health and use of health services in men, and 2) develop, implement and evaluate sustainable integrated primary and secondary prevention approaches to reduce the incidence and improve the management of cardio-metabolic risk factors, type 2 diabetes and/or cardiovascular diseases in men. Thus, the findings of this team research program using cross-sectional and prospective study designs as well as integration of the pertinent literature will improve the health of men by developing innovative health care interventions, tools and services that will better respond to men's cardio-metabolic health needs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Healthy Boys to Healthy Men: Engaging Boys and Men in Intergenerational Health Promotion
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORGINAL BOYS' AND MEN'S HEALTH; GENDER ANALYSIS; INTERGENERATIONAL ENGAGEMENT IN PROGRAM AND POLICY; INTERGENERATIONAL HEALTH PROMOTION; INTERGENERATIONAL TRAUMA AND HEALING; MASCULINE AND ABORGINAL IDENTITIES; PARTICIPATORY ACTION RESEARCH; POLICY ANALYSIS AND DEVELOPMENT; PROGRAM EVALUATION
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, the proportion of Aboriginal people who live in cities now exceeds the proportion in rural and remote communities. To date, a paucity of research has focused on the health of urban-based Aboriginal boys and men in Canada. Our program of research will fill key gaps in our knowledge regarding the health inequities experienceD by urban-based Aboriginal men and boys, both in Alberta and in Canada. Our Program of Research covers nine cross-cutting themes that are of key relevance for Aboriginal boys and men in Canada including: 1) poverty and food security; 2) access to health services; 3) intergenerational trauma and healing; 4) intergenerational engagement in program and policy development; 5) compatibility and integration of Aboriginal and Western conceptions of health; 6) addictions; 7) structural violence, as exemplified in child welfare institutions; 8) integration of masculine and Aboriginal identities;  and 9) resilience. A tenth theme involves ethics applied with urban Aboriginal populations.

Abstract-Résumé: Sexual violence victimization in males has been an area of gender neglect. Childhood sexual abuse, sexual coercion in dating, adolescent and young adult sexual assault have their impact on male sexual health, mental health, substance abuse, and suicidality. There is a need to clarify the specific pattern of elevated risks among male survivors, as well as a need to highlight the mechanisms that underlie challenges to healthy living and resilience for males. The emphasis on mediators plays a foundational role for intervention innovation and building upon established intervention models to address male trauma issues, and service delivery models that may be more suited to males.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Team in Male Health (TIM) Network
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN HEALTH; CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH; FRAILTY; MALE HEALTH; METABOLIC HEALTH; MORTALITY; MULTIMORBIDITY; MUSCULOSKELETAL HEALTH; POPULATION HEALTH; TESTOSTERONE
Abstract-Résumé: Testosterone is a hormone that is thought to be associated with several health conditions in men. These conditions include the metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, memory problems, depression, musculoskeletal disorders, multimorbidity, frailty, and mortality. However, testosterone's role in these conditions is not well understood. We propose to put together a team of scientists who are trained in different healthcare fields. This team will study testosterone's effect on male health taking into account other parameters associated to aging. The team will accomplish this task by using information from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA). The CLSA is a study of 50,000 people between the ages of 45 and 85 years. The information from generated by the Team in Male Health (TIM) will be used to design new studies to evaluate treatments that can target the deficiencies associated with testosterone in the context of an aging specific profile among men.

TitreApplicationTitle: The HPV-SAVE Study Team:  HPV Screening And Vaccine Evaluation in men who have sex with men
Keywords-MotsClés: ANAL CANCER; HIV TRANSMISSION; HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: Infection by certain high-risk strains of human papilloma virus (HPV) is the major cause of several serious cancers in men, including anal, penile and oropharyngeal cancer. Anal infection by high-risk (HR) strains of HPV is much more common in men who have sex with other men (MSM), particularly men who are co-infected by HIV, and our own work has shown that HR-HPV infection prevalence exceeds 90% in HIV-infected MSM from Ontario. However, optimal protocols to screen for and treat anal HPV and pre-cancerous lesions have not been established. In addition, not only does HPV directly cause important disease in men, but infection enhances the sexual transmission of HIV through mechanisms that are not clear.   This proposal brings together community and internationally-recognized experts in HPV disease and mucosal immunology to better define the optimal approach to HPV screening and management in HIV-infected and uninfected MSM, and to understand how this common infection enhances HIV transmission. This will provide critical information to improve the health of MSM, and will provide additional rationale for the free and timely provision of HPV vaccine to this community.

TitreApplicationTitle: HIV Prevention, Risk Perceptions, Behaviours, and Health Care Access Among Gay, Bisexual, Two-Spirit, and Other Men Who Have Sex with Men in the Context of Changing Social-Historical, Messaging, and Socio-Sexual Environments
Keywords-MotsClés: GAY AND BISEXUAL MEN'S HEALTH; HIV/AIDS; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; MIXED METHOD DESIGN; SEXUAL HEALTH; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HELTH
Abstract-Résumé: First diagnosed in gay men, the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) continues to have a disproportionate impact on gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (hereafter, referred to as MSM). Over half the people in Canada living with HIV are MSM, and they account for about 70% of all new diagnoses among males in BC and about 75% of new diagnoses among men in Ontario. The HIV prevalence of MSM who participated in Canadian national M-Track surveillance was 15.1% (11.1%-23.1%). Senior, junior and community-based researchers in BC, Alberta, Ontario and Nova Scotia have come together to articulate a focused research agenda designed to reinvigorate HIV prevention for MSM. We hypothesize that MSM's sexual, physical and mental health experiences, their risk perceptions and behaviours as well as their access to and use of health services are influenced by social, legal, media, and sexual environments, which have all changed dramatically over the past three decades. Our objectives are to: (1) examine how the four environmental domains (sociocultural and legal landscape, media, perceptions of risk in changing virtual and real-world communities, access to appropriate health care and social services) impact the experiences of sexual, physical and mental health and health care access for a diverse sample of MSM across Canada and influence their risk and resiliency for HIV and other STIs; (2) identify policy and program changes that would reinvigorate HIV prevention for MSM; and (3) enhance capacity to conduct research on the changing social environments and determinants of health for MSM and to develop appropriate programs and services. To achieve these objectives, we will use a two-phase mixed method design to collect information. Phase 1 will involve an online, cross-sectional questionnaire (n=1000) recruiting MSM from four provinces. In Phase 2, we include 400 in-depth interviews recruited from the online survey to explore research questions qualitatively.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mobiliser les savoirs et les communautés pour une approche intégrée de la prévention du VIH et de la promotion de la santé sexuelle des hommes gais ou ayant des relations sexuelles avec d'autres hommes.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCES AUX SERVICES DE SANTE; ANALYSE D'IMPLANTATION; ANALYSE ECONOMIQUE; APPROCHE SYNDEMIQUE; HOMMES GAIS ET HRSH; MOBILISATION DES SAVOIRS ET DES COMMUNAUTES; PREVENTION COMBINEE VIH/SIDA; RENFORCEMENT DES CAPACITES; SANTE SEXUELLE; SCIENCE PROGRAMMATIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: Les hommes gais ou HRSH, comparativement aux hommes heterosexuels, presentent plus de problemes de sante mentale, de violence conjugale, d'habitudes de vie nefastes, de troubles alimentaires ou de probleme d'image corporelle et d'infection par le VIH et autres ITSS. Or, chacun de ces problemes de sante a fort probablement comme determinants communs divers facteurs personnels, interpersonnels, sociaux et structuraux qui doivent etre pris en compte. La comprehension de ces facteurs syndemiques et de l'intersectionnalite est majeure pour orienter les actions de prevention des ITSS, incluant le VIH, et de promotion de la sante sexuelle chez les hommes gais et HRSH. Le projet propose ici regroupe des utilisateurs de connaissances, des chercheurs et des collaborateurs provenant de tous les milieux vises par le processus de mobilisation. Sous l'angle d'un modele integre d'application des connaissances et selon une approche de science programmatique, l'objectif general poursuivi par l'equipe est de mobiliser les savoirs et les communautes pour une approche integree de la prevention du VIH et de la promotion de la sante sexuelle des hommes gais ou HRSH. La programmation de recherche comporte 4 axes. L'axe explicatif et interpretatif, permettant l'exploration de banques de donnees existantes pour tester des hypotheses permettant de mieux orienter les actions par une meilleure comprehension des enjeux relatifs a la sante sexuelle de ces hommes et a leur acces a des services de sante sexuelle. Sous l'axe interventionnel et operationnel, les connaissances ainsi produites seront appliquees pour orienter l'action. L'axe processuel permettra d'analyser le processus de mobilisation et ses effets alors que l'axe de renforcement des capacites, creera des conditions favorables au developpement des competences des acteurs en matiere de prevention combinee, de partenariat, d'application des connaissances et de science programmatique.

TitreApplicationTitle: HIV Prevention for Gay and Bisexual Men: A Multisite Cohort and Development of New HIV Prevention Interventions
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; GAY AND BISEXUAL MEN; HIV INCIDENCE; HIV PREVENTION; HOMOPHOBIA; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; SEXUAL HEALTH SERVICES; SEXUAL RISK BEHAVIOUR; STI INCIDENCE; SUBSTANCE USE
Abstract-Résumé: Half of new human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infections in Canada occur among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM). Over the past ten years, there have been important developments in HIV treatment and prevention. For example, the use of antiretroviral medication therapies (ART) has been recognized as having the potential to act as a preventative measure at both the individual and the population level. In 2010, the government of British Columbia introduced a large scale program to "seek and treat" people living with HIV that involved prescribing ART to treat individuals and prevent the spread of the virus. This policy of "treatment as prevention" has not been implemented to the same degree in Ontario and Quebec. Canada has therefore begun a natural experiment on the effectiveness of this approach. We have created a national team to collaborate on HIV prevention among MSM in Canada in order to understand the effects of cross-provincial differences in the number of new cases of HIV and to address critical knowledge gaps in HIV prevention. Our team has 3 overlapping goals: (1) To develop the first ever national mulitsite study of new cases of HIV/sexually transmitted infection (STI) among MSM; (2) To build research capacity for HIV prevention research for MSM across Canada; and (3) Using an active, bidirectional Knowledge Translation approach, design and test HIV prevention programs for community and public health settings. Our cohort study objectives are: (1) To examine sexual behaviour and recreational drug use among MSM over a period of three years follow-up and to monitor changes in these behaviours as access to ART expands; and (2) To examine the effects of biomedical and sociohavioural HIV prevention programs on the number of new cases of HIV and STIs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Connecting Policy and Practice Through the Health Sectors and Across Health Disciplines: A SPOR Network in Primary and Integrated Health Care Innovations
Keywords-MotsClés: CONNECTING POLICY AND PRACTICE; HEALTH SYSTEM TRASNFORMATION; INTEGRATED HEALTH CARE RESEARCH; PATIENT ENGAGEMENT; PRIMARY CARE REFORM; SPOR
Abstract-Résumé: We are a team of researchers, clinicians, and policy makers who are proposing to form a network that will work together to transform the healthcare system of NL. Evidence from around the world suggests that health systems with a strong foundation in primary care (e.g., care from a family doctor or nurse practitioner) are the most effective and efficient. In NL we face a number of challenges in delivering primary care. Many other countries and parts of Canada have taken steps to reform their primary care systems to maximize effectiveness. NL has made little progress in this regard. The network we are proposing will bring together a large team of clinicians, researchers, and policy makers from across the healthcare sectors with patients/citizens/families who will work together as partners in healthcare transformation. Potential impacts from this work include i) improved primary care delivery with decreased dependence  on international medical graduates and more  appropriate care delivered by the most appropriate care provider; ii) improved communications and integration of the healthcare sectors; iii) more efficient care of high needs users and better chronic disease management; iv) improved child care and smoother transitions between child and adult care; v) greater incorporation of patients' needs and perspectives in the design and implementation of our health care system. To achieve our goals we have begun to assemble a team of investigators that includes those with experience and productivity in cross-jurisdictional and integrated health care research and program implementation. The combined efforts, skill sets, knowledge, experience of this group together with the leadership capabilities of our tripartite leaders will form a network capable of creating sustainable transformations to our health system.

Abstract-Résumé: As part of the SPOR Network, we envision to develop, evaluate and scale up existing and new integrated primary health care models using a variety of approaches with a specific focus on patients with complex needs. Embedded in the models will be an examination and management of patient's and health care provider readiness for change. We will also include new technologies for patient self-management of chronic conditions such as web-based self-management support and monitoring programs, alternative care models like group-therapy and improved access to information and treatment within specific cohorts and the full scale use of Electronic Medical Records to ensure appropriate distribution of patient records. The short term objectives are to expand the membership of the Network collaborators and partners within and across sectors of care such as, education, social services, mental health, pharmacists, patients, and Canadian and foreign experts to meet the ten SPOR Network requirements and to engage in discussions with other provinces to explore the possibility of an Atlantic SPOR Network. Over the medium term the objectives are to assess the impact of existing integrated primary health care models in the provinces, to develop patient oriented interventions based on the provincial priorities and upstream innovations such as healthy aging, integrated primary health care and self-management of chronic conditions and to develop system oriented interventions based on provincial priorities such as  improved access to community based integrated primary health care, urgent care and the coordination of care. The long term objectives are to create a practice-based learning and research network integrating horizontal and vertical care with a rapid assessment component using administrative and new data focusing on scaling-up to improve care and reduce costs and to create primary care research capacity.
